It's... Pretty much a giant ad for Dota. That's all. Quite a shame really, it started off great and I was pretty interested. However past the 40 minute mark I started to see trends in the video. Half the footage was of Dota gameplay, the other half emotional issues of the players and how their parents feel. I don't see how us learning about how some guy's girlfriend dumped him and made him start smoking has anything to do with competitive gaming, yes, people who play video games aren't robots, thanks, let's move on.
On top of that... Why is this video all about Dota? There are other esports games, competitive gaming has been around since Quake, and I think the only game I saw (and I really mean SAW, not even heard) was Counter Strike, and that was for about 20 seconds total. Considering Valve makes both games, I don't see how pointing out CS is also competitive and showing some glimpses of CS players would have hurt at all. In fact, I think a total of 8 minutes of the video was all that was mentioned about how Esports are slowly becoming more popular.
You'd think a documentary claiming to be about e-sports would have more than 1/30 of it actually be about how e-sports is becoming a real sport. Come on Valve, you should know better than this. The video made me want to play Dota, that's about it. I was considering showing this to some people who don't think highly of gaming, up until the 50 minute mark where I realized they were going in circles and talking more about their personal struggles and how they became part of an esports team.

So how do you take an old legendary game, and update it to modern specs? Well, one way to do it is to keep everything the same and update the UI and graphics. That's the safe way.
Then there's this game, which most definitely does not take the safe way, but manages to not just pull off carrying the X-Com name, but also stand on its own next to the old classic, while keeping some of the same spirit. That takes a lot of talent to pull off, especially since the classic is X-Com: UFO Defense. One of the greatst PC games ever.
You play as the Commander of XCOM, the anti-alien organization, and the game is split between base management in a 4X-lite-ish way and turn based tactical combat where you control each soldier individually. And each soldier is its own person, they have a name, they get skills as they fight more aliens, and they die horribly if you make a curcial error. Or even a small error on the higher difficulties. Or no errors on Impossible and the game hates you. And this is no fantasy game. You die, there's no coming back.
The two parts of the game are linked together. You go out, kill (or capture) aliens and their tech, use it to reasarch new technology for your troops and aircraft, and send them back out to kill/catch even tougher aliens so you can get even better tech. The trick is to stay on pace with the aliens, bascially. Because you can, and probably will, lose the game if your strategy part is lacking. Or if your elite squad gets wiped out and you have no backup team.
Basically, the game can be played for 20+ hours and lost. But that's kind of the fun, too. Until you unlock the secrets behind the aliens and make the final counter-assault, you can lose the game. There are stakes, and if you get complacent, Chryssalids will eat your men. Or aliens will launch coordinated attacks on your funding nations and get them to withdraw.
Overall, this is a fun game. Frustrating, difficult, brutal... but fair. But when your Sniper makes that clutch shot, your Assault gets a perfect flank, or you're bringing home the biggest, baddest alien you've seen yet... alive. It feels good.
Then the alarm goes off because aliens are blowing up Sao Paulo. No rest for the secret para-military alien-concealing/killing conspiracy.

Teleglitch is a clunky twin stick shooter with the pretensions of a roguelike. The worst parts of being a roguelike,with the uneven difficulty making it boring until  the seconds before you die and you have to repeat, and repeat, and repeat.  The basic shooting/combat mechanic is passable but movement through the levels is a chore since you have no idea what the hell you are looking at. There seems to be some kind of deep meta game with a cool variety of weapons, items, and enemies.  It's too bad it all ends up being pointless window dressing because the basic gameplay loop is so unsatisfying.
Graphics wise the enemies are very generic retro pixel art, and there is not much you can do wrong or right with a single pixel for each limb.  It is not an exaggeration to say that Robotron in 1982 had more detailed characters.  The shadows swinging around to show line of sight are obnoxious and distracting.
The backgrounds and levels however are godawful.  The color palletes and mystery blobs make each level a modern art puzzle smeared over a low resolution pixel canvas.  Is that a door, a table, a wall, a gun, a plant, a light, a rug, a dead body, a crate, or a brown lump?  Can I interact with it or move through it? The graphics certainly won't tell you, so you will have to memorize it through one of your 50 plays through the same area.  A more elegant minimalist approach to the backgrounds would have suited this kind of game much better.

tramite "humble bundle", un sito dove si comprano pacchi di giochi per il pc a pochi dollari, ho rimediato un piccolo capolavoro roguelike dal nome avveneristico: Faster Than Light.
Un gioco ben fatto dalla grafica retrò che vi fa sin da subito immergere nella più incredibile ambientazione sci fi.
All'inizio potrete scegliere la nave con cui iniziare il viaggio (a dir la verità di base ve ne da solo una, le altre le dovrete poi sbloccare), la ciurma inizialmente composta da 3 elementi dove potrete customizzare sesso e nome, ed infine avrete armi e miglioramenti dati di default in base al modello di nave scelto.
Il gioco è formato a livelli o "galassie", livelli a loro volta formati da mappe dove vi potrete spostare da punto a punto cercando di raggiungere l'uscita della mappa posta solitamente dalla parte opposta dell'entrata.
In ogni punto dove andrete a spostarvi potrete trovare di tutto: da ragni giganti a piattaforme disabitate ma nella maggior parte dei casi dovrete vedervela contro altre navi spaziali.
Il gioco è impostato in maniera altamente strategica e manageriale. Infatti risulta fondamentale l'utilizzo della pausa in game (barra spaziatrice) in modo da ideare bene il piano di attacco in base alla tipologia di nemico che si ha di fronte.
Le navi, compresa la vostra, sono formate da stanze collegate,le une con le altre, da porte. Quasi ogni stanza ha la sua funzione: vi è la stanza armeria dove si gestiscono le armi dell'astronave (raggio laser, missili, cannone a Ioni, etc.), la medicheria dove si possono curare i membri dell'equipaggio, etc.
Se vi fanno "saltare" una stanza, cioè ve la mettono fuori uso con un missile o qualcos'altro, non potrete utilizzare la relativa funzione. Per esempio, prima sono morto perché mi hanno distrutto la stanza adibita alla diffusione dell'ossigeno, non ho fatto in tempo a ripararla con l'equipaggio e quindi son schiattati tutti miseramente.
Le armi sono moltissime, come i droni utilizzabili (ho nella nuova partita un drone che gira intorno alla nave nemica e gli tira raggi laser ogni 4 secondi) o i miglioramenti, come ad esempio piu' % di trovare "scrap", una sorta di valuta, dovrebbero essere rottami, quando si distrugge una nave nemica.
La difficoltà è abbastanza elevata anche con facile. Ho perso partite dove ero messo benissimo solo per una piccola distrazione.

Antichamber is easy to dismiss as a Portal clone at first glance; it is a first person puzzle game wherein you move from chamber to chamber, equipped with a puzzle “gun” which interacts with your environment.  But while Portal deals mostly in learning the rules of its mechanics and then adding complexity to those mechanics, Antichamber is a game which aims to subvert your expectations about how a puzzle should fundamentally work.  It makes you question the unspoken rules that video games abide by.  Frequently, it is simply brilliant and mind blowing, though occasionally it’s too obscure or random for its own good (especially in later parts of the game).
There’s no real story to speak of in Antichamber, but the entire experience is expertly accented in a very sterile atmosphere and minimal graphics.  Sound design is also minimal, but well done.  Certain audio cues can give you hints to where you are in the world, and the simple tick-tock of a clock can become a fixture of an entire portion of the game.  It’s definitely a polished game which looks and feels nice.
Of course, the real meat of Antichamber is the puzzles, and it’s hard to say much about them without revealing part of what makes this game special.  Suffice it to say that it is one of the most unique and creative games that I have ever played.  Environments are frequently non-Euclidean in nature, and rely heavily on perspective or understanding the rules of the universe which Antichamber itself has defined.
There is inherent difficulty in designing that kind of puzzle; if you don’t abide necessarily by the rules of physics or perspective that we’ve come to rely on, puzzles can have arbitrarily hard solutions.  For the most part, especially in early parts of the game, Antichamber does an excellent job of staying consistent and teaching you the ways of its mind-melting world.
But in the later hours, you are bound to run into situations where a puzzle solution will feel almost entirely arbitrary.  Frustration will set in, and occasionally solutions don’t have the satisfying payoff they were designed for. There was one instance where I resorted to some online hints because, it turns out, I had completed an earlier puzzle in a non-traditional way and didn’t have the resources the game expected me to have.  It took quite a bit of digging before finally understanding how I was
to complete the prior puzzle so I could complete the current one.
One very smart addition to curb some of this difficulty is the ability to, at any point, press escape and jump out to the central hub of the world.  From there, you can see your progress and also a map of the entire area you have so-far discovered.  You can jump in to any area you’ve previously visited, and I found it helpful to jump from puzzle to puzzle I didn’t know how to solve.  Typically inspiration would strike somewhere, and my frustrations would yield relatively quickly.
Overall, Antichamber is a smart, mostly incredible puzzle game.  Moments of frustration are almost inevitable here, and for the most part the balance is hit just right so that frustration results in joyous satisfaction when you make progress. It occasionally missteps and frustration just leads to greater frustration, but it’s easy to forgive when so much of the game is so good.  Highly recommended.

Much like the beloved TV show, South Park: The Stick of Truth is ridiculous, over-the-top, and crude. South Park has taken its shots at the world of video games before, but never with this kind of reverence. At the same time, the game is a celebration of seventeen seasons of the show, drawing references from fan favorites across the entire span of its run. Amazingly enough, the South Park stuff aside, it's actually a really good RPG as well.
South Park: The Stick of Truth puts players in the role of the new kid in town. He and his parents just moved to the quiet, Colorado mountain town in order to get away from some bad thing that happened that he has conveniently forgotten about. After being shooed out the door by his parents and told to go make some friends, he discovers that the children of the town are embroiled in what has to be the most amazing LARPing session of all time, all to decide who controls the miraculous Stick of Truth, which gives its bearer control over the universe. He naturally gets drawn into the game, but behind the scenes, the weirdness of South Park is at an all time high. Aliens, secret government organizations, underpants gnomes, nazis, zombies, nazi zombies, and Al Gore all threaten to bring the town to the brink of destruction, unless the new kid can become cool.
It should come as no surprise that Stick of Truth looks and feels just like an episode of South Park. The game begins with a terrific character customizer that allows players to generate their own nine-year old kid in the South Park style. Some players may be disappointed to learn that only male characters can be created, but there are story reasons for this, and rest assured, the girls of South Park get their day in the sun as well. Similar to Fallout 3, the appearance of the new kid determines the appearance of his parents as well. The town of South Park has been faithfully recreated, including the vast majority of landmarks seen throughout the show's seventeen-season run, including Jimbo's Guns, Skeeter's Bar, City Wok, South Park Elementary, City Hall, and even Canada. The story possesses unique elements, but also draws from the show's history for events, side quests, and even the miscellaneous junk items.
Of course, exploring South Park isn't as easy as it looks. There are a number of places the new kid won't be able to get to, at least not right away. There are locked doors that require keys to open, and rooftops and small spaces that require special abilities to access. In fact, the interactivity of the environment is one of the game's strongest aspects, and even plays a role in combat. By using the various special abilities at the new kid's disposal, as well as the special abilities of his friends, players can find multiple routes through the game's areas, and even make combat easier by defeating enemies beforehand, sometimes in surprisingly ridiculous ways.
Stick of Truth's combat involves simple but engaging turn-based battles reminiscent of the Paper Mario series. Near the beginning of the game, players can choose one of four classes — the fighter, the mage, the thief, and the jew — and each class has its own special skillset. Each class learns five special moves that can be used by consuming power points, and can spend points earned each level to upgrade their power. In addition, the new kid can also summon powerful beings like Jesus and Mr. Slave to assist in battle, and harness the magical power of... his farts. He can also bring a single ally into battle, though they can be switched out on the fly at the cost of a single turn.
Once battle begins, combat takes place turn by turn, "just like in medieval times." The new kid and his ally can perform one healing ability and one attack ability each turn. All attack skills require some sort of timed button input to perform effectively, though they are mostly very easy to perform, and the ones that require a bit more finesse are still plenty powerful even if the player fails.
Unfortunately, the game tends to be rather easy most of the time. This is partly compounded by the ease of which players can gain experience. The game caps out at level fifteen, and if players are ardent about completing side quests and exploring the town, the new kid will reach this cap well before the end of the game. The game is much more challenging in the first few hours than it is later on, despite an adjustable difficulty setting. That said, the ease of play is still dictated by successfully performing attacks in combat, and a string of bad inputs can quickly change the tide, right up until the end of the game.
Players can also collect a huge assortment of weapons, armor, augmentation items, and accessories like wigs, make-up, and glasses to further customize their character. The number of customization options are mind-boggling, so players should have no trouble making their character their own. Players can also get permanent passive bonuses to various combat functions by earning perks. Perks are earned by gaining facebook friends in the town.
One of the most surprisingly excellent aspects of South Park: The Stick of Truth is its audio. The fantastic voice talents of Trey Parker and Matt Stone are certainly wonderful on their own, but an even greater surprise is the music. Not only are there some terrific orchestral pieces that help set the tone, the game is filled to the brim with the goofier songs from the series' history, often playing on radios scattered throughout the town or during particular battle sequences.
Some players may wish to be cautious, however, as even by South Park standards, Stick of Truth is particularly crude. Not since the 1999 film South Park: Bigger, Longer, and Uncut has South Park pushed the boundaries of good taste as far as they have here. Players will engage in battle beneath the bodies of two people making sweet, sweet love, perform an abortion, and delve deep inside a man's ♥♥♥♥♥♥. There are alien anal probes and just about every bodily function imaginable, and anyone who is even remotely offendable should stay far, far away.
The best thing about South Park: The Stick of Truth is the little things that help bring the town to life. Fans of South Park are definitely not going to be disappointed, and fans of RPGs won't be either. Although the game is fairly short, the quality of the experience is undeniable, and the humor and multiple classes give it a fair bit of replayability as well. And as Obsidian games go, it's also one of the most stable. I didn't encounter a single issue. It took a while to get here, but the wait was well worth it: South Park: The Stick of Truth is sweet.

I remember the first time I played this game; I went to GameStop on my fourteenth birthday and bought the game for the Nintendo 64 and It scared the crap out of me.
About six years later I played it for the Sega Dreamcast, which by then was obsolete, and it scared the crap out of me.
Now that steam has released Shadow Man and I am almost thirty, it is not scary at all. I still love this game because of the unique atmosphere and story.  I will go down the list and give my opinion on the games features.
Story: You are the Shadow Man and you must hunt five serial killers in both the world of the living and the world of the dead and collect dark souls in order to stop the end of all things. While the basic story is not the most original, the specific details and voodoo theme really make it unique. 7/10
Lore: I gave the story a lower score simply because I wanted to address the lore on its own merit but, if combined with the story, the score would have been a 9/10. As far as the lore goes, the game is loosely based on an earlier comic book and centers around a different hero and for that reason; I won't go into the comics. This Shadow Man, Michael LeRoi, was an English major that dropped out of school, became a cab driver, and one day some gangster/Mafioso types left a bunch of cash in his cab. He quickly paid for his sick brothers operation and bought his family gifts. The gangsters of course murdered his family and Mike ended up spiraling downhill, becoming an assassin for a local voodoo priest/crime lord in exchange for protection. Long story short mama Nettie, a voodoo priestess, implants the mask of shadows in mikes chest, the voodoo crime boss is killed and Nettie gives Mike control of his bar. At night he becomes the Shadow Man and fights the dark forces. This long back story, the bios of the serial killers, the origins of the prophecy, the voodoo references, and the characters stories give this game a very interesting lore behind it which adds heavily to the gameplay. 9/10
Graphics: This game came out in 1998 and even for the time it was not the best looking game but it certainly was not the worst. I can’t rate this game graphically in any fair way since it is going to be 20 years old in a few years. For its time 7/10 today’s standards (which should not affect the score) 2/10
Sound: The vast majority of the atmosphere comes from the sound track of the game. While there are not a large variety of level themes, there is enough to make the levels have their own feel and they all fit the environments and add to the immersion without being overly repetitive. The only particular cases are two areas in the asylum where the background screams, laughing/crying, and sounds of torture play so frequently that it becomes obvious the music is looping. This is not a big deal though and these are some of the most frightening levels because of this. The sound effects are very fitting for the game. Fire sounds good, screams sound tortured and in pain, the sound of hooks digging into flesh can make a less then strong stomached person cringe. The voice acting is not perfect but it was, for its time anyway, very good. The characters all have unique and interesting dialogue and the actors express emotions like anger, fear, and confusion believably.
Overall Sound: 9/10
Music: 8.5/10
Sound FX: 9/10
Voice Acting: 9/10
Gameplay: This is the make or break category for any true gamer. The Gameplay here is not unique by any means. It is a platformer like Tomb Raider, and a pretty good one. There are items to collects that serve specific purposes, weapons to find etc. The main gameplay centers on finding 128 dark souls, each making you more powerful. These souls literally work the same way as the stars on Mario 64. The first coffin gate requires no souls to unlock the second requires 1, then 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128 to open the level 10 gate. Not all souls are required to finish the game and some are very hard to find. The enemies are interesting and range from basic Zombie Mothers to psychos in gas masks wielding hooks to weird BDSM man/dog creatures clad in bondage outfits. There are 5 unique serial killers to hunt down and kill for their souls. Each one has unique character models, voices, and their own level. The final boss, while not particularly difficult is a great villain and fun to fight. Overall 9/10
Overall Game Score: 8/10
Bugs: While there are not too many noticeable bugs, there is a particular problem with the collision detection that occasionally cause the character to stick to doorways upon entering/exiting. This problem is in no way a game breaker however and I think would be of minimal concern for most players. Occasionally while fighting, the music may skip if you are attacked and die under the right conditions. This is rare however and most players likely won't encounter this.
Whether you are a fan of survival horror, platformers, or dark brooding adventures, shadow Man has something to offer everyone. With Fast paced gameplay, interesting story and level design, this game is truly and underrated gem of the late 90's.

Shadow Man is a game which I revisit every year in the autumn, the perfect horror themed game, no jump scares but a lot of disturbing visuals and sound with a twist of dark humour. The graphics have not aged well but it doesn't affect the gameplay value conisdering this is from 1999.
The game is based on the comic of the same name (More specifically Volume II: the Garth Ennis era) and it does capture the feel of the comic very well. The story is about a Shadow Man called Michael LeRoi who is told of a premonition of impending apocolypse and you have to stop that from happening using whatever Voodoo powers you can get. Along the way you get help from Nettie, a Voodoo priestess and Jaunty, a dead Irish man with the head of a human skull and a body of a snake with a sense of humour.
I have played and own all versions of the game (N54, PS1, Dreamcast and PC) and I can safely say that this, along with the Dreamcast version is the full, definitive game with no cutbacks like the N64 and PS1 versions. The game is pretty difficult if you are playing this for the first time. You would often get lost and backtrack certain areas but that is a good thing since the worlds (Liveside and Deadside) are very immersive, this is best played in the dark and in the night for the ultimate experience.

A very poor HOG game with little to no redeeming factors. Buy at your own risk.
There is very little good to say about Crystals of Time. The soundtrack is pretty nice, but extremely limited, often stopping for minutes of a time leaving you in silence. The story is pretty much non-existent and the characters uninteresting.
The worst part is the gameplay and the presentation however as the game is littered with horrible design decisions. The area is very open with many rooms to explore and return to. Unfortunately, the areas that need items are often very vague as to what is needed (“I should find the missing item first.” is the games favorite line… instead of giving some kind of hint what I’m actually trying to do there) and HOG item zones will activate with little rhyme or reason. For example there is a greenhouse which when you first visit does not have a HOG zone… but one activates later without giving you a single indication or reason to return to the greenhouse. Thus, you are forced to use hints or to go through every single room each time you are missing an item. As moving around in the game is very slow (the minimap can only take you to a few select locations) and the locations are very uninteresting to explore the game pretty much forces you to use hints a lot.
The minigames and HOG sections themselves are uninspired. The items you search for are randomized and when you return to search the same area you often have to look for the same items again (even items that you previously took and used). Many objects are badly sized, coloured strangely, sometimes wrongly named and there is very low sensitivity to your clicks, e.g. you have to click very precisely and sometimes that is not enough. I once clicked 5 times on a chain and it simply refused to work making me believe it was the wrong item. It wasn’t.
The time travelling gem that changes the scenes is nice… I guess. However, very little is done with it in the sections I played (I only found the first crystal before I finally decided this game was not worth playing). Only means you have to keep an eye on the crystal to see if you can change the time in a room. Anyway, I bought the game for about 1 Euro and still feel a bit cheated. Avoid.

At first I thought this game was excellent. It had a great atmosphere and the music is truly lovely - melancholic but modern.
However, the game fast gets repetive, falling into the lazy traps that many hidden object games do.
The good points:
1. The music, as  I've said before is lovely. It fits nicely with the atmosphere and although it's not that varied it doesn't prove distracting, it adds to the experience.
2. Many of the mini puzzles are interesting and provide a bit of a challenge and variety.
3. The first 30 mins or so of gameplay are excellent, the diary gives you hints as to what you need to do and you don't mind skipping between locations to complete tasks/find objects.
The bad points:
1. In order to solve many 'puzzles' you need to collect objects to complete an item. Often these objects are hidden in completely non-sensical locations meaning that you have to trawl through all the possible locations of hidden object scenes. This could be so much better if you thought 'Ah, I need a pipe, I think I'll try the storeroom' rather than 'Ah, I need something to fix this damn boat and the diary is giving me no clue, I'll try every location until I happen to stumble across the correct hidden object scene - one of the master bedrooms'.
2. In order to fix these 'puzzles' as I've said above, you have no real clue what you need to collect - there are no prompts - and so this undermines the puzzle element and just makes it a grind.
3. The diary soon becomes of no use whatsoever. The 'clues' you pick up don't really help and there are no prompts.
4. It feels very much like the game had a great germ of an idea but then didn't have the time to finish it.
Overall a disappointing experience.

This game has won awards in Germany for PAEDI 2016 Awards Outstanding children’s software and it is easy to see why that is.
The animations and illustrations are impressive and brilliantly colourful, bright and packed full of fun.  Ideal for an inquisitive youngster!
I wish there were more games like this, as a parent I search constantly for ways to help teach my little one in new and creative ways and sometimes an educational game is just the ticket!
PROS
======
-	Fun & Educational.
-	Beautiful animations, vibrant, happy and fun.  Perfect for a child’s reading book.
-	Interesting storyline and characters.
-	Easy for early readers and more advanced readers to enjoy, even by themselves.
-	Each time you play there appear to be slightly different items on display in some of the chapters.  This encourages repeat play (important for reading).
-	Fair price.
CONS
======
-	As good as this is I think more could have done on the assisted reading front; coloured text for important words, perhaps an option to have the words spoken….even single spoken words upon a click.  This would enable young children to learn even when playing alone.
-	Inconsistencies around how the story Text boxes are dismissed caused a few accidental quick click dismissal incidents….As a result you don’t know exactly what to do.  It is easily overcome but a frustration none the less.
-	Some of the chapters are way too quick…single click completion.
-	The game is a mobile port, nicely done but not fully utilising the PC opportunities.
-	Language translation is fine 90% of the time, but a small amount of questionable rhyming word selections will stand out to adults.

"Shadowrun Returns" is an isometric turn-based RPG that relies heavily on dialogue and its namesake to keep it afloat.
Having never played the original "Shadowrun", perhaps I missed out on the excitement of cameos and resurging nostalgia "Shadowrun Returns" was designed to invoke. Instead, I was left playing a game filled with forgettable characters, bland visuals, predictable plot, cliché themes, and monotonous gameplay.
What kept me hooked, at least for a while, were the dialogue options, the promise of deeply customizable character progression, and the writing. Each of these elements, though engaging at first, quickly fell flat. Dialogue options exist mainly to give the illusion of meaningful decision making. Leveling and skill point allocation became a chore, with little incentive to diversify playstyle. Most disappointing, however, is the script: It starts out with some clever quips and paints a narrative that is tempting to dive into, but loses depth and character at an alarming pace.
At a staggering discount, the point at which I purchased the game, perhaps "Shadowrun Returns" is worth the investment -- probably moreso if you already have fond feelings for the franchise. I have also been told the next installment, "Shadowrun: Dragonfall", is an improvement (and I plan on playing it at some point), and perhaps "Shadowrun Returns" is a stepping stone to enjoying that next chapter. As a standalone title, however, I cannot recommend this game to players who are not already in love with Shadowrun or have somehow not had their fill of cookie-cutter cyberpunk experiences.
Games available on Steam in the same vein as "Shadowrun Returns" that I would recommend include the XCOM and Baldur's Gate series, as well as "Transistor".

Shadowrun Returns is a turn based RPG set in the near future where metahumans (elves, trolls, dwarves, and orcs) mix with steampunk tech in Seattle's urban landscape. Character creation is pretty wide open, you can be any metahuman or just create a human. You specialize further by picking a class which range from the archetypical fighter to a hacker who can plug themselves into cyberspace to an honest to goodness mage to a drone operator.
The story is engaging for the first two acts, but does feel like it overstays its welcome by act three. The conversation aspect of story advancement seems more like flavor text, it typically has no real effect on the over arching plot.
I enjoyed the theme, combat, and setting. The wide variety of classes and races makes me want to play it again with a new character, but the main storyline doesn't really lend itself to multiple playthroughs. However, there is a lot of free content in the Steam Workshop so I will most likely create a new character for one of these community campaigns.

tramite "humble bundle", un sito dove si comprano pacchi di giochi per il pc a pochi dollari, ho rimediato un piccolo capolavoro roguelike dal nome avveneristico: Faster Than Light.
Un gioco ben fatto dalla grafica retrò che vi fa sin da subito immergere nella più incredibile ambientazione sci fi.
All'inizio potrete scegliere la nave con cui iniziare il viaggio (a dir la verità di base ve ne da solo una, le altre le dovrete poi sbloccare), la ciurma inizialmente composta da 3 elementi dove potrete customizzare sesso e nome, ed infine avrete armi e miglioramenti dati di default in base al modello di nave scelto.
Il gioco è formato a livelli o "galassie", livelli a loro volta formati da mappe dove vi potrete spostare da punto a punto cercando di raggiungere l'uscita della mappa posta solitamente dalla parte opposta dell'entrata.
In ogni punto dove andrete a spostarvi potrete trovare di tutto: da ragni giganti a piattaforme disabitate ma nella maggior parte dei casi dovrete vedervela contro altre navi spaziali.
Il gioco è impostato in maniera altamente strategica e manageriale. Infatti risulta fondamentale l'utilizzo della pausa in game (barra spaziatrice) in modo da ideare bene il piano di attacco in base alla tipologia di nemico che si ha di fronte.
Le navi, compresa la vostra, sono formate da stanze collegate,le une con le altre, da porte. Quasi ogni stanza ha la sua funzione: vi è la stanza armeria dove si gestiscono le armi dell'astronave (raggio laser, missili, cannone a Ioni, etc.), la medicheria dove si possono curare i membri dell'equipaggio, etc.
Se vi fanno "saltare" una stanza, cioè ve la mettono fuori uso con un missile o qualcos'altro, non potrete utilizzare la relativa funzione. Per esempio, prima sono morto perché mi hanno distrutto la stanza adibita alla diffusione dell'ossigeno, non ho fatto in tempo a ripararla con l'equipaggio e quindi son schiattati tutti miseramente.
Le armi sono moltissime, come i droni utilizzabili (ho nella nuova partita un drone che gira intorno alla nave nemica e gli tira raggi laser ogni 4 secondi) o i miglioramenti, come ad esempio piu' % di trovare "scrap", una sorta di valuta, dovrebbero essere rottami, quando si distrugge una nave nemica.
La difficoltà è abbastanza elevata anche con facile. Ho perso partite dove ero messo benissimo solo per una piccola distrazione.

Gameplay: Plays like Lords Of Arcana. Which is basically a hack and slash Monster Hunter. Attacking feels great, the hit boxes are broad, and UNLIKE Monster Hunter, you can toggle being able to see enemy hp. There are a variety of weapons to choose from, and a variety of "classes" to equip. Each class offers different skills to use during battle such as: Attack boosts, defense boosts, party support, unique attacks. Each one levels up as you use it more. There are missions (which can be done both online and offline) that involve slaying small monsters, clearing waves, collecting items, and last but definitely not least, slaying large monsters (or Onis). This is where the game is the most fun. A party of four against a large enemy, just like Monster Hunter.
Sound: The game is primarily Japanese. This means all the dialogue has english subtitles.
Graphics: Here's where people are complaining the most. The game is a little lacking in the graphics department and it is locked at 30fps. It's really no big deal, as the game still runs smooth enough (provided your specs are on par). 60fps would be lovely though. The game looks as it does on the PSVita, since it was orignially on PSVita/4.
Controls: Here's another issue with this game. The controls are intuitive, responsive, and fluid...on a controller. I would not reccomend playing this game on keyboard. Most annoyingly, you cannot type in text boxes with the keyboad, or navigate through a menu with the mouse.
Online: There are issues here as well. What's important is that the game runs flawlessly online. I haven't had any issues in the lobbies I played. Whether it was 2 or 4 players in the room, there was no noticable lag.
What I have a problem with is the lack of chat. You are limited to quick chat commands. There's no way to type, no way to voice chat, and you can't even check another players steam profile to add them. If you want a party to be fully coordinated, you'll have to form it outside the game.
What's also annoying about the online (and the lack of chat makes this worse) is that you have to exit the loby if you want to purchase, craft, or sell any items. So if you're trying to make a sweet sword, and you're not sure how many more parts you need for it, you'll have to go offline to check the blacksmith. You won't be able to tell your peers you'll be right back, and they may just assume you've quit.
Overall, the game is very very enjoyable. A solid pc controller, a voice/text chat group outside of the game chat, and hopefully eventually some graphical optimization (fps unlock at least) would make the game even better.

This was my first hidden object game. Got it for free, so gave it a try, even though I'm not a big fan of Myst-like games (which I assume is what all HOGs are based on.)
From what I could gather, the story is about a woman who visits an old mansion and decides to clean it up. The mansion's owner must have thought that women really liked cleaning up, because he regularly trashed the place again. Or maybe that's how hidden object games are supposed to behave, and don't ask too many questions.
Graphics are beautiful. Some screens are only transitory and I'm surprised they spent time on them to begin with. Mini-games are okay, some are classics like the towers of Hanoi, some are interesting, others are too obscure but thankfully there's a Skip button, so casual gamers like me will never get stuck.
There's only one song in the game, and it plays in a loop. Normally this would be a major drawback to me, but the one song is good enough that it didn't hit on my nerves, and I actually liked having it in the background. (Edit: nope, there's more than one song, but they're all fine.)
Text is in broken English (like, they're trying hard but ultimately it's obvious it's not their native language, and I'm French so I would know), and the ending is as abrupt as an ending can be. Seriously, it's just three or four sentences, then "thanks for playing". That's a serious offender to me, but I guess the whole thing is about the journey, not the destination. Whatever. The complete lack of character interaction and dialogues is more problematic to me, you end up feely very lonely. Thankfully, if played in multiple short sessions, this isn't too much of an issue.
I don't know how good a flagship this game is for HOGs, but I'm guessing it's not the worst. I personally enjoyed it, even though the time travel mechanic was really underused: there are like, 3 places in the entire game where you can travel in time, and it's only to find a less dirty version of that same room so you can play yet another hidden object scene.
Will probably play another couple of HOGs in the future, perhaps better rated games, just to see if they're worth more of my time.

This review is specifically for *Enemy Within*.  Enemy Unknown was a great game too, but now that Enemy Within is out, there is no reason to play just the original.  In simpler terms, if you did not play Enemy Unknown, BUY BOTH Enemy Within and Enemy Unknown and play Within only.  Beyond needing to own Unknown (because Within is technically an expansion) there is no reason to play Unknown at this point.
If you have played Enemy Unkown, Within adds a number of new features that are really cool (mech soldiers, bio augmentations, another dynamic through another faction, and soldier customizations).  I had played all the way through Unknown myself twice and even though Within follows the same overall story, everything felt more fleshed out.  They also added a number of new maps with Within and I'm not sure I have actually played the same map in the same playthrough with Within whereas there was definitely a repetitive feel to the maps in Unknown.
The ability to customize my soldiers made me feel more connected to them / like each of them developed more of a personality.  Until I could really customize them, I hadn't realized how much their sameness in Unknown detracted from the experience.
Then you have the mech soldiers and the bio augmentations which add an aspect and are a lot of fun, though I'm not sure they were strictly necessary.  Fun though is the name of the game here.  Mechs are sort of ridiculous, but they look awesome and they're somewhat balanced by their inability to use cover (beyond breaking line of sight).  The bio augmentations are nice, but since I don't play hardcore I have only found a few of them to be particularly useful.  Still psionic defenses and snipers who can jump as high as they want is nice.
Overall, if you have never played Enemy Unknown and you like turn-based tactics games, I would recommend this game without a doubt.  If you have played Enemy Unknown I would still strongly recommend Within as I think it's a much more robust game now, but be warned that it follows the same basic storyline (it's just more fleshed out).

The game itself runs at a locked 30fps (This might perhaps be modded out in the future I mean just look at the original Dark Souls) and while some people might complain about ''hurr durr muh 60fps pc mustard race'' I personally feel like the game itself works just fine at 30fps.
It was also stated yesterday that the game does have some issues with certain Nvidia cards in combination with Windows 8.1 (GTX 560, GTX 570 and GTX 980) and I happen to be running Windows 8.1 with a GTX980. During my first 20 minutes of gameplay I ran into a crash while I was going to the village but that could be fixed by running the game in Windows 7 compatability mode and after putting that on I have yet to get another crash.
I've seen in the community that some people are having problems in the village with the frames going down as low as 15 and I do not have that problem on my rig soo the game runs at a constant 30fps.
Now as a Monster Hunter veteran and hunting genre lover I personally felt like this game was worth the price but I understand that most of you probably feel like it's way too high because you already own the game on another system but for a first time player it really could have been worse.
As a whole I highly recommend this game if you are into the whole hunting genre as the weapons are really fun to use and the oni's are fun to hunt.
Happy hunting everyone!

I was looking through my library of games on Steam to see which one I've played the most, and Risk of Rain takes the cake. I've played this game 40% more than my second most played game. So, I figured, it deserves a nice review from me.
I bought Risk of Rain in a steam sale (like everyone does) a while back when it was something like 75% off. I was honestly just looking for something I could pick up and play for a few hours and then probably never touch again. Despite the positive reviews I had quickly skimmed through, I still was skeptical because I've never liked a single rogue-like game besides Binding of Isaac. In most rogue-likes, once I die 5 or 6 times I usually rage-quit and never play it again. But when I booted up Risk of Rain, I was immediately blown away. The first thing I noticed was the music. The music from the first levels is always very mysterious. It got me to feel just as curious as the character I'm playing as is supposed to be. What planet is this? Who was that guy that crashed the ship I was on? What am I supposed to do? Then, as you progress through the levels, the music picks up as you become more and more determined to reach the end and escape this harsh and hostile world!
The game has a lot of replay value.
First, randomized items and enemies (unless you have certain acquired artifacts turned on).
Second, decisions. In Risk of Rain you decide whether to kill more enemies for money to open more chests, or go straight for the exit. And the balance between the two is still something I'm figuring out after having played for over 130 hours. I should also add that the mechanic of having to wait 90 seconds for the transporter to turn on while a high influx of waves come at you (including a boss) is AWESOME and creates many tense moments.
Third, length of the game. The game is just long enough that you don't feel helpless as you try again and again, and beating the game is feasible.
Fourth, character variety. The only thing I think you could complain about is also the one thing I happen to like about the game. That is, the characters are not balanced at all. Some are much easier than others. I personally find the huntress to be the easiest to beat the game with, as she can run and shoot at the same time, making it easy to kite enemies. And then I find the sniper's abilities to be really tough to master, and Acrid's melee abilities are hard to close-in with without taking damage. I think that this actually adds to the game. You may find other characters easier depending on your play-style, thereby making more options to present yourself with different difficulty levels.
All in all, the game is great. I highly recommend it, even at full price. It's a fun game you can get into, play for a bit, leave, and pick back up again the next day. I've been addicted for a while now, and I don't get tired of it. The music's very fitting, the graphics are pleasantly simple, the game-play is thrilling, and no two attempts are the same. That sinking feeling you get when you know you're about to die after how far you've come is absolutely the worst, and keeps me motivated to get better.

Some first impressions from my first hour of playtime regarding the port and comparability to Hyperdimension Neptunia:
First off, the game runs smooth even on my old toaster card. This is likely due to it being more CPU intensive to begin with, but even then I am seeing no hiccups with my i5-4460 and my HD5750, running Windows 10 Pro x64 - in other words, the game runs smoothly at 60fps (which is the default lock as per the .ini file, but may be unlockable).
There are no in-game graphics options to speak of besides resolution and a fullscreen/windowed/borderless toggle, but then you'll hardly need more, seeing the game's artstyle and heavy reliance on animated 2D backgrounds and sprites. Further graphics settings may be available in the .ini file again, and AA can be forced via your graphics vendor's control panel regardless.
Settings for controls, sound and so on are all there, including manual button remapping for your gamepad (which should help with getting non-standard Xinput pads to work), and Voice, Movie, Effects and BGM volumes have separate sliders, as they should have.
From a gameplay standpoint, the game is close to Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth, which it supposedly shares the engine with. If you've played Neptunia, you'll find it easy to get into the systems, though even after an hour of playtime, there are differences and additions in Fairy Fencer F.
Those differences include the Tension meter that raises/lowers your stats in combat and allows you to transform at a certain point (whereas Neptunia gave you more free reign with transformations), "boosting" weapon stats, learning new skills and what not through using them to earn and assign points, attaching Fairies to your characters for added perks, switching weapon styles to increase certain parameters like crit chance, speed and the likes, and Character Challenges which reward you with stat increases for various gameplay milestones.
These challenges also encourage cycling through your party members, as some of them demand a character to be the party leader or do things only the leader is able to. It is a nifty system I'm looking forward to explore more in-depth, as it should keep things fresh (if a little grindy in the higher ranks, I expect).
Overall, the gameplay system at least feels more complex in terms of customization and late-game options than Neptunia (though take my judgement with a grain of salt - I'm not that far in yet).
The story and characters up to now seem like a good combination. The character dynamic between the protagonist and his fairy partner are funny and lighthearted, which reminds of Neptunia, but appears far more grounded and less preposterous than Nep did. If Gamindustri felt too wacky and over the top to you, Fairy Fencer F might deliver a more enjoyable experience.
The basic plot is very simple in theory: Collect all the Fury weapons and revive the Goddess, explore dungeons, talk to people in towns (again, more grounded than in Neptunia, though very similar in execution), and fill your protagonist's stomach.
The art design and music are straight-up gorgeous, as would be expected from the team behind them (which includes Nobuo Uematsu as composer and Yoshitaka Amano on the art, two big creatives that made Final Fantasy so good in its glory days). Fairy Fencer F offers some top-notch, high quality art in the typical J-RPG/Anime style.
Overall, I am pleased with my purchase, and will continue playing it.

Now, let me open this review by saying that I freaking LOVE Half-Life! In case you think I've reviewed the wrong game, do not despair, I haven't, it's just I feel I need to share this declaration in order to set the foundation of this review. Right, let's get to it. After the HUGE success of Half-Life I was genuinely overwhelmed by the announcement that a sequel would be coming out. I’ve played HL2 when it was first released in 2004 and again recently. So, what did a fan (huge fan) of Half-Life think?
Confused.
You begin as Gordon Freeman having just arrived in City 17, from where you don't know and never do. A figure on a screen is broadcasting, a person whose name, once learnt has no meaning to you. The city and indeed the world has been conquered by a force called the Combine. Who they are or why they invaded is never explained (at least in no detail). You meet up with three colleagues from Black Mesa. One is Barney who we know escaped the facility before its destruction. The other two were last seen deep within Black Mesa yet here they are, alive and once again no explanation is given. This theme continues through the game, causing me to constantly scratch my head in thought. Only by reading online did I learn what the hell HL2 was all about, something that I should never have had to do.
Graphically HL2 was a huge improvement on HL, yet by today’s standards dated and lacking features that one would expect in a FPS. Weapons are your usual standard, with one exception. Enemies are varied including some old favourites.
I can't help but feel that HL2 was (and is) an incomplete game story wise. For me HL2 was not HL. Other than Gordon Freeman and the occasional G-man scene it felt nothing like the original, which was (and is) so good. The only level which reminded me of HL was Ravenholme, a rather scary place. I get the feeling that the developers, after the huge success of HL thought they'd make a sequel but had no idea what story to go with, no idea what to do as most scientists etc were killed in the original. There is no continuous flow from HL to HL2. It was not seamless. It was disjointed and full of storyline holes. As I didn't know who anyone was I found myself not caring what happened to them. I played through the game emotionless, uncaring and confused.
7/10

This game was actually one of my childhood favourites. I still remember the demo disk, which had you playing through the Asylum-map.  Entertained me enough to buy the whole game, once I spotted it in a gamestore by accident. The game has you running and gunning in the liveside (our world) and the deadside (A sort of purgatory). As you go, you collect dark souls and all sorts of useful items, both which help you continue your journey through the mazes of the deadside. You need a certain amount of dark souls to attain a certain "level" of sorts, which allows you to go through certain doors in the deadside. Same goes for the items: you need certain items to, for example, climb the rivers of blood or teleport to you another (useful) location. The game could be explained as 3D metroidvania-game. The souls and items are found non-linearly, so the game might have you running for an item which you've already gone past, but only now have the means to attain. This gives you more reason to explore previously visited levels, and at the worst could make you run around for a few hours, looking for that last soul or item you need to advance in the game.
All in all, I love it. The game gives you a constant feel of exploration, the items and lore are exciting and nothing I've seen in other games. The levels go from a setting of dark to disgusting; Babies crying and meat grinders working their way through the flesh of some poor soul. Despite the dark setting, it has good dark humour thrown in, to not make you take it so seriously.
Now, the negative stuff. The negative part is mostly tied to the engine; lack of features or bugs I don't remember encountering in the original. Some of them are annoying, some of them might outright stop you from advancing in the game. I played through the game from end to finish, gathering the max amount of dark souls and Cadeaux (sort of bonus item) to gain full level and maximum health bars. Here's a list I kept adding to, during my playthrough:
- Gamepad support is awful: The game plays best on gamepad, and the joystick/gamepad support is awful. It will not recognize half of the buttons on your gamepad, and there's a lot of buttons to configure to get the best out of the game. For me, this was saved by the fact that I noticed Pinnacle Game Profiler on sale the day I started playing this game, and the features of that program saved the experience completely. But this is not something you should have to do to get good gamepad-experience. Taking the extra gamepad buttons into consideration shouldn't be too difficult of a task, even when rewiving an old codebase.
- Crashing to desktop: The game crashes to desktop every now and then. Might be that you'll crash couple of times in an hour, might be that you get to play all day without the game crashing. This will make you learn to save your game often, since even losing the last 15 minutes of gameplay always feels excruciating.
- Enemies sometimes shoot through walls: I got killed a couple of times by an enemy I couldn't even see, but they were quite able to suck through my lifebar through a wall.
- You'll fall through floors (rare): Sometimes you'll just encounter a floor, that isn't actually there, making you fall into the abyss and having to reset your level progress.
- The climbing system is sometimes (more often not) broken: You can hang on to ledges in the game, allowing you much greater mobility than a standard jumping-game would afford. When trying to jump from the ledge to the actual platform, the game will force an animation on the character, which might force you through the wall of the ledge, and make you fall into the abyss (Again, losing some of the level progress). As a more major bug: in a certain part of the game you find the ability to hang on ledges that are hot/on fire. When you gain this ability, you are supposed to return to a certain level and make your way around a big flaming "barrel" by hanging on to the ledges and shimmying yourself around the object. But in this part the game is ALWAYS broken: after shimmying a couple of seconds, you will drop off the ledge. ALWAYS. As a new player this WILL make you feel like you are not in the correct place, and should look for a way forward elsewhere, causing many hours wasted. I had to carefully make my way to the very edge of the barrel, partly inside the object, and only then could I grab on the ledge, so that the game would allow for me to shimmy just long enough, that on dropping from the ledge, I would drop to the otherside and continue my journey. Awful shortcoming, and the reason I tipped this review into the negative side.
- Other minor annoyances, possibly existing in the original version: There are these certain underwater propellers you need to avoid in the game, by swimming through the blades. Sometimes when trying to swim through the blades, the game will simply think that you are not actually between the blades, and hurt your character. It's as if the graphics weren't totally in sync with the engine. In other part of the game I had to open a certain door with a key, but the door simply wouldn't budge. Luckily I found a way to the other side of the door and once using the key from there, the door opened. I'm not certain if this was in the original.
Almost all of these problems are rare occurrences, and might not detract from your experience, but I felt that there were enough problems to give a negative review, as a sort of warning to new players. As an old fan, I thoroughly enjoyed the experience, and haven't even the slightest buyers remorse. Should you feel like you want part of the experience, and don't mind the mentioned flaws in the game, I very much recommend you to buy and play through this game.

If you want to try an action horror classic that still holds up to this day, I recommend that you check this one out.

I play this game and I am TRYING my best to enjoy it.
Pros - Amazing art design for their cards. Lots of beautiful asthetics.

They give you loads of booster packs to begin with so you can actually get a deck going for yourself so they offer quite a lot to new players.
Cons - Despite everything they do for new players. You will be having to put money into the game to even start winning any games. They do give you loads of boosters to start but that does NOT mean they will give you cards that you can work with. Because of the different classes in cards your decks will always be missing cards to them for the decks to even work. You run into constant players who have these clean cut decks filled with the cards they need to win or reach their win condition. I cannot see any new person coming into this game and getting anywhere when it comes to playing against other players. I'm pretty easy-going when it comes to HOGs. I've played a LOT of them (thanks, Big Fish Games!). I like the puzzles, I like the hidden object scenes, and I'd say 99% of the ones I've played have at least some kind of reasonable story.
This game belongs in the 1%.
Pros:
+ reasonably nice graphics for an HOG.
+ I can play in windowed mode.
+ there's a map for quick-travel.
+ nice soundtrack.
Cons:
- typos and painful grammar; reads like a bad translation.
- awful storyline, completely unbelievable premise.
- puzzles have nothing to do with the story.
- some puzzles are completely unintuitive.
- HO scenes randomly reset.
- jumping back and forth between locations in the hope that something new will appear.
- unrealistic, pointless puzzles.
- some items in HO scenes are named badly.
In short, I can't really recommend this game. I wanted to; HOGs are generally fun, brain-candy games. I can usually finish one in a night. I'm halfway through this one, and I want to tear my eyes out. At this point, I'm only here for the trading cards -- and even those aren't dropping.

I'm not sure how I feel about this game. The core mechanic is inspired and interesting, but as is so common in the indie puzzle scene, it seems to need a bit more.
The opening puzzles are fun and quickly introduce what I have dubbed the double platforming mechanic. The slow introduction of other elements kept the game fresh and engaging in my short play through.
However, around level 25 the execution difficulty spikes. The camera becomes difficult to use and the controls (changing based on your perspective) become frustratingly easy to mess up. I overcame the level but once again hit the same problems only two levels later. Imporovements to camera control ( I have no idea how) or setting the controls so that they do not shift with perspective might fix this.
It's a shame as the game is interesting, but not enough for me to warrant putting up with this frustration. A more patient player (or one with better platforming skills) will likely get more enjoyment out of what is a quirky little game, but that is not my story.
Still, I will not be looking for a refund and I look forward to seeing what this developer comes out with next. So I'm recommending this, but leaving my thoughts. Buy this game if you want to see something interesting, but stay away if you're looking for a casual platformer.

InterSection is a platformer game with some puzzle elements. While the game may not seem much there are a lot more into it as it takes a simple idea and involves it into something more. I was pleasantly surprised of the use of its numerous mechanics as I unlocked each one of them and using them altogether!
The game consist of 2 platforms that always cross, or to say it better, 'Intersect' each other at your location. Essentially you play a platformer at 3 dimensions, each dimension follows you and has a Cube in it. To finish the level you must get the 2 Cubes to touch. As easy as it may sound at first, after some levels the true fun will start, along with some frustration and a mild headache. The game's mechanics ramp up at a good pace, having none of the special blocks at start and each added after a set number of levels. Each is unique and it interacts with the others in a marvelous way that level design highlights even more!
In general the game give you a feel of chilling, zen, allowing you to play at your own pace. The UI and music fulfill this idea by offering calm earthly colors, wonderful animations, platform design and chilling music at all times. Most levels are meant to be beaten either by moving among the dimensions or by some use of the puzzle elements the game offers. However there are few levels that feel like a huge rock thrown in the peaceful lake this game is. They require precision platforming or unneeded use of a repetitive, in that case, mechanic. While the later most people will find it boring and eventually beat the level, the first can lead to frustration and even quitting as there is no skip button.
Additionally the game has a small story that is unfold by few select levels with a DOS screen behind a single platform. You are free to read it or simply run to merge the 2 Cubes and move on.
However the gray part of the game is its controls. You move with WASD jump with Space and move the camera with the mouse, but you cannot customize them at all. While there is no need for anything complex as the required input is basic the game offers partial controller support, or even better, unfinished or accidental controller support. On the 360 controller I could use the left stick to move but there was no button assigned for jump and I could not turn the camera with the right stick. If controls where customizable I could perhaps bind jump to a mouse button at least...
Overall, I do not think InterSection is worth its cost, as there are only 100 premade levels and even with workshop support, I cannot see myself returning to check workshop levels after I've finished the game. But by no means it is a bad game, in fact it is a really good one and I quite enjoyed it most of the time (that level 27....AAARG). It is perhaps a great example that not every idea has been used, or every mechanic has been made as it's simplistic visual design hides a huge innovating idea behind it. If you want to experience a different kind of platforming, then I strongly recommend InterSection.

This review is specifically for *Enemy Within*.  Enemy Unknown was a great game too, but now that Enemy Within is out, there is no reason to play just the original.  In simpler terms, if you did not play Enemy Unknown, BUY BOTH Enemy Within and Enemy Unknown and play Within only.  Beyond needing to own Unknown (because Within is technically an expansion) there is no reason to play Unknown at this point.
If you have played Enemy Unkown, Within adds a number of new features that are really cool (mech soldiers, bio augmentations, another dynamic through another faction, and soldier customizations).  I had played all the way through Unknown myself twice and even though Within follows the same overall story, everything felt more fleshed out.  They also added a number of new maps with Within and I'm not sure I have actually played the same map in the same playthrough with Within whereas there was definitely a repetitive feel to the maps in Unknown.
The ability to customize my soldiers made me feel more connected to them / like each of them developed more of a personality.  Until I could really customize them, I hadn't realized how much their sameness in Unknown detracted from the experience.
Then you have the mech soldiers and the bio augmentations which add an aspect and are a lot of fun, though I'm not sure they were strictly necessary.  Fun though is the name of the game here.  Mechs are sort of ridiculous, but they look awesome and they're somewhat balanced by their inability to use cover (beyond breaking line of sight).  The bio augmentations are nice, but since I don't play hardcore I have only found a few of them to be particularly useful.  Still psionic defenses and snipers who can jump as high as they want is nice.
Overall, if you have never played Enemy Unknown and you like turn-based tactics games, I would recommend this game without a doubt.  If you have played Enemy Unknown I would still strongly recommend Within as I think it's a much more robust game now, but be warned that it follows the same basic storyline (it's just more fleshed out).

I've heard "this game is like XCOM." Scratch that, because it's nothing like XCOM. Sure there are some minor similarities in battle mechanics but that's where the similarities end. This game is good in it's own right. You've got a pretty interesting plot about finding your old friend's killer to make a couple of bucks. From there the story goes down a rabbit hole to uncover the culprit and turns into quite the adventure.
This game isn't necessarily about saving the world or some greater good. You're pretty low on cash and a lot of times I compromised my morals to make a couple bucks. Mercenaries don't come cheap in this run down futuristic, magic tech world and we've all gotta eat. That being said although this game is short, for an RPG you'll end up taking a lot of jobs and get to meet a few brothers in arms. There are many characters you'll encounter but aside from the handful you actually get to know a bit most are for fighting purposes.
There are numerous skills to customize your character with. When you complete missions or do good deals it rewards you with karma points pretty frequently to upgrade whatever you like. I suggest finding a particular specialty and sticking with it. When I started my I decided I'd be a decker with focus on melee skills. Decker was a good choice as there are a couple of situations later in the game that require that particular skill set. But I soon found that most enemies carry guns and you know what they say about bringing a knife to a gun fight. Charisma was an important skill as you can get more money by charming the pants off of people using your words. This also had a couple of layers to it as you learn new etiquette surprisingly it's the choices I don't expect that pop up in dialogue.
Like most strategy RPGs having a diverse range of companions helps in all missions but you'll end up hiring the same people who complement your style. Battles require a bit of strategy as AI isn't stupid. If you cluster all your forces in one spot an enemy will likely bomb your group. That being said you'll have more of the "kill all foes" variety of missions. How you do it is up to you.
This game is good but I would have liked to see more locations or other town like places you could meet runners in between missions. There are conversations referencing other places in the Matrix but sadly you never get to experience them. There were also a couple of bugs that froze my game during missions. They were random and seemed to fix it self after a restart but saving often helps. Hopefully all these issues are resolved in the Dragonfall sequel but in itself it's an alright game and you should try it if you're into tactical, futuristic RPGs.

You'll see from my 'Hours played' that I dig this game.  Just like anybody, when I started I had exasperated moments of, "UGH!  How was I supposed to survive THAT?"  This was really the first Rogue-like game I'd ever played so the sensation was new.  So I struggled, and struggled, all the while appreciating the awesome music and very nicely styled pixel art as I ran away screaming from Magma Worms.
Slowly, you get better.  You learn how to best combo the moves of the characters you grow to prefer, you figure out the attack behaviors of the enemies, and you learn which items are the most useful.  And here's the good news- the gameplay itself is so simple and satisfying that you feel encouraged to do so.
One of the things I like the most about this game is that depending on how you play- you could go from blank state to pixel power house in about 15 minutes.  It doesn't take very long to get a hold of a good stock of items, and so when you die, you never feel like, "How will I ever get that back?  I invested so much time!"  A sense of improvement and reward comes quickly.
I would say the number one feature of the game is 'Replay value'.  Because there are literally almost 100 items (might even be slightly more) and nearly all of those items have stacking effects, you will never go through the game with the same equipment.  And items add on infinitely, there's no cap- most of them with permanent passive effects that will dramatically change the way you play.
On top of that nearly infinite combinatorial variety, there are 12 characters, all of whom feel very unique!  And I've beaten the game with all of them, so while many people claim that some are objectively better- have faith that they are all at least playable.
Even on top of THAT there are the artifacts- very reminiscent of Halo's campaign 'skulls' which would activate permanent gameplay adjustments and the various combinations of those can make for extremely different run experiences. (Love Glass: 10% Health in exchange for 500% damage)
As I talk about all of this variety, I should emphasize that the game never feels overwhelming in the choices/complexity.  In fact it's pretty simple- stage to stage you just kill monsters until you can find the teleporter, activate it, survive the larger waves of monsters + boss, buy up items in chests/ drones, and then go to the next level.  But there's plenty of complexity to explore and play around with as soon as you want some variety.
Some of the fun, once you get good enough, is just seeing, "How ridiculously powerful can I make myself?"  The difficulty increases as time goes on but it does hit a limit eventually, and if you can survive at that limit?  You're pretty much on your way to being 'unkillable'- a satisfying state to reach as you repress memories of being rotfl-stomped by a Sand Crab at Lv. 1.
Unfortunately, the online co-op is pretty hard to set up.  Lots of people have trouble with it- I rarely have success playing with people who aren't in the room with me.
That being said, this is still my favorite indie game- I cannot recommend it highly enough.

This review is based on what i have played on PC for Fairy Fencer F (フェアリーフェンサーエフ)
Fairy Fencer F (フェアリーフェンサーエフ) is a 2013 fantasy role-playing game developed by Compile Heart's for the PlayStation 3, which will take around 45-50 hours to complete 1 playthrough, depends on individual.
A long time ago there was a conflict between a goddess and a evil god. The two deities didn’t fight directly, but created a large number of special weapons imbued with their godly energy, each containing the life force of a fairy for others to use. Eventually, these powers sealed each other and the power vanished from the world. Going into modern times, warriors that wield the powers (Furies) are known as "Fencers."
Fairy Fencer F places you in the role of Fang reluctant hero that is more interested in his next meal, becomes a Fencer—warrior chosen by The Goddess to become companions to fairies, who are magical beings who can transform into a variety of weapons called "Furies" and warriors that wield them are "Fencers".
Fury weapons are said to be incredibly powerful, so Fencers constantly scramble to acquire them. By a strange coincidence, fang finds himself rescuing a young woman named Tiara, who is also a Fencer as well. This fateful encounter between two Fencers has dire consequences, and Fang soon finds himself involved in the ongoing conflict between the Goddess and Vile God.
Unlike most JRPGs, you don't equip any new weapons in Fairy Fencer F. Since each Fencer is bound to one fairy partner, you instead upgrade your fairy to increase its capabilities and powers which is unique. (Unless you have the DLC weapons then equipping weapons will affect stats)
The dialogue and voice acting are both well done, and the soundtrack is really nice as the soundtracks blends perfectly with the action going on in your screen.
As for the combat the characters special attacks have flashy animations. It is like watching a really cool anime. For example, Fate franchise.
To sum it up Fairy Fencer F is a enjoyable way to spend 45-50 hours for 1 play through, and would definitely recommend it to, JRPG fans, Anime lovers or those who want to try somethwing new.

So I had been wanting Teleglitch for awhile. It's been in my wishlist for several months, but next to all the other games there, it wasn't really a priority of mine to get it. I thought, "Well, that's a neat little game. Looks like fun." But other than that, I didn't think much more of it.
And then PC Gamer posted an article about how the game was free with Humble Bundle. Like, literally free. Not "buy one get one free", but actually
So it only took me about 3 minutes of juggling with my e-mail, my Steam account and Humble Bundle in Chrome, and BAM! Free game. How awesome is that? (You can get this game for free as well by putting your e-mail address into Humble Bundle's site, and then logging in to Steam and activating the game key. As long as you do it before the end of November 2014.) So that's cool! I got this $13 game for free. Something for nothing. Now for the review!
Teleglitch is reminiscent of other roguelikes available on Steam like FTL and Binding of Isaac. One thing I like about the game is that the lore is actually revealed through walking up to computers in-game and accessing databases, which makes it feel like scanning terminals in Metroid Prime. Sounds are very precise and make you feel like you're actually in a desolate facility, and it feels very immersive. Unlocking lore, killing enemies, and crafting items will help you fill up your Info section which basically gives information and lore on specific aspects of the game. Once you kill an enemy, your info will be updated permanently, and you can view everything in a Risk of Rain monster log style layout.
The graphics and gameplay make Teleglitch feel kind of like a top-down Doom 3. It has a unique inventory and crafting system as well, and although it took me a little while to figure out how to use it, it actually is really important to craft things in order to survive. For instance, you can combine RDX-250 (an explosive charge) with an empty can of meat that you just ate out of, and a box of nails, to create a one-shot-use weapon called the 'cangun' that explodes and sprays shrapnel in the face of your enemies. Pretty awesome. And there's plenty of other goodies you can craft besides that.
The combat system feels nice once you get the hang of it. It's fairly simple controls. WASD moves your character, right-click and hold to aim, left-click to shoot, R to reload. Alternatively, you can simply left-click without aiming to jab in front of you with a knife while a weapon is equipped. Your inventory is always open and off to the side, so mousewheel up and down will select different items or weapons. Left-click will also use items if you have them selected instead of a weapon, for instance using medkits or eating canned meat. Bombs and explosive charges work similarly. Simply left-clicking will drop them at your feet while holding right-click will aim and left-click will throw. Explosives have a very short fuse and will damage the player if he/she is too close. Overall, fighting in the game is very fun, but ammunition is typically scarce. This makes ammo conservation a must as the player struggles to manage resources. Hearing the telltale *Click* after pulling the trigger on a now-empty gun is never a fun sound when there's mutants and zombies hurtling towards you at running speed.
One thing that kinda surprised me and bummed me out is that there is, in fact, no music in the game. It does make the game feel a bit creepier though, not having a soundtrack to cover up the dead silence and occasional noise. But if you absolutely need music, the developers have made a $2 "Guns and Tunes" DLC that adds music to the game as well as some additional guns. It's worth two bucks for a game like this. Alternatively, you could probably play your own music in the background just as well.
The DLC actually doesn't update the game's files with the music, which seemed kind of minimalist to me at first, and confused me because after buying it there was still no music in the game. But as it turns out, the music from the DLC instantly becomes available in your built-in Steam music player after buying. So what does this mean? Well, all you have to do to listen to your music is open the Steam music player by right-clicking "Library" and then clicking on "Music". Then, find your Teleglitch Soundtrack, select it, and hit "Play", just like you would with any game. Put it on repeat and shuffle it if you want, then you can go back to your games library and load up Teleglitch. It sounds inconvenient, but it's actually not that bad at all.
I really think I'm going to enjoy playing this game over the next few weeks, So far, it's exciting to play, and creepy enough that it's uncomfortable playing it alone in the dark at night. Teleglitch seems like it has a lot of potential for the surprisingly difficult rougelike game that it is. If you are able to get this game, you would have to be hard pressed to not enjoy it.
