Back in 1999 before Acclaim's demise they released an interesting third person shooter with item collection/area exploration mechanics reminiscent of metroid/castlevania that flew under the radar called Shadowman. This game is the PC Port version of that title. It was also released on the N64 and Playstation but they were little more than watered down versions. Between the two, the N64 was the more stable and easier to play through version.
As you go through the game you collect "dark souls" throughout the land of the dead, known as deadside.
The dark souls have two functions:
1. Increase the amount of damage you can charge into your basic weapon, the shadowgun. The gun can be charged like Megaman X's X-buster for increased damage shots. Higher levels of shadow increase the max damage of a fully charged shot and increase the distance it travels too.
2. Enable you open "coffin gates" which can only be opened if you have enough dark souls, which is measured by the levels of shadow on your shadow meter. Different coffin gates have different shadow level requirements. These gates seal off the accessible areas and levels of the game.
You will also find other useful items ranging from keys, other guns and voodoo weapons and voodoo artifacts as you attempt to stop five serial killers and their unknown master from unleashing an army of immortal zombies from deadside to the land of the living, liveside.
This is a third person shooter with dual wielding capability. You will wield two weapons to kill your enemies however most of the enemies you kill won't drop a health pickup unless you execute them with your basic weapon, the Shadowgun. You can still kill enemies using different combos of weapons but the enemies won't drop a health pickup after they die. To execute an enemy you just shoot it until it enters a sort of "stun-state" then you shoot it one more time with your shadowgun to gain a health pickup when the enemy dies.
You can hold down a button for a nice little lock-on feature that doubles as a Doom-style strafe. Therefore you can sidestep enemy fire as you missile them to death with your weapons. Although this is a third person shooter some of the more agile enemies are a little easier to shoot using the free look. Don't hesitate to use it if the lock on is causing you to shoot at the floor or at a wall while you're locked on to something on the other side.
The game has a strong horror theme to it. You're an immortal voodoo demi-god that has to travel to deadside(basically hell.) and you fight zombies and disfigured creatures. That's just the first few hours of the game. You fight nastier stuff like torture-loving psychos, asylum retainers that sound like wild boars (Don't ask.), and even serial killers later on. A “few” things will try to jump out at you but it's rare actually. The highlights of the horror come from the atmosphere and background music. Stages like the Asylum's Playrooms and the Asylum's Undercity are really going to make your skin crawl.
Like the original pc version it still has gamepad support. I can't imagine playing this on a keyboard honestly.
In terms of difficulty, most stuff is easy to go through. Dying just sets you back a little bit or to where your closest teddy bear warp point was. The only real hard part is just the final boss battle's skill cap is astronomical compared to everything else you fight in the game. It will surprise you.
Outside of this the only other noteworthy feature added is the option to watch previously seen cutscenes.
The only detail that will probably turn you away from the game is the age. Most first person shooter games outclass this one but during its time it was ahead of other games of its kind.
In the end, this gem is worth your time. It's also good for a scare.

Resident Evil games are tough to write reviews for without drawing comparisons with previous Resident Evil titles, and so if someone were to ask me what Revelations 2 is like, I'd describe it as Resident Evil: Code Veronica wearing the skin of Resident Evil 4, with a dash of Resident Evil Zero thrown into the mix.
So let's clear one thing up to begin with, Revelations 2 is the best Resident Evil title since Resident Evil 4.  It's not got ridiculous areas, bright sunlight and african tribesmen trying to spook you like Resident Evil 5 and it's non-sensical and stupid plot with a total lack of horror.  It's not an over-the-top action-fest with a terrible plot, forgettable characters and balls the wall pacing like Resident Evil 6.  What it does have is some decent horror atmosphere, interesting enemies and monsters that can and will often take you by surprise, some cool mechanics surrounding the two characters you control and it's not too bad to look at either.
Revelations 2 can most likely be considered the swan song of the Resi 4-esque games of the series, with Resident Evil 7 being shown as what appears to be an attempt at putting a foot into the door of the already overcrowded first person indie horror games that infests Steam as so many other PC marketplaces, but as a final battlecry before giving up and copying what everyone else is doing, Revelations 2 takes the best of all the Resi games since 4 and slaps them all together into a rather enjoyable experience.
The other plus is that you get to play as Barry Burton, who hasn't really shown his face in a Resi game since Resident Evil: Gaiden on the Game Boy Colour, and it's nice to see him as one of the stars of a fully-fledged 3D Resident Evil title for once.
And for the finale, Raid mode has returned, and it's super fun.  Running around picking up loot, improving weapons, blowing monjsters away all to a super awesome soundtrack, it could have been a release all on it's own, but to get it coupled with the main game makes the entire thing truly worth the money.
As someone who normally can't stomach Resident Evil games too much, and as someone who normally HATES zombie games because of them stagnating the game market and lacking all originality, I can actually say this game is really good, and I do recommend it to long-time fans of the series, or people who just want a cool and spooky shooter.

The soundtrack starts off wonderfully, with the very first song you hear when playing being fantastic, but it soon ends with the same looping song. It's a nice song, but variety is the spice of life.
The story is not very well shown beyond a few sparse notes. You don't really know why you're doing what you're doing beyon the brief cutscene at the start.
Gameplay is a little "ram your head against the wall". There are some parts where you have to rely on the hint system, which is a weak way of padding the game out. It makes it satisfying to figure out the right answer for yourself, but those moments seem rare.
The ending is very abrupt, having you slot three crystals into a machine and use your special crystal you change time. Then it just ends. The hint/time crystal is underused in its time aspect. There are a grand total of two rooms besides the ending where you can use the time crystal, which is a bit of a shame.
In all, this is a good game, but needs a bit more polish to be truly great. I recommend this as a time killer, as you can blast through in about two hours.

I was gifted this game and I guess I let it sit unplayed for too long! It's a fun strategy game that I found myself pretty invested in after only about an hour. While a lot of people knew what they were getting into because of the original game, I was unfamiliar with it.
The game is a fairly straightforward strategy game along with a base building element. You receive periodic funds and materials from missions to either upgrade gear for your soldiers, research technologies, and keep the world at peace with satellite coverage and UFO interception. The game does a pretty good job of making sure you aren't able (at least not easily) to do everything, so you have to somewhat plan out what you want to do in order to make sure things go smoothly.
The way the campaign progresses in pretty neat. At least, I hadn't seen it before. The game will tell you a specific thing to research, or item to build, or facility to construct, but the game doesn't seem to give you a deadline to do it. If you wanted, you could just kept the game going forever. But at the same time, going for too long without being able to protect the council/countries means that you have to keep progression in mind. It almost seems a little like Persona, of all things.
The core gameplay was pretty great, there is a ton on emphasis on positioning. Cover is basically the determinant of whether your unit will live or die. I lost 3 units pretty fast before I started being more careful. It's always really neat in these types of games to watch as units fall into roles and favorites become clear over the course the of the missions. I ended up with 2 snipers (which are fairly over powered, as everyone has probably heard) 2 supports, a heavy, and an assault. Each one ended up being used in a way that felt organic. I didn't need to meticulously plan, I just tried things to see what worked and what didn't and it all flowed so well.
I wished class changes could be decided. Unsure why it had to be random. I had other issues with manual saves and weird locks up that happened if a certain outcome was forced (say, attacking two of the elites with a grenade, they normally have a reaction cutscene but didn't work with 2 of them). I also wished there were a few more things fixed in place instead of just random missions on procudural maps. The few that were there were pretty nice. Some more enemy variety would have been good too, couple annoying recolors with are just boring.
On normal, the base game got a bit easy but the last mission certainly upped the difficulty. Once you know what works, you simply just repeat it every mission while spending your money at the base. For me that meant keeping snipers back, having a shotgun running around, and a tank absorbing blows while some medics pranced about. So the game loses a little magic at this point, but luckily this is right as the campaign was ending so it didn't overstay its welcome.  I am also hopeful that the expansion content will help some of these issues. I am certainly interested in trying it at some point down the road.

Killing floor 2 follows the same great tradition as the first game.  Essentially, you play up to 10 rounds in an increasingly difficult wave-based arena over a series of maps ranging from simple to intermediate levels of complexity.
If you didn't hate that summary, read on.
What I love about this game is that there are very few griefers.  In fact there are measures to allow a group of people to deal with that and bans get thrown around when people are being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
In terms of game quality, it's first rate.  The game looks great, it plays with a very solid frame rate, and it has very few bugs that I don't see people appreciate often enough.  Play a game for long enough, you'll find bugs, trust me.
Balance.  Can we talk Balance?  Taking a lot of ideas from the first game, many of the same classes made their way back and the balance quality (I think) is very much still here.  It's rare to find a game this well balanced.  At the end of the day, whatever class you choose, you'll have to really bring it at the higher difficulties, and those high difficulties are required if you want to level your characters at a decent rate.  (The higher difficulty levels give xp modifiers).
Enemies are designed with love and care and they crunch and explode satisfyingly.
What don't I like?  After you level 2 or 3 characters, the game does begin to feel a bit repetitive.  You'll need to take little breaks here and there to get it to feel fresh again.  This isn't a knock on this particular game, all games feel repetitive after you grind for a while.
The potential here, of course, is to offer more game modes.  At the moment there's just one:  Survival.  In the first killing floor they had mission based stuff, and I suspect those game modes are coming soon.
As a counter point to my negative critisism, you should know that TRIPWIRE have ALWAYs been very good at supporting their games and offering FREE updates twice or three times a year.  If they continue in that vien, I know I'll be playing this for many years to come.

A must-buy for puzzle junkies and game designers everywhere, Antichamber is a master-class in puzzle design and technical execution. Non-euclidean space remains largely unexplored in modern gaming, even though the ability to produce such geometry (convincingly) has been available for at least a decade. Antichamber dives head-first into this unexplored space, unflinchingly forcing the player to think outside established conventions as the game unfolds, then folds right back up.
As you begin to master the maze, you will be rewarded with power over mysterious cubes, each color having it's own abilities. Antichamber's puzzles involving these blocks end up being as intriguing and as entertaining as it's spacial puzzles, not content with just one challenge, moving around, Antichamber forces you to think resourcefully as well as the maze only has a limited supply of the precious blocks.
Many will highlight the game's visuals as criticism, and it might be true that Antichamber isn't exactly stunning artistically, but the pure ingeniousness of the level design quickly sweeps those concerns under the rug. In fact, the game's combination of sterile-white hallways and colorful, kaleidoscopic segments give Antichamber a unique feel, as if strict laboratory experiments are being carried out in the land of "Dr Seuss", or perhaps more accurately, "Alice in Wonderland".
Antichamber sits confidently next to Portal on the top shelf of ingenious, mind bending puzzle games. It is a testament to the fact that truly great games come from the minds of dedicated and passionate game designers, not marketing teams and analytics engines. Antichamber is a must-buy for apprising game designers.

TLDR review... It's a 5.5 - 6 of 10 score, and cheap especially on sale (5-7$), it's almost 'FTL II' (slightly more casual), but be braced for bugs.
-----
Full review... A solid, generally enjoyable, FTL clone. Since that company is working on "Into the Breach" right now, this is probably as close to an 'FTL II' as you're going to get for the near future.
Now to clarify, when I say 'clone' I mean, this game damn near served in the first Battle of Geonosis. It's that much of a clone. If you liked FTL, your odds of liking this are probably north of 95%. If you didn't like FTL, unless your complaint was having to rush (this game doesn't force you to race a wave), you're probably not going to like this game.
It's biggest flaw, unquestionably, are the bugs. Your captain will run off into space. Ship fights will lock and, because of the rogue-like nature of the game, break the save the instant they do. That don't happen often but they also aren't rare. It sucks but avoid long games, anything over 12 sectors and your odds of a save ruining bug get too high. Otherwise, expect a game breaking one every ten or fifteen games or so.
Space Rogue won't revolutionize your view of gaming, it's not a very deep game for the most part, and it doesn't go too many places FTL didn't go a few years ago for you, BUT...

Chance of Precipitation is a 2D platformer that gets mad at you for being in the shower for too long. As time goes on, the difficulty rises until a transparent shadow emerges from the steam with a pot on it's head, challenging you.
.it creates a fun sense of urgency to quickly find the teleporter to the next level and efficiently deal with every enemy so you can proceed, but not so quickly that you barely have any money for the bus fare. It uses an item system somewhat similar to Binding of Isaac: you find and collect stackable passives and can carry one usable item with a cooldown. They do not however, affect your physical appearance (with the exception of one.)
one of the things I really love about this game is that despite how terrible your RNG may be, your items (with a few exceptions) do not directly affect your actual damage, which increases as you level up, so your deaths will 80% of the time be your fault.
The one thing there is for me to really complain about is the characters. a good chunk of them are very interesting and cool, but you'll be spending a lot of the game kiting enemies as you'll usually die pretty quickly otherwise. As such, it makes the Huntress definitively the best as she is the only one who'll automatically target enemies near her for all of her skills. Melee characters also tend to have a very hard time because of this, despite being probably the most fun to use. While the game is still very enjoyable, it is a bit of a crucial design flaw for a game like this.
in short, Chance of Precipitation is a girlfriend who is absolutely terrible to you but is way too cool to not hang around. You may be a masochist. Congratulations.

Now, let me open this review by saying that I freaking LOVE Half-Life! In case you think I've reviewed the wrong game, do not despair, I haven't, it's just I feel I need to share this declaration in order to set the foundation of this review. Right, let's get to it. After the HUGE success of Half-Life I was genuinely overwhelmed by the announcement that a sequel would be coming out. I’ve played HL2 when it was first released in 2004 and again recently. So, what did a fan (huge fan) of Half-Life think?
Confused.
You begin as Gordon Freeman having just arrived in City 17, from where you don't know and never do. A figure on a screen is broadcasting, a person whose name, once learnt has no meaning to you. The city and indeed the world has been conquered by a force called the Combine. Who they are or why they invaded is never explained (at least in no detail). You meet up with three colleagues from Black Mesa. One is Barney who we know escaped the facility before its destruction. The other two were last seen deep within Black Mesa yet here they are, alive and once again no explanation is given. This theme continues through the game, causing me to constantly scratch my head in thought. Only by reading online did I learn what the hell HL2 was all about, something that I should never have had to do.
Graphically HL2 was a huge improvement on HL, yet by today’s standards dated and lacking features that one would expect in a FPS. Weapons are your usual standard, with one exception. Enemies are varied including some old favourites.
I can't help but feel that HL2 was (and is) an incomplete game story wise. For me HL2 was not HL. Other than Gordon Freeman and the occasional G-man scene it felt nothing like the original, which was (and is) so good. The only level which reminded me of HL was Ravenholme, a rather scary place. I get the feeling that the developers, after the huge success of HL thought they'd make a sequel but had no idea what story to go with, no idea what to do as most scientists etc were killed in the original. There is no continuous flow from HL to HL2. It was not seamless. It was disjointed and full of storyline holes. As I didn't know who anyone was I found myself not caring what happened to them. I played through the game emotionless, uncaring and confused.
7/10

The city of Harran is beautiful, even if it is filled with the dead, and only a few remaining survivors. This game is everything I could hope a survival horror game could be. This review of Batman Arkham Knight will be shorter than my normal reviews, because the game was released more than 2 years ago, so there’s not much I can add to the conversation at this point. I waited so long to play this game because of its well documented technical problems on launch.
But as a fan of Batman – particularly the previous Arkham games, the Telltale adventure, the Bale/Nolan film trilogy, the Gotham TV show, heck I even liked Batfleck in BvS – I never completely forgot about Arkham Knight. I saw it on a 75% off sale recently and decided it was time to take a chance ... and I’m glad I did. I guess the most important thing I can say is that I didn’t suffer any technical problems – no crashes, no framerate drops, no stuttering. (i7 6700K @ 4Ghz, 16GB ram, GTX 1080 8GB vram)
The story is pretty good. Batman has arguably the most interesting collection of villains out of all the comic book characters that I’m familiar with, and many of the old favourites return in this game, along with a couple that were new to me.  There’s also more screen time for Batman’s allies, including Robin, Nightwing, Oracle, Alfred and Jim Gordon. Voice acting is superb all around.
The combat system is just as enjoyable as the previous Arkham games, especially when you get into a good rhythm of hitting, countering and using gadgets. The variety of enemies forces you to use different tactics from one encounter to the next.
My only real complaint is the Batmobile. I’m not a fan of vehicle sections in most games, and its the same in Arkham Knight. Vehicle combat was dull, chase scenes left me feeling like I was doing more damage to Gotham than the actual villains, and you even have to use the Batmobile to solve alot of the puzzles.

Shadow Man is one of the greats of classic gaming.

The game keeps you locked in with the inhabitants of Deadside lurking around every corner. At 30+ hours of gameplay, this is one of the longer games from it's time period. It's full of surprise encounters that will keep you looking over your shoulder at all times, Shadowgun at the ready.
The graphics are actually pretty decent, especially when compared to other 64 games. Be mindful though, this is a game from 1999; so don't be expecting your latest Crysis engine visuals. An added bonus, is that this game is indeed compatible with the Xbox 360 controller!
This game would be a tough cookie NOT to recommend. It is jam packed with hours upon hours of gameplay, has an awesome storyline; and still has the ability to scare the pants off of you 13 years after it's release!

I wasn't sold on this game at first. I kinda hated it and saw it as RE6 trying to wear a cheap The Last of Us guise. After some time though I have quickly come to prefer this game over the original Revelations.
The story mode in both scenarios initially seems like a two player escort mission, but it becomes apparent that the more feeble characters (Moira and Natalia) actually have a skillset that synergize with the gunslinger types (Claire and Barry) and create a cool co op dynamic, more interesting than the likes of previous co op oriented games in the series.
The real draw, as with Resident Evil Revelations, is Raid Mode. This time around it may seem casualized, but again, it becomes apparent that the changes made are for the better. One example is a medal going from the original's "No damage taken" to the sequel's "No herbs used", which ends up being balanced out as enemies now come in more dangerous varieties. Load times within missions have also been done away with, and the sheer amount of levels (built using RE6 maps with Revelations 2 enemies) dwarfs the original game. You won't be spending any time deadlocked trying to level up your character before you can finally have a decent shot at attempting the next level over; instead you'll be picking which you should do and with what character.
Must have if you like Assassin's Creed, zombie apocalypse games, or fun.

In short: Its a great game, I definitely recommend it. It combines fast paced combat, cinematic storytelling, open world exploration and logic based puzzles. What I liked about the game:
+ the story is good, the mystery of the Arkham Knight's identity is well done (also you can guess it about half way through)
+ the game has a cinematic feeling to it
+ graphics is beautiful and detailed
+ the city has a dark, Gothic style combined with retro neon signs, shops, billboards
+ the game-play is similar to the previous installments, apart from the Batmobile, which gives new variety
+ group combat is even more fluid, dynamic and context based (environmental take-downs)
+ there are new enemy types, each requiring different tactics to beat
+ the size of the open world is just right, it is densely packed with side missions and challenges. It does not feel tight, but it avoids having big empty areas that would feel just padding
+ the progression system is good, you get XP for combat and missions, but you also get upgrade points for side missions and challenges, so there are multiple ways for you to get new skills
+ one little touch that I liked, is that the people react to story events and random dialogues change according to what the situation is.
Some of the negatives:
- just as in the previous games of the series some puzzles are illogical and frustrating, but most of them are fun
- I experienced frequent and annoying crashes and freezes
- the ending is a bit too drawn out.

In 2005 an arena combat shadowrun game emerged, it was a tremendous mistake. It singlehandedly destroyed the beautiful and weird property that wizkids had cultivated for tabletop gaming, for an entire digital audience. I salvaged a disc from a bargain bin a few years after it's release, and died a bit inside realizing titles meant nothing. It'd be like going to your favorite restaurant on your birthday, and getting food poisoning.
Flash forward to Harebrained's inspired idea to do this franchise right, and goodness did they.
The controls are so streamlined you could replace candy crush/angry birds for your toilet gaming habits.
The Lore is solid. This game was written by someone who not just played the tabletop, but obsessed over the subject matter so long, that they could re-create the vivid world of megacorporations and magic, and they expanded on it so well, that even their truly inspired players could use their tools to tell their own cyberpunk stories.
This game is an accomplishment, not just a successful game- not just a beautiful deluge into the gritty future of fantasy, but the redemption of an entire franchise.

This is another that I recommend with reservations. That is to say, as part of a bundle or a really huge discount, because it actually does have enough positive elements to it to be worth owning, even while there are major negatives. To begin with the bad, I need to say that the game is linear to a ridiculous extent. Basically, you find hidden objects at a location to gain a needed item, wander around/backtrack to find the next hidden object area that is active or reactivated (yes, you read that right, and you will in fact play most of the same areas multiple times by the end), and need to solve these hidden object games, mini-games, and collect items, as well as performing tasks, all in one precise order, regardless of if you already know you need something that you find before the official time to collect it, etc.
On the bright side, there is a very generous hint system available, that will tell you exactly where you need to go or what you need to do next, which saves you a great deal of random backtracking to find the next location. Also, there are elements to the story that are fun, and the minigames that make intermittent appearances offer a nice change of pace from the hidden object scenes. So, it is not a great example within the genre, but is fun enough if you get your hands on it as a bargain title.

Lego Marvel Super Heroes is an action adventure game developed by TT games and published by Warner Brothers, releasing in 2013 on PS3, Xbox 360, Wii U, PS4 and Xbox One, and of course, PC and Mac.
Game play is similar to that of other Lego titles, you are able to take control of around 150 characters straight out of the Marvel Universe, and each of them have their own abilities. Each of the game’s levels consist of a series of puzzles which use specific characters special abilities, as well as breaking objects to them build other items to help you traverse the environment. In between each level, you enter a free roam type area around the streets of New York. The free roam contains opportunities to complete small side missions which are narrated by none other than Deadpool.  When in the main missions, there are a few side actives to complete too as well, which include Marvel co-creator, Stan Lee; this segment of the game is called “Stan Lee in Peril”.
The graphics in Marvel Super Heroes is very much the same as other Lego games, you will find it very hard to fault the visual department of this game; it looks colourful, animated to perfection, everything in the game is made out of Lego, so it has that childish charm that is just gorgeous. There is a wide range of resolution options, but a lack of any other graphical choices, other than texture quality which still only has two levels, high and low.
There is really no difficulty in the game, there is no penalty for dying, since you just respawn straight away, you will be stumped for ideas on a few of the puzzles and you will just have to experiment with your characters in order to progress. The boss fights are all uniquely challenging and offer various different waves of battle for you to learn.
The game’s level design is perfect; there is an in game “brick counter” which you can fill up by breaking other Lego objects in game for other smaller bricks. I played the game with my partner and we made it our aim to fill this counter on each level, this adds another challenge to the game, and lets you have the satisfaction of breaking tons of Lego and collecting thousands of smaller bricks. On top of this, there are also plenty of small Easter eggs too, which the odd appearance from Deadpool (who doesn’t appear as a main character in the story).
We finished the game in just under nine hours on co-op mode with collecting 100% of the bricks on each stage. What makes the Lego games repayable is that after you complete a level, you have the free play option unlocked – this means you can play as any character on that stage to unlock special areas for more side missions and collectables. Whilst on the subject of collectables, there are so many to find! On top of the regular cast of characters, there are over 100 more to find and discover whilst completing side quests, achievements, and finding items.  Complentionists will have a field day with this game.
Sadly we did run into a few technical problems during our play through. The main one being one of the levels just freezes all of the time; this is a known bug and the only way you can progress is purely by restarting the level and hoping you are lucky – thankfully this bug is right at the start of the stage, so you don’t lose much progress.  Another issue we ran into was fairly annoying, in that characters can sometimes get stuck in the environment, this isn’t too bad if you are able to kill the character with another player, but sometimes this isn’t possible so the only way you can get around the issue is by restarting the level; this can sometimes be painstakingly annoying if you are right at the end of a stage.  We did have a positive experience both using a 360 controller and the Steam controller to play though. I would strongly recommend anyone picking this game up to use either of the two controller options.
I have come to the conclusion that Lego really make fantastic games; and Marvel Super Heroes is no different. You have two of the biggest franchises in the world today and combined them; you have a recipe for success straight away. We had such a blast whilst playing and I would strongly recommend Lego Marvel Super Heroes to any fans of Marvel or Lego out there. The regular price of £14, 99 is spot on as well. If you can get it any cheaper, do not hesitate to pick it up, you won’t be disappointed.

Huge oversight on the design of this game, is that noncombat "skill checks" for interacting with the environment can only be done by your character.
What this means is, say you have three hired mercenaries on your team.  One of them is the "hacker" role.  You go to a computer in a noncombat situation, and want to hack it.  You have no hack skill, but the hacker merc you hired has plenty of hacker skill level to break into the computer.
But the game doesn't let your use your hacker to open the computer - only YOUR character's hack skill is checked.  So, there is NO reason to hire a hacker, since they can't be used to hack in noncombat situations.
Utterly stupid.  If you don't take the hacker role for your character, you literally have NO ability to hack outside of combat situations, since your hacker mercearies can only hack in combat.  Thus, hacker mercs are pretty terrible.
There's things like Strength checks too.  Like, your character is not strong enought to move a fridge, but the troll you hired has enough to move it.  But again, it's not combat, so your troll can't help you.  WTF.
AND THERE'S SO MANY BUGS!  Scripted events fail to trigger, game freezes, can't progress in missions...Sloppy.
NOTE:  The later sequels, Dragonfall and Hong Kong, have fixed the hacking oversight.

LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is the best thing to happen to Marvel games since 2006's Marvel Ultimate Alliance. It's a warm and witty, multi-layered approach to the brand that ties in hundreds of Marvel's most iconic characters, settings, and stories. While you can knock out the campaign story in around eight hours, the world is rich with content, and I've found myself up late every night for the past week playing for "just one more hour." It may not offer the challenge or player-driven context of this year's other open-world games, but those games would be hard-pressed to deliver as much fun and happiness as you'll find in Traveler's Tales latest.

Free to Play gives a much needed and much appreciated look on the competitive gaming scene, and even gaming as a whole, that's incredibly realistic and down to earth. You can truly respect the sacrifice some people have made, wholly immersing themselves in their passions. It's something that's gut-wrenching and emotional to the core, showing you just how hard some people work, how much they care, and again, what they've lost. It helps break what's left of the stigma surrounding "gaming" in the western world, giving any person willing to watch the insight and realization that gaming is a true dream for some people. These are real people doing what they love and striving to be the best in the world.

PSA: I will often use XCOM and X-COM in the same sentence. Just for those unfamiliar....
XCOM = Enemy Unknown & X-Com = UFO Defense / TftD
X-COM: UFO Defense. A strategy title that, to this day, is still hailed as one of the best - if not
best - strategy games of all time. Firaxis certainly had some big shoes to fill when they announced that they would be rolling out a remake of this classic. Does it live up to the hype? Why, yes actually.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown gives an impressive updated look to X-Com. The graphics are fantastic and I enjoy the art style they went with. Many of the enemies of old are still here, Sectoids, Chryssalids, Ethereals, Mutons, the Cyberdisc and even Snakemen (reimagined into the covert unit Thin Men). All the units look great and play as you might expect them too from previous games.
There does come a time to nitpick unfortunately in a review and this is it. With a series as complex and enjoyable as X-Com it must be done.
This has been completely streamlined in XCOM from how it used to be in X-COM. Instead of having a topdown view as we are used to from X-Com we have a side shot of an underground honeycomb styled base. This isn't as big as a blow as many might be thinking as multiple bases no longer exist in XCOM as well as base defense. That's right folks, one base and no longer needing to defend it from the alien invaders.
I chose a broad term to cover a few things here, mainly country funding, manufacturing and research. Funding used to primarily be based on performance in X-COM. Missed a ship/landing site/terror mission/failed?
Well - too bad Sir - the aliens are winning.
In XCOM: EU they have added the addition of satellites into the game to give you a more hands on approach to dealing with countries and their 'panic' level in the situation room. Should a country's bars fill completely into the red they will withdraw funding and side with the alien invaders. Satellites bring that bar back down but require time, funds and the building of satellite arrays in your base. Satellites can be shot down, but even playing on the highest difficulty I have never had it happen.
Manufacturing and selling produced materials, equipment and alien tech was a huge part of X-COM and it has now been removed. Research also feels much more easy, the tech tree less elaborate and not requiring near as much risk in high ranking alien captures to reach end game.
Many people have a large number of gripes with how these particular topics are handled. While I do enjoy the streamlined process of combat, I do miss the solider management, more complex combat and inventory management. Gone are the days of having a set number of 'Time Units' (TUs), now we have a two-action system for soldier combat. Usually comprised of moving a short distance then firing/item use or one action abilities (firing first, item use first, sprinting a longer distance, special skill use in some instances).
Soldiers come in four flavours: Assault, Support, Heavies and Snipers. There is a reason for this....FOUR MAN SQUADS! Yup, that's right, you start with a four man squad and work your way up to six (with Officer Training). No more fifteen+ man squads of rookie cannon fodder.
This can pose a number of problems if a certain class is in the infirmary or K.I.A:
1) Assault: This is your front line trooper. Able to dodge enemy reaction shots, auto fire in close proximity in the enemy turn and has excellent mobility and health. If this trooper goes down capturing aliens does get slightly more difficult.
2) Support: No longer will you have revives, smoke grenades or any decent heals. This is the medic class.
3) Heavies: Suppressing fire and of course, the one use only Rocket Launcher. This makes dealing with the packs that enemies now travel in incredibly easier with AoE damage and cover destruction.
4) Snipers: Well, sniping. An incredibly powerful unit that can use team member's forward spotting to shoot aliens from across the map (with Line of Sight).
The aliens themselves now travel in packs and seem to have smaller numbers. If you should happen to find an alien 'unit' a cinematic will play giving that unit a free chance at movement. Usually this means the unit will move into cover, but at the end of a turn this can give the aliens a free advantage to rush or flank your troops, essentially decimating them. No longer will you spend hours combing a map hunting for that one alien hiding in a corner somewhere at least....right?
Finally we come to the inventory and to be honest it doesn't look good. No longer can soldiers interact with alien/friendly corpses, weapons or items on the battlefield.
Why? Because the inventory system no longer exists.
Ammunition is now unlimited, grenades/rockets are one use (without a specific +1 perk), medkits have a limited amount of charges, many of the accessory items such as flares (No more night fighting!) and grenade types are now gone, alien weapons/equipment/tech can only be acquired from a successful mission and
if the alien has been stunned for capture. This means if a mission is going badly you can't pack up your stunned alien with it's equipment, hop in the skyranger and take off. This goes the same for soldier salvage.
Any fan of the original X-COM understands and dreads that which is mind control. Many a time has the hapless soldier been immediately mind controlled out of the carrier only to fire a rocket/lob a grenade into the skyranger on the next turn to kill his defenceless teammates. Not so in XCOM. Mind control is a much more short range affair and seems to really require much more obvious Line of Sight to the player. Due to these shorter map distances it's incredibly easy now to take out the offending psionic and free your unit on the next turn in most circumstances.
All-in-all XCOM: Enemy Unknown is watered down slightly and streamlined for the modern crowd of gamers. Part of this is most likely due to it being ported onto consoles (or ported from consoles to PC, I don't recall which at the moment), the generally low complexity of most modern AAA titles and the lack of difficulty which helped make the original so memorable.
Is it worth the money? Certainly! Especially now that it has been out for a bit and tends to go on sale every Steam Sale.
Is it as good as the original? No, but it stands proud and the developers have done an amazing job modernizing what is surely one of the greatest games ever made.

Antichamber is a 3D first-person puzzle solving game. With an extremely minimalistic artistic scheme and no story to speak of, the only thing it has is the puzzles and the very aesthetic. The three-dimensional space isn't one; the corridors loop in on themselves in utterly impossible ways, and it is possible to go upstairs to go down, go downstairs to go up, or end up in the exact place you started by going forwards or backwards. The whole thing is very confusing to navigate, furthering the theme of disorientation, but a few puzzles hold it back from greatness.
Story
There is no story, only motivational posters on the walls.
Gameplay
The core of this game is the gameplay, and the core of the gameplay is the puzzles. Your goal is to escape the antichamber, and the exit is visible from where you start... or so you think, anyway. In reality, you pass by this door four times, and each time it has a different poster behind it until you finally are allowed to leave by truly finding the exit.
Early in the game, you discover that the layouts of the rooms are not, in fact, three-dimensional but rather can change around you by completing various tasks, walking in certain directions, or even looking in certain directions. The environment serves to disorient the player, as well as a puzzle element, forcing you to figure out the proper way to navigate the environment. Some puzzles can only be solved by backtracking as the area behind you has changed; others merely SEEM repetitive when you are actually making very subtle progress.
Later, you gain the ability to manipulate cubes with a gun. It starts out with just the ability to pick up blocks, then deposit them elsewhere, but over the course of the game you gain the ability to place them continuously through slits in walls (allowing you to fill up certain sort of "wall gauges"), pull them around with your gun (allowing you to, among other things, ride cubes, as well as allowing you to solve some puzzles where the cubes are behind glass and only by moving them can you solve the puzzle), and eventually the ability to multiply cubes and place (and suck up) large sheets of them, allowing you to easily construct staircases and create platforms.
The puzzles vary from quite simple to fairly difficult, though most of the puzzles take very little time to actually solve, and very few of the puzzles are reflex based - rather, it is mostly purely about figuring out exactly what you are supposed to do, or how you are supposed to get cubes into various places which destroy your cubes or otherwise make your life difficult.
The puzzles are mostly fairly reasonable, but there are a few puzzles which are only solvable in fairly strange ways. The worst, amusingly, is one of the simplest puzzles in the game - the final exit is barred by a barrier surrounded by a force field you cannot grab cubes through. The solution is obvious - you need to suck away some of the cubes with your gun. But there is no apparent way to do so - there is no source of cubes you can use to solve the puzzle with, and there's no apparent way to grab the cubes. The actual solution is to walk down the stairs and shoot through a very narrow slit between the ground and the bottom of the forcefield - it doesn't require anything clever, merely that. It was a very disappointing and annoying puzzle.
Overall, though, the game feels like it has a reasonable difficulty level, and most of the puzzles make sense, though a few require you to remember some semi-obscure mechanics of the cubes, such as the fact that creating a continuous outline of cubes will fill in the middle of them (something which only comes up a very small number of times, then not again for a long time... at which point it is integral for solving a puzzle that more or less obsoletes the mechanic thanks to the gun upgrade).
One interesting aspect to the early game is that there is a timer on the wall which counts down from 90 minutes. It is constantly there and prominently displayed, ticking away, and it really encourages you to rush to try and solve the game. Interestingly, the timer has no purpose whatsoever - the only purpose is to mess with the player, as absolutely nothing happens when it runs out other than a message being displayed on the wall.
Graphics
The game looks very sharp. The graphics are clean and crisp and the environment is suitably strange. My only real complaint is that some of the washes of colors on the wall just don't look quite as clean as the otherwise aseptic environment would suggest they should.
Final Summary
Antichamber is a very reasonable puzzle game which will likely take you a good 6 hours to complete, possibly longer depending on whether you get stuck on some of the puzzles or attempt some of the puzzles that you cannot solve before you're supposed to do so. The constantly shifting environment is wonderfully confusing and the puzzles are mostly reasonable, but the game lacks the character of games like Portal. It is puzzles, puzzles, and nothing but puzzles, and if you're expecting anything else out of it, you will be disappointed. If you want to try your hand at a puzzle game that gives you very little guidance beyond the controls, though, this game might be for you.

Overall, I'd say that this game might've been okay in 1990, but it's 2017 and trying to pull of stuff like that is just cheap and a bit cringy.

Comparissons to FTL are going to happen with this one as honestly, the combat is basically the same. Turn based with pause. Send crew to various stations as they are needed (sometimes to man them, sometimes to repair a system). Target your weapons on the various enemy systems to take out the ones you think will be most advantageous to take out, then wait for them to recharge and do it again. That system worked for FTL and works fine here.
The main difference gameplay wise is that there is no pursuit here, you are pretty much free to explore at will and the map is more open and diverse than the FLT one. Lots of random events that are all reasonably interesting, and 5 main scenarios you can choose from at the beginning of each game. The scenarios will give you overall direction, but you are still free to explore withiout pressure. In fact I recommend levelling up your crew and ship a bit before pursuing the main quest.
Your crew gain XP and level up and you can choose what areas they are going to improve with each level, or leave it on auto. At level 3 you can specialize in a skill so you can end up having people expert in shields, engines, weapons, etc. You also collect resources in the form of tritanium, which you use to improve your ship systems, such as shields, engines and weapons. Improving weapons for example will increase the amount of weapon slots available and the amount of energy they can draw. Improving the ships computer will increase the amount of modules you can have installed. These do various things such as set fires on the enemy ship, or make weapons temporarilly do extra damage to an area of the enemy ship. New weapons, modules and drones can be found as spoils of war or bought from various space stations. There is a fair variety so you can pretty much tailor your ship to your play style.
One interesting thing is that after each playthrough finishes, you get a certain amount of  "Space Points" depending on how well your last run went. These are permanent and add up over consecutive plays. Get enough and you go up a level which will unlock new ships, new starting perks, and new starting scenarios for the game, which you will then have access to on sunsequent  playthroughs. You can only have two perks equipped at once, but some of the later ones are quite powerful and very useful in facing the difficulty of the later scenarions. The scenarios are all multi part and reasonably long for this style of game. There are 5 in all and they scale in difficulty.
All up its a really solid space exploration rogue like that does enough different from FTL to actually feel like its own thing in the end. The character levelling and ship upgrades have a decent depth and the "Space Points" that carry on from game to game unlocking new content the more you play is an interesting concept. I realise FTL had unlockable ships too, but some of the ways of unlocking them were quite random and convoluted. Here, so long as you keep plugging away, you will keep getting new unlocks.
It's worth noting that the graphics are really quite good compared to FTL's basic streamlined graphics. The music is quite nice too. Nothing incredible but some nice laid back ambient music that compliments the space exploration on offer.
Recommended. Especially for fans of FTL.

I bought this game because I wanted to give a positive review, but unfortunatly, I feel that this game is truly is a dissapointment. From the screenshots, description, and video, this game seemed like a unique and challenging take on the platforming genre. Unfortunatly, what hampers this game are the things that should have made it great. This game has no instructions on what each obect represents and how anything interacts. Some things are done well, like how you can't see verticality, so you must learn to think like that and memorize how jumping works, which is both intuitive and unique in a way that greatly benefits the game as an experience. Even now when I understand the game, it still isn't fun. The puzzle mechanic of switching lights from blue to yellow in order to activate a door was cryptic and confusing. Also, the music (besides the menu music) was absolutely horrid, and is the reason I had to quit to the menu even 5-10 minutes or so as I just couldn't bear it. The sound design is also harsh on the ears, as the noises made by the enemy is really unpleasent, which is why I had to turn off everything and go silent. This allowed me to see the visual and mechanical problems with this game, which are abundant. The color choices for certain objects was distracting, since many "things" look similar, and the colors overall left a lot to be desired. The gameplay is bland, and the game itself it absurdly difficult, as enemies have so much health that you might as well avoid them, and they are place in really inconvenient positions. The AI seems to be horribly put together, and the mix of fighting this "things" while also trying to solve puzzles button puzzles never meshed well. This game is stupidly difficult due to the problems I have already stated, but also because of the extremely long levels, that makes memorization of enemies and the puzzles mechanics a must, and turns the game into annoying and tedious trial and error. As well as all this, it seems as if the game only has 9 or so levels, which is certainly not worth the $3 price tag. Honestly, and regrettably, I feel that this is an exercise in what not to do with a great, innovative, and unique idea.

I was introduced to Risk of Rain by a friend. Normally, horde survival games aren't my forte. Being intimidated by this game at first... it was worth the "risk".
This indie class based side-scrolling action rogue-like survival game has plenty of content to keep you entertained for hours on end. Single player will mostly be played for unlocking characters-- As where Multiplayer is where the general amount of time will accumulate. There are twelve classes to choose from. Each with their own strengths and weaknesses. You will quickly learn which classes suit your play style, which are good for soloing, and which class works well co-operatively. Starting from level one, you will gain experience from kills and the amount of money you have left at the end of each round. Each character has four unique skills assigned to them. One main ability and three supporting abilities. When supporting abilities are used, a cooldown will initiate. When the timer reaches zero, you are free to use them again. The game moves smoothly and feels great. Finding items on the battlefield will help your character's weaknesses become irrelevant. Ranging from extra attack speed to constant area of effect attacks... You will be pleased with the progress you've made. These items may stack, increasing the effectiveness. Small enemies, elite enemies, and boss enemies will work together as an army to bring you down. There's a difficulty meter that grows the longer you play. The larger the bar is, the more monsters that will be summoned to end you. This gives you a choice of how you wish to play. Quickly: Weak, with few enemies or-- Slowly: Strong, with many enemies. How will you play?
Play with friends, conquer the masses, feel accomplished, and go home a hero. Worth every penny.

Still a Classic!
Shadow man was one of the many great games I owned on my n64, and one of my many games I just never managed to finish it (damn you mission impossible!), this was mostly due to it being in French (I lived in Swiss) and so I couldn’t understand what to do, but also of its complex levels structures. Nonetheless I still did enjoyed the game and found it had quite a unique atmosphere. 11 Years later I finally decide to have a go on it again, and what a surprise I must say!
The Story
In Shadow man you play as Michael LeRoi who possess voodoo powers and can travel both worlds of the living and dead. Summoned by Mama Nettie, he must travel to Deadside a place where all living things go after death. Here he must stop a great evil being “Legion” along with five serial killers who are trying to gather dark souls to bring pain and suffering to those of the living world. Michael must travel to vast lands and fight his way through them in order to gather these darks souls before evil does.
The Game
Apart from the straightforward story the game is offering, it still offers plenty of insight and character background for each main good or evil characters. The story is unique and quite pleasant if one decides to follow it; the game is dark, gory, and has a gothic (kickass!) soundtrack which helps to further get involve with the game. The voice cast is brilliant, especially Michael, and I must say that for its time the graphics weren’t that bad as some people claim to be. Indeed the graphic was something that didn’t really bother me; I value more gameplay, over graphics.
If offers a large number of different distinctive environments which become available once the player has gathered the necessary number of dark souls and item. This game offers quite similar mechanics seen in other video games such as in “The Legend of Zelda”. Another similar factor to Zelda would be that you are free to explore any level (as long you have the necessary number of souls), so even though it is quite linear, it still offers some freedom. However due to the large levels, the first time navigating through them can be quite a hassle because they tend to become like a maze, and so this is where perhaps having a mini map could have come in handy.
Through each level the player must solve puzzles, defeat enemies, swim, jump, climb, collect cadeaux, items, souls, were only some may be only obtainted if you possess the right ability or item. The player can fast travel using a teddy bear, and save his progress whenever he/she wishes. All the items and weapons you gather are store inside an inventory and Michael can equip two items at the same time, this makes life much easier rather than continuously scrolling to the desired item.
The Good
•	Amazing Soundtrack
•	Great story
•	Great voice acting
•	Long and enjoyable game
•	Good graphics (at those times)
The Bad
•	First time navigating a level can become quite a hassle
•	Can take some time getting used to the camera and controls
•	Some back tracking is needed to further progress through the game
Final Verdict
In overall I really do enjoy the game and recommend it to anyone who enjoys action adventures games like Tomb Raider and The Legend of Zelda. It has a deep story with an enjoyable soundtrack, and for the price I can guarantee you that its more than what it is worth for. Additionally steam are kind enough to give you the entire soundtrack, a avatar, and some PDF’s of the games map, quick reference card, and a neat strategy guide that will definitely come in handy!
8/10

Amazing game from beginning to nearly the end. If I had to pick 3 words to describe this game they would be: Immersive, Terrifying, and Awesome.
The city of Harran is beautiful, even if it is filled with the dead, and only a few remaining survivors. This game is everything I could hope a survival horror game could be. You have an entirely massive open world that is alive. You have the freedom to run, jump, climb, and soar through the air. You have a multitude of ways to deal with the infected, from your bare hands, to guns, to a massive range of weaponry. Drop kick a zombie off the side of a building, plunge your blade into their chest, break them apart limb by limb and then crush their head with your foot, or blow them up with some dynamite; it's all up to you. You have the opportunity to save people, and help them. The night mode in this game is downright amazing, unlike anything else I've encountered in any other game ever. It's intense, it's terrifying, it's immersive, it's creepy, it's.. everything you would expect in a world filled with zombies at night.
This game is worth the $60 bucks I paid, for sure. I have no regrets. I spent 72 glorious hours playing this game. The challenges are fun, they're sometimes very difficult. The side quests are interesting, and are a great compliment to the main story. If you're looking for a game that will truly immerse you in its world and leave you wanting more once it's over, this is the game for you. Come and enjoy the world of Harran for yourself. I don't think you'll be disappointed.

One and a half years later, I decided to pick it up because of The Fractured But Whole, Just So I could start with the original.

The story is basically a play on the hobbit (maybe its lord of the rings I dont know.) The boys have come up with a game where basically there is a relic called the Stick Of Truth. Whoever controls the stick, controls the universe.
There are 2 sides in the game, The humans and The elves. You start off on the humans but eventually you have the choice of the humans or elves, however this dosen't last long. I wont spoil what happens, I promise.

Also, there are action commands, which require you to push a specific button at the right time. There are also fart attacks that you learn at different points in the game. These are Dragonshout, Cup-A-Spell, Sneaky Sleeper, And Nagasaki. These will be used a lot in the game for various uses.
The Humor is definitly intact, with many references to the show, ands very innapropiate content, some of which got taken out in other versions of the game. There is one perticular one that I won't mention.
However I have one minor complaint about the game, and thats it's length. I honestly wish it was longer, since I got through in 2 days.
Overall I think this is a very solid game, and i'm excited to see what theyre going to do with coon and friends, especially with mysterion.

As far as HOGs go, it isn’t that bad.
A read through the reviews before playing this and it came across pretty negative. I trade spare bundle keys a lot and thought well, I may as well get rid of a spare key for a new game so I thought I’d give it a try. I honestly think it’s not that bad.
The story line is somewhat intriguing. Again, for as far as HOGs go. They are usually pretty cheesy storylines and they usually all fall under the same categories. Master thief, ancient treasure hunter, detective and so on. It isn’t an amazingly riveting plot, but it’s not too shabby.
Items blend in well and the art is nice, which is always a good bonus for HOGs. A few items blended in a little too well but it wasn’t a problem. It still didn’t take that long to find, just slowed down the momentum.
The puzzles and game mechanics are good, a few interesting puzzles in there. Nothing remarkably challenging though.
One thing that did kind of bug me with this game was the backtracking. Oh the backtracking… it kind of felt at points like you had to go back and check every scene you’ve already been in to be able to find everything you needed. Which was a tad tedious. The main setting is in a massive house, so backtracking and checking every room after you’ve made some progress wasn’t all that fun and took away from the feel of the game a bit.
But apart from that I would say I still recommend this one. It’s a nice addition to the genre. Although I would have to agree with quite a few people out there saying this isn’t the best HOG on the market. It’s decent, but it’s not the best. If you are a real fan of the genre and buy them more for the object finding (like I do) then the storyline/everything else then I’d say yes.
Hidden object games are pure cheese as it is, I don’t imagine many proper gamers actually enjoy these kind of games and I don’t really blame them. I can’t imagine most major gamers hopping out of COD and into this. So if you’re that kind of gamer and are looking to at least try this genre, I would say to go with a different, higher rated one.
All in all it’s decent.
TL;DR : OH THE BACKTRACKING… the story is alright, the art/item blending is decent, the mechanics and puzzles are good. If you can get past the backtracking then it’s a decent addition to the genre. Get it. Do it. Naaaow.

Let's take a seat and remember what was the library of PC games in this past 5 years. FPS, RPG, MMO, more FPS, more MMO, some RPG, but so few excellent strategy games. Especially a turn based strategy games that many people thought already dead in this modern era of video games. But Firaxis proof the Turn Based Strategy games isn't dead. Turn based strategy is not bad, turn based strategy is not only for old school gamers. Start with their infamous Civilization series and now they re-imagining the franchise that so many people will tell you it was the best strategy game ever. The XCOM series
XCOM Enemy Unknown is Firaxis attempt to live up a lovely strategy game franchise that were almost dead with Microprose's financial failure, studio that made original XCOM, in late 1990's. Firaxis as a studio that founded by some former employee of microprose and specializing for making strategy games has done a really good job to bring this franchise back to market in these days. Reviving old concepts, removing something that they found not suitable, add something new and polish the olds it to made it suitable for today's demand, but not literally dumbing it down. Firaxis made XCOM Enemy Unknown as a one of the best turn based strategy games that been released in these past years
Earth is attacked by extraterrestrial alien forces that come from outer space. They spread terrors on earth. Killed and abduct people and destroyed the cities with unknown motive or goal. The council of nation that been founded prior of the game acknowledge the global alien invasion has begun. Then they decide to activate the XCOM Project. The most elite paramilitary and scientific organization as the first and the last line of earth's defense. And you are the XCOM Commander. You have full authority in the organization for commencing military operation, deciding the the research project, controlling the building of facilities as well as items prodution, and train and recruit the soldiers.
There are two main gameplay session in this game. Headquarter management and field combat operation. The headquarter gameplay are quite similar with the original game. In here you strategically decide what the R&D team do to counter alien invasion and pointing where the military operation will be heading next. Do it wrong, like put a wrong priority in research and development, wrongly manage your resources, or take a wrong decision which abduction mission to do maybe will result panic in one or many founding country. If that panic not attended at the end of the month, the country will leave the XCOM project and you will defeated if 8 or more founding country left.
The field combat in this game is really amazing. Very tactical, engaging, and addictive. It is a turn based strategy with position decide everything in your team success. Get your soldier in a best place and the right time. Consider. Don't let your soldiers get flanked, or even worse, don't let your soldiers out of cover or the game will teach you a very hard lesson. A dead soldier can't be revived in any means so they would become unavailable for entire playthrough. So a careful thinking and decision is the key to success in every mission. You will never want to lose every experienced soldier in your squad.
The customizations are decent. Every soldiers are customizable, even you can't edit their class, sex, and nationality. You still can edit their name and appearance freely. Making them as cool as you want or as stupid as you want. Your call. In loadout section you can edit their weapons, armour, and gadget. This game has wide collection of loadout that come produced by research and development teams of XCOM. Speaking of experience, in every mission your soldiers can gain experience from killing the aliens to rank up. Your soldiers started as a rookies with unknown class potential. When it reached the rank squaddie the game will randomly decide what class that soldier would become. There are Assault, Heavy, Support, and Sniper class. Every class has their own specialized equipment and role in the battlefield to complement each other. After squaddie rank in each time you level up there will be two different ability that you can choose. Only one ability per level up and you can't undo it. So there would be many trial and error to find out what's the best squad composition and ability build. Unfortunately sniper class in this game are really overpowered once they reach the highest level. I have heard some people beat impossible mode despite having 30 dead soldiers in memorial thanks to always bringing two snipers in his team. Started as a really weak class but once they reached max level, a Colonel Rank sniper in a right position can wipe out an entire squad in single turn, or at least, killed so many of them. Glad seems they nerfed Snipers in XCOM Enemy Within.
Beside soldiers, there are also S.H.I.V. a mini tank that can subtitute a soldier in squad slot. They are strong and pretty much "replacable". But unable to take cover and level up. Taking them to the team when so many of your soldiers got injured or simply to try a different composition can add some variety in gameplay.
The map design in this game are well made. Each map has their own flanking point, high ground, ambush point, something that can be used to take cover, and many other. Making every mission give you an engaging experience. Eventhough the country your mission take place has nothing to do with in which map you will do the mission. But this game has wide variety of maps. You won't feel a repitition immediately. It's completely possible for one playthrough for only experiencing once of every map. Or skiped some variety of map.
The developer conciously create the story of this game like how the story of B rate movies are. It was corny, especially if you count the woman scientist who has annoying German Accent (I hate you Doctor Vallen, especially your useless advice), and an ending whose the formula already used in any other movies or games. Well that's just how original XCOM did in their story too. And Firaxis keep it that way to respect the original game. So I can't judge it was a really bad idea at all. Especially their story presentation basically are good. It still can be enjoyable but don't expect a really amazing narative from this game.
Buuut.. the narative maybe won't made you exploding your anger, or laugh and cry. Yyour actual game experience does. This game forged an emotional connection between you and your soldier as you can customize your soldiers like changing their appearance, name, and put some tactic so your soldier will level up accordingly, deciding what kind of ability they got when they level up. And in the battlefield, thanks to a wrong decision you as commander made or maybe just because of a little bad luck, PEW PEW PEW.. The aliens blows your soldier head. Breaking your heart. You are sad, angry, you start rewinding the all the memory you have with him. He was the survivor of the entire mission up untill now, you named him after the someone you know. If he was a real people, he must be really respected among other soldiers because of his experience in kicking alien's♥♥♥♥♥ But now, he's lying on the ground. The other soldier panicked, making her shoot her own team mate, in so many random things that can be done by a panic soldier, she choosed to shoot her own team mate, killing him!! You sad, angry, smashing your mouse, swearing in the front of your monitor, promising he will be avenged and that female soldier who made the situation gotten worse than how it should be will be dismissed if she made this mission alive. All that shocking experience are here and for a good reason.
My verdict is 9 out of 10. It is a really amazing and addictive game, it can make you sit in front of you PC for hours just for one more missions. It was rare to find a good strategy games like how this one did

Antichamber is a 3D first-person puzzle solving game. With an extremely minimalistic artistic scheme and no story to speak of, the only thing it has is the puzzles and the very aesthetic. The three-dimensional space isn't one; the corridors loop in on themselves in utterly impossible ways, and it is possible to go upstairs to go down, go downstairs to go up, or end up in the exact place you started by going forwards or backwards. The whole thing is very confusing to navigate, furthering the theme of disorientation, but a few puzzles hold it back from greatness.
Story
There is no story, only motivational posters on the walls.
Gameplay
The core of this game is the gameplay, and the core of the gameplay is the puzzles. Your goal is to escape the antichamber, and the exit is visible from where you start... or so you think, anyway. In reality, you pass by this door four times, and each time it has a different poster behind it until you finally are allowed to leave by truly finding the exit.
Early in the game, you discover that the layouts of the rooms are not, in fact, three-dimensional but rather can change around you by completing various tasks, walking in certain directions, or even looking in certain directions. The environment serves to disorient the player, as well as a puzzle element, forcing you to figure out the proper way to navigate the environment. Some puzzles can only be solved by backtracking as the area behind you has changed; others merely SEEM repetitive when you are actually making very subtle progress.
Later, you gain the ability to manipulate cubes with a gun. It starts out with just the ability to pick up blocks, then deposit them elsewhere, but over the course of the game you gain the ability to place them continuously through slits in walls (allowing you to fill up certain sort of "wall gauges"), pull them around with your gun (allowing you to, among other things, ride cubes, as well as allowing you to solve some puzzles where the cubes are behind glass and only by moving them can you solve the puzzle), and eventually the ability to multiply cubes and place (and suck up) large sheets of them, allowing you to easily construct staircases and create platforms.
The puzzles vary from quite simple to fairly difficult, though most of the puzzles take very little time to actually solve, and very few of the puzzles are reflex based - rather, it is mostly purely about figuring out exactly what you are supposed to do, or how you are supposed to get cubes into various places which destroy your cubes or otherwise make your life difficult.
The puzzles are mostly fairly reasonable, but there are a few puzzles which are only solvable in fairly strange ways. The worst, amusingly, is one of the simplest puzzles in the game - the final exit is barred by a barrier surrounded by a force field you cannot grab cubes through. The solution is obvious - you need to suck away some of the cubes with your gun. But there is no apparent way to do so - there is no source of cubes you can use to solve the puzzle with, and there's no apparent way to grab the cubes. The actual solution is to walk down the stairs and shoot through a very narrow slit between the ground and the bottom of the forcefield - it doesn't require anything clever, merely that. It was a very disappointing and annoying puzzle.
Overall, though, the game feels like it has a reasonable difficulty level, and most of the puzzles make sense, though a few require you to remember some semi-obscure mechanics of the cubes, such as the fact that creating a continuous outline of cubes will fill in the middle of them (something which only comes up a very small number of times, then not again for a long time... at which point it is integral for solving a puzzle that more or less obsoletes the mechanic thanks to the gun upgrade).
One interesting aspect to the early game is that there is a timer on the wall which counts down from 90 minutes. It is constantly there and prominently displayed, ticking away, and it really encourages you to rush to try and solve the game. Interestingly, the timer has no purpose whatsoever - the only purpose is to mess with the player, as absolutely nothing happens when it runs out other than a message being displayed on the wall.
Graphics
The game looks very sharp. The graphics are clean and crisp and the environment is suitably strange. My only real complaint is that some of the washes of colors on the wall just don't look quite as clean as the otherwise aseptic environment would suggest they should.
Final Summary
Antichamber is a very reasonable puzzle game which will likely take you a good 6 hours to complete, possibly longer depending on whether you get stuck on some of the puzzles or attempt some of the puzzles that you cannot solve before you're supposed to do so. The constantly shifting environment is wonderfully confusing and the puzzles are mostly reasonable, but the game lacks the character of games like Portal. It is puzzles, puzzles, and nothing but puzzles, and if you're expecting anything else out of it, you will be disappointed. If you want to try your hand at a puzzle game that gives you very little guidance beyond the controls, though, this game might be for you.

I'm gonna sum this up based on how it feels to me:
This is FTL casual edition.
It has the basic concept of FTL where you take your ship, jump from point to point through random generated systems, encounter random events and so on. But what it lacks is the time pressure.
In FTL you have the constant threat of the enemy forces looming over you and you are forced to speed rush through and get to the end or be over run. In space rogue you are taking a leisurly stroll through the galaxy at your own pace, you are the captain of your ship and your time is your own.
Sure there's missions you can do and jobs you can take, but you can move back and forth through the systems, even revisting old systems to make sure you didn't miss anything, or to visit a shop for something you couldn't afford before.
The game can have it's challenging moments, and after you've beaten the game you unlock a host of customizable difficulty settings; but no matter what you make the settings, you never have that looming pressure of being forced to advance.
In FTL you can lose simply by not jumping forward fast enough. In Space Rogue if you are losing, it's likely because you jumped ahead too soon and didn't fully explore the early systems.
If you've ever played FTL and thought "I want to take my time and explore everything!", you will probably enjoy this game.
If you haven't ever played FTL... yea go buy that first...
Combat is very similar, though space rogue is a lot less micro management. In FTL you had to micromanage power issues and pay attention to things like teleporting your crew back before the enemy blows up. In space rogue your power is pretty much handled for you, systems are either on or they aren't and even your crew is auto teleported back when the enemy blows up.
You still need to prioritize room targets and direct your crews actions, but again there's less pressure and fewer tedious systems to ponder over.
I love FTL, but there's definately room for Space Rogue in my game rotation for when I'm just not feeling that hardcore.
Side note: I have enountered a few game breaking bugs, but the devs are still active and were very interested in examining the issue (they asked for save files), so the game is still being worked on and patched, which is a plus. They seem to be talking about adding more content as well. There's a decent game here already, and it seems likely to keep improving a little.

I am cautiouly editing this review after many more hours and days of gameplay.
This game is fun for the most part. If you enjoy horror and being under pressure to survive, this game is well done. The monsters are interesting and creepy, the maps are well put together and have a decent appearance, along with many custom maps made by players. The learning curve is *kinda* steep, but doable with some effort.
But I'm giving this recommendation with my list of negatives as well. The player base is kind of wonky; good games tend to require some teamwork, but you'll often play with a bunch of people who want nothing less than to run off on their own after joining your game to fight alone. This always confuses me.
The game has a 'surprise' mechanic I call 'Surprize Buttzeds'. Basically if you don't check your back at all times, you can have ANY type of enemy spawn literally within hitting distance of you, inluding the toughest ones. And then you die. It's THE most frustrating aspect of the game because of the aforementioned aspect of your team spreading out and not covering you.
The game could have more weapons, which they are working on, and NEEDS more characters, which I don't know if they are or not. Gameplay can feel a bit repetetive after a while because of this.
Overall though, it's a good game, and the devs are working to keep it both interesting and fun, which I highly approve of (and am appreciative of).
