Firstly, i didn't expect this to appear on steam, but am so glad it did. One of my favourite games on Dreamcast didn't disappoint with it's mature theme, dark and heavy atmosphere and disturbing soundtrack.
It's few downsides (slightly samey at times, slightly clumsy controls, and it's a bit grindy in places) were far outweighed by the upsides. I never really cared for stories in games but this one had a great one. It's quite original, involving the hunt for 5 serial killers with an interesting take on who Jack the Ripper really was. It's quite a brutal tale at times.
It's a big game, with lots of exploring to be had although it's actually more linear than it seems. Not a bad thing. The game also gets better the farther you get, the opposite to most games these days...
The soundtrack is also worth a mention on it's own. It's incredibly fitting to the mature theme of the game. It's really weird and disturbing. Youtube 'the playrooms' for an example.
This PC version was a port of the Dreamcast version (or was it the other way around?) and is far far superior to the PS1 and N64 versions in everyway. If you've only played the game on the latter 2 machines or never played it at all i really do recommend it. It's a great experience. It's a great price also :)
PS. This steam version, although not mentioned on the storepage, does contain all the extras found elsewhere. Including the soundtrack, avatar, map and a good quality complete guide. Which i'm sure you'll peek at now and then;)

If you're a fan of the whole story-based seek and find with a few puzzles thrown in as I am, you'll want to buy this game because it's an example of the genre. It is not, however, an example I would recommend to anyone who doesn't regularly play those sorts of games, because it's a middling example of what these games can offer at best.
The story elements are pretty good, but the game fails in most other aspects. The seek and finds are tediously repetitive, the graphics are grainy and low resolution (adding to the tedious nature of the seek and finds) and the ending to the game is ultimately unsatisfying. There are also some language/translation issues, which can be problematic in the seek and finds. A few times an inaccurate term was used for an object (worm instead of caterpillar), and other times archaic and inaccurate terminology was used.
The journal entries were nice, and the quick travel map was a good idea, but I wish it were possible to zap to more locations with it.
If you regularly play these sorts of games, go ahead and pick this up, but you'll probably finish the game in an hour or two, so make sure you buy it at a price that makes the short length worthwhile. Everyone else, there are way better games in this genre I would recommend before this one.

It's hard to say that I'd recommend this game when you have Arkham Asylum and Arkham City as the standards set. Those two games created fantastic atmosphere, and presented fantastic storytelling with beautiful visuals and authentic voice-acting. Combat was high-energy and complex if you made use of your gadgets, and stealth felt rewarding and tense if things weren't going entirely your way. Whilst the combat of this game is improved on, and this shows with every new title that has followed, the introduction of the Batmobile into your arsenal happens to be the game's biggest downfall; revolving too much of the game's combat around your vehicle made you feel more like a tank rather than Batman, which is when the game is at it's worst.
The performance issues can definitely affect your experience; study the required specs back to front, and if you're unsure if you can run the game, then I suggest against buying this. I have a 6GB GTX 1060, 8GB of DDR4 RAM, and a Ryzen 1700 and got huge dips in framerates regardless of what I was doing, and the game would constantly freeze for a solid 4 - 10 seconds, before stuttering again, and ended in me getting frustrated and quitting. However, when it isn't freaking out, I got a solid consistent 60 FPS when flying around and driving, and the game does look gorgeous, as all the Arkham games are. The game was taken off the market to iron out these issues, however plenty of them still exist, and that should be taken with a grain of salt
The story - a little hit or miss. It'll keep you engaged, and there'll be plenty of familiar faces and voices, you'll definitely get a kick out of it if you've played the previous games. However this is one of those times where I would recommend either reading up on the story, or actually playing Arkham Asylum and City in order to get the full effect.
So, what's the summary? If you have the rig to run it, then expect issues but a good time overall. It will get tedious, but what's left behind that is a really fantastic Batman game that has fixed a lot of the issues that have hung around since the beginning. Note on Performance: Both on my GTX960M Laptop, I managed to get straight 30-40 on low settings and on 1070, my framerate with everything maxed out is around 80-90. So it's fixed. (Still not perfect, but it works).
If I have to put this on a spectrum from 0 being Big Rigs quality and 10 being absolutely perfect, I would put it at 8. The missions, combat, gadget variation is fantastic. Like previous Arkham games, combat is quite arcade-y in the fact it's not just button mashing, but also perfecting timing, priority, and deciding which takedowns to use. Stealth on the other hand is more strategic. On Hard Difficulty, being detected even for 5 seconds could mean death. Lucklily, you have a wide range of gadgets. Use voice synthesizer to fool thugs into checking the ammo crate you've sabotaged, electrocuting them out of the field is just one way. Or you could knock out one enemy, spray an explosive gel on the wall on the right, wait for 3 more to come then knocking out then by a single button press.
Gotham is varied, from the old city buried beneath the surface where gangs and henchman triumphs law and order, to the modern skyline of Founder's Island laced with drones and watchtowers ready to take you out at any moment, to the dark corners of Ace Chemicals where Scarecrow's deadly toxin are being perfected. As with the missions. On one mission you will investigate a serial killer who hanged their victim and branded them as broken while playing out loud the blight opera music, while others you stop a cult from killing its own people.
Still, it's not perfect. Getting to 100% completion where you'll unlock a secret ending (I won't spoil here) is frustratingly difficult. The Riddler race tracks and finding all 240 trophies, challengers, and destructible is impossible without a guide. Other missions involve you racing through the entire Gotham to find hidden watchtowers, checkpoints, or bombs scattered throughout. It's a frustrating task as sometimes when you have one bomb left, you've searched everywhere and cannot see it.
Otherwise, I would recommend this game outright apart from what I've described above.

Let me just start this review of by saying: This game is a real deal for the strategic lovers. However, is not the '93 XCOM with updated graphics. If that's what you wanted, don't buy this game and sail to other shore.
As I said earlier, this game is quite different from the original X-com: UFO Defence. However, this change in the gameplay mechanics has not worsen or dumbed down the actual enjoyment you can have from this title. They may have simplified the tactical combat, but simplifying doesn't always mean lower the standards to make the game easier or giving less losing strategic depth. What Firaxis has tryed to achieve in this process of "simplification", has been nothing than trying to make the game easier to understand, while maintain and in some aspect improve the strategical depth of the game.
XCOM: EU does the latter.
The strategic base management is probably even more complicated than it was in the original, due to the fact that you just own one base. (Satellite cover & aerial support can be provvided to the other continent in order to have bonus, and try to keep the panic level on controll {more country in the x-com project = mo money!}).
The tactical combat is, as I already mentioned has been symplified from the original game.
But, what are this changes?
Say goodbye to the "time unit", now all of your soldier are limited to 2 actions per turn and shooting instantly conclude the turn for the soldier who press the trigger.
The new combact system involve the player to make more sophisticated decisions on the battlefield, trying to make the units working together as a team and the cooperation is vital in order to make them survive till the next aliens threat.
Instead of having 14 soldiers scouting in every direction, you have a much more restricted group of soldier  (max squad 6, previous research inside one of the facility), which is also an additional challenge itself and it make the combat much more closer and personal.
Losing a man in action could be much more devastating than in the past, not just for the limited ammount on the field, but also because losing a specific specialization could possibly harm the entire unite and the success of the mission. Ammo is no more important, but guns still need to be reloaded. You just doesn't need anymore to equip your soldiers with ammo. The newest feature, and the number one feature that make the game even more tactical, is the completely new cover system. Now, when you move your soldiers across the map, you actually need to think about being flanked or flanking aliens, because shooting enemy in full cover is not  going to be a easy task. I've come across a situation where my assault soldier tried to flank an alien but revealed another groups of enemy in the process left him for an exposed easy shoot while my support has already throw a smoke grenade trying to protect my other assault, so I had put my heavy to suppress the flanking alien giving the enemy less chance of hitting the flanked soldier.
It might have killed the nostalgia factor a bit, but this system is faster and makes every decision more important and much more rewarding at the end.
8.5/10 the game is absolutely brilliant.

This review is completely honest and serious.
After playing this game for over 100 hours I finally questioned why. I've come to find out that this game applies so much to life. Your first attmept of each session is always a tease. You do really well but never will beat a high score, and you'll always mess up on something simple and stupid and question yourself like "Gaaaah how'd I let that happen!?" It's just like beginners luck. However as you play the same difficulty a few more times, for example when I play on Hardes♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mode, I start dying at around 20-30 seconds...A LOT. It's frustrating but I know that I can do better considering my high score is about 119 seconds. And then after playing for about 5 minutes I start averaging around 60 seconds with my fair share of early mess ups. And if I play long enough I will eventually make it extremely close to my high score but never reach it. And when I do finally beat my high score after doing this same thing I just decribed serveral, and I mean several, times, it's wonderful. However, I don't feel fully accomplished and I want to keep doing it and get an even higher score. My goal has gone up. I think to myself if I can just reach my high score and beat it I'll finally be set, I'll finally be happy with my score! And you never are, you always want more.
Just like in life. Everthing that you want to do starts off great. Then you hit bumps in the road, sometimes more and sometimes less, and then you get to where you never would have thought possible. And then you're so happy, but that high of happiness only lasts briefly for after it fades away you want more of whatever it is you're achieving. Rinse, Recylce, and Repeat.
Super Hexagon is a real life simulator. 10/10 would live my life again to the fullest...if it can ever be attained.

-- Controller support... I still can't get to work. It works in the menu outside the game, then I can only get keyboard controls to work within the game... and you can only get to the in-game-menu by keyboard (Esc key) then the menu is mouse-controlled only! WTF.
--== Original review follows ==--
Not ok.
The game is one level, randomised each time you play it.
The randomisation just makes it feel more a game of chance than skill.
Gameplay: You traverse a map trying to collect stars and buttons which spawn. The stars are for increasing a score multiplier (which goes up to 20), the round buttons which spawn - if you don't run into them by the time they get to full size, start moving about and become a hazard, the cross buttons which spawn - they give you points, and sometimes make enemy buttons shrink or disappear.
That's it. There's really nothing much to this game. No feeling of progress. No emergent gameplay that reveals itself after a while. It's pretty slow-paced, too.
If stars / buttons spawn closer to you than the enemy, you're going to get more multipliers, survive longer, and end up getting a higher score. It's more luck than anything.
It's just one very bland thing, and you've seen everything and got bored within 10 minutes.
Also - no joypad support. And the only thing a person might come back for - the global leaderboard - seems to be broken. It was showing me the person at the top of the leaderboard, and then someone else's score - not mine, not a friend. I think I ended up being around 40th best in the world. So bored, though.

Mirror’s Edge is a game in its own league because there aren’t many – if any – like it. The gameplay consists of running, jumping, sliding, kicking, etc. You’re in (almost) constant motion. The learning curve is steep and you’re required to have a lot of patience. You might not even get full enjoyment out of it if you’ve just played through the game once, unless you get the hang of it straight away. Now, at first I thought that the game’s just unfair and unnecessarily difficult... until I stopped making things too complicated for myself.  Unfortunately, that happened about an hour and a half before the end of the main campaign. I expected all the routes to be very linear and complicated but the truth is that there are many ways to get from one place to another. I just had to open my eyes, learn how to notice things and think simply.
•	The game is at its best during chase sequences and, fortunately, there’s a lot of them. You can actually feel the thrill of being chased while you’re running away from enemies.
•	The graphics are gorgeous and the visual style is quite fascinating. I saw some wonderful greens, oranges and blues. A real sight for sore eyes.
•	You can run through timed race tracks that are fun to complete. A good way to hone your skills.
•	Running feels very smooth once you get a hang of the controls.
•	There are some really exciting moments, like running towards a fast approaching train.
•	The soundtrack is really cool and fits the world and atmosphere perfectly.
•	Standing on the edge of tall buildings gives vertigo.
•	Early on in the game the routes might seem confusing or not obvious. Often it’s not clear where you’re supposed to go, the indicators are misleading and so on. What I learned is that the routes that make you think, "There’s no way in hell I’m supposed to go that way", turn out to be the right ones.
•	The game’s very bright, so it may be straining on people with sensitive eyes. The brightness can always be turned down but I found that this makes the game lose some of its visual appeal.
•	Reloading autosaves may place you slightly ahead of where you just were and that might create some confusion.
•	The main campaign is short. I believe it can be completed in under 5-6 hours.
•	Trying to grab onto ledges and jump off things can sometimes be very frustrating to the point of ragequitting.
•	If you’re afraid of heights like I am, then the possibility of falling to your death from tall buildings might create some actual anxiety (or it may be exciting, in which case this point belongs with the pros, not the cons). I must admit that I felt a bit anxious because, whenever you fall, you watch Faith fall until she hits the ground.
In conclusion, I'd say that I recommend Mirror's Edge to people who: a) want to play something completely different because this game truly is like no other, b) are looking for a thrill and c) aren't put off by minor gameplay related annoyances.

This game has a lot of undeserved negative reviews. Here's what I hope is something a little more impartial.
Space Rogue is an obviously FTL-inspired game in the same genre. However, this game is not, nor does it try to be, "FTL, but better". If that's what you're expecting, you WILL be disappointed (and that's likely the source of the negative reviews). Instead, Space Rogue should be recognized as being "Kinda like FTL, but different in almost every aspect".
So, aside from cosmetic changes, what's different? It's quite a long list. First, here are things that were removed:
- You have no Fuel count, no Missile count, and no Drone count. The related systems are always usable.
- There are no Doors, Cameras, or Piloting subsystems. Your ship is always able to jump/evade, you can always see inside both ships, and the doors always permit passage.
- On the default difficulty you have no time limit and can jump around between systems all you want. (Higher/custom difficulties can impose a time limit for a more FTL-ish experience.)
Here are things that were added:
- Monster fights, where instead of an enemy ship, you fight some tentacle monster, crystalline creature, or whatever.
- A new section, the Main Computer, and its associated Battle Cartridges. These give short-term boosts with a cooldown on them such as cloaking, shield boosting, setting fires in the enemy ship, instant repairs, etc. This replaces systems like the Cloaking and Mind Control systems from FTL with something more flexible.
- A new section, Life Support, which is a combination of the Oxygen and Medbay sections from FTL.
- The ship's hull is now an upgradeable ship section. Upgrading it increases the ship's max HP.
- Persistent events that occur at random and have a global effect (both you and enemies) for some number of jumps.
- A new currency/resource, Tritanium. Credits are used to buy weapons, drones, and repairs; Tritanium is used to buy Battle Cartridges and to upgrade/install ship systems. You don't buy systems, you just install them into your ship when you have enough Tritanium.
- A new enemy-only section, the cargo hold. Destroy it during the battle and the ship dumps the cargo in it, which results in bonus rewards after the battle ends.
- One of your starting units is designated as the Captain; if they get killed, this is a game over.
- Units come in different classes (engineer, navigator, or warrior). Engineers repair stuff and can man specific systems to make them more effective. The navigator (who is your captain) can man any system. The warriors fight well but can't man systems.
- Units gain EXP and levels. At a level-up you can choose a bonus to one of their stats (HP, damage, repair speed). Level 3 engineers pick a system that they can man.
- Roaming ships can appear on the map, resulting in an extra event if you arrive at a system with one still in it.
- There are multiple missions.
- An extremely intricate custom difficulty option has been added. You can tweak almost anything in the game to make it harder or easier, and you get more in-game experience for harder games. You can also make the galaxy bigger for a longer game.
Here's stuff that's been changed:
- Ship sections have HP counts that are typically multiples of 50, and weapons do numeric damage as well.
- Your shield's value is also numeric.
- When shields are brought down, some of the leftover damage punches through and damages the targeted ship system.
- Missile weapons have a salvo size. Once you fire all the missiles in the salvo, the salvo has to be reloaded, which usually takes about 4x longer than a normal cooldown.
- You still have a certain number of weapon/drone slots, but these go up as you upgrade the corresponding system.
- All battles start paused, and all your weapons are ready to fire immediately. Your opening salvo can count for a lot.
- As long as your teleporter is online, your crew will automatically be brought back upon destruction of an enemy ship, even if the teleporter is still recharging. This allows for more aggressive teleporter usage.
- New content is unlocked just by playing the game. Whether you win or lose, as long as you make progress, you gain experience. When a game ends for good (you win, or you lose and do NOT load the last save) that experience is cashed in and you unlock new ships, new missions, new perks (basically, permanent bonuses that lead to a specific play style).
Finally, here's stuff that's exactly the same as it is in FTL:
- Missiles ignore shields.
- Shields block energy weapons and flak ("cannon", in Space Rogue) weapons.
- There are different races that do different things, though Space Rogue obviously has its own unique set of races (plus, of course, the common and uninteresting humans).
- You can win by killing all the enemy crew (BUT - and I think this is a bug, not an intended mechanic - if your teleporter is offline when this happens, you lose your boarding party as if the ship had been destroyed!)
- Hull breaches suck oxygen out of a room and get repaired before any other systems in the room.
- Fires can start in a room and must be put out by the crew.
- You can't jump out of a system until your engines charge. The enemy must do the same if they want to try and flee.
- An in-game tutorial does an excellent job of showing you the ropes.
- Shops are your friend, and can repair you too.
So! Ultimately, the real question here isn't how Space Rogue matches up to FTL, but whether or not Space Rogue is fun. And I think that yes, it is, as long as you take it on its own value and don't try to make apples-to-oranges comparisons to other games. It has lots of replay value, and if you're bored of FTL, it's a good way to re-experience the genre. Whether it's better or worse is purely subjective, but the one thing you can say with 100% certainty is that it's different. And that's a good thing.

I am cautiouly editing this review after many more hours and days of gameplay.
This game is fun for the most part. If you enjoy horror and being under pressure to survive, this game is well done. The monsters are interesting and creepy, the maps are well put together and have a decent appearance, along with many custom maps made by players. The learning curve is *kinda* steep, but doable with some effort.
But I'm giving this recommendation with my list of negatives as well. The player base is kind of wonky; good games tend to require some teamwork, but you'll often play with a bunch of people who want nothing less than to run off on their own after joining your game to fight alone. This always confuses me.
The game has a 'surprise' mechanic I call 'Surprize Buttzeds'. Basically if you don't check your back at all times, you can have ANY type of enemy spawn literally within hitting distance of you, inluding the toughest ones. And then you die. It's THE most frustrating aspect of the game because of the aforementioned aspect of your team spreading out and not covering you.
The game could have more weapons, which they are working on, and NEEDS more characters, which I don't know if they are or not. Gameplay can feel a bit repetetive after a while because of this.
Overall though, it's a good game, and the devs are working to keep it both interesting and fun, which I highly approve of (and am appreciative of).

See this is having mixed reviews so figured I'd throw in my oppinion.
This is a "first impression" if you will, I just picked it up in the winter sale and have only played though one run so far (~3 hours in).
First: This is not FTL, it's very much a "FTL-like" though, it copy a lot of things from FTL, like the combat system and so on, but the overall game still play different.
One of the things is does not copy from FTL is the sense of urgency and scavenging your way. It's a lot more laid-back. There is no time pressure and no fuel to worry about, you can backtrack as much as you want and visit every single node on every map at your leisure and fly back to a station to repair as often as you want. Drones and missile weapons also have unlimited ammo, and just do a little less damage and have a bit higher cooldowns to compensate. This does make the game considerably easyer than FTL (my first run was a win, and it wasn't even close except one seemingly unkillable space monster I just ran away from). A nice little "quality of life" change is that your boarding party is automatically beamed back to your ship when the enemy ship explode (as long as your teleporter is not offline), so you can be a bit more reckless with boarding.
[Edit:] Seem I misunderstood, all difficulty settings, including the ability to customize difficulty is available from the start, you only unlock ships, perks and scenarios.
Progression is pretty straight forward. At the end of a run you get "experience" based on quests completed, ships destroyed and various other goals and then your main profile level up, winning my first run got me to level 3 which unlocked a new ship and a higher difficulty setting. This makes progression quite liniar, you just have to keep playing, no convoluted random quests you have to complete during a run to unlock a particular ship, on the flip side it means you can't rush to unlock any particular ship, you just get them at the level they unlock at.
To help with re-playability you also unlock more scenarios as you level up, where FTL always have the same main quest (get to the last sector and kill the boss), there are several different ones to choose from (once they are unlocked). The starter quest involve finding a kidnapped scientist (with some twists), later ones have more epic threats.
Overall I'd say it's a fairly competent FTL-like that should appeal especially to those who find FTL too punishing with it's time pressure. There are higher challenge levels available, but you can always play on easy and indulge your power fantasy blowing away enemy (or neutral) ships left and right as well.

An absolutely gorgeous, yet utterly lifeless hidden object puzzle game with a nice soundtrack, where your goal seems to be running around back and forth instead of actual puzzle solving.
Despite the fixed resolution, Crystals of Time is one of the most beautiful hidden object puzzle games I have ever encountered… and sadly almost one of the most boring ones.
For starters, it has almost no story: you get a few lines of explanation at the beginning, then one ‘Congratulations, you won!’ screen at the end. Even the titular crystal of time is wasted, it serves next to no role in the game.
Speaking of which… the gameplay mostly consists of running back and forth between half a dozen HO scenes to get your next key item, and after using said item you yet again search the entire house to find the one HO scene that opened up. Repeat a few dozen times until you win. No real sense of progression or accomplishment, just monotonous clicking and searching.
Still, if you find it on sale, or really want to play it for the exceptionally well-drawn HO scenes, it may be worth a try.

After more than year of reading reviews and reading about technical difficulties, I finally broke down during one of STEAM's sales and picked up Arkham Knight with the Season Pass. I wasn't sure what to expect, given the tons of complaints, but with most of the bugs having been resolved on the PC port, my latest jaunt through Gotham turned out to be pretty enjoyable.
Gameplay wise, if you've played any of the other Arkham games, you'll know what to expect. The controls are similar, the atmosphere is similar, and you fight pretty much all the same bad guys you've already locked up. In fact, early in my playthrough, I admit I was a little underwhelmed. I actually was getting a kind of "ho-hum, been here before" feeling that made me question if I was going to have the attention span to finish. But as the game progressed, I started to get into the  story. There were some interesting nuggets and story-telling devices which compelled me to stay engaged, and the story, for the most part, got better as it went along. That's good work for a development team producing its 4th of 4 very similar games. The writers did a very good job of making Batman's relationships with his allies and enemies add weight to the overall conflict.
Another game mechanic I applaud the developers for was the rapidity with which you aquire most of Batman's hand-held gadgetry. In the previous Arkham games, even though you spent hours collecting all these amazing toys with which to fight crime, you had to start over at the beginning of the next game, which always felt narratively silly to me. I understood it from a gaming point-of-view (you don't want players to start out overly awesome at the very beginning), but Batman pretty much spent most of Arkham City trying to get back all the stuff he had at the end of Arkham Asylum. I guess rich guys just don't really take care of their stuff? In Arkham Knight, you gain access to all of Batman's gadgets by about half-way through the game, which seemed far more logical from a narrative standpoint. This made more sense with the addition of the Batmobile, because now you could spend time during the later parts of the game adding features to your car, which we didn't have access to in the previous games. It was a good way to to handle improving your character's abilities, I thought.
The one part I dreaded after reading several reviews and talking to a friend who played Arkham Knight was the addition of the batmobile. I don't generally enjoy driving in video games, because I think so much is lost with the lack of g-forces and the feel in my hands of the car I'm trying to drive. In Arkham Knight, the batmobile seemed to have almost zero traction, which got really frustrating in chase challenges. Arkham Knight required a little too much use of the batmobile for my tastes, but it wasn't as bad as I feared. I could have driven more, had I wanted, but you have some options to reduce your reliance on it, if you wish.
My primary critique of the story is more of a game design issue than a narrative one. This is the first Arkham game to actually require you to complete all the Riddler challenges to see the full ending. I won't give any spoilers away, but even after you capture everyone else in the game, you still have to do every Riddler race and find every stinking trophy and solve every riddle and break every object to see the finale. How much time do people have? I found about 100 of them before I got sick of it and downloaded someone's save that had all but one left to find. Had I completed all the challenges on my own, I'm sure it would have constituted at least 50% of my time logged in the game. You might love the challenge of completing the riddles on your own, but be warned.
Must have if you like Assassin's Creed, zombie apocalypse games, or fun.

I got Arkham Knight a few months back as part of a Bundle Stars sale for $5.  At that price, I figured that even if it was still buggy and had performance issues, I'd only be out five bucks, and I had read that it was essentially fixed, the launch issues resolved.  In short, at least on my fairly beefy rig, it still has significant performance issues, enough that I don't think it worth continuing.
I have a 4790k overclocked to 4.7ghz paired with a 1080ti, a combination able to play demanding games like Mass Effect Andromeda and Rise of the Tomb Raider at resolutions well above 1080p with all settings maxxed and stay at or above 60fps.  At 1080p, most games stay at or above 120fps at max settings.  Arkham Knight struggles with 1080p/60fps, even with Nvidia Gameworks stuff turned off and other settings lowered.  It never got out of the 40s in the early game car chase sequence, regardless of settings.  These, alas, were not the only issues I encountered, leading me to abandon my initial attempt to play the game.
Additional technical issues:
Switching resolutions while tweaking settings randomly caused the game to jump to my second monitor, where it would stay until I exited and restarted the game.  This is the only game I've played that does this.
In group combat, sound is out of sync, with audio severely lagging behind animations.  This is a problem unique to this game.
Attempting to play the game in a borderless window, a solution that resolved the monitor jumping issue, resulted in fuzzy text in menus.  Also an issue unique to this game.
Sound, particularly Batman and Oracle's voices, is distorted.  Also an issue I'm not having in other games.
Even using an SSD, loading times are unusually long.
Despite using a controller, I kept getting mouse and keyboard prompts.  In the opening section, for example, I'm waiting for something to happen, and eventually get a prompt to press spacebar.
Menus have design issues.  For example, sometimes X is used to confirm a selection, sometimes A.  At other times, A cycles through configuration choices.
You cannot manually save your game.  Outside of a game based on procedural loot generation (Diablo, Borderlands), this is simply unacceptable.
Cutscenes play weirdly in that they all start at 30fps, then switch to 60fps, then back again.  The diner scene did this several times.  It was really annoying, creating a stuttering effect.
Gameplay:
The one early Batmobile section was pretty bad.  I found the Batmobile difficult to control, and the controls didn't work as described.  For example, X is mapped to both brake and reverse, which seems a strange design to me.  I would get stuck on a building, tap X to shift into reverse, and the car would stay in drive.  I never did figure out how to put the car into reverse, prompting several checkpoint restarts.
In that same Batmobile section, I was constantly fighting the camera.  I would move it up to get a view I found comfortable, and seconds later, the game would move it back down.  At times, the game would actively be resisting repositioning of the camera.
The two close combat sections were made more difficult by the lagging audio.  When the sound of Batman's hits come well after the blow lands, it makes getting a good rhythm going difficult.
I didn't get far enough into the game to get to a predator room, which is unfortunate, as those are my favorite parts of an Arkham game.  Given the problems I had with the close combat and racing segments, though, I don't anticipate that my experience would have been any better.
The amount of destruction and number of pedestrians run over in that long, boring chase sequence, made it abundantly clear to me that, even had the game been running smoothly, I would likely not have enjoyed this.  Batman destroying property and killing pedestrians seemed wrong in BvS, and it feels wrong here.
Positives:
Gotham looks pretty.
Conclusion:
Technical issues prevented me from going very far into the game, and those parts I did play weren't very enjoyable.  I can't fairly evaluate the story, as I only got the opening part of it before frustrating gameplay and technical issues made me conclude this wasn't worth the frustration.  Those that did get a smooth gameplay experience without framerate or audio problems may indeed have had a much better experience, but mine relatively short time with the game was filled with frustration.  It's not as bad as the original PC release of Bioshock 2, which had game breaking bugs that were never fixed, but those that were there in my sessions with Arkham Knight are more than enough to keep me from attempting a full playthrough.
If you can get it to run well, it may well be a wonderful experience.  It certainly wasn't for me.

This game is very hard, but can be very rewarding and enjoyable once you get a handle on things. Once you get used to how Chaos Engine does stage layout - with lots of walls and stairs appearing or vanishing to create new paths - and get a better handle on positioning, distance and pacing, the game becomes a lot more manageable. But expect your first couple of runs to end in misery - it happens to everybody.
They made some changes to the game with this port but for the most part they are minimalistic and geared mainly towards making the game look and play better. The new save system let's you enjoy the game without having to punch in long passwords for one, but it won't help you cheat like an emulator would.
Picking the Navvie (one of the six playable characters) makes things a little easier for beginners. His initial stats and powerful weapon makes him a very sturdy character, and his special is a no-nonsense smart-bomb. The other characters are more technical and require a little more knowledge of how the game works to use properly.

So far the game has been super fun. The loading on it is a bit long, but that isn't too much of a problem. Game play wise, the game is really fun. Haven't tried multiplayer yet, but the story mode is great.

The good: for a game from a small company, this is quite brilliant. Athmopshere is top-notch, story is very well written, UI and game mechanics are mostly very good, and while some character builds definitely make things much easier, it is possible to play the game through in many different ways.
The ambiguous: the game has excellent, relentless pacing, it proceeds like a well-oiled machine. I did appreciate a lot that the playing time was not at any point artificially expanded by making the player travel back and forth in trivial missions of killing and/or collecting umpteen this-or-that. On the other hand, this could also be interpreted as lack of content by some, but the main storyline is so strong and offers so many hours of high-quality content that at least I felt I got my money's worth and then some. Also, given the small budget there is no voice acting; I did not miss it in the slightest, but some may have a different opinion.
The bad: there's not much, really. Some aspects of the Shadowrun world are not in the game, but I never missed them, the game is really impressive and highly enjoyable as it is. And it would be nice to have an option to switch the fighting mode on and off, or at the very least be able to switch the active character when not in the fighting mode. Minor things that I almost feel ashamed to bring up, all things considered.

Solid proof of concept. I draw comparisons to this in my mind to the first Assassin's Creed. These are both games where the developers wanted to try something new and their respective publishers gave their teams a limited budget and resources in order to complete their visions. Mirror's Edge 2 once it comes out could be so much more than it's predecessor. With a proper story line, characters, some more inventive and less linear level design, and more length it could be the beginning of another series for EA.
The games art design is it's major strong point. The use of whites mixed with strong primary colors and the lighting system developed by DICE created beautiful landscapes and indoor environments that makes me wonder why more real world architects haven't implemented this design choice.
The story line in this game is non existent and inconsequential. Without spoiling anything all that needs to be said is nothing is accomplished and the main characters are worse off at the end of the game than they were at the beginning. There is no depth given to the main characters, no back story explained, and motivations of all the characters are extremely shallow. The main conflict between the cities government and the rebel groups is not touched on at all, and the main plot of Faith's has nothing to do with this far more interesting backdrop.
Game play is what makes this game worth it. I do not believe that there is a game out there that does first person platforming as well as this does. The game play alone is enough to warrant a purchase of this game and create the consumer desire for a sequel to see it more fleshed out. However there are times in which the controls can be less than stellar, such as preforming a disarm on an enemy and preforming rolls after falls can sometimes fail even though the input is preformed perfectly and it is not clear what else the player could be doing incorrectly.
One other small issue with this game is it's length. I believe this is due to what I stated earlier. That this game felt like little more than a proof of concept for DICE to present to EA and DICE was not sure what to do with the story or level design in order to flesh this out to a reasonable amount of time. It is very short, I completed it in about 5 hours on my first play through, and this game does require a fair bit of trial and error. Meaning you will die and have to replay areas over and over again until you figure out the way to get through that works for your style of game play (pacifist or gun running)
So for 20 dollars I cannot recommend this now 5 year old game with a 5 hour length. For a sale price (and this game does go on sale often) it is very much worth a play through and let us hope that Mirror's Edge 2 does what Assassins Creed 2 did, and improve upon the formula. However with EA in charge I do not have much hope for it.

I love cooking games. Ever since "I am the Chef" / "Ore no Ryouri" on the Playstation, a fantastic, but little known Japanese arcade cooking game that never got a North American release. I have played them all. *Very* few games impress in this genre. "Cook Serve Delicious" came closest to that winning formula, which was about multitasking and arcade-quickness. This game falls more under the "Order Up" category, a game for the Wii that I found to be very fun. If you are a fan of management or tycoon games, or cooking games, you will get sucked into this and find it hard to pull yourself away. It has both frantic multitasking *and* really in-depth management.
Run around like a chicken with your head cut off serving both humans and aliens throughout the work day, then do some dishes and settle down at the computer to re-stock your ingredients and see if you have any budget left to upgrade your kitchen with more machines, more fridges, more counter space, get things organized for the morning, etc.
Getting prepared for the day in the morning is important. I put tomatoes next to the grinders, make sure I have some pre-ground sausages ready to go... This game even has farming, and cloning animals! I imagine it will take me quite a while to get to that level. Just saving up for some basic kitchen improvements is tough to budget for.
The only technical problem I found was a short pause when putting ingredients into the 'meal maker' machine, the game must be doing some hard thinking then, parsing the huge recipe menu. I do hope this game gets optimized more though.
Don't leave your meats out, they will spoil quickly and you'll end up with filth from the grinders.

This review is completely honest and serious.
After playing this game for over 100 hours I finally questioned why. I've come to find out that this game applies so much to life. Your first attmept of each session is always a tease. You do really well but never will beat a high score, and you'll always mess up on something simple and stupid and question yourself like "Gaaaah how'd I let that happen!?" It's just like beginners luck. However as you play the same difficulty a few more times, for example when I play on Hardes♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mode, I start dying at around 20-30 seconds...A LOT. It's frustrating but I know that I can do better considering my high score is about 119 seconds. And then after playing for about 5 minutes I start averaging around 60 seconds with my fair share of early mess ups. And if I play long enough I will eventually make it extremely close to my high score but never reach it. And when I do finally beat my high score after doing this same thing I just decribed serveral, and I mean several, times, it's wonderful. However, I don't feel fully accomplished and I want to keep doing it and get an even higher score. My goal has gone up. I think to myself if I can just reach my high score and beat it I'll finally be set, I'll finally be happy with my score! And you never are, you always want more.
Just like in life. Everthing that you want to do starts off great. Then you hit bumps in the road, sometimes more and sometimes less, and then you get to where you never would have thought possible. And then you're so happy, but that high of happiness only lasts briefly for after it fades away you want more of whatever it is you're achieving. Rinse, Recylce, and Repeat.

For one, this game has almost all the great elements of a roguelike. All the levels are semi-generated (same rooms, but in different order), there's lots of items, and decision making heavily impacts your gameplay. Are you going to keep your pistol or turn it into a nailgun? how about a cannon? every item you get can be used for multiple things, and making these decisions.
The magnet for example, with this you can either build an armor piercing railgun or a bullet reflecting magshield. Different approaches and strategies call for different items, and finding that sweet spot between choices is very enjoyable.
Like most roguelikes, some elements are random each time you play. This is different in Teleglitch. The starting level is almost always the same, due to the fact that the same items and amount of enemies are always found. This changes in later levels though, where more choices and customization are given. 2 level choices are given after the 1st area, each holding differently placed items and enemies. After this, level choice can impact major aspects. The playthroughs might start out similar, but no 2 games will ever end the same.
Teleglitch is a fun, time-consuming, tough as nails roguelike that's worth at least some time. I don't recommend it to anyone who can't take a hard challenge. Only 0.7% of players actually beat the game, and the 2 or 3 difficulty curves can really push away some players. Imagine Dark Souls with it's training wheels taken off

I downloaded this expecting it to be a completely broken game where there was nothing to do except explore a potentially creepy setting and play with the non-threatening glitches (I especially looked forward to getting stuck in a ceiling, falling into a lake, and going to the edge of the map from other people's reviews), both of which I like to do.  But, there's an actual game in there!  :o  And it works.  It is very short and I would have loved it to be much longer and more in depth, but it really is completable and had a lot more to do and was more in depth than I was expecting (see above).  It feels like there was going to be more to it but resources ran out and they had to make it as complete as they could with what they had.  It was also a lot easier to figure out what I was supposed to be doing to progress the storyline than I had thought after reading the reviews.  It seemed straightforward enough to me from reading the short intro and the things the characters said, but it seems logical that many people might not have been able to read the menu to change the language to one they could read.  Or had the benefit of the review that gave tips for what to do before first playing, like I had the fortune of reading before I downloaded the game.  It is still fairly glitchy and some of the glitches are game-breaking, like the one I found where you fall through the ground and just keep falling forever until you quit or load a previous save, but most of the glitches I found I could get back out of again.  There was a recurring glitch I kept encountering on forced-walks where I would get stuck on things that I found can be stopped simply by pressing ESC and then Resume.  I found that tactic to work on a few movement-related glitches.  :D  But not ones where you end up inside objects or terrain...  Those have to be walked/jumped back out of, even if not from the same location of entry.  I was able to go up most of the ladders I found, but only with a lot of effort and ingenuity.  ;)
Overall, I recommend this game to only a few kinds of gamers:  people that like really short games, people that like to explore new places even if they are very small maps, people that like creepy games but not super creepy things (even though I found the trees to be fairly creepy since I'm not used to trees doing that, but I'm pretty sure that's mostly because I haven't had much access to games that use that technique), and people that want to have as many games as they can as this game is free and they can use it to increase their Library without the restriction of money.  I do not recommend this game to you if:  you need your language translations to be perfect or near perfect (I played in English and found that while there were odd phrasings and misspellings and such, it was still understandable aside from a stray couple of words), you like to keep only a select few games in your Library, you don't like short games, you need lots of depth and substance, you don't like sliding and not being able to jump on slanted surfaces, glitches make you angry, you can't stand walking only with no run or sneak options, and pretty much if you have any game intolerances at all.  xD
It has very little replayability unless you want to try every single possible string of actions.
Though there are few people I will actually recommend this to, I have to give it a Recommend because I got quite a bit of enjoyment out of it at 5.1 hours, and plan to get more enjoyment out of it, and it deserves some kind of commendation for that.  ^_^

I am downvoting this game for one specific reason: there is no undo button. When you are looking at a 30x30 grid or bigger, it is easy to accidentally mark boxes in the wrong row or column. So let's say you marked about six or seven boxes in the wrong column, and then you realize your mistake. Which boxes did you just click? You don't want to unclick previously marked boxes because you did the logic for those twenty minutes ago! It's almost impossible to not ragequit when this happens.
Otherwise, this is a great logic game. I like the fact that the solution pattern doesn't make a picture. (However, I understand why purists are upset at a picross game with no "pic".) I wish it were more user friendly.
BTW, if someone were to create a sudoku game with 16x16 and 25x25 grids, I'd be all over that. BUT IT HAS TO HAVE AN UNDO BUTTON.

For the obsessed only. Half the game is spent walking from place to place trying to find the hidden object spot that's reactivated; you'll replay most of them 3-4 times each, and it's always the same. No new items, old items are never removed. The game is obsessively linear; even if you have an AHA! moment and know you'll need something, you can't grab it. :( And when you need several items in a row, it doesn't activate all the rooms at once, only one at a time, so you can be led along like a good doggie and never veer off the path. The time mechanic would have been kind of cool, but it was woefully underused. I don't even need to go into the story, which is appropriately bad for this kind of game; the ending was a joke, though, basically "congratulations!" then dumping you back to the title screen. Graphics are mediocre; it usually wasn't hard to tell what something was, but everything looked cut-pasted with no consistent lighting, plus the usual mindlessly hiding long things on edges.
The worst part was the misspellings and the wrong words, like calling a butternut squash a pumpkin, or a cutting board a "trencher", or a vaccuum tube an "electric lamp", which is actually an important story item. It adds up to some real confusion, and makes you wonder how much of the game was just phoned it with a visit to wikipedia.
The music is actually pretty good, rather haunting. If it wasn't punctuated by long segments of no music at all, it'd be the highlight of the game.
If you're desperate for a puzzle, give it a shot, but there are many better options.

I didnt get to experience the ending because I was locked out of the Knightfall Protocol, because I didnt clear the Riddler sidequest. This was really annoying, I finished all the other sidequest apart from the Riddler's. Normally the game would let you receive the incomplete ending as long as you clear some of the sidequest of the game. However if you clear 14/15 of all missions apart from the Riddler, the game would lock you out and make you finish it 15/15 (Riddler) to get the complete ending. Which was really annoying, I dont want to collect all 200 plus Riddler trophies to get the secret ending. I just want to receive the incomplete ending. So I just ended up just watching the ending thru youtube, which really broke the experience for me.
Now on the gameplay side the game was good. The inclusion of the Batmobile was great. You can really see the production value on the animations and the attention to detail they gave to the map of the game. Combat is still the same as previous games. Story was kinda okay, the reveal of the villain's identity didnt really worked for me. The main villain wasn't good as well compared to previous Arkham games. And they went overboard with the Batmobile gameplay. The Batmobile combat and chase sequence gets really boring after sometime, and there's a lot of that sequence. So be prepared to get tired of those. Overall the game is good, just not as good as the previous Arkham games.
And also I would like to commend them for cleaning up their screw up with the PC launch. If you've played this before the patches, you would know how bad of a PC port it was. Good thing they were able to turn it around (after MONTHS). It now plays good, with some hiccups here and there.

Probably one of the best, if not THE best turn-based tactics games out there. Before I start with the good, I think I should look at the bad.
First thing that comes to my mind for what's bad about this game is its value for money. The Xbox 360 and Playstation 3 have what's essentially a Game of the Year edition (dubbed XCom Enemy Within: Commander Edition) which comes with the base game, the Elite Soldier cosmetics, the Slingshot Pack, and Enemy Within, all for an MSRP of how much you'd pay for the base game on Steam. Because of this, you're better off waiting until March 4 for the Complete Edition (Essentially the Commander Edition for PC)
Another issue i have with this game is that it does not illustrate your soldiers' line of sight. More often than not, I found myself moving a soldier to a piece of cover where I would think has a good shot at an alien, though I end up wasting his or her turn due to a lack of line of sight. This is even more of a nuisance for players who enjoy using Snipers with the early-game Squadsight ability.
And now for the good: While it's a difficult game in its own right, it certainly has enough content for several playthroughs. While you may get intimidated by the fact that you're often outgunned, you'll learn to get used to the combat. However, shooting aliens is only half of the game.
The other half of the game consists of the XCOM Headquarters, where you will need to research new technologies, arm both your soldiers and aircraft, shoot down UFOs, and manage global panic. Oh, and because you'll find yourself dealing with simultaneous abduction events, you'll find yourself having more problems with global panic than the actual combat, but this doesn't necessarily make the game unfair, as the resources to maintain panic are reasonably accessible.
The final verdict: GET THIS GAME

I wanted to like this game; I really did.  I thought it would be kind of like a steampunk version of X-Com, and I think it tries to be, but it doesn't quite succeed.  It has all the elements, plus more detailed story and dialogue (and an interesting version of hacking), but in the end it just feels unfinished.
For one thing, it's very short.  Just when I figured the intro section was about to end and the game would open up into a greater world with choices, I realised instead that I was starting the final mission.  The game runs straight along a pre-planned path with only a few options of whether to follow very minor subquests.
The combat itself is ok, but not very challenging and less engaging than I expected (again, comparing to X-Com).  The dialogue is reasonably good, if relying at times too heavily on film-noir-type descriptions.  The character art is surprisingly amateurish, like concept art that they never got round to finishing.  I don't know whether it was intentional, but many characters' faces are oddly asymmetrical.
There are plenty of references to a wider world that you never get to see.  Apparently some of the NPCs are familiar characters from the Shadowrun PnP game, but given that this was meant as a reboot it would have been helpful to explain some of the setting or give us some background on the NPCs.  (What exactly happened to bring the world to this point?  Why are there all these fantasy races in the future?)  Instead, it's all done with a nod and a wink, assuming anyone who plays the game will be familiar with the background already.  Not great for welcoming any new players to the fold.
The game offers a wide range of classes and weapons, so much so that I thought I would spend many hours replaying it with various characters -- and here's where I think it really fails.  The first time I finished X-Com I jumped right back in at the start, and I must have played through it a dozen times over the years.  With Shadowrun Returns, I started another game with a different class...and quickly got bored clicking through the dialogue trees, which in turn revealed how thin the rest of the game was.  I think this game saps its replay value in two ways: (1) being so story-heavy and (2) having so many missions that require various skills that they had to supply NPC companions to do those things, meaning that you've already played as every class by the time you finish a single run-through.  This undercuts the one thing that would have made up for the lack of content, because there's very little new to do on a replay.
They had the makings of a good game here, but they just didn't go far enough.  It's almost like a demo to convince a producer somewhere to fund the full version of the game.  In the end, I can recommend this only to fans of the original Shadowrun, and only if you can get it on sale.

Shadowrun Returns is a light tactical RPG focusing on story and pretty graphics. The game is fairly short (~10h), but just the right length to not overstay its welcome.
The gameplay elements are fairly simple as far as Tactical RPGs go, and those looking for challenging and meaningful systems should look elsewhere. It is still entertaining though, and perfect for those looking for a more casual experience.
The real meat of the game is the story, the setup and the writing. The plot is of a noir detective style with conspirations and social commentaries mixed in, well written, served by beautifully hand painted 2D graphics.
The only complaint would be that such an interesting universe: a blend between Blade Runner and D&D, deserved a more traditional, long lasting, content rich RPG. As it is the game is highly enjoyable as a little tread, but it's missing momentum, exploration and more involving combat. Well worth on a Steam sale though.

Yo, I'm Whit.
So, this is one game I missed out on during the last winter sale but I finally got a deal again!!! I have to admit, I was a bit nervous paying for a game I knew wasn't going to last very long but once I sat down and played it I was thrilled.
So for starters, this isn't your average run and jump game. This game is all about timing, quick thinking and having a visual of where you want to go. Thankfully the game assists with the visual through it's bright colors in a mostly bland world of roof-tops and you're not just limited to one path to reach your destination which definitely makes the player feel in control.
Now, I played the game on normal (I plan to run the hard difficulty later) and I gotta say the intensity picks up dramatically as you progress. The tutorial at the beginning is by far a neccessity if you want to finish this game without a "RAGE QUIT" as the controls are simple but execution is more complicated. I died alot... usually because of half-second too early jumps or from the shoddy combat/disarm maneuvers.
Combat in this game is probably its weaker side. It's pretty basic and you will probably never use it (until the last two levels where I felt it was neccessary) but it also angered me at times. Disarming a foe, while fun, is a total pain in the butt, ESPECIALLY against SWAT guys with machine guns and shotguns and stuff like that. I would do my slide-kick combo (I personally preferred the wallrun-kick combo just to watch them spin around xD) and run around to disarm them while they bent over in pain and it only worked like twice and I still ended up getting killed.
The story is pretty awesome even if it is short and the level design as I mentioned earlier was totally awesome. With the addition of people shooting at you (with half decent aim might I add) and even special enemies that free run just as well as you do plus they have tazers or something like that. Anyways there were three consecutive levels I enjoyed so much that I had to go pee three times during those three levels. I personally blame the music for that somewhat embarrassing fact.
Which leads to the music and sound. Definitely gets your heart pounding during chase scenes hearing Faith's sharp breaths with every stride her feet made. Every surface had a different sound. The music just made it all the better mixed in with all the police chatter definitely put me right in the center of the action.
Whit's Breakdown:
Story: 4/5 (Short but sweet)
Combat: 2/5 (Not really vital to this games life)
Sound+Music: 5/5 (IT MADE ME PEE 3 TIMES IN 3 LEVELS MAN!!!!)
Difficulty: 4/5 (I'll replay on hard and see if it changes)
Replay Value: 4/5 (There are nifty little easter eggs in the form of drop bags hidden in every level. There's 30 to collect I only found 11.... I kind of wasn't paying attention during the intense chases xD)
In the end, Mirror's Edge gets 4 hidden messages from "The Janitor" out of 5

I was honestly not expecting to like this game as much as I did.  Upgrade your ship, explore the galaxy, improve your crew's skills, and do it all with the knowledge that you are probably gonna die soon.
My worst death was when I was in one of my best games.  After a major ship battle, I was unable to repair my oxygen supply in time.  So everyone on my ship died nearly simultaneously.  Bummer.
If you're ok with hard games, I'd recommend this.  There are some decent mods available as well, including a few which make the game easier.  You could say that it's cheating, but I actually had a lot of fun being a little more powerful.  It's almost like the game is balanced really far against you, and the mods make it barely in your favor (in line with most games, I think).
Update:  After playing through this game many more times over a few years, I've become extremely impressed with it.  There is no game that gets across this feeling of exploring the universe.  Obviously, it lacks a lot of features that other space games have, such as landing on planets, building a trading empire, or dogfighting... but there is absolutely no other game that I can find that does what this game does.  It feels a lot like Star Trek: Voyager... traveling a long distance, with episodes for each jump, and seasons for each sector.  I wish I could find something else that scratched this particular itch as well as FTL.  But FTL is one of a kind.

My friend bought a four-pack for around $7 for some of his friends, and I was gifted it. I highly recommend doing that, since the multiplayer aspect is great, but it does require you hosting and using your public IP address.
Risk of Rain is a rogue-like side-scrolling shooter (originally released in 2013) where you can choose from multiple characters (which act like classes) for different play-styles that will run great on any computer.* It is a perma-death game, but like most rogue-likes there are some things that you are able to save certain things. I have spent 40 hours on this game, and by now I can tell you that I had a great time throughout all of my runs. You also come across chests which cost money to open, and give you an item. These items spruce up the gameplay a LOT, and add a ton of super fun things your character does. There are three difficulties you can choose from before starting a game (in order of easy to hard): Drizzle, Rainstorm, and Monsoon. There are also artifacts you can find in the game that can add gameplay boosts, such as having enemies drop bombs that can harm you whenever they die, and having you be able to choose your item when a chest drops one.
The gameplay consists of killing lots of enemies until you find the teleporter which is in random areas around the map. Once you find the teleporter, the boss will spawn and you have 90 seconds until you can teleport away (teleporting away requires you to kill every enemy on the map). Once you kill everything and activate the teleporter, you are whisked away to another location. This continues for five more levels until on the sixth level, you are on UES Contact Light, which is where the final boss
is located. Once you beat that boss, you beat the game, but don’t worry, there’s a ton of replay value.
One of the best aspects that I’m very grateful Hoopo Games added is the ability for you to host a Multiplayer game and play with your friends. There aren’t any servers hosted by anyone else (as far as I know), so you have to host your own server, which includes you port-forwarding and using your PUBLIC IP address. Luckily, all my friends know each other personally and are fine with sharing IP addresses. We have a ton of fun playing this together.
-Multiplayer support
-Cheap
-High replay value
-Good controller support
-Great gameplay
-Fun things to spruce up the gameplay
-Confusing story (at least for me), but it’s the gameplay that matters for me on this game.
-Having to use public IP address for servers (not a problem for me yet).
-Crashes occasionally (about 5 times in my 40 hours of gameplay, not too bad).
I rate this game 10/10, because there aren’t a lot of devastating cons and it met all my needs for a great game, even in 2016.
Side note: I've almost played this more than I've played Fallout 4...

Excellent top-down shooter with smooth controls, intuitive and rewarding crafting system, intriguing storyline, chilling sound and visceral graphics that produce a truly scary atmosphere reminiscent of the original Silent Hill games.
There is no music here, and with good reason. It really adds to the ambience that you're alone in this scary place, and you need to be able to hear every single creak in order to survive.
The difficulty will really test your skills, but it never gets frustrating. At one moment everything might be going great, you have plenty of ammo, health and supplies, and at the next a small dude with a machine gun mows you down.
The combat is extremely satisfying, be it melee, one on one, or one on dozens. When you're in a tough spot, you hold your breath, and when you beat it, you breathe a sigh of relief. I haven't experienced this level of engagement in gaming since... Hell, it's been a while. And the fact that a small indie title does it is just amazing.
Buy this game!

Honestly this game is considerably bland. I'm not saying that as someone who hates this genre either, I enjoy quite a few of these games, especially a few I picked up cheaply from Big Fish (which are what I will be comparing this game too.)
First we can start of with some of the major issues with the game;
There is next to no indication of areas you can travel to, I spent a good while of my gameplay being stuck all because I couldn't find the correct pixel on the screen to get to the right area.
Going from that, items are very picky about  being placed in the right place. A good example being early in the game where you have to place a fuse in a fusebox below the mansion to light it up. However simply placing the fuse in the box isn't good enough, you have to specifically put it in the place where it would actually go. Logical? Yes. Fun? No.
In true hidden item game fashion many random items are scattered around in completely random places. Although some of them are almost completely unseen without the use of a hint.
Story? There was barely a single drop of story to be found in the entire game. I honestly didn't know what I was doing or why I was doing it for most of the game.
Unlike many of the Big Fish games I have played there was no voice acting and no characters built up. For example when using a wrong object in the wrong puzzle would give you a small "I don't think this will work," or a joke about how silly a combination may be, even if it were logical. This game has none of that, half the time I'm stuck retrying my combo to see if I simply missed the tiny area it wanted me to place an object in.
The areas themselves don't look so bad, but they don't provide much atmosphere besides 'spooky (maybve haunted) mansion wooo'
Overall this game really is below expectations, leaving much to be desired. Though if you can pick it up cheaply and really enjoy the genre you may find some enjoyment in it.
Score- 3/10

Stock assets. Pre-rendered models. Jumpy framerates. Cancelled patches. Unity Personal Edition.
...Are you scared yet?
The above are just a handful of "features" that make Bloodwood Reload a terrible game. And for all of those inevitable "but it's a free game, how can you not recommend it!" comments I'll get, because I always do, would you recommend a mayo and dirt sandwich just because it was free? Moving along...
So the general idea of Bloodwood Reload is that you're a guy named Frank Bates, visiting a small, unnamed village that's supposedly in central Europe. Frank works for the White Wood Company, the largest logging business in the world. When good ol' Frank gets wind that there are some weird red trees in this unknown village, he heads there to investigate the matter. Nothing of real importance happens, and the ending isn't even worth making it to. Besides, you'll have figured out who the "bad guy" is from the beginning.
The game is beyond cryptic, with no indication of where to go or what to do at the beginning. There are lights strewn around the village, and usually that's a good starting point of where to go; not in this title. To be fair, I nearly quit the game after wandering around the small map for about 10 minutes with no clue what I was supposed to do since the whopping two people I could talk to were "busy" and ushering me away. Luckily there's a guide in the Community Hub that'll help out if you really want to play this garbage.
The framerate spasms as bad as Hillary Clinton when she hears a loud sound, the controls are too slippery, the walking animation has the screen bobbing up and down sporadically, the textures are muddy, the models are awful, there's too many spelling and grammar mistakes to count (slightly forgiven due to the developer having another first language, but there are some real doozies in here), one of the characters you need to talk to disappears randomly, there are white lines outlining almost everything, it's all stock material... as you can tell, the list just goes on.
Even though Bloodwood Reload is free, and even though it only takes about 15-20 minutes to complete if you know what you're doing, it's still not worth your time. There are better free games to play, like Cry of Fear... that game is absolutely amazing. Also, what is up with the store page tag of "shooter"? There's not even so much as a weapon in this game at all, much less a gun. Beware.

I took a chance on this game because it was on sale for a dollar.  While its heart is in the right place, this game just doesn't live up to the standards set by other games in the genre...
Navigation is a bit of a problem on some screens; it can be hard to tell which direction the arrows are pointing, and whether there is a new area to explore or not.  Speaking of navigation, I really hope you like backtracking.  The majority of this game involves running back and forth across the map to re-do hidden object puzzles you have already completed.  There is almost no way to tell what room you will have to backtrack to next, so do yourself a favour and just click the hint button.  It's better than wasting your time running around willy-nilly.  At least the game is kind and lets you instantly teleport to a handful of pre-selected screens from the map, mitigating some of the backtracking monotony.
The point and click puzzles were a little challenging, not because you couldn't figure out what needed to happen, but because some puzzles could realistically be solved in more than one way, and the "intended" solution didn't always match up with my adventure-gaming expectations.  (For example, did I really need to backtrack across the mansion to find a pair of tweezers when the small pliers that were already in my inventory would have easily gotten the job done?)  Combine this with the fact that some puzzles require you to be pixel-accurate, and it can be hard to tell whether you are doing the right thing and it's just not taking, or whether you need to use another item altogether.
I also had an occasional problem with disappearing, reappearing puzzles.  First with the crane, and then at one point in the greenhouse, I completely lost the ability to interact with a puzzle, even though I had the right items in my inventory.  Each time I had to leave the area and come back later for the puzzle to reset itself.
The hidden-object sections were not bad, although they mostly followed the "we're going to put a bunch of things that don't belong together on shelves, and have half of them completely blend in with each other" style of puzzles.  For instance, having a paintbrush hidden inside the leg of a chair, or having a machete hidden along the trim of a cabinet.  For the most part, the items were easy enough to find, however a few of the puzzles were especially blurry and undelineated (I'm looking at you, hazy greenhouse).  The listed object names were fairly straightforward, and there were only two instances when I felt they needed a more clear word choice.
Another minor thing that bugged me was the fact that the "dust in sunlight" flavour animation looked remarkably close to the "puzzle here" animation, which was mildly confusing at first.
The ending, as I had been warned by several other reviewers, is a huge let-down.  For all the effort they put into the story, they should have written a more satisfying conclusion.  It just feels like it builds up to nothing.
As far as what the game did right:
- They had a pretty decent musical score that fit the atmosphere well, and the voice acting was on point.
- The story was compelling enough.  I liked the way it unfolded through scraps and clippings.
- The art and backgrounds were quite well-drawn, on par with the most of the larger studios.
- There were a variety of interesting locales on the map, and the use of time travel to enhance a few of the screens was a fairly novel surprise for this genre.
- The mini-games were quick, fun little diversions that enhanced the otherwise repetitious gameplay.
- The hint system is pretty good at giving you directions on where to go next.
If you are thorough and click on everything, use the hint system to minimize backtracking, and have decent hidden-object and adventuring skills, you will finish this game in one sitting with minimal trouble.  However, if you are looking for a challenging game, with intriguing puzzles that seamlessly blend the HOG and P&C genres... this game is not it.
Overall rating: 4/10

I'm kind of neutral on this game, but there's no option for that and I didn't think it deserved a "no" recommendation, so I went with "yes".  This is a relatively linear puzzle-solving / hidden object game.  You explore areas looking for items you need to solve puzzles and progress through the story.  It's basically point and click to perform actions and move through the world.  Overall the game's not bad.  The hint function is great if you're having trouble finding a hidden object or need a pointer on where to go next.  At least some puzzles seem to have a "skip" option, and I almost used one, but luckily solved the puzzle before I got frustrated enough to skip it.  (This was where you have place tiles with pictures of objects next to their elements -- earth, wind, air, fire.  The puzzle's help didn't say which way the tiles need to be placed; IIRC, it's clockwise.)  I didn't see any scoring or major limitation on hint usage, beside having to wait a short time between hints, and I was never stuck for very long so the game never got frustrating, which is definitely good.  It only took me about 4 hours to play through it, so it's not especially long either, another thing I tend to like.
Some of the parts I didn't like as much?  The game seemed to involve a lot of backtracking through the same few locations in order to get everything you need.  And that's not necessarily because you missed them the first time around.  Sometimes progressing in the story causes old areas to have new items you have to go back to and pick up.  This got a little annoying at times.  There wasn't a whole lot to the story; enough to keep it going, but it wasn't exactly compelling to me.  The ending scene upon completion of the game was rather short and didn't exactly feel satisfying after spending ~3 hours to reach it.  There are at least a few typos in the text -- not enough to really affect anything, but enough to notice, and this is something that really shouldn't happen.  Especially here where there are no voice-overs to listen to and you have to read all the notes, proofreading should have caught and corrected these before release.
So overall the game was fine.  It was generally an enjoyable way to kill a few hours since I never got stuck long enough to really be frustrated (hints helped a lot here), but it aso had some issues that detracted a bit from the game.  I'd say if you like this sort of game in general, wait for a sale or bundle deal before getting this.  I think you'll be happier with this if you don't pay full retail value for it, even though that is only $5.
