Shadowrun Returns has been out for awhile. I'm late to the party but figured I would leave a quick review for anyone that shows up after I did. In keeping with the spirit of today's digital world I will make this brief.
Shadowrun Returns is a top down, isometric view computer role playing game (CRPG). Story and dialogue are delivered through text (NFPWDLTR). Combat is tactical and turn based, incorporating gunplay, melee, and magic into a system that plays a bit like Xcom, or Wasteland 2.
Combat is handled on a grid with an action point (AP) system. You move your character and any other runners (think mercenaries or other temporary party members) into and out of cover, shooting, swiping, using spells and or abilities to defeat your foes.
There is more to it than this but for the sake of brevity I will leave the rest up to you to figure out. One key point to reiterate is that this is turn based. Each unit on the field, both friend and foe take a turn. They move/shoot/swing/cast/use an ability then on to the next unit. If you are going to enjoy this game you must be comfortable with this type of gameplay. This is NOT real time with pause (RTWP) like Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale.  This is NOT real time top down like Diablo or Sacred.
I like all three types of gameplay but your mileage may vary. If you do not like turn based combat then do not buy the game, you won't enjoy it. If you you aren't the biggest fan of turn based but really enjoy RPG's and are interested in the Shadowrun setting then put the game on the easiest difficulty setting, plow through the encounters, and have fun building your character and playing through the fun, albeit linear story.
This is a short (for an RPG) game. The central storyline involves you, a runner, a dead buddy, a murder mystery intertwined with a larger murder mystery intertwined with a larger mystery mystery. That's about as spoilery as I am going to get.
The story is passable but it won't knock your socks off or anything. Progression through the story is quite linear, this can be good or bad depending on your mood. If you just want to play a short and straightforward RPG adventure then you will have a good time. If you are looking for something with a branching storyline featuring heavy choice and consequence (C&C) this won't do it for you.
Dialogue and story play in tandem with your choice of character quite well however and the game throws ample skill and stat checks at you in dialogue throughout the game. This will provide you with possibilities for higher paying rewards, avoidance of combat (in some situations), chances to receive additional intel, and alternative solutions to some quests.
The best part of the game in my opinion. I am biased on this as I really enjoy the Shadowrun universe. The blend of high tech and fantasy with cybernetics, hacking the matrix, and wielding magic, all co-existing in the same world is a strong draw for me.
The skill based character system is very well done and you can make some really unique builds if you so desire.
Once you get a feel for how the stats and abilities work my number one suggestion is to create a fully custom character. The templates provided throw points into stats where you won't need them. Create an idea for your character and try and specialize in two key areas while maintaining a sense of durability that shares a direct relationship with the difficulty you choose you tackle.
The only negative in this regard, and it is significant, is the way the hired Shadowrunners have been built. It's almost like the developers either don't understand their own mechanics (unlikely) or just wanted to build a bunch of gimps for you adventure with. If I were to alter this module in any way the first thing I would do is rebuild the stat and ability allocations for all the hired mercs.
Introductory I think is the best descriptor here. The Dead Man's Switch (the primary story module for Shadowrun Returns) serves as an introduction. An introduction to the gameplay systems, the dialogue system, the storytelling style, and the editor for the game. It feels like an introduction for both the players and the developers and while it leaves plenty of room for improvement I still had a great time.
I played from start to finish over the course of one long weekend. Steam says I clocked 15.9 hours.
I played a Human Decker/SMG/Toughguy. My ending stats were something like: (Body -7-, Quickness -7-, Ranged -7-, SMG -3-, Dodge-6-, Intelligence -7-, Decking -7-, Charisma -2-) My main character was always the most deadly in a fight and I could hack the matrix like an awesome nerd.
I can definitely see myself playing this again just to run through the story with another build. I already have several character ideas.
CRPG enthusiasts that enjoy isometric games with turn based combat and can look past the linear story. Think of it as the introductory module for a larger role playing experience in the Shadowrun universe as imagined by Harebrained Schemes.
Gamers not interested in having all of the story and dialogue in a game deliverd via text. Gamers looking for heavy C&C in the storyline and or branching storylines based on player agency. Gamers who do not enjoy RPG's.

Teleglitch is a retro pixelated roguelike survival top-down shooter with zombies. In other words, it’s a perfect storm of indie game clichés. But it proves that it’s lack of imagination, or flawed execution, that makes a bad game out of those clichés.
I can’t explain exactly why, but Teleglitch perfectly captures the feeling I remember of playing DooM for the first time as a kid in the mid-90s. That is to say, it’s absolutely nothing like the DooM I actually played, and everything like the DooM I remember. To me, that’s the absolute best kind of retro.
The exact mix of those indie game clichés is part of what allows Teleglitch to deliver that DooM-like experience. Randomly/procedurally-generated rooms keep everything fresh, so you’re always encountering rooms for the first time, with no idea what lurks in the corners. The scarcity of ammo and health means you have to worry about every shot. And the way the enemies accelerate as they get closer to you makes the back-pedaling panic that much more intense. And the walls actually extend upwards toward the camera, creating a really interesting variation on the top-down perspective.
But the wealth of terrible games using a similar mix of elements suggests there’s more to Teleglitch’s evoking of the first-time DooM experience. I can’t put my finger on exactly what it is, but I like it.

Two things I would like to point out before I get into the "meat and potatoes." The first is, I hate writing reviews this early into playing a game (13 hours.) Second, I really want to give a positive review and hope with some further developer involvement this game will get there.
So I can not, in this game's current form, give this game a positive review. The forums are riddled with bugs, some of which I have experienced first hand. The bugs ruin what could have been a quality FTL:Faster than Light clone.
So let's talk about the bugs and if you care to keep reading, we can talk about the game and it's mechanics. The bugs start with some freezes related to graphics cards. This game has crashed with both AMD and NVidia game cards on my personal computer and my laptop, respectively. I will admit my cards are both a bit outdated, but the drivers are still fully supported and can run all but the highest end games on high settings with my drivers up to date. The freezes force a restart, which runs into our second problem, saves being corrupted and failing to load.
Now we start over. New map, randomly generated, nice rogue-like and FLT experince. Mildly annoyed, I try again. This time, one of my crew members walks right off the map instead of to his assigned position. Interesting bug since he doesn't have a space suit. I see him on my crew roster, but not on my screen. After several restarts hoping he will appear, he does. I continue. This time the drivers crash causes my computer to see the windows 10 blue screen of death. A restart of my entire system over a $20 game. I give it a last attempt, only to see my save locks the game up in a loading screen.
There are a few quick  fixes to this that I could recommend, but some of them would ruin the rogue-like aspects of the game. The first would be a user manual save that I can go back to, which is not in the spirit of the game, but would allow us to avoid losing the game to a bug. The second and more obvious fix would be the developer fix all of these bugs so we can lose to the rogue-like ships and random events. Like I said, I want to see this game succeed and losing to the game is part of it. Losing to bugs just sucks.
So game mechanics time. I really like the game aspects. Solid ideas all around. FTL comparisions and differences. You are not being chased across the galaxy by a fleet. You can go back to areas, explore everything and yet still be challenged. Once a game is finished, you gain account experience and level up. New ships become available and new story lines become available. Also once you have died and lost or lived and won your first time out, you can now change the difficulty. Before running into all the bugs, I was able to lose one and win one game getting me to level 5. This opened up 2 new ships and 2 new story lines. The difficulty settings allowed me to change the galaxy size and base difficulties. The harder the base difficulty, the better the weapons that start to become available. Hence the shop will sell much higher weapons (and more expensive) in a level 9 area compared to level 1 area.
Your crew levels up based on experience, they have different classes, navigator (your main crew member and unique,) warriors and engineers. They will naturally migrate into their class with you being able to choose small amout of leveling of health, repair, damage and specialties as they level up. Different races, some are better warriors, some are better engineers.
4 different ships, each with it's own strengths and weaknesses starting out. Each ship is gradually upgraded, but a unique twist... Ships starting with weak shields, will have weak upgrades. So ships with strong weapons, will have slightly stronger upgrades. This is better seen than explained, but I noticed this from the 3 ships that I have ulocked. The first ship has level 1 shields. This protects against 150 damage (approximately 3 hits) then resets after about 8 seconds. An upgrade gives me 50 more shield boost a slight increase in system health and slight increase in the reset timer. Ship 2 has 140 shields, about a 9 second reset timer and the upgrade only gives me 30 more protection and the reset is slightly less. So is ship 2 waeker? Not on your life! It has much higher strengths in hull life, weapons damage (when upgraded) and has to be played differently. These differences add to the game's overall replay value.
There are other subtle differences between this game and FTL, but if you decide to get this game you can find them for yourself. I am just tired of talking about a game that I plan on putting on the shelf for a few months before I give it another shot. Once the bugs are fixed, this game has potential. I would put this game on your wishlist or follow it in the mean time. Until then, it remains a buggy FLT clone that I simply can't recommend.

While I was originally drawn by the boast of how difficult Teleglitch was as a rougelike I found myself actually a little disappointed at first as I breezed through the first two levels, slashing and shooting my way through hordes of mutants and zombies who seemed to be rather ineffectual at best.
I wrote the difficult off as exaggeration, much like I did with titles such as Dark Souls, where the difficulty of the game comes down to memorizing patterns until encounters become trivial at best. It was then I was met with level three, which was a life support facility. Aside from a close brush with a sudden horde of 20 or so zombies, things proceeded smoothly.
I then found a secret which lead me to this big sprawling area with a huge button. Being the curious sort I pressed it, and in seconds was torn to ribbons by three rather extremely large red gentlemen with automatic weaponry.
Thus is Teleglitch so far, and it is a rather masterfully done atmospheric game, proving that survival horror themes work well in a roguelike setting. While the game for the most part doesn't really offer anything spectacular, as the current theme likens to a lot of roguelikes where you encounter a new enemy type and then die to it, it does offer promise in it's crafting and item management system.
The only two negatives I have about the game, is that in one, I feel it is not random enough, as indeed there is limited differences in each playthrough I have had so far and the other, being more of a problem with the genre itself, is that sometimes the game just refuses to give you anything useful and then you die.
So if you like roguelikes, give it a whirl, especially if you catch it on sale. But if you are prone to frustration, I'd probably pass.

To make things short for half the people reading this article - if you're a FTL fan, or you at least liked the game - just straight up to a "BUY" button, Space Rogue definitely worth every cent.
As for the others... Story begins.
It didn't took me much time to get the game after I got news that Space Rogue finally met it's release date. Being a FTL fan myself, who explored it in various setups, got all achievements and killed that big fuggin battlecruiser in all possible and humorous ways, it was hard to pass on.
Key features that FTL-fan or any other rogue-like player will find here:
1) Stories.
Here we have so far four main quests to dive in. Each one is unique and requires certain playstyle in order to complete it. Stories told here are fun, and each time you finish any you hunger for more. Matching it's Difficulty, it provides refreshing and fun experience on each run.
2) Difficulty.
Highly customizable difficulty is what I really liked in this game - you can adjust gameplay to your playstyle, competing for more ending scores and satisfaction. It strongly remind of Space Rangers 2 game pre-start options, and fits the game nice, boosting it's Replayability.
3) Replayability.
What Space Rogues did good - it's replayability value is quite high. If you like your very first run, you can be almost sure you'll run it at least 4 more times even without difficulty, ship or any other changes. Pre-launch customisation, randomised encounters, fights and events combined with various game mechanics and arcade elements is fairly good here, allowing you to use different tactics for achieving victories battles, approaching events and storyline missions in numerous ways. And of course - can't forget open space to explore, no timeframes for approaching main battles and so on.
4) Atmosphere.
The very first minute of the gameplay told me - that's it. It was all the FTL needed - arcade elements, longer and wiser storylines, multiple miniquests and deeper (in a scale, not in design) atmosphere.
Someone can argue about the last point, but Space Rogue made it very smooth with transition of 1950s atmosphere - soundtracks, dialogues, ship designs which looks like cars from prev century - pretty neat, if you can feel it.
5) Gameplay.
You can read all that above. Balanced difficulty and combat, encounters, miniquests, various mechanics and arcade elements, packed and booster with Random God. It's pretty attractive, nuff said.
6) Graphics.
Visual designs is... OK. Can't say they are perfect all around, especially planet and some ship designs, but it's roughly ok, fitting the atmosphere of the game pretty well.
Only need to insert few more coints about 3D art and animations stuff. It's neat and certainly looking fresh, comparing to all other rogue-like indie stuff which comes with pixel art retro-style nowadays. Not that I don't like 2D graphics, just Space Rogue's 3D is o-k.
Totally looking towards more content like new racers, ships, quests, encounters, crew customisation and planet designs in future.
Or even, oh lord, full text quests and planetary combat in TB.
Cheers, people.

Teleglitch is a rogue-like, atmostpheric, survival horror game set in the future and populated only by things that want to murder you. Ammo is scarce, health is only replenishable by healing items and all of your foes madly crave your blood. You'll face mutants and their larger counterpart, gun-wielding guards, zombies, merciless bosses and a whole load of other truly challenging baddies. The shadow effects in Teleglitch: Die More Edition are beautiful and dynamic, providing a real sense of nausea, desperity and oppression via your knowledge you're probably going to die. When playing this game, I'd highly reccomend wearing a headset, the sound quality is great and the noises themselves are so disturbing, heavily atmospheric and psychologically painful, you'll feel tremendous joy in conquering this game's daemons. Like I've already said, this game is really hard, you may feel totally confident in your abilities and gear one minute, and then be forced into a corner whereby you can either run into the screaming crowd of mutants and other repulsing eyesores trapping you in, or headfirst into the 'void' behind you, a black lump of nothingness that anybody, or anything, unfortunate enough to touch it is atomised instantly. Overall, Teleglitch is a difficult, immensely atmostpheric b*stard of a game that'll keep you coming back for more, and making you it's b*tch in the process. The Guns 'n' Tunes DLC available for the game is a steal at 99p and is a nice cherry on top of this gruesome cake. However, the game's asking price itself is a tad steep, but I've seen it 80% off countless times, in said times, I definately recommend that you pick it up.

This game is either really hard or really easy. It depends on your reflexes and, to a certain degree, your luck.
Risk of Rain is a lot of fun if you're willing to sink some time into it and unlock some things. Unlocking things is done by playing through the game and completing tasks - some easy, some time consuming, and some that truly test the limits of your skill. Unfortunately in order to unlock every item, you have to be good with every character. There's more than a few item unlocks that require you to go undamaged for an amount of time, and that's quite a task when there's enemies everywhere.
Now, the items I'm talking about. You've got two types of items - use items and passive items. Naturally you can only have one use item, and the variety of use items will often keep you wondering which would be better at the moment... Early on I prefer a disposable rocket launcher, but later, when I have the cooldown low enough to make it indefinite, I prefer to make my character invincible 100% of the time. Passive items, on the other hand, you can have an indefinite amount of - you can have one of each, or a hundred of each, up to the point of breaking your computer. Much of your damage and survivability in this is determined by the items you've picked up throughout that run. And since death is permanent, you don't get to keep any of the items if you screw up - you start over from the beginning, much like a newborn, naked and screaming in an unforgiving world.
Characters are each relatively unique, and they all have their own playstyle. Items that are overpowered on one character might be completely useless on another, and monsters that you found easy when you could hit and run may be more difficult when you play someone who's less mobile. Every character has their strengths and weaknesses, and they're all different enough to feel like their own entities. Two characters may be good at the same thing, but the way they go about it may render items that were amazing for one useless on the other. An example - Commando and Huntress both play a multi-target hit-and-run style. Commando has higher attack speed and a skill that gives him some precious seconds of invulnerability, but the Huntress is capable of movement while attacking, making her more reliant on movement speed items than the Commando, who would prefer lots of extra attack speed and on-hit effects. And not everyone is ranged either - you have melee characters as well which, personall, I find to be too difficult for my tastes, but are in their own right powerful. One is a DPS monster who's cenetered on Damage over Time, another who's got more mobility than damage. Every character has their strengths and their weaknesses, and they all, to a certain degree, require you to be skilled with their use... some more than others.
The final mechanic, and the one that more often keeps people coming back, is the artifact system. Artifacts, much like items, can be picked up in the field. Unlike items, though, their effects can't be used until you return to the menu - live or die. When choosing your character, any artifact you found in any prior playthrough can be used to change the way the game is played. One that eliminates chests, forcing you to look to the endless horde for your loot, or another that renders you an unstoppable force of destruction with skin made of paper - one hit to kill, one hit to be killed. Artifacts can be combined, as well, and one of them even requires you to do one run, all the way through to the final boss, with every other relic active. The artifact system allows you to change the way the game is played to suit your mood, whenever you feel you need the change. Just be careful what you wish for, not all artifacts are meant to make your life easier.

Shadowverse is an amazing game cursed with a terrible art style. There is no doubt that the developers wanted to tap into the Otaku market, and as a result there is a lot of fan service. This is what initially put me off of the game. Getting past that major hurdle, almost everything about the game is very strong for someone who loves card games.
Unlike other digital card games, there is a lot of depth here. The only way to really get a complex card game on the PC was to find one that started as a physical card game and was converted to digital, or accept a lot of compromises to the core gameplay.
There are seven classes, and each is very distinct in their style;
-Swordcraft has officers and commanders. Officers typically get buffed by commanders. There is a lot of haste creatures and this class has the best curve in the game. As a result the decks out of here will be the most consistent, but also rely on creatures. The decks falls over to taunts.
-Shadowcraft relies on its units dying. Everytime a unit dies it produces a shadow. Cards will have an effect and then a necromancy effect. Using some of the shadows will activate the necromancy effect. Because this class relies so heavily on things dying, exile/banish counter it very hard.
-Bloodcraft has vengeance, which activates when the commander goes under 10 life (out of 20). Like Shadowcraft, when vengeance is active, some cards have bonus effects. Because the leader has to be low, it is a high risk high reward. Blood is very susceptible to quicker decks that can outpace its lifeloss and make better trades.
-Runecraft relies on casting spells. Everytime a spell is cast, things with spellboost get a bonus. Stack enough of these and cards can become free or effects can become stronger. The class relies on having both spells and spellboost in hand, without both any deck will fall on its face.
-Havencraft is the control class. It uses amulets, which are artifacts with a turn timer that either do things immediately, or when they die. Haven aims to win the game by controlling the board and achieving victory through a slow grind. Quicker decks that don't give Haven time to setup often win.
-Forestcraft relies on generating tokens and playing a bunch of them. Play two or more tokens in a turn and cards can get stronger. The downside to this is Forest can produce a bunch of tokens and combo them, but it lacks a consistent finisher relative to the other classes.
-Dragoncraft gets bonuses when they hit 7 mana. There are a lot of ramp cards that aim to get to 7 as soon as possible and play big creatures. Dragon lacks stronger finishers as well, but has a lot of tools that happen to be neutral.
The mechanic that seperates Shadowverse apart from other games is the evolve mechanic. Whoever goes first gets 1 draw and whoever goes second gets two draws. Beyond that, the person who went first can evolve at 5 and the person who goes second can evolve at 4.
Evolution adds +2/+2 to most units and gives them haste against any creature on the board. Sometimes units have effects that trigger upon evolving. Depending on deck style a person is favored for going first or second to get more evolutions.
Aggro wants to close the game out sooner and doesn't really need an extra evolution, so it benefits from going first. Control wants to keep the game going so they need more evolutions and extra card on two. Combo also wants to go second.
As mentioned above, the three classic card game archetypes are present. Aggro is countered by control. Control is countered by combo. Combo is countered by aggro. This isn't a hard rule, but it is good enough to use as a rule of thumb.
The game is very generous towards new players. Card games are money pits, anyone who has played one can attest to. There are 30ish packs a player gets right after finishing the tutorial. Play against the hardest two difficulties of bots for the 7 classes and get 2 packs each, coming out to 28 packs. Play 20 private matches against unique people and get another 2 packs.
There are more then enough free packs to craft a tier 1 deck without too much trouble. A player that wants to dump some moeny can also get a cheap precon that brings the player up to speed.
The game has a certain element of random chance, it is a card game after all, but the random abilities are kept to a minimum. If something targets randomly, it is because the effect is very undercosted and generates value as opposed to being the norm for the card design.
For a card game the production values are good. There is a campaign for each class that is a really good tutorial. There are also some unique rewards like card backs and class cards that make it worth playing all of them.
Sound design is good and does what it needs to. Not much else to really say, it is minimalist.
Graphically the game can get very busy. The UI is also a mess. The developers should try to make it clearer so a newer player can follow all the effects easier.
One thing to note, there is an option to disable enemy emotes. Check this because its an amazing setting I wish all card games have to avoid BM.
The PC port of the game is awful. It technically works and does what it needs to do, but its clear this is a mobile game first and foremost. There should be more settings to make playing on a PC the preferred option.
With that said, it does support cross platform play. Tie accounts together and it is easy to jump between, say a computer and a tablet. Really nice touch to have the game on all the platforms.
The game is well worth looking into and something I can't recommend enough as someone with a stupid amount of time into other card games.

As an example of a game I had today, I played Swordcraft and just because I can I choose to run Tsubaki, a legendary 4,3. The game devs are also very generous in terms of how many free packs they give. And you can also get a lot of bonus gold from beating all of the AI on expert in the practice mode. I have a nice amount of legendaries spending no money.
Now for the issues, and yes this game does them. Moreover it has only one issue in my eyes that bugs me, seriously bugs the hell out of me. Broken cards, ridiculous aggro and low healing. Runecraft is pretty broken with spellboosting right now, and it irritates me whenever I go up against it even if I manage to win. And decks that go face and only go face tend to rub me the wrong way.
Imagine this combo that I ran as an example Dark Dragoon Forte a 6 cost 5,1 legendary that can attack immediately, and then Urd a 4 cost 3,3 that destroys a follower and immdeiately brings it back to life. You play Forte and attack for 5 then you play Urd on it and evolve Forte giving it +2/2 and attack again.... For 12 damage in one turn.... in a game with 20hp max.... while leaving a 7/3 which I forgot to mention can't be attacked in play....
Just going to leave that there.

For the price it's a steal for any gamer and will open up a new exciting experiences. Just like the SNES game did for me many years ago.
Give it a go, you won't be dissapointed.

To be quite honest, as long as you simply look at this as a linear hidden object game, you won't be disappointed.   It's extremely forgiving- to the point where there's no time limit, no penalty for errors or hint abuse, and no bad end.
You play as the daughter of a very successful cat burglar, who has vanished on his latest caper- a house on the coastline of the northeastern United States, where a scientist and his helper have vanished.  Your job is to collect hidden objects and find key items in those puzzles to open the path in front of you, leading towards your father and discovering just what happened and whatever went wrong to get the mansion in this state.
There's a fair amount of puzzle-solving, but the game will tell you outright if you're missing any pieces to the puzzle you're working on- so if you still need other pieces, you'll be able to find out right away instead of wrestling with it for three hours and realizing then that you were missing a piece.   There is plenty of backtracking, and none of the items ever change places.
If you can grab it for five bucks, it's a good game for the younger crowd, but those looking for a deeper offering may want to give this one a pass.

I've reluctantly bought the game because of the Mixed reviews, but I love the FTL idea. After about 7-ish hours of gameplay, I am absolutely amazed at the bad reviews Space Rogue has. The game at least at this date, after realease, plays EXACTLY life FTL. You can have good runs, you can have bad runs where things just don't go your way. But it absolutely doesn't seem to have a ridiculous difficulty as people tend to describe it.
Pros:
-Plays just like FTL imo. That's a good thing.
-Better graphics than FTL
-Interesting weapons, not better but interesting enough.
-Interesting and numerous different events
-Possibility to play a big galaxy with no turn limit.
-High Galaxy customisation (after reaching level 1 or 2 i believe, means you gotta do a few runs 'till you can configure your galaxy) Imo this is a good choice because it lets you play the game "vanilla" without making it too easy/hard from the beginning.
-A bit more complex crew levelling system.
Cons:
-Sometimes the game gets stuck and you need to restart it, happened maybe 3 times in my 8-ish hours
-Low number pf playable ships, I think at the moment there are only 4. Easy access to them, with one 4-5'sh hours run you can unlock them all.
-Different species don't usually have different parks. So far only 2 species out for 5-6 that i have met have any perks at all. Also stats seem to be the same for everyone. A human space marine will have the same stats as an Okhama space marine etc.
-Missing complexity: You cannot vent atmosphere to extinguish fires; no systems like ship doors, cameras, you don't have energy management(as someone mentioned)  little details that FTL had and worked great.
All in all, really good game. People need to write about it because those mixed reviews are not descriptive of the current released version.

The game shares a lot of similarities with FTL, offering the same basic gameplay and features: random maps, permadeath, high difficulty, ship management, and crew orders. Space Rogue feature quests, which are essentially scripted encounters with enemy ships and creatures. There are plenty of game options to tweak the difficulty, although the “easiest” setting is still quite challenging. Time is given to revisit past locations, and dynamic events can change game attributes slightly. The energy system has basically been removed, eliminating a strategic aspect of FTL, and the oxygen and medical bays have been combined into one precious location (which really causes problems when it is constantly targeted by the AI). Crew members can level up, improving stats and granting new abilities. Balancing the minor new features the game adds, oversimplifications in other areas negatively impact the gameplay, making Space Rogue an unnecessary tribute.

Teleglitch is a rogue-like, atmostpheric, survival horror game set in the future and populated only by things that want to murder you. Ammo is scarce, health is only replenishable by healing items and all of your foes madly crave your blood. You'll face mutants and their larger counterpart, gun-wielding guards, zombies, merciless bosses and a whole load of other truly challenging baddies. The shadow effects in Teleglitch: Die More Edition are beautiful and dynamic, providing a real sense of nausea, desperity and oppression via your knowledge you're probably going to die. When playing this game, I'd highly reccomend wearing a headset, the sound quality is great and the noises themselves are so disturbing, heavily atmospheric and psychologically painful, you'll feel tremendous joy in conquering this game's daemons. Like I've already said, this game is really hard, you may feel totally confident in your abilities and gear one minute, and then be forced into a corner whereby you can either run into the screaming crowd of mutants and other repulsing eyesores trapping you in, or headfirst into the 'void' behind you, a black lump of nothingness that anybody, or anything, unfortunate enough to touch it is atomised instantly. Overall, Teleglitch is a difficult, immensely atmostpheric b*stard of a game that'll keep you coming back for more, and making you it's b*tch in the process. The Guns 'n' Tunes DLC available for the game is a steal at 99p and is a nice cherry on top of this gruesome cake. However, the game's asking price itself is a tad steep, but I've seen it 80% off countless times, in said times, I definately recommend that you pick it up.

This game was quite interesting and a little puzzling. It's early access, but rather polished. Yeah, there is a lot that can be done to improve it, but all in all it is a solid game! I was nervous at first because it seemed so similar to FTL. However, there are a lot of mechanics at play here that really help distinguish it from other space games.
One thing I like is how there are a lot choices with almost every part of the game. You can choose what weapons to buy, what planets to mine, what crew to hire, even which missions to take and the direction you want to go to get there!
Yes, it's a little glitchy and I wish there was more content, but I don't think it was a waste of my time. I have faith that if the developers continue to polish and refine it, this could be a really great game.
So is it worth it? In short: yes. Long story: maybe. If you have never played a game like this before, or if it simply interests you at first glance, check it out. You might just be surprised by how interesting this game is. But if you are a grizzled veteran of gaming with a degree in space games, you might find too many allusions to previous games. All in all, it isn't fair to determine one game's level of fun by comparing it to another. Yes, it is similar, but I challenge you to find any game that isn't like at least one other. So if you like space, exploration, survival, or the tough decisions a captain has to make, give Space Rogue a look.

Decent game, although it feels like I've played it for more than 4 hours.
Has a lot of potential, about my only worry is content.  Just seems like other than completing the main quest tha you are playing there is no other goals to reach toward, no real end game or side content I guess.  No playing space merchant or doing bounty missions other than an occasional random quest.  No home base or fleet to build up.  No enemy territory with wars happening or sides to join.  Not saying this all has to be in there, just that it doesn't really expand on the base options FTL had.  In FTL you were always on the edge of death so you didn't really notice, here you are traveling around rather carefree mostly and you can feel the difference.  And while there is a decent assortment of random events, I'd say still more are needed since a few common ones still pop up too often.
Should probably add that there is no manual control over doors for some reason.  Enemies can just walk around your ship as they please which is a bit odd.  Also you can't open an airlock into space to vent the ship, which was an extra tactic for fighting enemies or dealing with fire.  You cannot reassign energy throughout your ship like in FTL either, which really made you feel like a captain when things went pear shaped and you had to make choices.
Stability wise, lots of little bugs and the occasional crash, but nothing gamebreaking that I encountered.  I would just reload my save and it would turn out fine.  Game is pretty solid for the most part.
Now all this might sound bad, but I'm just getting it all out there.  I really like how relaxing it is to play compared to FTL, yet it still has that same addictive visit one more system vibe going for it.  Not worrying about fuel and not having something chasing you is really nice.  Art style is great as well and everything is easy on the eyes.  I rather like the extra systems that provide buffs or debuffs on the enemy as well.
TLDR - A lot more relaxing and simpler version of FTL.  Fun to pick up and play if you need to kill some time for a bit, but long periods of play will probably bore you.

First of all, this game can be hard to get in to. Mainly because it's hard. There are some things that you will only learn not to do once you have died repeatedly by doing them. And that can hurt, especially when you are a couple of hours into a run. Permadeath hits hard when the game lasts so long.
But that really steps the tension in this game up a level. The game does a very good job of making you scared, in a few ways. There's a clever viewpoint system that makes tight corridors feel claustrophobic and open areas make you terified of a redguard standing on the other side. I'm impressed by the sounds. At first I was dissapointed that there was no music, but I have learned that it really matters that you are listening out for footsteps, to tell whether there is a giant zombie on the other side of that door or a group of gunmen approaching. I feel that the ambiant sounds of the facility could be more detailed, however.
When you are attacked and are not ready, it's a panic, which is the last thing you want to do. Switching through weapons, trying to remember which one still has ammo left over, trying to work out where to run that you aren't going to be swarmed, and firing off rounds and MISSING! Missing really hurts in this game. Ammo is scarce.
Overal. If you don't want a tense, hard, painful, roguelike that punishes you for every mistake, this isn't for you. If you are willing to deal with that for the immensely satisfying experiance of finally beating those robots of doom, with 2 health left, healing up again and finding enough ammo to last you for ever, you'll like this. I really do. Favourite rogue-like. I think it really starts to shine when you actually get good at it.
Oh I'll give some advice too, for best enjoyment. I'd play the arena mode a fair bit first, so that you don't get disapointed that you died because you aren't used to the controls yet in your first few runs. Then i'd go into the 'story' and have some fun.

One of the best CCGs around. I definitely recommend it, it has a lot of depth and enough unique game mechnics to differentiate it from any other CCG (the rest of the CCG scene is suprisingly lacking in that aspect). You have amulets who can't attack or be attacked, being powerful passive effects that are permanent (unless removed) or have a countdown until their destruction. You get to evolve your followers, making them stronger/have an extra effect and they can attack enemy followers the same turn. This and the limit of 5 spaces on the field (you have to fit both followers and amulets on the field) makes the game's pace feel pretty fast. Pretty much any class is viable if you can play well, however the meta can get somewhat ridiculous with the persistency of certain classes in ranked games ("cough" Daria "cough"). It isn't as bad as some people make it out to be thought. The art is anime-styled and it is beautiful (albeit inconsistent at times).
The Devs are also pretty cool, you get a lot of free packs regularly, they don't treat you like crap and make expansions often.
So yeah, give it a try - for me, it is better than its biggest opponent, Hearthstone, and it will only keep getting better in the future.

Brutally difficult and unforgiving, while still being a lot of fun.
You'll quickly realize the levels are built from sets of static modules and be lulled into a false sense of security. Any sense of familiarity is your enemy just like the inhabitants of the level, because you can never be sure what's past the next doorway.
The graphics and audio are minimalist and retro, reinforcing the game's bleak theme very well. At times, they can begin to feel repetitive, but if you're fretting about that while playing you're probably not focusing on your own safety and will soon die.
The UI feels unpolished at first glance but it does its job and fits the aesthetic of the game. There's something very visceral about putting together a nail bomb on the run from a horde of angry mutants, and the UI lets you get the job done. I do wish the HUD made vital information like health and ammo a little easier to see or highlighted it somehow.
Overall, if you like feeling like you really earned every inch of progress you made, this is the game for you.

InfiniPicross is a fun little Nonogram/Picross game which randomly generates all its puzzles, to the user's size specifications.  It's worth pointing out that there are NO curated puzzles on this one - it's literally all just random puzzles, but the game's solver ensures that all puzzles generated are solvable, and I've found them to be enjoyable to play through.  There have been a couple of issues at launch which the developer's been extremely responsive about fixing, so I have no qualms about it from that angle!
The implementation is basic but very competent, and it's nice to be able to alter the game's "theme" to suit, as you can see from the screenshots.  There's also an editor to alter the theme however you see fit.  I'm unlikely to switch them around now that I've got one set up to my liking, but it's a clever feature.
If you're in the mood for a Nonogram/Picross game on your desktop which will never run out of fresh puzzles, I'd definitely recommend this one.

Played it a lot on phone, so I have more hours than this.
The big thing most will care about is how pay to win it is. The answer: it's not. It's extremely fair to free to play players. Pay to play will always have an advantage, of course, but it's nothing that's insurmountable and card decks/currency can be easy to get. You will have to grind a bit as a free to play player, though.
As for the actual game, it's a pretty standard online TCG. Nothing particularly stands out, though the balance is pretty bad. But, if you've played Hearthstone as most probably have, you already know what to expect.
Graphically, it depends on your preferences. It's extremely anime-style, with girls wearing questionably skimpy clothing and the few men looking like they walked off the front page of a teen magazine. Most of the cards are well-drawn and everything is pretty crisp.
Sound is pretty mediocre. The English version has bad voice acting and the music is as generic as you can get.
As for performance, it runs pretty well. I do have a pretty good system, though, so I don't know how it'll run on more mediocre systems.
It has a "story" mode but the story is mediocre and the battles are just AI battles that are easy to win with a little thinking.
Overall, I'd recommend it if you don't like Hearthstones graphics design, haven't played Hearthstone or another TCG or just want a good anime-style TCG. But if you're heavily invested in Hearthstone already, don't like anime or TCGs then don't play it.

Crystals of Time is a fun little hidden object game for anyone looking to kill three-or-so hours without too much mental commitment. There are a handful of puzzles, the difficulty of which range from very easy to moderately difficult, yet the mere activity of going through and solving them is satisfying enough. While the game is pretty straight forward, with only the occasional possibility of getting stumped, you can use the time crystal Ashley Ford starts out with to give you a hint--these are visual cues that trigger the player's understanding of what to do next instantaneously. There were, perhaps, a few too many of the "hidden object" sessions, but these are trifling and take only a few minutes to complete, even when you're presented with two or three to complete in a row. A big hint I would have found useful: if you come to a place where you seem to have run out of things to do, return to the places where you have scavenged for hidden objects before; often you will have to do another round of object finding in order to come up with the next item needed to proceed in the game.
One of the strongest elements to Crystals of Time is the artwork. As the entire experience plays out in a series of still pictures (with some minor animation at times), the player is treated with a wide array of stunning visuals that range from the vast, brooding insides of a sprawling mansion, to a glittering moonlit coast. It is an art style which is relatively simple, but detailed and colorful enough--with an excellent use of source-light shadings--that it never gets tedious to look at. In addition to the art, the soundtrack is both simple yet effective, adding to the atmosphere of the game in a substantial way. And, although there are only three-or-four songs to be had, the game designers were smart enough to allow for long stretches of silence between each play so that they don't get redundant.
The story, on the other hand, isn't very remarkable. It's pretty shallow and without any real character depth or interaction. Still, in a simple hidden object game such as this, it's not really all that imperative. The surface-deep story matches the overall casual nature of the game, and it's not really a knock against it; this game is light fair, enjoyed best when entering into it with a hankering for a nice, noncommittal gaming experience. I did, however, run into one glitch which probably won't happen reliably with every play-through: the journal somehow got locked up halfway through the game, and with each proceeding entry, the text overlapped upon the previous entry, rendering the book virtually useless. Thankfully, the game is clear enough that it did little to hinder my progress.
After all's said and done, Crystals of Time comes recommended at it's cheap $4.99 price-point, and is a no-brainer on sale for two dollars or less.

Let's get one thing straight off the bat.
I hate the Dead Island games.  Not because I'm some zombie contrarian, rather (even though I'm not a zombie trope fan) because they're poorly made and boring.  Combat was floaty, controls were always a tad wonky and I'm pretty sure there's no story at all in any of them.  Not one that serves an actual purpose anyway.  They aren't terrible games, but they're terrible games.  Wait.
Next thing to get straight: this game is not a Dead Island clone with a visual update.  Not even close.  In fact, I'm nearly convinced Techland had nothing to do with this game considering how tight the combat is, the fluidity of movement and environmental aesthetic.  Even the sound design is wonderful in this game.  It is the polar opposite in technical aspects from it's spiritual predecessors.  Dying Light is not only a brilliant zombie game but a fantastic game in general, and reigns on top of the heap of refuse thrown at people in the hopes that not being able to watch Walking Dead for hours at a time will drive them to spend money on unfinished, unrefined garbage.
Let's be clear here, when it comes to zombie shooters, the choices are ridiculously varied in terms of price, quality, depth, stage of development and, in the end, outright value.  DayZ is an uninspired, spastic mess and makes H1Z1 look like Psychonauts, even in it's definitely unfinished state.  Dead Island has either been played or is not worth playing.  We've all been through our Left4Dead phase and that wore out.  I'm not even going to address the remaining limitless amount of awful "zombie, survival, horror" titles clogging the Greenlight and Early Access sections, I think we all understand.
What matters here is Dying Light is none of those.  It is the king.  For once someone has nailed melee combat in an FPS that feels visceral, satisfying and rewarding.  The difficulty curves perfectly, starting out difficult if surrounded by daytime zombies and downright impossible at night, and peaking once you wield weapons capable of dealing massive damage, slicing through a horde of day walkers only to be humbled by what nighttime offers you.  Narratives are more organic and, while the story is certainly uninspiring, flat and brings almost 0 character development, the real engaging moments of gameplay have nothing to do with the script.  Whether it's a co-op stand against waves of zombies, a solo night run across open areas, hunting a particular creature, adeptly scampering up buildings and sending pursuing zombies down into the street below, the tone of the game and the pace of travel/combat makes the little moments the most satisfying (as opposed the ending of the main story arc which almost made me have an anyeruism).  That's the magic games lose today.  Publishers want studios to pump out a simple story able to be burned through just in time for the DLC to release and gameplay just competent enough to get you there.
Dying Light shines through for one simple reason: it's fun as hell.  It's simply enjoyable to play, to explore and to find new places, new weapons and new ways of eviscerating these helpless meatbags.
That's more than I could say for Dead Island.

Crystals of Time is the least fun I've ever had playing a Hidden Object Game.
The biggest problem is that the game is completely unintuitive. If you don't have the object you need for a puzzle, you'll need to check one of the two dozen or so rooms to see which one has had a hidden object puzzle suddenly pop up. I found myself using the hint button everytime I didn't know what to do, not because I was truly stumped, but because I didn't feel like searching every single room.
When you get the item, you might not even know what to do with it. Maybe you missed the background object it interacted with or you forgot which room it went in or you just don't know what it does. Granted, this could be a problem in any HOG game, but it seems especially bad here. Unless I missed something, inventory items don't have descriptions. On top of that, went you find something that needs an item it just tell you, "I should find the missing item first." No allusion to what that might be. Sometimes it's obvious, but when it's not it's annoying. Again, not because it's challenging, but because it feels like lazy game design.
A good HOG will kind of lead you down a path. Something will impede your progress, you'll solve it and move on. As you move on, older areas kind of get left behind, new puzzles are prominent, your mind makes connections between new items and the rooms you've been in. Here the game more or less just lays out a pile of screens and says, "Okay, figure out which of these seven locked doors need this key."
On top of these issues you have some really uninspired puzzles (a bunch of which amount to finding five similar objects  and bringing them to the same place), bland environments, over-recycling of HO screens and bad writing. There's a lot better HOG games out there. Don't settle for this one.

a big improvement on the first game.
PROS
-Overall, the game feels a lot smoother.
-Much better, smoother animations.
-More perks.
-Multi-perk weapons. For the longest time in the first game, I wanted the ability to use the Firebug Trench Gun with the Support, or the M203 M16 with the Commando, and now you can.

Definitely a very cool title.
A clearly FTL inspired space rogue-like with the same, and if not more depth and feel. Space Rogue features the greatest asset to come from FTL, the real-time and pausable combat system. You choose which subsystem to fire your weapons, and where to send your crew.
Space Rogue is a cartoonish and colorful play on many aspects we all enjoy from a good rogue-like experience. Get as far as you can, with the limited resources available. Gain ship parts, new weapons and crew members, while trying to stay alive to make your next run easier and more enjoyable. You WILL die and restart plenty of times. Each giving a new generated galaxy to overcome.
Unlike FTL, when you die you are rewarded a score. These points go towards your overall level, and when gained enough levels, you will unlock additional missions and ships.
Being in early access, you can assume that it is unfinished, unpolished and not fun, but that isn't the case with Space Rogue. If you liked FTL, to pretty much any extent, you will get plenty of hours out of this game. More galaxy to explore, a better looking and colorful game screen, and a less linear exploration model. Many things, are improved over FTL and some things fall short, but you can't have the two games be perfectly indentical. You should see most of the differences for yourself.
Space Rogue offers, in my opinion, a more detailed and enjoyable galaxy to explore, and an overall more immersive setting than FTL.
The music isn't half bad either.

Teleglitch is a really good, really hard, really interesting game. It's a game full of a lot of things preceded by the word "really". Words that can be used to describe the game following the word "really": brutal, fun, atmospheric, scary, tense... actually, it'd be too long of a list, so I'll stop here.
The graphics aren't exactly what you would call... good. To be frank it's a top-down blurry and pixalated mess. However, it's a top-down blurry and pixelated mess that actually works really well for the story and somehow manages to portray the tense horror of the situation very well.
Sadly, however, the perspective gets a bit rough on the eyes (and the stomach, when moving quickly). In the past this wasn't too much of a problem, these days are particularly rough on me as I have frequent migraines, and it seems particularly adept in triggering one. Honestly, even though I really enjoy the game, I can't play it for more than a few minutes at a time and haven't even attempted to do so in months. It is a really good game though, and highly recommended.
It's a shame the developer made cuts in the game, which explains why it's so short. Other than that, it's unique and deserves a sequel, which is coming up.

The big thing most will care about is how pay to win it is. The answer: it's not. It's extremely fair to free to play players. Pay to play will always have an advantage, of course, but it's nothing that's insurmountable and card decks/currency can be easy to get. You will have to grind a bit as a free to play player, though.
As for the actual game, it's a pretty standard online TCG. Nothing particularly stands out, though the balance is pretty bad. But, if you've played Hearthstone as most probably have, you already know what to expect.
Graphically, it depends on your preferences. It's extremely anime-style, with girls wearing questionably skimpy clothing and the few men looking like they walked off the front page of a teen magazine. Most of the cards are well-drawn and everything is pretty crisp.
Sound is pretty mediocre. The English version has bad voice acting and the music is as generic as you can get.
As for performance, it runs pretty well. I do have a pretty good system, though, so I don't know how it'll run on more mediocre systems.
It has a "story" mode but the story is mediocre and the battles are just AI battles that are easy to win with a little thinking.
Overall, I'd recommend it if you don't like Hearthstones graphics design, haven't played Hearthstone or another TCG or just want a good anime-style TCG. But if you're heavily invested in Hearthstone already, don't like anime or TCGs then don't play it.

Crystals of Time starts out well enough with an interesting (although one-dimensional) story and interesting enough exploration of the surroundings; but as you progress through the game it becomes incredibly repetitive and feels random.  The hidden object scenes are done fairly well; but you'll see each scene 3 or 4 times throughout the course of the game.  The items you're searching for seem to randomly change; but you'll see repeats making things way easier.   The game also does a really poor job of providing hints or rationale for why you're revisiting areas to progress the story.  It's really typical to go from area to area to see if a new item or section has become interactive with no rhyme or reason for any of it.  This became really tedious so I started using the hint system just to find out which room I needed to go to next.   If they didn't repeat the hidden object scenes and reduced the amount of random backtracking it would have been a shorter game; but way better in the long run.

The enemies don't really get stronger, so eventually you become this god amongst men. I personally still found the game enjoyable even until the end, but I can see where some people would have issues with the way the game turned out.
Then there's the multiplayer, the coop was alright. You got to play everything you could alone, but with pals. Of course, this only compounded the whole issue with the game being easy, because I didn't see any kind of added difficulty when playing with other people.
There was also a versus, where 1 player controlled super zombie fought against up to 4 player controlled humans. I don't really know what to say about this. It was unbalanced. The matchmaking was terrible. But once again, I actually really liked playing as the hunter zombie. The main issue being how hard it was to actually find a match. I'm guessing there were many more zombie players looking for matches than vice versa. This ended up in 10+ minutes of refreshing and hoping you join a game before someone else steals the spot.
But I digress. Great game, few flaws. I got my moneys worth. 8/10

Note: I received a free copy of this game with a hardware purchase, but bought the DLC Season Pass myself.
I have thoroughly enjoyed the previous entries in the Batman: Arkham series, even including Arkham Origins, which had its issues but was entertaining enough.
When Arkham Knight first released on PC it was beset by serious issues and a high-profile public drubbing ensued as a result.  I was fortunate enough that the game was playable on my PC at release; although the framerate was on the low side, I had no other serious game-breaking issues.  Since it has been patched, the performance is significantly improved.  I can understand that for a lot of gamers, the poor care taken with the PC port and the weeks between its original release and it being patched will have tainted the experience sufficiently that the game is ruined for them.
For me, the game was a fitting end to the series.  The story is solid, the voice acting is as good as ever and the graphics are simply incredible.  The inclusion of the Batmobile is controversial and perhaps too much of the gameplay is built around it.  That being said, the controls are responsive and the animations for it are good - it feels like it has mass and seeing it bounce on its suspension or crash through scenery makes it seem quite real.
The combat is the best its ever been, with a dazzling array of combinations.  The trademark Free Flow system is finely tuned and the animations varied.  Having had several games to perfect this system (which has spawned many inferior imitators), Rocksteady have clearly reached the pinnacle of their craft in this installment.  There are new, more challenging enemies, new moves and variety but all built around an extremely solid basic concept.
The game itself is reasonably long with a good amount of side quests, Riddler trophies and the like.  There is a lot of DLC content, some of which is fairly light on content, rather disappointingly, but does provide some closure for a few plot threads and characters.  The sheer number of extra challenge maps, race courses etc. is absurd; once you account for the different vehicles and character combinations, I think it would take months to complete every possible iteration.  Whether or not this is a positive or negative is debatable; I completed 100% of the challenges and collected all of the achievements in Arkham Asylum and have managed progressively less with each successive game.  Personally I think it's probably a bit too much, but equally it does increase the replay value somewhat.
I am not ashamed to say that I really enjoyed playing this game - now that enough time has passed since its release, it's likely to be a lot more affordable as well.

I was a little hesitant to buy this game at first, not knowing what to expect from it, and not really having played any Zombie  games in the past.  Here is my short review:
I didn't really know what to expect when I purchased this game, not having played the previous Zombie games on the PC or consoles, so I was a little new to the "surviver" type genre.  When you start the game, it is fairly tough, since you suck at running, jumping and climbing.  This makes things a LOT harder, and you die quite a bit in the early stages as you are getting your♥♥♥♥♥owned by monsters.
However, as you start doing things, you get better at combat or running or general survivor, and by the time you get to about level 8 or so in the 3 Skills, the game really starts to improve a lot, as the parkour system really starts to shine.  You can run and jump and climb faster, and run longer, and the game just becomes a LOT of fun.  Before all of this, its sort of annoying, but after you get that stuff down, its a blast.
I would do most of my quests during the day, I only went out at night a few times.  Initially I got my♥♥♥♥♥totally kicked, because I didn't realize Firecrackers were so useful, but after you "learn" the game, it becomes a lot easier and a lot more fun.
The story is decent, though nothing to write home about.  There are a few "arena" style fights, which I detest, but I did ok with them here and the developers have made it so that when you respawn, the monsters you killed stay dead so it doesn't get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Exploration and Crafting REALLY are important in this game.  If you take the time to upgrade your weapons, find blueprints, etc, etc, you end being a major killing machine in the last 1/3 of the game.
Graphics:
The graphics are fairly good, not the best I have seen, but pretty solid on my PC.  I was running them maxed out, except for textures which were set to medium due to some weird slow down issues on my SLI 670 FTW versions due to it loading too much into memory.  This wouldn't be an issue with 4gb cards but mine are 2gb.  The zombie models, buildings, etc are all pretty well done.
World Design:
I found the world design to be pretty decent overall, I just wish it was a little bigger or had a few more areas to explore that were different, but what is here is pretty good.  The buildsing have a fair level of detail, the sewers are well designed, the parkour system is built decently into the game, etc, etc.  I enjoyed it for the most part.
So would I recomend this game?  Yes, its a good deal of fun.  You might find the initial part of the game to be a bit annoying and hard, but give it time, and before you know it, you will find your guy leveling up and blowing through the game and having a total blast.
F2P Friendly, enjoyable to play casually, overall fun game to get into.

At launch, this game was very, very buggy and the overall launch was a tragedy. It was really, really bad.
But when I played through it every single bug I had heard about has been fixed. I had absolutely zero issues with this game, no bugs, no crashes, no problems whatsoever.
( I will point out that my experience was on my own high end pc, so I can't comment on what the experience would be like on an older pc, but it seems that the game is much smoother in general these days)
I'd recommend you play the earlier installments before you play this, namely Batman Arkham Asylum, Batman Arkham City, and Batman Arkham Origins. Not just because otherwise the story will make no sense to you, but also because the earlier games are on sale quite often and PHENOMENAL games in their own right.
With that being said, The game itself plays like Arkham City and Arkham Origins, essentially, but with tweaks to the combat here and there.
There is the added bonus/caveat, depending on your opinion of it, of the introduction of the Batmobile to the game. To some, it's a godsend. To others, a series of unavoidable, unskippable and quite frankly very frequent car/driving segments. Also, it's not just driving, but also combat segments involving the Batmobile. You'll see what I mean if you play the game. Now, I personally had absolutely zero issues with that aspect of the game, but I grew up playing driving games and I had a blast. It's just worth mentioning that one of the biggest complaints I've heard regarding the game is about the "god damn Batmobile segments", so if you think you wouldn't enjoy that, it's absolutely worth considering that it WILL be a frequent part of your game experience.
I played the game on the hardest difficulty (and I don't usually do that) and I beat the whole game without wanting to smash my controller. Essentially, it may not be as bad to you as it is for some people.
Now, the overall game itself was a phenomenal experience for me. There are flaws, most of which I can't really specify cause they'd involve spoiling certain things of the story, but none of them warrant hesitation towards buying this game.
Furthermore, the game's not brand new anymore so it does go on sale here and there, but even for the full price I think it's worth it.
If you like Batman or the Arkham franchise at all, add this game to your steam wishlist and wait for it to go on sale and I can almost guarantee you won't be sorry.
Highly recommended.

Pros:
- Nice visuals, awesome portraits, the art style is very fitting and immersive.
- The combat system is enjoyable but could use some polish.
- Dialogues and NPCs in general are very well written.
- The story is part dumb, part engaging. It fits into the setting, altough it somewhat turns downhill towards the second half. The writing is good for the most part though.
- The setting, I personally love the setting.
Cons:
- The combat, despite its solid foundation feels cheap and too easy.
- The decking sections are super boring.
- The game is waaay too linear for an RPG. It takes away from the awesome dialogues when you know you can't change a drek no matter what you say/do.
- The music is rather forgettable.
- The spell effects are down right ugly.
- The game world is gated behind loading screens and comes in small chunks. In this regard it's similar to Deus Ex - you're being teleported from location to location, thus the world seems small and contained.
They did an awesome job of bringing Shadowrun to PC, but sadly it's just isn't that good of a game. Feels more like an interactive novel, an introduction into the world of Shadowrun. The dialogues, the NPCs, the visuals and the cyberpunk distopia, the immersion of being a runner... it's all there and it's a pleasant journey for the fan of the setting. It's just it doesn't feel like you're DOING anything, other than watch the game play itself.
It's like this GM friend who's got this really awesome story he wants to tell you... but you can't alter a thing, your PC is but a pawn in his hands and you can only sit, listen and bask in the ambience. And if the story was indeed as good as he promised I would have enjoyed the ride way better.
Either way, if the story was better or the gameplay was more polished the score would have been higher. As is the final score sits somewhere around 6-7/10. Still, the game is so cheap these days, and the setting is so awesome you should buy it anyway.

Arkham Knight's initial launch on PC was a disaster. Numerous problems plagued the game even for those with high end rigs. It also was the first example of consumers excercising the new refund system on Steam.
The developers eventually said that many of the issues may be unfixable (for whatever reasons). However that didn't stop them from trying to continue to peddle DLC.
With that out of the way, how does the game hold up now? Well it is not without problems but I have been able to play it with only some stuttering here or there. As before, these instances of stutter happen during batmobile sequences. It wouldn't be as intrusive if not for the annoying frequency of 'horde mode' encounters (more on this in a bit).
Arkham Knight revists Gotham with many of the same characters. To avoid spoilers, the gameplay is largely the same from Arkham City with a few tweaks here and there with regards to combat.
There is plenty to do in this vast city scape. Unraveling the puzzles of the riddler, stopping bank heists orchestrated by Two Face, and a plethora of other side missions sure to delight fans.
The main story of course revolves around the titular Arkham Knight who leads a organized millita. Yes there are tanks that roll around Gotham. In some sequences you either duel them or have to catch them in the Batmobile. This is often where slowdown can rear it's ugly head.
Is Arkham Knight worth picking up? Yes with the caveat "when on sale." I picked the game up for about $7 during a sale and feel comfortable saying at that price, it's an easier pill to swallow. I have certainly got my money's worth from it. Hopefully WB has learned their lesson and will think before outsourcing another PC title to a third party studio.
UPDATE: Now that I have largely finished the story I thought I would give my overall impressions of the story while avoiding spoilers. The overall plot is decent enough. During the game you will encounter a variety of villains and recognizeable characters. Like the other Arkham games, Arkham Knight makes use of Batman's recognizeablle and stellar rogues gallery. They draw from a variety of sources and you will find even some more recent villains from well known modern Batman stories. The way these encounters are handled is you complete a series of missions before ultimately bringing them to justice. Each of them has a nice bit of story attached to them and I genuinely enjoyed these.
The biggest pitfall the plot runs into is that you are eventually presented with a few sequences that make the rest of the plot utterly predictable if your a well versed Batman fan. That aside it is a nice bit of fan service.

Way back when, back in the days of the Amiga 500, The Chaos Engine was one of those games that I kept coming back to and playing over and over again, even though I never actually saw the end of the game - not because of a lack of skill, but because the RAM on my Amiga always crashed as soon as I'd finished the final boss battle.  So, naturally, when the game resurfaced a couple of decades later on Steam, I jumped at the chance to get stuck in once more.
At first glance, the game feels pretty close to the one I played in the 90s: the soundtrack is as great today as it was back then, and the gameplay has pretty much the same feel - right down to the Brigand ally always nipping in to steal the bounty from the enemies I just killed.
However, there's something that just seems...off.
Some of it could be put down to the resolution, as the options seem to boil down to having it look great in a small window or having it look ugly when blown up to full screen, and it isn't the rose-tinted spectacles telling me the game looked better in the 90s because watching a walkthrough on Youtube has the game looking better.  Or it could be that, having played the game with joysticks back in the 90s, playing it on a keyboard simply feels unintuitive, which given the speed the game is played at is an issue.
The main issue, though, is the game calling itself a remaster just feels disingenuous.  Compared to an emulated version of the original, this version isn't as smooth and is just plain slower, which is a double kick in the teeth when you consider the system requirements.
I still love the original game, which can be tracked down by fair means or foul, but this simply is not the original game.  It may look and sound similar, but the pile of tiny yet significant flaws mean this just isn't The Chaos Engine of old, merely a poorly programmed port that does the original a disservice.

It's a reasonable take on the FTL genre, but not quite good enough yet. The potential is there, but it needs plenty more work.
Pros: Nice graphics. That's essentially it. (And the room-on-fire animations need work!)
Cons: Crashes a lot, at least the Mac version does. Two complete lock-ups in an hour and a half of play. I've not tried the Windows version, but it's safe to assume that is no more stable. Takes over the entire Mac in full-screen mode, preventing task-switching. And windowed mode is, like with 99% of games, utterly unplayable due to not fitting properly on the screen (i.e. there's no borderless option).
Limited keyboard control, e.g. dialogs require mouse input. Mouse control is a bit laggy and unresponsive. The music (at least the initial title music) is repetitive and annoying. Selecting your crew and moving them around is clunky compared to FTL's interface.
It's difficult to see what your drones are doing due to the zoomed-in perspective, although granted the zoom level can be adjusted somewhat. But the graphics are designed to be viewed large and close-up. Due to their isometric design, it's not always clear what's going on. It can also be difficult to tell your crewmembers apart at a glance, but I guess that'll come with practice.
Can't de-power rooms, which is a nice micro-management mechanic in FTL. Also there's no manual door control, so you can't defeat boarders by flushing the atmosphere. Missile-based weapons don't use ammunition either, which essentially means they're identical to lasers, except pass through shields. So why would anyone use lasers?
Upgrade window doesn't tell you the effects of a subsystem upgrade until you have bought it.
I don't like the cartridges, they're of limited use and fiddly. They're like the curses in Diablo - you have to keep re-casting them.
Bottom line, they seem to have taken FTL, beefed up the graphics, and simplified the gameplay. Granted, improving on FTL (at least the iOS version) is a difficult task; but the fact remains that Space Rogue - while not a "bad" game - is nowhere near as good. Yet.
Oh yes... and their support email address, as given by Steam's game support page, DOES NOT WORK!

This game is pretty easy to explain.  You move a triangle clockwise or counterclockwise around a hexagon in the center of the screen,making an effort to avoid being crushed by six walls closing in on you.  Your goal in each level in the basic Hexagons is to survive at least a minute, after which the speed of the Hexagon walls will increase as you enter that Hexagon's "Hyper" mode.  This also unlocks the Hyper mode in question from the main menu, allowing you to skip right to the more challenging segments.  Surviving a minute in Hyper mode will allow you to truly complete that hexagon.
Despite the straightforward description however, actually playing this game is a frantic test of reflexes, as even the default speed is very quick and easy to be overwhelmed by, at first.  The patterns of incoming walls can be incredibly difficult to wedge between, requiring percision and speed.  This could easily become frustrating in any other game, however, Super Hexagon mitigates the frustration with its quick game over-to-reload time.  With the press of a button, you're back in the action and at it again, learning from your mistakes, and seeing the time until a game over in a stage slowly rise to the minute mark.  Not many will complete this game (I doubt I will), or even one stage in it, but when losing doesn't feel like much of a waste, it manages to remain fun regardless  The exelent aethetics, from the pumping beat and the flashy background certainly help as well.
In one sentance: A simple to learn, but extremely challenging and addictive game, with vibrant visuals and a catchy soundtrack.
I highly reccomend giving it a go.

It's been spoken that developers were inspired by FTL but I want to clarify why it's not the clone but the genre evolution.
When I play chess or checkers I see the patterned field, I see some units and I see similar moves. Thousands of years passed and many of strategy games evolved to thousands of strategy games on computers, on paper. There are also  'tactical' games which came out of strategy ones. They differ much or not.
I'm observing the next 'step' of FTL-like game mechanic but not the clone. It could be Warcraft-like mechanic with many units-ships which their pros and cons against each other with space station which makes them or it could be something with shooting involved mechanic. That's JUST a matter of choice.
Why I'm talking about it in this way? I saw many comments like 'a
it's just another FTL', 'I'd play FTL better', 'They didn't make any new features' etc.
Just imagine it's a new genre and play again. Don't judge it from the point of 'cloned' game, it's NOT. There are plenty of different features: non-linear gameplay, starting conditions, friendly simple graphics, and many-many of little ones that you'll find when you play more than couple of minutes.
Besides:
a) the game is STILL in development;
b) developers ARE REALLY listening to what people write. And you can trace how crucially it changed from start to the point of 'now'.
So it's up for us: to help improving it or keep judging 'Unreal' to be a clone of 'Quake'. It really has a great potential and may be we'll see more 'FTL-like' genre games.
PROS:
- non-linear gameplay
- you can choose the level of difficulty by setting starting conditions
- nice simple graphics
- plenty of events
- nice music
- FTL-like gameplay
- still in developement, has a potential
CONS:
- balance (just my opinion)
- just sandbox, no deep campaign (I would prefer that)
