I really wanted to like Burning Cars, and would love to be able to recommend it, but it's just not really very good.
I love top-down racers, and played rival indie racer, Blaze Rush, to completion as well, but where Blaze Rush is adrenaline-fuelled, manic fun, Burning Cars is just a bit silly, and rather frustrating.
The graphics are good, and the sounds are acceptable. The courses are not too bad either, and the variety of powerups and obstacles is reasonable, if fairly standard fare for this sort of game. But the physics are a bad joke, seeing your vehicle (of which there are really only two: a truck or a buggy) bouncing around ridiculously, hanging in the air, rebounding with seemingly more force than it hit, and being unable to turn (especially in hard mode) at any sort of speed.
Even the upgrades and weapons are disappointing, with the different models of truck only differing from each other in minor ways, and only a very limited number of different weapons available.
It's sad, because from reading the brief credits and messages, it sounds as though the indie developers of Burning Cars really put in a lot of effort over five years to bring this game to completion. It was a really nice idea, and I wish I could recommend it, but the fun and replayability is just not there.

At least you get what's on the tin: you will see a few burning cars. But how's the game? Unfortunately, not great.
Burning Cars is a simple racing game: you drive trucks and buggies around a racing course. To spice it up you can equip the cars with machine guns, land mines and nitro boosters. The race course is quite literally littered with caustic waste and trash but also some helpful power-ups.
The game has two difficulty settings for the championship: Easy and Hard. It emerges that the two difficulties are very different from each other because of the very different car physics. Too bad that in effect there's only one championship, unless you count taking the same championship again (after losing it) with fully upgraded opponents.
I delude myself being a hardcore gamer, so I of course chose the Hard setting for my first championship. The first thing I noticed was that the car physics was outrageously, punishingly stiff (because of the difficulty level): the car simply does not want to turn. If you happen to turn the wrong way (fairly common occurrence), it is extremely hard to turn back the right way, and it takes aeons to do so. Combined with the issue that the interfering opponents can easily push you and turn you the wrong way, your race could be doomed early on. Yes, it is hard but not in a satisfying way.
Next thing I noticed that there are no brakes, i.e. you can't brake manually. Nor can you change the controls, so e.g. I was stuck with 'F' for boost, even though for me Shift would have been way more convenient.
Funnily and thankfully enough, the bad physics affects the opponents too. They get stuck and drive the wrong way as much as you do. Often you can still win an apparently losing race because the AI opponents are derping in a difficult corner where they simply can't get out because of the physics.
I mentioned weapons and corrosive wastes: unfortunately, they are rarely that useful or hurtful, because the opponents (and you too) will respawn almost immediately after dying. You will even retain some of your speed and will face the right way, thus making dying often a helpful occurrence. Yet you can't respawn on the map yourself: if you get stuck outside the course (happened to me several times) or fly completely off the map (also several times), you have essentially lost the race. If you happen to die out there, you simply respawn at that spot again, which to me is a huge oversight.
Because of the championship mode (it's the only mode but nevertheless a redeeming factor of the game), between races you get money and can buy upgrades to your car. These include better armor, weapons and paint for that extra touch.
You can also buy more expensive cars, which might be better than your previous one or perhaps not. On Hard mode the buggy was basically unusable for me because its turning was even clunkier than for the truck. It would get stuck driving towards a wall, unable to turn to either direction. Quirky enough, it would turn right more easily than left (maybe the equipment affected physics but I'm uncertain of this), making some turns impossible. While faster than truck, maneuverability was more important anyway with the clunky controls. This also meant that the AI buggies would often get stuck somewhere together and I would then win the race with little effort.
Easy mode was more like what I was expecting. Turning was reasonably easy for both types of cars and for a while it was very easy to win the races. However, on Easy mode the buggies were OP when compared to trucks. They were extremely fast and even trucks with nitros couldn't catch them, so I bought one as well and afterwards everything was easy again, except for the fact that too much speed would (hilariously enough) fly me off the map a few times, losing a couple of races.
Disappointing, Burning Cars is just good for an easy 100%: it only took a couple of hours to grab all achievements. Frankly, the original Micro Machines and Death Rally games are much better breed of the genre. Only get this if it's on an extreme discount or in a bundle. Even then I'd only recommend it if you wanted some easy achievements or really, really like top-down racing games.

It didn't take long for me to absolutely love this game to bits. It seems simple - a difficult top-down shooter with zombies and pixel graphics. Seems pretty mainstream at the core.
But there's way more to it that makes it stand out from most other games in my eyes - that it has actual atmosphere. I can count the number of game franchises I've played with true atmosphere on one hand: Metroid, Fallout, Dark Souls, System Shock, and now this game. What is "true atmosphere"?
I like to define it as ambience in a game to the point where it shrouds you in all sorts of mixed emotions, whether it be fear, cheerfulness, or isolation. In the Metroid games, you're alone on a planet and for the most part are the only "human" lifeform on it. The Fallout games you could argue don't really have true atmosphere, but what I'm talking about is the exploration part of the games (even the classic ones). Turn off the radio, go into the vaults or subway tunnels in Fallout 3/New Vegas, and you'll see what I mean. THAT'S true atmosphere.
And it just so happens that this simple-looking game is a mixture of Metroid and Fallout, with a touch of the sci-fi from System Shock 2 and the difficulty/unforgivingness of the Dark Souls games. Despite how awful the graphics look in the screenshots, the game has a beautiful way of approaching its graphical style. It plays on the style of glitches on a screen, and makes those as realistic as possible. They contrast from the rest of the game's visuals, and as a result it adds something to the game that I can't really describe. The game doesn't really have music - it's all ambient sound, which is extremely realistic. For most of the game you'll be getting used to the hum of power generators, and it makes the setting both peaceful and ominous.
The gameplay itself is well-done. The controls may seem awkward at first, especially with a controller, but you get the hang of them quickly as your life depends on it. Literally. If you can't get the hang of the controls and get yourself killed, you have to restart from the beginning, hence why it's considered a roguelike. This motivates you to be careful about where you set foot, because a single stupid mistake can make you lose everything. You get more powerful as you go along, though. There's a crafting system in place that lets you combine various things you find in the levels - which are semi-randomly generated - to make improved versions of guns you find. This is extremely reminiscent of Fallout 3.
Another comparison I made to the Fallout/Metroid duo is that in both games, you find out the lore via exploration. In the Metroid Prime games you have to scan walls with alien text on them to get stories about the civilizations that once lived there. In the Bethesda Fallout games, a lot of the lore is learned from holotapes and working computers that you find around the Wasteland. In Teleglitch, you do the same thing. The game introduces you to the main story through an intro, but after that you have to read logs present on computers that you find in the various levels. And just as in the Fallout and Metroid games, sometimes the logs can have a dark sense of humor.
In conclusion, I HIGHLY recommend this game, otherwise I wouldn't have written such a long review of it. If you're looking for a creepy atmospheric survival shooter roguelike game, this will more than surpass your expectations. It's THAT good. Trust me, get it.

If you have no patience for cyclical puzzle games, then avoid this like the plague.
However if lateral thinking is your thing then I suggest giving this a go.
I'd be lying if I said there were no similarities to Portal here; the first person puzzle POV, the single manipulative 'gun', and at a stretch the level design are familiar. Yet the object here is think about how each puzzle can be solved by manipulating small cubes, lasers and even the very levels themselves; and each puzzle may have different routes and different solutions.
You will find yourself entering the same rooms over and over again, either by your own volition navigating the starting menu, or by the seemingly random teleporting. But as you progress to upgrade your gun, previously impossible rooms will seem so simple to traverse.
I will however mention one point that may put people off; the visuals.
Some may say vivid, others seizure inducing; take your pick. Though this may play in its favour as you shouldn't be sat at the monitor for too long anyway (guilty as charged).
Replayability isn't really there, unless you wish to try your own speed run, and the way the cube physics works takes a little trial and error to fully utilise.
A nice added bonus is the 'developer rooms' dotted around detailing the build process of the game over the years.
These aren't mandatory to complete the game; you could get to the exit without visiting many of the rooms but the completionist I am kept me going.
All in all I liked the game; it is a fresh concept, taxed the mind, and even though it wasn't painfully complicated, I still felt accomplished to complete the game.

I'm going to preface this by saying one thing: Dying Light is a game that is far from perfect. There are a large number of problems with the game that cannot be overlooked, such as a number of achievements not functioning properly, and some other glitchy environments and setpieces. The game probably should have spent another month or two in testing in order to work out some of the small bugs that can in some ways interrupt the immersive experience that the developers want for Dying Light. This game needs some polishing, in all honesty.
However,
This is a game that is worth your full attention.
It feels like eons since I have had this much fun in a video game. This is a game that I don't want to stop playing once I start, and I feel like everyone else should have the opportunity to experience the intense amount of fun that I have had with this game.
The multiplayer works very well. The drop in/drop out system is rather fluid, and this game's atmosphere and play style work well with multiple players. Also, drop kicking zombies back and forth between your friends is pretty cool.
While the weapon selection is limited in a sense, I have never been so satisfied with swinging swords, machetes, and baseball bats into hordes of undead, and watching the unholy carnage pile up. Zombie smashing is fun again.
My last point comes to that so-called 'X-factor' that we gamers look for in games. It's that sense that we've just found a game that makes us feel like an utter badass as we do whatever it is that the game's objective is. It's that feeling that makes us not want to turn away from the game just so we can kill one more zombie, or grapple to one more rooftop.
Dying Light has that X-factor for me.

For an early access game, my first impression is a positive one. Unfortunately, Space Rogue is held up to the high standards of Faster Than Light (FTL), even though it is a different company, designing a completely separate game. It does, however, have large amounts of borrowed UI and  game mechanics, making it appear much like FTL. The game is very similar to FTL in many respects and at the same time it is its own game. If you enjoyed FTL and want to try a new type of strategy for this budding genre, this game will probably be fun for you. If you're expecting a 100% clone, you will be disappointed (and why aren't you just playing more FTL?).
Judging the game purely from a genre standpoint, it holds its own. There is a level of difficulty and challenge to everything you do. The game's strategy is deeper than space battles and economics, as it requires you to weigh in risk and probability. I've read several reviews complaining about the amount of failed events you find, but to be honest, I felt like it added another layer of challenge. Even if you skip events to breeze by without extra hull damage or lingering effects, eventually, you will find yourself wanting more Tritanium (A critical resource) than you can't always collect by doing missions or battling pirates.
I look forward to playing more of this game and I can't wait to see what the developers continue to do with it.

Burning Cars is a barely average top-down arcade racing game in the vein of Micro-Machines.  The game consists of playing through a 16 race campaign in either easy or hard modes against 3 other a.i controlled racers in order to win championship points and gain money to upgrading your vehicle.
Probably the best element of gameplay is the marketplace where you canupgrade your vehicle, engine, paintjob and install nitro boosters, armor, weapons and defences.  As the tournament progresses better versions become available to be fitted in the garage screen.
Unfortunately  the actual racing is not great.  Gameplay controls are pretty bad and making a mistake is unforgiving especially on the bends and in tunnels.  At least with keyboard and mouse.  Whats more the vehicles behave wildly when trying to right them to face the correct way.  This is compounded by issues with some walls not being completely smooth causing your car to jerk out of position without an apparent reason, causing you to lose places and most likely the race.  Even if you have nitro boosters present.
Limited combat takes place during the race with any car being able to equip itself with machineguns, shotguns and mines.  Though these only have limited charges unless refils found across the tracks are picked up.  Other refils include: health, nitro, ammo, armor and temporary speed boosts can also be found as you drive.  If the combat had been gratifying then perhaps the game could have seemed better than it otherwise is.
Game duration is also incredibly short.  Both campaigned completed and 100%d achievements in 2 or so hours.  Thankfully the game was purchased on a massive discount.  Otherwise I would have wondered why I had bothered at all with it.  There are much better games of its type out there.  I suggest you try those.  Ultimiately Burning Cars just provides more agony that ecstacy.
However to be fair to the developers if you can look past the games faults bear in mind that the game took five years to get released you could buy it on a massive discount sale.   It does have some nice moments 'when' you manage to keep control of the car and manage to destroy your opponents.  I wouldnt recommend this game but... if you want an easy 100% completion, there are not so many games that can be completed in such a short amount of time.

Even the most recent Death Rally, out in 2012, which was quiet bad, looks good compared to Burning Cars.
First, the story : there is none. Just read the "story" on steam page, that's it. So its a championship taking place in an open-air sewer island, with radioactive waste. You get to drive a trash truck against 3 other drunk bums, shooting and ramming on each other to get first place, get money and points for the 16 rounds of the championship. Now the weird part, the game is called Burning Cars, buts it's not really about cars, only trash trucks and flying buggies.
Those vehicles are armed with various stuff from shotguns to mines dispensers, and nitro, and upgrades. That's for the "Burning" part of the game, you'll often catch on fire driving in those green slimes and from opponents attacks.
About the racing aspect, it's the most tedious and masochist part of the game. Driving those things feels like there is no steering wheel, its a pain to take a turn, like if the tires got glues on the concrete. No handbrake or brake at all to take some drifts in the tight turns. You're lucky if you don't hit a barrier that will throw you into the sky or in reverse direction, especially with those buggies. The walls are also glued, because if you come too close from them, good luck to get off it. Easy tournament let you restart a race, so hopefully you can make it first place, as the opponents are sometimes dumb as hell and got stuck in a wall. Nothing more to add about the gameplay, it's just horrible. Take a careful look at the trailer video on Steam store, it'll show you all the pain you will get about the no-steering and flying on wall thing.
Thankfully, the achievements are quit easy to accomplish, the most frustrating is the hard tournament which will accept no failure, because you can't restart the race when it turns bad, or you go above a barrier or even out of the map, falling in the black void forever... There is steam cards too, but it's only to grab some money they won't make from selling the game itself.
Its a real shame because graphics are ok, of only physics was good, with more environment variety, and a multiplayer mode.
Don't get this game, unless you get it in a bundle, its pure pain and frustration for a masochist price. You've been warned.

If you have no patience for cyclical puzzle games, then avoid this like the plague.
However if lateral thinking is your thing then I suggest giving this a go.
I'd be lying if I said there were no similarities to Portal here; the first person puzzle POV, the single manipulative 'gun', and at a stretch the level design are familiar. Yet the object here is think about how each puzzle can be solved by manipulating small cubes, lasers and even the very levels themselves; and each puzzle may have different routes and different solutions.
You will find yourself entering the same rooms over and over again, either by your own volition navigating the starting menu, or by the seemingly random teleporting. But as you progress to upgrade your gun, previously impossible rooms will seem so simple to traverse.
I will however mention one point that may put people off; the visuals.
Some may say vivid, others seizure inducing; take your pick. Though this may play in its favour as you shouldn't be sat at the monitor for too long anyway (guilty as charged).
Replayability isn't really there, unless you wish to try your own speed run, and the way the cube physics works takes a little trial and error to fully utilise.
A nice added bonus is the 'developer rooms' dotted around detailing the build process of the game over the years.
These aren't mandatory to complete the game; you could get to the exit without visiting many of the rooms but the completionist I am kept me going.
All in all I liked the game; it is a fresh concept, taxed the mind, and even though it wasn't painfully complicated, I still felt accomplished to complete the game.

This game is pretty easy to explain.  You move a triangle clockwise or counterclockwise around a hexagon in the center of the screen,making an effort to avoid being crushed by six walls closing in on you.  Your goal in each level in the basic Hexagons is to survive at least a minute, after which the speed of the Hexagon walls will increase as you enter that Hexagon's "Hyper" mode.  This also unlocks the Hyper mode in question from the main menu, allowing you to skip right to the more challenging segments.  Surviving a minute in Hyper mode will allow you to truly complete that hexagon.
Despite the straightforward description however, actually playing this game is a frantic test of reflexes, as even the default speed is very quick and easy to be overwhelmed by, at first.  The patterns of incoming walls can be incredibly difficult to wedge between, requiring percision and speed.  This could easily become frustrating in any other game, however, Super Hexagon mitigates the frustration with its quick game over-to-reload time.  With the press of a button, you're back in the action and at it again, learning from your mistakes, and seeing the time until a game over in a stage slowly rise to the minute mark.  Not many will complete this game (I doubt I will), or even one stage in it, but when losing doesn't feel like much of a waste, it manages to remain fun regardless  The exelent aethetics, from the pumping beat and the flashy background certainly help as well.
In one sentance: A simple to learn, but extremely challenging and addictive game, with vibrant visuals and a catchy soundtrack.
I highly reccomend giving it a go.

A game like Antichamber should not be played by people like myself; games that have puzzles that go beyond merely logic, reasoning, memorization or problem solving and into the realm of beating your head against it until a solution reveals itself do not sit entirely well with me. This is more an issue with myself than those types of games for sure, but while Antichamber does take a couple of cues from Portal, this title is a drastically different experience that, while at times went way over my head, I can still recommend to people who want a puzzler that's different from your Trines or Professor Laytons or Mysts.
I'm really the wrong demographic for this kind of game, but Antichamber's advertising suckered me in since I wanted an exploration-based puzzle game in similar veins to La-Mulana; puzzles that were made to crush lesser minds. While I did get that vibe and happily did so, Antichamber sometimes felt like it could get away with whatever it wanted and did so with crossed arms and shrugged shoulders to the player. The Steam store page does say, quote, 'Antichamber is a mind-bending psychological exploration game where nothing can be taken for granted. Discover an Escher-like world where hallways wrap around upon each other, spaces reconfigure themselves, and accomplishing the impossible may just be the only way forward'. 'Accomplishing the impossible' may sound quite romantic to a player thinking about buying the game, but there are some cases where the impossible is possible, it just requires a ridiculous solution. To talk about these cases would just be absolute shameful spoilers and would take away from your experience, but the big pro tip here is that just when you think you've tried absolutely everything and are ready to give up, you actually haven't tried absolutely everything and need to try again. Not every puzzle in Antichamber is this 'impossible', as for a majority of the game your challenges are quite tame; blocks, switches, platforming, interacting with the environment, toying with some anomaly that's keeping you from progressing... Many of these can be solved just through expirimentation, trial and error or simple application of your brain, and for quite some time you can chug through the game at a steady rate, only meeting major opposition when you near the end of the game - And I mean major. Again, perhaps I'm the wrong kind of person for this kind of game, but at some point I ran up against puzzles where just nothing clicked and I found myself spinning my wheels in perpetual defeat, and that's where my enjoyment of the game took a heavy drop.
What kept me from really getting sour on the game is that at just about any time you can return to the main 'hub' room where you can look at a map of the 'facility' (players have insinuated there's a story some kind, but there's no plot in Antichamber at all) and then teleport elsewhere. This means that you can zip around the game and try assaulting a puzzle again or from a different angle, never being stuck against just one challenge forever until you complete it. This is an absolute god-send of a feature, and one that no doubt has kept many players (including myself) from quitting the game with a bitter aftertaste. It's also incredibly useful since you can stumble upon shortcuts or alternate exits everywhere that will take you all over the place, sometimes not quite in the direction you wanted to go. If you keep hallway-wrapping into a room you've visited or accidentally fall off a bridge that melts if you're looking at it, being able to warp back and try again keeps frustration down to a minimum, especially when you're trying to find the matter 'guns' to further manipulate blocks that you need for switches, platforms or other impede your progress.
The 'guns' is the aforementioned cue from Portal, and how they help you get around the game is the other. Again, to talk in detail about the puzzles you'll encounter would be shameful spoilers, but each new gun upgrade you find unlocks that much more of the game, with a myriad of possible solutions and new challenges to run into, which is a good feeling of constantly asking yourself 'what's next?' when you unlock this door or find a way past this chasm. You'll be looking forward to the next puzzle and not to the designs of the rooms as a whole since the game's sterile white environment at times feels just downright oppressive on the eyes, save for the splashes of bold, full colors that are strangely relieving when mixed in with the 'music' that is nothing but ambiance noises that I feel were designed to keep the player as relaxed as possible when hopping around the game trying to figure out a new solution. Color doesn't play any sort of theme like in Okami, but it does serve as something to take hold of your attention and to differentiate one route from another to avoid confusion.
While it sounds like I haven't had the greatest time with Antichamber, I walked away from it (and completed it) quite satisfied with the experience I had, and some minor technical hiccups like major frame-rate hitches during transitions and broken floor geometry were just that - Hiccups. Antichamber brings to the table a wildly different kind of puzzle game that sometimes can feel like it's cheating in order to challenge you, but overcoming these challenges brings personal accomplishment that is its own high. My overall enjoyment of the game left something to be desired, but I can still happily recommend Antichamber to those looking for a puzzle game that doesn't follow conventional rules.

Teleglitch is amazing, a must have for any diehard gamer.  It's brutally hard, I still haven't been able to get to level 7 yet (I probably need to use to learn the knife better), but you rarely feel cheated from your many, many deaths.  Like Nethack, all your problems could have been avoided in hindsight.
The graphics of the game, while extremely rudimentary, actually add to it; I love how much horror shows through, even though the monsters and worlds are just a few blurry pixels.  The storyline is interesting, and vividly describes the terror of the world you're living in, with a touch of humor as well.  If you're not interested in reading the computer logs to know how things got they way they are, they're also completely avoidable, and never forced upon you.
All of the monsters have their own unique personality (and freaking TRICKY movement patterns!  Those stupid small ones, yeeeeeaarrrgghhh!), and none of them seem repetitious, or rehashes of earlier versions.
The best part about this game?  THE CRAFTING SYSTEM!  Holy heck, I wish EVERY crafting game was as intuitive as Teleglitch.  Instead of needing a wiki article explaining how to make things you'd never have known exist, all you do is press a single key, and the crafting menu pops up, showing your entire inventory, what can currently be crafted from it, and what each of those items will cost you, using an easy to follow line diagram system.  Crafting is so easy, it can be done on the fly, during fights!  It couldn't be improved upon, except possibly to see items you can't craft yet, so you know what they take, but IMO, that would take away from the fun of discovery in the game, and add very little.
Teleglitch is a game I'll always be happy to own, and if I had somehow pirated it (why? it's SO cheap!), I would actually pay money for a retail copy to support the designers.  I collect games like they're little works of art, and am proud to display this in my collection.

Teleglitch is a game which pushes roguelikes into real time quite well. A departure from the typical turn based roguelikes (which I do enjoy), there's an additional element of action, forcing you to act without having any time to plan your actions.
The story is pretty typical with an experiment gone wrong, with the facility gone to hell. Aside from the monologue between levels, terminals are scattered through the randomly generated areas, with small bits and pieces to inform you of the various devices in the game, as well as things you can do to make your life more manageable.
Graphically, this game does well. Without attempting to try and make the graphics realistic, the pixel style is a nice step up from the grid-based tile setup, and the lighting flickers to just show the outline of the enemies ahead.
The sounds are minimalistic, and the eery silence will make you strain to listen out for any of the encounters that could be lurking in the shadows. Weapons sound the way you'd imagine, although they are a vast contrast to when you're not in combat.
Gameplay in Teleglitch is challenging and unforgiving, layering pressure with every level as you struggle to manage materials, deal with the enemies, and escape from the current sector.

I really like this game.
It is unashamed and frankly completely transparent about its inspirations, namely Diablo. References to Diablo abound, from the slurry old Sage standing next to the well, the trek through the ruined cathedral down to the depths of hell, and also the first boss (which I won't spoil). However, it is its own game with its own merits that merely uses Diablo as a platform from which to launch its own trajectory.
The game uses cards to represent its loot, and your character has a limited number of slots to equip cards to. While you can change them out at any time, only cards that are equipped will provide their effects. At first, I wasn't sure about the card system. This game isn't really a deck builder, which is how another review presented it to me. At least, it's not a deck builder by the strictest definition. There are no random draws, and every card you collect becomes a permanent part of your inventory. No shuffling, dealing, or stacking odds in your favour by omitting certain cards as is the norm with deck builders. Cards are persistent and essentially act as items, equipment, or spells in the same way any drop in Diablo would. The fact that they are cards kind of misrepresented how they work, for me. However, it's part of the pop-up book flavour and really it's just a cosmetic decision. What matters to me is that the way you use them has meaningful gameplay inplications and which ones you choose to equip essentially represents your character build. Some cards have great synergy with others, and it feels good to encounter a pack of enemies that your build is perfectly suited against, and sometimes actually terrifying when you come up against others that seem like perfect counters.
I was initially in danger of not finding the meat of this game, and losing interest early. To begin with, the cards felt kind of inconsequential, as the game seemed quite easy - the enemies were predictable, their behaviours exploitable. Being able to attack anything at range even with a melee weapon felt like I could cheese my way through the whole game. The cards didn't seem to matter too much - my first one gave me a chance to block projectiles, and really that translated to a very small and random advantage against enemies that died in a couple of hits and rarely hit me anyway. However, don't let the slow start fool you. Once the game ramps up its enemy variety, and starts introducing mechanics that change the battlefield, disrupt your mechanics, and more, the magic starts to happen. It doesn't take too long for it to do so.
Level generation is what you'd expect from a Roguelike that borrows from Diablo - you see the occasional familiar piece, but all in all it is a competent and varied system that never lets things get stale. The fact that you have to stick to the path initially worried me that the game would lack depth, but it has clever systems (namely in enemy behaviour) that are built around this which make it work. Discovery is part of the excitement, so I won't warn you what any of them are.
The "Flexiscope" system is wonderful. Essentially the game breaks itself down into chunks and allows you to tell it how large you want the chunk you're about to enter to be, scaling the difficulty and rewards accordingly. If you've got only 15 minutes to spare you can select the small size option and still have a relatively fulfilling run. The system learns from your playstyle and average completion times of each size and builds a more accurate idea of how long it will take you to complete any given size over time. This system is pretty cool as it means you don't necessarily have to set aside an afternoon to properly enjoy this game, as is the case with many RPGs.
To top it off, the game has great ambient audio (which is something the first Diablo absolutely nailed compared to its successors), very competent voice acting, and polished presentation. The previously mentioned pop-up book style kind of rubbed me the wrong way at first, because I wasn't sure it was going to adequately convey the isolation and claustrophobia of being a vulnerable human stepping into a dungeon of evils, but it grew on me. They took a risk with the art direction, and it paid off because of their commitment to it and their undying vision of how it would all come together.
If I have to list some negatives, it would be that the game feels slightly too easy with my current build. This will likely be remedied once I complete it and unlock another playthrough at a higher difficulty setting, though, so don't read too far into it. For posterity, though, I'm more than 3/4 through the game (in my first playthrough) and have not yet died once, although I admittedly have been close to it and was saved with some potion spam and some prioritization of enemies.
Another issue I find is that there are sections of the game where some cards feel like the "best" to use. This could be because I am invested in their play style, and have upgraded them - using a non-upgraded alternative card lacks a lot of the punch I'm used to. I've also felt lucky with some of the legendary drops I've received that matched the way I want to play. However, there are at least two cards that I feel I simply could not have survived particular encounters without. I plan on experimenting with different builds in the future, but knowing what I know about the enemies that appear and the formations you encounter, I think it's going to be hard to try anything drastically different.
If you like dungeon crawlers and/or Roguelikes, you owe it to yourself to give this a go. It's familiar enough - it has all the elements that you enjoy about those games and many of the staples that the genre demands, which includes the cliches (but in a fun, self-aware way). However, as familiar as it feels, it does everything in its own little nuanced way which gives it some new life in a frankly cluttered genre.

It's a bit weird writing a review of a game that I first played over ten years ago, but here I am on Steam just after buying a state-of-the-art gaming laptop and installing Half Life 2 to see how well it plays on it.
The answer to that is of course 'amazingly' - but I was not of course expecting my new machine to struggle when playing it as it could probably do it with one arm tied behind its back.  It's more of a question of why I am still coming back to an old game that I've played through many, many times and will probably continue to do so until I am physically incapable of holding a mouse and using a keyboard?!  It's a curious question indeed, but it is one that I'm going to have a pop at answering all the same.
You see, Half Life 2 is one of those rare games in that absolutely EVERYTHING was done perfectly.  From the graphics (which were really ahead of their time and still don't look bad, all things considered), the sound, the likable characters, dystopian storyline and the gameplay mechanics all gel brilliantly to make it quite simply one of the best games ever made - and it still holds up well to brand new games.
There are so many brilliant moments in the game, from the tense chase scene at the beginning as you run up the stairs to escape being captured by the combine soldiers, to the superb driving & hovercraft sections, being attacked by the flying hunter-killer gunships, pinned down by snipers, the spooky jaunt through Ravenholme and the terrifying encounters with the huge robotic walkers.  And all of this is held tightly together with realistic supporting characters and a narrative that drives everything along beautifully.
A special mention has to be said about the audio in HL2, as it has some of the most memorable sound effects you'll ever hear in gaming.   The sound design is just incredible and even thinking about the game evokes the sound of combine radio chatter, thumping gunfire, the sound as the gunships spot you and the chittering noise of the headcrabs.  There are few games that sound as good, even to this day.
So why do I keep coming back?  Because it's bloody excellent and, like a good movie, only serves to get even better over time as it's easy to appreciate how much of a breakthrough title it was and paved the way for so many modern titles.
It's impossible, of course, to not speak about the two episodes that come after HL2 as they are just as vitally excellent as the game that spawned them and add even more to the excellent storyline and character development.  And then it ends on a cliffhanger and we're all left wanting more.
...But are we going to see a Half Life 3?  I honestly hope so.  Valve would be fools to not eventually deliver the goods and come out with a sequel to what is undoubtedly one of the most loved games ever made.  Come on, Gabe!  Do it!

Now, I'm a big fan of these hidden object adventure games, and I can safely say that there are some amazing ones out there. Sadly, "Crystals of Time" is not one of them.
First of all, the game pretty much leaves you to your own devices for the most part. It's hard to tell which rooms you're supposed to go to next; I kept having to press the hint button to figure out where I was supposed to go. Not only that, you can't easy-jump from room to room using the map; it only leads to certain general areas of the house, the garden, etc. As a result, there's a lot of backtracking involved, and it quickly gets annoying.
Second, the so-called story in this game really has no bearing when you actually start playing. First of all, why does a thief need to break into an abandoned mansion? And those "crystals of time" that are supposed to be super-important? Yeah, you spend most of the game looking for the crystals, but actual time traveling literally only happens in three rooms of the game. Nowhere else! This results in the ending being one of the most anticlimactic I have ever seen. We're introduced to all these characters and pieces of a story, but they don't seem to completely fit together.
As for the puzzles themselves, they're fine. I was pretty much able to figure them all out without any difficulty. But if you like a good story to go with your hidden-object adventure games, I do not recommend this one. At least, not unless you like sitting for thirty seconds waiting for the hint button to recharge.

Crystals of Time, for me, felt like a very nostalgic game. It's a simple point-n-click, hidden object, game. The graphics are beautifully rendered and painted. It's definitely a very casual game that you can always go back to whenever you want. The story is pretty basic and straight forward.
Some people might find it an annoyance to have to wander around to get clues and objects.
But really, all you need to do is access your map to get closer to the rooms you need to be in.
This isn't an mmorpg, don't think that you'll be able to click on everything and expect to find secret spots.
Crystals of Time has very simple game mechanics, you only click what's necessary.
So if you're a fan of simple, no frills, games and want a relaxed playing experience?
Then yes, you'll probably enjoy Crystals of Time.
But if you want to be able to poke around more and get more in depth?
This may not be the game for you.
For what it is, I find it to be a well made game.
The developers knew exactly what they wanted and stuck with it.
Even technically, there was nothing inherently wrong with the gameplay.
It just all boils down to personal preference.

This was the Shadowrun I wanted when I couldn't get *into* it back on the SNES. The story is deep but easy to get into, and while the engine feels sluggish, four hours in my first sitting is an excellent indicator of how engrossing this world is. I've heard it described as the 'weakest' of the rebooted series, but that is only a testament its success.
What's fun:
- Intelligent, thoughtful and entertaining writing
- Fantastic character design and visual astectic
- Thematic, moody music that is unintrusive
- Dresden
- Combat is fluid and engaging
- Smooth difficulty curve with a storyline around which you are the focus
What's not fun:
- The interface is very bsaic; getting the job done and requiring more of a learning curve than the gameplay
- Cover based combat is introduced without any guide
- Shopping can be confusing as you can't see what's in your inventory at the same time (a feature in RPGs since the early 90s)
The 'not fun' aspects are very minor quibbles as I easily found the patience to learn the system. It's nice to see a game that doesn't insult its playerbase, as games often do. Having to remember and/or double check your inventory before purchases is hardly a chore.
Any fan of cyberpunk and fantasy needs to give this one a try, and it can be had quite affordably via various bundles online.

This is a great turn-based strategy RPG whether or not you're familiar with the Shadowrun universe.  If you're already familiar with Shadowrun and have been looking for a new Shadowrun game... well you probably already own this but if you don't, get it.
Gushing aside, this was the first of the Harebrained Schemes Shadowrun games and the least polished.  The story is pretty linear and offers little opportunity for exploration, which is a shame because this is a setting begging to be explored.  This could be a plus though, as it offers a focused story experience that you can play through in a dozen hours or so.  And then you can move on to the vastly super sequel, Shadowrun: Dragonfall.
Combat resembles the new X-Com games, where most characters have 2 "action points" which are used for moving, attacking, using special items or magic spells, or performing an "overwatch" type action where the character will auto-fire at any enemies that enter their cone of sight.  There is also the Matrix, which basically functions as another combat map with a different set of abilities for the decker (Shadowrun's "hacker") that enters it.
Overall it's a great game, but not as great as its successors.  The game can be played through in ~15 hours and there's not much reason for replay.  Definitely worth picking up if you enjoy turn-based strategy RPGs like X-Com or Final Fantasy Tactics.

I do reccomend this game. but as the reveiws are "mixed" right now these are a few reasons why.
Right now in early access this game is VERY frusterating. I think the developers released it a little too early because:
Areas that desperately need development.
1) It is riddled with game ending bugs that will lead to unavoidable crew deaths/ship explosions. They have an auto-save feature that lets you reload in case this happens but some of the bugs will corrupt your save game and you have to start over.
2) Many of the events are still very rudimentary. e.g. Would you like to stop at this space station? Yes/No. Yes. You       scratch someone's ship and lose x amount of credits. You have no option to choose what you do at the space station and once the event is over you cannot return to it. That's just one event example.
3) The UI during combat often obscures ship rooms both on enemy and player ships making targeting/repairing very annoying.
Why I recommend it:
1) This game is NOT FTL and should only be compared to it in that the format is the same. After you take FTL out of the equation, it's a decent game.
2) When the above deficiencies are corrected this game is going to be awesome.
3) This game has potential to be the best game of its type at this time. They have a mod manager tab in the start menu which will allow users to augment this game and further improve its playability.

Summary:
I like this game. A LOT. After more than 80 hours of gameplay, I'm still not tired of it. Space Rogue has earned my STRONG RECOMMENDATION. Buy it!!
Gameplay:
This game is really well thought out and super fun to play. It is a very enjoyable Rogue-like/permanent-death space adventure game with pretty graphics and great customization options. Your ship can be upgraded with an in-game resource to support more and better equipment, and equipment can be found in missions or purchased from trading outposts. A wide variety of weapon classes, drones, and "cartridges" lends additional depth to gameplay as each type has its own strength and weaknesses. There is a huge spectrum of difficulty customization available if you want it, and harder challenges are rewarded with a higher XP multiplier. There is even a "Workshop" feature where anyone can design new quests and share them within the user community, which gives the game almost limitless depth.
-----
Even though I love this game, there are still some bugs that need attention from the developer. Please consider the rest of this review a bug report for the developer's benefit, in hopes that this information can help them identify and resolve these bugs. Please don't let this distract from the positive review. Below are the issues I have experienced over about 30 hours of gameplay in version 1.3:
Minor annoyances:
-Broken, missing, or unlabeled hotkeys
-Saved positions for some crew members are sometimes forgotten
-Enlarged enemy ship view obscures bays in your own ship. Could my ship veiw be shifted to the left to utilize the empty screen real estate? I see this view in some of the screenshots on the store page, but I can't make it look like that in game.
Major annoyances:
-Equipped weapons, drones, and cartridges sometimes disappear, leaving empty spaces
-Crew members occasionally vanish without a trace
Critical issues: (possibly related to the "major annoyances" above)
-Unable to access ship screen or trading screen at bases. The game is still playable, but can't repair or upgrade ship. When this happens, the number of weapon/drone/cartridge slots displayed at the bottom of the screen changes and they become unclickable.
-Game stops responding completely and "end task" must be used to close it. Unfortunately, the game sometimes auto-saves this state, which means the game will load into this state and the saved game is ruined, requiring starting over to resolve.

Ace Team is known for making surreal games and this is definitely their most surreal of the bunch. That's probably the only good thing I can say about it, because the gameplay is an absolute glitchy mess and it isn't nearly as polished as their other releases.
It simply lacks polish in every area imaginable; the combat system is obtuse as heck, so it definitely ain't Dark Souls or Punch Out!!, you have to backtrack a friggin' lot and you only have a map with general directions, so it's very likely you'll get lost a LOT and it only gets worse with respawned enemies, so instead of enjoying the weird scenery, you try to traverse as quickly as possible to avoid every respawned enemy.
The story presentation... I don't know if it's intentional or not, but it's a jumbled mess that borders on the surreal. I get the general gist of "order vs chaos", but the way the characters deliver their dialogues is just weird and sometimes a bit jarring, also the audio mixing is all over the place, the music is incredibly loud and you can barely listen to the characters speaking, but even with the music lowered, the dialogue mixing is still uneven.
It's a shame though, because the world is absolutely fascinating to explore and even look at, that's until you see a rabbit running backwards, all sense of wander wears off almost immediately. I guess you can decide for yourself is that was intentionally part of the surrealism or not.
I would only recommend it just to experience the weirdness of it, because it's definitely quite tedious and frustrating.

is the sequel to ACE TEAM's pugilistic brawler set in the bizarre and fascinating world of Zenozoik. Ghat and his sister Rimat must explore the land and meet unusual characters along the way, on a quest to rid zenozoik from an oppressing force of a dark and otherworldly realm. Like it's predecessor, in zenozoik you handle things with your fists first and ask questions later. Unlike it's predecessor it's brighter more colorful and a bit less subtle and disturbing. This sometimes works to the games benefit however, since some of the places you can explore look outstanding. There is a large variety of enemies and the combat has been a just a little improved. It's also a much longer game than it's predecessor, and you'll be exploring Zenozoik and collecting achievements much longer than before. I feel the soundtrack is very unique, although sometimes hit or miss in regards to appropriateness to the level design. The story is told with quite a bit of dialogue and cutscenes, for better or for worse. But the game is still very fun, and if you have a friend why not give the COOP a try?
+ Improved Graphics
+ Much longer than the original game
+ Interesting variety of settings and enemies
+ The Night/Day system is quite good
+ Much more open-world and free-roaming than the original
+ Has cooperative multiplayer
+ RPG elements offer depth to the gameplay
+ Feels somehow different from the original
+ Combat isn't as fun or engaging as the first game.
+ Story isn't as interesting or abstract as the original
+ Music sometimes feels distracting and unfitting
+ It starts to get repetitive after a while.
+ Imagery/themes feel toned down compared to the original
If there was to be a ZC3 i'd recommend keeping the RPG elements, Keeping the world-exploration/quests and expanding the mythos without revealing everything. Keep the audience craving more of Zenozoik. Also keep it dark like the original. I feel the somewhat sanitized atmosphere of ZC2 (Probably at the Publishers request) might be hurting the game's creative potential. Keep it dark, weird and mysterious! (And also seriously add more variety to the combat, it feels lacking.)

Book Of Demons is a fantastic hack and slash dungeon crawler, even for a game that is in early access it has an extremely solid base game that I hope they will build around and continue to expand upon as they move out of the early access stage of their game.
So where to even begin with this game... Well let's start of with how the game works and what makes this game just so damn good. To start off with the game has a option before you even begin the game for you to decide how long you want the dungeon to go on for until you reach the end of that section. This sort of mechanic isn't usually shown in many games nowadays, and it really helps with those people who don't have too much time on their hands to play hours upon hours of games everyday. You only want to play for 5 minutes? We've got you covered! Want to go for an hour long play through? No problem, the game is very nice for giving you this option as it provides the player with a reasonable playtime if you're short on time and only want to play through part of a dungeon for a couple of minutes.
As well as this useful mechanic, the game also provides a deck building mechanic that aid you upon your quest. Even though there isn't much depth to the deck building side of the game, it provide a variety of different play styles, so being able to mix and match cards will be up to your own personal preference. There are 3 different types of cards, artifact cards, item cards and spell cards. Artifact cards are basically passive cards and the ones that I used throughout the entire game, there is a nice variety of these cards, as well as legendary and magical types of each card. Some of them will allow you to cause enemies to slow, whilst others will give you a chance to stun enemies, and even regenerate health. Items cards are basically consumables, healing potions, town portal, toxic bombs etc. and the final one being mana cards, which are spell cards. I personally never used these cards, and never really felt like I needed to.
Now, something that I was slightly concerned about was the way that your character could only move on the set path that is built in the dungeon. I mean why would you need your character to only be able to walk across a one block path? For me this kind of limited the way I could play the game, but didn't make ruin the enjoyment of the game for me. I would've liked maybe a bit more freedom to move around on these set paths, maybe make it 2 or 3 blocks wide so I can move around a bit more. I suppose that the game was designed like this with a purpose to make it more challenging, but for me it didn't really hit the mark. It's a small thing, but something that I think would make me want to play the game more.
Speaking of dungeons, the game provides procedurally generated dungeons each time that you choose a length time to play through. I really enjoyed this aspect of the game, as this keeps the game fresh and allows for a nice amount of replay ability once you have completed the main storyline of the game. However, I feel like it was slightly lacking a variety of different 'tiles' that are used to piece together each dungeon. I would of like to see a bit more variety with these 'tiles' just to make the dungeons seem different from one another.
So does the game provide a nice amount of enemy types that co-inside with the randomly generated dungeons in the game? Yes it does, there is wide variety of enemies that you will encounter at different part of the game, all of them having different fighting styles whether they shoot projectiles at you, or run at you knocking you out for a few seconds, every enemy feels well thought out and put together. You will find different enemies in all 3 different areas, from demons to ghosts to goat things each area has it's own arrangement of enemies that you will have to adjust your play style to in order to effectively kill them.
Needless to say, the graphics in this game are extremely unique and something that I personally haven't seen much of when it comes to gaming. It's kind of like a pop-up book world, but combines it with dark dungeons that really seems to fit the game and the atmosphere in general. All the characters and enemies look very nice, and it's all very consistent throughout the game.
+ Choose the length of each dungeon, from a 5 minute run to an hour run. Very useful for people who don't have too much time to play games for hours upon hours.
+ Even though the deck building isn't very in-depth, it does provide a different play style being able to mix and match different types of cards to suit your play style.
+ Procedurally generated dungeons makes the game have better replay value.
+ Nice variety of enemies throughout the game, most enemies are contained in one of the three dungeon areas.
+ Very unique graphics that isn't really used much in gaming nowadays, works well with the game itself
+ Good length storyline, 12 - 15 hours of gameplay + freeplay mode for more of a challenge.
- Only being able to walk on the set path that is provided, kind of limits where you can go but for me didn't ruin the enjoyment of the game all that much.
Overall this game is extremely well built and put together, even though it's still in early access. The game provides a nice length main storyline (will last about 12 - 15 hours) as well a free play afterwards so you can continue going through these dungeons. I for one am very excited to see where this game goes next, and can't for more game modes, and more storyline (maybe) as the game continues to get updated. Would defiantly recommend this game to any fans who enjoy a good dungeon crawler.

Antichamber combines challenging puzzle solving metrics with a beautiful art style to create something that I can say is truely unique. As some puzzle-solving games suffer from prolonged gameplay, Antichamber uses random topsy-turvy, vertigo-inducing elements to make something as basic as walking interesting.
__________
Story: Put simply, there is none. Antichamber revels in the moment of the game's experience to give you an entertaining on-the-spot experience.
Graphics: Fantastic. The use of cel-shading is phenomonal. Colorful, yet simple environments. While it may not be the BEST looking cel-shaded game, it still is nothing to scoff at.
The Game Environment: Strange, hilarious, and unpredictable. False floors / doors, teleporting, gravity platforms, second dimensions, this game has it all.
---One scenario: You walk into a room and observe window-like objects in the corner of the white room. Walking up to it, you notice the window seems to peer into another room, something like an Alice In Wonderland moment. Turning around to look for more clues where to go next, the room behind you has transformed into another room completely, looking exactly like the blue room you saw in the window. Woah.
Gameplay: Like I've said before, it's nothing short of a wild acid trip. The puzzles are challenging and have many of those "Ah!" lightbulb moments as you explore different gameplay mechanics.
____________________________________________
Overall, it's a must-buy, regardless of whether you really enjoy puzzle-type games.

There are a large number of problems with the game that cannot be overlooked, such as a number of achievements not functioning properly, and some other glitchy environments and setpieces. The game probably should have spent another month or two in testing in order to work out some of the small bugs that can in some ways interrupt the immersive experience that the developers want for Dying Light. This game needs some polishing, in all honesty.
However,
This is a game that is worth your full attention.
It feels like eons since I have had this much fun in a video game. This is a game that I don't want to stop playing once I start, and I feel like everyone else should have the opportunity to experience the intense amount of fun that I have had with this game.
The multiplayer works very well. The drop in/drop out system is rather fluid, and this game's atmosphere and play style work well with multiple players. Also, drop kicking zombies back and forth between your friends is pretty cool.
While the weapon selection is limited in a sense, I have never been so satisfied with swinging swords, machetes, and baseball bats into hordes of undead, and watching the unholy carnage pile up. Zombie smashing is fun again.
My last point comes to that so-called 'X-factor' that we gamers look for in games. It's that sense that we've just found a game that makes us feel like an utter badass as we do whatever it is that the game's objective is. It's that feeling that makes us not want to turn away from the game just so we can kill one more zombie, or grapple to one more rooftop.
Dying Light has that X-factor for me.
I'm not saying that you've got to put a hundred hours into this game, but again, I'll say, this game is worth your full attention.
Give it a go.
Good Night, and Good luck.
Regards,
Jman

Half-Life 2 is a First Person Shooter developed by Valve and released late 2004. This is actually the first game I owned and played on my steam account, I cannot speak highly enough of the whole Half-Life series.
Half-Life 2 starts on a train arriving at City 17, you play as the protagonist “Gordon Freeman”, get used to that name, because everyone knows it and exclaims it when they see you.
Not long after getting off the train, you come across old acquaintances Dr. Kleiner and Barney Calhoun, they send Gordon on his way to join up with an underground group known as the "Lambda Resistance".
I won't risk saying and spoiling anything about the rest of story; this is one of the games that I contrast against many other story telling narratives – because it's so well done. Even replaying the game after so many years, Half-Life 2 is still a very enjoyable game and I believe the series will survive the test of time to become a staple in video game history.
As you progress through the game you unlock new weapons, and explore new area's, you can switch between your weapons with the scroll wheel or number keys, sometimes you double up on the same weapon categories
All of your standard FPS's are in the game, your basic “go to”
weapons are: The crowbar, pistol, and Submachine Gun.
The weapons you unlock are:
About half of the achievements in Half-Life 2 are unlocked on your first play through, the other half are Easter eggs, or various objectives challanges.
The hardest/longest achievement is Lambda Locator, which requires you to find each Lambda Cache.
As you play through the game you will sometimes come across a “λ” Lambda, that means there's a Lambda Resistance weapons cache nearby.
The standalone price for Half-Life 2 is $9.99 you will probably come close to nine hours of gameplay within this game. I've personally replayed the story several times so for me it was a great value.
However, I have a better recommendation; if you are thinking about getting Half-Life 2, Half-Life 2: Episode One, Half-Life 2: Episode Two, and/or Portal, you should purchase
for $19.99, you will get all of the afore mentioned game titles.
Story: Excellent, a personal all-time favorite of mine. Gameplay: Solid controls, solid physics, solid, solid solid. Even after all these years the game is still very good. Achievements: Fairly doable 100% completed game. Price: Fair, but I suggest getting the Orange Box deal.
I recommend this game to people who enjoy darker serious stories, FPS's, or don't swear by the latest game releases

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

Just like the first Killing Floor, this game comes with a great soundtrack and intense gameplay that makes your blood pump like crazy. You can feel the adrenaline pumping like hell if you're playing for example Farmhouse on Hell on Earth and all your teammates are dead when it's round 10/10 with 200 Zeds left, and you keep telling yourself that you can make it through this, over and over while you hear those terrifying Fleshpounds and Scrakes spawn, ready to bash you open and eat your intestines while you're burning/shooting/sawing through all those pesky Clots, Cysts, and Gorefasts standing in your way while everything is running after you, round and around the barn you keep on running, you don't even have the time to stop and think, you just got to keep moving for God knows how long while blood is splattering all over the place.
Now with that long introduction out of the way, let's get started.
Killing Floor 2 is a co-op survival horror game, very similar, if not identical to the first Killing Floor, (but with better graphics) where you're supposed to survive a bunch of waves (with friends, of course, unless you have none *Sad face*) while loads of zombie-mutants trying to kill you. At the end of each wave, you get access to the trader. Where you can buy weapons and such. ''-How do you buy weapons at the trader after each wave?'' You may ask. Simple; you kill Zeds to get money. (That's what the Zombies are called in the game) That's why you need to be the player being most out in action. I mean, you don't have to be out in the action all the time, but if you want Dosh to buy stuff, you sure gotta kill- kill- kill!
I pre-purchased Killing Floor 2, and it's still as fun as it was back in middle of 2015.
''-Uh, doesn't it get pretty repetetive after some time? They release new maps and all, but not new items and cool updates too, right?''
Well, they do. They release new bosses, (they've released The Patriarch which was the boss of
the first Killing Floor, and they've got more coming) new perks, (wait, no, they've released all perks now, I believe) new and old weapons, probably some DLC coming, maps, (obviously) new game modes, and much more.
Speaking of maps, on every map in the game that's a Tripwire server, will there be collectibles. Like for example; on the map 'Prison', the collectible is a soap with a rope around it to keep around your neck. ;)
Keep in mind now: The collectibles look different on each map. Unless Tripwire hasn't made a model for it yet. If it hasn't got a model yet, it'll just be a Dosh-sign with a rope around it. Kind of like a necklace. You can look for them, and if you find ten of them on each map, you'll get an achievement. I don't know why I'm writing this, but if you're new, and want a little ''easter egg hunt'' in your violent zombie-slashing game, then this game is definitely for you.
By the way...as much as they have updated the first Killing Floor, I am 100% sure that they will always have something planned for this game to update. Even if it's just crates with cosmetics, new skins, whatever. They'll always have something up their sleeves.
The characters are as funny as always; mean, ironic, sarcastic, funny, and insulting. There's one thing I'd like to mention about the characters that is really neat: Is that they've all got different voices now. Before, in the first Killing Floor, all the male characters had one guy doing all the voices. When I say ''doing all the voices'', I mean that they took one guy, and copy-pasted his voice. So every male character had the same voice actor. Even though that guy sounded awesome, it was kinda weird having Pyro from Team Fortress 2 going around with the same voice-lines as Harold Lott. Vice versa with all the female characters.
I have nothing else to say about this game really, I've never experienced any lag or desync for that matter. So you've just got to buy the game, and judge for yourself. Because trust me, it's worth it, and you won't get tired of it either. Unless it's something wrong with you, and you don't think it's fun to slash through endless amounts of zombies with stunning graphics.
Nah.

You'd be forgiven for thinking at first that FTL had just undergone a facelift. The game plays very, very similarly. Welcome to Space Rogue, another entrant in the opening wave of "FTL-Likes" to go along with Convoy. It's been quite some time since FTL came out, and to be fair nobody has really gone out of their way to try and cook up what FTL achieved, indeed, FTL set the bar so ridiculously high there was a sense anyone trying would have to differentiate themselves pretty hard lest they wind up being seen as a poor version of FTL. So far we've had things like Death Skid Marks (Excellent), Convoy (Reasonable) and now we have Space Rogue. Space Rogue however hews closest to FTL's formula, in so much as it puts you in command of a ship which you fly through sectors of space.
In the current iteration of SR, events are taken from a nice diverse pool, and most of them end up with combat. Unlike FTL there's not a lot of subtlety going on, the vast majority of the time you'll be murdering whatever gets in your way, or you'll be getting rewarded FOR murdering whatever got in your way. There are the rare, thankful occasions when that's not the case, but in this game, combat is the norm, not the exception.
This would be fine if combat was solid and satisfying, currently it's rudimentary. It takes a lot of cues from FTL (with the PiP view of the enemy ship) to allow for specific targetting of areas of the enemy ship, but unlike FTL there's no real benefit to nuking the enemy engines, life support or navigation. Right now the only things that matter are shields and weapon systems, and maybe the medic bay if you have the right facilities.
This is a shame because in some areas it genuinely improves over FTL's combat model, such as the concept of ammo weapons having a shorter reload between shots and then a "long" reload as the clip is refilled with ammo. There's program "Cartridges" which allow you to conduct cyber warfare on your opponents, such as setting fire to target bays, puncturing sections of the ship, and sending their crew into a panic. These are seriously good steps forward.
Equally there's the navigation system, unlike FTL you're not time constrained, so you'll be moving back and forth between sectors, completing quests. Right now it's a very barebones system, with planets you've cleaned out not being of importance or note once you've dealt with them, but there's always the possibility of systems becoming event markers so that after an extended period, sectors become more difficult, forcing you to keep pressing onwards and preventing you from farming for easy planets and mining opportunities.
There's potential here to be sure, there's definitely a good idea of where the game is going, and there are some intriguing possibilities in the future. Right now however, it's a case of "It's a lot like FTL but... not really as good." and that makes it entirely impossible to recommend -yet-. I say yet because there's a patch due in the next couple of weeks, in other words, put this on your wishlist, and watch this space. There's a very good chance that the game will start improving significantly, and that my opinion of it will move more towards a cautious recommendation, and then eventually a wholehearted recommendation.

At best Mirror's Edge is fast paced and brilliantly exciting. Leaping across buildings, sliding and rolling through a beatifully stylised city, the parkour can be fast and fluid with a real sense of freedom. Dodging bullets and racing through buildings, disarming guards and finding quiet moments by sneaking through air vents is all great fun. For odd bursts of thirty seconds or so, this game is brilliant.
Then you find a jump which is just too pixel-perfect and takes thirty tries to get right, or the slightly awkward combat and inconsistent level design keeps getting you killed, or despite the hint system it simply isn't obvious where to go next or how. As well as being frustrating in themselves, these events break up the pace of the game and take the shine off the best parts.
If it were consistent, this would be one of the best games ever made. As it is, it is a variable experience which is superb in parts and well worth playing overall.

olive 1 tablespoon oil
salt and pepper, to taste
DIRECTIONS
Slice the tomato in approximately 1/4 inch thick slices. Do the same for the mozzarella.
Alternate layers between the tomatoes, mozzarella, and basil. (i.e. tomato slice, mozzarella slice, couple leaves of basil, beginning and ending with tomatoes).
Drizzle with olive oil and balsamic vinegar. Season to taste with salt and pepper, if desired.

Best roguelike I've played in a long time; solid controls, good crafting system, and a firm but completely fair difficulty. Another great feature is that it has checkpoints so you won't be spending 99% of your time playing the first couple levels (one of my major beefs with some roguelikes). I was also pleasantly surprised that a game like this would have Steam Cloud integration; started it up at work one day and I got to start at the checkpoint I left off from at from home! All in all Teleglitch is a great game that is well worth the price tag, especially if you get it during a Steam sale.
Minor nitpicks for the developers (hoping some of these get patched in):
-loading screens from the main menu to the selected checkpoint would be nice (maybe just the caption screen preceeding that level?) Even though it only takes 5 seconds to generate a level, it still feels weird when the main gui becomes unresponsive.
-scattering dead enemy bodies around each level and having a few of them randomly get up would add to the scare factor
-the story text needs a bit of proofreading; hell I'll even volunteer to do this given how few errors there are.

Good setting, decent enough story (retelling of the warrior who turned on his organization to help the people), and fun mechanics. Comparisons to Dead Island are inevitable, so borrowing from that it's a far more stable, far less buggy, far better done version of Dead Island (at release) with parkour and a day/night cycle that changes the power dynamic from the player to the zombies.
The combat system is fun, if not a little klunky at times. I took several hits from monsters that looked like clear misses, so I had to learn what Dying Light considered to be a hit. Also -- the power difference between firearms and melee weapons was pretty much the difference between a bat and a gun in reality. Even with the drawbacks of firearms (the sound alerts a tougher type of infected) I was never really discouraged from keeping my ammo full and carrying 3 guns in my 4 active equipment slots. I thought Dead Island made melee and throwing weapons far more entertaining, so there's one for Dead Island.
I enjoyed playing and beating the campaign, and from it have really only one complaint.. and this will be a totally predictable mechanics spoilers, but don't read if you don't want to know the final boss fight is a quick time event. Good game though, best of the story driven zombie stuff to come out in the while.

If you liked Dead Island, this game is Dead Island, with the fat trimmed off, everything polished and parkour thrown in for good measure. It was honestly one of the more fun open world games I've played in a while and zipping around the city was a blast. It's also far more stable than Dead Island ever was, though I still ran into several bugs (most which I took a screenshot of). The combat, movement and exploration is all great. The story...is dumb. And stupid. And hits about every zombie cliche in the book. Hell, it hits more of them than Dead Island did, and that's pretty nuts. The main character is actually not all bad and has some funny lines, and the side characters aren't too bad even though they fit stock zombie genre cliches (young feisty teenager smart aleck, badass lady who takes no♥♥♥♥♥♥ raving villain who shouts the hero'sname and talks endlessly about how CHAOS IS THE TRUE ORDER, etc.) I think some of this was somewhat self aware, but as this game was trying to take itself seriously, self-aware winks and nods are kinda silly. The only other big con I can think of is that the first few hours are rough as hell. Your character can run about five feet before getting winded and every weapon breaks in about five seconds and you can only swing them for a short period. Honestly, though...push through, because once you start getting some skills, it all becomes really fun.
tl;dr - Story and characters are lame (for the most part) and the beginning of the game is a bit rough, but its fun exploration, movement and combat is top notch. I say this as someone who feels pretty meh about zombie games, so take that as it is.

Have you ever had a dream where you would walk through a door, and then walk through it the other way, and ended up somewhere other than where you started? Have you ever looked at all the assumptions you make while playing a video game and wondered if there's a game that invalidates all of them?
Put both of those things together, and you have Antichamber.
Antichamber is a game that is based entirely on subverting all of the expectations you have when it comes to video games. However, unlike some games along the same lines, which punish you for those expectations (coins kill you, spikes are bouncy, etc.), Antichamber is remarkably kind about it. There is quite literally no way to play Antichamber wrong. It's a game less about success and failure, and more a game about introspection and philosophy. That's not to say that it's one of those stupidly pretentious games, either. It's a game that sits in a comfy chair across from you, smiling mysteriously and responding to your ideas with "Really? That's very interesting. Tell me more.". It's a game best played when you're feeling philosophical, and it makes a point of ensuring that you always feel that the entire game was designed entirely around you and your life experiences. Honestly, I don't think I can describe the game completely without ruining the experience, but I enthusiastically and honestly reccomend this game.
It might be rough around the edges, but this game is very fun and easy to play! I can't wait to play more.
