It's a bit weird writing a review of a game that I first played over ten years ago, but here I am on Steam just after buying a state-of-the-art gaming laptop and installing Half Life 2 to see how well it plays on it.
The answer to that is of course 'amazingly' - but I was not of course expecting my new machine to struggle when playing it as it could probably do it with one arm tied behind its back.  It's more of a question of why I am still coming back to an old game that I've played through many, many times and will probably continue to do so until I am physically incapable of holding a mouse and using a keyboard?!  It's a curious question indeed, but it is one that I'm going to have a pop at answering all the same.
You see, Half Life 2 is one of those rare games in that absolutely EVERYTHING was done perfectly.  From the graphics (which were really ahead of their time and still don't look bad, all things considered), the sound, the likable characters, dystopian storyline and the gameplay mechanics all gel brilliantly to make it quite simply one of the best games ever made - and it still holds up well to brand new games.
There are so many brilliant moments in the game, from the tense chase scene at the beginning as you run up the stairs to escape being captured by the combine soldiers, to the superb driving & hovercraft sections, being attacked by the flying hunter-killer gunships, pinned down by snipers, the spooky jaunt through Ravenholme and the terrifying encounters with the huge robotic walkers.  And all of this is held tightly together with realistic supporting characters and a narrative that drives everything along beautifully.
A special mention has to be said about the audio in HL2, as it has some of the most memorable sound effects you'll ever hear in gaming.   The sound design is just incredible and even thinking about the game evokes the sound of combine radio chatter, thumping gunfire, the sound as the gunships spot you and the chittering noise of the headcrabs.  There are few games that sound as good, even to this day.
So why do I keep coming back?  Because it's bloody excellent and, like a good movie, only serves to get even better over time as it's easy to appreciate how much of a breakthrough title it was and paved the way for so many modern titles.
It's impossible, of course, to not speak about the two episodes that come after HL2 as they are just as vitally excellent as the game that spawned them and add even more to the excellent storyline and character development.  And then it ends on a cliffhanger and we're all left wanting more.
...But are we going to see a Half Life 3?  I honestly hope so.  Valve would be fools to not eventually deliver the goods and come out with a sequel to what is undoubtedly one of the most loved games ever made.  Come on, Gabe!  Do it!

I personally enjoy driving the batmobile around Gotham like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ but some people don't. I feel that this batman game edges farther away from the comic book realm of the prior games, and more towards a serious tone, which I personally enjoy. Shadowverse CCG is, as its title implies, a collectible card game.
If you've played Hearthstone: Heroes of Warcraft, then you'll have a general idea as to what Shadowverse is.
The main difference between Hearthstone and Shadowverse is the evolve mechanic.
Evolving gives your creatures more stats and/or different effects. For example: A 2 mana 2/2 can become a 4/4 when evolved. Evolving also allows them to attack the turn they are played, but can only attack other creatures and not face. This mechanic alone makes me recommend Shadowverse.
Shadowverse is also VERY f2p friendly. You recieve so many packs and arena tickets just from playing the game, and it isn't pay-to-win in the slightest.
If you pay you can unlock pre-built decks and cosmetic items such as hero skins.
The reason why I currently prefer Shadowverse over Hearthstone is that Shadowverse doesn't have the wild/standard formats that Hearthstone does.
If you want to use cards from every expansion, are interested in the evolve mechanic, and like f2p friendly games, give Shadowverse a try.

My short review: An above average game with a potential of very long gameplay in raid mode.
Lets begin with cons for long review:
- If you already know a lot about resident evil, the story is predictable and ordinary. There is not much additions to what we already know.
- There are additional characters to the story but their personality is mediocre and their contribution to gameplay is somewhat neglectable.
- There is no co-op story mode. Only a split screen option is available. Why not add a co-op mode when you have such a nice potential?
- I did not experience much frame drops, maybe because they have updated the game or my rig is powerful, but there is a general consensus about frame drops and visual glitches in the game.
- The voice acting is strong for some characters and weak for others.
- Boss battles are mostly about waiting for an opportunity and evading attacks like a robot.
- The story mode is short. I think i have completed it in 12 hours in casual difficulty.
- If you have first Revelations game, do not expect a whole new game from this one. It feels like a remake. (First game is also nice)
At this point i read the cons above and realized that they are over powered by pros. That is why i recommend this game. Here are the pros:
- The story has more than 1 angle. And if you pay for extra episodes, they reveal more background.
- Switching to the other character in story mode is seemless. There is no waiting or a loading screen or etc.
- Since there is no co-op story mode, it is nice to experience and change identity and style on realtime basis. you do not always shoot, sometimes you just point where to shoot :)
- There are puzzles in the game. Some easy and some hard. You will be satisfied with puzzles.
- The horror is mostly because having multiple zombies and creatures converging on you. You will like trapped most of the time.
- There is a nice inventory management and weapon customization. You must find weapons parts to upgrade and customize your weapons and this makes it a survivor game. You have limited inventory space and you must use, combine or get rid of some of your items sometimes.
- The raid mode is the best aspect of this game. Raid mode is a level based zombie slaughtering mode in a specific map design. Yes there are tons of maps and monsters and even characters from older games (Revelations and RE6) but this actually works for the better if you play this game first. It is like the whole package. But some of them are DLC unfourtanately.
- The weapon customization is the same as in story mode in raid mode. Weapons can have 5,4,3 feature slots to enchance. You can find weapons in crates in the missions. Or if you have coins you can buy it on the store. The game is also connected to a website and you can claim prizes in there.
- Your characters will be leveling up and missions will require stronger characters as you progress. You have to equip skills for your character and some missions can be easily beaten with a specific skill. For example, if you have multiple enemies coming to you, you can use a freezing bottle and a magnum with incresed damage to frozen enemies. This is a lot of variety.
- Weapoen customization parts have plenty of choices. Long range, close range,easy hit, anti recoil, daze, capacity, reload speed, more damage to frozen or burning enemies, shoot 2 or 3 at once, shoot freezing or burning bullets, firing rate, hooming bullets... The list continues. This can make a disavantage of a wepon dissappear. Increase firing rate for you sniper rifle and be awesome :) These parts have levels and you can combine to parts with the same level to make a better part with higher level.
- Weapon parts or weapons are earned in missions and there is a jukebox (literaly) to evaluate or sell them. Selling before evaluation gets you more conins but you can sell your parts and weapons in the store afterwards.
- Raid mode is hell of a fun with a friend. You can decrease your level (can be incerased again) and take on challenges like playing a mission 30 levels above you.
So if you are not a RE veteran and looking for a survival horror game and if you don't have first revelations game, this game is a very nice choice. I think raid mode is better than the first revelations and RE6, and story is above average. Just buyinhg the first episode and jumping into the raid mode with a friend can be very satisfying :)

I finished this game in a couple of days. Would I recommend it? Sure! It's just not for everyone.
To get an idea if this game might be for you, consider the following questions:
Is a well written story important to you? Do you like cyberpunk and fantasy? Do you like the combination of both? Are you okay with reading most of the dialogs because there is no audio?
If you answer all or most of this questions with yes, this game is probably for your.
To be a bit more clear about whats awaiting you check my pros/cons list:
+Very well written and interesting story and interesting characters
+Very Immersive a lots of lore from the Shadowrun Universe
+Buildiung a character is easy, yet you still have lots of options
+Nicely drawn maps in an oldschool isometric view
+Very good character portraits (for player characters as well as npcs)
+The game runs on very old computer without problems
+The game has an editor and there are tons of mods to play
-Fights are far too easy. Tacticts were not required, although I played on the highest difficulty. The most important reason is probably poor AI, also the balancing is an issue.
-The game is rather short. I finished it in under 20 hours and I did every side quest I found, browsed stores extensively, read every dialog and reloaded a couple of times when I wasn't satisfied with the outcome of my actions. Some oldschool rpgs took me far more than 100 hours to finish. I am rather slow. A fast player (not speedruner) would probably not need more than 10 hours or so.
-The maps look nice, but are also very linear and there is not much interaction. You rarely find any treasure, you mostly just buy rather generic new stuff.
-Enemies do not drop their weapons or anything. Most drop nothing and if they drop anything its story realted (mostly keycards)
-The interacting with items and picking up of the same is bit tricky. Sometimes you click and nothing happens
-Decking (hacking) is not well integrated and rarely needed. It doesn't play the important role it should
-There is no system of initiative. The enemy always attacks first, even if you seem them first.
-No multiplayer

What really works for me in XCOM is the constant urge to move forward against the urge to carefully prepare for the unknown.  The different strategies required to most effectively utilize the strenths of the different classes (especially once they get into their respective skill trees) encourages a dynamic, and most often edge of your seat approach.  As the game develops, there are plenty of little intricacies you can use to more fully capitalize on a class too - gear, weapons, even machines.  Your guys feel powerful and yet fragile.  Its so gratifying when your sniper can double tap for 30+ damage.  But with the fist pumps come the sighs on the other hand....
While there is a tutorial, there were some key aspects of the game, most notably the economy, which I didn't know about until further into my game, which was frustrating because I'd already allocated my precious money in another area.  Its unforgiving, and can be a real handicap.  A few times I rolled my eyes at the "bad guy pop out one shot critical - my captain is dead" factor - while that adds to the risk, and thus the fun in escaping with another victory, the setback the next mission is palpable and frustrating.
Overall a risk taking game that I really enjoyed. Its plenty of hours and highly engaging.  9/10.

This is a very fun game as long as you take it for what it is. Yes, the similarity to FTL almost hits you over the head, race/species, battle scenarios, and ship interiors are among the things that scream FTL! ...but one can argue that any game of similar genre will have a similar design. There are quite a few differences however, whether they're good or bad depends on your expectations. If you're expecting a FTL clone with a face lift you might be disappointed, in my 15 hours of play time I found Space Rogue to be a much simpler game, but this might just be due to the fact that I have been unable to move past lvl 2 space (because of bugs that force you to restart), or perhaps the game is meant to be more suited for a younger crowd and/or casual gamers. Then again we have to remember that it is an early access release, and for all we know it might still be missing a lot of its content.
Even though its very enjoyable to play in its current state, there are plenty of things that remind you its an early access game. You know little things like your captain walking right off your ship only to die in the cold vacuum of space, which of course means game over. Your boarding crew disappearing with the (very much intact) enemy ship after defeating the enemy crew, or getting stuck in a bugged battle only to quit and reload your game in the very same spot with no way to move forward. So there are some bugs that will force you to restart your adventure, and the lack of crew/ship customization options as start of game make restarting the game a killjoy.
My advice to anyone finding the Mining mini-game more frustrating than fun is to start a custom game with more Credits rewards and less XP rewards. The game considers this a fair trade for the balance score of 1, and you'll find that your crew still levels up fairly fast, and now you might even have the credits to level some of them up. Though mainly it'll make mining, or rather repetitively failing at it, less of a hassle when you have the funds to try and try again. I have no knowledge of what the odds actually are of landing your mining probe and mining, but it surely feels like they're stacked against you, but as long as you think of it in terms of 50/50 chance, and make peace with the fact that you'll fail half the time no matter what, you'll be more likely to laugh it off than curse at your screen.
This game is definitively still a work in progress, but shows a lot of potential, and is already a lot of fun to play around with,

This is an extremely hesitant not recommended and let me tell you exactly why. Many of you guys reading the review section are almost undoubtedly fans of FTL and you are wondering. Is this a blatant ripoff? Are there any differences? If so, do they make Space Rogue stand out enough on its own to justify a purchase?
In my opinion right now, no. But, it has potential to be as good and even better than FTL and this is from a guy who played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of FTL several times with and without mods and beaten it several times. (Didn’t play on steam). I managed to reach the second last zone in Space Rogue  several times in the campaign and they have a lot of work to do if they want to surpass FTL.
Differences
Power – This is a difference that primarily affects battle. In FTL, power is doled out by you to the various systems and this adds a layer of strategy in battles where you can boost the power to your shields, weapons and engines but at the cost of taking power away from other systems like the medbay.
In space rogue, there is 0 power management as each system will have power independent to the other systems and how much power available depends on how much you upgrade each system with Tritanium, a separate resource from credits which you acquire from mining. Without power management, Battles become less hectic and chaotic but also more focused. Some may find this a positive, I personally find this a negative.
Battle – Battle is largely the same as FTL and veterans will be familiar with hull breaches, enemy troops teleporting onboard, fires and the way shields and hull damage works. Weapon types are also fairly similar but there are some unique to Space Rogue but not many.
Crew - There are 3 kinds of crew available to you. The captain who is well, the captain of the ship, engineers and warriors. Unlike FTL where different crew members can man stations and improve its efficacy, the captain is the ONLY crew member who can man a station.
Why this is so is beyond me, as the ability to man stations with your crew members and have them become more skilled and level up is a fantastic part of FTL. There are different species but the only difference between the species stats. So, unless you are a data/stats min max kind of person, it will reach a point where you go eh whatever and pick randomly. Crew is a missed opportunity here and needs more work to be more engaging and more relevant to the ship instead of being wrench monkeys or gun drones.
Resources - The amount of resources you get throughout the game is so pitiful to the point where I was backtracking through cleared systems just to grind out to credits and tritanium I needed. By the way, levelling up your crew costs you credits which.... is stupid and extremely cost prohibitive.
Random events – This is where FTL and Space Rogue take a different approach. FTL’s random events could have devastating effects, but never does it go “oh you know what? I think your hull doesn’t have enough holes. Here, lets fix that by having a system randomly explode and oh yeah fires too cause why not”. Think I’m exaggerating? Heh no. I found it infuriating and blatantly unfair that my ship could suffer damage literally just by travelling to another planet.
This is of course the worst example of what could happen, but there are a ton of other encounters and most of them seem to end badly for me one way or another. Sometimes I do come away with a nice haul of credits but most of the time.....
Now lets talk about mining. *Huge sigh* Mining is goddamn expensive as it costs credits to send a drill down to a suitable planet. I’ve mined literally every single planet that could be mined and even backtracked to earlier systems just to see if i can scrounge up some tritanium to upgrade my ship and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ let me tell you that mining is stupidly unfair and not fun. Send a drone down, lol it hit the planet too hard and made a whole planets worth of ore sink so deep that it becomes un-minable just because your drone landed a little too hard.
Oh the drone below the planet surface explodes for no reason (yup that’s the reason you are given, your drone blows up for reasons unknown) and not only do you lose ALL the resources you mine, but your ship IN ORBIT ABOVE THE PLANET SOMEHOW TAKES DAMAGE TOO. Send your drone down, lol some mockconglers shoot it down and tell you to run off and there is nothing you can do about it. Oh hang on, your drone actually made it to the surface, that’s fine I’ll start drilling.... oh♥♥♥♥♥♥I found unstable tritanium and your drone immediately blows up and again your ship takes damage. Oh crap, I found a trap on the planet THAT SUCKS MONEY OUT OF MY SHIP IN ORBIT.
After reading all that, you might think, well I’ll just not mine. Well you won’t get very far since mining is literally the only efficient way to get tritanium which is needed to upgrade your ship and since mining is stupidly unfair and unfun, its very likely that mining will cause you to lose both credits and hull integrity and set you back even further than before.
Aside from the stupid random events and how most of them are basically out to screw you over in every way imaginable, the game is pretty damn fun. While it may seem like I didn't enjoy it at all, I did get the "FTL feel" back again but way too many problems. The progression needs work. The difficulty spike is pretty crazy and I had to flee many battles to backtrack to systems I already conquered to scour them for credits and tritanium to get my ship to a level where I would not get blown up instantly.
The game does have a lot of potential and I believe it could be great if the devs make the improvements that Space Rogue sorely needs as it moves along in early access. But right now, Its just an echo of a great song that is FTL.

At best Mirror's Edge is fast paced and brilliantly exciting. Leaping across buildings, sliding and rolling through a beatifully stylised city, the parkour can be fast and fluid with a real sense of freedom. Dodging bullets and racing through buildings, disarming guards and finding quiet moments by sneaking through air vents is all great fun. For odd bursts of thirty seconds or so, this game is brilliant.
Then you find a jump which is just too pixel-perfect and takes thirty tries to get right, or the slightly awkward combat and inconsistent level design keeps getting you killed, or despite the hint system it simply isn't obvious where to go next or how. As well as being frustrating in themselves, these events break up the pace of the game and take the shine off the best parts.
If it were consistent, this would be one of the best games ever made. As it is, it is a variable experience which is superb in parts and well worth playing overall.

I picked this one up for cheap during the summer sale. Now, I'm not actually a fan of slow, plodding strategy games like this one, but with a price tag of $2.50, I thought I'd check out what all the fuss was about. So far, that $2.50 has been Steam Summer Sale MVP, because while FTL can be a slow, contemplative strategy game, it is also so, so much more.
The best way to describe Faster Than Light is that it is a "Star Trek Simulator." You are captain of a Federation starship on an mission to deliver vital information about the Rebel leaders, all the while outrunning the oncoming rebel fleet. Using your wits, weapons, and a little luck, you attempt to complete your mission of crossing the galaxy via waypoints, having many adventures along the way. During your trip you will encounter hostile alien races, dastardly space pirates, or high-tech weaponry.
An aspect of the game worth noting is that the game uses a random event generator similar to The Binding of Isaac, making sure that Faster Than Light delivers a unique game experience with every playthrough. Also worth noting is that the UI, while seeming a bit confusing at first, is actually very intuitive to understand after the basics are understood. The combat engine is done absolutely brilliantly, especially with the inclusion of the option to stop time at will and analyze the situation. FTL rewards both careful preparation as well as snap decision-making, and it makes for a very enjoyable gameplay experience. And finally, the writing and storytelling are compelling enough to make repeat playthroughs worthwhile.
I have never played a game like this before, but it latched onto my brain in a very short timespan. It is just the right balance of difficulty, storytelling, and fun, and will keep you coming back for more.

This game seems simple at first, but it really pulls you in. It got that Diablo addiction as you go down deeper (exactly like Diablo 1 actually) . They  added all 3 classes at the time of this review, making this game immensely replayable . Love how you can select what size dungeon to generate based on your time available . This is perfect for quick short bursts, i have been playing this in 15min stints resulting in me increasing my dungeon sizes as i get more hooked. For a game in early access it is very stable and seems feature complete (i did not notice anything missing or broken).
Pros:
The graphics are a rather unique cardboard cutout design which does the job. This definitely seems to make the game perform extremely well (can most likely play this on a tablet). Some might not like this if you are coming straight out of say Grim Dawn / Diablo 3 / Wolcen , but give it a few dungeon runs, it grows on you.
The card based skill system combined with how you upgrade cards and have to manage your mana pool to equip them is very satisfying to play around with. Love how you have to constantly weigh up between more passive skills vs. active skills etc.
The game is definitely taking its inspiration from Diablo 1, and there's a ton of throwbacks and humour around this. The game does innovate quite a bit in the actual combat which can be both good or bad. I like that there's various mechanics that you need to take note of with different enemies , like enemies being immune until you do something specific (i.e. killing their guardians first or  destroying their shields first by clicking on a specific shield icon etc) or being able to reduce poison time by clicking on your poisoned health bowl. Even getting stunned has a little mechanic to it allowing you to get out of it faster if you are swift with the mouse.
Cons:
It can get a little chaotic with the clicking when there's alot of enemies and you need to click precisely on specific icons (i.e. to break shields you have to click on the actual enemy shield which is often a tiny thing to click).  Luckily there's skill cards that make this easier.
The game is still in early access and they juuust released the final 2 classes. I started with only the warrior class available which would have been a con, but no longer.

This is a game that comes from the mind of a mobile developer. One of its selling points is the option to have a short play session—an issue that often is crucial for mobile, but hardly relevant for a PC gamer. The control scheme also feels like it was made for a touch screen. There are many mini-games that boil down to grabbing things floating on the screen. To heal poison, you have to click the bottom left with your cursor, even though normally you keep it to the center of the screen—an idea that would be handy of the game was controlled with your fingers via a mobile device, but doesn't translate well to PC.
A lot of its other elements feel clunky as well. While you can instantly teleport to the end of a dungeon when it's 100% clear, looking for that one pesky pile of gold you've missed means backtracking—excruciatngly slow backtracking. And pray that your final enemy isn't a gargoyle or a ghost: both can hide and must attack first... or ignore you, making you run past them a dozen times, groaning.
As for the presentation, I'm pretty sure that Deckard Cain voice is borderline copyright infringement.
also borrows heavily from
with its combination of stylized visuals and gritty narration.
Does it all mean that the game is bad? No. It's all right. The treadmill does its job, injecting you with satisfaction via a steady stream of achievements and other small rewards. The idea of a small-budget simple Diablo-like is laudable, and you get enough fun for the price.
I do, however, feel that the 'Overwhelmingly positive' rating gives the wrong impression of
being some sort of a hidden gem.
It's not. It's just all right.

I'm a sucker for these LEGO games. I'm a sucker for Marvel. It all just worked so well for me. I loved flying around New York City.

Review time! This time we're discussing LEGO Marvel Superheroes. I'll give you the breakdown of the goods and bads of this game. So lets hop right in.
OVERVIEW
If you are familiar with the LEGO games, this one does not differ. LEGO games are one of the few games that are rated E that really are enjoyable to everyone. It doesn't matter how old you are, this game is fun. Like all LEGO games, this game is packed full of puzzles, cheesy one-liners, and a huge range of playable characters.
PROS
This game is entertaining through and through. Both the campaign and the side missions are fun to play. The open world is huge and there's around 136 playable characters to collect (You can even be Stan Lee, who has several superpowers) along with a bunch of vehicles. Deadpool is one of the rarest characters in the game and has his own set of missions that need completed in order to unlock. Like all LEGO games, you can play campaign missions over again with any character you would like (and you'll need to do so if you are looking to 100% the game). Achieving 100% is usually the primary goal of the LEGO games, but many people just play whenever they feel like. I have not quite achieved 100% but I do intend to in the future. As far as the Marvel aspect goes, the characters/storyline do not necessarily follow the movies or comics. This does not take away from the experience at all (unless you're one of those weird die-hard comic guys). You can find almost every character thinkable in the Marvel Universe (except for a few, but I can't think of any off the top of my head).
CONS
There aren't many cons, but there are definitely some that need noted. LEGO games have NEVER been meant for PC, there are a set of PC controls, but they are awkward, and don't even use the mouse. If you're going to play this game, I HIGHLY recommend using a gamepad. If you don't have a gamepad, don't worry, the game is still playable, the controls are just going to take some getting used to.
Another thing about controls, while flying, if you run into the side of a building, you will come to a jolting halt and the camera will be a bit weird in adjusting. As you improve your flying skills, you'll run into this problem (no pun intended) less and less.
The other large con is that you cannot kill civilians in the open world, which is a real shame. While there are enemies in the open world, you can only fight them during side missions or while at The Raft (The prison). This is very disappointing, but I heard it might've been required to maintain the game's E rating. Still, a shame.
VERDICT
This game is super fun. If you are a Marvel fan, or loved the other LEGO games, or both, then you really need to get this game. Even if you haven't played a LEGO game before, I recommend you give it a try. Pick it up on sale if you can, but I paid full price and have #noregrets.

WOW. Cygames has demonstrated astounding levels of artistry in terms of card design and game balance.
Like any other competitive card game, you have your tier one decks. But they do not dominate the ladder in a way that is restrictive to people who want to experiment or play lower tier decks (provided you're a decent player, and willing to actually try to build optimal strategies).
Though only two expansions have been released at the time of writing this review, both have introduced powerful and interesting cards into the meta that create new and powerful tier 1 strategies, but do not break and dominate the game.
Not to mention, arena 'Take Two' is an elegant take on drafting, and the arena meta has been quite fun and healthy.
The flavor of the game isn't really my style, but the art is far from ugly. Visuals are well-crafted, and I find myself often interested or amused by the flavor text displayed during the loading screens in-between matches.
Of course it's hard to talk about the merits of Shadowverse without bringing up the Hearthstone comparison. As a long-time Hearthstone player with multiple Legend finishes, I can safely say that I'm moving to Shadowverse, at least for the time being. It simply lacks the problems that have been plaguing Hearthstone since the introduction of 'Standard' mode: Cygames is willing to take risks in card design and encourage decks that feel different from one another, and is willing to make relatively quick adjustments to game balance if something goes wrong.
I cannot sing enough praise for this game, as someone who plays or played many TCGs and CCGs actively and competitively, I can say without-a-doubt that Shadowverse is quite the achievement, and I'm excited to see where it goes from here.
Oh, and don't let anyone tell you that you can't play this game competitively for free; be smart with how you liquify cards and spend your in-game currency, and you can easily build top-tier decks within days of one another.

LEGO Marvel Super Heroes follows the general trend that LEGO games usually take - easy, but sometimes unforgettable. I believe it is evident now that every LEGO game is pretty much identical. This game takes a LOT of Marvel characters and mashes them into a relatively straight forward story. It is better than LEGO Marvel's Avengers, mostly because the dialogue is much better. Graphics wise it looks relatively cute, but the open world cities are not especially great looking. The locations vary throughout the missions, from Asgard to the X-Mansion. Unfortunately as with any LEGO game, they are amazing initially but ultimately grow really repetitive and downright boring. Because the game is relatively easy there is an almost apparent feeling that there is no challenge, and I didn't find it too fun after a while and certainly wanted it to end. Gameplay is the same as any other LEGO game. I wish they'd make a standalone LEGO Spider-Man game, it would be pretty damn good. Couch co-op is definitely an option. You can play keyboard (player 1) and controller (player 2) and it does work! Sometimes co-op is much more convenient to solve puzzles than to do puzzles by yourself. Controls are customizable thankfully so it isn't a pain. The most fun characters tend to be the big guys, like Abomination, Hulk and The Thing, since they are mobile and can hit a lot of things.
Is the PC version good, though? Well, yes. And, kinda. With a spice of no. It barely has any options to tweak graphical settings, and it has some weird problems. I can play it at 720p at about 400fps but then you switch it to 1080p and things mess up. For some reason, during some cutscenes, the game drops in frames. It certainly is not game breaking, but you will notice it and it is really weird. (I am running a GTX 960 2gb, Intel Core i5 4590, 8gb RAM.)
The story is pretty decent, the game is fun while it lasts and there certainly is a lot of content to be discovered.
I don't regret buying this at £3.74, but if you have played A LOT of LEGO games and are getting sick of them, I don't recommend this game to you with a full heart, and therefore you should get it on a sale, because you will be much more forgiving on yourself.

Somehow it's a cool thing lately to hate on Hearthstone. Some suggested Shadowverse as much better alternative. But after playing it for 3 months or so I'm already sick of it. It's just too simple, primitive even. No hero powers, no secrets, positioning doesn't matter, everybody plays aggressive
I'm judging from the position of player who never attempts to seriously climb the ladder. Doing same thing thing over and over is not my thing. I'm either doing daily quests with some fun decks or playing the arena. And you can't have fun with either in Shadowverse, because:
- even lower ranks are riddled with robots playing their carbon-copied meta decks. To complete vast majority of quests you have to WIN, compared to Hearthstone, where there are many different types of daily quests
- arena is set up in a way that prohibits any deliberate deck building. Only 15 choices of two pairs from 60 cards compared to 30 choices from 90 cards. You end up with lots of unplayable cards in a deck.
And then there's Dimension Shift. When Hearthstone developers try to stop non-interactive decks, Shadowverse developers decided that having a card that takes my turn away from me is a great idea. IT'S NOT! It's like playing a fighting game with your bully older brother, who, seeing that you are about to win, punches you in the face, takes away your controller and laughs hystericaly while beating your defensless character. This is unacceptable in CCGs, imho. "Win a game" cards too. Although I encountered that joke of a card only a couple of times - nobody runs it because you either aggresive in Shadowverse or you lose, control is not a thing here, again, because of Dimension Shift. These should not exist in any CCG.
I heard, "but Hearthstone, blah-blah, freeze mage, pirate warrior". With both I can do SOMETHING, not just watch helplessly while opponent has 2-3 turns in a row. And these types of decks are nerfed constanlty in Hearthstone. Not in Shadowverse though, everything is according to keikaku here.
I know, my "for fun" decks won't works against meta in hearthstone too, but I usually don't encounter those in my 20-15 rank (or they are weaker incomplete versions I can have an even match against), but there was a time up to 50% of my opponents in C rank ran dimension shift decks. Game starts - Runecraft opponent, whelp, I already know how this will play out.
So, overall, I don't reccoment this game. Why waste time on it when there's a better alternative
To add some positive - I do like most of the art (even though it tends to be too busy) and they give out quite a lot of packs, so it's easier for beginners than Hearthstone

I'm suprised I haven't made a review yet for this game, and I can't even think of anything stupid to write other than "with a bang and and a boom!" and "let's do this right." multiple times.
I was rather skeptical of this game when most of my friends started playing it, having never played a card game like this before, you can probably understand why, but I'm glad I picked it up. This game was kind of hard to pick up and understand at first (again, having never played a T/CCG before) and even after trying to learn it I'm not that good and play one class almost exclusively but I still like it.
Before you start asking if it's pay to win, it's not, you get so many free card packs and in game currency just for playing and the only thing in game you have to spend crystals  (paid for currency) on are the prebuilt card packs which you can just write down the cards from their info screen and make them yourself. While a lot of the current meta decks are based on using legandary cards for the current newest expansion, rise of bahamut, you don't need them as a lot of other cards will work well. (Mordecai will always be the best card) While there are moments where you might be cheated out of a victory becuase your win condition card is on the bottom of your deck there are cards that force a draw of a high-cost card and you can use mulitples of that card in your deck.
Ragequiting is also apperently a thing that happens a lot when people know or think they can't win, to the point where people I have fought would sit there and wait to see if I quit. So the only thing I have to say about that is: even if you think you're saving us both time, it doesn't make it any less cowardly.
So yeah, this game is fun, even to just collect the cards, so if you've been thinking of playing a CCG or have played a lot of them I would recommend this for you. The only other bad thing I'd say about this game is that the english translation was rather poorly done.

This game can be absolutely rage inducing. But stick with it, because it is awesome. But If you get frustrated easily, this is probably not the best choice of purchase for you. Soldiers sometimes miss ridiculously easy shots until they gain some rank, while the aliens hit in absurd situations. That happens, and it’s a pain.
But if you get past that, this is a really good game. It is immensely satisfying to see a plan work and pull a mission off nicely. The feeling of immersion is great. I did two playthroughs (normal and classic) and both times I started getting attached to my soldiers quickly, having favourites, cursing when they got hit and so forth - in my opinion that’s one of the most important aspects of what makes this game good. It also has this “just one more mission” urge to it. Building a base, developing new gear and then deploying it on a mission with your favourite soldiers is a great mix and keeps you hooked. Map variety is quite good, there is little chance you’ll play in the same setting twice during one playthrough.
Concerning “Enemy Within”: I think it’s a good expansion to the base game. Introduction of gene mods and mechs is a nice addition and offers some new gameplay, though I feel some power creep is taking place (mimetic skin + low profile = constantly invisible sniper). Exalt missions are a good change of pace and a welcome addition also.
Can’t comment on the multiplayer as I have not tried it. I have absolutely no regrets about buying this game, though.

I've just finished the second one of these game 'Dragonfall' and intend to start the third straight away later tonight!
These games offer so much to the player who likes a 'story'. If your an impatient conversation/cutscene clicker then simply DONT buy these games, you will get so little from them!
But if you like to get your teeth into a decent storyline, turn based combat and a polished product then these games may well serve you well.
The Shadowrun universe is compelling and interesting. It's not your run of the mill fantasy/sci fi fair, it's rich deep and complex and the PDF that comes with this first game goes quite a way into giving you some of the details. Again this is for people who like to delve and read lore, those who care about backstories and where their characters will be adventuring.
The graphic style of the game I think is perfect! The detailed world is welcoming, it draws you in and the art team have done so well in bringing the Shadowrun World to lfe. It's hand drawn feel adding to its charm.
Character progression is good, although a little linear feeling, in that like most games nowadays you need to build your characters in certain ways to really get the most out of them. That said theres plenty of different ways to build your character and enouigh difference in the classes to keep you interested.
I played the first game as a Decker and had plenty to do as I progressed through the game and I played the second as a Rigger and again found the gameplay excellent.
The second game is better than the first and theres no requirement to play the first, they are standalone stories but if you were to skip this first game you would be skipping some of the best narrative there is out there today.
Harebrained schemes obviously care about their writing because it's very profesional, head and shoulders above most similar games out there.
The game isn't perfect. It's short (which can be forgiven as a first foray into a new universe - the second is MUCH longer and even better written, if thats poossible.) and it has anoying ommisions of functionality that we come to expect as game players.
You cant for example swap out inventory items between team mates, often leading to frustration because wanted items are passed to your 'stash' rather than simply handing them to another team member who has room for them! An odd choice of how to do things that sadly made it into the second game too!
Aside from some other small niggles I find it hard to say bad things abaout this game, and its sequel Dragonfall because I had so much fun playing them.
Do yourself a favour, buy them!
TL:DR - This game is not for you.

This is one of my favorite games of all time. It is a very unique experience and when you get the flow it's amazing. Some people have complained about the combat systems, but to me it's actually better that the combat is difficult and clunky as compared to a real first-person shooter. This is a running game and the protagonist is not Rambo -- so the combat reflects that fact. You can pass basically any mission without needing to kill people, and it just emphasizes the importance of becoming good at running and dodging.
The level in the glass-walled skyscraper where you have to parkour your way up is my favorite level.  It's a beautiful level and has fun jumping/climbing challenges.
Be forewarned that you will likely not pass each level on the first try, so there is a lot of re-doing levels as you learn where to run and when to run. This pure gameplay focus is similar to a platformer like Mario Bros., and is NOT like a modern shooter game. The story is also throwaway and didn't add much for me. With the right mentality and approach I was not frustrated by this fact as the game is not super long. I enjoy running the levels enough and trying new approaches to the same problem that the need to re-run levels didn't bother me. Going back to certain levels and re-playing every few months is still fun. If you cannot stomach this type of approach and intent then don't bother!

"Space Rogue" immediately reminds me of "FTL", especially the portions where you can move your crew around the ship and manage your ship's resources.  Even the rooms and the pacing of combat have the same general concept.  "Space Rogue" does take it a step farther in a few places, giving you the ability to mine planets for minerals (just to cite one example), though you can't grind for minerals by revisiting planets you've already been to.  In addition to this, the customization options for when you're setting up said sandbox are fairly vast.  All of these things appeal to my inner sci-fi geek...I mean, what "Star Trek" fan doesn't dream of commanding their own ship?  I think it's safe to say that if you enjoyed "FTL" (it's one of my favorites), then you'll like "Space Rogue" too.  The price is a bit steep considering that the differences between this and "FTL" are few and far between...I sincerely hope that more content is coming to justify the price variance between the two games.

Some first impressions, hopefully they help. Production values are very good overall and far more polished then many EA games. Often overlooked by non-English developers is translation and spelling which had no issues either. Soundtrack also impressed me and really added to the atmosphere. Fans of FTL there is a lot you should love about Space Rogue. Do think it's priced a little high but I'm not someone who put 100-1000hrs into FTL either. If you are that person the value seems to be there but depends on future content as well.
Gameplay involved jumping around the galaxy while heading toward your main objective. Every planet visited triggers a random event of which the game claims to have included around 200 or so. I didn't run into any that seemed familiar after several hrs of play. Clearing each sector gives you the the ability to heal your crew members, patch up the ship, install upgrades and level up crew members. Currently the game includes a basic tutorial and campaign. Campaigns seemed to be made of many solar systems with a single jumpate at the end. Each solar system also contained at least 1 central trade station where you are able to buy and sell along with repairing your ship.
Storepage mentioned it was randomly generated so I put it to the test and created around 10 new games, all of which were entirely different. Main plot line, planets, galaxies, faction reputations and wars all seemed to change dramatically between sessions. Much like all rogue-likes the RNG system can be a complete pain in the rear sometimes but it does go both ways. Several games I played did manage to get stomped quickly at the start. As long as you hit a few planets successfully will soon receive upgrades or be given extra crew members through minor victories making life in space much easier.
With mod support along with listening to community feedback the sky is the limit. Should keep fans of the genre going for some time. Feel free to ask any further questions, will do my best to answer them asap. Cheers folks and happy gaming. :)

A SECOND LOOK AT THE REQUEST OF THE DEVELOPER:
I am leaving the original review below, so that you can compare for yourself, if you'd like.
While the changes are really nice, I have to give a reluctant maybe to this one.
If you're REALLY into rogue-like games, then you'd probably enjoy the punishment you need to endure to get up to a high enough level to be able to tweak things like difficulty level, but for myself I'm not really willing to invest that amount of time beating myself up so that I can get beat up a little less.  My main enjoyment with a game is being able to go through the content.
I'm going to address my commented items below, in order, for clarity's sake:
Mining:  They have made one large improvement to mining that I think is quite good - your ship no longer takes hull damage EVERY drone that hits an event.  It takes three events for this to happen now.  While a vast improvement, I am still confused how my ship in space takes hull damage from planet-based mining.  (Developer:  An easy workaround here is to a) do shipboard systems damage related to drone work, like the main computer, and the engines, or b) have a large credit expenditure for the retrieval and repair of said broken/exploded drones; if no money is available, they lose the drone and it's drilling chance for a number of turns until your engines make another).  I still lost 8 hull to a mining incident, which made me hesitant to continue mining, even though it was my main source up upgradable parts.
Away Teams:  Despite efforts, I never ran into an away team dialogue.  I can't comment on this one, sorry!
Jumping to Planets:  Happily, this seems to be fixed!  I jumped to a dozen different places and wasn't damaged for simply moving myself along! Yay!
Ship Combat:  This is the big sinker/floater, still.  While I wasn't destroyed on my first encounter I was destroyed on my second encounter.  And, after restarting I was destroyed again on my first encounter by... Psionics.  A giant space squid?  Great... but don't make it the damned spaghetti monster with shield-penetrating triple wave psionic beams at literally the second planet I fly to!
Also, while I'm on space combat:  Boarding parties should scale with my crew/ship abilities.  I don't know, maybe make an algorithm based on the level of my ship's systems for toughness of boarding parties?  And, if there is already something like that, please dial it back a touch.  I had to continuously repair this one open gash in my ship hull in a tiny 2-slot room while trying to defend my ship from another ship while trying to beat down a boarding party.  Moving crew between my (destroyed, and still trying to fix that, too) healing room, and the hull rupture at the very furthest point of my ship was infuriatingly slow... no sense of urgency from my crewmembers who seemed to think that walking is about as brisk a pace as is possible.  While this whole way of combat is fun sometimes, it's not fun when you know you're just really slowly losing the fight.  If this was simply a review of combat it'd be a solid thumbs down.
Pop Up Dialogues:  They didn't kill me every time, or cost me money.  So, that's quite a bit better!
Other things I noticed:  Damage indicators have been VASTLY improved.  The captain still appears to be the only one that doesn't just stand around when put on a station; but, I'm still not certain if he's doing anything to give a positive benefit or stat to the station he's on.  I also noticed many little changes here and there that have added to the ambience of the game, however, they aren't game changers in and of themselves.
Overall:  The game is definitely getting to where it needs to go, and while this is a vast improvement on the previous iterations it's still not really hitting the mark at the core of it's gameplay.  With some more combat improvements the game could definitely be a hard hitter.  (Developers:  If you want me input on those items, you can feel free to contact me directly.)
It's getting there, it really is.
I wrote this review on May 5th, 2016.  Almost exactly one year after the previous review.  And, still:  Hopefully in a few months when you read this they'll have a playable game out there, and my opinion will be outdated, again!
Until then, happy gaming in whatever game you choose!
TL:DR
Much has changed, combat still frustrates, ship go boom, crew go poof, shinier game, buy it? maybe, devs working hard, captain is a mad scientist.

The Chaos Engine: Remastered
This is a worthy remastering of the Amiga/SNES/Genesis classic from the early-mid 90's
If you're looking for the definitive version of the Chaos Engine (Soldiers of Fortune in the US), then this is that version. Of the three classic versions, the Amiga CD32 version had the best graphics and sound while the consoles had much snappier loading times. With the Steam version, you not only get the Amiga version of the graphics (more advanced color palette and animation detail) and sound, you also get the incredibly fast loading times.
Also, the Steam version comes with achievements, cards, matchmaking and some image enhancement options. I highly recommend playing this game at the original, intended resolution. Scaling it up to "HD" will only blow up the pixels to a size that is nearly unbearable to look at. However, if kept at the original size, one can really appreciate the exquisite pixel art of the Bitmap Brothers. Smoothing can enhance the visuals even more, but, again, it is best left at the original resolution.  As for the added bloom effects, they are successful at enhancing the already impressive original explosion animations and other elements of the game world. I would put this game on a list of examples of games that use bloom to great effect without overdoing it.
My review is really focused on whether or not this is a good port. If you're unfamiliar with the Chaos Engine, I recommend checking out some of the other reviews here to find out if its your kind of game.

Antichamber is a weird game to review, as it stands on a league of its own. It's not trying to be a good game. On the contrary, it's actually throwing most conventions out the window, and challenging the player to see it through.
Let's say it's a first person puzzle game. If you need a comparison, Portal would be a decent choice. However, where Portal clearly gives you the mechanics and expects you to use them to solve the puzzles, Antichamber makes you dig a lot to find those mechanics and how it all fits and interacts. The game is purposely trying to bend the players' minds at every turn, and it certainly succeeds in doing exactly that!
I'm not going to do the usual review on this game. It simply wouldn't work, and would achieve nothing. So I'm going to try to convey the game's fundamental aspects, and you'll then judge for yourself if you're interested enough.
The game also has some Metroid-vania elements regarding its map. However, while those games obey "real-world" rules, Antichamber laughs at them. The whole game is a non-Euclidian maze (meaning it doesn't obey 3D geometry rules -- when you turn back, the rooms may have changed; maybe you can go down enough that you're back where you're started; you get the idea). However, you are given a very useful map, which functions almost as a progress meter. With its use, you'll know *some* of the connected areas, but above all else, you'll know when there are still ways to uncover in a given room.
Antichamber is essentially about sheer willpower and deconstruction. You're not given anything. Instead, you need to find it yourself, and then experiment with your new tools to solve more of the puzzles. The game also has a few signs with messages, giving you feedback for your actions (and the meaning of life, if you're so inclined). It works almost as
. The game is about learning for yourself. About having to learn to progress. Since the knowledge you had previously (as conventions) doesn't work, you'll have to start from the very beginning. To solidify your discoveries, the game usually gives you a short phrase (and picture) to relate it to life itself. And it helps giving context to what you're doing, setting it all in stone.
Eventually, you'll be able to make the game's logic almost conventional, weirdly enough. You adapt to the weird world you've been thrown in, and it feels great to realize how far you've come.
There are lots of branching paths, each leading to a new puzzle. However, you have a Hub Area in which you can jump into every puzzle directly (after you've found it). It would be impossible to complete the game without it, since traversing the map is everything but convenient. This is also something that goes well with the fact that you'll be stuck a lot.
Either you haven't learned a certain mechanic well enough, or you're lacking a certain tool for a puzzle. But you'll be forced to turn back. And the game helps you with that a lot. So you'll be constantly trying out new puzzles, and shying away from others. It's fine. The game was made with that very intent, and it uses that to its advantage, avoiding a lot of frustration.
Another aspect is that there are mostly no wrong actions. Everything is a choice, and the game responds to everything you do -- it may just not be the answer you were looking for.
I've seen the question on the forums "What's the point"? Well... there is not point, other than discovery, and basically deconstructing the world until you master its own way of thinking. You don't have anyone to save or kill. No reward waiting for you either. But curiosity will certaily keep you moving forward -- well, maybe not technically forward... up and to the right, maybe. Maybe backwards, who knows? -- and it's incredibly rewarding to solve some puzzles that were particularly difficult to you.
It is a very, very unique game. And it's hard to explain what it is or why anyone should play it. But I'll say this: it's the game I'd recommend to most people, even if they're not into games. And that's because it's an unique experience, not necessarily tied to traditional games. The same may happen with movies or even music. People may not like movies all that much, but there are some that are worth watching anyway, for one reason or another.
Again, it's on a league of its own. It also shares some similarities with Fez, in that regard. However, Fez requires you to take knowledge from outside of the game, while Antichamber requires you to throw all knowledge away.

There are also some Dev Rooms that will give you some information about the development of the game. It's nice that they're there.
If you want to be challenged, dazed and confused... Definitely get this game. And play it through without a guide, otherwise its charm is all lost. Persistence is important, but it's one of the most rewarding games I've played in a long, long time. And it works nicely as food for thought as well.
I have never played anything even remotely close to Antichamber (not saying it's the best game I've ever played, simply that it's very different from everything else I came across), and it's a well executed game. It's interesting not only in concept, but in practice as well. Give it a go!

Risk of Rain is a roguelike platformer that escalates in difficulty the longer you play. You play as the only survivor of a cargo ship crash on a hostile planet, hoping to survive long enough to escape. Standing in your way are lizardmen, giant crabs, living flames, and all sorts of other monsters. On your side, you have your gun and your wits.
That's not quite true. You also have the contents of the crashed cargo ship scattered across the planet. Every area comes with chests you can spend money to open. These chests contain items that can give you extra health, the ability to deal critical hits, and other effects to even the odds against the endless waves of enemies that will stop at nothing to murder you.
The core gameplay is simple. You start somewhere in a semirandomly generated area. Your goal is to find the teleporter that will take you to the next area. Kill the monsters that spawn to gain money and experience. Leveling up increases your stats, but money allows you to open the chests and operate the shrines that are scattered around the map for items, as well as activate drones to aid you im combat. When you activate the teleporter, you are given a countdown where you must stay alive, as the boss of the area and even more enemies spawn around you. When the countdown is over, enemies stop spawning, but you still have to kill every single one left before you can move on to the next area. When you do, all your money is converted to experience, so there's no rushing the next map for chests right out of the gate. You have to survive through five areas before you get the chance to enter the final map and face the final boss, but you can continue looping back through the five areas as many times as you want (or survive through, at least).
The items you receive are random. Sometimes you run into machines that allow you to choose one of three, or ones that spin a roulette that stops on your cue, but for the most part, you aren't given much choice in what you pick up to help you. It may be the experimental drug that increases your attack speed, or the ukulele that adds a chain lightning effect to some of your attacks. Other items are activated manually, stopping time or granting you a shield of invincibility, with a cooldown between uses. As is standard for more modern roguelikes, there are persistent unlocks for completing certain tasks, increasing your item pool for future runs.
The big draw of the game is the fact that the game gets more difficult the longer a run gets. Indicated by a dificulty meter that ranges from 'Very Easy' to 'HAHAHAHA', more and stronger enemies spawn the higher the difficulty gets. Even if you've filled the meter by 40 minutes, the difficulty still increases beyond that. At the higher difficulties, even bosses spawn on their own, without the prompt of a teleporter activation.
Enemies also come in elite versions. Marked by a noticeable color change, these elite enemies have added effects, like increased health or explosive attacks, and gain more as the difficulty rises, like shooting homing missiles, healing nearby enemies, or teleporting directly to where you are.
There is also a difficulty you can choose at the start of the game: Drizzle, Rainstorm, or Monsoon. Depending on the mode you choose, you may start with shorter or longer teleporter countdowns, along with slower or faster difficulty scaling, and minor adjustments to enemies. Of course, Monsoon rewards you for playing on a higher difficulty with increased chances of unlocking cool stuff, whereas Drizzle prevents you from unlocking anything besides items and doesn't even record high scores.
Anything you kill outside of Drizzle mode has a chance to drop a monster log, which gives insight into the backstory of the game and the survivor's thoughts as they fight their way through the planet. Meanwhile, every item you've picked up can be viewed in the Item Log, with details of their effects and a little letter attached to each one. You did crash on a cargo ship, after all! Reading the Item Logs gives you a peek into where the items were intended to go, often with a little dark humor.
You're given 12 characters to unlock on your runs through various methods. Every character comes with a set of four skills, which range from invincibility-granting combat rolls to just swinging dual pickaxes around like madman. Every character favors a different style of play, like the Huntress who excels at kiting, or the close-quarters Loader.
When playing on Rainstorm or above, the maps can be generated with a hidden area and a puzzle to unlock Artifacts. These Artifacts can be activated when you choose your character, changing the way the game works. There is one unique Artifact per map.
Find Honor in the Desolate Forest and face enemies that are all Elite!
Bind yourself to Kin in the Dried Lake and be swarmed with armies of only a single type of monster!
Fall victim to a Distortion in Damp Caverns and lock yourself out of a random skill every minute!
Face your enemies' Spite in the Sky Meadow and watch them all drop bombs on death!
Become as fragile as Glass in the Ancient Valley, dealing five times the damage with only one-tenth of your health!
Find a mysterious Enigma in the Sunken Tomb, locking you to an activated item with a random effect every activation!
Gain the power of Sacrifice in the Magma Barracks, making enemy kills the only way to get item drops!
Take Command in the Hive Cluster and choose the items that drop!
Fill yourself with Spirit in the Temple of the Elders, making everything run faster the lower they are on health!
And if you can beat the game with all of them active at once, you will be rewarded with Origin, a sinister Artifact that gains the attention of the teleporting Imps that will invade periodically to kill you.
Final rating: 120/120 seconds, kill remaining enemies!

Risk of Rain is genuinely one of my favourite games on Steam. Through the suprising lack of rain there is an masterfully crafted rouge-like that doesn't shy away from mutilating your very soul on multiple occasions. It's frustrating as hell but in genius way, every death making you want to do it all again and prove the mocking death message wrong. There is no sort of proper story like some other rouge-likes, but it doesn't need one when you are gunning the heck down avian bird thingys with the much needed help of an electric ukelele - the story is that you're a rather small pixelated guy person, just go shoot some things without worrying about why you are doing it. As mentioned before this game is frustrating, which goes hand in hand with it's pretty steep learning curve, but every death along this curve seems constructive towards you as a player. Every time a robot guy smacks you in the face you still feel a peculiar sense of accomplishment, and every time you unlock a new character you may even find yourself shedding a tear  - which is something most games can't say they do. If you just want to play the video game equivalent of frolicking in a field then this game might not be for you, but if you are one of the two people in the world looking for a frustrating way to pass the time on a rainy day (hue hue) then maybe consider giving Risk of Rain a go. You never know, you might even enjoy yourself.

An interesting twist on the digital ccg formula with a unique "Evolve" comeback mechanic and very diverse classes. Reminds me of Hearthstone in all the best ways, and even goes beyond it in some aspects.

P2W vs Hearthstone: Either very (generous / heinous). Booster packs are somewhat 'fair', with rates for each card revealed officially. Many bronze/silver tier cards are viable. However there are 2~3 really powerful class legendaries that you (want to / have to) stuff the deck with full three copies for serious jump in win rates - Game allows you to buy the same starter deck three times for that reason more or less.
Gameplay: Some matchups can be very stagnant. They do their own thing, you do yours, and maybe once every three turns Haven and Rune will react to your turn. Hell, if the game let them do it, I'm sure they'd throw single target removals against an empty board out of force of habit. Aggro Swordcraft floods the board every turn and doesn't care how you deal with it, but at least there is a war of attrition to be fought there.
In the end everything is balanced because everything is OP, sort of. Except poor fairies, combo system isn't friendly to them yet.
Audiovisual: You're playing this instead of Hearthstone because of dem waifus. Illustrations are large enough to appreciate them as CCGs tend to be.
Overall: Nice distraction, probably worth investing a few starter decks, good fun being in the middle of the pack playing suboptimal decks, but the climb to top isn't appealing.

XCOM is more than just a turn-based strategy game. You begin as a mostly weak military organization set to keep alien invasions at bay. As you complete missions and capture and examine aliens, you can research and acquire their technology to make yourself even more powerful. Begin with a group of rookies shooting with cheap assault rifles and end with a team of elite soldiers with plasma weaponry, advanced armor that lets you climb up walls, and psionic abilities to decimate alien opponents.
Investments and time management are a necessity in normal mode and absolutely critical in the game's famous "Classic" mode, which requires several difficult decisions and sacrifices to complete the game successfully. XCOM is a fun and challenging time on its own in this respect apart from the already excellent combat system.
XCOM: Enemy Within is also a great "true" expansion to the game that adds lots of great weapons and story content. It's a hell of a lot more relevant than today's cheap DLC injections into every video game.
Try Ironman Mode for an extra challenge. Every decision you make sticks to one auto save, so you can't reload if you make a mistake.

Wow.  I'm impressed.  To be honest, I was skeptical but very intersted in trying the game.  I mean, come one, a fusion of parkour and zombies and wrapped in yet another FPS?  *sigh*
Surprise.  The free-running core gameplay mechanic inside of a zombie apocalypse story ... well... worked extremely well.
The free-running movement system is a subtle master-piece.  Such to the extent that it is so easy to take for granted, as it doesn't not flaunt itself in your face by means of hand-holding color highlighting, or by visually separating climbable objects from non-climbable objects.  In contrast, the mechanic, once learned (and quite simply, I'll add), rarely tries to guide you or make itself evident.  It just works, and really well.  If you see somethign in the game that (if the game was trying to be realistic and immersive) you feel you should be able to climb, then you have an extremely good chance of being able to.  I was impressed.
The environments themselves do a great job of making you feel as though you are a very exposed and endangered survivor in a very hostile environment.  If you make too much noise, you will attract attention to yourself, and faster moving zombies will seek you out.  During the day, the environments are saturated with hordes of undead shambling enemies, and at night the game becomes much more intense and difficult as a very lethal, nocturnal zombie type emerges, and, for the most part of the game, you have no choice to run from if they see you.
As for the story... The overall broad plot has been done a million times:  Man saves world.  The details between the start and finish, however, are unique and refreshing.  The characters have a lot of personality, the events that shape the story are interesting and do a great job of immersing you into the fiction.  I enjoyed the story, and I would have liked to have seen it continue beyond it's ending.
The action in the game is also quite good, though at first can feel too gamey.  Weapons break much too quick, and the crafting system feels too abstract and far-fetched, especially when you pull out machete, wrapped in electrified cable, with a small blow-torched strapped to it.  Once you get used to the extremely flimsy weaponry that looks like they belong in a dead rising title rather than this game, you'll find that the combat system (independent of the idiosyncracies with the weapons system) is very well designed and implemented, as the character changes the motion of his arm intuitively as you aim for a zombies neck instead of their leg, or their head instead of their torso, etc.  With that in mind, if you aim your attacks right, you will be able to control the amount of damage you do to your enemies, as a swipe to the neck with a sword is likely to decapitate a zombie in one shot, or a swing to the forehead with a hammer will likely explode a zombies head.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game.  Get it, even at full price.

Killing Floor 2 is the sequel to the popular survival shooter where you are pitted against massive waves of zeds which want to feast on your flesh.
Killing Floor 2 for me at the very least is improved in every way possible. It fixes a lot of the problems the original had, but it brings new problems along, but in general Killing Floor 2 is still a fantastic game.
There's no story to speak of in Killing Floor, but there's is a story in general. There's a virus which turns people to zombies and civilians band together with soldiers to fight the virus on the streets of Paris, London and Germany and in general all over the world.
Gameplay wise, this game is played mostly in a survival mode. So each game you have to survive for a few waves where you then face off against two types of bosses. One is the Patriarch and the other one is Dr Hans. Patriarch has a mini gun and a rocket launcher to fight you off and Dr Hans has a toxic gas and explosives.
The game also let's you pick a certain class like sharpshooter, gunslinger, firebug or support. These classes are built on what play style you prefer, so if you like burning everything alive pick firebug, if you like to use ranged weapons use Sharpshooter.
Now I felt that the classes in the first one were all balanced, while some were overpowered all of them had great qualities which made them fun to play, this time however I feel that that classes are a bit off. Like the firebug class not doing a lot of damage with the flamethrower.
The game also has new classes like a SWAT class which uses SMGs and a Survivor class which is a jack of all trades so you will find a class that suites you the best.
Graphically the game looks great and runs great. Fully maxed out the game runs fine even in the moments where the screen is full of stuff being ripped apart.
The soundtrack is also great, where you listen to heavy metal while shredding through waves and waves of zeds. While not every track is great, a lot of them are really good.
Overall Killing Floor 2 is a great sequel and has a ton of replay value. It's definitely one of the games you can come back and play from time to time. While it has slight issues with classes and other stuff I highly suggest checking this game out.
Final Rating:
9/10
Pros:
+ Runs and looks great
+ Fun gameplay
+ Tons and Tons of replay Value
Cons:
- Classes aren't balanced

Shadowrun Returns is a story-driven RPG with something akin to XCOM's combat system (albeit a few tweaks and more customization per character).  There isn't any choice that drives the plot in a different direction but there are multiple ways to deal with the smaller scenarios you're presented with, such as how to get into a blocked off area.  These ultimately do not affect the larger story but it's nice to have these smaller interactions in lieu of that.
Also, some dialog options are locked behind choices you make during character creation, and occasionally others are behind skill checks.  So that plus the multiple routes in each level makes up for what I imagine were budgetary constraints that prevented a multi-path narrative.  It was a Kickstarter after all.  I don't know if this is the case for the future titles in the series, so don't judge those based on this.  I'm only talking about the base game.
The skill system in this game is satisfying, using a steady stream of points instead of levels.  I like all the different ways I can customize my character.  The classes all feel varied and interesting, and they fit the world really well.
Shadowrun is well written, even if the story is not revolutionary.  It has fast paced dialog and isn't overly wordy, like the aforementioned Pillars of Eternity, or most games which people claim are "well written."  It doesn't bog you down in detail, yet it also provides quite sufficient descriptions to give you a good understanding of everything.  Sometimes the world's "slang" feels a bit cheesy (like using 'frag' instead of ♥♥♥♥).  I love a world that has its own slang, like in Clockwork Orange, but that slang was far more believable.  I don't believe for a second that people would say frag and stop saying ♥♥♥♥.
Even with a bad story, I'd still be interested because the world that this is set in is fantastic.  It's a cross of D&D, Blade Runner, and Deus Ex.  I've not played any of the other games/tabletop games in this ruleset before so the whole thing is new to me, and I really found myself drawn into it immediately.  The only critique is that it's too bleak to be plausible.  No society with the technological capability of this one could crumble to the place that this one does.  Still, it is a work of fiction, and it's established well enough to overlook the unlikeliness of it.  The story deals with serious subjects like drug addiction, racism, torture, etc. but it also manages to keep a lot of levity in there as well.  It takes itself seriously enough, but not to a point where it's brooding or depressing at all.
Overall it's a nice little game which I've enjoyed far more than many other releases.  I avoided the game for its middling reviews, but I am upset that I did in retrospect.  I'd have liked to play these games earlier when I was searching for something to play.  I really love the XCOM type combat, the classes are all interesting, the story is sufficient, and the world is really great.
And this is gonna seem strange, but there's some real oomph to when characters get shot, and that has made me want to play the game almost more than anything else about it.  There's something about when games make something feel right that I just love.  I played Spiderman 2 on PS2 for dozens and dozens of hours just because of how web slinging felt correct.  I remember playing San Andreas and thinking about how differently each of the cars felt from one another, and how they all felt right in their own way.  This game, the way it feels when you shoot someone and it makes impact, it just feels correctly made.  I realize that there's probably nothing more subjective than to say that I enjoy the way it feels to shoot enemies in this game, but it's my review, so whatever.  Get the game.
