is linear story-driven game with turn-based combat. You are a mercenary in a sci-fi world that also got few drops of magic and your goal is to find the murder of a friend of yours.
The story plot is generic: You are called by your friend who was recently murdered and you have to find his murder. On the way you gonna meet other runners and people that will show you that there is more than meet the eye.
Even with the generic plot, the writing is solid and often you see that there are several approaches in a conversation that is based on your stats and etiquette. But dont worry if you cant talk your way out, few bullets can do the same or maybe a few slashes or fireballs.
The combat in Shadowrun Returns is turn-based with Action Points and cover. If you played X-Com : Enemy Unknown , the combat will be old friend of yours if not then you will be in luck since combat is simple enough to learn but it can be hard to master.  First thing first : being melee you are allowed to walk and attack with 1 action point( more if the target is far away) while for range you cant run and gun. Instead  you will want to get in cover before you start spreading love/bullets/magic. If you arent fan of direct attacks you can instead use drones/spirit to do the dirty job.
We should not forget and the AoE skills mainly because there is friendly fire so you have to be careful when you use them. Especially if there is low hit chance because if it misses, the AoE will hit somewhere near the targeted zone.
Cover is mainly to reduce the chance to be hit but at times it may seem broken . Once I went behind a target that was in cover and my hit chance got reduced(in pointblank range) which was weird.
Once you are familiar with meat-world combat you will have to encounted and the Matrix which can be accessed only by deckers . Combat in the matrix is the same but you use different skills and death in the Matrix means disconnect and damage to your real self.
Thats one area which lacks content. While you have on your hands several kind of gear to use, you will find that there isnt much variety in it and you will just look for the higher numbers.
First you have your outfit that provides armor and bonuses to different stats. Then you have your weapons melee/range/drones/ spells , Then you have slots for skills and last but not least you have consumables : medkit, revival kits,grenades , spirits.
If you arent fan of using spells/magic then you will be glad to upgrade yourself with cyberware. Cyberware provides you with improved stats at the cost of your essence(the ability to use spells) which is a fair trade if you count on melee or range weapons.
But still Equipment pool is lacking a lot.
Here we are with the best part of this game. I mean what is an RPG without a decent character customization , huh?
While you can pick one of the 5 premade classes you are better off with making your own class and the customization deliver just that. There are 6 main stats : Body, Quickness(Agility), Strength , Intelligence , Willpower and Charisma. And each one of them got different branches that offer different skills(only Body doesnt have any those since its mainly to increase your HP).
Quickness is important for your range gunners . It allows you to spend points on different gun types : Pistol,Shotgun, SMG and Rifle. It also let you increase your points in dodge which makes you harder to hit with physical attacks. It also allows you to specific actions in a conversation.
Strength is important for your brawlers because it let you spend points on close combat : melee weapons or unarmed.In the same tree you will find and the throwable stats. And just like quickness, you can pick unique options during a dialogue.
Intelligence is important for your techwizards: hackers or drone users. Hackers are useful when you are investigating because you will often find hackable objects that provides useful information. Also only Hackers(deckers) can enter the Matrix to provide you with extra information. Drone users on the other hand will be able to use higher level drones . On top of that Intelligence also contain the Biotech branch that increases the amount of HP you recover with medkits. And just like the other stats you are given unique dialogue options every now and then.
Willpower is the main stats for mages. Increasing it will allow you to equip more and better spells. It also increases the chance to hit with them.
Charisma is the main stats for spirit users and sweet talkers. Its most helpful if you try to talk your way out of a situation. It also allows you to have different etiquettes.
Its worth noting that different races got different limit on some stats, And a friendly advice from me : Never try to be a Jack of all trades because there arent enough Karma points to let you do that. Instead focus on 2 stats and let other shadowrunners fill the weak spots(yes you can hire other runners on some missions).

Companies are trying to cash-in on the huge zombie genre push. Most of the games are absolute garbage not worth playing for free.
Dying Light is most definitely
garbage, at all, and it's nice to be able to say that given the trend over the last several years.
From my perspective there are two main categories. Low budget small team and corporate.
For low budget (and cost) I believe the best value is
7 Days to Die. It's worth supporting. The developers and the community are active and the results are outstanding considering the size of the team and budget constraints.
So what about corporate, big budget high production value? All the ones I've seen so far are total s h i t, and then there's Dying Light. I found it on a whim. I've been avoiding zombie games after so any are just worthless un-fun trash.
I saw this one properly supported DX11 and after reading extensively about the game it seemed to be the real thing.
Dying Light stands out so far. I've just put in a couple days of intense addictive play. Excellent quality in almost every aspect. If you want a solid FPS POV horror action RPG - yes, it
have actual RPG elements - without the ignorant 3rd person POV crap then Dying Light is a good bet.
The price is high but that's been the trend in the industry for awhile. Considering how many other pieces of crap exist at or near the same price-point this one smashes their skulls, completely.
It'll start you off at a manageable pace getting your feet wet (soaked in blood). If you're paying attention you'll notice how the pace and danger gets more intense. It's done pretty well.
The main city is huge. I'm just now in the 2nd smaller city, but small is relative it seems pretty huge and there's a LOT more interior areas here. That plus the distinct architectural differences, number and type of enemies feels right.
So overall there's a gigantic amount of action-packed fun doing all kinds of stuff in both cities, and night time is where you'll find real terror if you've the spine for it.
The visuals overall, flexible rag-doll dismemberment, weather and just about everything else is outstanding. It does take a good rig to really enjoy all its glory, but if your rig is strong you'll like what you see.
I play on a huge LED TV five feet from me in a dark room and it's
intense, and a lot of fun. My visuals are powered by twin GTX Titans (and many other fast components) so I simply have no frame of reference if it sucks (nor how bad it sucks) on mid range equipment. But if you've got some power this game will use it.
The big negative is the ignorant durability system. A steel pipe, beefy sword or oak table leg wears out and breaks after bashing in just a few skulls. There are several methods to eliminate this stupid aspect of the game, just do some research.
With the durability issue removed there's a real gut wrenching, meat chunk factory load of fun to be had if you want to shower in gore for awhile.

I've had this game (and the first one) sitting in my library for a while now, the way "bundle fillers" usually do... but I gotta say, these games were a nice little surprise.
Starting by the universe they present: Everything is weird as hell, but it feels original and interesting and if you're like me, you'll be hooked instantly and will want to know more. The first game serves as an introduction to the universe by way of a rather limited (in scope) and more personal story about the main character and his "family"... The second game serves as both a continuation of that story as well as a deeper exploration of the world they live in. And it's all a breath of fresh air among the countless traditional fantasy/sci-fi plots that plague every game these days.
Moving on to the gameplay... well, it's basically an FPB (as in first person brawler) and it does its job well. Whereas the first game was very restricted in terms of gameplay (a succession of "arena-like" levels with almost no exploration allowed), the second one is definetly more of an "open-world" and allows you to just go and explore this beautiful strange world you're punching weird creatures in. In fact the game will reward you for exploring which is nice.
What I liked about this second game is the freedom it gives the player in terms of gameplay. You can approach this as a straight arcade brawler game and just go into the Arena mode. And even in the story mode, you're still free to roam the world and explore or just rush through the main story line and punch your way to the end.
A lot of people might complain about the repetitveness of the open world and the respawn mechanics, but hey, they game provides you with an effective run mechanic which will allow you to bypass most fights (except the story-scripted ones) if you're not in the mood, or you can chose to take the time to punch everything in your way.
If you're not so much a fan of punching all the time, the game's got you covered with several ranged weapons lying around and a perma-weapon that will make your life much much much easier (not gonna spoil it but look for it very early in the game) for those who are more into exploring and playing the game for the story.
Yeah there are some quirks and issues with this second game, but overall it's definetly an improvement in every regard to the first one, which was rather basic (but effective). Better graphics too as well, which is appreciated in such a lush and strange environment. The voice acting on both games is top-notch too, and the music is very good and fits well to the atmsophere of the game.
So if you're like me and have had this game sitting around in your library, I definetly recommend you give it a chance (and the first one as well, although not really needed). And if not, you might want to consider putting it on your wishlist, since I think it gets a hefty discount on every steam sale at this point. It's very much worth it if you enjoy weird fantasy worlds...

*Hints for first time players*
A.) To aid with the white line effect- when playing in 1920x1080 downgrade graphics via the launcher from “fantastic” to “good” . This does not entirely eliminate the white lines, but it reduced their effect dramatically on my rig.
B.)language selection- select “opciones” - left click “idiomas: castellano” - left click one more time for english.
C) turn down mouse sensitivity- either just above the language selection, or in game hit Esc- options. I would suggest next to lowest setting, if not lowest.
To be as constructive as possible, the game is down right slippery. One defined tap down on an MX brown switch and my character moves an additional 2 or 3 strides in any direction. Honestly it made me feel like a wet noodle for the first 30 seconds when combined with the mouse sensitivity that felt unnecessarily quick at default settings (in my opinion). The textures, specifically on the buildings, struck me as a homebrew skyrim, and i have no issues with that, except for the white line bug other comments have mentioned. I don’t want to make too much of a big deal about the language selection as it was simple enough to change if you’ve been playing games for a decent part of your life.
But there are issues that made the game a displeasure to play. First off, the crashes. My game hung twice in my very brief play through. On my first boot up i was stuck inspecting the hay cart within three minutes of playing the game. Then i got stuck on a loop of going up and down the stairs inside the inn, until eventually i was stuck near the top of the stairs until i Alt+F4’ed. Of course there’s no auto save (or not that i experienced) so 20 minutes into the game I’m launching it from the start for the 3rd time.
Second issue is the lack of direction. I found the crow bar, the tankard, the matchbook, the lantern, the rock, and the key.I filled the tankard with beer cus I like to party. Then I spoke to the farmer (incoming meme on the English translation), the inn keeper, and the priest that’s too busy to talk to you. And like many other players the game ground to a halt. Was not sure what i was missing, and there wasn’t so much as a journal or objective list to give me hints.
There are several miscellaneous bugs I’m sure the developer intends to patch. The priest and the farmer often try to walk and are stuck in quick sand, then after loading my save they wouldn’t quit walking away from me during interaction. And one old school glitch by the barn where you can slide through the fence and walk towards the level boundary.
It’s a free-to-play experience that’s both new to steam, and needs a lot of fine tuning. Preferably if anything were made a priority, it would be a hint system that would help players find what the objective of the game is, if indeed that objective is actually obtainable. Without it, a lot of players may feel like they’re searching for the entertainment, and not receiving it. The free-to-play market is a fickle place for gamers like myself that have a back log of unplayed games, and first impressions are often love it or uninstall.
I hope my tips at the top helped someone get their feet wet a little quicker while they were browsing through the comment section during the download. If not, I still did my good deed for the day, and Santa Claus has to bring me presents now!

This is a return of an old classical 2 players game. This is not a new remake. As I noticed they changed only three things:
1. Added a filter that makes pixels look smoother. Can be disabled, but I really liked it (steam store screenshots have it turned on).
2. Added autosave of the last unlocked password. No need to write them down on a sheet of paper. Handy.
3. Not only local, but also a network multiplayer (2 players coop campaign).
None of these features really make this game better or worser than it was before. I hightly recommend it to those who played this game years ago and liked it. It's still the very same fun game. On the other hand, mashing Fire is still a need as this way you shoot faster than if you just hold Fire key/button.
For those of you who didn't... Well, it's a good 2 players coop game, played good if using the same computer (keyboard or controller for each player). The game is of average difficulty. It can kill you really quick if you are careless, but not unbeatable and doesn't require super reaction or precision. No combos, dirty tricks, you can play it straight out of the box. A lot of guessing elements appear later in the game and make you life easier or harder depending on your choices. This game will not take much time, it has autosave every half an hour or an hour at later stages when you reach a new world.. or if you loose all your lives before that :D. If everything goes good, you'll be able to complete it in one go in somehting like 3-4 hours. Six different characters and different special power (unlocked later) give this game some replayability, but not too much. Finishing it 1-3 times will probably be enough for most players.
If this sounds fun - you should try it. If not - pass by, this game is quite good, but not a must see.

The offline play remains pretty true to the SNES version, but the special power button seems sort of bugged out. I was playing with a 360 controller and it get mapped by default to the L trigger, which seems to be sort of wonky. Luckily you can remap the controls, but it still seems sort of sticky to use. Other bugs include leaderboards showing The Priest in lieu of some other characters. I was doing a play with the Thug/Brigand and the leaderboard shows Thug/Priest, for example.
The enhanced graphics are ok, but not that great. It looks like a photoshop smooth filter was applied to the character models (the map seems the same?) and a bit shinier of explosions, but that's about it. You can switch between either graphics instantly while in game, though, which is nice. There's a nice "how-to" menu that explains the formerly bamboozling upgrade system and explains the powerups nicely.
I wouldn't really recommend this game at its fullest price point unless you're a bizarrely huge fan of the original game(s). I'd wait for a steam sale for its price to drop substantially to really justify it, considering you can find SNES roms of it for free.

The year is 1887 and a number of very strange things have begun to occur all over the world. First of all a dinosaur is found trapped in rock just south of Berkshire. However, when examined it appears that it's a lifeform not known to man. At the same time a theatre in Paris suddenly disappears into the earth, the Statue of Liberty crashes into the heart of New York destroying everything in its path, and half the population of Bavaria are turned into wolves, stalking the countryside for innocent victims.
Central to these strange happenings, Great Britain descends into anarchy as the landscape begins to alter and change disturbingly. Unknown to everyone the source of the disturbances is coming from the south of Cornwall where Baron Fortesque, bored of making pasties and fighting off Spanish trawlers, has decided to build a massive steam-driven engine with the power to transform matter. It grows out of control andt he Baron becomes imprisoned within the engine, transforming him into a deformed creature of evil. Now fueling itself, the Chaos Engine continues to inflict its evil curse on the world.
Two brave soldiers (the game can be played co-operatively) must enter the grounds of the mansion and make their way to the resting-place of the dreaded engine - The Hall of Machines. Stepping forward for the task are six unique individuals: the Mercenary, the Brigand, the Gentleman, the Navvie, the Thug and the Priest. Picking the right two men for the job is essential if you're going to have any chance of getting near the evil device.
Each character has different statistics covering speed, skill, intelligence, strength, health and weaponry and it really does matter who you choose as if you pick a strong yet stupid computer-controlled partner in single player they may well stand around while you are getting shot to pieces (though picking a weak yet smart character may leave you with too little firepower and thus end up with you getting shot to pieces also).
Whoever you choose, you must then fight your way through four worlds, split into four individual levels in order to achieve your goal. Viewed from a top-down perspective, the title takes a somewhat unique approach to the standard shooter. While action consists of going around blasting anything and everything that moves, there is a subtle strategy at work in the game mechanic. As well as blasting there are endless puzzles to solve, some of which are incredibly tricky to work out. Solving puzzles leads you to secret areas or even to a different exit from the level.
In order to leave the current level a set number of nodes must be activated in order to activate the exit door. Doing this is easier said than done as you are usually surrounded by all manner of nasty creatures. This fills the game with an incredibly intense atmosphere that is built up in equal measure by the bleak graphical style and the outstanding industrial-tinged techno soundtrack. Graphics are fairly simple but contain subtle elements of detail that make you believe you're making your way through a truly disturbing place; this coupled with a dark and menacing colour palette is incredibly effective in creating the chaos-themed world that the title is set in.
Something else that Elevates the game to the next level is the outstanding soundtrack. One of the most potently powerful musical creations in the history of gaming, the soundtrack beautifully accompanies the action with its continually brooding and sinister nature, hinting that you are only scratching the surface of evil and at any minute the true horror is about to greet you. Simply stunning.
In terms of how the game actually plays, we are presented with a strange juxtaposition of styles. Although you are constantly under threat from numerous nasty creatures that all need blasting to bits, the game has a somewhat structured pace to it. Far from the breakneck speed of other top-down shooters such as Smash T.V., The Chaos Engine makes you think more carefully about what you should be doing, Go aimlessly wading in with all guns blazing and you will die, simple as that. Instead, players need to stand back from time to time and think how best to deal with the creatures. This is mainly because certain creatures take forever to kill so you need to make sure they are going to be dead before they reach you. Also, you cannot move and shoot at the same time, so you have to move up the screen then stop in order to pick off enemies (bringing even more strategy to proceedings).
There have been some improvments made, such as the smoothing of graphics and getting the game to understand a proper 360 degree axis to allow for better movement and shooting with control pads and analogue sticks. However, this is effectively the same game as before - it's now just a bit more friendly for modern PC's. It feels old school and a touch dated but the strenght of the game is such that is remains something worth playing.Perhaps more could ahve been done but at least it can't be accused of ruining the atmosphere or feel of the game.
The Chaos Engine is one of the most original and inventive shooting games that has ever graced the planet. With a difficulty setting that starts at hard and goes to ridiculous, it's a very rare thing to meet someone who has made it all the way to the end. Regardless, it's a genuinely exciting experience and any true fan of either retro gaming or shooters should have this title in their collection. It is a strategy-tinged, puzzle-filled, full-on, adrenaline-pumping ambient shooter, and you need it, but it might seem a touch slower than you remember.

I've read a lot of negative things about Shadowrun Returns. After a few hours of playtime, I can now understand where those less-than-stellar reviews came from. However, from a pure "entertainment perspective," SR is still plenty of fun and certainly worth it's purchase price (especially when on sale for only $2.99).
Let's get the most negative thing out of the way; Shadowrun Returns isn't much deeper than your average FPS. It certainly has RP elements, but the way you're shuttled through the story and the way missions play out is completed limited. For example, you can't really choose where you want to go when you leave a building. You just go where the next mission is, automatically. Or, if you're in a mission there's only one "action indicator" so you click it, go to the next, click it, etc.  Because of this gameplay mechanic, I would actually liken this to more of a point and click adventure than an RPG.
One secondary dig - The fixed camera position is part of what gives this game it's charm but it also sucks hard at times. I understand that HBS couldn't (on an indie budget & team size) fully realize all their locales in 3D so you could pan the camera, but my god... not being able to see your character is awful. They didn't even bother making buildings go transparent.
So far it sounds terrible, right? Perhaps for somebody that has a ton of games to play this isn't worth your time. On the other hand, I absolutely love two things about this game. First (and obviously), I love the Shadowrun universe. There may be other games that have combined magic/technology/combat in the past 20 years, but this feels "OG" to me since I remember playing Shadowrun on SNES.  Also, I love the graphics. This could go both ways for other players, too. I like the clean esthetic instead of the standard, modern "concrete texture" everywhere. I would wager that if they did THAT, I would like it more but this look stands out against the competition for now.
Anyway, overall, I say to get this if just to help support smaller developers. I've read parts of reviews of the follow up games (Dragonfall & Hong Kong ) that said they fixed problems in the original reboot. If you're on the fence, based on that info, I'd say to skip this game but definitely buy one of the sequels instead.

Lots of fun, but plenty of issues.
First the good:
* Rich world and great atmosphere.
* The combat is fun, though a bit repetitive. For an RPG, this game is on the short side, which is probably just the right length to prevent things from getting too repetitive.
* Good story. Some parts are amazing. Some parts are just OK. I think it averages out to good.
Now the bad:
* More than two years after release, there are still some glaring typos in plot necessary dialogues (such as extraneous words that clearly don't belong).
* Movement is often awkward and slow. After finishing an area, you'll stay in turn based combat mode; this kills a bit of the fun of exploring a floor you've cleared.
* Very linear. I found two side missions which were both very short.
* Terrible point-and-click targeting. I found myself walking past targets I meant to attack and unable to move to squares behind allies simply due to not being able to target the right square or creatures.
Overall, the good outweighs the bad. It's worth a play and will probably take you about 15 hours at a leisurely pace.

Among the most enjoyable games I've played in the past 5 years, Shadowrun Returns gives oldsters everything they've been hankering for for years - and then some.  Although the story is somewhat simplistic, and the entire plot occurs very much railroaded, the gameplay is tight and enjoyable and the characters relatively memorable.  Even more so, the fact that you are given a choice to play someone who is mercenary without being Bioware Evil was refreshing, and speaks to the core of Shadowrun.  Reliving some of the most famous scenarios and plotlines from the older editions also gives veteran Runners a treat, and can help bring newer Runners up to speed rapidly, without bogging them down.
That isn't to say that this game doesn't have flaws.  Melee is bad - just BAD.  The rules don't even resemble the rules present in the tabletop RPG, and so this game would be completely insufficient for helping someone ease into the actual game itself.  And the villains are largely one-dimensional; maybe fitting for an RPG that was spawned in the 1980s, but not nearly as satisfying as the more nuanced villains who have appeared in more recent fare.
But at the end of the day, Shadowrun Returns is quick, dirty, and enjoyable - exactly the way a Shadowrun should be.  If you think of it less like an extended campaign with deep ideas, and more as a short arc between longer sections of a real campaign, its relative lack of depth becomes more bearable - as does it's short run time.  With it's drop in price, anyone who hasn't picked this up should, however.  It's very fun.

The best aspect is probably the game's ability to generate atmosphere. Considering the fairly 'primitive' graphics (although the lighting and some of the effects are really cool), Teleglitch does an amazing job at generating tension - with procedurally generated levels, no less.
Speaking of the proc-gen levels, it should probably be noted that the levels are only 'psuedo' proc-gen. You can expect some or all of the elements to appear in a given order and layout in a particular level in any play-though. I think this is a good thing, as it allows the player to develop a strategy for how to progress, but at the same time doesn't get boring on repeated playthroughs - which there will be many of it's a hard game.
If you like roguelikes, system shock-esque sci fi horror, arena shmups or a combination of the three, Teleglitch is worth playing.

I'm not much of a reviewer, but with the amount of mixed reviews going around for this, I figured I would throw my 2 cents in.
I love this game. It's fun as hell, but like most reviewers have stated, it starts slow. You're not a fighter when you first start. It's hard to go rage mode in the beginning, but that makes the rewards of playing so much better. I'm about 15-20% through the game at this point and I feel like a pretty solid fighter. It's a blast crushing zombie skulls and kicking them while they're down. And the co-op is ridiculously fun. I've never been a co-op player. I mostly play single player or the type of multiplayer that is just a kill the other team scenario. Well, once I finally tried the co-op, I was hooked. It moves a lot faster and your group will slaughter any and all zombies in your way. The night runs are insane, so be warned.  And when a group of 4 players knocks a zombie down and they start kicking it while it's down, I can't help but laugh with delight (I'm twisted).
The graphics are beautiful, but it's demanding. I had to do a lot of tweaking to get it running smooth at the higher settings.
The sound is really well done, especially when you "make loud noise" in the game. It attracts nearby zombies and the sounds they make as they get ready to come after you are creepy as hell.
The story is meh....It's nothing special, but it's there. It's not bad, but it won't keep you on the edge of your seat. Don't expect much from it.
The gameplay is fun as hell and easy to pick up on.
I hope this review was helpful to some of you and thanks for reading.

"Killing Floor 2 itself was a nice treat since last time we played it was a year ago while it was in an Early Access stage. Now it's a finished game with far more content than there was when we first bought it. I joked that in terms of violence (which I've become very desensitized to - not because of games; I've had no problem with violence long before I began gaming, thanks to the news and the public education system), KF2 is an overbearing, super conservative parent's nightmare in terms of how gruesome it gets at times. Very cinematic too, though I say that because it periodically has "slow-mo" scenes like in action movies where a gunman dives through a window or something and shoots 10 people in slow motion, called "Zed (common slang for zombies, not just in the game) Time", which is really cool." - From my Facebook.
In terms of original review content... well I summed it up from my Facebook post. Still, Killing Floor 2 is a blast. In terms of graphics and the game engine it runs competently on high graphics settings (in-game, I mean), which is nice given the jaw-dropping amount of gore featured. I somehow broke a trend where I was usually ultra-conservative about ammunition, but somehow morphed my style of play into turning my weapons into a typhoon of bullets (which one of the game's classes allows me to do, I'll cover that momentarily) that would ultimately leave me empty. I ended up using my knife for once, and MY GOD the effects. I chopped two zombies in half; one horizontally and one vertically. All while a massive tsunami of blood and gore effects fly every which way. So if you're squeamish, Killing Floor 2 is going to be a living hell for you.
But the other side of Killing Floor 2 is the gameplay itself. Let's discuss that. I mentioned classes; Killing Floor 2 is a very, very teamwork-oriented shooter. Up to six people rally up to fight 4, 7 or 10 waves of mixed zombie types - I estimate there to be at least 10 distinct zombie castes (though technically this game's antagonist force aren't really conventional "rise from the grave" zombies; more like genetic experiments or something), from typical brainless walkers to big fat guys to shriekers to INVISIBLE zombies. The amount of zombies is scaled to the number of players, however the game is much, much easier with teammates; makes sense, given how that's sort of the intention. Oh, and there are the bosses, which are damn near impossible to bring down alone.
Classes themselves: spawn as different roles with different specialty weapons. They get really specific and creative in this game, I should say - a post-initial release addon was in the form of a "Gunslinger" class which focuses on all sorts of pistols with an emphasis on dual-wielding them. Said class, when leveled, gets to choose one of two perks every five levels until the player reaches the max level of 25. There are typical classes, such as the "Commando", which favors assault rifles, and then more obscure things like the "Firebug" which focuses on flame-oriented weaponry as the title might hint. When I say "specialty weapons" I refer to weapons that the classes boost. The Commando, as I said, gains experience by killing zombies with assault rifles, which include a Colt 9mm SMG (don't ask why a submachine gun counts as an assault rifle; by the way, this is the weapon that the Commando will spawn with), an L85, an AK-12 and a SCAR-H (which is technically a battle rifle). You can use other weapons, like the Gunslinger's pistols, but you won't gain any experience for the Commando if you use those weapons instead of the assault rifles.
Killing Floor 2 might look like ANOTHER zombie shoot-'em-up co-op game, but it's a damn good one that simply deserves to be played. It's a grindhouse supreme with awesome effects, a rockin' soundtrack (no seriously, the soundtrack is tons of rock and metal music, which is also really well composed), creative classes, varied enemies, good performance on a technical level, and is just a really well-made game.

I normally love the top down shooter genre, and this game shows a lot of promise. But on the whole the experience is very lacking.
The game tells you levels are procedurally generated, but the variation they do have is far more limited than you would think. Each level has the same rooms, just arranged into different places with some awkward hallways stringing them together.
Other reviewers have commented that it's hard, but most any game can be made just as hard by removing any save functions. The overall effect of removing save points and deleting saves when you die was more tedious and frustrating that I have to slog through the same areas again. And again. And again. If that's your idea of fun I can only imagine what kind of abusive household you must have grown up in.
Another frustration, the knife (which you will have to use a ridiculous amount for a top down "shooter") does not automatically keep attacking. I had to download an auto-clicker just to spam left clicks for me because you will wear out your index finger and mouse in short order otherwise. If that sounds too technical for you or if you plan on playing on a console without a turbo button controller you should not buy this game.
The painfully low resolution makes it hard to even know what you're looking at, which in later levels when enemies start carrying guns will regularly prove fatal. The flavor text you pick up from terminals is probably my favorite part, but if I wanted to indulge my bookish side I'd be better served by ordering a book. At $15 it's hard to say it's not worth the price, but it certainly isn't worth the time.

Inventory is basic, but inconsistent. Some objects you can use by clicking on them and choosing the action, but some objects require you to open your inventory and drag something to it. Why couldn’t it be one or the other for everything? More inconsistency.

I'm really split on this game, which rarely happens.  The premise of the game is great, and the way the different elements (squad, economy, panic levels, air defense, etc.) tie together is well done.  The reason I don't recommend it, is sadly due to issues that could be very easily solved with a couple options in the game menu.  The actual battles take far too long, due all the triggered events, and having to watch the enemy take its long turns (this also bounces the camera around, which is annoying).  Get close enough to an enemy to discover them on the map?  Get ready for a little cutscene.  Is one alien boosting another?  Get ready for some multi-second animation.  It doesn't sound like much, but for as many turns, and as many battles as you have to do, they really add up.  And yes, this is with disabling the action cam in the menu.  I'm fine with the cinematic style being the default, but give us an option to cut out all that fluff.  When it's my turn, I'll survey the map, I don't need to see 4 enemies scurry behind a wall, 1 miss a shot, 1 heal another, etc.  The best solution would be to offer which actions the player wants to see.  All movements?  All actions more than just movement?  Only shots that hit and surpression?  Would've been an easy drop down option in the options screen, and made a world of difference.

Risk Of Rain is a Rogue-like, difficult game with 2D pixelated graphics, and definatly in my top 10 games on steam. The game itself is pretty solid and provides a ton of replay value. It has some RNG in the game which adds to the replay value of the game itself. It has Multiplayer which is really fun when you have a few buddies to help you through the game.
Risk Of Rain is a Rogue-like game, which means that you know this game isn't going to be easy. It has perma-death and survival elements in the game that really make the game what it is. When you first start off playing this game you might die, A lot. You will not complete this game in you're first few runs. You are going to need to learn and adapt to your situations and how you're going to survive this. The game is really fun, even though you might die a lot and get fustrated you'll want to come back to it and play 'one' more time. The basic of what you have to do is to find the portal, activate it and then survive until you kill all the enmies on the area then teleport to the next area. As 'easy' as this sounds it's really not. You are kind of up against a timer in some aspects, the longer you are staying in the area the harder it'll get. But why would you stay in the area and not go straight to the portal? Well to collect items you need to open chests, to open chests you need enough money, to get money you need to kill enemies, to kill enemies you have to wait until they spawn. So the process forces you to stay in a area to get the items that are in the chest. A really coll mechanic if you ask me. The game has a nice variety of characters and powerups that you collect on you're journey. Other collectable include secret artifacts that you can use to modify you're game to make it a bit different. For example one of the artifacts will called Glass does the following: Deal 500% damage, but have 10% health. There are 9 others and you can put these into you're runs if you want to variey you're gaming experience with this game. This adds replay value and makes this game really enjoyable. There are a few glitches that I have encountered while playing the game, such as when you start a new run you will just continously fall through the world, and sometimes the enemies would freeze and you can't kill them or do anything.
The game itself really has done well with the pixelated graphics, Especially all the animations of the characters and their own personal abilities that they have. That along with the huge amount of enemies that you encounter throughout playing a few runs is really impressive. Some of the bosses are really well animated with their attacks as well. Everything just really seems to fit in with this sort of game play that this game has to offer. It doesn't seem lazy with the animations that some games have, it really seems that the developers put a lot of effort in the animtations and general art style of this game.
The music and the soudns kind of bring this game down a little bit. The sounds are a bit generic for my taste and the music isn't really all that it could be. If the game could add some more music and some more variation then I would really like to hear that. Otherwise for the time being I will be listening to my own music while playing this game.
This game is really fun. If you can see past some of the generic sounds and repeptitive music of the game then it is really fun. The graphics for this game are superb, and the animtations are in no way 'lazy.' Each character and enemie have their own custom animations. It also has a high replay value which is wha you want in these difficult, perma-death rogue-like games. Really fun with friends or playing solo!

Zeno Clash 2 is the sequel to ACE Team's fantastic Zeno Clash, which should already be obvious by the name. Seriously though, I must congratulate ACE Team, since they delivered a great follow-up to an excellent game.
In this game, we still play as Ghat. After the events of the first game, the North Golem has established a prison in Halstedom, and imprisoned FatherMother in it. However, Ghat isn't happy with the Golem trying to impose his rules, and so he, along with his sister Rimat, start a "quest" to kick the Golem out of Zenozoik.
The combat system has been greatly improved; now there's a lot of different attacks, and you can chain them up into powerful combos, and weapons have received changes as well; they now feel a lot more satisfying to use, although nothing can beat punching the face of every opponent you meet with your bare hands. Now this game is a lot more open than the first one; while the story progress in a linear way, the game world allows you to revisit areas after you acquire new abilities, allowing you to find new paths and such. There's also an air of RPG mechanics, since you can level up certain stats, and a few characters offer you sidequests which reward you with new weapons, abilities, or allies.
The game also features a coop mode, with the second player taking the role of Rimat. While in singleplayer you can call Rimat and another ally for some battles, it's in coop that the combat system shines. Not only will you both be kicking and punching your way around Zenozoik, but having a second player opens new possibilities: your friend can grab an enemy for you to kick at your pleasure; and it'll also make some of the fights more interesting, having someone to help you out that isn't AI controlled. It also features a challenge mode with three different maps: the Colosseum, where you fight 50 waves of enemies, with a brief time between waves to buy allies or upgrades (this one can be played coop, too!); the Framerate Arena, where you must keep killing enemies in order to keep your FPS count over 25; and the Rock of Ages challenge, which is like the Colosseum, only that you control the boulder from Rock of Ages, one of ACE Team's games, and you can only buy allies in the store.
The soundtrack is top notch; with different tunes for each area, including day and night tracks (yes, the game features a day/night cycle), and combat music. Very well done, in my opinion. And the level design leaves nothing to be desired, the world in Zeno Clash 2 is even more bizarre than its predecessor, and that's great. You'll find lots of interesting locations while you travel through Zenozoik. Another great thing about this game is that it fills a lot of details regarding the history of Zenozoik, while still leaving some things unanswered, which makes me wish for a third game, even when it does a good job at wrapping up Ghat's story, I still want to see and learn more of this world.
Well, I think that's enough for Zeno Clash 2. If you enjoyed the original, then you should definitely get this one, as it has everything that made the first one, and takes it up to eleven.

There was a lot of hype surrounding this game - and to be honest, I was pretty excited about it, too. Maybe I built it up too much. I wanted this game to make me question everything I ever believed in. A WTF around every corner. I expected a mind-blower, something that would change the very way I think.
And you know... there were a lot of WTFs around a lot of corners, but nothing really challenged me to let go of my assumptions, or force me to rethink my methods of navigating non-Euclidean spaces, or anything like that.
Antichamber is just a regular puzzle game. A lot of the WTFs are just gimmicks specific to a room or a puzzle that you need to figure out largely via experimentation. Most of the time, you wander around confused until you accidentally stumble upon the answer - and you realize that OHHH you can walk through a certain wall, or WTF if you walk back the way you came, you end up in a new room. There ARE a handful of situations that require logic or problem solving, but these aren't mind-blowing or assumption-shattering; they're just challenging and really hard to solve.
I had to come back to this game several times to complete, because I often found myself in a rut or travelling in circles after about an hour or so. And then, it was hard to come back to because I would remember how frustrating it was. For the total amount of time the game evoked the sense of wonder and discovery, I ended up spending way more time feeling stuck.
Antichamber felt more like a house of mirrors than what I wanted it to be... BUT I think my initial expectations were a bit unfair and somewhat unrealistic. For such an experimental game, Antichamber is really well-made. While the concept itself is ambitious, the mechanics are creative and seamless, and the game looks beautiful. Like many indie games, the game begins without telling you anything, and although frustrating at times, the process of discovery does yield a few satisfying moments. For all that it's worth, I did enjoy exploring its labyrynth of tricks and gimmicks - at least when I wasn't moving in circles. It was a unique experience, and I definitely don't regret buying it.

Quite enjoyable aesthetically pleasing game that I put a decent amount of free time into.
Art 8/10 - Enjoy the anime type art style, but due to the large amount of artists art can be very stratified and different. I personally don't mind the revealing art whatsoever, but be warned. This game most likely isn't for children 13 and under.
Gameplay 9/10 - Generally follows 3 main ideas similar to another card game Hearthstone. You want to control your card advantage, board presence, and tempo. By itself the game would be pretty mediocre (one of the reasons why I quit HS), but Shadowverse introduces the evolve mechanic. Evolving creatures generally boosts stats and lets them instantly attack into another creature. I personally love the huge tempo swings experienced from evolves and that keeps me invested into the game.
Developers 9/10 - Some games often dump progression into a strict meta (Such as HS pushing the aggro meta). Despite the undesirable and often unfair games, the problem isn't the meta, its the developers' responsiveness to the desires of the community. I personally feel that the developers of Shadowverse (actual players of other card games) understand what is happening to the ladder and are making a step which will benefit the most. One thing we don't need is sudden, rash decisions in designing such a large game. Shadowverses' developers have not gone to balance too many cards yet so that aspect is uncertain. What is certain, however, is that Shadowverses' developers are one of the most F2P friendly card game developers. They often give out free packs making it super easy to F2P, something I will capitalize next.
Free To Play-ability 10/10 -  Starting the game gets you 30-40 packs for free, which can almost always provide you with enough vials to craft a competitive deck for ladder. Free packs from promotions and tons of quick rewards only speed up the growth of your collection. As of now, Shadowverse is the most f2p friendly card game (Out of HearthStone and Magic [Haven't tried Evoker yet]).
Is there any pay to win BS?
Shadowverse also offers the sale of crystals, which can be used to purchase more packs and pre-built decks. Despite the initial view that spending money leads to a greater advantage, skill and knowledge often play a greater factor in determining the outcome of games than solid card quality. Therefore I would say this game is almost completely free of pay-to-win because you can still lose running a deck with terrible card quality but if you have a decently competitive deck a lot of the games come down to skill.
Edit: With the new expansions coming out and releasing cards on a new level of power, I would have to modify my original statement. Card quality does matter now.
Is it worth it for a new player to spend money?
Shadowverse is excellent for new players as they offer the magic of pre-built decks. Pre-built decks are great because they offer a solid selection of cards and guarantee necessary legendaries for a craft. They cost 500 crystals for the first purchase (increasing to 750 for ever subsequent purchase), which is literally only 5$ during a crystal sale. I feel like they carry their value as they bring in critical legendaries (which of course can be crafted if you don't have spare change) while introducing how crafts should be played. Currently, the most valuable pre-builts are the Bloodcraft prebuilt (control blood), Forestcraft prebuilt (almost every forestcraft deck uses cards from this pre-built), and Shadowcraft prebuilt.
I would definitely rate Shadowverse a solid 9/10 overall due to its defining characteristics, solid gameplay, and f2p aspects. I hope you have the same enjoyment I did while playing this game, and don't be too competitive while playing. After all, its a card game.

This review is based on the PC version.
Overall, a good port. I have the Amiga original, which still holds up in spite of graphics and sound from 1993, largely due to its excellent gameplay. The Steam port (at least on PC) is nearly identical and therefore the same praise applies. If you like the original, you will like the port.
I have one complaint, which for most people probably won't matter, but it is worth noting. Why did they have to go and mess with the original colors? I'm not talking about the hazards of trying to emulate Amiga hues on another system. Some colors in the game were deliberately changed, like the color of those little white cyclops guys with amber eyes (my avatar), whose white skin gave them a cool, creepy alien look. In the new version they are green with purple eyes, which makes them look more "cute" than creepy. They also seem to have brightened up the frogs too much, and the "mossy" gear backgrounds seem to have been changed to "rusty". More demerits! So far these are the only major, deliberate color changes I have noticed. Overall the colors are close enough, and admittedly, most people won't notice the hue changes or care.
If you have never played the original, don't be put off by the slightly-blocky-by-today's-standards graphics. The game is fun and addictive and definitely worth the ten bucks they are asking for the port.

Gameplay has many similarities to Hearthstone, but that's when learning the basics. Each class as you can expect has their own mechanics, but even with (right now) three expansions there's good versatility to create all kinds of Decks. Sure that there's the fear of facing the meta/tier decks on higher ranks, but its card pool allows creativity enough to make many things work together. Finally there's its unique feature called Evolution, a limited resource that can turn arround games or give you an immediate answer against opponent actions. This mechanic is what makes the game stand out compared to others, as managing its use is the main learning curve of the game.
The game also gives a big welcome to new players with several rewards on the go, and along a very friendly card pull ratio soon enough you can build a solid deck in a pair of days. And even if you are in bad luck is not difficult to make low budget decks with the cards available. However keep on mind that some classes are harder to learn than others, being the main challenge to learn the game (Like Swordcraft is newbie friendly by summoning and boosting small monsters, while Havencraft requires stalling and shortcuts for their cards to start working). There's also Take Two (Arena or Draft format), which by default gives you a pack by trying and other bonuses the more wins you get, and you can get tickets for free by simply playing Ranked.
With all sorts of ways to earn packs with high pull ratio, a diverse card pool allowing many strategies to work regardless of budget, and many game modes to tutorial newcomers through all its mechanics, is a solid card game which sets you ready to face other newcomers and experts after a few hours learning. Just keep on mind that the game is quite aggro encouraging with its Evolution mechanic along certain effects, so might give you a negative experience if you don't learn the matchups. Overall, a solid game for anybody who wants to try a card game but don't wanna wallet through to make a decent Deck, as well those who got tired of other card games and wanna start with a solid build immediately.

It's certainly The Chaos Engine.
That's unfortunately where the praise ends, and admittedly, some of it isn't the games fault.
Online co-op is absolutely dead, immediately rendering one of the selling points of this quick and dirty rerelease moot. Of my 100+ friends on here, 2 own it, and they never want to play it, so I've been unable to try it out regardless. I'd hope that when you do get in a match, it at least runs well, but considering how quickly the search results for the online matchmaking went from "player found" and then dropping back to the menu, to outright failing to find anyone, I doubt it.
You can stretch the window to fit your monitor, but that looks just as terrible as it sounds. You'll want to leave it in the native resolution, which, thankfully, is bearable. It's just amazing that they give you the option to change the resolution, when all it does is stretch the game window and make it look like a big square of mud. The supposed graphical filters that they include just make things look worse.
I loathe this statement, but I am left to wonder if The Chaos Engine has been a victim of time. On it's own merits, just as a game, it simply isn't very good. Enemies are ruthless, and the characters all feel identical outside of their weapon and maximum health, despite the game adamantly stating they are very much unique in nature. I never saw a reason to play as anyone other than the high health characters as a result of this. If I was going to be dodging bullets all the time, I'd rather have a lot of chances to screw up than only a handful before my game ends.
After each stage, you are able to increase your characters attributes. This should be awesome, but it is absolutely hamstrung but constantly having to babysit the other character. You already only make a handful of coins a level, but when playing solo, that amount is automatically cut in half, with half given to the AI. Because, you know, that's fair. So the most you can ever really do is buy an extra life for yourself, or maybe increase your maximum health. Those interesting, possibly viable upgrades like increased movement speed, firepower, and such? Don't even think about seeing them in action. Your little AI friend needs an extra life.
When you are actually on the field playing this mess of a game, enemies spawn from generators much like in a Gauntlet title. In those games, everything was restricted to movement in the four cardinal directions.
The Chaos Engine hates you, so you are stuck moving and shooting in the four cardinal directions. Meanwhile, enemies can move wherever they damn well please, and some can shoot in 8 directions as well. Are you having fun yet?
To complete a stage, you have to shoot all the posts in the stage to open up the exit. There are unlisted hidden posts that can open up secret exits, but the game isn't enjoyable enough to make that an enticing idea in the slightest. When you finally complete a stage, you really just wish you would run out of lives already.
Luckily for you, the game has some mercy. When you do run out of lives, there is no continue option. You just lose. You can "continue" from the main menu, but this just loads you at the start of the last stage you were on, in whatever horrible shape you were in before you got murdered. So that's great.

The reason why Zeno Clash 2 wasn't tagged as a FPS is because you only "shoot" 10% of the time, while the other 90% is spent in melee combat. And while first person melee combat is a thing nowadays, most of them see players in sword fights or other similar melee weapons combat. Zeno Clash 2, however, focuses more on martial prowess, with emphasis on punches and kicks strung together into stylish combos, all seen from a first-person perspective. Playing Zeno Clash 2 is like watching one of those kung-fu action movies where the viewers get some interactive scenes to determine the plot advancement.
In some ways that is a great concept and a fresh introduction in the gaming industry, but it could be a bad thing. Despite the available number of moves and combos the players get in the game, unless you actually memorize each and every one of them you'll find that you'd end up repetitively spamming the same attacks anyway.
Overall it is a good game, maybe not the best game in the market, but good enough if you need to kill time. Or, in this case, punch and kick some time.

I'm giving the game a thumbs up, only because there is no neutral stance, and the game does not deserve a thumbs down.
The game has potential, and the basic concept is great... However, the physics, size of maps, and team-size limits leave a lot to be desired.
Physics: Turret rotation speed is actually pretty good, in terms of being realistic (something which some tank games make horribly quick)... and that's where the positives end. I find turning to be a huge pain in the backside, as there seems to be a delay, and if you have been hit you sometimes seem to veer off to one side for no reason. And don't get me started on collisions. Hitboxes which are in places they shouldn't be (such as an invisible wall on the main map, if you manage to spawn on the overpass), fences which you can/can't pass through (some you can, some you can't, even though they look the same), and generally poor maneuverability; I expect a tank to pretty much stick to going straight when I am not telling it to turn... game thinks otherwise.
Size of the maps: I will say that, as of the time of writing this review, I have yet to play online multiplayer, however, the size of the maps lead me to assume the multiplayer side of the game will be a little frantic. As the maps are quite small, meaning there's no real way you could pull off some crazy ambushes, or something, like you would on a larger map. However, if always being in the action is your sort of thing (personally, it's not mine) then you will like the size of the maps, as they aren't so small that you will always spawn next to an enemy, but you will spawn close enough to one that you won't be without action for more than a minute.
Team-size limits: In multiplayer, I can understand there being a limit to how many players (+ AI) you have. But in arcade mode? If my PC can handle 50 tanks, let me have it! Don't limit it to just 14 tanks as a maximum. Yes, larger maps would be required to enjoy playing with 50 tanks. But 10 vs 10 (or some variant of 20) would still be doable on the current maps, without it feeling crowded.
Some side notes: Personally, I adore British tanks, and the fact there's only 3 to choose from is a little annoying. I'd have been fine with seeing 4 WW1/WW2 tanks, and the Cheiftan, if it meant the British tank lineup was of a similar size to the other nations'. But at least this doesn't make the game worse.
So far I have only really talked about the bad. And there's not a lot I can say in favour of the game as it stands right now. I put this game on my wishlist a while ago thinking it'd turn out to play sort of like "Girls Und Panzer Der Game", and ho-boy was a kinda disappointed. I expected to be drifting round corners and destroying tanks twice my size... But that's not what this game is. It's got the anime vibe, sure, but change the anime characters for portraits of "army-looking men" and change the voices to something a little more gruff, and you have a tank battle game.
The textures aren't great. The physics are crap. The maps are small. The team sizes are tiny. The British tank lineup is pitiful... Yet I am still giving it a thumbs up. Because it is a fun game to play. Is it frustrating that a round misses, when you feel it should have hit? Sure. Does it feel good to see that stupid little Panzer in flames in front of you? Of course it does.
Now look at the price of this game. Is it on sale? Buy it. Unless major changes are made to the game (I will update this review if one of my above gripes are fixed) it isn't worth full price. 75% of the price? Sure, I'd settle for that.
If they added more game modes, or fixed some of the many bugs in the game, then I'd have no issue with the game at full price. Hell, if they fixed some of the bugs, and added some of the features I'd like to see, then I'd say it's worth more.
The game has a lot of potential, which is why it's getting a thumbs up. It isn't great, yet. But as long as people know they aren't buying a perfectly polished game, then the devs can keep developing it. It's not often I say a game should be in Early Access, but I feel this game needed it.

This is a top-down roguelike sci-fi shooter where you play a bunch of pixels trying to get off an abandonded planet. You'll spend hours upon hours being chased down by zombies, mutants, brainwashed soldiers and various robots trying to reach the teleport to the next level. The goal is to survive until you reach the final teleport to be able to get home again.
I bought the game because the unique dystopian psuedo-retro aesthetic intrigued me and not because I'm a fan of roguelikes. I'm wasn't even all that familiar with the genre. The game definitely turned out to be more than a few hours distraction though, and being a gamer that enjoys challenges I'm now 40 hours deep into this with all the achievements cleared. Without any regrets, I might add.
Mechanically the game performs very well. The keyboard and mouse controls are precise, the game runs smooth and I didn't experience any glitches or crashes. I played the game on an iMac and the port runs just fine. The only hassle was playing with a Magic Mouse, meaning I had to rebind the second mouse button and the mouse wheel to the keyboard. The graphics are either awesome or absolutely terrible depending on how you look at it and what your preferences are. I think they suit the game perfectly.
So after playing the game extensively I can only recommend it, especially if you appreciate a good, hard, maybe even brutal challenge. It's a game that achieves what it sets out to do more or less flawlessly, even though I'm fairly certain it therefore speaks to a certain audience - those of us that get a kick out of that merciless difficulty.

Zeno Clash 2 is the sequel to the original weird game of the same name Zeno Clash, it's one of those games that is weird and unique in it's own way. Zeno Clash 2 is developed by ACE Team, the same people behind the wonderful rock game Rock of Ages and the first Zeno Clash game and published by ATLUS, the original game was developed with Valve's Source engine, this time, the sequel was developed on the Unreal Engine 3
The story continues right after Zeno Clash, so people who are playing this before the first game may get a bit confused, thankfully there is a prologue that tells you the story so far, I'm not going to explain the story to avoid any spoilers from the first game. The story as the same as the first game isn't the best but get's the job done, however the story is way more boring than the first game in my opinion
The game's graphics are wonderful and are greatly improved from the first game, obviously due to game engine changes. Weird and creepy but magnificent and unique. All the environments, characters and enemies are unique in their own way althought people like me who have played the first game will know all the creepy and weird characters from the first game
The music and sound are also top notch, very well composed. The only thing I would complain about is the combat and gunplay. It's way more awkward and hard to fight enemies, plus you get hit from all sides which if you're own low health, you'd be dead in an instant, also, whilst fighting you focus on one enemy and that enemy only, and if you need to move away to find some health you can't...
Another thing I would complain about is the FOV, now thankfully I do not suffer with motion sickness but good god is the FOV really bad in this game, the camera is too zoomed in and you can't see anything surrounding you, thankfully there is an FOV wide option which gives you a wider view, however, Ghat's body does clip through sometimes, another thing I'd complain about is the length, it's short, just as the same as Zeno Clash, and I finished the game in one whole sitting. If it were a bit longer I wouldn't have complained about the length, but maybe it's a good thing
I'd also recommend turning subtitles on, because volume levels are all over the place, some characters voices you can hear just fine whereas others you can't, also there are many more creatures talking in this game so you won't understand most of the gibberish that comes out of there mouths without having subtitles on. Plus the voice acting is not as good as the first game, the side characters voice acting is bad and some of the main characters make a return from the first game but sounded like they didn't care in voicing this game...
Zeno Clash 2 is not as good as Zeno Clash, there are a lot of problems with this one that the first game did not even have and this game had a better game engine then its predecessor, however Zeno Clash 2 gets the job done and I'd recommend it to people who finished the first game and want to know what happens after

That game, guys ... THAT GAME !
X-COM : Enemy Unknown and his expansion Enemy Within were a total surprise for me. I bought them during a christmas sale totally randomnly. Then I remember that after my buying, I discovered it was a turn-base combat system... I actually never really like that genre. But ! With that game Firaxis got the genius formula to transform a reticent player toward turn based games like me into an absolute fan. The idea of giving 2 main phases : the combats in turn base and the facility gestion in real time is simply genius.
The combat system is wanted to feel "squad tactic"-ly and it's a total success. You have everything to think about : choosing the good soldiers to deploy (Do I need a 2nd sniper or should I remplace it by a mech ?), thinking about the positioning, the good covers, knowing when to fight or when to retreat ... Even the environment is part of the equation : You can naturally destroy walls and ruin an enemy cover (And dont try to cover behind a burning car ... You'll have a pleasant surprise !)
But what really sold the turn-base mode for me are the little animations you can see during the actions. Like when soldiers/alien are attacking or moving. The camera sometime switch from tactical view to 3rd person and give this game all the dynamic dimension it need.
This game is hard. Every mistake is fatal. And god, that's so good to play it.
I totally recommend this game. If you ever see it on sale one day, dont hesitate and give it a try. You'll be surprised !

I've played Shadowverse for around 35 hours and I would like to say this game is great! I love the way they used a HS style and managed to make a unique game.  Allow me to make a few comparisons to its big bro HS.  What makes the game stand out to me is being able to evolve cards.  Shadoowverse has many things which make it unique much like HS. This means 2nd player will be evolving a card on their turn before the other, but the 1st can get board control faster.  And board control is everything in a game where you choose which minion you want to evolve for value.
2. Evolution cards allow cards to be two cards in one!  When you evolve a card it can attack a minion that turn. (not the hero tho)  So most cards will get a +2/+2 buff when evolved but most cards will have an ability which activates when it is evolved.  A card thus is a triple edged sword in this game.   The common cards are usually balanced in stats with more rare cards, but the evolution of a card can allow a cards function really shine.
Just like HS and its hero power each class has its own strengths which are unique to that class.  There is a dragon deck which can be compard to the Druid from HS, getting extra orbs for bigger minions.  Then there is a Vampire deck inwhich he harms himself and his cards become more powerful at 10 HP. THere are 7 classes total.
The game gives us a few things I can mention like taunt, charge, spell immunity, bane, and life leech.  The game starts you off with 20 life instead of 30.  Making going face early game more viable with a strong evolved card with early board control.

The F2P model is rewarding.  Within 20 hours you should have a good start on your first base set, not to mention everything else you earn along the way. I recommend this game to anyone who has tried HS and say what it offers is unique executed very well.  Give a HS style game with some twists a shot!!!

I played all games in Arkham series and this one really makes you feel like you are vengance, you are the night and you are the Batman.
PROS
+Amazing graphics. I have a GTX 965m in my laptop and I played 50 60 fps on high settings. Visuals are amazing throughout the city.
+I had the season pass from the beginning so I don't have any idea which suits game gives you without it but still you have various suit options for both Batman and other allies/villians like Robin, Nightwing and Harley Quinn. However original one is far the coolest one in my opinion.
+BRILLIANT STORYLINE. Game tells you about the time after the 2nd game Arkham City which ended with Joker's death and now everyone thinking that Batman crossed his only redline and killed Joker himself. As you go through the story it really gets into you and unlike the other 3 games, this one is far more emotional with Poison Ivy, Jim Gordon, schizophrenic Joker and everyone around Batman. As Rocksteady announced this game as the last Arkham game (I refuse to believe so) it is more like a goodbye game and I guess that's why it focused on emotions after all. You get to have 3 endings and %100 ending is totally worth the time you get to spend for finishing all those ridiculous Riddler riddles.
+Nice soundtrack. Especially in cut scenes the sounds they use makes it 50 times more intense then it could be.
+BATMOBILE. You get to drive a freaking tanky Batmobile to fight drones and other tanks and you can also remotely controll or call it which increases the Batmany effect a lot more. Also with season pass I guess, you get to drive different types of Batmobiles including the classic ones from the movies which we all loved like 2008 Dark Knight trilogy or a more nostalgic one like 89 movie. Also you get to use lots of different dressing options of the current one.
+Lots of side quests and 4 more with dlc's. You get to face with old enemies of Batman and reunite with some sort of friends.
+Also with dlc's you can play with other heros from Batman. For example you can play as Harley Quinn or Robin or Catwoman and a few more which is a must to try in my opinion even though they dont take 1 or 2 hours to finish them all. Still they might be something to focus on more in the next(hopefully) Arkham game.
CONS
-Sometimes it gets to be a bit repetitive especially with tank fights. But if you enjoy using batmobile it is actually better cause that way you get to use batmobile for a real reason other than just driving around.
-Even though it's coherent in terms of storyline, still its really annoying that you have to finish all those idiot Riddler quests to see the actual ending.
-Can't think anything else.

Hopefully one day we'll see some proper Bitmap Brothers remakes, but I don't regret having paid the £6.99 for this in the meantime.

The extensive launch coverage devoted to the famously terrible/broken PC port of Batman: Arkham Knight obscured a critical fact about the game: for all of its visual polish, it is remarkably un-fun.
In a nutshell, this game is not only a barely-altered recapitulation of the games that came before it in the series, but  it is an incredibly tedious and poorly implemented one at that. Batman: Arkham Knight fuses all of the most repetitive, workaday, ditch-digging aspects of lazy/procedural open world design (think Skyrim, but somehow even MORE soullessly check-list-y) with gameplay that is dogged by hit detection, navigation and context-sensitive control issues that are honestly shocking to encounter in a triple A title.
Moreover, Arkham Knight is a game that constantly reminds you that it exists solely because an executive somewhere wagered that there was still a percentage to be made off of Rocksteady's excellent work on Arkham: Asylum. Say whatever you want about UI and control, the big picture "design" of this game, such as it is, ultimately amounts to little more than an exercise in walking to checkpoints, solving the simplest imaginable puzzles and mashing the attack button.
The sheer unambitious cheapness of the game was a constant source of frustration for me, but nowhere is the money-grubbing cynicism that animates every slap-dash feature in this game more assaultive than in the completely idiotic and nonsensical implementation of the Batmobile.
Not only is the implementation of open world driving worst in class (even if your class was GTA 2: it's that bad), the endless, mandatory tank mini-games involving the Batmobile are literally the reason I had to put this game down for good. It's not just bad and it's not just arbitrary, you can actually tell, when playing through the Batmobile tank mini-games that the developers/designers were given a feature to implement without any kind of meaningful goals or definition of done and basically just pawed at it until it was time to ship.
Just a total failure from conception to delivery.
All of that said, the bright spot is, as one has come to expect from the Arkham series, the writing. Batman eavesdrops on bantering henchmen whose frequently hilarious "flavor" dialogues not only break up the monotony, but lend depth to an otherwise punishingly repetitive procession of lame set pieces. The plot, while simplistic, is literally carried on the back of excellent, engaged scenario and "quest" writing that was clearly done by guys who care deeply about Batman.
But even given that, and even at fire sale/bargain basement prices, you should definitely avoid this game.

A parkour game mashed with first-person shooter elements. That is essentially what Mirror's Edge encompasses. Upon hearing about this game I was immediately excited and curious by the notion that it was different from many other 'first person shooters' I had previously played. The screenshots looked enticing and the trailer was amazing.
Picking up during a Steam sale was perhaps one of the best purchases I have made on Steam.
The game is exciting, fluid and dynamic. The mere feel of jumping over buildings in a huge, modern and visually striking city coupled with the stunningly real feeling of vertigo, is something unique to this game. The controls are excellent which give the feeling of power and strength that your character, Faith, encompasses. This along with the stunning graphics, which scaled remarkably well on mid-range hardware (i7 3630qm, GT 740m), being still able to run on 'highest' on full resolution; are just a couple of the reasons why this game is rather excellent. (I recommend turning off the crosshair and HUD. This increases the feeling of immersion)
For all these good points however, there are some negatives. This game is not perfect. The story is rather short and forgettable, revolving around some sort of political conspiracy; and I felt the cartoon-like cutscenes clashed with the photorealistic nature of the rest of the game, pulling me out of the immersion. Several stages were also poorly designed which left me dying repeatedly until I managed to accomplish a semi-impossible feat (I'm looking at you last level). But this could have perhaps been due to my incompetence at the game itself...
When taken as a whole however, Mirror's Edge is amazing, which leaves me eagerly anticipating its second instalment.
