I used to play the first Killing Floor game, and only just got into the game about 6 months before the early access release of KF2. Man, I was terrible at the first game. But I used to look up guides, and youtube videos, the wiki and all kinds of information about the game: it was fascinating to learn about all the little intricacies that the game had to offer. To be fair, I couldn't learn them all by the time KF2 came out.
As soon as I downloaded the early access version of KF2, I was immediately impressed. The more I learned about the game - and thanks to players like simplecat, q3.railgun, devante and many others - I learned a lot about the game and how much time and effort that went into the balance of things. The Berzerker EMP grenade was the perfect setup to headshots from Commando, Zerk nailgun and shotgun blasts from Supports; the problem was the remainder of the community was too stupid to figure out such simple and interesting options for *teamwork*. And even if they did figure it out, they weren't doing it all by themselves, so it just wasn't quite as satisfying for them. So, they complained.
When the Incinerate 'n' Detonate update came along, I quickly learned a lot about the Demolitionist perk. I understood very early, just how intricate and complex the combinations of weapons used could result in quick takedowns of 6-player Hell on Earth difficulty fleshpounds. Most of the people I played the game with at the time either didn't understand, or didn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥that there were things you could do as a team that worked well together. I say this as a player that doesn't consider himself the best of the best, but I did - and still do - consider myself a lot more team-oriented than most of the players I came into contact with.
Myself and a good friend at the time put a massive amount of time and effort into learning the complexities of the game that the developers at the time placed into the game. I believe - but cannot substantiate - that the people who left the company in the latter part of the previous year were the people that had the most positive impact on the direction of the game up until that point; the game was simply more team-focused. It wasn't called "co-op survival" for players to be anything but co-operative: sadly, the community lacks the presence of mind to really run with that. I say this with regard to the community at the more serious end of the game: the Suicidal and Hell on Earth difficulty players. Naturally, the players at the more casual end of the game are fine: they're looking to blast faces and have a little fun. There's no expectation that these players ought to pay the game's complexity any degree of concern.
After the Gunslinger update back in early December last year, things started to go downhill; lots of people started to notice it, too. Not much really happened until the "half-of-a-Sharpshooter" update back in ... I think April this year. There was talk from the team that they would be reworking the resistance and affliction systems. Most of the players that had in-depth knowledge about the game, pleaded with the company on their own forums to leave the systems be. Many of them felt a deep sense of doubt that the company could actually improve on something that was already deep, complex and rewarding for players that actually had an interest in figuring things out. If I remember correctly, simplecat himself said words to the effect of "please don't change it - it's interesting and challenging as it is". Undeterred, the company went on to create the new resistance and afflictions system.
In my opinion, this completely toppled the delicate balance of the game. Railguns two-shotting 6-player Hell on Earth scrakes solo, Gunslingers simply unloading entire .500 magazines into fleshpound heads for decaps: every single remnant of depth to the game was erased in one. fell. swoop. Despite the pleas from the more knowledgeable and experienced members of the KF2 community, the developers didn't really revert their changes. Zeds still have little "seeing stars" animations and aren't stunned or otherwise incapacitated in ways that make all perks relevant like it used to. There's an element of "do-it-yourself, this isn't really co-op anymore" to the game and that's how it's stayed ever since.
I uninstalled the game six months ago, and only recently went back into it. To be honest, I'm not particularly surprised that they managed to undo all the good work that this game had going for it in that first six or so months. Naturally, plenty of people that don't know much about the game [and presumably don't really care] will say this review's not accurate, not helpful, and downright negative. That's fine.
You can say whatever you like, but the players that knew the game from the start, knew what it could have been, and the disappointing cesspool it's turned into now. If you're a smart consumer that likes genuinely co-operative games, then I'd suggest to give this game a miss. If you're the kind of player that revels in the Call of Duty-style pretense of co-operation - whilst actually being the complete anti-thesis of co-operative play - then this game is for you.
Either way, enjoy.

NOTE: I've had this game for awhile now but never really got into it until recently, so I haven't racked up many hours as of yet.
TL;DR: Just get it, it's a fun game.
We'll start with the pros and cons of Killing Floor 2 (KF2)
Pros:
-Amazing Graphics
-Gore (lots of it)
-Nice variety of perks (classes) to suit all playstyles
-Adequate character customisation
-Lots of different maps including community-created ones
-Accurate physics (I guess it doesn't make much of a difference)
-Gameplay just isn't as boring as other games of similar genre
-Good soundtrack (if you're into metal like me)
Cons:
-Gets kinda repetitive
-Only two bosses (I think)
-Skins
-Perks are somewhat unbalanced
Overall the game is a step up from your run-of-the-mill FPS/Survival like CoD zombies. The perk system allows players to change their playstyle and loadouts during and in-between games. The character customisation is a cool but not really neccessary feature that lets you add more personality to the preset characters. Owning certain games and performing various actions will also unlock new characters (and sometimes weapons) for you as well, like owning Chivalry will unlock Tom Banner and the Zweihander.
The wide selection of maps from both the devs and the community do help to spice up the somewhat repetitive gameplay, and the "horror" theme adds to the atmosphere of each map.
As stated, the game's gameplay kinda get "bland" after a few games, this has been fixed by the new versus mode, which is a fun addition.
The perks in the game are naturally supposed to be balanced, but, with every game, some are more powerful than others. Undoubtedly the "Berserker" class is probably the best, being able to destroy Zeds with a decent selection of melee weapons, while also being able to tank the hits. Other perks however, such as the SWAT (in my opinion) are just plain bad. Some balancing is required, but I guess the not-so-great perks can be put to good use in the right hands.
Final rating: 9/10

Mirror's Edge has done something not many games do. It combined visuals and gameplay into such a unique experience that you cannot find in much games. Mirror's Edge takes the term 'parkour' to such an extreme level. You're literally traveling from building to building. With your FEET. The only other game I can think of that takes free-running to such an extent would be Assassin's Creed, only first-person and modern. The visuals, thankfully made with the Frostbite engine, are spectacular. Especially if you have the right PC setup. The style is amazing, with the mostly white metropolis brightly lighting up objectives and significant building with color-schemes for every level. Not only are you running from enemies, but you have to fight them too. In most situations, you choose between fight or flight. Stealth is an option, but a hard one. After taking out an enemy, you can pick up their weapon and use it against your enemies. The thing is, there is no ammo count; you only use the ammo in the clip and discard the gun. This enthuses players to go the traditional parkour gameplay of the game. The game is not that long, since I beat it in a short 4-hour session. But it has decent replayability, being encouraged to try to beat your time throughout the levels. The story... is pretty dull. I won't talk about the story, but it's a bit cliche. For the price, I think this game is definitely worth buying, with its original gameplay and concepts that you can't really get anywhere else.

Regardless of the money, I don't feel playing through this game was time well spent. The world is bigger. It's less linear. There's more exploration and more characters. The gameplay is still boring and limited and frustrating. The characters and the writing don't have any emotion in them, to say nothing of the flat, dull voice acting.
What did make me happy was the lore and history of the universe getting fleshed out. That was the best part by far. Inevitably, it was drowned out by the other elements, and we're left with a story not worth telling. The events of these games don't actually seem to affect any real change for either the characters or the world they reside in.
I have to give some props to the art direction. There are some beautiful moments of pure imagination. I'd probably buy some of these landscapes and levels as artwork. The problem is they're more fun to look at than to play through.

Let me start off by saying this: I generally don't like absurdly difficult games. I play games to relax and unwind, and, while a difficult puzzle game isn't bad once in a while, games that have a tendency to relentlessly pound you into oblivion tend to be entirely too frustrating to be relaxing at all.
That was an important disclaimer, because I'm sure there are plenty of people like me. To those people: This game is absurdly difficult. It is absolutely brutal. It can be frustrating as hell, especially when you've managed to make it half an hour+ into the game, and you get killed because of your own stupidity. With that said, this game is ALWAYS fun. I have died after hour-long runs, and still wanted to immediately go back in for more. Perhaps I'm a glutton for punishment, but again, I typically don't enjoy that sort of thing.
Thankfully, you are still making progress in the game. There are things to unlock, such as new items, artifacts, and, of course, new characters, so your time in the game is rarely wasted. The game is an absolute blast, and I have gotten every penny of my money's worth out of it so far.
If you like fun games, be they frustrating, impossibly difficult, or just the casual variety, as long as you like platformers with light RPG elements, you will definitely love this game. Look at the pictures, read the description, and read the reviews... If you haven't already decided you'll hate it, then you'll absolutely love it.

X-COM : Enemy Unknown and his expansion Enemy Within were a total surprise for me. I bought them during a christmas sale totally randomnly. Then I remember that after my buying, I discovered it was a turn-base combat system... I actually never really like that genre. But ! With that game Firaxis got the genius formula to transform a reticent player toward turn based games like me into an absolute fan. The idea of giving 2 main phases : the combats in turn base and the facility gestion in real time is simply genius.
The combat system is wanted to feel "squad tactic"-ly and it's a total success. You have everything to think about : choosing the good soldiers to deploy (Do I need a 2nd sniper or should I remplace it by a mech ?), thinking about the positioning, the good covers, knowing when to fight or when to retreat ... Even the environment is part of the equation : You can naturally destroy walls and ruin an enemy cover (And dont try to cover behind a burning car ... You'll have a pleasant surprise !)
But what really sold the turn-base mode for me are the little animations you can see during the actions. Like when soldiers/alien are attacking or moving. The camera sometime switch from tactical view to 3rd person and give this game all the dynamic dimension it need.
This game is hard. Every mistake is fatal. And god, that's so good to play it.
I totally recommend this game. If you ever see it on sale one day, dont hesitate and give it a try. You'll be surprised !

With Marvel in particular, some of the levels are nearly unplayable including Sandstation and the Good, the Bad, and the Hungry (not to mention the Circus mini-level). The controls when flying or driving are also particularly difficult whether you use the keys or a video game remote. Unless the developers find another more reliable interface, it would be better to resolve these glitches to ensure that the game is more user friendly for PCs. It is not worth its selling price and I can't recommend it.

Antichamber is a puzzle platformer that can stand with the likes of the Portal series.  While the 3D graphics are minimalistic,  the challenges that are presented will force you to rethink HOW you approach the problem.  There's no enemies or creatures to defeat, only puzzles with a special block gun (& upgrades) that you'll find as you explore from room to room as you eventually find your way out of the space known as "The Antichamber".
Armed with only the basic controls & a target timer (which is something you can COMPLETELY IGNORE, as taking longer than what the game notes is perfectly OK... it's just a challenge that you can partake in), you explore the various rooms & the unique challenges they can present.  The game has a very surreal feel as it takes advantages of things that cannot be done in reality
.
While the game DOES NOT have any save support, it DOES offer shortcuts to players who are perceptive to find them... as well as secrets for those who wish to uncover every secret The Antichamber has to offer.
If you love the Portal series, you'll definitely enjoy Antichamber as well!

-Nice Campaign mode
-A few start-up packs
-Animated character portraits
-Everything's voiced
-Evolve Mechanic to help recover from slow starts
-More than 5 cards a pack
-Potentially strong currency generation
-Daily login bonus
-Excellent motivation if you ever wish to commit suicide.
Cons:
-One Daily Mission slot is consumed by "Link to another device" by default. Steam version cannot link to another device, so players are denied a Daily slot.
-Daily missions use the Hearthstone mandate of "Win," making for a frustrating string of losses for classes people don't want to play. Only one mission may be rerolled a day.
-BRUTAL demand for good cards and Hearthstone-esque crafting restrictions. People will restart entire accounts just to stand a chance with their initial draws.
-No Matchmaking on Unranked.
-Ranked becomes an invincible wall of meta decks as early as Beginner 2, making progression and income slow to achieve.
-Strange emphasis and overvaluation of "Take Two", the Arena mode, which is five matches guaranteed, despite the appearance of being kicked out with no reward after one loss.
-Immense RNG power. Imagine a set of fingers being smashed repeatedly with a hammer. That's what it feels like to have bad luck in this game.

I think it is past time I put in a review for a game that has absorbed one hell of a lot of my life.
Its worth noting that, as I write this, the game has only been "officially" released for about a month, however, I have played on and off since the first day of Alpha.  I have currently put 243 hours into this game, and 297 into KF1, which shows, if nothing else, that I like these games a lot.
Is it like KF1?
Probably not.  It looks like KF, it feels like KF when you play it.  But the classes are different, leveling is faster and more rewarding, the guns are more restrictive (due to its age) as are the maps (custom included).  There are now microtransactions akin to CS:GO.  There are new zeds, but they are mostly variations on the current ones, and so far only crawlers, clots, and soon gorefasts.  There are two bosses, which is very nice since some classes have a distinct advantage against one vs the other (sharpshooter wrecks hans and commando can make the patriarch fight a joke).  The game also feels easier, by and large, but that could be a result of time put in.
In short, it's not the same game, and some people really hate change, but to me, this game is a lot better as a whole, it just still feels young.
There's a lack of custom maps and mutators in size and scope of the original.  That isn't to say there aren't some amazing maps out there (Mario64 & Kokiri Forest), as well as old maps that have returned thanks to the community (West London, Mansion, Office, & Biotics Lab).  But the much larger maps that incorported some interesting mutators (like the RE and Aliens series with custom zeds; Mysterious Trees [my absolute favorite] with random spawning of massive hordes of zeds) have yet to return.
I'm going to focus on the cons more here in an attempt to be more critical.
PROS:
- Very fun weapons (pulverizer & microwave gun notably)
- Zed diversity is increasing, which is much appreciated (still hoping for scrake and fp diversity)
- The classes feel well rounded for the most part.
- it feels and looks like an improved KF1
- they are bringing back holiday events!
CONS:
VS mode, just as a concept, feels like a waste of time by the Devs
Microtransactions.  I don't particularly mind the concept, but it seems the free drops consist of one of 5-6 things at this time.  That should be a expanded to a greater diversity as new items are released to bring market cost down a bit.  Or at the very least implement more into the game, make some market only and others earnable through achievements or something.
Classes:
- Survivalist needs refined (but as I write this, I'm sure that's currently happening)
- I like most of the other ones, commando seems boring nowadays, zerker will benefit from more tankiness (but they are doing that currently with the taunt and shield), and demo escapes me.
- still hoping for LMG
- would be nice if they increase the level cap or add prestige with benefits someday
Guns:
- Every class could benefit from more t2-t4 gun options.  I'm sure this is coming, but its been slow thus far.  Its a bit frustrating to get into a monotony in buying certain guns certain waves to hit the end "set" which seems necessary for a boss fight.  Diversity would really be helpful.
- I think there needs to be some weight distribution or more utility in the "t2" set.  In several of the classes, I never buy the t2 weapon unless there is some odd money constraints (e.g., death/late join).  Weapons such as the xbow, hunting shotgun, trench gun, and vlad go by the wayside because they are sufficiently better than t1 to justify not conserve money waiting for t3/t4.
Talent Trees:
- Every talent tree should have three options per tier, not two.
- Some of the talent trees are very forced (a healing-dedicated medic must choose the left side.  Since there is only one   healer  class, it'd be nice to see an option of HoT vs big heal / big cd vs armor regen.  Or maybe I've played too many MMOs.
No mysterious trees.

All around a great game with a few minor inconsistencies. 8/10.
The Good:
The graphics are very good and the maps are open and absolutely filled with free-running opportunities.
The parkour is great when it works.

There is a huge difference between nighttime and daytime gameplay, which makes for a very broad and content-rich game.
There is a good enough variety of zombie models.

A plethora of Easter eggs and minute details that are either plain fun or really add to the atmosphere of a doomed city.
Weapons are DEADLY.
The Bad:
I've experienced several extremely frustrating deaths due to the game deciding I didn't grab that ledge or deciding I didn't press MMB to use my grappling hook. The free running mechanics just don't work 100% of the time like they should.
My game will freeze and lag when zombies latch onto to me or swarm me. Spitter bombs also cause this. I exceed the recommended specs and play with no view distance and medium textures.
Your attacks are often canceled far too early (IMO) by zombies triggering the escape animation where you must mash F or press E (if you have the skill) to free yourself. The zombie may be feet away from you, and you cannot control Crane once the animation is triggered.
While the walker zombies have a good enough variety, the special infected do not. They all look the same.
Walkers are extremely easy to kill, so an inconsistency arises when facing certain types of special infected. Normally, the zombies just feel like vulnerable zombies but there are these outlandish and hard to believe special infected that feel too much like boss zombies. Some would argue, but I feel they just don't mesh well with the rest of the game. It's as if they are relics from Dead Island.

Great open-world game to explore (within reasonable boundaries). The story isn't as bad as I expected from "just another zombie game"; there's a true sense of personal conflict with the main character and his role that plays out in his interactions with the survivors and the group he's affiliated with. The dialog that brings this to life doesn't always feel forced or clouded with a sense of perfection (at least from the main character... the NPCs can have some rather "meh" dialog that you simply have to stomach).
The running "parkour" element is something I can appreciate from this game that Dead Island did not have. It gives you a sense of urgency, a sense of being able to outrun and outmaneuver your pursuers and doesn't force you to take all threats with a bloodied weapon head on. With that addition, players familiar with the Dead Island series will notice many similarities particularly with the inventory, crafting, the sense of looting for materials and more. Overall, a much more fluid experience in regards to movement and gameplay.
The game has its own fair-share of glitches and problems. Updates appear to be occurring regularly enough, but from what I've gathered, AMD users beware as this game could still be largely unplayable. Be sure to do your research. Additionally, some of the achievements have syncing issues, so if you're an achievement buff, make sure to regularly save before you make any contributions as the syncing could be extremely slow at best, or not even occur at worst.
Overall, very good game and am pleased with the purchase. While there is room for improvement, I'm confident in saying that this is one of the better-handled games of the "zombie genre" to date.

I've been playing this game since the very first day it was released on early access. Back then it was very bare bones and only had 4 classes in the game.  I have had the chance of seeing it grow and change drastically over the years, finally culminating into the complete game we have now. I believe that game is worth buying.
This is a very enjoyable co-operative first person shooter. You and 5 other people try to survive against increasingly challenging waves of ''zeds''; cloned monstrosities set loose upon the world by the Horzine Corporation. The soundtrack is death metal and it's bloody as hell. It's a very cathartic experience.
There is an extremely large and varied arsenal of weapons to choose from split between 10 classes. The developpers, Tripwire, used to be infamous for their long development times and lack of communication with the community but they've definitely addressed that problem recently. Updates are frequent and fast, and they always release new images and previews to let people know what they're working on. Even though the game left early access, it's still going to be constantly upgraded.
The 10 perks can all be leveled up to level 25, which can take a bit. Furthermore, there are several difficulty levels that drastically alter the gameplay ( they change the zed behavior, making them more deadly) as well as custom maps. All of those things add tons of replay value to the game.
Don't know what else there is to say about Killing Floor 2. It's not the most complicated of games but it has tons of content, replay value and fun. You should get it if you like fun.

Some background. I am a massive game nerd. I love both board games and video games. I own quite a few FFG-games as well. I never played Mansions of Madness first edition.
We played the first 2-star scenario that was said to last 60-90 minutes. It wasn't the best experience, and neither of us wanted to play the game again. What went wrong?
First there was
:
- massive pop ups that cover most of the graphics. And you can't drag the popup out of the way, or minimize it temporarily. This is 2017. Not 1983.
- the app is a nightmare. No pun intended. If you accidentally click (because you tried to get rid of that massive popup), and the story moves on, you can't go back. No back-button.
- only the first part of the story and the ending has voice acting. All the rest of the text you need to read.
- buttons are sometimes unresponsive.
- developers, if you are so dead keen on having an app that accompanies a board game just to be cool and hip, then why not make a tutorial scenario? Just explain everything, You made that app. So USE its possibilities! Now you still need the rulebook to look up rules.
- you know which characters are in play, developers. You ask for that input. So why do you use that information arbitrarily? Sometimes, the app uses that info, and sometimes not. Be consistent.
That's the app. I probably forgot to mention something, but I think it gives some idea of what the app is about. It feels like it was quickly put together by some amateur.
Now,
itself:
- rules were missing, in both the app and the rulebook and the reference book. Maybe we overlooked, but there were quite a few instances were something happened with for instance the character with the lowest Strength. But what if there are 2 or even more people with the same Strength? It wasn't mentioned anywhere what to do in such case. Or, as one of my fellow players mentioned: "You would expect this to be noticed during the first playtest?"

Do not doubt that this game is great. And though my review is going to be entirely criticism, I do recommend it. Perhaps I should wait until I've beaten the game before I write this review, but I don't see that happenning within this lifetime.
My most major gripe is the Guard enemy. I appreciate how they transition the game from a leisurely stroll through the abandoned facilities to a nervous twitch-inducing slow crawl through every corridor, but they just seem too hard. I can't even count the times I've stepped out of the start point in level 4 with full hp and armor, only to suddenly find myself dead from the gang of three guards waiting on the other side. And when you're playing a rougelike where every death means starting all the way back at Level 1, it can be rather trying to die so instantaneously.
Even the super cyber guys in Level 5 don't bother me as much as the Guards do, because you know what you're stepping into before you fight them. The Guards just pop up behind you and then death. Yes, you can wait at the edge of a room and wait for them to patrol past you, but honestly, camping a corner for 5 minutes to survive isn't quite my idea of a good time.
If I'm alone on this, then by all means, disregard all of my ranting. I may have just not gotten the hang of it yet. But if this holds any water, could I please request that their strength be dialed back just a little? Maybe boost the strength of the mutants and zombies to compensate, because honestly, I don't feel like most of them even in huge groups are even half a threat to my character. Or if not that, could the Guards AT LEAST have a noise to notify that they've spotted you? It would be nice to know if a zombie with a shotgun is about to pop up behind you and void your last 15 minutes of progress.
Two other small gripes:
-Could we have a noise that sounds a little more terrifying when you're melee attacked? Becuase the one the game has now sounds almost comical.
-Some ambient music would be nice. The atmosphere in the game is already pretty solid, but doesn't always suit it during the more intense moments of gameplay.

Occassionally you will go through quite clausterphobic spaces, such as hallways or offices, which can turn into very tedious areas to navigate or know where to turn. There is a key that will turn your camera to where you need to go (the ALT button), but I found myself using it almost constantly. A directional arrow onscreen would be helpful as to where to go, or even a glowing halo of the next door you must pass through would be much better alternatives.

Antichamber is a puzzle platformer that can stand with the likes of the Portal series.  While the 3D graphics are minimalistic,  the challenges that are presented will force you to rethink HOW you approach the problem.  There's no enemies or creatures to defeat, only puzzles with a special block gun (& upgrades) that you'll find as you explore from room to room as you eventually find your way out of the space known as "The Antichamber".
Armed with only the basic controls & a target timer (which is something you can COMPLETELY IGNORE, as taking longer than what the game notes is perfectly OK... it's just a challenge that you can partake in), you explore the various rooms & the unique challenges they can present.  The game has a very surreal feel as it takes advantages of things that cannot be done in reality
.
While the game DOES NOT have any save support, it DOES offer shortcuts to players who are perceptive to find them... as well as secrets for those who wish to uncover every secret The Antichamber has to offer.
If you love the Portal series, you'll definitely enjoy Antichamber as well!

The weird thing about Book of Demons is that I don't find Diablo 1 particularly compelling (LOVE 2 and 3), but is this game ever fun. It seems to be a whole pile of concepts - Diablo 1, but its papercraft, and also all your items and skills are cards, and you're also a particularly human shaped train. And I love almost every single thing about it.
The only thing I dislike is the movement system. The procedural dungeons are a series of smallish rooms, which really works well, but you only travel through them on what is effectively a small network of rails. And that gives me a headache, especially when I start going down a long straight corridor with a dozen archers at the end and all I can do is slowly eat 50 arrows as I laboriously make my way to them.
On the other hand, Plexiscope, a system that lets you choose the length of your playsession down to within a few minutes, is absolutely brilliant and now I want it in all my ARPGs and rougelikes.

First of all, this game is not easily comparable to Portal. They have similar aesthetics; you are in first person, you are some voiceless being, and you simply interact with the very concrete world around you to solve puzzles as they arrive, until everything you've come across is no longer a mystery. The similarities stop there. Portal is linear; it has humor, it has lore, it makes you feel your situation like you are a character in a world with the odds against you, and it pushes you forward through each puzzle with just enough to solve it and move on.
Antichamber, in this aspect, is the exact opposite. You will not feel like someone else, like someone installed into the lore, or like a character who needs to escape from their situation. You will start with absolutely no clue what you're doing or what you can do, and you will come across each challenge using only a portion of it, and then have to return to a room later just to suddenly realize what everything was supposed to do all along. All the pieces of the puzzle will click together. Then you move forward.
Every single room in this game is available to you at all times. It's not linear, not at all. If you run into a dead end, you press your Escape key, return to the start of that room and try to figure out what you did wrong previously, or jump somewhere completely different all the way across the map and find out what you can now do that you never used to be able to. However; things are still connected. There's nothing meaningless. You'll have to fail a lot in order to succeed in the end.
I've addressed these specific things about Antichamber because the majority of the complaints in the Negative reviews section seems to be built on the idea that these are bad things. Tedious trial-and-error, statements trying too hard to sound wise, a lack of any direction to what needs to be solved next. Are they bad things? Do they go against the definition of a puzzle game? No. Those kinds of things are purely subjective. In this review I am not telling you to buy this game. I'm not going to try to convince absolutely everyone that this game will be in their taste. I have told you what Antichamber is.
The only honest reviews you read from the Negative section about Antichamber will be the ones that say "This game is not my cup of tea."

Much smaller in scope, but just oh so right!
Few will mistake this for a main installment. Both the story and magnitude feel very much like that of a side-game.
However, in a series that has turned to high-octane action and explosions, this game's return to darkness and tension feels like a breath of fresh air. It is maybe the fact that it doesn't need to be bigger and better (as numebred sequels are wont to) that allowed the devs to just focus on a smaller, more personal story, and pack its much tighter location with all kinds of horrors and disturbing shadows. (This is not to say there isn't action in here, but it's less about being a terminator and more about fighting for survival).
The game is divided into 4 episodes, with 2 parts each, one for RE veteran Claire Redfield and Moira Burton (Barry's daughter), and another one for Barry himself and newcomer Natalia Korda (a little girl with the power to sense monsters from a distance as well as other invisible threats). Each half runs for about 60-90 mins and feels distinct in its gameplay style and mood, complementing each other perfectly while offering different challenges. Claire has more enemies, but less ammo, whereas Barry is armed to the teeth, but some deadlier enemies call for a stealthier approach. In short, the game offers variety and remains interesting while running as long as it needs to, no more, no less.
It is fair to say that the RE formula has grown stale at this point, and, true, Rev 2 sticks to it in many ways (even with the novelties it brings to the table, its feels none to different from RE4), feeling perhaps like it treads on quite old ground, which isn't helped by it being more of a budget title. However, with all of its faults and somewhat recycled gameplay, it does offer what Capcom has perhaps failed to provide in recent installments, a scary RE game. Its switch from open spaces filled with gun-toting enemies to smaller, darker rooms with monsters ready to pop up from the shadows (or not), and its overall grittier, even depressive, atmosphere, is something that makes Rev 2 easily a bonafide return to form, and absolute recommended for fans of old-school RE.

Great game.  Similar to hearthstone but without a lot of the problems that hearthstone has.
Tons of rewards for new players to help them get right into the game.  After the tutorial they give you 40+ free packs and then from beating the ai with the characters you get free take two tickets (draft mode) and unlock some great cards that you'll be using in your decks for a very long time (some are standard in high ranked meta decks).  Their individual stories are interesting and not too long.  They give you a daily reward just for logging in and 3 quests.  If you want to be a free player it's far easier to do so vs other ccgs.
The evolve mechanic is great.  Starting on turn 4 The player that went second can evolve a minion which gives it a buff (and on specific cards triggers an ability) and allows it to attack on the turn it's played.  The player that went first gets two uses of this ability, the player that went second gets three.  It really helps balance out the initial advantage of going first and leads to very interesting gameplay/stratagies.
The draft mode (take two) has you choose two cards for your deck at a time between two pairs of cards.  This leads to some very interesting decisions.  Do you take the two cards that are both just ok quality or do you take the pair that has one good card and one not so great card.
If you do want to spend some money they have several pre-built decks for you to buy that have strong legendaries in them and are worth the $.  If you just want packs they have a daily deal where you can buy a pack a day at half the normal price.
I love the card art in this game, it's very well done.  The animations are great as well.
The makers of this game really seem to care about their players time.  I've gotten many free packs from when they were a couple of hours late on an update... and I wasn't even around trying to play the game at the time.
Highly reccomended.

For the price of £0.84, you obviously get Episode One of Resident Evil Revelations 2 (this is on a sale, though). And let me tell you it is so much worth it!! The game does in fact have quite a bit of content to play through - the main story took me around 2 hours or more to beat and it was alright to be honest - the story is quite decent and leaves the player with a lot of questions at the end inevitably leading onto the other purchasable chapters. But what I must say to you is that you MAY want to buy the other chapters too! Due to how much fun I actually had, I think I may! While the actual mission environments are really closed off and give this claustrophobic feel to them, it is also really dark and maybe even a bit creepy. Unfortunately though it wasn't too scary. I haven't played RE4 but I surely am interested to! A scary game I have played would be Dead Space and this game doesn't exactly come close. However other than the story mode there is the Raid mode which is essentially a shooting gallery in much different environments (first raid mission is in a snowy environment, which is not present in the first episode of the story) to the main story mode. Graphics aren't too good or too bad, but it runs at a silky smooth 60fps through and through. Gameplay is pretty good and in the second half of EP1 it felt a lot like The Last of Us, which is certainly a good thing. At one point I was really frustrated due to continuous fail but regardless this game was a lot of fun and I certainly am looking forward to playing the other episodes!
For £0.84, don't let this one pass you!!

The combat is the biggest part of the game. Happily, it not only works fantastically by itself, it actually fits into and around the story. It doesn't bog down the story ACE Team is trying to present, and the story fits in with the fighting so that you don't feel held back by cutscenes or dialogue keeping your from punching more dudes. The punches and weapons have impact as well, sending oponents reeling, dropping their weapons, or even sending them flying. Unfortunately, that goes the same for you: when the enemy hits you, you feel it.
I love this game. I've never been a big fan of beat'em-ups but somehow this game really gets me excited. The characters are vivid in more than just their off-putting looks and the story is fascinating. The environments have made a huge change for the better, becoming more open and vibrant. However, don't let the openness fool you. This game is still very linear; not quite as linear as the first one, but it is very far from open world. However, you are free to explore the various locales as many times as you want.
The story is one of this game's strong points. ACE Team's writers crafted a world that really feels alive and sets itself apart from similar RPG titles. It works hard to connect every thread from the first game into this one and expands beyond its predecessor in the way a sequel should. The story is far from perfect, of course. A few points could easily have been skipped and nothing would have been lost. However, those points are interesting in their own way and add to the life of this world even if they add nothing to the main plot.
Zeno Clash 2 is worth every penny. It provides a great story both as a standalone and as a continuation of the Zeno Clash world, and the combat is superb, fitting in perfectly with the story and shining as a testament to first person beat'em-ups. It isn't terribly hard, but it won't be a walk in the park either.
A really good game. Animations can look a little cluncky but the story and solid enough gameplay make this a title worthy to recommend.

I generally enjoyed my time playing Shadowrun Returns and I'm not sorry I bought it.   Having said that, I cannot recommend purchasing this game.  The writing is excellent; the setting is awesome; and the graphics, though a bit basic, are quite charming.  The battle system isn't bad either (although some of the endgame encounters are tedious).  The problem is the story and its length.  The setting and characters are compelling, but the story itself is bland and incredibly short.  You can finish the game in about 10 hours.  Ordinarily I wouldn't hold the length against a game, but here it felt like the story ended before it ever even started.  Things were just starting to fall into place and then all of the sudden you are in the last mission.
To make matters worse, the modding community for Shadowrun never took off, so you're stuck essentially with the main game's short story and maybe a little extra.  The amazing promise of the game just isn't realized and that's a shame.

This game is amazing. The soundtrack by Chris Christodoulou is fantastic, one of the best soundtracks in an indie game, it's like a mix between rock and roll and the kind of music that pumps you up for teh adrenaline filled experience you have through the game. The rouge type elements keep you on edge, which is a good thing because you need to manage your time VERY WISELY, because every 5 minutes you spend in the game, the game gets increasingly difficult, so basically, if you aren't extremely skilled at the game, and you've spent 40 minutes in a round, you'll likely be killed in the next minute or so, unless of course you've already activated  the teleporter and defeated the enemies spwaned by it and are simply trying to get the achivement. The classes are also a fantastic aspect of the game, because they all have different styles of play and each class can appeal to a specific gaming style, for example, my favorite class is the Enforcer because he is the most realted to a Tank-type character in the game, but I know that the Sniper and Bandit are also very popular for being sort-of Ranger-type classes, which are usually the most popular in these kind of games because they can deal massive damage as well as being able to dodge attacks with relative ease. The story and collect-a-thon aspect are also very unique and rather fantastic because of the joy of getting/unloking new things as well as getting better at the game at the same time, and the story is simple and sweet, just like how these kinds of games should be, the only downside to having a simple story is not being able to talk about it without giving away spoilers. The non-spolier part of the story is in the intro of the game, you are a mercenary hired by a shipping company to guard the cargo of a shuttle; however, during the flight, a mysterious entity teleports onto the ship and blows a massive hole in the ship, destoying it. In the aftermath of the ship's destruction, you awaken in an escape pod, and have crash landed on a vicious planet where everything wants to kill you, but using your wit, skills, and whatever cargo you find throughout the world, you try to make it off the planet alive. I hope this review can convince anyone who reads it try out the game, take it from the 94% positive rating, this game is worth every last penny you spend on it.

Teleglitch is a definate must have for people looking for a challenge, and I would recoment it to anyone and everyone.

Nothing too groundbreaking or innovative, just a very solid tactical strategy game.

What can I say? This game is truly a masterpiece. An easy 9/10.
By the time I have started playing this magnificent game, most known bugs were already fixed. In fact, I have not even encountered a single bug after 50 hours of immersive gameplay.
The graphics are just plain beautiful. Rocksteady Studios has obviously been exploiting the potentials of Unreal Engine. The amount of detail in this game is absurd. From the ugly dirt sticking on the Batmobile to the small cuts in Batman's cape over time, it truly is astonishing. I also have to commend the water flow in this game. It seems very realistic for me. The gameplay is amazing. The amount of gadgets and combos you can do makes every encounter unique. Overall, this is a game I will truly recommend to everyone. And to think of it, I actually got this game for ₱199.98 ($4.02) when it was on sale. It feels like this game is worth around $60+.

This is a movie based on three Dota 2 players who make their way to the Dota 2 Internationals for the $1 Million Prize from their humble origins to the tournament. While yes, most of you will scream at your PC and say, "Why risk your life away from gaming? Get a real job!". The point is, these three players that were documented in the film gambled their life away for video games because they geninuely want to play video games in a professional level, mind you.
This movie shows strongly how society generally scoff video games as a time waster, yet a fun medium. When society hears people who want to PLAY video games as a living and make a professional earning out of it like a sports player would, that's the kicker. The contestants' families are mostly stressed over this because it's such an unheard thing, and if you lose? You go home with little or no money.
The presentation of the movie, though, is coordinated very well. Cinematography, lighting, all the elements of a documentary video are there. It even has extras and deleted scenes bundled up as well.
My summary? Free to play, free to see the cringe and spaghetti of various familiy members and loved ones, and free to see a  quality movie. Heck, you don't even need to buy it.
Even if you HATE Dota 2, it's still interesting enough to see the lives of a gamer at stake.

Initially, this game was great. It felt like a perfect mix of balance, lack of RNG, and fair progression, but somewhere along the lines it quickly did a 360. For those of you coming from Hearthstone seeking something new, I will start by saying that even at its worse this game is better than Hearthstone, but don't expect to be impressed after you've spent some time getting familiar with it. If you are looking for a CCG with balance, a minimal amount of RNG that has no overbearing effect on gameplay, and a decent amount of progression within reasonable time as mentioned above, Shadowverse fails to deliver.
Contrary to first impressions, the imbalance within Shadowverse derive from many reasons, with one reason being its blatantly overpowered legendary cards. The meta boasts cards such as Seraph (a card that if not answered using a specific spell within a certain amount of turns automatically wins its user the game), Prince of Darkness/a.k.a Satan (a card that guarantees victory, assuming the user is not near death, by replacing the users hand with blatantly broken spells and minions), Daria ( a card that promotes reckless play by not only giving its user a whole new hand full of cards when needed, but also significantly lowering the cost of the cards aquired. Daria can also have her cost reduced, which makes it easier to play her on an early turn), and much more. Another reason are the types of decks that are standard to the meta. The main four types of decks you will come across (unless you are in the beginner ranks) are braindead agrro face decks, control decks that aim to stall the game until they can drop a game winning legendary, one turn kill cheese decks, and snowball decks aiming to constantly flood the board with minions until you finally run out of answers. I've recently made it to B0, and although not a super high rank, I have only come into contact with those four types of decks for majority of my time playing this game. It's gotten so repetitive and nervre wrecking that I hesitate to start the game now. If all of what I have said sounds bad so far, don't even get me started on the RNG. If you draw a bad hand and don't get anything playable pass turn 3, you may as well surrender. It gets even worse if you draw bad AND get matched up against a face aggro deck. You have to sit there with your thumb in your mouth while being whacked in the face as you watch them flood the board on perfect curve.

Not much to say here except for it's infinitely better than the amount of time it takes to progress in Hearthstone. Where the progression falls short within Shadowverse is that you usually need multiple amounts of different lengendary and gold cards within the same deck to make it viable. It can be quite expensive is terms of vials (similar to dust in Hearthstone). The way to get around this is by usually making a cheap face aggro deck, but this is a horrible option for anyone who doesn't like to spend all of their game time mindlessly rushing face.
In general, I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone looking to play it competitively and advance in rank. This is the type of game that would best be played logging in to complete daily missions, maybe having a couple of unranked games, and then logging out. If you still wish to play it competitively, just be prepared to be met with a wall of cancerous decks (which you will be eventually forced to play as well if you ever plan on standing a chance) and games completely depending on RNG as you move through the ranks.
Although it has no pc version in the US, a game I would recommend sticking to is Mabinogi Duel. You'd most likely have a better time with that than both Shadowverse and Hearthstone. It does everything better while offering a more intriguing storyline and cards.

I've been playing this game since the very first day it was released on early access. Back then it was very bare bones and only had 4 classes in the game.  I have had the chance of seeing it grow and change drastically over the years, finally culminating into the complete game we have now. I believe that game is worth buying.
This is a very enjoyable co-operative first person shooter. You and 5 other people try to survive against increasingly challenging waves of ''zeds''; cloned monstrosities set loose upon the world by the Horzine Corporation. The soundtrack is death metal and it's bloody as hell. It's a very cathartic experience.
There is an extremely large and varied arsenal of weapons to choose from split between 10 classes. The developpers, Tripwire, used to be infamous for their long development times and lack of communication with the community but they've definitely addressed that problem recently. Updates are frequent and fast, and they always release new images and previews to let people know what they're working on. Even though the game left early access, it's still going to be constantly upgraded.
The 10 perks can all be leveled up to level 25, which can take a bit. Furthermore, there are several difficulty levels that drastically alter the gameplay ( they change the zed behavior, making them more deadly) as well as custom maps. All of those things add tons of replay value to the game.
Don't know what else there is to say about Killing Floor 2. It's not the most complicated of games but it has tons of content, replay value and fun. You should get it if you like fun.

Welcome to Far Cry: Zombie Edition. Dying light manages to upstage it's fairly obvious muse in that the story and mechanics in Dying Light far exceed what has been achieved by the Far Cry series. Having said that the influence of Ubisofts giant is cleat throughout this zombie smasher and it even sadly continues the narrative whereby the American Hero saviour ends up in generic backward country to show the locals how things should be done. That distasteful line aside the free-running works extremely well .
The protagonist is fairly unlikeable as he seems to spend much of his time whining about doing what he agreed so happily to do in the first place that being stabbing everyone in the back for money.
Mechanically very solid game. Free-running being partly based on looking makes it miles better than the free-running seen in other titles even if it takes some getting used to and the dense urban landscape makes for an interesting playground. The shift between day and night makes a huge difference to the way you have to play which makes it a shame you can simply skip this transition by sleeping the night away for the majority of the game.
The game on the PC however is still plagued by crashes and issues with interacting with hardware in weird ways which really cuts into the strides it has made in making an immersive experience. Still needs a few more weeks at least of patching to be stable.
Overall I would say it shows serious mechanical improvement on the FarCry series it is so obviously ripping off and even manages to inject some interesting storyline between bouts of shouting 'USA! USA!' but be warned it's not as polished as it thinks it is.

Within minutes of booting Zeno Clash 2, I knew something was wrong.  The change from the Source engine to Unreal 3 made everything feel a bit off.  Ghat's move set was greatly expanded from a handful of brutal moves to a large selection of hard-to-master combos that I knew right away I wasn't going to bother with.  If Zeno Clash is Double Dragon, then Zeno Clash 2 is Street Fighter 2.  Ghat, who felt strong and capable in the original feels weak and flimsy here.  The story, which was tight and thrilling in the original is now flabby and not nearly as interesting.  Gameplay in the original involved being placed in one intense situation after another, with occasional breathers to allow story progression or to admire the strange world you inhabit.  The lead characters were constantly on the run, constantly pursued and constantly in danger.  In Zeno Clash 2, you're allowed to manually travel between hubs, mostly at your own pace, bashing respawning monsters and poking around in hiding spots for colored moths.  It's not quite "meh, this is kinda stupid" but it also is a far cry from the "holy cow, this is constantly awesome!" feeling I got from the original.  Zeno Clash 2 is definitely an inferior sequel that was made less interesting and less fun by trying to add more to the core mechanics that made the original so great.
BUT... Is Zeno Clash 2 a bad game?  No, it is not.  It's still a fun 1st person fighter/shooter.  It still exists in a wonderfully weird world that is a blast to exist in.  It has a perfect challenge level.  It's achievements are relatively fun and easy to get.  It's story, while inferior, is still decently written and enjoyable.  And yes, hunting for moths can be fun.  It's not the same KIND of experience and not the same QUALITY experience but it is still just barely good enough to earn a recommendation.  BARELY.

Zeno Clash 2 is the follow up to Zeno Clash, developed by ACE Team for PC, PS3 and Xbox 360, being released in 2013. The game runs using the Unreal 3 Engine, unlike the previous game which used Valve's Source engine.
The game plays basically the same as the first; no new features have really been added, apart from the secondary weapons. The whole game focuses on hand to hand combat with a light amount of gun play. Whilst the gameplay is very much the same, it's still has an element of fun to it, which is hard to find in melee fighting games. You are able to block and dodge enemy attacks, each time you do this you gain a little bit of a boost to your special attack bar, which allows you to perform a pretty mean looking double punch right to the opponents face. The element of gun play is very basic; again like the first there is something odd with the way you control your character when equipping the gun, you can't seem to holster it and go back to punching, you just have to whack your opponents with it instead - I found that a bit strange.
Graphically, the game is a bit of an improvment over the first, but not really four years’ worth of improvement. Whether that is testament as to how good Valve's source engine is or whether it should class as a negative point towards Zeno Clash 2, you decide. The game still does look nice though. Just the right amount of lens flare being used in moments where it should. There are some really beautiful environments to feast your eyes on, and some really interesting enemies and NPCs to check out too.
For the plot, it is absolutely necessary that you have finished the first game for you to understand what is happening; it begins right where the last game left off, but this time your companion is Rimat, who was actually an opponent in the last game. The story is set around freeing Fathermother, a character again out of the first game. The story is OK, it does seem a little dull at times and feels like a little bit more action is needed to make the characters you meet along the way to have a bit more character to them, as they all seem very generic and bland.
Whilst we are on the topic of generic and bland, that brings me on nicely to the game's audio. The voice acting in this game made me physically cringe with how bad it is. Every single one of the characters sounds so awfully awkward whenever a line of text is spoken. The game certainly took a step back compared to the first here. I have to admit though, the sound effects when punching enemies are really satisfying, nothing like a hearing a good old squelch as you smash a walking shrimp in the face.
Zeno Clash 2 can be played on a few levels of difficulty; if you managed to complete the first game you should be at least playing on Medium, the easy mode will be a walk in the park. There is a nicely put together tutorial which can be done before you jump into the story, however it is completely optional, so much that it's not included in the main game, and you have to select it from the main menu. You are able to select which allies you bring into a fight with you, some are more powerful than others, and so once you work out who is the best, you won't have any problems beating many of the enemies you'll face.
I actually felt as if this was almost a bit like an open world style game, with various different zones to explore, you have a couple of options of where to go next after completing objectives. Each of the zones has its own theme and style to it and each of them has plenty of things to see in. Throughout the game you will encounter giant sea shells, these acts as the games "treasure chest" system, and in them you'll find health pots, special ability bonuses and many more different items and weapons. You'll also come across butterflies and item boxes which also add bonuses onto your character; as well as just plain talent upgrades, which let you choose how you spend the points in the regular RPG style, HP, damage etc. etc.
I was a bit disappointed when I found that I completed the whole game in almost four hours. The only saving grace for that is that Zeno Clash 2 actually has a multiplayer mode in it, meaning you could play it through once on your own then team up with a buddy for a second play through; however I have finished it single player and don't really have any urge to play it through again. The game does have a few achievements this time. And they actually work unlike the first games.
Zeno Clash 2 has a wide variety of graphically options as well as an FOV option (which you will need to set to wide or else you'll get motion sickness) which is nice to see in a PC game. However I still encountered a couple of crashes; which I couldn't for the life of me work out why it was happening. It just seemed to happen at random times; other than the crashes I was able to play the game fine. I was running it at full graphics on 4k resolution and had a steady 60 FPS all the time. Keyboard and mouse are the only viable option here; but controller is supported too.
To sum up, Zeno Clash 2 fell a little bit short of my expectations compared to the first game. The shortness of the title really doesn't help, but if you feel like you would want to connect up with a friend to play this through, you may get more mileage out of it at full price, however I cannot really recommend what is a four hour game for £10, 99, when the first game is half the price and has more than double the amount of content in.

Quite a quaint little game, VERY arcadey, however, once you get the hang of it, very fun. Yes, yes, there are still flaws with the game, but, I'm remaining optimistic and hoping that sometime down the line, there will be solutions presented (for example, team selection in arcade mode is a tad uninuitive, since the game was originally made for only two factions, but now there are five.) Still, if you're able to get a good grip on the controls, have a somewhat powerful system to run it on, and are willing to put up with a few unintuitive parts, then you can have quite a bit of fun! There's even quite a few features that are implemented, and can be greatly expanded upon in due time, however, the developer (yes, one person) does have quite a bit that they're working on, and are very responsive and quick to look at issues, from what it appears.
Overall, I'd say this is a very fun game, may not be the greatest tank arcade shooter, but, it is, indeed very fun. ...If only there were more people to play with for online games, ah well, can't have it all.
Also, a couple little tips, at least with the current state of the game: With tanks, using explosive rounds is preferable since you can deal damage to both the chassis and turret, but it has a higher shell drop. Armor piercing are much better at sniping in tanks, and it appears against flat angles, does more damage than explosive to the compenent that was hit. And, if you want to rank up fast, currently, going on the flat arena map, and going up against a large enemy team composed of Type 89's (Japanese WWII era medium tank) with kills required set to 0 and a time limit of 10-20 minutes is the most efficient way.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a real-time strategy... turn-based... space ship... Star Trek... simulator? In this game, you control a space ship that is on the run from the rebels with valuable information regarding them in the war between them and the Empire. As you can tell, this game takes a lot of elements of its lore from specific source material like Star Wars and Star Trek. In this game, by default, you control the space ship, the USS Kestrel, though other styles of ships are unlockable. You can rename your ship and the three crew members you get. Your ship has multiple systems that you must manage, such as Oxygen, Weapons, and Shields. You have to run away from the rebel fleet across eight sectors, all the while fighting other ships, trading with people visiting stores, and making decisions. The best part abouth the decisions is that there is always a possibility of a postive or negative outcome. Depending on the type of situation that you are in, you decide whether or not to try that decision. Theoretically, the game shouldn't take more than two three hours to beat, you'll die and restart so much, the game's lenght will probably triple. The game has a very nice pixelated art style that I love (hinting at the origins of my name) and the price is very cheap considering the quality of the game. FTL: Faster Than Light gets an 8.5/10.
-The Pixelated Gamer

Apparently this game has strong ties with its TV show counterpart, but I am being ignorant for it as I've never even heard it, so this review is based on purely the gameplay/technical aspect of the game alone.
South Park is a light RPG with cartoonish graphic which is full of (apparently) comedy from start to finish. I am not a type that can stomach this kind of disgusting jokes in-game, though.
From a quick glance, you might think it's suitable for children, but no it's not. Even the rating says it's not,
The gameplay is fairly simple, you control one character on 2D map, can move right left to explore the areas, unlock new rooms and do some quests to progress. The map is fairly large, but there's a quick travel (think about Waypoints in Diablo 3) so you can deliver quest items around faster.
Being an RPG, there's bound to be battle screen. The battle screen is loaded when your character comes in contact with enemy - more or less Mapped Enemies - so there's no annoying random battles, because you can avoid battles if you want (except boss battles or forced fights). When in battle your 2 characters take turns like traditional RPGs, can use items, skills or magic. The standard aspect of RPG battles still applies here, as enemies often have strong resistance against certain elements, so you need to research the enemies first before attacking.
The sound/OSTs are so so for my taste, nothing really caught my attention. But the good side is that the game is fully voiced, meaning you will hear characters speaking whether in battle or in map/normal exploration.
From technical side, I've heard about a bug where you will get skipped cutscene during certain event, see this link:
, but I didn't encounter it. Still, I did as what advised and saved my game before it's too late. As a whole, the game is very smooth on maxed settings on my laptop, and I can play with my xinput Logitech F310 controller without issue as well.
Once you beat the game, it won't end like Final Fantasy 7 for example, where you can only replay the game from your last savepoint. You'll be allowed to return to the map to continue your sidequests, along with your latest equipments, that you haven't finished. But there are missables so if you fail to get them in the first place, you need to restart your playthrough from the beginning / new save.
DLCs are garbage, don't buy them - what an awful quick cash grab from Ubisoft, but it's to be expected. However, for some unknown reason, this version does NOT contain uPlay. Hooraaaaayyyyy! One of redeeming point of this game for me.
So am I going to recommend the game? Absolutely, despite its flaws for me, but only when it's discounted. I personally paid this game for like 2 USD on legitimate/endorsed Steam key distributor for 12-15 hours of entertainment - well worth it. So if you haven't bought it, chances are you will be able to get the same price like me in the future.

South Park has always had a rough run in video games. From the original South Park video game for the original Playstation and N64 to the more recent South Park: Tenorman’s Revenge, pretty much all South Park games have been less than spectacular. None of them have even truly felt like a real South Park experience. Well, South Park: The Stick Of Truth is here to change that. South Park: The Stick Of Truth is an RPG developed by Obsidian Entertainment, the developers behind Star Wars: Knights Of The Old Republic 2, Dungeon Siege III and Fallout: New Vegas. The game has gone through a lot in its development time. Originally planned to be published by the now defunct THQ, it then vanished only to be re-risen by it’s new publisher Ubisoft. I am quite thankful that Ubisoft has made sure The Stick Of Truth has seen the light of day because it was a truly fun experience.
The game begins as the gang is engaging in a war over the stick of truth, a stick which gives it’s holder ultimate control over the universe. You are the new kid. Your parents tell you to go out and make some friends and shortly after, you’re sucked into the world of the game. The game offers you four different classes to choose from consisting of Fighter, Mage, Thief and Jew, all of which are self explanatory with the exception of Jew which plays like a paladin would. It also offers three different difficulties which are Easy, Normal and Hardcore. For my first play through I chose to play as a Mage and it played exactly like you’d expect a Mage in an RPG would. As I progressed and leveled new spells and abilities became available and it played out as you would expect in a standard RPG. The leveling system is straight from the books as well and is pretty much on par. Without giving too much information away the story plays out pretty much exactly as you would expect from South Park. It’s absolutely ridiculous, but in an extremely fun and entertaining way. The game progresses from the boy’s tiny Lord Of The Rings stylized game to a world filled with chaos with no one realizing just how ridiculous and insane everything has become.
The game play of The Stick Of Truth is pretty unoriginal but it worked out perfect for the game. The fights are turn-based with you and your buddy up against your enemies. The HUD is nice and easy to use and makes battling an easy system to master. When not in battle, you are either running around completing side quests or working on the main quest line. The main quests are generally longer and much more complicated and will take you across a variety of locations where as the side quests are generally short and to the point. There were a few “find and kill” side quests but not enough to be an annoyance. The main quests were really where the majority of the fun was but you will definitely need to have done side quests in between or you’ll be too low of a level to actually compete with any enemies you may encounter on the main quest. The loot system consists of both finding and collecting items from defeated foes. You can loot anything from money, to weapons to armor to potions to a turd (which can be used to gross out your enemies). The map of South Park is not overly huge so you’ll end up going back and forth to many of the same places multiple times. If you don’t feel like running you can take a fast travel (thanks to your little bud Timmy) but I found it much nicer and only slightly longer to run it. If you’re playing the uncensored version of the game while free roaming around town you may enter locations and spot random events going on. In general, they were pretty hysterical but I am sure that none of them have made it into the uncensored version of the game.
The Stick Of Truth also has a collecting system were throughout the game you must try and collect all of the 30 chinpokomon scattered around South Park. Along with this is another collection goal to become friends with everyone in South Park on Facebook. Both systems were nice and added slight side goals, but at the same time I felt both were a bit on the easy side. Collecting friends generally would just happen by playing through quests or talking to people while roaming town, while the chinpokomon were, with a few exceptions, generally hidden in plain sight. Still it added a bit of extra content and a few things to do other than questing. Almost every character from the South Park universe does makes an appearance in the game so if you’re dedicated it will take a lot of searching to find everyone.
In many ways, Stick Of Truth actually feels like a new South Park movie only much longer and more interactive than a movie could be. The animations and voice acting was done by South Park Studios so when you end up in a cut-scene it really feels like you are actually watching the show. While playing the game the animations are just as great but it does feel somewhat different. It could just be due to the fact that you are busy playing and not just sitting back and watching a scene. Obviously the game carries it’s own unique story but the game contains more references, to episodes of the show, than I could count. Whether it was completing a side quest to help Mr. Hankey find his children to helping Mr. Kim fight off the Mongolians there was a lot of nostalgia from past events. Unfortunately, while the main quest line focuses on the new story a good portion of the side quests are actually geared towards reminiscing on past episodes rather than building onto the new story. It isn’t a problem but I would have preferred to have seen the side quests add more new content into the new plot. You will also find references everywhere by picking them up as junk items or even simply having the references be a part of the actual world.
The Stick Of Truth is a game which has plenty of replay value as well. My first play through took me about 16 hours to complete entirely. Every single quest was done. Now normally for an RPG I would expect a longer game but this one felt right being shorter. The game was extremely well written and was fully enjoyable and I think pushing it on longer may have actually hurt the game. Once you’ve completed the game you’ve still got three other classes to go back and play through, or you can go back as the same class and choose a different faction to side with which will change the story, though only slightly.
Overall, South Park: The Stick Of Truth is a great game. It is the South Park game fan’s of the series have been waiting for. The fighting systems are well balanced and play smoothly, the cut scenes and voice acting feels straight out of the show and the story is one that is humorous and could only make sense in the world of South Park. South Park: The Stick Of Truth gets a 8.5/10.

I got this game for free by preordering Bioshock Infinite on Steam. I enjoyed this game sooo much more than Infinite. I like to think that I actually bought this game and got Bioshock for free. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a turn-based tactical strategy game where you command a squad of soldiers battling an alien invasion. It’s actually a remake of an old PC game of the same name. I never played the original, but I’ve heard it has some UI issues that make it unintuitive and difficult to learn. This was the opposite. It was easy to get the hang of and felt familiar to me as someone who has played several games in this genre before.
XCOM also has a “permanent death” element where if one of your soldiers dies on the battlefield, he dies forever. Which made me restart a battle a few times when one of my best soldiers died, even though I probably would have won anyway. Soldiers can specialize in several different classes: Sniper, heavy, medic etc. and you can upgrade your soldier’s gear and abilities and what not. Nothing too groundbreaking or innovative, just a very solid tactical strategy game.
Check this out if you like turn-based strategy, I enjoyed this game enough to finish it twice. It’s quite addictive. And difficult.

You are nothing. A wanderer, adrift in a mysterious world that is otherwise physically impossible. Your memory is time and time, deceived. Deja vu moments and memory gaps, contradictorty as they may seem, plague your mind.

well...

Your tool shall evolve as you progress, as the quotes you encounter unfold a story of pictures.
You will create plant life, gardens of inward growth. Your gardens will transform into animals, primitive snakes of sorts, slithering upon command.
You progress, a plague, a virus, horrendous, beautiful, but limited in dimension.
Your final form, a carrier, a harbringer of death, a black hole, a plague. The end of all, yet a beginning of a life of wisdom.

Enjoy the game that teaches you more about life than society ever will.

TL;DR: Hidden Resident Evil Gem, eith episodic gameplay.
Okay so what people may or may not tell you is that, apart from getting these in episodes, there are essentially TWO games.
MAIN GAME:
Traditional Resident Evil humor and writing. Hopefully you played a bit of RE1 because BARRY! You get references all over the place.
Gameplay feel right in between RE4 and RE6. You do a little bit of dodging like in RE6 but instead of THROWING yourself on the GROUND like some sort of action hero, you just do a side hop, good enough to dodge attacks. This is pretty solid since you can move around while aiming. Honestly if they remade RE4 with these mechanics, you wouldn't need another RE game because it would be more perfect than it is.
Also 10/10 to Barry for going to a spooky island and bringing not only a pistol, but a revolver and a rifle.
Gotta manage ammo a bit more than RE4,5 and 6. Feels good.
7.5/10 game, and that is having 5 as a pass.
RAID MODE:
Mercenaries on crack and way more fun IMHO. This is the reason I keep coming back to the game.
You start with a character and a pistol, then you choose the first mission. In missions you will find chests with "albums" as well as ammo. Missions are pretty straight forward (kill X amount of enemies, go to the end in X amount of time and defend X) and are a blast to play. You get 3 herbs per mission. You level up after missions when you get anough XP. You use the skill points to get per level to upgrade skills which actually change up how you play.
After a mission you can unlock an album or sell it for cash. The album tells you what gun you are unlocking and the skills have their own icon so you know what you are getting. Now this may make you think that you have to pay for gold to unlock items, but believe me, you don't. I am overburdened with gold. You can play daily missions and free missions for gold. you will never need to do this because you will find a few types of weapons and sell the rest (I personally love Shotguns and handguns).
Some characters have some skills unlock early, some characters have more weapon slots to use and less skills. Some specialize in grenades. Claire for intance is an all rounder who like pistols. Barry has more weapon slots to begin with but fewer skills. I got Wesker in the full collection edition and he obviously had ONE-A PUNCH-U SKILL-O
This section is easily a 8/10
All in all fun times that I didn't expect. Seriously after the dissapointment of RE6 this is awesome.
