Arkham Knight combines much of the grit of the Rocksteady titles with the poor design choices of WBs Arkham Origins. While the story itself is well worth a playthrough, constant issues will definately keep you from a second one.
The Good:
Graphically the game is the best it's ever looked. Light and fog effects are gorgeous (when turned on) and the turbulent ocean effects were jaw dropping.
Gameplay had a fairly steady difficulty curve, provided you are going through all the side missions you will feel like Batman by the end, perfectly timing combos and flying through predator encounters.
The story is still where the game shines. The voice acting is completely on point and the main story has real weight to it. While it is the weakest of the trilogy it still stands on its own as a solid end to the series.
The Bad:
The one issue that will plague you from start to finish is the loading. Having a "seemless" city to prowl around in sounds great at first, until you feel your hard drive chunking away trying to keep up. This is the legacy of Arkham Origins. This is especially an issue when you upgrade the speed of your grappler​. Speeding between "zones" without loading screens at crazy speeds creates hiccups and loading wheels constantly. This drove me crazy in Origins and it's back with a vengeance in Knight. My only solution was literally pausing the game and waiting for my HDD light to calm down then resume. It took me completely out of the immersion of flying around Gotham like a boss.
Then there is the story. Without giving anything away from the get-go the story really starts to paint Batman as a real schmuck. It feels very forced, almost like the story he forcing his decision making rather than creating it. In the end much of Batman's arc feels forced. The writers wanted a result and bent and contorted their characters to get it.
Verdict:
If you have played the first 2 as I have, this is pretty much a must play, just for completion. Just like Mass Effect before it, this final entry feels forced and crushed under the weight of its own success.

This is what I'd call a "thinking persons" resident evil, certainly not a typical run 'n' gun scenario.
I'll make A few points rather than a review because I could analyze the hell of of RE, revelations 2.
Firstly, graphics are graphics....what can I say. It ran nice and smooth on my rig, which is getting dated, running a 5+ year old AMD fx 4100 with 8gig of ram and a radeon rx270. At 1080, at max settings, never dropped below 60fps and I guess that's to be expected because its not exactly a new game and nor is it revolutionary with what it presents. Still, it's good to know that you can crank up the settings and enjoy the crisp gory detail.
Speaking of gore, the setting is eerie, possibly the most "disturbing" entry to the series (Until RE7 arrives...), while the fear effect wears off eventually, the sickening gore and images are apparent through the whole game. You get the feeling you're playing a Silent hill game crossed with Dead space in the Biohazard universe.
And that's exactly how the game plays. I can see how they encourage replaying the game, you're rewarded with BP, which is basically the games currency to buy upgrades, extras, special unlocks, artwork etc. If you find enough gems and hidden items, accomplish certain things in the game, you're rewarded BP. To me, it's too overwhelming, there are a lot of unlockables and you'd have to invest a lot of time to unlock everything. By the end of the first playthrough, you probably have over half of the special abilities \ passive abilities if you invest all of your BP, enough to make a 2nd playthrough more enjoyable....so you can earn more BP to unlock the extra costumes, artwork.....etc etc. Need I say more? At about the 25 hour mark, it seems like a bit of a grind unless you're a hardcore RE fan. Me....I have a steam backlog like you wouldn't believe and I've got no time for that.
All in all, it's an interesting story, worth the investment and even one playthrough, purely for the purpose of the ongoing resident evil canon.

This CCG has its own cancer deck(s) of course, but it's still good enough to recommend, since my experience is: a tiny bit of frustration, which quickly goes away, and a whole bunch of fun, that you won't forget any time soon. Most of the following is very subjective, so that's an other reason to try the game, but of course reading different opinions might help you decide if the game is for you, so here we go! (I'll try to stay objective, where I can. Tl;dr: check the "OVERVIEW" part.)
THE LOOKS:
The animations on the cards in a lot of cases look great, even if the mostly anime style drawings are not to your liking. And even if they're not to your liking, they are mostly very well drawn. A lot of the cards are drawn in this style, but definitely not all: some of them give a "classic" fantasy vibe, so they're just pleasant to look at. The overall look of the game however can be a little bit confusing/too much at first. There can be a lot of effects on the screen at the same time, which can make the game look less appealing.
THE SOUNDS:
I've seen some people complain about the voice acting. While it's not the greatest, it's definitely not that bad, and I don't even think it even has to be great. This is a free card game after all, and for its "price", it delivers. I've seen (and heard) a LOT of very bad voice acting in games and movies too, and if you're experienced, you can clearly see the effort they put in the voices. The music is not horrible either, but it IS made of few minutes long loops, so if you don't like that... well, you're gonna listen to your own music anyway after a while, so in this case you'll just start sooner. Not that they're bad loops though. On the other hand one thing I really like is the voice acting of the cards (that speak). In most cases they're consistent with the creatures' personalities, sometimes even if it changes when you evolve them (Lucifer). I also love that you can make emotes clip into each other, but again, some do not like that you can spam 3 emotes/turn. I agree however, that there could be more emotes, as sometimes I feel I can't react to the opponent's emotes appropriately.
GAMEPLAY:
You can decide on your own, if you like the voice acting and the look of the cards (or rather, their "anime style" drawing). But don't judge it only by its looks! The game itself has some pretty good and unique mechanics, so even if the look of the game is not your favorite, it is still possible to have fun thanks to the variety of these mechanics, and the comebacks that seem to happen quite often, especially in lower ranks.
There are a bunch of unique features too, like Private Play Take Two (which means that you can play arena with a friend for free). But you are constantly reminded, that not everyone has the same idea of "fun" as you do. There ARE cancerous decks with cancerous "combos" - the most recent being the Daria Runecraft deck. At lower (than Master) ranks at least half of the games I've played were against aggro decks, though it IS possible to win against them with a good enough control deck. Of course if you'd like to depend only on the free packs you receive, there's a chance you won't have all the necessary cards, so making an aggro deck in most cases will be much easier. This, however won't be as fun imo, as playing a control/midrange or a less easy combo deck.
OVERVIEW:
I think this game you'll just have to see for yourself. There's one very important thing to keep in mind though: you're here to have FUN. Yes, there are less balanced cards, yes, there are copy-paste netdecks. But overall the game delivers. I really enjoy most of the matches, and when I meet said netdecks, I still have fun. How? I guess I just know that this is a game. If you only care about ranking, just copy a deck and off you go, but if you care about the adventure the possibilities have to offer, try different combinations of different cards!
BUT! Before you make an okay deck, and start to rank up like crazy, remember: the game becomes MUCH harder, after you reach rank C/B (depending on your deck). In lower ranks it is easier to complete your daily quests. If you want to stay in lower ranks until you have a decent enough deck, then it's a great opportunity to try "worse" decks. Let the experiments begin! In this way you'll gain experience (literally and in-game) which will be very useful, if you'd like to know   your opponents AND the possible combos you can pull off with your cards that you've never used before.
All in all Shadowverse is a great experience, especially if you know how to treat it (as a game). Don't be afraid to give it a chance! You can't waste your time if you're at least a little bit interested in the game. I hope this helped you in some way!

Clair is the agressive player in the pair with Moira being more support focused. Throughout the world you can use moria flashlight and natalia pointing to find hidden objects. They range from herbs, ammo, to BP which can be used to purchase skills to improve your characters.
The game features RAID mode, just as the previous resident evil game did. It has been improved with more missions, weapon variety and the gameplay hooks you in pretty quickly. The enenies are always challenging so you never feel like it is a cake walk. If you aren't a fan of the story then just purchasing the first episode for $6 and playing RAID mode is alone a good enough reason to purchase the game and you'll more than get your money's whorth.
The story is compelling and you find yourself hooked pretty soon. Clair and Moira are absucted and find themselves in a prison. from there you encounter many obstacles, overpowering enemies will be a big one. The game uses the world around you to your advantage in how you deal with your enemies. Claire and Moira , as well as Barry and Natalia's team work is truly something to behold.
The enviroment around you looks amazing objects are crisp and clean, effects are great. This is a game worthy of being in your library. If you are a Biohazard fan or new to the series, definitely give this series a shot.

I feel obligated to review this because of the obscene amount of hourage I have. I am not a serious gamer but for some reason I've racked up more hours in Risk of Rain than pretty much every other reviewer who's written about it. This is mainly because I am very bad at the game and have spent many hours repeatedly restarting, due to mediocre hand-eye coordination.
Risk of Rain is a roguelike and it is excellent at being a roguelike. In my opinion, it balances a slow build of achievements and unlockables with the permadeath feature. One advantage of this setup is that the player has time to get used to basic game modes and items before moving onto more difficult or more complicated aspects of play. Unlockables came at just the right pace for me - although the game was frustrating at first, I never got bored, and was always excited for the next item to try out.
It has cute graphics - I love how tiny the main character is. The landscapes are minimal but have a huge amount of atmosphere. I love feeling immersed in the setting of the game. I run it on a gaming laptop, and if I've been playing for more than an hour I usually have to turn them down a bit to keep my framerate up. Less powerful laptops will struggle with this game so don't be fooled by the simplicity and pixelated style.
I found gameplay to be very difficult, but non-gamer friends did not have trouble with it. Mileage will vary depending on playstyle and character chosen, but this game does have a certain skill/strategy aspect, especially later in the game. It's not intellectually taxing but I like getting to make strategic decisions and figure out what abilities and items will work best for each character. I also like that the game doesn't seem to funnel the player towards a certain playstyle or outcome. If you want to linger on a single level for three hours, or buy only goat hooves for an entire playthrough, or stack barbed wire so heavily it covers half the screen, you can be its guest. I tend to like sandbox and simulation games for the sense of exploration and choice I get from them, and I got that from this game.
Not everyone will know what I'm talking about on this point, but RIsk of Rain does really well (for me) at inducing that exhilerating feeling of tension when the difficulty starts to ramp up - I'm elated every time I beat a run, even though I've beat it tens of times before. (I love the ending; it's neither over- nor under-done in my opinion. I feel a pang of emotion every time I get there. But I don't want to give anything away :) )
One thing the game really has going for it is the short playthrough time. The longest games of RIsk of Rain I've played have lasted about 70-80 minutes. So it's easy to sneak in a game between classes (I do that more than I probably should...).
I'd highly recommend Risk of Rain to those who aren't frustrated by roguelikes, and those who don't have much time to game but still want to feel immersed in a fast-paced, exhilarating alien universe. (Also, from a sample size of two in which I am one member, every single autistic person I know has become obsessed with it, so there's that.)

While I like this game a lot, others may not, depending on what they're expecting.
If you are expecting any edition of the tabletop role-playing game, or the Genesis or SNES console games, you will be disappointed.  Shadowrun: Returns plays something like a simplified version of tabletop rules that never actually existed.
I liked the plot, combat, and music.
Opinions on the plot vary widely.  If you have an aversion to reading, this game is
for you.  Almost all of the plot is delivered via screens of text upon entering an area, or text dialogs.  There is no voiceover.  Some people complain of purple prose, or that it seems to have been written by someone that is immature, but the writing is superior to that in
video games, including most other RPGs.  I personally do not perceive any of these problems, and have never seen examples cited.
Screenshots do not do the combat system justice.  Some of the interface is only displayed when it is relevant.  For example, the action point cost of movement, and the effectiveness of cover, only appear when you prepare to move, and when cover exists in the area you mouseover.  The combat system is relatively simple (which is reflected in the user interface), but like Chess, can be quite difficult.  The difficulty is selectable at character creation, so if you find the game too easy or hard you can adjust it.  Since almost all RPGs are combat-heavy, it's important that it not be mindless and repetitive.
The music is hard to describe.  It is not ambient.  You
notice it.  I especially like the theme on the title screen.
I didn't like some things about Shadowrun: Returns.
It is very linear, and most decisions will not affect the ending.
The gameplay in the matrix is very similar to meatspace.  It's not so much that the gameplay in the matrix is
as it doesn't feel
.

Story is a wonderfull thing. It can make you cry, make you smile. Well this one made me confused and bored. The problem with Kane and Lynch is hard to pick at one thing though as story only shares the blame. The others would be the stale mechanics, and the bland characters.
I want to start with mechanics as this is a huge problem how it's designed and how it works in this game, Especially a shooter. For some reason it was a good idea to make it so you were practically the worst shot in all of gaming. The hit marker wasn't even how I aimed, I always aimed my shots slightly to the top right as thats where all the shots somewhat went. Even then it was difficult to get a shot on someone. The way aiming worked was that you always aimed in the area your crosshair took up. Confused? Well imagine the crosshair as a circle instead, because you aren't aiming directly center ever. Even in close range I didn't bother shooting and instead went with a takedown instead. The only weapons I ever used were the sniper and shotgun since the sniper was always accurate, and the shotgun was a wide spread. When I didn't have these weapons I was annoyed at the amount of time I spent in gun fights just to hit someone nevermind killing them.
Now the story. Out of what Square Enix has put out, it's a shocker how bland this story is. Now it isn't bad, but it isn't good either. The story is very cookie cutter. You need to save your wife and kid. The way it was introduced reminded me of John Wick how this insane criminal comes out of retirement to destroy an organization he once belonged to. Of course it's different as Kane (the main character you play as) is instead broken out of prison and such. It has this plot that could go in many directions but doesn't. It leaves questions unanswered, the main character is boring, and halfway through the game it turns into some military shooter. I'm not joking. You go to the jungle with army gear, tanks, rpg's, and helicopters. This caught me off guard so much, I thought this was Lynch's memory since I didn't know much about him. Any character brough up has these interesting topics and relationships that are never explored. Like how is Kane known to this organization. What did he do that made his family hate him? Lynch is blamed for his wife's death but believes it wasn't him despite his violent blackouts. There is so much here that it kills me that not in this one or the sequel they touch on these subjects.

Anicon: Cat’s Path is a fun little otome game about Clena and her adventures with a family of boys who are cursed to turn into animals. In this path, the story is focused on the cat, Kad. He’s a super shy cat who transforms into his human form quickly due to feeling embarrassed by Clena’s actions.
I’ve been waiting for the release of this game for a while now. I’ve been looking forward to Zeiva’s Dragon Essence for years now, but this game was announced and I thought it sounded like something I’d love to play in the meantime.  When I first heard about, I thought it sounded cute and fun. And that is what this is. A cute, fun, lighthearted game. It doesn’t have a deep story or anything of the sort. Clena has one mission set by a character and the rest of the story is just moments that happened throughout the year. It felt very episodic in that way. Still, it was funny and an enjoyable read. The artwork was gorgeous as well.
I’ve been playing Zeiva’s games for years now since they released their older flash games on deviantart and I’ve always thought they were enjoyable and quirky. This one’s no exception. I do, however, have a recommendation for them—switch the engine from flash. Flash is kind of a dying breed nowadays and it’s not very secure. I recommend switching to a VN engine like Renpy or Tyrano Builder or if they don’t want to go for those, HTML5 is a choice. It’ll also make implementing Steam features more easily, since the game doesn’t have Steam overlay which sucks because I would have loved to share some funny screenshots I took of my favorite character—the snail. It would have been nice to have the in-game achievements implemented onto steam as well. It’s those extra things that make everything even nicer. I also would have liked the game to have a widescreen option. I couldn’t play it on full screen on my PC. When I tried, the screen would go completely black. It never showed up properly, so I had to play it windowed the entire time.
Leaving those things aside, I do recommend the game. I think it’s cute, fun and perfect to play when you want a shorter game that doesn’t get exhausting. I’m looking forward to more paths, and I would really love a snail path!

These things were minor annoyances, though. I got to take a team of Badasses from one Badass Crater of Badassitude to another, and kick♥♥♥♥♥all the way to Badassdom with a steady supply of bublegum. If tactics are you cuppa, then gie this bad boy a shot. Well worth it.

For a long time, whenever someone would ask which Traveller's Tales Lego game they should guess. I couldn't give them an answer. They were all about equal in quality, just pick one that is an ip you like. No longer, I can definitively say that Lego Marvel Super Heroes is the best Lego game Traveller's Tales has made to date.
It has the greatest variety of useful  characters, the most activities, the largest world to explore, and just the best looking visuals and writing. It is also more challenging than most Lego games. Especially if you are going for 100% completion. There are some collectibles (and rescuables) that are quite the head scratcher.  This is enhanced by the open world. Easily one of the best looking open worlds in this type of game. Clearly Traveller's Tales best most detailed open world.  People on the street will often respond to whatever character you are controlling. Every place is properly detailed. It must have cost a lot to create it since they are reusing it for Lego Marvel Avengers. Lego City for the WiiU is a close second.
The game shows the staff at Traveller's Tales that worked on this game really loved Marvel comics. There were many deep references that casual fans, and Cinematic fans would miss but would delight long time fans. Not that you would need to be a long time fan. The entire game has plenty of clever writing, humor and sight gags to entertain fans and non fans a like.
Let me stress this isn't a perfect game. There are some glitches that happen from time to time. There is one area inside the Statue of Liberty where characters will often slide off platforms and to there deaths for no apparent reason. The driving and flying controls in the open world are particularly frustrating in race events. Nothing that kills the general game play or fun, but if you are trying for 100%, you will get frustrated sometimes.
Also if you are suffering from Lego game burnout, you might want to take a long break before playing this game because its easily the most Lego of all Traveller's Tales games.  If you are ready for one, this is the one to get. At least until Lego Marvel Avengers or Lego Dimensions comes out.

I'm usually not the biggest fan of turn based tacticals...but this game is ALMOST pure gold. I say this because there is some bs to it. But I can't start with that. Not with a game this good. In XCOM: Enemy Unknown you take the role of a commander overseeing an operation to eliminate the alien threat. You will be making critical decisions almost all the time; and some of these decisions may force you to rely on luck. You will be responsible for keeping other countries faith in your project, thus earning you 1 or more bonuses: money, scientists and/or engineers.
These countries have a panic meter; and when this panic meter reaches full they will withdraw from your project permanently and you lose their bonuses. Certain missions and requests will pop up from time to time to time reducing panic or giving you more of the 3 bonuses. The more scientists/engineers you have, the faster you build/research. And we all know what more money does. Not only do you need to think critically on the field but with resources as well. So having a lot of money won't cut it for everything. Satellite coverage alerts you to enemy UFO presences and reduces panic. Satellite coverage is the way you get bonuses.
I could go on and on but those are the basics. The only thing that is a downside to this game are the 'Thin Man' aliens. They have a poisonous spit that literally never misses and they've even spit through walls and any other cover. This is annoying because poison instantly takes away that units turn up to 4 turns. They also blow up when they die creating a poisonous cloud then as well...so watch your units' paths so you don't run through. Other than that small problem, the game is worth every penny. Think smart, play it safe and have fun!

Mirror's Edge is a good game.  Certainly not great, as it has plenty of flaws. Which can range from more time-intense arenas like being chased by police across rooftops, to calm but very complex parkour puzzles (like using scaffolding to ascend multiple stories of a skyscraper).  The best part is, the controls are easy to master and the game feels fluid and responsive.  I also like how the designers used color to help navigate the player. The story is okay but they could have done a lot more with the world they created.  7.5/10

Antichamber is a great puzzle-based non-combat FPS game. It's a game that requires you to accept that while the world does not follow the rules you already know, there is always logic that can get you where you need to go.
Some of the puzzles involve your perspective or your movement, but most of them involve finding and using the matter gun.
The matter gun begins with the ability to pick up and put down small colored blocks, necessary to activate switches, prop doors open, and even build platforms. As you progress through the game, you will be able to upgrade the gun to manipulate the blocks in additionals ways, which in turn allow you to solve more advanced puzzles  on your way to the exit.
While the "essential" doors need to be completed in order with corresponding gun upgrades, the game is actually somewhat open in allowing you to explore and solve less-important puzzles and unlock new areas. Most of the puzzles are not required in order to reach the end, but many of them serve to teach you how the world works and how to use your gun (once you find it). Scattered throughout the entire game are over 100 posters to find. Some are hidden, some are out in the open. The posters feature a simple illustration and life lesson, which often ties to the puzzle at hand in some way. The posters add an optional collection factor for obsessive completionists.
There is no real danger to your character. You survive falls of any distance, but since much of your progress is upward, you may still be frustrated to find that you fell down to an area  you've already solved and may now have to waste time catching up.
The starting area functions as a hub room, keeping track of which posters you've found and providing a map of areas you've visited. You can always warp back to the hub room if you get stuck, and you can use the map to warp to an area you've seen, so it allows for quicker travel in the late game.
Out of all the games I've played this past year, Antichamber is one of my favorites. I'd recommend this for anybody who likes the puzzle solving aspect of Portal games, though it doesn't have the same atmosphere and snarky comedy.

Revolutionary for it's time, but mediocre by today's standards. I bought and played through all Half-Life games and their respective DLCs in order to understand what all the hype for HL3 was about, and also hoped to find some good games while I was at it. Was very disappointed.
I don't usually do this pros/cons thing, but the only other option would be to write an essay or make a video, the latter of which would require me to play the game again, so let me break it down for you.
Pros:
-Really great atmosphere and world building, good artstyle, shame the story falls short.
-Graphics are good and still hold up.
-Gunplay and controls feel as smooth as any other source game.
-Character model eye pupils move independently, along with many other amazing leaps and bounds in video game technology that you probably care about a lot.
Cons:
-The gameplay is about as lackluster as any other modern shooter, with tedious pre-school physics puzzles to fill the gaps between engagements and artificially extend game length.
-Essentially a long glorified tech demo.
-Boring missions, most of which consist of getting from point A to point B and killing everything in your way. Never feels like you're actually doing something meaningful.
-AI isn't very intelligent.
-Interesting but unfinished story, conveyed mostly through random bits of newspaper and other junk strewn about the environment, that you will most likely miss.
-Required to buy episodic DLC in order to progress the story, which still doesn't go anywhere, and still hasn't been finished.
-Mute blank slate protagonist complete with annoying mary sue sidekick who has a hard on for you.
-Protagonist just goes with the flow and does whatever anyone tells him to do, zero player choice.
-Many other boring characters.
-G-Man, who the ♥♥♥♥ is he?
Thank you.

9/10: Rounds out Rocksteady's Batman games with a Halloween hosted by Scarecrow. Drive around in the Batmobile, go tank mode, or leave it all behind to swoop majestically around Gotham.
Batman, already dealing with Joker's infected blood from the previous game, is starting to hallucinate Joker while desperately researching a cure. Things then get drastically worse as Scarecrow and the mysterous Arkham Knight, threaten the city into evacuating, leaving them along with Penguin, Two-Face, Harley Quinn, and more to wreak havoc on Gotham. Can Batman keep it together long enough to prevent Scarecrow from releasing fear toxin on the populace, or will the Batman finally pass the breaking point?
Honestly, it builds pretty safely on the previous titles mechanics. The combat is still flows and is made even better by the several team-up fights, grappling up buildings and flying around feels quick, and Predator mode gets you feeling like a ninja. The Batmobile sometimes felt clunky to drive, and fishtailed a lot, but I enjoyed blowing up hordes of militia drones using tank mode.
Personally, I liked bringing the Joker back this way, as a voice in Batman's head. I don't know if I'd have enjoyed Arkham Knight quite as much without his commentary running alongside it. There's plenty of other villains running amok and tons of militia outposts and checkpoints to populate the area between main missions with extra tasks, so the game definitely feels full.
Still, there's a finality in this game that makes me wistful. Rocksteady's Batman games stuck out for me because I enjoyed how smooth the combat was and the rush of grapple-launching into the air to fly to the next mission. While I'm not about to spend my time going through every AR challenge they packed in, I can say I'm satisifed by Batman: Arkham Knight, even if it may be the end.

Take your time and watch Free To Play. In brief:  A modern classic of 4X gaming.
I'm not going to explain Civilization V.  If you do not know what the game is about, I suggest checking out any number of Lets Play videos out there.
Pros:  Massive number of variations on play, and the various Civ bonuses lend real depth to how you tackle long term strategy.
Cons:  The game only really came into it's own after multiple expansions.  If you are going to pick it up, go for everything at once.  Many times gameplay will devolve into hitting "End Turn" while you wait for something significant to happen, and there can be a flood of useless information late in game as you try and home in on your victory path.
Who would like it best:  Fans of multi-faceted strategy games, history buffs, people who prefer long term open ended games.
Who may not like it:  People who need a plot to frame a game from beginning to end, those who hate DLC, people who dislike turn-based gameplay.

This game is NOT for 7-year-olds. It is tense, atmospheric and above all, terrifying.
The game is set in a fairly industrial environment, full of manufactured mutants and insane zombified guards, all out to get you. (There's a reason they call it Die More Edition) Each map is full of secrets and rather nicely-realised graphics - though some of the assets could do with a little more detail, such as some of the pipes and the flooring.
Ammo and weapons are very scarce, so you need to make every shot count - otherwise you're left with a knife and your own patience. There are a variety of guns as well as a bevy of things to stick together to create something better - for example, if you find 12 tin cans, you can make 2 plates which can then be made into an armour vest. It's important to look around for bits of stuff to make useful things out of - but, again, beware the nasty mutants. Many of them knock off as much as 10hp per hit, and bearing in mind the game has perma-death, this is rarely a good thing.
And the titular teleglitches dotted around the maps make the most horrific noise - sounds like the very fabric of reality is being tortured, which it essentially is. Each time you play, the map is completely different because of said glitches.
Essentially, if you're after a solid top-down shooter game that can make you cry out in horror, with elements of roguelikes, this is the game for you!

Let me be very clear: this is a bad game.  It is also a bad game that I have played through two, maybe three times.  That's because despite its (myriad) flaws, it is also a singularly unique game that builds a world I was fascinated by.
Those familiar with the works of Michael Mann (particularly Heat) will feel right at home with the tone and setting of this game.  What I enjoy most about Kane & Lynch: Dead Men is the fact that it goes all-in on its telling the story of two irredeemably corrupt and incompetent individuals.
The lead cahracters have good intentions (or at least think they do), but screw everything up to such a degree at every turn and to such a level that you would be foolish to send them on a simple grocery run to the local market.  Like watching a train wreck in slow-motion, it's horrific yet impossible to look away.
As games tend to be sold as power trips or escapist entertainment, it's unfortunately rare for a game to place you in the shoes of somebody that you actively detest.  However, taking this risk opens up so much in terms of unique and exciting storytelling.
So, yes -- the game hobbles by on sloppy cover-based shooting mechanics that repeatedly get you shot while you think you're hiding.  The graphics were dated when this game released in 2007, and age hasn't helped that.  The final act of the game, while narratively engaging, is a downright slog and includes the single worst stealth sequence that I have played in ages (so much so that you need a step-by-step guide just to keep you AI teammates from ruining everything immediately).  Even its high point, the story, has some giant holes and leaps of logic that can pull you out of things.
Despite all this, I recommend it -- but only if you're willing to overlook its shortcomings.  I also highly recommend playing it in co-op with a friend, as it adds a lot to the gameplay and characters with multiple perspectives.

I've heard FTL described as a rogue like crossed with a space sim. Though having only played one other rogue like (Azure Dreams on the PS1, just FYI) I feel like the label is fairly justified. Nothing carries over from each playthrough but the new ships you unlock and can play as, and each play through is pieced together from different parts in a seemingly random way.
A very slow paced game, but can feel frantic at times if only because of the urgency of problems that can occur. It can be frustrating succumbing to death in a playthrough that was going perfectly until one small mishap, and you will feel a lot of attachment to a crew and ship that are doing well, but you will sever that attachment quickly after hitting the retry button and starting afresh. Definitely worth picking it up, and definitely a worthy leader in the Kickstarter game trend.

I'm quietly confident that I'm not the only person on the planet to have been very excited by the IDEA of the first edition of Mansions of Madness, but a little disappointed by the results. I'm glad to say that the app-powered second edition finally delivers the goods, and despite my initial misgivings about the idea of a board game NEEDING an app in the first place, I'm happy to say it's the digital enhancement in question which finally makes this highly ambitious idea "work".
Yes, that's right, I did say "board game". Not "board game adaptation"...board game! So if you're not willing to: a. move miniatures around a bunch of cardboard tiles, and b. spend quite the bucketload of cash in order to attain said board game elements, you may want to skip this review and Store page altogether.
Oh, and did I say "bucketload of cash"? Now, now, I know that's anathema to Steam customers worldwide, since you're such a bunch of whining pansies who post no end of negative reviews reading "I spent five dollars to get this game on sale, and only got ten hours worth of gameplay out of it. RIPPED OFF. ♥♥♥♥ YOU, GABEN." Yeah, sorry, but you people can just kindly ♥♥♥♥ off at this point. Modern board games are for people with MONEY. Or at least a willingness to spend some money on entertainment that perhaps offers quality over quantity (me, I'm mostly a pauper, but I'm still willing to shell out upon occasion).
Not that this game doesn't offer potentially tens of hours of moderately varied entertainment - possibly more, once they  start releasing more expansions and whatnot - but you probably won't be getting thousands of hours of amusement out of your hundred-dollar-plus investment. To me, that kind of math is more than acceptable; if you're not that kind of person, then it's back to your Left 4 Dead 2 or Call of Duty, and no awesome tabletop fetishism for you. Some of us still enjoy a bit of TANGIBLE materialism every once in a while, evil capitalist pigs that we are.
This does bring us to the inevitable question, though: why, in Cthulhu's name, do we need a video game app in order to play a board game? Why would anyone think it's a good idea for these two rather disparate mediums to meet? Well, I was pretty skeptical too, but I gotta say, after this - my first foray into such territory - I'm mostly sold. MOSTLY. Erm...let me explain some more...
Yes, this could have been done purely-and-utterly as a video game. As far as I can deduce, there's no good reason why that couldn't have happened. EXCEPT: Fantasy Flight Games are a board game company, this is a second edition/complete rethinking of an earlier board game of theirs, and besides all this, sometimes tiles and miniatures and cards and dice are JUST ♥♥♥♥ING COOL. Simple as that.
The first Mansions of Madness tried hard to be the closest thing possible to the classic tabletop role-playing game The Call of Cthulhu transmogrified into somewhat simplified "board game" form. It didn't quite succeed, not least of all because it required one of the players to be the Keeper (also known in other tabletop RPGs as the Dungeon Master or Game Master).
This was its first mistake: a competitive board game, in which it was basically God versus the human investigators, and more often than not, God had the upper hand (what a ♥♥♥♥ing shocker, eh?)! I mean, it was an interesting experiment, trying to transfer such traditional RPG-ish elements into a board game, but as a competitive game it didn't fully work because the investigators and the Keeper weren't really playing the same game with the same rules. It wasn't a level playing field, in other words, and while the designers tried their damndest to make it one, it was all a bit "square peg in round hole"-ish by the end of the day.
Enter the app.
In this new version, the app plays the Keeper, leaving all the players (or just yourself, if you wanna Nigel it up and play alone) free to be the investigators and get on with, well, investigating! And this is where Mansions of Madness 2nd Edition succeeds admirably in being perhaps the best compromise between the worlds of board gaming and tabletop RPG-ing that I, at least, am thus far aware of (though I'll obviously have to check out Descent: Road to Legend in good time). The amount of "agency" granted to the players in this game is quite impressive, and there is a genuine feeling of "adventure" as you explore spooky mansions and other mysterious locales. It's certainly the closest you're liable to get to a single-player tabletop role-playing game this side of your wildest, wackiest dreams.
Sure, you don't get to do crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥like "I'm going to amass my own army, butcher innocents, and crown myself ruler of the whole kingdom", but then this wouldn't be a board game any more; it'd be a fully-fledged RPG. Given this game's somewhat more narrow, yet still admirably high ambitions, I think they've done a sterling job. I'm still not quite sure how far this app-driven board game thing can be taken - nor am I sure how far it SHOULD be taken - but I can safely opine that it works quite a treat in this instance. The gaming world truly is our communal oyster, and I for one am keen to see what bold new treasures await us in the future. To the cosmos and beyond!
Verdict: 9/10.
(PS Love the sometimes shamelessly Resident Evil-style music! Always a bonus in my book.)

I bought this game as soon as it was available on Early Access, and plugged away at it for 200 hours. I'm giving this game a positive review, but I must say I'm very disappointed by the full release of this game.
Graphics:
The game looks great. It's not perfect, but the graphics, fire and particle effects are very nicely done, the gore engine is amazing and the whole game is just big beautiful bloody mess. Environments look unique, none of the official maps look alike, none of the guns look like generic wastes (aside from some of the starting weapons, which is to be expected) and overall the game looks wonderful.
Sound:
The guns sound wonderful. Seriously, I love the sound the shotguns and explosives make. The only weapons I can't stand the sound of are the Medic Assault Rifle, and the melee swings for most weapons. I feel like the berserker's hammer swings just don't sound meaty enough. They don't have much oomph behind them, they're not particularly crisp or even that loud. I know I could turn the sound up, but doing so would make every other weapon shatter my ear drums.
The soundtrack isn't exactly my style of music, but it fits the game perfectly. The fact that I can turn lyrics on or off only makes it that much better.
The voice acting for this game is a lot better than it's predecessor. The fact that there's so many new and different voices now makes the game feel so much better to me. I love Mr. Foster, but I also love Skully. All of the female voices sound pretty decent as well.
The game sounds good, but I wouldn't say it's perfect. Some weapons seriously need some different sound files.
Gameplay:
There are a bunch of different classes, each of which do something better than others. Berserkers are tanks and can clear mobs of enemies without dropping hundreds of dollars in ammo. Commandos can lay down long ranged, accurate rapid fire support to soften up enemies. Supports can keep doors up and provide ammo to his allies, as well as heavy, close-ranged burst damage to his enemies. They all play really well, and they handle in a way that's unique.
Then there's the Survivalist special snowflake. This is one of the issues with the game a lot of people seem to have. When this game was fully released, all that was added from the Early Access version was an assault rifle for the demolitions class, and the survivalist class, who has almost no special abilities at all. He just uses the weapons from all the other classes. The fact that the update that released this class took so long after the previous update where they added maps rubs a lot of people the wrong way, myself included. Also, the idea that an Early Access game that didn't even have all of its maps done yet had developers spending time, money and effort creating weapon skins for microtransactions over finishing their game's levels was a less than promising concept to me.
I'd give this game a solid 8/10, especially when I consider the Steam Workshop support this game has. Just the other day a friend and I played a full recreation of Bikini Bottom where we murdered zombies in various copyright free Spongebob places
It's a great game. It's a lot of fun. I just wish the developers hadn't released it the way they had.

(Detailed)
This game may not the best game you will ever play, but it certainly lives up to its bill. Anyways, let's go over the good and the bad:
The Good!
The old school RPG they promise is real: This really does play like an RPG of old, and if you have been looking for a turn-based RPG, then this will be something you can get into. You have many different options of attack, from regular atttacks to techniques/Justice Skills to healing skills, using items, etc. The exp. in this game feels really in place, as (until you get to the Elite section) you never really have to worry about grinding too much as you generally stay around the level of your enemies. This is nice if you hate grinding in games. There is alchemy among other things to make yourself stronger, and there are a few battles you might be able to skip if you want to. The game flows smoothly as a turn based RPG with a good battle system that can get you hooked on the game. Also you can get a helicopter early in the game to just zoom yourself to the dungeon you want to go to, but you don't have to use it. Still its a nice perk to avoid mundane walking around. Your team is pretty balanced as well, although you must use the same 4 heroes. There is a general healer/buffer/magic user, two main dps, and a flex member which can heal/dot/damage/etc that is generally your most durable.
The Bad!
While the good generally outweighs the bad, (I know this part is bigger but most of these things are pasable for me anyways) there are quite a few bad things with the game. Besides a few bugs here and there (I auto-won a battle once without using a move, and lost battles during the elite fight when my team was still alive). There are some things which I can forgive since its an indie game, and some that might lure people away.
1.) This is probably my biggest gripe with the game, which is the story. Of course I did not finish completely, but if you are looking for an RPG with an immersive story that keep you coming back to find out what happens, this game is not for you. There is minimal character development, as well as just story in general. There is a story, as you are trying to cure the aggromites that are making everyone in the city hostile to others. But, that's mostly it. Bosses tell you they are sorry for the anger they had, and you get told of new missions to help find the cause of the aggromites... not much else... and no cinemas either, just text. The story is a bit more minimal than a GameShark Pokemon game. Do not expect anything like an Undertale or Kingdom Hearts in terms of story here!
2.) Can't see where you are on the map. Eventually you learn the map, and you might not care too much with a helicopter and if you want to explore anyways, but I do kind of wish there was a marker that let you know where you are on your map.
3.) Gear is bland. There is gear in tiers, and upgrades, but that's it. Gear is Chest T1, Chest T2, etc. They are all the same, as in there isn't gear centered toward healing, magic/physical damage, etc. Weapons can vary slightly, however your heroes will only have 1 or two options. There is no real rarity in gear or finding gear off bosses either, you buy all your gear at the shop. You might be able to find rings (which are REALLY powerful) in chests, along with other cool things, but enemies generally won't drop anything cool except a few bosses might drop alchemy recipies. (And potions, but that's not REALLY that cool to get off enemies).
4.) Graphics. This plays like an old school RPG. The graphics are pretty much that as well.  Of course, this is an indie game, so you shouldn't come in expecting amazing graphics, so I can let this one slide. They are not the WORST graphics you will see either.
5.) Equipping upgrades requires you to unequip the item, find it in your inventory, then putting them in, then reequipping the item. Not a big deal, as the game does tell you that, but it is a bit of a bother/ time waster.
All in all, the good outweighs the bad in this indie game. It is certainly not a perfect game by any means, but it does deliver what it promises.

The SNES Shadowrun was the jewel of my cartridge collection. I've honestly lost count of how many times I've played through it. With that in mind I started up my journey into Shadowrun Returns with a healthy dose of nostalgia and optimism, and at the end of the journey I came away happy, if not entirely satisfied.
Unlike the Shadowrun of yore, Returns plays like an odd crossing of point & click adventure and turn-based strategy. Your runner is investigating the death of an old friend, and in each scene spends most of their time navigating dense dialogues with the many NPCs on hand. You might also be tasked to click on an object or a door, but the vast majority of the non-combat gameplay is talking. It's good talking, though, with some very colorful characters and attentive writing. The parentheticals get a little too heady and poetic for my tastes, but they set the scenes well enough. Overall the game nails the Shadowrun setting, which goes a long way towards keeping me interested.
Combat is the other side of the coin, and while it works better than the ancient art of "stand in place and shoot forever", it's not without its flaws. Your crew and the enemy forces each take turns expending the action points of their members on a grid map with cover objects, much like in the recent XCOM. AP is spent a little oddly, however. Each move within a certain range costs one AP, whether it be a single step or a dash to the edge of their range. With melee weapons this is fine because the melee attack is included with the move, but ranged weapons cost at least one AP just to fire, so getting into an ideal position and firing can be a costly proposition. Doubly so when the sight lines around the environments are not terribly consistent, and it costs a full AP just to reload. It's an imperfect system that works well enough, but could definitely use more polish.
There are plenty of ways to kill people though, and enough skill points to earn through the game to make the most of them. You have melee, five different firearm types, drones, and two kinds of magic, and that's not even getting into the support skills. Unfortunately, there's not much reason to diversify, and the game even tells you as much. High ranks in skills are very powerful, and spreading your points around won't give you the ranks you need to pass skill checks or hit later enemies. Plus, you hire party members from a large roster of shadowrunners who can easily fill in the gaps for you.
These gripes are really part of a larger trend with Returns. You can buy weapons, armor, and other upgrades, but they are unevenly spaced throughout the game. There's not much to interact with in the many levels, and no real branching paths to explore. You can be a decker and get into the Matrix side battles, but they are few and far between. Your hired runners have no personality and can't be interacted with other than ordered around in battle. Even the story, built on some genuinely good writing, is small in scope and lacks any sort of proper build-up. It all points to a game not fully realized, a lot of potential without a lot of substance. The whole time I was playing, Returns felt more like a demo for the game engine than a full product.
That's not to say it wasn't fun. I thoroughly enjoyed the 8-10 hours it took to complete, and aside from a particularly annoying final mission, had no major complaints about it. The issue is more a lot of little shortcomings mounting to give Returns a very half-baked feel. It's definitely worth playing, and I'm very interested to follow it with Dragonfall, but I wouldn't fault anyone who checked out after a few hours. Shadowrun Returns is a good enough Shadowrun game, and now I want a better one.

I'm a Master rank player (highest rank ingame) with several hundred hours playtime on the mobileversion, but since the Rise of Bahamut patch I simply can't recommend Shadowverse anymore. I used to love this game, but with the Rise of Bahamut patch the competitive aspect of this game went down the gutter.
The game has become an RNG fest: extreme machtup based deck winrates up to 61,9+%, also winrates for the same deck that differ around 12,2+% based on whether you go first or second (Source:
- set filter to Master rank). More than that - an infestation of hyper-snowballing decks like daria and cancerous  insta-win cards like Seraph (draw Odin in time or lose the game) or Dimension Shift(: 1 player with 4-turns in a row "interactive and fun").


: Some new numbers arrived - we're seeing matchup based winrates up to 78,3% when going 2nd. (Source:
Aggro-Daria vs Swordcraft(class average!)).
As somebody who achieved the highest rank in Shadowverse I just can't recommand the game (post Rise of Bahamut) anymore. RNG might not be as obvious as in Hearthstone, but Rock-Paper-Scissor-matchmatcking determines a vast majority of games.
I used to love Shadowverse, but with skill becoming less and less of a factor, I - as well as other top rank players - are personally losing the fun in this game.
If you're not into competitive gaming feel free to try Shadowverse as your to-go casual cardgame, it has a lot of aspects that make it more interesting than Hearthstone. From a Master rank's persepective on competitive play I just can't recommend it anymore, though.
Also a warning: Avoid the Reddit Shadowverse community, it's EXTREMELY toxic and due to the average low ranks you are likely to get REALLY bad advice.

Dying Light is a brutally fun game in a fantastically detailed environment with really satisfying ways to wreck zombies, what more could you want? DL really is the next evolution of Dead Island with you playing as Kyle Crane, a mercenary working for the GRE, an organisation looking to help the citizens of Harran recover from the Zombie outbreak, or are they?
I found the DL storyline is decent with events, characters and twists you've probably seen in plenty of movies / games previously. Unfortunately the subquests let DL down somewhat with subquests generally being monotnous & dull. Fetch quests make up the majority of the subquests and I found myself laughing that there was a zombie apocolypse going on outside but someone at Tower HQ wants you to trek to a deserted island to pick some lavender plants to make Tower HQ smell prettier...come on now.
The game is beautiful on PC & Xbox One (haven't played it on PS4). There are some tech related issues with the PC version currently but Techland are on the case. Do yourself a favour before the endgame boss battle where you'll find yourself climbing a massive tower - when you've got up near the top, just stop and look around and take in just how beautiful Harran is, Techland has done a great job with a sprawling city in obvious despair. The sound quality throughout the game is also on point with the ambient sounds of Harran a real highlight.
The movement system is superb. The parkour elements really make the movement in the game a free flowing experience & I found things like drop kicking or shoulder charging a Zombie from the roof of a 6 floor block of flats just a hell of a lot of fun! Minor gripes were the grapple needs to be available earlier on so you can get your "Just Cause 2" grapple goodness going in combo with your parkour moves and the fast travel system needed to be expanded, too limited as it stands now.
The enemies are varied & fun to take out. Night-time Harran is a real highlight, not only because movement & kill XP is doubled, but a certain enemy type comes out to play and this particular zombie is a vicious customer if you let it discover you as it'll let other similar zombies know where you are and then the heart pounding chase is on.
If you're a DI vet, you'll notice a number of zombies back in different forms. Two enemies to look out for are the Infected, high speed Zombies who are attracted by EXPLOSIONS!?! and make sure you listen out if you swing and miss them as they haven't quite transitioned fully from human to zombie yet so they'll beg you not to hurt them. The other enemy to look out for later in the game is one that most games seem to steer clear of, with Dead Space being one that has done them before. It's a high pitched enemy that when I came across it for the first time, I was just like "what just happened?" Human enemies are also spread throughout Harran, they're generally good fighters in close quarters combat but their ability to block nearly 100% of throwing items you throw at them with their machete is pretty annoying. As the game progressed, I just found myself pulling out my Police Rifle and mowing human enemies down instead. You'll also find as you level your character up, you will become a zombie slaying god. Techland recently announced a "Hard mode" will be released in March for free which is something I'm looking forward to level the playing field a bit.
DL also offers co-op & multiplayer components but I only played single player so I won't cover off on either of those features in this review.
Overall Dying Light is a fun & enjoyable game which has a fantastic movement system and provides really satisfying ways to kill the zombie hordes which afflict Harran. I had some gripes with the game but they really are minor compared with the positives the game contains. If I were giving scores, DL would get an 8/10 from me & I'd recommend you pick it up. Enjoy!

In brief:  A modern classic of 4X gaming.
I'm not going to explain Civilization V.  If you do not know what the game is about, I suggest checking out any number of Lets Play videos out there.
Pros:  Massive number of variations on play, and the various Civ bonuses lend real depth to how you tackle long term strategy.
Cons:  The game only really came into it's own after multiple expansions.  If you are going to pick it up, go for everything at once.  Many times gameplay will devolve into hitting "End Turn" while you wait for something significant to happen, and there can be a flood of useless information late in game as you try and home in on your victory path.
Who would like it best:  Fans of multi-faceted strategy games, history buffs, people who prefer long term open ended games.
Who may not like it:  People who need a plot to frame a game from beginning to end, those who hate DLC, people who dislike turn-based gameplay.

Despite it's obscurity and lack of publicity, this is actually a really good quality game. It easily matches the quality of a lot of AAA first person brawlers, even though it was made by a relatively small team of devs. It's pseudo-open world, consisting of a collection of medium sized areas seperated by brief loading screens.
The brawling mechanics are impeccably designed and make for a smooth fighting experience that remains challenging up until the endgame. It's action packed, and you'll be frequently accosted by bizzarre looking bandits and other enemies who want to beat you up. The story is weird and unique, and the universe is original and nicely realized. There are some truly beautiful and surreal environments to run through that are a pleasure to look at.
The world is populated by strange and wonderful creatures, some you will have to fight, and some you will have to talk to and join forces with. It's never boring, and you'll keep playing just so you can see what happens next.
I recommend playing the original Zeno Clash (also an absolutely fantastic game) before playing Zeno Clash 2, as there are story elements in ZC2 that might not make much sense if you haven't played the first one.
If you like surrealism and weird action-packed worlds where nothing is what you expect, you'll love ZC1 and ZC2.

Risk of Rain is a 2D action-packed platformer which has the player - a survivor of the UES Contact Light - exploring a strange planet, fighting hordes of monsters and collecting a multitude of items in an attempt to ultimately escape and win the game. Although you may, to begin with, find surviving past the first level or two very hard, the controls are very easy to learn and most players should be able to get to grips with the mechanics quickly. A range of characters are available to unlock, each with their own unique play style and discinct feel; something I love is that none of them seem too powerful or too weak compared to the others, meaning that you won't only want to play with one character all the time. Many items can be found while playing to give you certain buffs and boosts, and as each one has the potential to completely alter your game, opening every chest is an exciting event. An online co-op mode is available for you to play with others, although I was disappointed that you can't simply host a game and let anyone join; a friend has to connect to your game with your own IP address. Another negative point is that the levels, while being very well-designed, are few in number, so you'll quickly memorise their layout; perhaps having randomly generated levels would have been more interesting. Overall, however, Risk of Rain is a great game with brilliant art and music throughout, and it's definitely worth the cost.

Antichamber is a great puzzle-based non-combat FPS game. It's a game that requires you to accept that while the world does not follow the rules you already know, there is always logic that can get you where you need to go.
Some of the puzzles involve your perspective or your movement, but most of them involve finding and using the matter gun.
The matter gun begins with the ability to pick up and put down small colored blocks, necessary to activate switches, prop doors open, and even build platforms. As you progress through the game, you will be able to upgrade the gun to manipulate the blocks in additionals ways, which in turn allow you to solve more advanced puzzles  on your way to the exit.
While the "essential" doors need to be completed in order with corresponding gun upgrades, the game is actually somewhat open in allowing you to explore and solve less-important puzzles and unlock new areas. Most of the puzzles are not required in order to reach the end, but many of them serve to teach you how the world works and how to use your gun (once you find it). Scattered throughout the entire game are over 100 posters to find. Some are hidden, some are out in the open. The posters feature a simple illustration and life lesson, which often ties to the puzzle at hand in some way. The posters add an optional collection factor for obsessive completionists.
There is no real danger to your character. You survive falls of any distance, but since much of your progress is upward, you may still be frustrated to find that you fell down to an area  you've already solved and may now have to waste time catching up.
The starting area functions as a hub room, keeping track of which posters you've found and providing a map of areas you've visited. You can always warp back to the hub room if you get stuck, and you can use the map to warp to an area you've seen, so it allows for quicker travel in the late game.
Out of all the games I've played this past year, Antichamber is one of my favorites. I'd recommend this for anybody who likes the puzzle solving aspect of Portal games, though it doesn't have the same atmosphere and snarky comedy.

Cyberlike, tatical strategy, turn-based rpg. A lot of great things about this game however, there are a lot of flaws as well.
The graphics are nice. The artwork is fantastic. The story is interesting. Shadowruns is a great series!
Not to mention, the game editor produced some amazing community content.
I especially love that it's compatible with my tablet pc. You don't need a keyboard to play.
As a result, I spent my long subway rides progressing with the story which was a great way to pass time.
However... this game is extremely linear.
There are dialogue choices, but most of the time.. They don't matter. Most, if not all, dialogues end the same.
Most importantly, the gameplay is extremely linear. There's not much exploration and the paths are clearly laid out for you. Adding to that, there are very very little side quests to actually do. There are just optional objectives that give you extra karma or help a little with the main quest.
A little bit about the combat:
Because it's turn-based, it takes a while for each battle. There's no way to speed up the process so battles often take longer than you'd expect. Adding on top of that, You can only save out of combat - Be prepared to finish or don't start it at all.
+ Interesting story
+ Can be fun, depending on your own preferences
+ Great time-passer
+ Amazing artwork
+ Great community content
- Linear gameplay & plot
- Linear dialogue
- Slow combat
Despite it all, Shadowrun Returns is a great place to introduce yourself and start the video game series. The sequels are a huge improvement as well. I recommend that you play it!

Me: So what do I do then, Antichamber?
AC: Restart the game!
Me: Wait, what? Oh, I can go back to any area I've gone to on the map. Hey, Antichamber, this map doesn't make any sense, nothing lines up.
AC: That's because they don't have to!
Me: Then it doesn't seem to be a map. Oh, at least the map shows me where I'm going if I look at it. Okay, I'll go back to pick up some more blocks- Wait, I don't have any so I can't go anywhere. Antichamber, where are all the blocks?
AC: You need to start from the right place so you have enough blocks!
Me: So why let me start here?
AC: Uhhhhh....I tricked you!
Me: Great.
--A short while later--
Me: It looks like I'm stuck again, Antichamber, I think I'll reset.
AC: Okay! Hey, look your timer ran out!
Me: Timer? What? Oh, you mean the thing that says 'Live life by your own watch' above it? Why put it there then?
AC: Because it's smart! It makes you smarter!
Me: Thanks, Antichamber, I figured that out a long time ago.
Ten minutes later I left my job working in a day care for 'indie' games.
Antichamber likes to think it's smart, and, at the beginning, it is, the puzzles are actually pretty clever. However, as the game continues, the fact that it likes to throw something completely unrelated to the previous puzzles at you while smugly preaching at you via meaningless and pretentious 'life lessons' on signs, it starts to grate, and badly. Antichamber doesn't have any ground rules, it can throw whatever it wants at you, and rather than being interesting, it just becomes annoying because of just how badly the game conveys progression; every puzzle starts the same and they eventually merge into a seamless blob of white hallways where none of the choices you make affect your environment. As I illustrated above, it is the game equivalent of arguing with a small child, one who thinks he's smarter than you. Games are supposed to have rules, of what you can and cannot do, and what the game can and cannot do. Antichamber, on the other hand, can do whatever it wants, while your rules stay the same. In a debate, this is known as 'moving the goalposts' and it is an extremely cheap method of getting your opponent to keep arguing, and in a game it is a cheap and annoying tactic of trying to keep the game feeling fresh.
This is not a game intended for people who liked Portal. Portal had rules of what both you and the game can and cannot do with portals, while Antichamber does whatever it wants and laughts because you were foolish enough to assume that it would follow some kind of 'thread.'

Decent XCOM-style tactical RPG romp. I had fun with it.
The good:
The fluff is real nice. If you're a fan of the tabletop game, you'll appreciate all the little touches Harebrained has put into this game. Even if you aren't, they really nail oppressive, foreboding cyberpunk atmosphere. Genre purists may be put off by the lolD&D fantasy elements, but the game does a good job of blending the two without making it too jarring of an Axe-Coppy mishmash.
Lots of good Workshop support means that you're not going to run out of content any time soon, either. Once I figure out how to get the editor to run on Linux I think I'll try my hand at making some UGC, too.
The bad:
The graphics leave a bit to be desired -- the art is good and the textures and models are too, but there is a lot fo cut-and-paste when it comes to the animations. A lot of attack spells are literally recolored fireballs or lightning bolts. Likewise, the voice acting is so bare-bones it might as well not even be there.
The ugly:
The game's biggest failing has definitely got to be the character building. The game is class-less and level-less, but it still encourages you to specialize to an uncomfortable degree. On top of that, some builds, like Decker, are so specialized that unless the campaign you're playing is specifically designed to acommodate them, you're seriously gimped. If you spend your EXP wrong you can end up pretty screwed down the line, and there is no way to go back and redistribute. Do yourself a favor and don't overwrite saves. I had to swallow my pride and dial down the difficulty setting to get past a mission right at the end of the first arc in the main campaign, "Dead Man's Switch".
Your call on this one, folks.

There are quite a lot of butthurt, original X-Com fanbois slamming this game and giving it terrible reviews, which is utterly ridiculous. It’s like bashing a modern platformer b/c it doesn’t force you to get through 100 levels on 3 lives. XC: EU isn’t perfect but it’s still a lot of fun and doesn’t deserve to be trashed.
It may not be as complex as the original game but it is still very tactical and turn-based, despite many claims here to the contrary. Not sure how some reviewers can compare this to Call of Duty or Mass Effect. Idiotic. There are still difficult decisions to make, as in do you dig open another level of your base, buy another plane, buy another satellite, or research better weapons? Should you investigate that UFO you just shot down or wait b/c your medic & sniper are still recovering from wounds and you’d have to take too many rookies into battle? If you don’t plan & pay attention to what you’re doing, you will have to start all over. You also end up getting attached to your squad members even though they never speak and it’s hard to resist the urge to reload when they die (or when you get faced with a very inconvenient random event between missions one game hour before finishing research on that new armor).
Some here are even complaining about the “cutscenes” during missions which are actually cinematic visuals of your characters doing what you tell them to do. Sorry, I never got tired of the camera zooming in on one of my guys rounding a corner & shotgunning a baddie at point blank range, or my sniper coolly raising up his rifle & blasting another before they could attack a vulnerable squad mate in the next turn. These are a very cool touch.
Where I will knock the game is that battles do feel a bit skewed in the AI’s favor. Whenever you stumble upon the enemy, they always see you and essentially get a free movement turn to shuffle around. So if the last guy you move in a turn happens to be the one the aliens see, they immediately get a free move and then will move right away again since their movement turn just started, which most likely means they will swarm whichever squad member is closest. This makes most levels take a long time unless you reload after finding out where the baddies are, as you don’t want to move around the map too quickly.
And the battles do end up becoming a bit tiresome by the time you reach the end of the game. No way around that after sinking hours & hours into the game.
Overall, though, it’s an excellent game. Regardless of whether or not the original X-Com is better, XC: EU stands on its own as a great experience.

I bought this game as soon as it was available on Early Access, and plugged away at it for 200 hours. I'm giving this game a positive review, but I must say I'm very disappointed by the full release of this game.
Graphics:
The game looks great. It's not perfect, but the graphics, fire and particle effects are very nicely done, the gore engine is amazing and the whole game is just big beautiful bloody mess. Environments look unique, none of the official maps look alike, none of the guns look like generic wastes (aside from some of the starting weapons, which is to be expected) and overall the game looks wonderful.
Sound:
The guns sound wonderful. Seriously, I love the sound the shotguns and explosives make. The only weapons I can't stand the sound of are the Medic Assault Rifle, and the melee swings for most weapons. I feel like the berserker's hammer swings just don't sound meaty enough. They don't have much oomph behind them, they're not particularly crisp or even that loud. I know I could turn the sound up, but doing so would make every other weapon shatter my ear drums.
The soundtrack isn't exactly my style of music, but it fits the game perfectly. The fact that I can turn lyrics on or off only makes it that much better.
The voice acting for this game is a lot better than it's predecessor. The fact that there's so many new and different voices now makes the game feel so much better to me. I love Mr. Foster, but I also love Skully. All of the female voices sound pretty decent as well.
The game sounds good, but I wouldn't say it's perfect. Some weapons seriously need some different sound files.
Gameplay:
There are a bunch of different classes, each of which do something better than others. Berserkers are tanks and can clear mobs of enemies without dropping hundreds of dollars in ammo. Commandos can lay down long ranged, accurate rapid fire support to soften up enemies. Supports can keep doors up and provide ammo to his allies, as well as heavy, close-ranged burst damage to his enemies. They all play really well, and they handle in a way that's unique.
Then there's the Survivalist special snowflake. This is one of the issues with the game a lot of people seem to have. When this game was fully released, all that was added from the Early Access version was an assault rifle for the demolitions class, and the survivalist class, who has almost no special abilities at all. He just uses the weapons from all the other classes. The fact that the update that released this class took so long after the previous update where they added maps rubs a lot of people the wrong way, myself included. Also, the idea that an Early Access game that didn't even have all of its maps done yet had developers spending time, money and effort creating weapon skins for microtransactions over finishing their game's levels was a less than promising concept to me.
I'd give this game a solid 8/10, especially when I consider the Steam Workshop support this game has. Just the other day a friend and I played a full recreation of Bikini Bottom where we murdered zombies in various copyright free Spongebob places
It's a great game. It's a lot of fun. I just wish the developers hadn't released it the way they had.

While it's fun and all when you're the one accomplishing it, it feels really uninteractive when you're on the recieving end. Still, the devs are really generous with free packs. Does it make up for the repetitive and uninteractive gameplay? YMMV.
If you know Hearthstone, the digital collectible card game by Blizzard, then it's simple : while being fundamentally a japanese copy of Hearthstone, Shadowverse improves the formula in many quite important ways : more complex, less reliant on RNG, more generous in F2P content, and less greedy for the paid-content. However, in the competitive end of the game, you'll run into the same "problems" with a specific metagame and over-represented decks that tend towards short "aggro" games (but less aggravating than in Hearthstone).
If you don't, then let me elaborate a little : Shadowverse is a digital Collectible Card Game. CCG are a peculiar kind of games. They not only function as games, with rules, goals, a winner and a looser, but also as collection, where the goal is to "collect them all". As such, before considering investing time, and maybe money, into said game, you should be perfectly aware of one thing : collectible games are expensive. They're designed to make you pay to complete a collection, and what you pay is the feeling to make progress in that collection.
Not that it's impossible to play as a F2P! In fact, Shadowverse, in comparison to other CGG, is quite generous with its free content, and you can reasonnably expect to open roughly three free packs every two days. In comparison, Hearthstone is more like three packs in four days.
Imo, the best way to handle this kind of game is to manage your expectations : what is your goal?
- complete the collection? This game is kinda cheap for the collection aspect, investing roughly 90 dollars every three months should be enough to get one exemplary of each card (and yes, this is cheap...for this kind of game)
- be competitive? Because you get quite a lot of free stuff, you can reasonably make a free competitive deck by destroying all your useless cards and crafting the ones you will use.
- have fun by making weird decks? Shadowverse offer a "random" mode with rewards, Take two, which is quite cool and balanced.
Just note that doing everything at once will be really difficult.
That being said, Shadowverse is probably your best bet, because of how beginner-friendly it is. Good luck!

Parkour is fantastically difficult to translate to a video game. Regardless of how streamlined the controls are, a majority of users will probably experience some frustration after failing to grab onto a ledge (which leads to death) or missing a ladder (which leads to death). Even though I felt like Mirror's Edge did a much better job of porting parkour techniques to the video game world, I also recognize that ME was significantly more linear than Dying Light. I had a pretty low standard going into this having just finished Far Cry 4 (press space here...no wait, back up two steps, press space he--...nevermind, you went too far, move forward). Having said that, though, the free running aspect of this game was pretty good. I wouldn't call it spectacular, but I wouldn't call it mediocre either.
While I enjoyed DL's melee combat, I do take issue with how they introduced guns. It seems like you go from finding one or two guns with very limited ammunition to receiving supply drops from the NRA. The abrupt change from almost exclusively melee combat to having more guns than Lil Wayne's entourage felt like a way to rush through the latter third of the story. I still used my tried-and-true melee weapons when I could, but guns added a large amount of imbalance to an otherwise polished system. Had they introduced them more slowly and limited the amount of ammo available at shops, it might have not felt so forced.
By the way, I hated the music. The soundtrack was, for all intents and purposes, terrible. It felt like the composer was having an identity crisis: post-apocalyptic zombie world meets Snake Plisken and every bad 80's action movie soundtrack ever. It would have been one thing if the game's atmosphere didn't just share a few commonalities with Escape from LA (protagonist thrown into destitute situation to recover documents, only to realize they expose a deep-rooted conspiracy by the people who sent him), but I never got the feeling from the game that's what it was trying to accomplish. The soundtrack just didn't belong.
Irrespective of all these issues, I found the game enjoyable.
