Tokyo Warfare is the spiritual successor to the 1996 arcade tank shooter called Tokyo Wars (I have never played Tokyo Wars btw). The objective of the game is to eliminate your opponent a certain amount of times to claim victory. You have the option to play as the Japan Defense Forces or the Red Star.
The gameplay is fast and the tanks move well for the most part. You have the option to fire either armor piercing rounds, explosive rounds, or a machine gun. During gameplay, you have two health bars: turret armor and chassis armor. Getting either one of these damaged can cause some negative side effects such as your tank having a slower fire rate because the barrel is damaged or even having your tank completely immobilized because the tracks are completely ruined.
As of now the game has only three maps: Arena, Naniwa-Ku, and Oi Terminal. Arena seems to be a map that tests how well each player can maneuver since there is virtually no cover, Naniwa-Ku seems to be a map based on close quarter battles with its small streets and super tight alley ways, and Oi Terminal seems to be a mix of close and long range battles with the main area being a container yard with lots of cover to go by as well as corners to turn.
Well after mentioning all of this, I think it is safe to address the many faults of Tokyo Warfare.
First of all, Tokyo Warfare has no kind of in game tutorial. This could lead some players to be completely confused as to how to play the game or even how the game works overall. You are able to download the manual for the game but that makes me wonder why they couldn't just add the manual in game.
One issue I have with the gameplay is the constant bobbing when moving your tank. This makes aiming and shooting a lot harder than it needs to be. The camera bob even gets in the way when you are moving. I am not sure if this was to replicate how being in a tank feels like but this just comes off as very annoying.
Another issue with the gameplay that I have revolves around the two ammo types which are the armor piercing rounds and the explosive rounds. The two ammo types seem to function extremely similar to one another as they seem to eliminate the target in about the same amount of rounds fired. The only difference I was able to spot was that explosive rounds have some splash damage to them.
My next issue comes from the map pool. Now I know that the Tokyo Warfare team is small but would it have hurt to have at least another map or two? I don't know maybe this is just me being a bit picky.
While I am on the topic of maps, one of the more annoying problems I have with the game comes from the map design. On both Naniwa-Ku and Oi Terminal, It is very easy to get stuck on things such as a little piece of the wall poking out or even by something completely unknown. This can become aggravating as this can allow an enemy player to acquire a cheap shot on you just because you are unable to move due to being stuck on something you should not be on.
Tokyo Warfare was a game I was really looking forward to. I was amused at the idea of a fast paced tank shooter. Sadly, the current issues with the game prevent me from enjoying the game as much as I would like to. On the plus side the devs are active on the forums and are willing to take feedback to improve the game. My review may change in the future but as of now, I have to sadly rate this game down. I believe this game has a lot of potential and I am hoping that the devs make the necessary changes so that Tokyo Warfare can become a better game.

*Btw if the devs are reading this, in the about this game section under the "moar" section, vehicle is spelled as vehycle.

If you liked the first game, you'll absolutely LOVE this one. And if you disliked the first, this one is vastly improved!
+The combat has been improved, with a many different combos added into the game. A new fighting style where each mouse click controls each hand rather than light attack and heavy attack independent to each mouse click. A fighting style mixed with an RPG, how quaint!
+A skill system! You can level up strength to hit harder, stamina to fight longer, health to be tankier, and leadership to command stronger allies!
+Allies! You can collect allies throughout the game that will assist you in fights. Definitely helpful if you plan on playing singleplayer rather than coop.
+The game provides an easy to access tutorial that will give you a refresher on any newly added combos should you need it.
+The story expands very much upon the previous game, answering many questions left from the first game while also creating a very entertaining original story for this game.
+The graphics are vastly improved as the game moved from the source engine to the Unreal engine for this game.
+The world remains one of the most imaginative worlds i have ever seen, and with the lore expanded upon in this game I cannot help but drool at the idea of another sequel. MORE ZENO CLASH MORE!
+The iconic great voice actors return from the first game, with new ones that are just as great at fitting their roles!
+The characters you love and hate return and more are added, each of them with their own background and interactions to be discovered. Deadra's still my favorite!
+CO-OP! YESSSSS! Now i can enjoy Zenozoik with a friend! He plays as Rimat though, and the first Zeno clash taught me to hate Rimat. But seriously, the co-op rules. Makes those 1v8 fights so much more bearable.
+This game was much longer than its predecessor. It took me 6.6 hours in coop wheras its predecessor took me 3 hours. And whereas the previous game held one challenge mode where you ascended a tower or descended a pit, fighting all enemies you see, this game provides three challenge modes.
#1. The Colosseum. A Singleplayer/Coop mode where you challenge your opponents.
#2. Rock of the Ages. A silly mode where you play as a rock that runs everyone over while also recruiting an army of allies from the game. All the characters! This mode is so fun I could play it endlessly, it was even expanded on and turned into it's own game!
#3. The framerate challenge. You fight binary opponents in an attempt to keep your framerate above 25fps at all times. It's quite strange, but provides quite the interesting challenge.
This game was ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic, and I really hope a 3rd one is in the works. I give this a 10/10. This is one of the most memorable games I've ever played and one I will revisit ten years from now simply to relive this classic. It's a rare day I give a game 10/10, but this one earned it. It's not revolutionary or particularly innovative, and you're pretty much always aware it's a "budget" title for the series, but Resident Evil Revelations 2 is a rock-solid addition to the franchise, and I hope that RE7's seemingly drastic new direction doesn't mean we'll never see something like this again.
The main campaign is relatively long if you take your time to explore every area. It's kind of a mixture of classic and modern RE gameplay - it isn't exactly terrifying and it's still action-horror (you probably won't find yourself running out of ammo too often), but a lot of the tension and dark, grimy environments bring back a bit of that old school feel. It's definitely a little more reserved than Resident Evil 6.
You'll be switching between two fairly separate storylines, and each of them has two playable characters. This includes Barry Burton, who makes his first canonical appearance since the very first game, and is arguably one of the best protagonists the series has had recently, as he manages to be a "badass" while still actually feeling like a human being instead of some kind of completely invincible action hero.
There's a decent amount of variety between the various playstyles - you'll generally have one character that's useful for scavenging for ammo and hidden items, and another that handles the weapons and the rest of the dirty work. This, plus the fact that you can switch between two characters on the fly, means that unlike RE5 and 6, it's actually a completely valid option to play this on your own instead of co-op, although the (offline) option for that is also there.
The campaign would be enough for me to recommend RER2, but the action-focused Raid Mode ensures that it can potentially provide hours upon hours of content - and a surprisingly hefty amount of it is available even if you just buy the first episode. Practically another game in and of itself, it's somewhat addictive and has online co-op to boot.
Nobody plays Resident Evil for its highly intellectual storytelling, but - probably at least partly due to its episodic nature - there's even an attempt to come up with a fairly interesting plot here. Coming from someone who rarely even takes notice of story in video games, I think this is the only time I've found myself being somewhat invested in the story of a Resident Evil game. It doesn't really resolve itself in the best possible way when everything's said and done (there's also a good ending and a bad one, depending on a choice you make in Episode 3), but for my money it's still more compelling than most of the plotlines from the rest of the series.
Oh, and feel free to install the film grain removal mod... the game can be a bit of an eyesore without it.

Zeno Clash 2 improves upon its predecessor with longer punch combinations, new combat options, upgradable skills, and the ability to take or leave allies. These improvements complicate however, making intuitive systems less natural but more robust. It's a double-edged sword, and some of the original's charm is lost along the way, but that dichotomy mirrors the central conflict of the game. Just as the instinctive freedom of Zenozoik is supplanted by the growing complexity of its society, so too is the charm of an organic experience supplanted by the deepening of its systems. As unavoidable and regrettable as that may be, it doesn't hold the game back at all. The sequel continues the story of this bizarre world to a deeper and more satisfying conclusion than the previous game. If you found yourself somewhat let down by the ending of Zeno Clash, don't let that hold you back from playing the sequel. You might find yourself judging the original differently after they're both finished, as I did.

Risk of Rain is a 2D action-packed platformer which has the player - a survivor of the UES Contact Light - exploring a strange planet, fighting hordes of monsters and collecting a multitude of items in an attempt to ultimately escape and win the game. Although you may, to begin with, find surviving past the first level or two very hard, the controls are very easy to learn and most players should be able to get to grips with the mechanics quickly. A range of characters are available to unlock, each with their own unique play style and discinct feel; something I love is that none of them seem too powerful or too weak compared to the others, meaning that you won't only want to play with one character all the time. Many items can be found while playing to give you certain buffs and boosts, and as each one has the potential to completely alter your game, opening every chest is an exciting event. An online co-op mode is available for you to play with others, although I was disappointed that you can't simply host a game and let anyone join; a friend has to connect to your game with your own IP address. Another negative point is that the levels, while being very well-designed, are few in number, so you'll quickly memorise their layout; perhaps having randomly generated levels would have been more interesting. Overall, however, Risk of Rain is a great game with brilliant art and music throughout, and it's definitely worth the cost.

Allow me to present my opinion of this game in the form of an argument with a five-year-old:
Me: Okay, so, hi, Antichamber, what do you have for me today?
Antichamber: Puzzles!
Me: Nice, that's what I was looking for. So what's this first one?
AC: Staircases!
Me: Okay, I see that. Let's see what happens if I go up this staircase...Surprise, I'm back where I started, interesting. It looks like the same thing happens if I go down. So what do I do now, Antichamber?
AC: Look! I made a sign for you! It has stick figures on it!
Me: Thanks, that should help, then. Let's see, "The choice doesn't matter if the outcome is the same?" Thanks, Antichamber, that's pretty obvious already.
AC: Hahahaha! I tricked you.
Me: Great, well, I'm going backwards, aaaand, hey I'm somewhere else.
AC: I knew you were going to do that!
Me: So I gathered. How clever of you.
--A couple of minutes later--
Me: Hey, it looks like this is a dead end. Antichamber, what am I- Whoa, the floor disappeared on me. That would be a surprise if you hadn't done that in the previous room.
AC: Hahahaha! I tricked you! I'm so smart.
Me: Well, since I'm down here, I might as well read this sign. Let's see, 'Life has a way of pushing us in the right direction?' Fascinating. Did you come up with that all by yourself?
AC: Yesss! I'm so smart!
Me: Cute.
--Later still--
AC: I got you a little gun thingy that shoots blocks where you want them!
Me: Ooooh, a new mechanic, nice. Let's try this out.
AC: See, you can use it to close switches and hold doors open!
Me: That would make sense. Okay, so I guess I go through these beams to open these doors? Okay, seems pretty strightforward. What do I need to do in this next room? It looks like there are ten switches I need to close here.
AC: Ha! You don't have enough blocks! You need to go back and get more. See! I tricked you!
Me: And the door closed behind me so I can't go back.
AC: Haha, you're stuck in here!
Me: So what do I do then, Antichamber?
AC: Restart the game!
Me: Wait, what? Oh, I can go back to any area I've gone to on the map. Hey, Antichamber, this map doesn't make any sense, nothing lines up.
AC: That's because they don't have to!
Me: Then it doesn't seem to be a map. Oh, at least the map shows me where I'm going if I look at it. Okay, I'll go back to pick up some more blocks- Wait, I don't have any so I can't go anywhere. Antichamber, where are all the blocks?
AC: You need to start from the right place so you have enough blocks!
Me: So why let me start here?
AC: Uhhhhh....I tricked you!
Me: Great.
--A short while later--
Me: It looks like I'm stuck again, Antichamber, I think I'll reset.
AC: Okay! Hey, look your timer ran out!
Me: Timer? What? Oh, you mean the thing that says 'Live life by your own watch' above it? Why put it there then?
AC: Because it's smart! It makes you smarter!
Me: Thanks, Antichamber, I figured that out a long time ago.
Ten minutes later I left my job working in a day care for 'indie' games.
Antichamber likes to think it's smart, and, at the beginning, it is, the puzzles are actually pretty clever. However, as the game continues, the fact that it likes to throw something completely unrelated to the previous puzzles at you while smugly preaching at you via meaningless and pretentious 'life lessons' on signs, it starts to grate, and badly. Antichamber doesn't have any ground rules, it can throw whatever it wants at you, and rather than being interesting, it just becomes annoying because of just how badly the game conveys progression; every puzzle starts the same and they eventually merge into a seamless blob of white hallways where none of the choices you make affect your environment. As I illustrated above, it is the game equivalent of arguing with a small child, one who thinks he's smarter than you. Games are supposed to have rules, of what you can and cannot do, and what the game can and cannot do. Antichamber, on the other hand, can do whatever it wants, while your rules stay the same. In a debate, this is known as 'moving the goalposts' and it is an extremely cheap method of getting your opponent to keep arguing, and in a game it is a cheap and annoying tactic of trying to keep the game feeling fresh.
This is not a game intended for people who liked Portal. Portal had rules of what both you and the game can and cannot do with portals, while Antichamber does whatever it wants and laughts because you were foolish enough to assume that it would follow some kind of 'thread.'

First, let me preface this review by saying that Zeno Clash is just about the best thing ever. I was going to write a rave review about it, but I foolishly decided to play Zeno Clash 2 first. The problems start with the tutorial/prelude. I might not have played the tutorial if it hadn't also been labelled prelude. As it was, punching Metamoq in the face with some voiceover recap of the plot of the previous Zeno Clash in the background sounded like just the thing, which should indicate how good the first Zeno Clash was. The first thing I noticed was the lack of filters. The first Zeno Clash had a hazy effect, which made distant objects blur and added to the atmosphere, and which I assumed was an attribute of Zenozoik. Not so, apparently, since that effect is gone in this game. Instead there is music added to the voiceover. Music was used sparingly in the first Zeno Clash, so the overall effect was that of excessive melodrama. Oh well, if a bit overdone, the plot is still awesome, and punching Metamoq in the face till it's over should be simple, right? After all, I defeated the last game, and know how this goes.
...
Not so much. It turns out that there's combos and stuff now. The 'lock on' key has been switched, which is a minor annoyance, but more annoying is that it's a bit difficult to connect with some of the attacks. I find out that the tutorial is glitched when I manage to check a box without fulfilling the requirements, and just stand there for a while, since the game won't move forward until I satisfy the /actual/ requirements. It's here that I start to worry that the game might be overcome by feature creep.
A worry which is not abated when I find that, despite beating the previous game, I am unable to do the '5-part launch combo' required in the tutorial, even more ironic since it comes after Metamoq's quote: "If you are satisfied and do what you feel you must do, no matter what that is, then you have reached perfection." Apprehensive, I finally quit from the endless nightmare of facing a downcast Metamoq and start the real game, hopeful that the tutorial was an ill-conceived quick add-on.
But of course, the problems continue into the real game. The combat system is now so complex that I have no idea what I'm doing in the first fight, and the AI manages to trip over itself without any clever guidance from me. In the first game, if you plan it right, you can have heavy enemies smash through lighter ones to get to you, or have lighter ones glare at you, unable to attack through the enemy interposed between you. You can even attack enemies from behind if they're distracted by picking up weapons, something which I had to exploit to defeat one scene.
But the AI in the first game is actually pretty good. It hides from your shooting range when it thinks it can, and does stuff like sneak up behind you. I didn't see any of that here.
What I did see wasn't much better. Somehow, combat looks jittery, and the lighting isn't the same. I saw a new creature design, with even more nudity, and knocked it out before stumbling across a most egregious example of feature creep. Remember how the 'lock on' key was remapped? It's now the key for 'exit area'.
To understand how terrible this is, you have to understand how the first Zeno Clash worked. You would sometimes walk places without fighting, and sometimes you would fight. Another example of Metamoq's wisdom.
Oh well, I exit, and the story goes on... and on. One of the great strengths of the first Zeno Clash was how much it did with very little dialogue. This is not the case here, where it takes three sentences for your sister to tell you that you're helping her break Father-Mother out of jail.
And then... nothing. Oh wait, a tower that says 'Level Up!'. Feature creep indeed! Let's go there, then get stuck before realizing that we have no skill points yet, pull out a map, which utterly butchers the charming minimalism of the one in the first Zeno Clash, then forget how to put it away, leaving us stuck, until we remember it was 'M', and run around aimlessly, and... we can talk to a person? Wait a sec, did we just get a quest?
When did this become an RPG, anyway?
Not the first Zeno Clash, not a good RPG. (-10)/10

Mirrors Edge is a game set in the dystopian future, where the people are under constant surveillance. You are a runner, a courier of sorts, who delivers written messages that are not supposed to be seen by the government.
The games has several interesting mechanics, the best ones focusing on simulating parkour. Faith, the protagonist, has a range of moves that allow her to move through the city landscape with great speed. This includes all sorts of jumps and vaults, wallruns, sliding under obstacles, climbing ledges, pipes and ladders, swinging and jumping from horizontal bars. The camera reflects the movement of the character - it bobs a bit when she runs, it follows  and spins with her as she tumbles. The characters hands and feet are also visible at all times. All this combined with a complete lack of user interface (with the exception of a small dot at the center of the screen that prevents simulation sickness) allows for great immersion and a unique experience.
The game features some combat mechanics, including punches, jump- and slidekicks, disarming opponents, but in my humble opinion, there are games that do this better, and its not the strongest point of the game.
The game employs these mechanics to provide various challenges and sources of fun to the player.
The great camera movement and parkour moves are used in some levels to provide a great speed-running experience, where the player focuses on the fluent and graceful run through the map at top speeds. This type of gameplay is reinforced with a mechanic called the runner vision, that highlights important objects that you can use in your run to maintain or even gain momentum. Its all about the mastery of the available mechanics and entering the Flow. This kind of fun can be found mostly in the early levels of the game, which is a shame in my humble opinion. Luckily, the game features a time trial mode, where the player can focus beating the levels in the fastest, most gracefull way.
The jumping has another use - in the later levels its used to build some sort of a spatial puzzle. The player knows where he has to go, because pressing alt makes the character face the destination. He just needs to find a way to get there. There is little left of the fast pace of the first chapters of the game. The player progresses slowly, looking around and trying to find the ledge, pipe, or wall he has to use.
The game also encourages a bit of exploration. On the maps there are some spraypainted symbols, indicating that there is a bonus hidden nearby. This works well with the later, puzzle-like chapters of the game, but not really so in the parkour-like ones. In the rush, when the player focuses on where to go next, to stay in the flow, its hard to spot those little red marks. Also, getting to them usually means taking a sub-optimal route, so that another contradiction in using these two mechanics together.
The game features combat, as was mentioned earlier, and its supposed to be a challenge for the player - its the only thing affected by the difficulty settings. The problem is, its not very challenging, at least at medium difficulty. (Hard is unlocked by completing the story). All I had to do to finish the story was jump/slide kick + pummeling the stunned oponent till he drops. For locations with multiple enemies, I had to lure out a single foe before unleashing my combo. I didnt find it challenging and not really interesting enough to try the game at hard difficulty. The "bossfights" of the games are mostly reduced to hitting the disarm button at the appropriate moment.
The combat is a weak addition to the game. It does not fit thematically - the runners arent thugs, and beating up or even shooting police officers feels a bit off. It wouldnt be so bad, if pummeling an officer was a last resort option for a player who couldnt outrun him - I've beat 3/4 of the game withut knocking out anybody, just running past them in tricky ways - but sadly there are levels where the player is outright forced to fight. It may be an elevator or a pipe thats very slow to climb, but some levels feature sort of a bottleneck that you just cant beat without being gunned down if the police officers arent unconciouss or dead. It gets even worse when you decide to pick up a gun - the game turns into a bad shooter. Faith loses her mobility, and the game reduces to "shoot one guy and then take his weapon to shoot another one".
All this makes me feel like the game focus drifts off while the player is getting near to the end. The start is very dynamic, the adrenaline is pumping, the player has various paths to choose from, and its up to him to decide which one is faster. With the games progession, a lot of this is lost, the game slows down with all the combat and puzzles. Of course, once you solve the puzzlle that the late levels are, you can try to complete it as fast as possible, but your choice of path is severely limited, and the challenge is all about flawless execution - not as interesting as the frst levels are. Perhaps it would be better for the game if the puzzle levels and speed-run levels altered throughout the whole story, providing a rollercoaster of thought and adrenaline, cutting out combat alltogether.Dont get me wrong - the engame isnt all puzzles and fighting, it just leaves an overall feeling of their dominance.
In my opinion, the game should use the fantastic immersion, movement freedom and speed as its focal point - those are the truly fresh elements that drew me to this game. The others we allready had, and sometimes even better. We had an excellent series of Prince of Persia games that started with the Sands of Time that gave us all the acrobatic platforming 3D puzzles we ever wanted. As for the fighting, its really nothing new either - just check out some old titles, O.N.I was published in 2001 and had better shooting/hand to hand combat! But a first person, challenging and captivating, immersive parkour experience? That one is fresh, that one is new, thats the thing I wanted to see more of!
There are two more elements of the game that I would like to mention: visuals and storyline.
Lets start with the visuals - the game is georgeus! Im not talking about the graphics technicalities, shaders, polygons and textures - Im talking about overall aesthetics and art style. The game is beautiful, the neat, clean and bright world of the future is a welcome change from the dirty, dark and mostly brown depictions that are so fashionable nowdays. The game is pleasing to the eye, the usage of well saturated colours is great - simply put, top scores for the visuals.
Sadly, the story is lacking. The setting was perfect for an inspiring story about fighting for what you believe is right, choosing the means you are willing to use in such a fight, about sacrificing yourself for others, about the true meaning of freedom and safety, the horrors of the world where everyone is under constant surveilance. Given the dystpian world, Faith's personal story and the strong start of the game, the base of a great story was there. The game does not tell that great story. It tells a weak story with no meaning instead. Not everyone sees games as an art form, but I think they can be a great new medium for delivering narrative and making people think - because in a written story or a movie, the consumer just observes. In games - he acts. Its a pity that such a great topic was wasted and a wonderful story was left untold.
All in all, it looks like my review feels a bit negative - but its not! I did mention all the flaws I found in the game, but they cannot eclipse the novelty and freshness of the title. The running gameplay is great, both challenging and rewarding, the aesthetics are wonderful, the experience unique. I think you shuld try this game - despite its flaws, you wont regret it!

EU is a great game on its own, with strong ties to the origins of the series in its gameplay and music. Tactical challenges abound as the conflict keeps escalating and more and more curve balls are thrown your way, and the balancing act of managing research, resources, and an increasingly impatient world council that is the metagame means even between missions you rarely get a breather. EW adds a ton of content worth the price, with two new upgrade trees for you highly customizable squads, a ton of new research byproducts that give you plenty of tactical options to experiment with, new maps, and two new enemy types to make sure you don't get too comfortable with your new toys. Play on the higher difficulties on Iron Man if you want to stretch your strategic skills to their limit, or stick to Normal if you want to just see the game through. Even then, don't expect it to get too easy. Good replay value, and rewarding challenges. A very strong GOTY candidate for me.

Gotta give this one a down vote.  It's close but there are just too many frustrating parts to this game.  If you enjoyed the other Arkham games, the game is on sale, and you really want to see what happened after Arkham City then go for it.  Just be prepared for a few rage quits.
The trick racing games... UGH!!!  Fighting tanks and racing around after crooks is OK but the trick races are just exercises in frustration.  Most are confined to dealing with the Riddler but I like the Riddler's other puzzles so the only way to see them is to go through the rage-quit-inducing races.
Checkpoint saves only.  LET ME PICK WHEN TO SAVE!!  At least this one isn’t as bad as Arkham Origins – this time they were smart enough to keep backup saves for you so, if something gets corrupted, you’ve got a backup you can go to instead of having to start the whole game over again.
Pointless upgrades.  They added a lot of new upgrades you can spend points on but many of them seem useless.  For instance, you can get an upgrade to throw your batarang at some enemies as you drop down on one.  That’s nice.  And then there’s another to shoot your grapple as you drop down on an enemy.  And another to shoot your electric zapper as you drop down on an enemy.  Why!?
The story.  Everything is Batman’s fault!  The bad guys blame Batman.  Gordon blames Batman.  Robin blames Batman.  Most of all, Batman blames Batman.  Hello?  Don’t you think that just maybe Scarecrow deserves the lion’s share of that blame?  What’s more, there were some big plot twists I didn’t like much.
The procedural combat system is still big fun… mostly.  It gets pretty hard to target properly with the masses of people you fight plus Batman sometimes just decides to go off and whack some completely different thug from time to time.  But it’s such a joy to watch!
It’s got a pretty complex combat system.  The key combinations are actually starting to get a little bit like a fighting game!  Once you get deeper into the game, you’ll find you really need to think about how you’ll be attacking some enemy strong points, too.
Good Riddler puzzles again!  Though it would be nice if the game would tell you if you don’t have some gadget needed to solve a puzzle.  Arkham City had the same problem.
The Joker is just great all around, same as in all the other Arkham games.
There’s a photo mode that’s pretty nice.  Like most console games, it forces you to keep the main character in the frame but otherwise the camera is free.  Be sure to check the options in there – you can turn off the game logo.
I didn't have an FPS counter up but framerate never got close to causing me a problem even with max settings.  I've got a 1080 and 16GB so no big surprise there.  A lot of other folks are having issues, though.  The game has a performance test in it so check that first thing.  If you can't get the performance up to snuff in the first hour, refund the game.
So overall I would give it about a 6.5 out of 10.  If you haven't played Arkham Asylum or Arkham City yet, definitely play those first.  Not only will the backstory help but they are both better games.  Play this one if you liked those a lot and want some closure.

This "Hearthstone" copy features a interesting, yet hard story mode and some excellent voice acting.
The story kept me busy for ~25 hours, which is surprisingly long for a Trading Card Game.
Step by step you learn the motives and backstory of the main characters and classes you can play and ultimately you fight against an AI that shows you how to really play the deck of the class.
But that's all there is. The PvP section of the game is filled with imba decks that will wipe out beginners within a few turns. Gamebreaking cards that destroy all of your units in a single swipe or just like that make every enemy unit evolve at once (which gives them a huge bonus) are enough to make everyone who isn't pay-to-win want to quit.
Because there are only 2 (free) ways to progress in this game. Either by gathering the low rewarding daily login bonus for the end of time until you can afford some decent decks with the ingame currency or playing pvp and get beaten in 6 out of 10 games because the game can't put you against equal players. From the remaining 4 games 2 will be players who quit right away or just do nothing to stall time (for whatever reason) and then quit. The last 2 of 10 are games that you might actually win. Totally worth it.
It's mainly because of the great story mode that I recommend this game.

-----V1.4 UPDATE-----
V1.4 bring us major updates...and awesome one at it.
Obvious one is the tank. Previously, you only have T80 for Russian and Type 10 for JSDF. Now Russian got T-72, T95 Black Eagle, and T-14 Armata while JSDF got Type 90. Maybe in future we can see modernized Type 74? Who know, but this new addition greatly improve the game.
Another improvement is a lot of UI get reworked. Some are necessary to facilitate new tanks, some are improving old UI. It certainly more user-friendly than before.
All in all, yes, i still recommend this game, especially for you WoT players who tired with random match.
-----UPDATE-----
Developer team quickly address some issue that really annoying, which is great of them (hey, after playing WoT for so long any kind of quick response is great in comparison). So here i updated my review, old review can be read down below. Note that i haven't try online mode, only arcade so far.
First, with X-axis and Y-axis sensitivity slider implemented, its way better. Disorientation problem still exist but with a little practice and lowering your X-axis sensitivity into VERY LOW, it become less problem than before.
The physic still need improvement (if you collide with some obstacle it can be quite... weird) and I will suggest to lower hull traverse a bit. Able to access gameplay option from main menu will be very helpful too(curently you can only access it when you are in match). Maybe in future we can see more tanks or factions, and new game mode or maps would great too, but for now this game is okay. I recommend it if you need some break from WoT or WT:GF; or if you got some spare money. At least your teammates AI in arcade can't be worse.

Put simply, Tokyo Warfare is a fantastic core game with some overarching issues that the developer is thankfully taking very seriously.
Wonderfully fun to play just like its spiritual 90's predecessor Tokyo Wars, it also looks great and maintains a certain otaku sense of humor. The environments are well-designed and the destruction is deeply satisfying. Unfortunately, it has started off with some issues (poor hit detection, spawn glitches, odd control issues) but I've been extremely impressed by the dev's response; the game has already been patched once and further patches are coming in 24-hour cycles to address criticism and bugfixes. The game is also somewhat barebones at the moment with only two playable teams/tanks and two city maps, however the dev apparently intends to add content regularly once the core game is satisfactory, which is fine by me.
That aside, the incredibly fun core gameplay and the dev's deep involvement with the community have encouraged me to stick with Tokyo Warfare despite its current flaws. If you played Tokyo Wars back in the day or are just hungry for a goofy tank battle sim, this is worth an investment; just keep in mind that it's an evolving product that will continue to recieve polish.

Short version: A game that is worthy of bearing the 'Resident Evil' title. By a smidge. Love having my favorite girl Claire back. 7/10 and only worth buying when on sale.
Some details I'd like to share:
*Story is....okay. The series honestly has never been "great" with story and still isn't. Granted, it's still a clear storyline (that's rather predictable at points) and it fits the requirements.
*Graphics are whatever. Player models are at essentially at its best. Everything else such as environmental textures are subpar. Environment design is mostly dull and boring, but only because most of the game you're in dungeon-like areas (which are inherently dull) so technically I guess they did it right.
*Gameplay is similar to RE6, yet not nearly as smooth. Compared to RE6, character movement feels a little wonky and less flexible, and dodging isn't as good (without upgrades to it, you can still get hit by lame basic attacks). At the very least, dodging is included and can be upgraded to be much better.
*My biggest pet peeve: Ally-controlled AI = ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and generally useless. Worst part of the game to me. Only pro is that the support characters (Moira and Natalia) can get hit a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton and not die because their health slowly regenerates as long as they are controlled by AI and are not under attack. I think they can die if constantly hit in a short amount of time but it has never got that far. Here's the issue: no matter which character the AI controls, the AI is the worst at falling back from enemies. Countless times I'm running away to a more advantageous position to fight and constantly the ally AI is either BACKPEDALING (and thus moving slower) white I'm miles ahead, getting caught running behind or adjacent to the enemy, or just generally staying somewhere in very close proximity to them. In short, it's like they're in awe of the enemies and want to get hit. Now, this is no problem if it's support characters getting left behind (regen thing), but if it's Claire or Barry, well♥♥♥♥♥♥ be sure to have extra herbs. They do not regenerate at all and just LOVE to be close to the enemies. Even worse, if you opt for the upgrade that allows the AI to attack (with VERY LOW damage and no ammo penalty), they'll do so while standing next to the enemies. Ugh. You'll understand more in Claire's campaign and facing off with Ironheads and their giant axes.

The app works well but has one huge issue for me personally:  you can't disable the second edition content.  I already own first edition Mansions of Madness and was looking forward to this as a replacement for the "keeper."  In first edition, the keeper controls all of the monsters and plays against the 4 other people who play the investigators.  This app plays the role of the keeper, however, so instead of a 4vs1 game we could play this 5-player cooperative.  The game would probably get more time on the table if someone didn't have to be the bad guy, and because of that, we have only played Mansions of Madness once in the 2 years I've owned it.  I've actually considered selling it since it never gets played, but I heard about the app and thought it might make a difference.
Nope.
Under the options, you can select what MoM content you own, so if you own first edition, you have access to the map tiles and investigators from that game.  This is great if you have both editions because it gives you extra content.  The problem is that I can't disable second edition content, I can only
first edition content.  So I can't use this to set up a game because there are 24 potential map tiles that it will use in the app that I don't physically own.  I don't really have a desire to drop another $100 to repurchase a game I already own just to get map tiles and the ability to use this app to play full co-op.
I do like that it offers a way to track monster health so you have fewer tokens to deal with, but I don't understand why you couldn't add the investigators in the same way.  The interactive puzzles are better than their physical conterpart, and having search tokens and various other story elements in a digital format is better than reading from the book.  There are only four scenarios, though, so that's kind of limiting the replayability (but I'm sure they plan on selling more through expansions).  Some cards in the app are used in the app while most others it just tells you to "add the card to your inventory."  I get that it's a "companion app" and not a replacement for the board game, but it just seems odd to only half-include some things.
Overall, not a bad companion app if you are just getting into the game and buy second edition right off the bat, but it's literally worthless without buying the second edition.  No love for fans who supported the first edition?  Sorry, but I'll pass.  The only good thing about this is that the first edition is out of print and becoming collectible, so I'll actually get something decent when I inevitably decide to part with the game for good.
---------------------------------------------------------
Edit:  Regarding most of the comments, you seem to be missing the point.  This app lets you incorporate the first edition content into the game.  That being said, it's possible to play using only first edition investigators, and the potential is there (since maps are supposedly randomly generated) to create a scenario using only first edition tiles.  It's all there.  It literally populates the game with the content that you tell it you own.  So, why then can I not make a map using only first edition tiles if that's all I have?  It doesn't seem like that difficult of a thing to allow in the app, but it seems to
not allow it so you
to get the second edition box to enjoy the app.  I understand this app was designed for second edition, but it's literally just the flip of a toggle switch to only use first edition content, so why won't they allow it?
After the amazing Descent app, I was looking forward to this doing the same thing:  taking control of the keeper/overlord so my friends and I can have a truly co-op experience.  Since it doesn't without purchasing what amounts to a $100 expansion, I'm disappointed.  I said the app was pretty decent, but I'm still disappointed by the lack of support/fan service for the first edition.  It doesn't seem like that much to ask for when the content is already supported by the app.  It's such an easy fix.  Why am I not allowed to be disappointed by that and give it a thumbs down?  Why is your only argument "It's for second edition, dummy" like that magically changes everything?  Sheesh...

I first played this game on the Xbox 360, and I will say it plays a lot better on PC.  The controls are flawed and the AI is far below average intelligence, these are things I think everyone can agree with.   This is a third-person shooter with poor game mechanics and really short levels.  However, it is one of the most brutally honest narratives I have seen in a game. You play the roles of two psychopaths: a schizophrenic and a mercenary. The game does nothing to excuse either character, they're both despicable. I would say Lynch is the more tragic one, having an actual mental condition and oddly a better moral grasp on life than Kane. The game doesn't try to justify its violence.  If you compare it to other third-person action games, you start to notice things like: Nathan Drake guns downs thousands of people in the pursuit of a non-existing treasure, and we call him the good guy.  I beat the game in about 5 hours, I could've beaten it in 3, if it weren't for the flawed gameplay. The game asks that you use a cover system, but enemies at times can shoot through the barriers you use as cover.  Towards the end of the game as you lead a coup de tete, your allies will be the death of you. To say the gameplay is frustrating is an understatement, but play it for the story. So much ambition went into the narrative of this game, I think they may have lost sight of the actual game mechanics.  I am a huge fan of Michael Mann films, and this was worth it for that reason alone.

What a charming and compelling game! It goes well beyond a typical puzzle game, drawing the player slowly into the alternate logic of its universe. Only very occasionally did it demand a tricky (to me) bit of eye-hand coordination. Upon solving a puzzle I never felt that sense of frustration one sometimes feels when a solution demands something absurd or that the player couldn't reasonably guess. Everything can be solved by experimenting to learn how things work and then utilizing the principles.
If I had to say something let me down, it's probably that I felt it didn't resolve in a narrative sense. Being faced with this alien world, with different rules and a sort of iconic tale being told in parallel, I was constantly trying to put together the larger "story" or concept. While there was a clear transistion into the conclusion, and while the actual ending was beautiful and gave me a primitive sense of closure just as a sort of transcendent spectacle, it didn't connect to a meaning as augured by the icons, etc. That may well be part of the point, and I respect that, but that lack of resolution is the one thing I wish could be different. Well, and of course, I wish there were more wonderful puzzles!
I recommend this, I have purchased it as a gift for others, and I look forward to more from the author.

A spiritual successor to Tokyo Wars, a great arcade game back in 96'.   Tokyo Warfare was a game I've always been hoping for since the Tokyo Wars arcade booths were decommissioned.  Though the Original Soundtrack doesn't live up to the standards Tokyo Wars set, the game play is still the same and it's great.  The simple and fast paced game play really is what makes this game great.  There are no complicated armor penetration values or angling of armor, 2 Factions, 2 MBT's, 1 Game Mode.  This may put off some, but sometimes simple is for the better.
As for bugs and glitches, there are a few minor camera clipping issues and sometimes you respawn on top of another tank, but nothing game breaking or big enough for it to matter.
I also hope to have full Japanese voicing for menus and in-game implemented soon, as the English voices sound rather cheap and as a native speaker it really is unbearable.
I maybe bias because of the nostalgia I feel from playing Tokyo Warfare, but the game is fun, and I recommend it for anyone who wants a game they can play for very short amounts and still have fun.

It's not often I write a review, but this game is well worth it.
For starter, I just want to say that this game has finally sated that burning desire to drive a tank that Girls Und Panzer instilled in me.
That aside, this game has a lot of unique and enjoyable aspects:
+Destroyable terrain
Crush cars, blow up support pillars, knock over vending machines, even destory a poor, innocent Chibi statue.  in other words, you get to be just a destructive as a tank should be
+Different camera angles
This is a big plus for me, since I really am not a fan of the 3rd-person viewpoint. Tokyo Warfare allows you to change your viewpoint mid-game with the press of a button, which actually come in handy a lot. I find that for tight maneuvering in alleyways, I usually switch to 3rd person for a better view, and then go back to one of the two 1st-person viewpoints for more open driving and/or combat
+Multiplayer
Yes, it has multiplayer.  I can't really speak too much on this one yet, since I havn't tried it, but it looks awesome.
+VR Mode, but not exclusively VR Mode
I'm very happy that this game didn't do what so many other recent VR games seem to be doing, IE making them exclusive to VR. I have never owned a VR headset, and never plan to, but being able to play this game just the same is a definate plus.
+Cheap!
Yup, this was a pleasant suprise. I backed the original Kickstarter campaign (which sadly was unsucessful), at a price roughly 60% more than its current price. Finding out that it's only $15 on Steam is quite a big suprise
+It keeps it simple
This game knows what it sets out to do, and it does it well. There aren't many fancy additions, but those aren't really necessary.  The core gameplay is solid and simple, and that's what will keep me coming back to it, over and over.
----------------
+/-Leveling System
Still undecided on this one, it looks like you unlock even more maps and stuff as you level up, but there doesn't seem to be too much to unlock. By my current level (level 5, I think?) I've already unlocked all but one map, multiplayer mode, and the secondary team. I guess it's more for the purpose of a Global Leaderboard...?
----------------
-Could use more maps
Yeah, I'll admit it, this game could use some more maps, and maybe even some different tank skins. However, this is a day-1 review, and the devs have said that they plan on adding more later, so this is only a temporary negative.
----------------

Not sure what to really think of this game. On the one hand, the combat system is fantastic. On the other hand against all the plot-important enemies you don't get to use it. There the game resorts to tedious trial-and-error action sequences. These are especially annoying to me since, hey, I have a shotgun, why would I enter melee with this bum? No seriously, I have a gun and the dude is standing 10 meters away flailing a machete, shoot him? No... enter illogical melee, It's a great sum of the storyline in general; a series of ownright stupid clichés.
Here's where I don't understand the game at all:
This game has the best combat system I've seen in a zombie game. Really. It is absolutely fantastic and a joy to use, especially when you get the grappling hook.
But instead of using the brilliant combat system, in the important stages of the storyline, the game resorts to arena-style combat where you are either "too tired to use the grappling hook" followed by stages where you have to marathon-sprint away from stalker-copies. Instead of designing the game around the combat system which is so much fun, they restrict it to conform to their idea of a stage and everything suffers for it.
The freeroam of the game is a 10/10 and rarely have I had so much fun, but as soon as you enter "quest stages" it's a mishmash of bad design decisions, combat-crippling nonsense and invisible walls to keep you to the designer's vision of what the challenge should be. This is a downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ way to handle a combat system designed to give you as free hands as possible in how you overcome your adversaries.
Dying Light takes all the best aspects out of Dead Island, Far Cry and Stalker, but somehow manages to include the worst as well. I'll recommend it because of the freeroam which is incredible amounts of fun at times, but stay away from the main storyline as long as possible. It'll leave you disappointed at best.

Dying Light has pretty decent story in my opinion. A lot of players complain about the story containing a LOT of cliches. I don´t honestly mind them, but the game uses pretty much every single cliche video games usually have. Parkour system is really good and fluent. There is also nice amount of crafting inside the game but it could have been more indept. A lot of people complain about melee system being a lot like Dead Islands. Well first off the game was made by the same developers + in my opinion there is nothing to complain about it.  One thing which the developers should look at is the fact that you can´t upgrade your weapons or add attachments like silencers or sights into weapons.
PERFORMANCE:
At launch the game was horribly optimized. Specially on AMD systems. I had 20-30 FPS on ANY settings at launch (7970 GHZ) even setting resolution to lower didn´t change FPS. Also the film grain effect also annoyed many people. I didn´t mind it. After recent patch I can run the game at 50-140 FPS (max settings except view distance which destroys frame rate). Techland also added setting to remove the film grain many people complained about.
If you like zombie games I think Dying Light is really good choice. Though if you aren´t that huge fan of zombie games I recommend you to wait till the game goes on sale.

[/spoiler]( if you are confused about sv's playerbase in numbers i can roughly estimate using this simple equation: 12000* + (12000 x 9**). an estimated total of 120000 million. )

THIS is because cygames want shadowverse to be a quniue game than heartstone to be a short battle that usually decides who win and who loses by the end of turn 10 (usually). just remeber that is the game shadowverse it's unique and how they balance decks is that they will buff/nerf cards. that is all.

I decided to expand on my previous review a bit.
Zeno Clash 2 is a first person brawler set in the fantastical world of Anarchy, Zenozoik. A society perpetually stuck in a sort of stone age, it will be unlike any other world you will explore in video games, and I really mean that. Wandering through this bizzare-but--extremely-well-thought-out landscape, grappling with it's equally bizzare inhabitants, is an experience I can't quite recommend enough. Between bar brawls in the seedy Halstedom, clashes with wildlife in the stunningly beautiful Rath-Bird fields, to defending yourself from the aggressive shrimp men tribe of the desert, the landscapes and enemies are extremely varied. The story is also very very good, but you have to dig a little to get the full experience (think Dark Souls), much is inferred by the environment.
The music is fantastic, though sadly the voice acting is a bit eh.
This game gets a bad rap for not being as focused as the first installment, and while it's true its not as compact, I'd say the best problem a game can have is that it's developers dreamed too big.
Zeno Clash 2 is one of those games I keep thinking about, again and again and again, at least once a week, even a year and half after I first played it. I can't get it out of my head, and thats a wonderful feeling.

This first person parkour game really strives to create something unique.  It almost achieves it, because when the level design flows well, you have a real sense that you are freely moving through the area at your own will.  However, the problem is that most levels have their flow broken consistently.  This is done by 1) combat: it relies on a counter system which is sluggish, unrefined, and just frustrating 2) poor level design: when a game is focused so much on moving forward, stopping to backtrack or search for your next path is not fun 3) unresponsiveness: sometimes it just feels like I should have made a jump or kept my momentum, but I didn't because the game dictated it so through its scripted animations that require a threshold to be met.
Do not waste your time or money on this game.  The story is bland and the gameplay is forgettable.

Marvelously difficult and with soldier customization and traits that give the brave few of XCOM more personality and emotional connection than plenty of RPG characters, this game, for the problems it may have, is, in my opinion, a fantastic strategy title.
Combining large-scale resource management and intelligence gathering, and even managing global panic levels, with squad-level engagements in a wide variety of objectives and maps, especially with the DLC addons, and all that can be influenced by the choices made in the skill tree of a single soldier, and wrap all that up in a situation so tense and emotionally demanding that I would personally get disheartened whenever I really messed something up that I'd have to quit the game and do something else for a while. And as far as I'm concerned, any game that can compromise me emotionally like that, and make me care about characters who hardly talk, has to have some kind of gaming magic behind it.
In XCOM: EU, the micromanagement doesn't feel like micromanagement, it feels like progress, like the player themselves has leveled up each time a soldier earns a promotion or when a squad can cover each other to fight off Seekers, Chryssalids, and a Sectopod at the same time without losing a single soldier.
I can't say much, personally, for the multiplayer, as I've not played it yet, but I don't often have an interest in multiplayer strategy games.
Excellent fun, solid combat mechanics, decent storyline. A rare gem; a genuinely worthwhile indie game.

Honestly, I'm impressed. I bought this solely based on the other reviews because my initial impression was a bit lackluster-- that this looked like some kind of Diablo-flavored reverse tower defense.
Gotta say though, it captures the essence of the ARPG genre and Diablo 1 very, very well. And then it manages to add interesting mechanic changes on top of that to keep it fresh.
The flex system is pretty amazing. Even if I do generally end up picking the longer ones, it's nice to have the choice to play a shorter quest and still progress if I'm short on time. It's not something you often think about with this kind of game but it's definitely on my mind now that I've experienced it.
The card system was something I was very skeptical about, but it works. The upgrade system isn't overly complicated but it is robust enough to make progression feel steady and meaningful.
Overall, I'm excited to see this come out of EA to see what the final product is like.

During the beta stages I had almost completely given up on this game, too many idiotic balance changes. Microtransactions being introduced before the games 1.0 release. And a versus mode nobody asked for ( and is pretty much devoid of players ) just to name a few problems I had. However since then Tripwire has made some worthwhile changes, and adjusted balance rather well (besides the Firebug and Survivalist classes). Microtransactions are still in, didn't expect them to go away but I'm still not a fan of their inclusion.
One thing this game has done well from the beginning however is making the combat just feel good. Almost every weapon has a real weight to it, and the visceral gore that soaks the map permanently is pretty satisfying to say the least.
There are still some broken promises, the one I'm most dissapointed with is the teased Hand-to-Hand class being replaced with the incredibly lackluster Survivalist, who is a master of none and isn't particularly fun to play.
Overall the "launch" of Killing Floor 2 felt very rushed, but if Tripwire continues to support the game, it could eventually live up to Killing Floor 1.

As someone who's never played Shadowrun previously, I'm pretty happy with the system mechanics and how the story folds out. I played it on Very Hard difficulty, which didn't actually seem all too difficult (if anything, I felt like my team missed their attacks more often than they should have). This is also based on the Dead Man's Switch campaign, which comes with the game.
I customized my character originally as a Rigger, focusing on Drone Control, with a few levels in Pistols. I later added Decking to my skills, keeping its levels even with my Drones, and it seemed to work out very successfully, in that I never felt that my character was over-reliant on my companions other than for additional damage output.
The game does have a couple of bugs in some places: the first major one I noticed was when I bought level 2 Decker abilities, where they did not show up in my inventory/stash at all after I bought them. I had to trust the game actually did register that I possessed them, as they were also absent from the store (which is normal if you already had it), and later on in the game, when level 3 Decker abilities were made available, the behavior seemed to correct itself.
The other major bug I found was in the room for the final battle (I'll try not to be spoilery). There are pieces in the room which are either active or inactive, and to keep the battle more manageable, you want to keep all of them inactive as much as possible. However, there were a few instances where I couldn't actually target an active piece (quicksave/loading fixed this), and a few times where a piece appeared inactive, but I knew based on enemy behavior in the battle that it was actually active.

Teleglitch is a top-down randomly generated shooter where the environments, enemies, weapons, secrets, and dang near everything else are places ina ny which way! This game prides itself on looking very low-res and simple while having the graphical effects for its gunfire and such be a very visually outstanding point. As the gameplay goes, the game plays wonderfully and is inrecidly responsive once you get your hands around the controls and functions. There's also a VERY large variety of weapons and objects you can fire, throw, combine, and such to handle the rather large onslaughts of enemies that head your direction. Another big plus is the atmosphere of this game which is vacant, gloomy, and downright sinister at points, the ambient sounds really help hit this point home too.
As far as any negatives go? This game is HARD. Like we're talking brutal hard, here. The game does punish you for mistakes and wrong moves will often leave you with no ammo, a few points of health, and a good swarm of enemies on your tail. So let that be a warning for those going in to get this game, it WILL test you. Beyond that, the game is very solid, plays great, and has a dreadful atmosphere, and if that's your thing, you should definitely check this out!

Not sure what to really think of this game. On the one hand, the combat system is fantastic. On the other hand against all the plot-important enemies you don't get to use it. There the game resorts to tedious trial-and-error action sequences. These are especially annoying to me since, hey, I have a shotgun, why would I enter melee with this bum? No seriously, I have a gun and the dude is standing 10 meters away flailing a machete, shoot him? No... enter illogical melee, It's a great sum of the storyline in general; a series of ownright stupid clichés.
Here's where I don't understand the game at all:
This game has the best combat system I've seen in a zombie game. Really. It is absolutely fantastic and a joy to use, especially when you get the grappling hook.
But instead of using the brilliant combat system, in the important stages of the storyline, the game resorts to arena-style combat where you are either "too tired to use the grappling hook" followed by stages where you have to marathon-sprint away from stalker-copies. Instead of designing the game around the combat system which is so much fun, they restrict it to conform to their idea of a stage and everything suffers for it.
The freeroam of the game is a 10/10 and rarely have I had so much fun, but as soon as you enter "quest stages" it's a mishmash of bad design decisions, combat-crippling nonsense and invisible walls to keep you to the designer's vision of what the challenge should be. This is a downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ way to handle a combat system designed to give you as free hands as possible in how you overcome your adversaries.
Dying Light takes all the best aspects out of Dead Island, Far Cry and Stalker, but somehow manages to include the worst as well. I'll recommend it because of the freeroam which is incredible amounts of fun at times, but stay away from the main storyline as long as possible. It'll leave you disappointed at best.

Zeno Clash2
8/10
The Good:
+ Although the gameplay is almost identical to the first, the level design has changed. Rather than being a linear adventure in the first game Zeno Clash 2 has large areas to explore interconnected with each other. This gives the world a more cohesive feel.
+ Each area to explore is unique and different from the last making it exciting when you reach new areas.
+ Both Zeno Clash games can not be faulted for being unoriginal. These games are some of the craziest, most unique and original ideas in a game. Everything from the world to the characters to the enemies makes for a very fresh experience.
+ Unique enemy designs
+ Artistically the game is nice with some really nice scenery, technically however I felt that it was average
+ Combat is fun, one of the few games that has done first person melee fighting successfully. In addition to straight combat, you can find weapons/guns or use your secondary items to defeat your enemies.
+ Some slight RPG mechanics. Scattered throughout the world are skill totems, fidning them gives you experience points where you can spend them on 4 attributes: Health, Strength, Stamina and Leadership.
Average:
-The game is somewhat easy, I had little trouble on normal and I don't think hard would have posed too much trouble either. One of the secondary items makes combat pretty trivial most of the time.
-If you never played the first game then you will not understand what the hell is going on. If you played the first then you will still be confused only slightly less. The story is decent but isn't presented as well as it should be and that is a shame because the story touches upon some interesting themes that should be expored further.
-The attribute leadership is somewhat of a useless stat. Leadership allows you to recruit allies to fight with you in many battles, a new addition to the game. The problem is, combat being easy and your AI companions being stupid doesn't make it a worthwhile stat, making it very meaningless.

The hardest action-roguelike I've ever played, and I love it.  Success is dependant on your own skill during the game's lightning-quick combat.  You must constantly be on alert for the slightest skittering or a heavy footfall, clueing you into the next reanimated monstrosity that's ready to come charging at you around the next corner.  Split-second mistakes can break you easily. The game utilizes a clever and very smooth inventory management system, and mastering it on-the-fly is vital to survival.
A very subtle, yet compelling story builds slowly as you wander through the darkened, shadowy corridors.  The game is thick with a brooding, oppressive atmosphere, steeped in hard sci-fi horror.  Sound design is amazing, and the graphics are impressive for being so deceptively simple.  One of the best indie games I've played - keeps me facing its challenge again and again, even as it brutally beats me back down so often.

To be fair, writing this review should be divided into two kind of aspects.
First of all, the technical issue, this game is barely out-dated so everyone can run the game flawlessy and I had nothing problem on running it on the latest gpu such gtx1060 with i7 processor. You have to install Windows Live first to run the game if you encounter error issue such the game wont start properly.
The second thing, ofcourse its about gameplay. So lets get started with the plot.
PLOT
You are Kane, an ex-criminal that do revenge against to your crime organization because they kill your family and must save your daughter that is kidnapped. In order to do that, you dont do it alone, you will be accompanied by Lynch, a troubled temperamental guy who swears alot. He helps you during the gameplay and mission which you must shoot everyone from police to Yakuza where the gameplay is basically just getting from point A to B and so on with interesting feature such as commanding your partner or your groups (on some mission) to face your enemy for killing.
Story-wise its over-used theme and the dialouge are territbe, for personal reasons, I cant see the reason why the writers here write their every single characters in this game have swearing lines that were not necessary and exaggerating in order to convince the character you play is not average good guy trope. Its like written by an edgy writer who thinks that character who swears a lot is great to convince the player that has unique personality, and the problem almost single of characters here sound same with angry attitude.
CONTROL
This game requires keyboard and mouse to control, so if you have controller/joystick its useless. The problem with the control mechanic is really awful in aiming for far range. You have to remember precisely which the keyboard button function for exact control. The most annoying thing that this game dont have "jump" button which in one mission I almost being stuck to continue my gameplay, and besides please be patient that your movement isnt smooth enough to move with confusing camera movement and auto-hiding feature that is glitchy. But overall, still you can enjoy game if you get used with default controlling mapping if you dont play this game often.
VISUAL
Its little bit out-dated but still cannot categorized into retro game considering this game came out in mid 00s. The facial movement looks stiff and sometimes ridiculously weird with characters moving their lips on dialoge unsynchronized and you can find bug here and there during the gameplay.
FUN
For the game that you can spend for more 5 hours, this game can potentially be fun for third-person shooting genre, but considering this game is not controller / joystick ready and have lack of story-line interesting plot. You can still add to your collection but for me, Its really hard to see what is the replay value from this game and maybe I never look back because the only thing makes thie game interesting is probably its kind of starter to explore third-person genre on PC that is "cheap" to try on Steam (bought on sale).

Risk of Rain is a game about running and gunning, collecting items, and proceding to increasingly difficult levels as you find teleporters in each level. The game harder the longer you play for, so taking too long in one area can cause the difficulty to rise too high to cope with.
PROS:
-Great art (although everything is pretty small)
-Variety of items and characters with vast uses and playstyles
-Lots of unlockables and secrets to find that can change the way you play
-Music is pretty good
-Very satisfying to play as you get good.
-TONS of replay value
-Co-op mode
-Three levels of difficulty
CONS:
-Extremely difficult. Still have not beaten the game. The enemies get harder fast and you often feel as if you are shooting ping pong balls at your foes instead of guns and explosives.
-Combat gets a little bland by the end of game as you are constantly running and dodging enemies with no room to do anything else. You'll pretty much use the same tactic throughout the game with less and less wiggle room for screwing up. Run left. Dodge. Get a shot at the enemy. Run right. Dodge. Take another shot. Pause for 2 seconds and die.
I would recommend this game to most people, but definitely not the casual gamer. It is very difficult and has a steep learning curve, but has great aesthetics and overall feeling.

People weren't kidding when they said you play through an episode of South Park.
The first game that Matt Stone and Trey Parker got to legitamently work on as they saw fit, South Park The Stick of Truth was not only an hilarious game, but a game that plays quite well as well.
Teaming up with Bethesda studios, the game follows a sorta traditional turnbased RPG battle system, abeit, if I had one gripe, too easy and simplistic. I hadn't had much trouble throughout the game, so if you expecting a challenge, go for anything above normal difficulty.
A phenominal thing about the game is that despite how it looks super fake, thats the magic in the game in which it's like a literal version of kids playing medival make believe, yet makes you feel a part of their world and forget that it's a game at times, not to mention the added hilarity of Matt and Trey's writing.
The overworld is cool as its the first time South Park was shown as a whole town, one you could travel through, chock full of references and songs from the show. From the movie theater to Jimbo's gun store to South Park Elementary, you'll get to see it all, and it's fantastic.
You also get tons of customization for your character, and throughout the game you can buddy up with some of the protagonists of the show, each with their own hilarious or cool abilities (mostly hilarious though).
All in all, even if your not a hardcore South Park fan like myself, if you even slightly enjoyed the humour then I'm sure you'll enjoy this game (it even pays homage to a certain classic zelda game at a part in it). If your a fan of humour and a pretty alright RPG system, then this game is a definite must.

Tripwire really out did themselves with this one. If you enjoy co-op games, look no further than this.  They took everything good about the original and brought it back even better and then continued to add on. The classes this time around feel amazing and really play defined roles and the ability to reconfigure the perks just adds a new level to the teamwork dynamic and can add new life to a class you may be getting bored of. The maps this time aren't as ridiculously massive as some in the original, though I hope they do bring back more maps from the origianl, but they make up for it by making the maps way more vertical and adding chokes that can either save you or ♥♥♥♥ you if you aren't careful. The Zeds this time around really provide a fun challenge. They really did a good job this time with the AI and how they react to differnet situations and instead of just having more health between difficulty spikes, they attack and spawn diffently too. Which brings me to the guns. The guns is this one are awesome. They look beautiful, they all handle differnetly and each gun in its own way requires it's own mastery. There are a few that I feel fall short, namely the microwave and rail gun, but that could just because they just aren't really for my play style.
Now for the the negatives. I have a few minor complaints that really amount to minor fixes that hopefully tripwire address in the future. There are a few levels that have weird sound files that really just distract, me atleast, from the game. My prime example of this is a sound file on one map that I think is supposed to be a dog whimpering but somehow can be heard over explosions and a symphony of chainsaws. Another problem I have is that it's a little too easy even at higher difficulty levels to manipulate the money system in the game in order to stack up large amounts of cash in the early waves, this causes you to sometimes see lone wolf players that really have no interest in trying to help the team which takes away from the fun.  The only major problem is player collison. You will get stuck on the stupidest♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes that any normal person would just step around. You will literally get stuck on the edge of door frames, small trees, bullards, and on other players in a wide open areas. Usually it's just a quick adjustment and you will be fine, but when you're being chased or about to be cornered, it can be the sole deciding factor in your death and it's absolutely maddening.
Overall it's a great game to play with your friends and a way to meet new friends. It's well worth the money and i look forward to dumping 200+ hrs into this game. I give it an 9/10.

Marvelously difficult and with soldier customization and traits that give the brave few of XCOM more personality and emotional connection than plenty of RPG characters, this game, for the problems it may have, is, in my opinion, a fantastic strategy title.
Combining large-scale resource management and intelligence gathering, and even managing global panic levels, with squad-level engagements in a wide variety of objectives and maps, especially with the DLC addons, and all that can be influenced by the choices made in the skill tree of a single soldier, and wrap all that up in a situation so tense and emotionally demanding that I would personally get disheartened whenever I really messed something up that I'd have to quit the game and do something else for a while. And as far as I'm concerned, any game that can compromise me emotionally like that, and make me care about characters who hardly talk, has to have some kind of gaming magic behind it.
In XCOM: EU, the micromanagement doesn't feel like micromanagement, it feels like progress, like the player themselves has leveled up each time a soldier earns a promotion or when a squad can cover each other to fight off Seekers, Chryssalids, and a Sectopod at the same time without losing a single soldier.
I can't say much, personally, for the multiplayer, as I've not played it yet, but I don't often have an interest in multiplayer strategy games.

Killing Floor 2 is (obviously) the continuation of the quite famous Killing Floor. Despite some minor controversy in early access it's finally entered full release. The only real way to play is online, as offline mode is mostly uninteresting and feels dull.
Everyone, especially the fans of the original, will be happy to know that the principle stayed the same. HOWEVER, almost everything has been improved. The classes (perks?... who thought of that) have been fleshed out better, new zeds look much better, there is a versus mode, everything feels smoother and weapon handling is even better. Everything is again accompanied by heavy metal, which goes alongside great and makes slaughter even more fun.
Every game basicly goes the same. You fight waves and waves of enemies, with some time to restock on ammo and buy new gear inbetween. In the end, your group faces one of two bosses with some interesing abilities, however nothing really out of the book. While you won't have much problem during easier difficulties, it gets much harder the higher you set it, making tactical play a must if you want to survive on suicidal and up.
There are 10 different classes and they all play differently. Surprisingly, all are viable and you are encouraged to have variety, as each class has different strenghts and weaknesses. Melee combat got improved immensely and the berserker class relies almost purely on it.
Zeds got a bit of an upgrade too. They are still almost harmless alone (minus some exceptions) but they can pose a threat to even the most experienced players in a group. You really have to work together, as running around alone quickly gets you killed.
And finally, versus mode. To be honest, I didn't really liked it, it kind of felt like a bad version of the same mode in Left4Dead 2. It's not really that well balanced (yet), but it's still fun to play, as constantly playing the same mode can get dull. That is also my worst gripe with the game, as you mostly do same things over and over again. There are no quests to keep things fresh, you basicly just kill everything untill the bell rings. I'm not saying that's bad, but it could be better. If weapon handling wouldn't be some damn great, I think people would get bored much faster.
Conclusion:
Great continuation of Killing Floor, a lot of much needed improvements. Could get boring after a while, but if the moding scene keeps things fresh and the developers keep supporting the game for years to come, I think Killing Floor 2 has the potential to be a great game for years to come. It's definately my favourite co-op survival shooter at the moment - sorry Left4Dead 2, your reign has come to an end.
Final grade: 8.2/10
