Shadowrun Returns is an old-school isometric cRPG in the vein of the classic Fallout games based on, as its title suggests, the Shadowrun franchise; one of the pioneers in the fictional literature best known for combining cyberpunk, magic, urban fantasy and crime elements into this unique lore. Initially started as a pen-and-paper boardgame, it was long “forgotten” by today’s generation or occasionally overshadowed by games such as the widely popular and highly-acclaimed Deus Ex – at least that is how I see it.
The gameplay in Shadowrun Returns is similar to many classic cRPGs. You manage a team of up to four Shadowrunners where you can choose from the story’s main characters to use or hire random, more specialised, Shadowrunners which suit your mission’s requirements. Just like in any RPG, you can pick a race and class for your character at the start, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. The combat mechanics are turn-based and generally well balanced, resembling the one used in the recently rebooted XCOM franchise by Firaxis Games, thus if you are familiar with it then that is good news because it is solid. In addition, by completing missions or triggering certain events in the story, karma points are earned to be further spent on enhancing your main character’s attributes which include the typical Strength, Intelligence and Charisma, to name a few, seen in most classic RPGs. For instance, investing lots of points into Intelligence allows your character to be highly competent with Decking or Drone Control specialities, or investing a lot into Charisma can unlock specific dialogue conversations to bypass certain key situations in the game (other attributes are used sometimes for exclusive dialogues too). In fact, the game does a good job in making sure the player cannot master all the available attributes, because as the game explains in its tips during loading screens: a jack of all trades is a master of none. As a whole, perhaps one of the key aspects of its gameplay aside from its good turn-based combat is how you can approach the narration by choosing your responses based on what personality you want your character to be like when talking to NPCs. While not all responses follow a choice-and-consequence pattern, some do actually have an impact on how things develope; and Shadowrun Returns provides a wide range of opportunities. Ultimately, this also increases the replayability of the game a great deal. One last addition is The Matrix which is like a cyberworld used by Deckers to hack into systems. It is an interesting concept but feels a bit underdeveloped as it can feel a bit of a chore most of times.
The art direction in Shadowrun Returns is at the very least appealing. The backgrounds, which do vary, are nicely drawn and the colour pallets used fit with Shadowrun’s universe and its cyberpunk roots, making it easily one of the best looking traditional isometric games out there.  The neon light effects used are also something to praise it for since they bring the game’s world to life, despite the lack of NPCs roaming the streets. Unfortunately, the character models, including their animations, are about the only things which look visually mediocre in this rather attractive game, almost making it look like it was ported from a mobile game. Moreover, Shadowrun Returns also boasts a brilliant soundtrack with a couple of memorable tracks, such as the one from the main menu (“Return of the Sixth World”) and “Puppet Masters”, which fit with the cyberpunk vibes of the game. Sure, while this soundtrack does sound slightly different to the one from the original Shadowrun game on SNES, it still sounds cool.
Without a shadow (no pun intended) of a doubt, Shadowrun Returns’ strongest aspect is its narration with its great character development. Whilst it takes a bit of time at the beginning to get to like (or despise) individuals you meet, eventually you will be surprised by how many who become your companions or allies will quickly turn out as memorable characters by the end with who you can at least sympathise. Starting off as a simple detective story in the style of Jack The Ripper which progressively deepens and deviates from just a simple detective case to solve later on, the “Dead Man’s Switch” story in Shadowrun Returns is mostly solid, even though it sorrowfully turns into a Fahrenheit (Indigo Prophecy) type of story in the last quarter of the journey. While it might not completely ruin the endgame experience, that latter part personally left me with a sour taste in my mouth. Despite featuring no voice acting, this does not ruin the experience either since it allows you to use your own imagination on how characters are supposed to sound like in the story. As a result, it might require a bit more effort and dedication to read some of its pompous written dialogues, and this will certainly not be everyone’s cup of tea.
Shadowrun Returns has some glarying imperfections though. Being an extremely linear (pretty much most of it is on rails) and story-driven game, it lacks any sense of exploration due to its contained maps and minimal interactions with their environments. This is something which might frankly turn off quite a number of RPG fans, old-school or contemporary. Clicking on certain hotspots, found only intermittently around places, usually pop up a text-box describing what the character is observing, but these are indeed very few throughout the game’s journey. For a text-heavy game, this aspect of interaction seems like a lost opportunity for further enriching the experience. On top of that, once a mission is completed or the area is cleared, in most cases there is no way to revisit an area afterwards. For a completionist, it is crucial to check everything prior to proceeding to the next area. The lack of a deep character customisation is another aspect that will not please every RPG fan out there since it is very basic and only allows you to choose from premade character models. Additionally, there is also no inventory customisation/management for your companions either which can cause some annoyances when planning your tactics prior or during combat.  One further frustration with the game’s design is its tendency to occasionally lock the player into combat even when everyone in the area is eliminated. This results in wasted time trying to move your team to the next objective location on the map as it is agonisingly slow due to its turn-based mechanics. And lastly, as much as the writing is top-notch, the game can sometimes drown you with its longwinded expositions from time to time which can be underwhelming especially for those looking to jump into action more often.
In conclusion, Shadowrun Returns is an adequate and faithful entry to the franchise, albeit a limited game, that should please any cRPG, cyberpunk/fantasy fans and even book readers out there to some degree. While it can honestly feel shallow in places, its stellar writing, good narration, memorable cast of characters, distinctive art direction and competent XCOM-like gameplay should keep most people invested in its relatively short 10+ hours campaign, even if its story loses some of its early charm near the end. This, however, remains a borderline recommendation as many things could have been done to further improve the game as a RPG since it can feel a bit basic. To get most out of it is to always remind yourself that it is a very story-driven experience foremost, so any notions of open-world or high-budget production values in the manner of The Elder Scrolls should be dismissed, otherwise you will be disappointed by your own misconceptions. The best way to describe Shadowrun Returns is like reading a long, but relatively good book (that will not really blow you away) accompanied by solid gameplay elements to justify it as a game -- because honestly, it is not too far from being no more than a visual novel.

Let me just start by saying that this is a game you'll either like or you'll hate.  It's very unforgiving and to be quite honest, like most roguelikes the random nature of the game can mean you may end up wasting entire swaths of your time just to get to a level that will absolutely punish you and you will die.  A lot of people have trouble with that kind of gameplay, while others find it rewarding.  This is more a commentary on the actual roguelike genre than the game itself however, but it is such an integral part of the game that I feel it nonetheless bears mentioning.  If you are the kind of person that gets frustrated by those kinds of games then this game is, without a shadow of a doubt, not for you.
Teleglitch utilizes a very low-fidelity graphics style.  Given the sound design and the lack of music, I am inclined to believe this is a conscious gameplay decision.  While the sort of voxel design it has certainly does seem rather unique, I can't say it really clicked for me.  It just doesn't seem to have enough creative soul to it to justify that appeal.  It certainly does have a very kinetic feel to the gameplay and graphics both however, so that bit was nice.
The gameplay mechanics themselves, however, work very well and it truly does the sort of roguelike survival thing very well.  The gunplay is very simple point-and-shoot, however it does have line of fire mechanics that are done surprisingly well given the perspective, and each of the guns you have handle in a very different fashion.  Some of the more powerful weapons such as can bombs or the high explosives involve a very survival-esque risk/reward mechanic whereby you can use them and they will be very devestating to the enemies, but given the timing window they could also be very damaging to yourself if you do not use the weapon skillfully. I find there generally enough of a skill ceiling to the gunplay and crafting that I find myself playing more in spite of an aesthetic that I don't find pleasing, which is praise for the game if I ever heard any.  As well, the difficulty of the game is obviously something the developer has put some thought in.  The levels themselves may be random but the progression itself has obviously been carefully tweaked, and they have abated the frustration of having to start over by including what are essentially checkpoints in that if you get up to certain levels you can start over from a further point than the beginning.
All in all I would say that is a mechanically-well-designed game that is somewhat let down by a very sparse flavour to the aesthetic and theme.  I would still recommend it to someone that is a fan of that sort of roguelike however, as it is a very strong game in that genre.  It doesn't add anything terribly new or innovative, but what it does, it does very well.

Somewhere in the future, on the edge of a particularly dark area of space is an experimental research facility. Said facility is doing some particular nasty military experiments and now you have woken up and realised it’s all gone to hell. Your only chance is to escape but that isn’t going to be easy.
Teleglitch is an action rogue-like come survival horror title viewed from a top down perspective. Controls are similar to Hotline Miami but it shares none of that games neon tone, instead using a rotten and decaying colour palette designed to inspire feelings of dread and despair as you explore the lonely research outpost.
The games visual style is at first jarring but you’ll soon begin to adjust to the haze of greens and blocky characters. It all begins to take on a certain grotesque beauty and certainly adds to the atmosphere. Sound is the other key component of the game and the outpost hums, bangs and clatters as you explore. Noises are designed to keep you on edge and you’re never quite sure if what you’ve just heard is the station or a monster lurking nearby.
The game follows a pattern of shifting momentum as you move from treating it like The Chaos Engine or Smash TV to running for your life from hordes of mutants and zombies. This change is brought about by what weapon you are carrying and how much ammunition you have left. A few monsters on their own aren’t much of a match for a well-equipped player, but having a few bullets left in a weak gun makes you creep around very carefully, even on early stages.
Teleglitch is a difficult game, something emphasised by the semi-random Rogue like elements of it. Level are randomly generated and randomly populated with monsters. This means you can’t just learn the layout of a level and then dash towards the exit.  It also means that on occasion you will be completely swamped by monsters almost from the off and you’ll need to adjust your strategies quickly in order to survive. Death is permanent and results in starting again from the first level so every move is crucial. There are checkpoints at level five and beyond which allow for a restart from those stages but then where’s the adventure in that?
Much like games like Spelunky the skill required here is being able to understand what you are up against and react accordingly. Doing this is your best route to survival, though it’s highly likely you’ll still be dashing around looking for the exit with hordes chasing you before long.
The important thing is you always want to dive back into the murky and rotten world. It has the same bite as all the best Rogue-like games and you’ll react with the same joy at finding a useful weapon or despair at opening a door to see hordes of monsters in front of you. You’ll die, a lot, but you’ll always want just one more go.
The other problem that a lot of games in this style face is repetition. Teleglitch does have some issues with regards to re-using environments but there are a wealth of different enemies to take on and a whole lot of different firepower to use as well. This, along with some suitably huge boss type monsters later in the game help to keep things fresh.
Overall, Teleglitch tries to bring something a little different to the Rogue-like sub-genre and succeeds. It may well be going through randomly generated dungeons again but this time there are enough twists and more than enough style to set it apart from its competitors. It’s a hard as nails survive-athon than no fan of the genre should be without and in a crowded market that’s very impressive.

Kane and Lynch is definitely a weird one to categorize. The gameplay itself is quite mediocre  hinging on bad in some cases. There is some pretty crap design issues as well. The cover system being complete garbage, and a crappy squad mechanic that doesn’t seem to work at all are a few examples. However where Kane and Lynch truly excels is in the story line. The game presents a rich crime drama with many mature themes. It doesn’t fall into the video game trap of the main character being relatable and deep down a “pretty nice guy.” Kane and Lynch are horrible people, they’ve done terrible inexcusable things. Even when Kane tries to fix what he is done he only continues to dig himself deeper into the mess that is his life. The game is really short clocking in about 3 hours. However I think in this case this is more of blessing as the game doesn’t exhaust you with its mediocrity (gameplay wise). So if you're looking for looking for a game with a good story and can put up with some less than stellar gameplay I’d say give it a shot otherwise I would just skip it.

FTL is one of those games that, if you don't dodge out of the gate, will grab you hard.  It's got that just-one-more jump thing, kind of like Civ. Alright this game has to be one of the more addicting I've ever played. Considering it is a roguelike platformer it does have some aspects that set it apart from others in the genre. First is the combat, the game has 12 different classes each equipped with 4 unique skills. One of these skills is their basic attack while the other 3 different skills which have a cooldown. The classes are incredibly varied with each having their own strengths and weaknesses. While I am definitely better with some than others none of them feel extremely underpowered and it is very possible to win the game with each. This variety of classes and abilities that range from damage over time, increased mobility, and temporary invulnerability allows the combat to feel much more varied than some of the other games in the genre.
The levels in the game are fairly limited but they change enough to keep it interesting. A complete run consists of 6 stages. For each of the first 5 stages there are two possible options for the level. For example in the third stage can either be a snowy level with steep cliffs on either side, or a level where the bottom half is underwater. Each of these levels is random to an extent. The levels are predesigned but there are different variations of each level so there is some variety added in that way. Still after a few playthroughs you'll likely see all the levels have to offer. The sixth and final stage is set in stone and is consistant throughout playthroughs.
The game does add replayability in several aspects. There are a decent amount of items in this game and a lot of them have interesting and unique effects that make it fun to discover new items and combinations. It is possible to cycle through the stages after beating stage 5 instead of going on to the boss, so it is entirely possible to rack up an insane amount of items and just mow down anything in your path. Getting to this point is challenging but extremely rewarding once you realize you are pretty much unstoppable.

Talking about difficulty the game is quite hard to start before you get the hang of it. Most likely people will try to take too long on each level farming in order to feel comfortable with their items and levels to defeat the boss. The thing about RoR is that there is a timer that is always increasing and when it hits a certain threshold the difficulty increases. In order to get better at the game one can't get discouraged at initial playthroughs. It takes a bit of trial and error to figure out the value of getting items/levels, vs. the value of getting onto the next level before the difficulty ramps up to far. Once this balance is reached the game is not easy, you still need to be aware of surroundings and plan your attacks, but it becomes much clearer what you need to do.

Of course it is always good to play with some other friends either online or locally. If they already have experience they could be of help in teaching you and possibly complementing you with characters that you havent unlocked yet. For the price you could easily get your money's worth. If its on sale especially, take a flyer on it, you could find yourself addicted trying to get better, at that price it would be worth it just for the soundtrack which I have to point out is amazing.

Well, where do I start?
This game is in no ways a bad game, but, I have to say that some of the decisions taken by Tripwire were kinda off-putting.
I've been following the development of this game since before the ZedConomy update, and I can see why some the early adopters are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at Tripwire.
To be honest, I don't really mind these MT's, since they are merely cosmetical, but I think they should have announced the inclusion of them at least 1 month earlier to prevent the huge backlash that it caused.
Now, the updates themselves were painfully slow, especially if we take in account that this game was originally planned to be out in 2015.
The PVP mode was really bad at the time of release, and I personally think that it was a mistake, and that the time and resources that TWI spent on creating it should have been used on adding content for the core game mode, like new weapons.
The Survivalist perk is underwhelming to say the least and, in my personal opinion, goes against the idea of having a Perk based gameplay. It's basically a Jack-of-All Trades which does a mediocre job at everything. Also, it doesn't even have weapons of it's own, it just uses weapons from the other "real" Perks.
Now, let's talk about the good things!
-It's a gorgeous looking game
-Well optimised, even a toaster can run it
-Fun gameplay

After 11 hours I finished the game and it was a good ride. There are good things about the game and then there are things that could be (way) better. Let's start with the good things first:
It certainly feels like a Shadowrun game. I've played the pen & paper RPG in the 90s and during the first minutes, the game gets the atmosphere right. It feels like the Seattle of 2050 that I had in my head (or at least very close to it). The artwork is well made and the soundtrack works nicely to support the setting.
You can choose how to play your character. While the decking part is a bit underwhelming, the choice between weapons or magic is there and quite well balanced. There's a good amount of freedom how to build your character and while it doesn't have a big influence on the outcome of the game, it still gives the game some depth.
Depth... that's the real problem with the game. The story is well written and while it does have a quite large number of twists, in the end it works well. The game is too linear though. There is exactly one optional 'Mr Johnson' run and that's simply not enough in a Shadowrun game. The game feels too much 'on rails' and while you can grab a few optional items for additional creds, there's almost no content you can miss out on. That in turn means there's almost no replay value except if you want to check out magic instead of weapons (or vice versa).
I still recommend the game, because it does give you a good amount of content and especially if you like Cyberpunk. 15 € is too much for it though, so grab it in a sale (they are frequent enough). I'm looking forward to play Dragonfall and see if they added a bit more flesh ;)

Dying light is an excellent game which I highly reccomend. Simply, its parkour is incredibly fun, the combat is brutal and the story, well, its all right, the protagonist is pretty basic but there are some npcs who are very well voiced and really get the atmosphere of a wasteland going. All in all I rate this an 8/10 as its brilliant apart from the story and some missions feel restricting or dull.
Below is a more indepth review.
Overall Dying Light is a great game, once you get into it. Firstly it helps a great deal if you have patience, you may find the first hour or so a bit dull and slow paced.
Thats because of the upgrade system, at the start of the game you are not some ninja warrior who can charge into a group of zombies and come out unscathed, nor are you a master of parkour. However as you level up you get to spec points into the skill trees, Survivor - all round skills, Agilty- parkour (some other stuff too) and Power- Attacks and weapon crafting you become a hardened survivor and the game becomes a lot more fun. You level up these skills separately so you dont worry about where you put your points. Personal favourite being the drop kick, if you run and jump then kick you do a double footed kick at whoever is unlucky to be in front of you.
Moving on to the weapon crafting, yes its like dead island but it still makes weapons fun. First off, weapons have a certain amout of repairs, so if it loses its durability you use parts that you find almost everywhere (bins, toolboxes, zombie corpses) to repair it. When there are no repairs left its useless and can be thrown away. There are upgrades for weapons which you can recieve as rewards or buy which simply increase damage, durability or handling, sometimes more than one. Then there are mods, mods are attachments to a weapon found in the form of blueprints which are then crafted and put on a weapon. Examples inclue "Ben Franklins Key" which adds electricity to your weapon. Others include fire, bleeding, poison and  impact (or something like that). I currently have a machete that electricutes and poisons my victims.
The rest of the game is filled with Story missions which (suprise suprise) advance the story, side quest which range from escorting people around town to restoring power to certain areas of the map or stealing batteries from busses in an overrun bus stop. There are also random events which mostly consist of some poor civilian being mauled by a zombie or a supply drop which you have to get to and retrieve before rival survivor groups do. The story is ok but if your looking to get this game for the story maybe wait for a sale or something.

Like B-movies, I tend to gravitate towards games that look like total shlock. Maybe I'll discover an unpolished diamond, or maybe I'll end up with Rock Zombie. I probably shouldn't complain too much, because thanks to this game, I got a foil card drop that sold for $8. That's more than triple what I paid for it and-oh wait. I'm a game reviewer, I'm supposed to complain too much.
It's that time of the year folks! It's another zombie apocalypse and only a trio of badass witches with guitars can save the day. The store page mentions Golden Axe and yep...you guessed it, Rock Zombie is nowhere near as good. I'm not even the biggest fan of Golden Axe, but it's still a competently-made hack & slash. Rock Zombie on the other hand suffers from a sincere lack of effort. It's like the developer actually tried to do as little as possible.
Let's start with the characters. Zoe and Crystal (red & blue) look okay, but then Sasha (yellow) looks unfinished. She's definitely missing polygons, and certain textures (like her eyes) don't look right at all. Each of the gals has the exact same attack animations and moves. I think they also have the same voice, which really doesn't make any sense. To top it all off, while you can unlock clothes and weapons that boost stats, it doesn't really mean anything. Zombies take and do about as much damage as they always will, no matter how much health and strength you think you're supposed to have.
During a zombie apocalypse, you expect the greatest threat to be the zombies, right? Oops. The zombies in this game are only here to waste your time, because you have to kill them all to progress. They'll do their meager little swings, and even attempt some groping maneuver, but you can clobber them easily with the guitar. Puking zombies are actually dangerous, but you can just hit them with the
beam. There are also spiders and marines, but they're not even worth considering. Your moves auto-track, so as long as you're facing the general direction of an enemy, you'll hit them. The whole ordeal is so mind-numbing you'll be lulled into a stupor.
The bosses really aren't any better. The first guy is a puker, so you have to be careful, but I created a fool-proof strategy within seconds of fighting him. I call it the "HORSESHOE OF UNDEATH". Basically you hit the guy, run around him, hit him again, and run back the original position. Alternatively, just picture a clock going from 3 to 9 and then back again. This strategy is what I like to call "TIME TO DIE (again)". You don't want to mix the two, because it could be troublesome. The second boss is a giant spider, that does nothing but lay eggs. The third boss is beaten as easily as running up to him, hitting him, and then running away. The finale is "difficult" in the sense that the wonky hitboxes will cause you to take a lot of damage and probably die a few times. On the bright side, by the end of the game you should have more lives than you know what to do with.
So if the zombies are weenies and the bosses are pathetic, how could you even lose? Well, it might have something to do with all the crap on the ground. Land-mines, spider-webs, puke, and all sorts of other dangerous objects are just lying around for you to run onto. This game is so boring you're liable to be half asleep while you play, so you'll trip over everything. As I said, puking zombies are actually something to worry about. So if you run onto two mines and get vomited on, well that's a guaranteed death.
Even then, I don't think that's any cause for alarm. There are plenty of extra lives to collect, and you get unlimited continues + game saves. The occasional death merely serves the purpose of reminding you that you're playing a videogame. This reminder tends to wear off quickly. Without any challenge, you'll fall back into the stupor, and mash buttons until the next accidental death. You can't even sucker a friend into playing this game with you. There is no co-op play of any sort, which is weird because the gals are perfectly color-coordinated for just such an event.
There are also vehicle sections, because of course this garbage game would have vehicle sections.
I played through Rock Zombie twice. It was one of the worst mistakes of my life.

I tried to give this game a chance, seeing if it could have ANY chance of being a decent game in the future, bad developers or not.
Downsides:
I played the game for an hour and a half on twitch.tv and managed to get 4 planes to take off and one to land. Each plane only ever needed one button press to get the plane going, which meant that all I needed to do was click once every 23 minutes (I didn't need to click anything for the plane that landed). As the start of the game, you get information overload, which is pointless, considering that all you need to do is click on the icon ontop of a plane and it does all the work by itself.

90% of the features the game CLAIMS to have are actually 'To Be Added' when you attempt to use them - Which would be fine if it wasn't a $15 game, early access or not.

Consider this recommendation as having a big asterisk next to the "thumbs up", because I was honestly on the fence about how strongly I actually recommend it. This game's story is going to become my go-to example for a work that needed more love. Because there is absolutely glimmers of brilliance in this game, with original ideas and a very interesting story concept.
It's a roguelite about a highschool girl whom, every time she returns home from school, winds up taking a magical path through a dungeon. One based on the route back home. This is thanks to an unwanted blessing put on her by a witch who is seemingly trying to turn her into a witch. Can Akari sort out her feelings that cause her to be pulled into this world, or will she surrender her humanity and completely become a part of the witch world?
That is a compelling story idea in my opinion, and certainly original a setup for a roguelike-type title! But the story doesn't really deliver on any of these ideas and a lot of what's happening has to be inferred because there aren't much in the way of story scenes or dialogue. Even the support characters in the form of the witches that Akari befriends in the game's main town aren't really given much chance to shine. I wanted to know not just more about them, but I wanted to see a lot more character development for even Akari herself. The story is very thin on the ground for such a great hook and it feels like they wrongly gave up on it.
How about the gameplay? Well, I have to admit. It actually impresses me how much this game does a good job of teaching the player how to ideally perform best in a roguelike, without even so much as a tutorial to do it. You essentially cast spells and make all of your attacks using your healthbar. Your healthbar is easy to replenish with frequent healing item drops and a backup health meter that quickly regens it anyway, though itself depleting over time. The game becomes a matter of juggling your resources and thinking outside the box with the spells you discover to eliminate enemies quickly and efficiently, without putting yourself in too much danger.  (even a light breeze will kill you if you don't pace yourself with your attacks)   Because roguelikes at their core are about resource management and application as well as eliminating enemies quickly, this is a great game to build good habits with. The boss fights in this game are also, unusually for the genre, mechanically interesting and demand thinking out each turn. All this makes this game easy to recommend to people who are interested in designing a game in this genre. On top of everything else, it's also really interesting how you use words as seeds to discover new spells with different keywords have different effects. You get frequent chances to do this and it's one more form of permanent progression.
Sadly, the game gets kind of grindy towards the middle and end. Eventually just having enough health to fight even the strongest enemies without being immediately knocked out becomes a matter of how willing you are to drive yourself into a wall over and over. Thankfully the game has a lot of permanent progression and very few truly rare items so it's not as frustrating as it could otherwise be, but with very little story payoff it doesn't feel rewarding to push through it.
Nonetheless, I'm glad I played it and I found some inspiration in its ideas.

Alright this game has to be one of the more addicting I've ever played. Considering it is a roguelike platformer it does have some aspects that set it apart from others in the genre. First is the combat, the game has 12 different classes each equipped with 4 unique skills. One of these skills is their basic attack while the other 3 different skills which have a cooldown. The classes are incredibly varied with each having their own strengths and weaknesses. While I am definitely better with some than others none of them feel extremely underpowered and it is very possible to win the game with each. This variety of classes and abilities that range from damage over time, increased mobility, and temporary invulnerability allows the combat to feel much more varied than some of the other games in the genre.
The levels in the game are fairly limited but they change enough to keep it interesting. A complete run consists of 6 stages. For each of the first 5 stages there are two possible options for the level. For example in the third stage can either be a snowy level with steep cliffs on either side, or a level where the bottom half is underwater. Each of these levels is random to an extent. The levels are predesigned but there are different variations of each level so there is some variety added in that way. Still after a few playthroughs you'll likely see all the levels have to offer. The sixth and final stage is set in stone and is consistant throughout playthroughs.
The game does add replayability in several aspects. There are a decent amount of items in this game and a lot of them have interesting and unique effects that make it fun to discover new items and combinations. It is possible to cycle through the stages after beating stage 5 instead of going on to the boss, so it is entirely possible to rack up an insane amount of items and just mow down anything in your path. Getting to this point is challenging but extremely rewarding once you realize you are pretty much unstoppable.

Talking about difficulty the game is quite hard to start before you get the hang of it. Most likely people will try to take too long on each level farming in order to feel comfortable with their items and levels to defeat the boss. The thing about RoR is that there is a timer that is always increasing and when it hits a certain threshold the difficulty increases. In order to get better at the game one can't get discouraged at initial playthroughs. It takes a bit of trial and error to figure out the value of getting items/levels, vs. the value of getting onto the next level before the difficulty ramps up to far. Once this balance is reached the game is not easy, you still need to be aware of surroundings and plan your attacks, but it becomes much clearer what you need to do.

Of course it is always good to play with some other friends either online or locally. If they already have experience they could be of help in teaching you and possibly complementing you with characters that you havent unlocked yet. For the price you could easily get your money's worth. If its on sale especially, take a flyer on it, you could find yourself addicted trying to get better, at that price it would be worth it just for the soundtrack which I have to point out is amazing.

Lays down the foundation for a really good game... and then leaves you wanting.
Can't say I had a bad time. I have really enjoyed my whole 10~15 hours of Shadowrun.
The art and music are good and true to the cyberpunk universe. The fighting is simple yet quite tactical and enjoyable, and while you will miss your 93% hit chance suspiciously too often, it's not too frustrating (definitely not as much as X-com) even in hard mode.
The storyline is the big star of the show, with a rivetting plot that you cannot miss or forget, simply because there is only one straight line throughout the game.
This is possibly the most linear RPG I've ever played, so if you are looking for open world or side quests, stay away from this. There is literally just one side quest in the entire game, and it doesn't seem to change anything.
There is however a lot of freedom on how to spec your character and its class, but this is also where it builds up excitement to leave you wanting at the end. There are so many options to choose from, which seemingly open many doors... most of which never become of use. If you want an example, you get rewarded a whopping 15 skill points after defeating the last boss, after which..... credit roll !
All of this feels like a prologue to something greater, like the devs just lay the bare foundations of the game and then vanished hoping the community would build up on it.
...and they have! The game has an editor and there are lots of community levels to choose from, finally offering you a way to use those interesting mechanics  which were underexploited in the main campaign, like the matrix hacking.
Whether you call it a cheeky dev serving you a teaser, a greedy dev letting the community do the work, or a wishful dev trying to unleash the public's imagination in true table top RPG fashion, the end result is still, a very well rounded game which will keep you entertained without overstaying its welcome.

Antichamber is an odd game to describe. Mechanically, Antichamber utilizes first-person puzzle techniques with aesthetic touches from other first-person narrative games. On many games this would be a one and done deal, but Antichamber's aesthetics and level design are top notch and gave me a lasting impression. The clean, white rooms with hints of color provide one of the catchiest visual styles I've seen from any game to date. With special regards to the early stages of the game, Antichamber challenges the player to forego their sense of reality and logic, to embrace the games universe as it creates a world with challenges that couldn't really be duplicated in real life. While the later part of the game foregoes a lot of this wonder in the face of more complex puzzles, Antichamber is still worth a playthrough if you need to reflect or simply experience a new take on puzzle games.

Teleglitch is a very interesting game. You play as a worker in an abandoned military facility after a teleportation experiment goes wrong, turning the facility into a blood-bath. Your goal is to make it out of this mutant-ridden facility in one piece, but doing so is very difficult. In your way stand numerous foes and halls that rewrite themselves each time you play. Adding to the problem is an overall lack of resources; budgetting your consumable items and having steady is imperitive if you want to survive. The game's aesthetics really wrap the experience up in a tight package, immersing you in the psuedo-dystopian environment. It mixes Atari-like graphics with a programming code-like GUI giving off a retro/scientific mix. Overall, I really enjoy this game. It's one of the few games that can make me truly feel panicked and alone while also being addictive enough to rope me back for another go after I've inevitably failed. Definitely get this game if you're a fan of rogue-likes (get it soon while it's on the Humble Rogue-like Bundle!)

Teleglitch is an excellent top-down Rogue-like with great visuals, creepy atmosphere, and a deep/awesome crafting system.
The visual presentation in Teleglitch is wonderful. You feel almost like you're watching from a CCTV system. The audio is pretty clean and helps immersion. However, enemy sounds could stand some diffentiation and to be brought a bit above the noise-floor to help with recognition.
The crafting system is brillaint. You have so many options to craft from the random bits and pieces scattered about. These items can drastically change the game, or even change how you choose to play the game. It is a central mechanic, and it is thought out well, and executed just as well.
The only thing I dislike about Teleglitch is the insistance that there be limited save capability. In order to resume from Level 3, you need to clear Level 5, and so on. If you aren't terribly adept at the game, it is likely you'll only ever see the first two (boring) levels, before the difficulty curve hits a brick wall.
So, I found myself wanting to explore more of the game, especially the cryptic computer logs, but being unable because I never could clear the first few levels. This is a pretty fundamental design flaw.

Mirror's Edge is bold in being substantially different from most other games. The art style is sharp and vibrant, which really draws you into the dystopian, perhaps Orwellian, vision of the future. In addition, the gameplay is fluid and addictive for the most part; it is only interrupted by the occasional questionable level design. The storyline is certainly not groundbreaking, but fits well with the rest of the game, and does trigger some moments of reflection in the player.
Overall, having played the single player story through three times (twice on console and once on PC), I can safely say that this game is well worth your time and money. Just don't go in with towering expectations. The time trials are a nice addition, which I'm sure will appeal to hardcore players looking to squeeze out the best time they can from a certain level.

Antichamber is, by far, one of the most unique, mind-bending video games ever made.  It's literally like playing in a world as imagined my M.C.Escher; nothing makes sense, rooms and hallways break the laws of physics, MADDENING perspective tricks are played on you, and, despite being completely sterile, and without a single other living thing (as far as I've played!), it's mildly terrifying.  The hints to solve the puzzles are cryptic, and carefully written as to not give them away, but, after some (possibly deep!) thought, give you an "a ha!" moment, where you don't feel cheated by being told the answer, or robbed of the accomplishment of solving the puzzle.
There's some weird central control room that has a map, and an ominous timer counting down from 1 hour... I have NO idea what happens when you run out of time!  There's no explanation given to the nature of, or why you've been placed in this world, which adds to the eerie gameplay experience.
Antichamber is HARD, and because of the clever, reality-bending gameplay, is mentally exhausting to play; a half hour or so is all I could take.  While I don't see myself playing all the way through this game, it's one I feel very guilty about missing out on.  I bought it primarily because it's so unique, I consider video games works of art, saw this as a must have for my collection, and wanted to support the developers of such an amazing piece.  Even if you don't complete this game, you have to get it, if only to experience it for an hour, and to make sure more works like this keep the video game industry alive, interesting, and vibrant.  2 thumbs up.

The game which made a base ground for Payday and Payday 2. It was not bad among other shooters 10 years back, but, after the time passed, it's not worth to actually play it anymore.
Let's forget about compatibility issues (GFWL isn't working, but that's no big deal anymore, just a game without achievements and multiplayer). What were the selling points of the game? Intense action? Oh, c'mon there are plenty of games with that, but alot better. Deep, troubling story? Oh, yeah, again, we have plenty of them around, about mass-murdering psychos like Trevor from GTA V, and even ever-drunk baldy Max Payne et cetera, cetera, cetera...
So, as a "pro" points for the game, everything's compromised. The shooting process itself is bad, the AI is very, very bad, and it's only getting worse (dumber) on the "Hard" ("Morphine") difficulty setting. Even the music (performed by Jesper Kid, if that rings any bells) isn't good and thrilling anymore.
All the cool level setups, borrowed from such Michael Mann's movies as "the Heat" or "Collateral", are no so great - since they were copied too many times, and since they're not original or well-made in the first place.
The story of betrayal, where betrayed betrays betrayer, and betrayer straighten things up by more betrayals... Well, it sounds stupid, but it still sounds better than it actually is in the game.
Note that Kane and Lynch isn't a bad game because it's about bad men. No, it's just a very mediocre shooter, which was lame at shooting and secondary-made from the start, and aged very badly. With all those tech troubles... Now it's just doesn't worth the hassle. If you want shootouts - look for GTA great heists, or the Payday 2 - they do all that what was good in the K&L much better.
So, my mark is 6/10. Game was worth a one go through in the time it was new. Now, it's better to stay away - unless you have some nostalgia troubles, which I doubt. Try a Youtube walkthrough, maybe? And remember, the shooting, especially aiming, is really bad there.

Solid game with a simultaneous turn-based system (similar to roguelikes). It is an RPG with a level system where the protagonist gets stronger as she explores the dungeon. Death removes your consumable items but your stats and magic remain. Other then staves (which you don't lose on death), there isn't really equipment in this game.
Gameplay is pretty fun. The majority of your deaths are going to be your fault because you messed up or didn't prepare adequately. Interestingly, all spells in this game are cast from health. You have MP, which is used for your spells, except if it hits 0 you die. I've gotten trapped several times without enough mana to cast anything and died. I've also cast a spell that brought my life down too low and failed to kill the enemy and then I got hit and died.
The spell system lets you create spells and name them, and the name determines the kind of spell it is. Putting "Red" or "Star" in the name gives you a fire-element spell, putting "Beam" or "Arrow" causes the spell to be an attack that shoots out in a straight line in front of you. It doesn't have that much variety and you'll probably see everything a few hours in but it's a pretty cool mechanic.
Story/writing is basic and there isn't much. I wish there was more, as I liked some of the dialogue in the game and there's plenty of unexplored ideas in the setting like the origins of the witch world and the background of the other NPCs. Translation seems fine, the spell naming system works well and there aren't any bad typos or grammar errors that I can see.
I would have preferred a manual or ingame bestiary that explains what the elemental weaknesses are. As it is, they get mentioned once or twice but not in too much detail and you have to figure most of it out yourself. They also say machines are weak to electricity but the only machine in the game is the tank which is a powerful late game enemy that didn't seem to be particularly vulnerable to electricity (or anything else really).
Music only has like one or two simple tracks that repeat all the time, so not good, though the ending credit theme is a vocal song which sounds nice.
Overall, a good game, relatively short and simplistic but worth trying if you're interested.

Kane and Lynch: Dead Men is a game developed by IO Interactive and published by Eidos Interactive
The characters are what really sold me in this mediocre action game. Unlike other series in which you play as "bad guys" who ultimately tend to do the right thing, Kane and Lynch are 100% scumbags
Kane is a self-serving, traitorous sociopath and Lynch is just completely mental. It's a real treat to see how they interact with each other and how their personalities affect the storyline.
The combat is good, not great. The cover system is a little wonky and the AI is outright terrible at times, but I was always having enough fun that these issues didn't bother me much. Shooting feels off at first, but as you progress and get a feel for the weapons, it becomes a total joy
You really get the feel of desperation that would accompany a heist gone wrong leading into a frantic shootout with the cops
The graphics are pretty mediocre, and look like what you'd expect from a non AAA game title in 2007. That being said, the levels you play in are more than interesting enough to make up for it
You'll go from banks and upscale office buildings to the streets and rooftops of Tokyo to Havana in the middle of a political revolution
Overall, this is a solid game with a few flaws that stand out, but definitely won't ruin the experience of playing as such interesting characters in such interesting situations. And for only 6.99EUR, you can't go wrong giving it a try!

So yeah, I highly recommend this game, it's really charming and brings out unique experience!

This is probably my favorite roguelike game that I own on Steam. I think it's a little more fair than Binding of Isaac, which can be frustrating because some powerups set you back and you can't get rid of them. This game just makes all of that an inventory system. If you decide you don't like a gun, you might as well ditch it, or try to make it into something else. You have SOME control over what you get because of the crafting system, so that's really cool.
In terms of the level design, I like that there are some items you can always find in a level (like the bunch of empty cans or canned meat in level one), but it never ultimately feels like I'm playing the same level twice, and the game is constantly surprising me with ambushes. This really enhances the survival horror aspect of the game as well, because you really never know what's lurking around the corner, or if you can even handle it.
This game is only missing one thing for me to consider it to be ABSOLUTELY INSANE, and that's online coop. Yeah, sure, you could argue that it would mess with the balance and atmosphere of single player. Just leave single player alone, then. Single player's pretty great as is. I'm just saying, I could convince a lot of people to start playing this game if they knew they could play it with a friend, and I imagine rationing ammo and health between multiple people would add an interesting layer of depth to gameplay as well.

From a beginner standpoint, this game is trying very hard to be quite impenetrable. Someone recommended this game to me after I got bored of Eternal, which, if nothing else, is a very cleanly designed CCG, but this game is a mess.
First impressions weren't great. I couldn't reach a menu to adjust volumes or play the game in fullscreen without finishing the tutorial. That's... real lazy. Once I did get into the actual game, a lot of other visual gripes started showing up.
For example, I found it difficult to tell what faction some cards were without mousing over them, because the only indication seems to be a tiny dull icon at the bottom of a card. The cards look basically identical. The text is oversized, and yet information about what a card actually does is still hidden behind a mouseover menu. Heck, the UI is such a shameless port that they even left in the little sparkly effect over the mouse cursor whenever you click somewhere.
The art is all pretty good, but the art style is all over the place. It's like they didn't have a style guide, and instead just commissioned half of deviantart to do hot chicks and called it a day. It seems to range all the way from chibi style to generic digital art to hyper-detailed fantasy pinups, and its real jarring.
I also had a lot of trouble just trying to learn the game, as the pacing seemed really off. I finished the first story campaign, which ends in a completely unfair fight where you just have to wait until the AI gets a bad draw. Learning to play is also challenging due to the speed of enemy turns and no clear visual cue about what actually is happening. Again, having text on cards, or at least taking a second to linger on effects, would help a lot.
Overall this game is just not very friendly to new players. Call me a noob if you will, but if a game cannot draw new players, it doesn't have much of a chance at growing, and right now this game is a horrible experience for new players.
There are some things to like about this game. I like that each card can be evolved, and has different art (sometimes its just a cheap recolor or mirror though). Voiced cards are cool, and the game seems rather generous with packs, giving you quite a stack to start out with. After that it seemed a lot worse though, and the packs I opened seemed rarely to have anything worthwhile in them.
Unfortunately for me, if all the game has is a few solid mechanics, but actually playing it is a chore thanks to poor design choices, then I am not having a good time.

Well, where do I start?
This game is in no ways a bad game, but, I have to say that some of the decisions taken by Tripwire were kinda off-putting.
I've been following the development of this game since before the ZedConomy update, and I can see why some the early adopters are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at Tripwire.
To be honest, I don't really mind these MT's, since they are merely cosmetical, but I think they should have announced the inclusion of them at least 1 month earlier to prevent the huge backlash that it caused.
Now, the updates themselves were painfully slow, especially if we take in account that this game was originally planned to be out in 2015.
The PVP mode was really bad at the time of release, and I personally think that it was a mistake, and that the time and resources that TWI spent on creating it should have been used on adding content for the core game mode, like new weapons.
The Survivalist perk is underwhelming to say the least and, in my personal opinion, goes against the idea of having a Perk based gameplay. It's basically a Jack-of-All Trades which does a mediocre job at everything. Also, it doesn't even have weapons of it's own, it just uses weapons from the other "real" Perks.
Now, let's talk about the good things!
-It's a gorgeous looking game
-Well optimised, even a toaster can run it
-Fun gameplay
All that said I'd reccomend this game to anyone who just wants to shoot some ugly ZEDs in the face.

Sometimes Antichamber is smile-inducing puzzling, and other times it is a source of hair-pulling frustration.  It certainly makes you think, but I think the biggest difficulty is that because it is so intentionally confusing at times, it's very easy to forget where you have and have not been.  Therefore I would recommend playing it in as connected a series of sessions as possible.  If you want to complete 100%, as my personality compelled me to do (!), then you will have a hard time "tying up loose ends" if you leave it too long, finding yourself _rediscovering_ the same exits from puzzle rooms that you have already completed and wasting a little time - which started to make me feel a bit bored.
I actually have a hard time knowing whether to recommend this game or not.  It's fun, and satisfying, but also pointless and infuriating.  A lot of the puzzles require _discovery_, and that can sometimes mean the dreaded "wandering round rooms not knowing what to do".  Sometimes you feel like you have to find the puzzle before you can actually solve it!
My guess is that some people will love Antichamber and some will hate it.  I found myself flip flopping between these extremes!

Not a rogue-like but still a great game. The combat and level design are very rogue-like but that's where the similarities end. There is no permadeath here. When you die you retain your level, your stats, your magic and your important items. You also retain most of your progress since there are checkpoints every 4 levels that you can skip to after you die.
The magic crafting system is kind of fun and the text parsing for naming spells works surprisingly well considering the rest of the translation is pretty bad. You pick up "Anonymous Magicite" and when you use it you get to give it a name. The effect of the resulting spell is determined by what you name it. Something like "Holy Beam" might give you a straight shot magic with the Holy attribute while "Fire Storm" might give you an AOE attack with the Heat attribute. You could also type in nonsense just to see what you get. There are tons of combinations of effects and crafting magic could be great fun except for one thing...
In this game you don't have HP and MP. Well, you do except you use MP for magic, you lose MP when you take damage and you die when you reach 0MP. There are no typos in that sentence. "So what the hell is HP for?", you ask. HP allows you to regen MP. You lose HP over time and when you use certain types of magic. If you're at 0HP, you don't regen MP. So think of MP as your health except you're playing a brawler where you're only allowed to use those special moves that cost health and think of HP more like a hunger bar. This actually has a serious impact on playstyle...
You see, you can't play around with magic much due to the health system. If you use high cost spells, you open yourself up to dying easily. If you use low cost weak spells, enemies can end up hitting you which costs you MP, anyway, so you should have just used stronger spells. Worst of all, if you're in a pinch you can't really do anything aside from teleport away. Heal yourself and you take hits which cost MP and then you attack back which cost MP and then if you don't kill all the enemies in one shot, they hit again which costs MP and you're probably dead. Basically, what it all boils down to is that you'll be running a very specific setup: your most efficient damage spell to exactly 1 or 2 shot enemies, a cheap ping to clean up anything with low health, a bomb in case you get overwhelmed and a wild card which could be a teleport, a heal or a protect spell. It's just odd how limiting the HP/MP system is considering how wildly creative the magic system is.
Overall it's a great game as long as you aren't expecting an actual rogue-like and I do recommend it. It may sound like I complained a lot but it's more a matter of being confused by the design choices than anything else. It's a fun game for what it is. Give it a shot. Give it a Giga Frost Shot, in fact.

Simple yet fun little rpg. More for the nostalgia factor.
Approached by a stranger in the night calling for help, you reach out and without a word they vanish. Moments later you hear the cries of creatures in the distance. Carefully proceeding forward you notice a bright light shining from the room ahead. What is this glowing crystal shaped object? The lightest touch suddenly sends a surge of energy that washes over your body. Voices in your head mutter words you cannot comprehend. Regaining consciousness you immediately notice the the creatures are now in your sight, without a thought a bright flash of light bursts forward toward the beasts. As they keel over you are not shocked, only now focused with a sense of urgency, to find your way out these once familiar streets that have seemingly turned into a dungeon. Traveling onwards, feeling much stronger from the experience of battle and now have some idea what might lurk beyond the next corner.
Pros-
Responsive controls and reasonable soundtrack.
Simple yet enough challenging enough to feel rewarding.
Combining a wide range of spells, some of which you get to name yourself.
Cons-
No voice work.
No achievements.
Repeated tilesets become stale quickly.
Unknown Spells named first, difficult to sort later.
IMO should lower the price a bit, several comparable products that offer more. Enjoying the game so I'll give it a thumbs up overall, keeping in mind what I've mentioned. Cheers folks.

Firstly, bias aside: this was the first LEGO title I ever played. In some ways I was spoiled to come to expect great things from all other LEGO games. Regardless, apart from some exceptions, LEGO Marvel Superheroes is a hugely satisfying experience from beginning to end. A stellar voice cast and clever dialog and references to popular culture that LEGO games are known for, along with an entertaining variety of level design and character selection made for hours of non-stop fun. A good mix of intuitive design and challenging puzzles, where LEGO Marvel Superheroes shone brightest was the open-world city of New York. Not all characters were notable (and there were so many of them), but I found a core group of them to be essential in combat, satisfying to control and well-designed in terms of abilities while interacting with the world. A must for any fan of the Marvel Universe, and a no-brainer for any fan of LEGO games.

Faster Than Light is a space semi-rouglike where you pilot a ship through space and micromanage the crew and systems onboard while trying to fight off enemies that will not stop until you're a pile of smoldering space-scrap.  It has a huge amount of hype behind it, and it is mostly well deserved.  The music is superb, the gameplay is fun and it's quite a charming game overall.  I would recommend picking it up, especially on sale - it hits $2.50 at times, and it is easily worth that.
FTL has awesome, addictive gameplay with a high amount of replayability; however, while it may seem infinite at first, it really begins to seem like you've seen everything the game has to offer after a few play sessions.  Games take awhile, and, while random, there isn't really that big of a pool of things that can happen to you out in deep space.  While there may be minor variances, it mostly boils down to: Warp into a place, oh no! there's a spaceship here, fight it, warp to the next sector.  Don't get me wrong, the game is a lot of fun, but after 4 or 5 runs, you can kind of expect what's going to happen in a future game.
To combat this, there are many different unlockable ships, all of which provide different ways to play, but that said, you really don't have much motivation to go unlock those after you've dumped a couple hours into it.
Pros:
Soundtrack
Fun gameplay
Interesting mechanics
Cons:
Not a very large pool of random things that can happen (wears out fast)
Games take a long time

So, I'm going to get my blasphemous heresy out of the way quickly... I actually prefer this game to the original X-Com: UFO Defense. Okay... So. I do miss some things like having multiple bases all over the world and having to defend those bases whenever the aliens feel like you need to be taken down a notch. However, I think that the satelites system is a reasonable compromise for streamlining that aspect a bit. The streamlining and tight focus altogether is what pushed this game over the original for me. Instead of doing your math to understand things like how far you can move and still be able to get a reaction shot in, that's all taken care of, by replacing the whole action points thing with giving you exactly 2 for each soldier per turn. I think that was a brilliant move, and makes the game feel like a nice and tight tabletop game. One that's not too overly complicated. So, the barrier for entry is very low, and it only takes a short bit to acquaint yourself with the mechanics to get you to the meat of the game right away: Strategizing. So, too, with all the streamlining and focus, I'm pleased that the game still provides you a good challenge to twist your head around. Just brilliant work by the team, and I hope that I can afford to get the expansion pack soon. I love this game more and more the more I play it, and I can honestly say that it's fast becoming one of my favorite games ever.

Originally I enjoyed this game. Then I started realizing how hard it was, even maxing out skill lines for each character, to do...anything.
There is no actual tactical combat in this; your team blindly follows your character until they blunder into an enemy group, who immediately gets to react and take cover and shoot you up. You can only take cover once you've already entered combat, and you cannot manually start combat; the enemy starts combat for you EVERY TIME.
Not only that, but there are either really bad bugs relating to gunshots to enemies or - and this is pure hypothesis I've come up with because there's no documentation beyond the description of Body - the Body attribute makes it so there's a chance for every single attack to only deal half damage...meaning every single attack roll has three rolls: whether you hit, whether you crit, and whether it's weak, and enemies have a higher Body score than you seem able to achieve and have a decent chance of hitting at anything but point blank range, meaning while they may not hit as often, it will hurt more. It got to the point I started quick-saving before ever shot, and my own experiences suggest that you need to take about 30% off of the shown percentages for attacks (even on the easiest difficulty level), because 99% misses about 1 out of every three attacks, and I've only occasionally landed hits with percentages below 55% (call it 1 in 20 or more).
Want a definite bug that's gone through every patch thus far? When firing an assault rifle on full-auto, once one of your five shots misses, every other shot misses. Always. It doesn't matter if you've got a 99% chance to hit; if your first attack roll is that 1%, you won't hit anything at all.
Oh, and you can't carry more than one weapon of a particular class, which means you can't carry both a sniper rifle and an assault rifle, because they're both RIFLES. If you want to have both long- and close-range options you have to split your karma points (XP/skills) on two SEPARATE weapons.
And my personal favorite screwed-up design option? Every conversation pretends you are by yourself. You can have (or be) one of the most skilled deckers ever on your team, but you don't have an option to ask him to hack a terminal except in very rare circumstances. You can have a troll on your team with tremendous strength, but it's YOUR strength that matters for bashing things down in conversations. YOU have to know things, rather than being able to delegate or actually ask your freaking teammate who's standing RIGHT NEXT TO YOU. I totally get some of this in games like Pillars of Eternity, because some of what you do is in the spirit world and only you can interact with it, but even there some of it irks me (because I should be able to have someone else light a fire with their face if they're the right race), but at least they let you use teammates for a lot of stuff. Here, though? We're seriously talking about maybe three times in the entire game where you get to use the skills of someone else on your team, out of hundreds of times skills and attributes are checked.
I wanted to like this game. I wanted to want the Hong Kong game that came out after. But after repeatedly coming across the stuff above, as well as the most recent problem I've had where there is endless combat heading into the final battle even when there are no enemies around, and my game is corrupting save games made during combat, which means I can either run the entire last level with nothing but autosaves, or run the (high) risk of having to start over from the beginning......I cannot like it, and I cannot recommend it to anyone unless they're incredibly masochistic. Finishing this game has become a task I have to force myself to do, and even then the game is preventing me from doing it with this corrupt savegame issue.

DISCLAIMER: Don't pay full price.
I feel like I will leave that disclaimer at the top of many other Recommendations from here until forever.
While Mirror's Edge is a beautiful and fun game, it is not worth the full money either. Well, perhaps it is, depending on your interests. Call me a Scrooge, if you will.
But I found the game terrifyingly short as I beat it in a few hours, and neither the time trials nor returning to the story for the collectibles really make me want to keep playing, so I find no replayability either. Hence, I believe it lacks enough to justify the full price tag.
However, the game is definitely worth playing and it's very fun. The parkour style running is interestingly done and lends to puzzle-like rooms very well, often livening up the game instead of making you simply run down a hallway over and over. The combat isn't too great, but it's not really a combat-oriented game, though I did like that sewer section where you can snipe at the guys in the tunnels.
As I said already, the game is also beautiful. Man, it may kill your machine if you don't have something new. I have a newer laptop which is able to handle quite a lot of gaming, actually, but full graphics on this game would make it churn heat like no other. It still ran beautifully, though, even with all of the settings maxed out, with the exception of a few places here and there which would lag the game into oblivion. Oddly enough, most of those sections didn't seem to have anything around that made sense with the lag, as I couldn't figure out why the game would die out in an empty hallway, for instance.
In any case, if you've been interested in the game, certainly purchase it on sale. I never thought I'd play it and eventually I bit the bullet and got it. I'm glad I did.

It's a definite sequel for a really enjoyable first entry Killing Floor, but with every aspect of it is much better, pumped up, more detailed, more bloody, more FUN!
The Graphics are amazing, and well optimised, it could run on weaker PC on normal settings, and this includes well detailed outlook, amazing animations which make the gory-fun more enjoyable, the splittings-cutting off-amputation fest was never that much fun for a long time (not that it would be a high priority for me or something, but this game is really about this).
The gameplay is also more polished, it is also up to date with it's well refined controls, where the fashlight can be on despite whatever weapon you have. The game engine can stand much more pressure than the KF1 ones, where even with bit of lag it was really hurtful to play through, here however you can maintain your enjoyment with a solid gameplay, where you can flexibly handle your aim and shots, your overall killing experience.
The music is also more brutal, hell man, it's more grindy just making the body-digesting procedure even better.
Only one issue I have encountered with is the Server Browser mechanic, which is highly pain in the hole, because it's just not practical at all, even KF1 had better one, so from this aspect it's kinda awkward... but at least it has also an automated server search where you can easily join a random game based on your filter setup.
Summary:

*Pros:
+ Bloodily beautiful graphics with plethora setup customizations, including special, powerdemanding-FX options
+ Hellishly polished gameplay, which put the KF overall experience on the next level
+ More brutal music in the background making the gorefest more authentic
+ It's just more enjoyable than its predecessor
*Cons:
- Awkward server browser in places
(-) It might not be as scary, or not on the same way as KF1 was
Overall: 8.5/10

TL;DR AT END
A brief, bleak experience, Kane and Lynch: Dead Men is a morally bankrupt piece of fiction. Nothing you do in this game is for "the greater good", everything is in the interest of the protagonist: Kane. The game begins with Kane being broken out of a prison transport and everything goes to hell from there, one selfish scenario after another, with Kane's psychopathic (literally) partner Lynch almost constantly throwing a wrench into our anti-hero's plans of redemption/revenge.
If that already sounds appealing to you, then have at it. But for me, personally, I did not find this game very enjoyable. It does nothing new or creative, little is inspired about its gameplay; its graphics have aged poorly; cover system is absurd; voice acting excluding Kane and Lynch is subpar, and the music is often times unfitting to the tracks' respective scenes.
To top it all off, the biggest gripe I have here is the story and narrative. The tale of Kane and Lynch is actually pretty damn good in it's own weird way. They're interesting characters who have interesting pasts. They say very little, but when they do talk it's typically insults thrown at each other. And the game says little about their pasts, which is what I find appealing: Kane and Lynch, as characters, are ultimately mysterious. Much like Eidos' Agent 47, these two pitiful, middle aged, nutjobs have a lot of mileage and know a lot that they're not spilling. I like characters like that.
It's a pity the story was presented in a poor manner. The writing was actually strong for the most part, but everything seemed very rushed in favor of the shootouts.
[And now for deep, pretentious "video-games-are-art'" theories below]
I also like transgressive art and fiction, which I feel this game is an excellent excercise in, on multiple levels.
Kane and Lynch are not normal, by any means, and lash out at the world around them in a very violent, shocking way which the developers seem to present to the player in a sort of "Look at this! Isn't this nasty? Isn't this so very, very awful?" tone. I kind of dig it.
In addition, Kane and Lynch is a BAD game about BAD men doing BAD things. Remember that multiple level thing I was talking about? This is it. True transgressive art is distressing to view, it's not enjoyable. Just like this game.
Call me a pretentious nerd or whatever: I like Kane and Lynch: Dead Men almost exclusively because it has poor gameplay. I say this in a similiar vein to how Spec Ops: The Line is a game that was intentionally made to be run of the mill and mediocre for narrative purposes. I feel Kane and Lynch was made intentionally mediocre and subpar for its own narrative reasons. The gameplay is so incredibly barebones that it's difficult to enjoy, but somehow it's not boring either; it just makes sense. I can't see this game having been made any differently, the almost painful mediocre tinge of everything 'Dead Men' presents to the player just sort of... fits.
Just like Spec Ops: The Line.
[Artsy stuff ends here]
"But, how did this game spawn a sequel with a bigger budget, a comic and now apparently a movie is in the works?" Good question. This game was a commercial success, and made quite a bit of dough despite all its shortcomings.
TL;DR: Kane and Lynch is not a good game. Much like its wonderfully transgressive and outrageously selfish protagonists, it's functioning (usually) but what's under the hood is old and nasty. Buy it if you like the Max Payne series, or if you like playing the 'bad guys' a la Hitman (also made by IO Interactive).
I'm recommending this game purely because it is definitely worth the asking price of seven bucks, and a no-brainer on sale. Is it worth five hours of your time? Probably not. Is it worth trying? Absolutely.
Pros
+ Environmental variety
+ Kane and Lynch
+ Challenging
Cons
- Uninspired gunplay
- Tedious level design
- Poor enemy variety
- AI is autistic
- Havana chapters are putrid
- The narrative was poorly presented
- Looked good back in '07, has aged poorly

This game is as good as you could ever hope for a 4x to be. I've not put nearly as many hours as many into this game, but I still can't resist its pull - my yearly playthrough always sucks me in.
The gameplay follows the standard formula (and in many ways defines it) of eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate. The paths to victory are myriad, and every time you play you will find yourself in the middle of a new story - one that pits Bismarck against Ghandi, and Queen Elizabeth against Attila.
The caveat that I'll issue is that this game is not great on its own; the expansions (Gods & Kings, Brave New World) are practically required for the new systems that they add and the revisions that they make to the core of the game. With these expansions, the game is trule a masterpiece.
The lingering negative thought I have is that the game does not support mods in multiplayer; other games have managed to support this, but in Civ V this was apparently not a possibility that Firaxis was willing to support. So, sadly, 90% of the content that has been generated by the excellent modding community since release is not available to play with your friends.
