Violence in our video games is a pretty common thing nowadays, and while there is nothing wrong with that I don't think that the true extent of violence's effect on people is looked at very well. You can gun down a bunch of people in video games and it seems that it doesn't have too much effect on the story, with exceptions to Undertale and Dishonored. Our protagonists kill so many people that they, reasistically at least, are either sociopaths who don't care about murder or have therapy bills up to the roof. Games seem to ignore this aspect in the story, and if anything try to downplay it by showing that they're emotionally stable and act just like normal people even though they've killed more people than some wars have, even giving witty one-liners like in GTA. Ultimately, it's an ignorable aspect of these games, and competent writers do a good job with making these characters likable, but you almost never see a developer make a ♥♥♥♥ed up character who can't think straight because of the killing they've done. That's where Kane and Lynch: Dead Men comes in. Made by IO Interactive, the studio known for the Hitmen games, Kane and Lynch: Dead Men looks at this issue from a much more interesting angle. Does it do it well, though? Let's take a look.
STORY: You're Kane, a former mercenary on death row for killing a bunch of people. However, when you're being transported to be killed, you and Lynch, a fellow inmate, are broken out by a mercenary group called The7. Unfortunately for Kane, The7 have beef with him for running away, leaving men to die and taking a bunch of cash. Kane is forced to get the money back, as they have his family held hostage and will kill them if he doesn't do it, with Lynch tagging along as help as well as someone to snitch to The7 if he ♥♥♥♥s up or tries to run. Things don't go as they should, and Kane and Lynch go after The7. The story is actually pretty solid despite some cliches, it provides a fresher twist on the story by putting it through the perspective of two guys who would be the villains in most other games and it feels like they put effort into it. It does jump around here and there, at one point they just robbed a bank in the US, then all of the sudden they're in a nightclub in Japan, but it could have been much worst in that regard and it's not too bad. There are two endings, both being kind of depressing, but are still solid and aren't horrendously sequel-baity. Sadly the game is pretty short, I finished it in about four hours, though to be fair, it feels like a complete story and, while some stuff here and there could be added, it feels about as long as it should be.
GAMEPLAY: 3rd person shooter. You can carry one primary weapon, one sidearm, and a couple types of grenades around with you. If you're downed during combat, Lynch or another AI companion will hit you with some adreneline, but if you go down in a close timeframe from your last hit, you'll OD on it, which encourages you to stay in cover as much as you can. Unfortunately for the player, the cover system is broken at best and at worst barely functions, as you only seem to go into cover at the ends of things that you can take cover behind, which feels weird. Shooting feels too loose as well, and while it isn't as bad as cover, it's mostly mediocre. You can also command Lynch and your later companions in crime, but unfortunately the command system is kind of barebones and the AI can be pretty stupid. Moving around is fine enough at least, but for the most part, the gameplay is average. I wouldn't say it's unplayable like a decent amount of people say it is, in fact it's far from it, but it's nothing special and the game is held back by it.
GRAPHICS, LEVEL DESIGN, AND PERFORMANCE: It's a game originally released on the Xbox 360 back in 2007, don't expect a pretty game. There are some bad looking textures even for 2007's standards, though it doesn't look terrible and some leeway has to be given to a game almost a decade old graphically. The performance is solid, I got a consistant 60FPS and if it ever dipped below that, I didn't notice it, and the cutscenes are pretty solid for that time. There are also a lot of cool levels, like a nightclub in Japan packed with people (who you can gun down if you want to), opium fields in Venezuela, and a fight in a construction yard which are nice to play around in.
CHARACTERS AND VOICE ACTING: Let it be known that you probably will not like Kane and Lynch, as they are not good people and the game does not go out of its way to make you like them. Kane seems to know right from wrong and he does know that he should be dead, he's just alive so he can protect his daughter and take out The7, but he is a sociopath who kills people and doesn't seem to feel bad. Lynch seems like a better character initially, though it turns out he is a schitzophrenic who has phychotic episodes even if he does take his medication, snaps easily and kills people while blaming his schitzophrenia for it which might not be the full story to why it's happening. They also don't look like the traditional protagonists; they're older, balding, Kane's nose is broken and he has a ♥♥♥♥ed up scar, Lynch is overweight, they look and act like side villains in a video game. With that said, I did kind of end up liking Kane and Lynch, at least to some degree. They both know they're killers and nothing more, which is strangely refreshing to play as. The rest of the characters are mostly irredeemable or unlikable as well, which feels right for a band of killers. The voice acting is top notch as well, which lends to making the characters feel believable.
MULTIPLAYER: There is co-op, though sadly online co-op is not possible, which is a real shame because it would be fun to play this with a friend. If you do play as Lynch during co-op, you get to see the psychotic episodes he goes through in the story through his eyes, which is a badass feature that they added which adds to the character. There is also an online mode which I did not bother with since I'd need to make a Games With Windows account and it's most likely dead anyway, though I hear it actually isn't that bad.
FINAL THOUGHTS: The gameplay is mediocre and while that does hold it back, Kane and Lynch: Dead Men has enough going for it that I feel condifent in recommending it. 7/10, I might be a bit generous to the game, and at it's original $60 I can see it being not worth it, but for eight bucks while not on sale, it's a bargain. If you do want to wait for a sale, I can understand that, but do pick it up at some point, because Kane and Lynch: Dead Men is something really special, and I'm hoping that IO Interactive do something with the franchise in the future.

Fancy walking around some nightmarish 1970s sci-fi artwork thumping creatures in the face (sometimes kicking them when they are down)? I'm not sure I did, but I had a lot of fun.
Zeno Clash is niche. It is also obtuse and unfriendly to newcomers. There are no tutorials (apart from a couple of screen prompts in your first fight); there's no journal, no quest log, no helpful NPCs offering guidance on what to do or where to go. There are entire sub-plots you could miss by not going into the right house in the opening city (which gives no indication it is a hub area). This really is a game in which you are dumped in a world, given the lightest of prods in the direction of a story - and then get left on your own. Persevere and you might end up loving it.
I loved it. The game is pretty short (6 hours or so), the controls are clunky (there's one fight which requires a special ability that will have you gnashing your teeth), but the combat is satisfying, the game is beautiful and it is unlike anything I've ever played (though I might now have to check out Zeno Clash 1).
If you are fed up of being spoon fed AAA baby food, this comes highly recommended.

This to me is what Resident Evil 6 should have been, and what sucks is that it had that potential, but due to a really action packed/compact storyline in the campaigns, it never got to really flesh itself out as a true Survival/Horror. But that's another review for another time. Resident Evil Revelations 2 picked back at the series roots, while doing its best to make cohesiveness with the immense success brought upon by the innovative changes that Resident Evil 4 brought (and yes, I would recommend that game in a heartbeat)
The Good.
Both different segments of the campaign, Claire/Moira and Barry/Natalia, have similarities overall, but just enough uniqueness to keep things interesting when each segment ends. The way you kill the enemies with the red pus on their bodies in Claire's campaign, along with a few others choices and actions, and having them impact Barry's was a nice touch of continuity between both. Both sets of characters had unique weapons and support characters. Claire's weapon set was definitely a touch back to her days starring in Resident Evil 2 and Code VERONICA, while Barry's was reflective of his attunement to the BSAA and preparedness for his investigation. Moira's crowbar/LED flashlight, along with Natalia's brick were nice survival basic touches. The finding of weapons/ammos scattered about the island, enemies no longer dropping items, along with the fact that no two ammo/support packs contained the same amount of said item was a really nice touch in the survival department. The sub-weapons and their combination system was also another nice touch of survival ingenuity, with healing items such as the tourniquets and disinfectant. The flow between switching characters was something that should have been implemented in RE5/6 as it really helped the flow of fights.
Story
The story overall was decent, the flow nice, and there was definitely a few high moments in terms of character progression and development. The only negative in that regard is that Barry and Moira were the only two characters that seemed to develop and progress in the entire campaign. Natalia and Claire were more or less simply 'there', which is really a shame on Natalia's part as she was a big mystery for a big chunk of Claire/Barry's campaign and even after it was all said and done.
The Bad
The game placed a very very heavy emphasis on ammo conservation, which for a survival horror is normally a very good thing. The only issue is the misbalance between the campaigns. In Claire's campaign ammo conservation is fairly easy as with Moira's flashlight, follow-up attacks and so forth. Saving your ammo for the bigger fights was fairly straightforward, but still retaining enough difficulty to make every shot count. With Barry and Natalia, it was easy when fighting the zombie like enemies and as Natalia's brick functioned similar to Moira's crowbar. But when fighting Revenants and zombies you’re forced more or less to strictly melee all the zombies and save your rounds for the Revenants/miniboss Revenants. The final boss was an ammo sponge for Barry’s campaign, leaving you nothing but (hopefully) the magnum and its hoarded rounds for the final phase. Unfortunately this made inventory a nightmare in Barry's case. The final boss segment was a little disjointed as the boss was fairly large in size for the segments you controlled Barry in the caves, and the shifting back to Claire in the helicopter felt a little awkward as well.
Final
Overall, the game was fairly good. I enjoyed the attention to detail in certain areas, and the character development for some. The combat was pretty solid, and the survival aspects added throughout both sets of campaigns really added a much needed survival note to the series. It has a few negatives, but the positives are what is mainly focused on. The series really seems to be going back to its well-established survival/horror roots, and RE7 looks to be only continuing on that path. I give the game a solid 8/10 and give it my firm recommendation to any player progressing through the series.

Think Paper Mario, or Mario and Luigi's Dream Team on Nintendo 3DS.  What I mean by this is not only do you have to choose an action, like attack, for example, but after doing so your character gets ready to do the attack.  At just the right moment you have to press "A" on the control pad for extra damage on that attack.  If you don't time the pressing of "A" just right, you'll still attack, but do much less damage.  It is the same for blocking an attack when it's the other guy's turn to attack. The story itself is great as well and includes many characters that you may have seen over South Parks many years of being on TV.  If you are a fan of turn based combat RPGs, as well as a fan of South park, then you will love this game.

This is a decent RE title. Honestly the series lost me at RE5. Unlike most fanboys who claim halfway through 4 was the death of the series (The end of four seemed to be an actions shooter while he first half seemed to be a horror shooter) I actually liked mostly all of them for individual reasons. Six is the only one that was total crap to me. This series has been all over the place really. Even the new one coming out (Resident Evil 7) which is a first person horror thriller.
Story: It was a decent game really. I started out liking the first few episodes. The concept behind it is very interesting. As a minor spoiler alert, I would like to tell you the actual setting of the game. Claire and Miora get kidnapped and taken to a island where they are toyed with by a woman named the overseer. She paces a bracelet on everyone that if they become o frightened a virus activates in them. This is a really cool concept to me. Barry comes to the island to recue Miora after he recieves her radio transmission. He meets Natalia which is his partner for the rest of the game.
The story how ever was dissapointing, while the concept was amazing. At times it had me thinking about how it is just another RE action shooter. The story failed to grasp me. The end is what upset me the most because it did not seem possible. It also was clearly setting up a sequel which I have interest in for only one part:
The Gameplay: This is by far the best part of this game. Reminded me a lot of RE 4 which is my favorite game of all time. Great mechanics and shooting. Little things like dodging or turning 180 degrees around on spot are little mechinics that make a whole lot of deference. Miora uses a crowbar because she refuses to use a gun. She is also equipped with a flashlight which I liked a lot. It added more the gameplay as well. Blind an enemy with her then uses partner fighting actions to tkae the infected down without using ammo. She also uses her flashlight to find objects which was tideous and was a hindrance cause it kind of slowed me down. I am all for hunting hidden things in games but this method was annoying to me. Especially since she points out things that physically cannot be in their locations or one would see with the naked eye. Natalie uses her finger to point at objects to my same dissapointment.
The shooting is great, most of the infected you interract with have specific ways to kill them. There is a specific bug though that is invisible to Barry and Claire that is really annoying to kill. That was my only gripe. There was a giant guy who threw fire from a barrel which was an interesting idea? But I actul]ally enjoyed my few interractions with him.
Overall: It is worth it for the gameplay and concept. The story is not that interesting at all. I played like an episode a day. It did not keep me to interested but was just a great shooter to pick up and play here and there. There also a few cool mods for this game outside of steam workshop.

I purchased Delicious - Emily's Home Sweet Home after watching someone online play through part of the Delicious series. This title was actually the one that made me decide to buy all the games available on Steam. I hoped that the game was just as fun to play as it was to watch. It turns out that it is.
Home Sweet Home follows Emily and her family, who moves into a new neighborhood. The sitcom style story follows them through different challenges and levels as they attempt to turn their purchased fixer-upper into a home. The time management gameplay is similar to the previous game, Emily's New Beginning, but the menus are different and the selecting items system is new. There are also regular challenges that players can opt into in order to perfect the game.
Pros:
- The game doesn't take itself seriously.
- Art is cute.
- Controls are simple - all mouse.
- Challenges are fun but still somewhat difficult.
- Most achievements can be unlocked simply by playing through the game.
Cons:
- Story is on the ridiculous side.
- Subplots aren't always entertaining or engaging.
- Entertainers sometimes get in the way.
- Some item grinding is necessary in order to get all the achievements.
Of the Delicious games I've played so far, Home Sweet Home is one of my favorites. I liked the new menu system and the new challenges. There are still flaws with it, but it's not a bad place to start for people looking into the franchise.

Emily's HSH is about what I expected from a Delicious Emily game. The QOL issues that earlier titles had are mostly gone (entertainers still get in the way a bit, and some dishes are incredibly similar to each other, but that's just a flaw with the entire series). The gameplay had that frustrating yet addictive quality that makes you ragequit, then restart the game (thankfully, erasing everything in the "branding" folder makes restarting the game quick and easy) with a new strategy that allows you to easily ace the level.
The plot also reached the expected level of sitcom insanity, as Emily's work as a temporary chef reconciles a series of wacky parents to their children (and vice-versa), all while a power-hungry councilwoman plots to demolish Emily's new home (to be fair, Emily's family did break her daughter's legs).
With that said - since the developer outright stated that the current bug-ridden condition of the game is here to stay, and even game breaking bugs like the Russian translation not working at all will never be fixed, I cannot in good conscience give this game a positive recommendation.
Edit - I note that the game's store page no longer claims to support Russian. I guess that's one way to fix things. Simpler than fixing the translation itself.

The best thing about LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is that it delivers almost everything a Marvel fan could want. From Abomination to the Wizard, this game is an A-to-Z (well, A-to-W) love letter to the Marvel Universe that starts with the Silver Surfer gliding across the title screen and ends with a credits song that could not have been better chosen. A few technical glitches and some carryovers from the franchise history keep it from being an outright masterpiece, but it easily ranks as one of the best superhero games I've played in years.
It starts with the characters. Where LEGO Batman 2 offers a sizable roster of heroes and villains, the campaign in LEGO Marvel delivers more playable heroes in a much more coherent story about collecting cosmic bricks around the world before villains do. The first mission starts with Iron Man and Hulk, but the selection of playable characters soon grows to include the rest of the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, loads of X-Men, and even Spider-Man. You'll even switch heroes mid-way through many of the missions, with Cyclops and Jean Grey rescuing Storm and Iceman during an assault on the X-Mansion, or the Human Torch flying in to assist Black Widow and Hawkeye as they infiltrate a Hydra base. The entrances and exits are all handled as part of the story, which gives you a chance to play several characters who all feel like they're part of a single narrative.
What's Next-Gen LEGO Marvel Super Heroes Like?
The same is true of the villains. You can start by chasing Doctor Octopus from the Baxter Building to the Daily Bugle, but you'll soon be flying off to thwart Dr. Doom's plans in Latveria and taking the Rainbow Bridge to stop Loki from stirring up the frost giants in Asgard. I particularly liked how each mission played out as a sort of protracted chase, with the heroes in pursuit of folks like Magneto or the Red Skull, while battling lots of lesser villains like Pyro or the Leader along the way. As great as it all is, telling such an earth-shattering story without major characters like Dr. Strange or Sub-Mariner present feels off. Still, when a game features lesser-known characters like Black Bolt, Captain Britain and HERBIE, it's hard to complain. Maybe they're saving Kang and Ultron for a sequel?
The puzzles in the LEGO games are almost always solved by matching the right power to the right problem, and the Marvel take on this mechanic is particularly inventive. Take
LEGO Marvel Super Heroes
LEGO Marvel Super Heroes offers an original storyline in which Nick Fury calls upon heroes spanning the Marvel Universe to save Earth from such threats as the vengeance of Loki and the hunger of Galactus, Devourer of the Worlds.
Great Games with Huge Casts
Super Street Fighter IV: Arcade EditionLeague of LegendsLeague of LegendsLeague of LegendsSkylanders Swap Force Black Widow for example. She, like Invisible Woman, can spoof security cameras, but Widow also has the acrobatic skill of Captain America, which enables her to access remote areas of the levels, and the brains of Tony Stark, which lets her use certain consoles that would be off limits to other heroes. Throw in a gun, and you've got a very useful character made up of a number of different power sets. Storm and Thor, for instance, can both use electricity to power up stations, but Thor can smash open walls while Storm can put out fires. Even though there are only maybe a couple dozen powers to share among them all, the various combinations of powers ensures that no one feels entirely redundant.
You will get a few power sets that seem a bit out of place; Captain America's ubiquitous shield switches seem a little arbitrary, as does the notion that Wolverine should be really good at digging and climbing. There are also a few that make sense but aren't particularly well implemented. The special sixth sense shared by characters like Spider-Man, Wolverine, and Daredevil is really more for recognizing what walls you can climb than for keeping those characters out of danger.
I finished the main campaign in under 12 hours, but I've been coming back to collect extra characters and bricks for days after. In between missions, there's a massive open-world map of Manhattan to explore, from the Statue of Liberty and Battery Park to the X-Mansion up past Harlem. There's also the massive SHIELD Helicarrier floating over the East River.
The city has loads of attractions, complete with characters to collect and challenges to beat. Over the course of the side missions, you'll help Heimdall take out frost giants on the docks, battle Sentinels in the streets, or take control of a neglectful boyfriend's mind and make him climb the Empire State Building to apologize to his girlfriend.
Experienced gamers won't find many of the open-world puzzles and challenges to be much of a contest; for the most part, you'll simply need to identify the type of task you're facing and then just go hit the right steps in the right order. It's clear that the challenges are aimed at LEGO’s young demographic, so gamers craving a challenge will be let down here. Still, if the allure of putting Daredevil on a motorcycle and having him race Ghost Rider through the Upper West Side sounds fun, the difficulty is sort of incidental. The rare exceptions are the timed challenges, or those that require you to search out objectives that aren't in the immediate vicinity of the challenge.
The biggest pain is the inconsistent, confusing flight system. It attempts to use the same control scheme from the missions where the up and down motion of the thumbstick moves your character toward or away from the camera. Now you'll use face buttons to control the pitch of your character's flight. The problem is that the button you use to ascend is also the button you use to accelerate, and I frequently found myself flying into the side of buildings or massively overshooting my objective. Even with a week or so of playing, it still seems weird to me.
Lego Marvel Super Heroes, Manhattan tour
Even with that one chief complaint, there's just so much to love about LEGO Marvel that I've been playing it a few hours a day for over a week now and am still finding new charms. From unlocking Gwen Stacy and making her jump off the Brooklyn Bridge to watching the heroes dance at Tony Stark's house parties, this game is full of the moments that make Marvel one of the best brands in entertainment.
THE VERDICT
LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is the best thing to happen to Marvel games since 2006's Marvel Ultimate Alliance. It's a warm and witty, multi-layered approach to the brand that ties in hundreds of Marvel's most iconic characters, settings, and stories. While you can knock out the campaign story in around eight hours, the world is rich with content, and I've found myself up late every night for the past week playing for "just one more hour." It may not offer the challenge or player-driven context of this year's other open-world games, but those games would be hard-pressed to deliver as much fun and happiness as you'll find. 9.5/10

one of the best first person shooters of all time, maybe even THE best.  This game was a huge tech demonstration in  a a way when it came out, the physics and graphics were WAAAAAY ahead of  their time.  There are physics based puzzles, mirrors and magnifying glasses work, and the gravity gun is charming and fun beyond words (I want one for realz).  The plot is never really laid out in nitty gritty in either dialogue or in writing, but if you pay attention the story and world are artfully crafted, and engrossing.  The Combine (the bad guys) are a fascinating foe, as cruel as they are alien, and they get fleshed out a good bit in this game and even more in the expansions (totally worth getting BTW).  whether you are burning headcrabs in ravenholm (we don't go there anymore), banging it out with Combine soldiers, or running over ant lions in the car, this game is a total blast.  The levels are linear, as is the style of the older shooters of that era (Halo, call of duty MW 1 or 2's story), but they are large and complex enough you dont feel trapped in a corridor and the world seems real and alive enough for you to buy into it.  The pacing is also notable, sometimes you bust through a door, amped up expecting a fight, only to find a welcome dialogue sequence, and the vehicle sequences and puzzles that break things up from time to time are a treat too (exceptionally well done, the puzzles will only bother really, really stupid people).  Last, but not the least by any stretch of the imagination, the audio is EXCELLENT!  Gunshots echo realistically in canyons and alleys, the chatter from enemies is really cool (especially the flatline when they die), the screaming and howling of the headcrab zombies is terrifying and unsettling, and the audio for the weapons is top notch.
overall, 9.8/10, and if you want to get all picky and don't like decimals, 10/10

A beautiful game with a very distinct art style. While in the actual game you're in a 3D environment, the story parts are in 2D, in style reminiscent of a graphic novel.
Gameplay can become quite frustrating at times, as timing is extremely important. You might find youself repeating the same part of the level literally dozens of times. After the first three levels though, you should probably understand how to solve most of the problems.
The tutorial, while going very in-depth and showing you practically every move you might need in-game, feeds you all the information in one five-minute session. If you're not one of those people that remember every combination of keystrokes right away, you might find yourself in a pinch not knowing what to do when faced with certain obstacles (going from personal experience: by forgetting I had the ability to double tap space while wall running, I added probably one or two hours of gameplay and frustration to my first playthrough). But once you get the hang of the controls and figure out the different ways you can use your surroundings to move around, most of the levels become a breeze.
While the story, in terms of development, is pretty predictable, there's a few aspects that make it (and the whole game) stand out. For one, the main character is a woman of Asian descent, who instead of being driven by some kind of romantic nonsense, is trying to save her sister. No one makes a deal about her being a woman, no one even acknowledges it. She's not special because of it. She's just another runner. And that is really great, in my opinion.
In conclussion: after two hours of head-bashing against the keyboard trying to understand the controls, it quite quickly jumped to one of my top 10 games of all time. The recently announced Mirror's Edge 2 is definitely on my watch list.

This is Hearthstone... but better. Basically, in every way. When I say "in every way" I really do mean EVERY. The campaign is better, the art is better (although that's
subjective - I like it, that doesn't mean you will). The basics of gameplay are the same, but once you're past the basics, it's all soooo much better.
Basically, if you were all like "I wish Hearthstone was more Anime, had a decent single player campaign, and was generous enough in single player to keep playing" then, you've found the right game.
Don't get me wrong - Hearthstone is the Original for this basic style of play, and I love the WoW universe as much as the next gamer, but this game has interwover plots, interesting added mechanics, and a generous (to put it lightly) single player deck expansion setup.
In short: If you liked Hearthstone, you'll like this. If you're an anime fan who likes card games, you'll like this. If you like Free To Play games that don't treat all of their players like potential whales, you'll like this...
And if you like none of those things, I basically don't care if I ever know you.
So... recommended? HELLZ TO THE YES!!

The game is visually beautiful and unique in its concept and execution. However, it is plagued by poor collission detection, far from excellent combat, and bad level design.
The visual aesthetic presents plenty of eye candy and a unique environment where every deformation becomes a potential foothold. The two or three colour pallet is very sharp and coupled with high-resolution textures and lovely lighting definitely delivers the artificial and sterile feel that the art department is trying to put across....just turn the brightness down.
However, none of this matters if half the game is set in claustraphobic ventilation shafts, small rooms, and narrowl subway tunnels that make the levels of Metro 2033 feel spacious and nonlinear. In the open levels, on the other hand, many of the structures serve as mere clutter.'
The gameplay is unique and delivers a very dynamic feel to movement which in other games may not have even been given much thought. Navigating the obstacle courses can be challenging and thrilling, with an emphasis put on quick pace, a keen eye, and an idea of how to get from point A to point B in an increasingly convoluted way.
Nevertheless, the levels leave barely any room for error, and timing is absolutely crucial. Press a button a millisecond too early or too late and you will be treated to the same falling animation for about a billionth time. It doesn't help that poor collision detection results in quite a few attempts where the character simply fails to grab onto a ledge that she is right in front of, or slide down right next to the wall that she could have pushed off of. This results in an absurd quantity of retries presented to you by a barely adequate checkpoint system. Not to mention that most levels are linear and you are given no other option but to retry the same minute of gameplay dozens of times over.
The combat is quite interesting as it doesn't focus on gunplay unlike an overwhelming number of modern games, nor does it rely on repetetive button pressing. Rather, it revolves around catching the right moment for a reversal, swift counterattacks, disarming the opponent, and use of the environment to overcome the more numerous armed opponents. However, all of this doesn't matter when the combat is restricted to two buttons, one of which is contextual and the aforementioned colission detection problems make using the environment very difficult, especially with such a narrow field of view. So instead of jumping on a guard, disarming him, and proceeding to move on to the rest, what most often happens is that the jump overshoots, and you end up riddled with bullets on the ground. This would've been fine if the combat was always avoidable, but there are some sections where the game will absolutely refuse to proceed until every guard has been disarmed and/or killed.
Finally, there is the story, which isn't half bad. At least it's original, even if a little unclear and full of names you can't hope to remember on your first run, as the story is often told while you are running, and thus concentrating on something else.
Overall, I think this is a brillian concept with execution missteps which made it barely playable. I'd love to recommend this game, but since games are meant to be played, not looked at, I'd suggest saving your money for something that you can actually play to relax instead of frustrating yourself.
And hell, there is a new one coming out soon, maybe that'll be better.

This game is as good as you could ever hope for a 4x to be. I've not put nearly as many hours as many into this game, but I still can't resist its pull - my yearly playthrough always sucks me in.
The gameplay follows the standard formula (and in many ways defines it) of eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate. The paths to victory are myriad, and every time you play you will find yourself in the middle of a new story - one that pits Bismarck against Ghandi, and Queen Elizabeth against Attila.
The caveat that I'll issue is that this game is not great on its own; the expansions (Gods & Kings, Brave New World) are practically required for the new systems that they add and the revisions that they make to the core of the game. With these expansions, the game is trule a masterpiece.
The lingering negative thought I have is that the game does not support mods in multiplayer; other games have managed to support this, but in Civ V this was apparently not a possibility that Firaxis was willing to support. So, sadly, 90% of the content that has been generated by the excellent modding community since release is not available to play with your friends.

A breath of fresh air in a dying genre littered with painful alphas and zombie slaying boycots. Dying light has brought the open world zombie survival back from the un-dead. The introduction video was all the convincing I needed! Within 20 minutes of gameplay, I found myself reliving the days of old, Dead Island.  Oh, the memories. Plenty of exploration, enough weapon mods to leave you salivating for more after every devastating blow. And graphics to die for, over and over again. Brilliant zone layouts with plenty of undead & human enemies to slaughter. An extensive crafting system with everything you could possibly need to get the upper hand (especially at night when the crazies get even more crazy). I've put over 30 hours into this game since its release and I can see myself putting at least another 30 into it with the addition of the DLC that I had already pre-ordered with the Season Pass.
Some pros and cons about this game:
Pros:
Fantastic graphics
Outstanding game play
DIY must have crafting system
Intelligent & god fearing AI (approach a couple of Rais's men with a shotgun and you'll see what I mean)
A skill tree to turn the most novice of player into Spiderman in a short period of time
A real sense of imminent "I'm so dead" moments
Great cutscenes and interaction (A truly heart felt feeling that can only come from the guys at Techland)
Insanely fun and sometimes outrageous achievements
Cons:
Lack of melee weapon variety and firearms.. seriously.. there really isn't that much to choose from.
The DLC.. and I can't stress this enough. The Season Pass was about $30. The first DLC was released a few days ago. As far as I can tell, it's only added a total of 2 new quaratine zones (Hard Difficulty), which I managed to fly through in less than 10 minutes. And I hope.. nay.. PRAY, that the remaining DLC to come will be worth that pre-purhcase price.
Overall, this is a brilliant game, and I would highly recommend it to anyone. Just avoid the Season Pass and DLC until a later date.. with any luck it will drop in price, SIGNIFICANTLY.

Antichamber is what happens when puzzle game designers strip away all tradition, get drunk, and decide to see how cruelly they can mess with gamers' heads. Then, when they sober up the next day, there's a hint of remorse as they patch over it with a few words of inspiration on the walls.
To be fair, their minimalistic game design it expertly crafted, to bring highly innovative challenges which really make you think. Much is based on perception and pre-conceptions. You may wander down a hallway, stop and turn around, only to find that the way you came has totally changed. You may also look a little closer through a viewing window, step back, and find yourself transported into a different room. This is all completely seamless, which messes with your head that much more.
This game teaches you that trying something new will be rewarding. It almost always knows which way you'll tackle a challenge first, then give you one of many reassuring messages alluding to the task, or life in general. It gives you motivation to try and try again, in different ways.
And you will want to, because finally overcoming a challenge that left you stuck for ages, makes you feel like
I will admit that I sometimes asked for help from a gamer friend smarter than I, but I implore you to hold out on walkthroughs for as long as possible. It would ruin the rush of completing the harder puzzles.
The lack of story and strange ending might remove you from being enveloped in the experience, but that's not what it's all about. It's about overcoming bizarre and difficult puzzles not like any other game out there.

have everything I like in a shooter, except for the bad AI, DRM and only local co-op. But these are just the bad aspects of this amazing game, Kane and Lynch are much more as a duo!
Kane is a man on the death row, but the sins of his past wouldn't let him die just like that, no. He had to suffer, so it starts. Meting Lynch sure shake things up, a psychopath heavenly inspired by
, a character in the movie
. This fantastic duo sets foot on a path fueled by revenge and the uncontrollable need to fix Kane's family, her ex-wife and daughter kidnapped by The 7, a group of top worldwide gangsters.
This is the starting line; travel the world hunting down The 7, and shooting mobs of enemies.
No doubt a huge hit by IO Interactive, a cover-based shooter with intense violence and major Holywood influences like
.
Although we only play as Kane, Lynch is definitely still there, together with some friends we pick up on the line. As an action game every level is priceless, from the start bank heist, to the prison breakout, or even the very famous night club shootout in Japan. Each moment in this game is amazing, the level design always makes me go back and replay it.
The stressful situations, Lynch looses it, the innocent people screaming... Such great free violence only video-games can provide!

The gameplay quality, however, makes me feel sad this had to be an issue... For starters the AI is terrible, and we're talking about some big issues here; enemies stop in the middle of the fight, your teammates without a clue where to go, the hitboxes are a huge mess...If this was not bad enough, the physics have issues too. Throwing a grenade can be challenging, you never know where they go by hitting an invisible wall or just crazy physics blocking their way.
Although we shoot most of the time, the hitboxes are the biggest issue for me, and make it almost impossible to hit enemies at some distances.
Being a console port doesn't help much either, the visual and performance options are there, but seem to make little difference in improvements!
From all the negative feedback, the DRM is probably the main reason, choosing GFWL wasn't a good idea in the long run plan, but the game still works (surprisingly).
I tend to forget about all of this when I'm playing
, with such good maps, and a story line worth of a TV Show, every problem gets swelling down, almost like every pill Lynch takes.
The soundtrack is worth a being checked out, and suits perfectly with the tension of the campaign. Co-Op action is still available, but local only, and that's a shame because the game does offer some great co-op moments!
I give
a positive review, but barely... Because the campaign is really good, and the story is so solid, it makes me go back and replay some amazing missions, even though they all play out the same way!
There is nothing more powerful than a father seeking revenge!

I want to like this game, I really do. I paid 30 dollars for it and I was hoping to get at least 20-25 hours of gaming out of it. Unfotunately, while the game isn't bad per se, it has some flaws that for me impair the game's playability and longevity. Firstly, the game, while graphically impressive, is very badly optimized. Some gamers can run the game flawlessly but my system has a 780m. The 780m falls between a 660 Ti and a 770 GT. The game itself recommends(not requires...recommends!) a vanilla 560 so consequenly, I should be able to run this game at 1440p, high settings and still get 60 fps.
But I simply can't. The best I can manage is 1080p, medium settings and 60 fps. In a twitch shooter, those settings neither look good nor play well. In short the game is a fat bloated pig on mobility architectures and lots of people play on mobility architectures. This is an oversight that strictly shouldn't have happened. I suppose if you're running a 970, this game isn't a problem but if you're one of the many mobility gamers out there, be wary of this game because the architectures are different and even if you do have the horsepower to run it beautifully the game may not be designed to take advantage of it.
Secondly the game is very repititious. The classes lack significant variation. Each round plays almost exactly as the last as you buy the same gear and get the same weapons. The fighting is frenetic, which on the surface seems great, until you realize that it's simply spamming everything with firepower until it drops. The maps are uninspired and level advancement is slowed. Thematically, the concept of people spontaneously turning into zombies with drills for arms doesn't do it for me either, personally.
Mass Effect 3 has a similar multiplayer component but has literally 60 different classes and over 50 different weapons. Did I mention that at least 25 of the class archtypes play *completely* differently? Some have a staggering array of powers and others are weapon specialists. The range and variety is truly wonderful. Characters feel well, handle well and shooting play is flawless. Graphics are attractive and the game runs on modest systems. The game has over 15 different maps that all feel/play differently and you can play against four different races which all attack/behave differently.
When combined with four different difficulty modes, lots of ammo types, equipment/character bonuses and a complex branching power/skill system, the game has every advantage over this one. So why am I bringing it up? Because the games are almost identifcal in their design and yet Mass Effect 3's multiplayer component was a throwaway mode that few players extolled or gave credit to. And yet the game comes bundled with a long, rich campaign and costs 10 dollars on Origin.
You could buy this, get the inferior product, for 30 dollars. Go play ME 3 multiplayer. It's ultimately the same product but better and you'll be a lot happier. If you've played Left 4 Dead 2, or Mass Effect 3 multi, this game is simply no great shakes.

Take my points with a grain of salt, as you may feel differently about some of these features but some things that personally disappointed me in KF2 are:
-The heavy, powerful feel of the guns in KF1 is somewhat gone, or at least comparatively lacking
-Despite characters being more unique and diverse, their personalities still seem flat compared to KF1
-The voice menu from KF1 has been severely downgraded to an awkward, minimalistic Overwatch-style communication wheel, which is lacking extremely basic options that were included in KF1 such as "Thank you", "Run" or "Look out"
-The gritty, horror-esque atmosphere of KF1 is replaced with a somewhat unfitting shiny, clean, futuristic sci-fi style
That being said, Killing Floor 2 still has many redeeming qualities that, in my personal opinion, outweigh the aforementioned letdowns.
+In my personal experience, when playing on Suicidal or higher, the game actually feels more challenging and fast-paced than the first game.
+Gore physics
+Great soundtrack
+Vastly improved graphics (obviously)
+-Significantly less grindy perk progression, though it almost feels a bit too fast at times
Overall, Killing Floor 2 is lacking a lot of the personality that made Killing Floor so great, but other than that, it delivers more of (and in a few cases, improves on) the violent, fast-paced, co-op horde-shooter gameplay that Killing Floor 1 did so well.

Oh my god, they killed Kenny. You ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s!
South Park is one of the few adult TV series I still watch, and I have fallen in love with Cartman, Kyle, Stan, Kenny, Butters, and the many other characters in the wonderful fictional world of South Park! So when I heard Obsidian Entertainment were making a game, I had high hopes but also I wasn't too excited for it due to other movie/TV licensed games in the past and the other mediocre South Park games in the past, however, Obsidian Entertainment and South Park Digital Studios did not disappoint!
If you are a long viewer of South Park (like me), you would feel right at home with its quirky characters, environments and harsh but funny comedy, people who are not familiar with the TV series however, would not really know what the hell is going on in the beginning, the characters, the offensive and crude comedy and the references to the TV series. You have to have at least some knowledge of the TV series before venturing out into the Stick of Truth
The style is the same as its counterpart on the television, and the character customization makes you feel like you are part of the South Park family and it made me feel like I am watching an episode of the show. The story is really well written and hooked me in for hours, with its sudden plot twists and same crude humour, it really made me feel at home.
The combat is simple yet very difficult (on medium, can't imagine it on hard), so much so that I had to lower down the difficulty to easy at some points because the combat became too hard for me. The items that you need to collect are sometimes stowed away either behind a tree or somewhere hidden, with the game being in 2D format, rather than moving around like you would do in a 3D game, in the Stick of Truth you moved either away from the game camera or move towards the game camera which made me hard to see where my character and buddy were going
The missions are spread out evenly across South Park and fast travel provided by TIMMY! can be used, and this is one of the few games where I carried on after playing the main campaign and continued some of the side missions which there are a total of 17 side missions, this is where it brings me to my complaint. I mainly focused on playing the main story rather than focusing on side missions, I did do some side missions here and there but mainly focused on the main story, however after the short 5-6 main story campaign you are allowed to go back into South Park and finish off the side missions, however, you feel like you are doing the side missions for nothing. The XP level is capped to level 15 which I reached in a matter of a handful of missions, then... nothing. You basically do the side missions for nothing and it made me kind of say, "Wow, after the main story, you literally do nothing, what a shame", which is rare for something like an RPG Adventure game like this one, it basically felt like an empty game after finishing the main story
But, South Park: The Stick of Truth is a must buy for any fan of the wonderful TV show, I'd might not recommend it to people who have never heard of or seen at least a few episodes of South Park, because you will have no idea what is going on. Also, this is not a game for the easily offended, this game and the TV series go into subjects that are deemed offensive to many people, but if you have an open mind, you would find it hilarious! South Park: The Stick of Truth stays true to the franchise and makes it even better!
Can't wait for the sequel!

It should be known that I wouldn't normally buy a runner game but this came with a bundle.
Pros:
- Catchy music
- Nice art
Cons:
- Clunky and difficult which wouldn't be a con in itself if you didn't lose all progress each time you die
- The arm pump from spamming xc was so bad I had to create a mouse macro
- If you don't get your xc rhythm back immediately after getting up you fall over again and its instantly game over, which is made harder when your already fatiguing from spamming xc on rather long levels
- Bananas move a little when you jump over them so not only do you have to allow for objects spawned close together requiring jump spamming but you also need to account for this as well while keeping enough momentum from spamming xc while your hand feels like its going to fall off
- Not really a massive con as you can change bindings before booting up the game but it would have been nice to have been able to do this in game, I didn't realise how inconvenient having enter bound for getting up would be and I don't want to have to reload a game to resolve this
Why they lump you with 10 levels and lose all progress on death I do not know, this would be much more enjoyable with 100 generated levels and not having to start all over again but it just seems its been made more difficult and anger inducing for the sake of it.
This small thing was the difference between me leaving a negative and positive review, as it stands I don't see any reason to recommend people parting with their money as there's nothing new here and nothing I feel has improved upon many already existing games of the same nature.

I am an old fart who enjoyed the original XCOM back in the day, so I really wanted to like this game.
But ...
Tactics in this new edition are poorly implemented.  It doesn't do much good to cover your flanks and move in support when aliens are prone to randomly spawn in the middle of your squad.
There is too much emphasis on individual character development.  Once you reach the mid-game, you can't afford to lose squad members -- the development tree is too important and it takes too many missions to get them up to speed.  In the original game you had to be careful not to waste the lives under your care, but when you are fighting aliens with vastly superior technology you would expect it to be a given that some of the good guys will die.
I dislike the reduced squad size ... playing with a team cap of 6 greatly reduces the tactical options when compared to 14.
Z-dimension controls on the UI are very frustrating, especially when you are trying to navigate a multi-level alien craft.  It can be extremely difficult to issue a simple command to walk up a ramp ... and the consequences can be severe when Arnold McBlaster decides to walk under the ramp instead of up it.
The effective range of an assault rifle is about 40' in this game.  If the baddie is outside that range then you can't even attempt the shot.  I can reliably plink a round from a 10-22 into a coke can at 50 yards, but these super military types using military grade hardware won't even attempt a shot at a gorilla sized target at a third that range.  Really?!?
On the plus side, you could tell that the game designers put a lot of effort into the visual styling of the game.  It just wasn't enough to cover up weak and even flawed gameplay.

Lego Marvel Superheroes is a advanced combot RPG game developed by Bethseda studios what combines advanced lore with fun mechanics of gameplay. The lore is rich and the open world elements make the game outstanding, also the next-gen graphics make it look straight out of the Unity engines cupboard. The story is about a teenager named Chad, who discovers on a week of mountain biking and parachuting that he has super mutant powers, the first power he gets is the ability to score sweet hatricks while playing football on the beach. The second power he gets is the ability to change into Elvis whenever he wants. I've saved the last for the best, his last power is the ability to turn into a biscuit when ever he so pleases. As it says in the game description it was highly inspired by Bad Rats, most of it is like Bad Rats, basically a upgraded version of Bad Rats.
The story revolves around Chad and his gang of extreme skateboarders. He lives in Canada and there is a very big skateboarding competition coming up and Chad is feeling insecure because his Girlfriend dumped him. Then, Chad requires his powers and fights all the evil crime in Canada, he doens't have to use his powers that much. Alot of childhood character make a appearence what can bring nostalgia into your brain, such characters as Johnny Neutron, and Ben 10. Like I said, the lore is awesome, when you come across a a landmark, you'll get a snippit of lore to find out about the certain object/landmark. My favourite was the bodybuildingorange because it supplied with lore that was not known to me, and it made my day. For the story I'd say it makes the game, but I've still got Gameplay to do, and other stuff, but the story is spectacular and I spent countless hours washing my body in it.
Lego Marvel Superheroes takes a change from the other lego games, adding in a XP system with a leveling up system, at first you begin at the NOVICE stage with very little perks, but as Chad progresses he levels up unlocking powerful abilities to defeat evil people, in his quest to become popular and win the Skateboard contest. The combat is amazing, including bloody finishers and great visual stunning takedowns (Non-Lethal and Lethal). One of the characters called Spider-Man can do a sick flip and snap someones neck, what personally I think is quite cool, plus it looks cool in awesome but blocky graphics. But, that's another section, for gameplay I'd say it's fantastic, good combat, good mechanics, and good takedowns?
The graphics are visuallly stunning as I mentioned, everything has a reflection, when I say everything I MEAN EVERYTHING it's like the floor of a bathroom toilet on every model, seriously it is. But anywho, the graphics are nice and saturated and colourful and really bring in the life to this game, this game in black and white wouldn't be as fun. It was obviously made on the Unity engine, making it stunning graphics and really demostrating what the Unity engine can do when you put lego blocks and make a game with them, cool.

Probably one of the only games since System Shock 2 that's been able to get this kind of atmosphere and experience down, with you often scraping by bullet by bullet, smashing things together and scavenging to desperately try to keep moving and keep alive. If I have problems with the game they come down to the graphics, procedural generation and writing of the game, and they are somewhat intertwined.
System Shock 2 was so terrifying because of the enemies being horrible mostrosities, perversions of what was once human flesh often now coupled with machine parts. Here, I feel like that's supposed to be the case, but I can't tell due to the simplistic top down style. This could likely be circumvented by having sound design that lets your imagination fill in the horrifying gaps for you, or writing for the datalogs you find to elaborate on the backstory of these things but no, that doesn't happen. The sound design seems to be content to the 8-bit aesthetic and the writing seems to be confused about whether it wants to be dead serious or a little tongue in cheek with its subject matter. I ended up skipping through most of the data logs given the total lack of personality or a good level of backstory handed out beyond the words "necrotic tissue reactivation" and "genetic tampering".
Also the procedural generation itself feels too cruel and really, really same-ey. The environment never really feels... I'd almost say navigate-able or "comfy". I don't expect it to feel Comfy obviously, it is a survival horror game, but it never really feels anything but stuck together out of different parts in a way that's jagged, lopsided and poorly balanced.
The reason resource management this strict works in games like System Shock is because the level design is manageable, it's obvious, and you can rely on things. You aren't going to end up luring enemies into a courtyard because the hallway feels so rough and fiddly to move around in that you will probably waste vital supplies.
This is a game that didn't need to try to be a roguelike or a procedurally generated game, or even one that needed to try to have a story.
Teleglitch could have made itself into a pretty good linear top down sci-fi survival shooter with a decent story, but instead it throws in procedural generation on top of the already difficult resource economy of supplies v.s. dead enemies, which just pushes things too far.
It could have simplified and just been a fun procedurally generated shooter where you explore a randomly drawn up location and try to survive that's slick, mean and embraces the retro aesthetic further. I
Instead it feels like it collapses under its own elements into a muddled mess of scrap metal, crafting, nails and ugly brown pixel art.
My recommendation: If you want to check it out, wait for a sale and don't pay anything under $5 for it.

Antichamber is what happens when puzzle game designers strip away all tradition, get drunk, and decide to see how cruelly they can mess with gamers' heads. Then, when they sober up the next day, there's a hint of remorse as they patch over it with a few words of inspiration on the walls.
To be fair, their minimalistic game design it expertly crafted, to bring highly innovative challenges which really make you think. Much is based on perception and pre-conceptions. You may wander down a hallway, stop and turn around, only to find that the way you came has totally changed. You may also look a little closer through a viewing window, step back, and find yourself transported into a different room. This is all completely seamless, which messes with your head that much more.
This game teaches you that trying something new will be rewarding. It almost always knows which way you'll tackle a challenge first, then give you one of many reassuring messages alluding to the task, or life in general. It gives you motivation to try and try again, in different ways.
And you will want to, because finally overcoming a challenge that left you stuck for ages, makes you feel like
I will admit that I sometimes asked for help from a gamer friend smarter than I, but I implore you to hold out on walkthroughs for as long as possible. It would ruin the rush of completing the harder puzzles.
The lack of story and strange ending might remove you from being enveloped in the experience, but that's not what it's all about. It's about overcoming bizarre and difficult puzzles not like any other game out there.

A breath of fresh air in a dying genre littered with painful alphas and zombie slaying boycots. Dying light has brought the open world zombie survival back from the un-dead. The introduction video was all the convincing I needed! Within 20 minutes of gameplay, I found myself reliving the days of old, Dead Island.  Oh, the memories. Plenty of exploration, enough weapon mods to leave you salivating for more after every devastating blow. And graphics to die for, over and over again. Brilliant zone layouts with plenty of undead & human enemies to slaughter. An extensive crafting system with everything you could possibly need to get the upper hand (especially at night when the crazies get even more crazy). I've put over 30 hours into this game since its release and I can see myself putting at least another 30 into it with the addition of the DLC that I had already pre-ordered with the Season Pass.
Some pros and cons about this game:
Pros:
Fantastic graphics
Outstanding game play
DIY must have crafting system
Intelligent & god fearing AI (approach a couple of Rais's men with a shotgun and you'll see what I mean)
A skill tree to turn the most novice of player into Spiderman in a short period of time
A real sense of imminent "I'm so dead" moments
Great cutscenes and interaction (A truly heart felt feeling that can only come from the guys at Techland)
Insanely fun and sometimes outrageous achievements
Cons:
Lack of melee weapon variety and firearms.. seriously.. there really isn't that much to choose from.
The DLC.. and I can't stress this enough. The Season Pass was about $30. The first DLC was released a few days ago. As far as I can tell, it's only added a total of 2 new quaratine zones (Hard Difficulty), which I managed to fly through in less than 10 minutes. And I hope.. nay.. PRAY, that the remaining DLC to come will be worth that pre-purhcase price.
Overall, this is a brilliant game, and I would highly recommend it to anyone. Just avoid the Season Pass and DLC until a later date.. with any luck it will drop in price, SIGNIFICANTLY.

Basically everything that isn't directly related to gameplay is pretty much great.
The story is awesome and gritty, the characters are fleshed out, the voice acting is very good and the graphics still hold up today.
The game is amazingly varied, which something that most games don't really have.
I'll be now giving some SPOILERS, so be careful.
You get to escape from prison, you get to break into a prison, you get to rob a bank and so on.
But now the negatives...
While the bullets exist from a realistic point, a.k.a. the gun, the aiming system isn't really configured to that fact and it still seems to think that bullets come from a straight line in the middle of the screen. That will be an issue when behind cover and shooting a sniper rifle.
Speaking of cover, the cover system is junk. And seeing as it's a 3rd person cover shooter, it's pretty damn pathetic to see this excuse of a "cover system" being implemented. It's an auto-snap cover system. So that means, no designated button and no real indicators to show which covers can actually be used. Also, once behind the cover, make sure you barely move. Otherwise you'll most likely walk away from the cover again and you might never get back to it.
The gunplay is pretty awful in terms of it feeling satisfying. You can shoot some enemies 4 times in the face without them even being fazed. There's no real feedback there.
The guns are very random in terms of their stats. The accuracy is the same on all of them. That meaning, the accuracy sucks for all of them. The game has a physical recoil mechanic, meaning that when shooting up, the camera also jerks up. Well, putting that in made them forget that an M16 should have a good chance at hitting a target at medium range when single firing. Well, there's no actual difference between spraying/burst or single firing. Only you deciding whether you can deal with the recoil jerks.
Overall:
Objectively this game is a 3/10. It's easy to see the glaring issues and it's way below average.
Subjectively, I enjoyed this game enough to finish the 4-hour campaign. Subjective grade: 5/10 - Just average.
(All games start at a 5/10 and move up and down based on their pros and cons)

Let me start with telling you that I played almost all RE titles ( excluding the lightgun spin-offs ) and that I thought, after RE6 things could only get worse.
But I was wrong.
Surprisingly this game wasn't bad at all. (Not counting the extra episodes)
Which mostly comes from it's coop aspects.
It feels much more Resident Evil like to slowly advance through the level, hoping to not run out of bullets and trying to survive the next onslaught of horrifying monsters which bare a striking resemblance to Dead Space's necromorphs btw.
Storywise the game is medicore at best, with a few plot holes here and there but it's RE after all and we all know how bloody trashy it's stories are.
You'll be mostly playing as Claire Redfield or Barry Burton. Both are being accompanied by either Moira Burton ( if playing with claire ) or the little Natalia ( if playing with Barry ). If there's no other player at your side, both will be controlled by AI which does a fairly decent job of not being to annyoing.
Same goes for the enemies AI. They are not smart by any means..but they are zombies after all..so I think that's ok..I guess..
Gameplay-wise this game feels much more like the old survival-horror games than the modern shooting galleries.
You often need to find a key, pull a switch or somtimes need to solve a puzzle ( there could have been more of those ).
Ammunition is scarce and herbs ( only green and red) are infrequent as well. Enemies tend to be bullet sponges, which can become annoying after a while.
This leads us directly to the weapons and some interesting aspects of gameplay.
While Claire and Barry don't hesitate to use guns, Moira does not want to use firearms, so her only way of defending herself is by using her flashlight to blind her foes. With her flashlight she also can be of use to look around for hidden items which Claire won't see without a light source.
Instead of wearing a flashlight Natalia is able to see enemies through walls, pointing out their weak spots for Barry to shot.
As I mentioned earlier this game really shines in coop, for it is much more intense for both players being in need of the other. With a playtime of approximately 12h it has a good length too. Especially for this price.
To put it in a nutshell : If you can grab a friend to play this togeher and you want to have a good coop experience and a good RE game on top, don't hesitate to pick this up. But please consider that this is still miles away of being as good as the old RE titles like RE2.
P.S. : This game features a lot of funny Barry references!

Overall, the revelations series is onto something great and I hope they keep it up and find that blend of new and old RE we've all been waiting for. Highly Recommend 8/10.

REvelations 2 is set between the events of Resident Evil 5 and 6 and is a step back to the roots of the franchise. The game is split in 4 episodes, each of which contain a story segment where you play as Claire Redfield and Moira Burton, and a segment where you play as Barry Burton and Natalia Korva, 6 months after the events of Claires and Moiras segment.
The Claire and Moira campaign certainly plays like old resident evil games. To me it was quite scary due to the excellent scenery design, and the fact that enemies do not drop ammo or healing items adds even more to the feeling of panic the game induces occasionally.
The Barry and Natalia campaign plays a lot like the last of us with more emphasis on fighting zombies, which isn't a good thing. The developers clearly tried to recreate TLOU with Barry being entrusted to take care of Natalia right from the start of the game. Sadly, Joel is an emotionally cold ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, while Barry is not, and thus the moments that are supposed to mimic character developing moments from TLOU fail catastrophically at delivering anything to the player. The only half-decent emotional moment is in episode 4, where Barry cracks up and tells Natalia about why Moira is afraid of firearms.
Natalia is a child and Moira, as said before, is afraid of guns, which is why both don't use them, instead, Moira uses a flashlight and lights the way for Claire while Natalia can see infected through walls (not explaining why because spoilers).
Both can see blinking objects on the ground, hidden in small crannies, point them out and make them up-pickable items.
Due to this, and Moiras ability to stun enemies by blinding them with her fleshlight, you will want to play as the defenceless character surprisingly often, which is a nice refreshment from the terrible shooting games who also happened to include things that are related to the Resident Evil universe, such the last 2 main installments in the series, the Operation Racoon City spinoff, and the more recent umbrella corps.
The plot revolves around the sister of Albert, Alex Wesker, and is fairly well-written (above average for the Resident Evil series i'd say) however it's really nothing special compared to heavily narrative-driven games, so if you want a story-heavy game this isn't what you're looking for.
This game is the result of the combined effort of lots of talented developers, and I can wholeheartedly recommend it if you're on search for a decent 3rd Person Horror-Survival shooter.

Oh my god, they killed Kenny. You ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s!
South Park is one of the few adult TV series I still watch, and I have fallen in love with Cartman, Kyle, Stan, Kenny, Butters, and the many other characters in the wonderful fictional world of South Park! So when I heard Obsidian Entertainment were making a game, I had high hopes but also I wasn't too excited for it due to other movie/TV licensed games in the past and the other mediocre South Park games in the past, however, Obsidian Entertainment and South Park Digital Studios did not disappoint!
If you are a long viewer of South Park (like me), you would feel right at home with its quirky characters, environments and harsh but funny comedy, people who are not familiar with the TV series however, would not really know what the hell is going on in the beginning, the characters, the offensive and crude comedy and the references to the TV series. You have to have at least some knowledge of the TV series before venturing out into the Stick of Truth
The style is the same as its counterpart on the television, and the character customization makes you feel like you are part of the South Park family and it made me feel like I am watching an episode of the show. The story is really well written and hooked me in for hours, with its sudden plot twists and same crude humour, it really made me feel at home.
The combat is simple yet very difficult (on medium, can't imagine it on hard), so much so that I had to lower down the difficulty to easy at some points because the combat became too hard for me. The items that you need to collect are sometimes stowed away either behind a tree or somewhere hidden, with the game being in 2D format, rather than moving around like you would do in a 3D game, in the Stick of Truth you moved either away from the game camera or move towards the game camera which made me hard to see where my character and buddy were going
The missions are spread out evenly across South Park and fast travel provided by TIMMY! can be used, and this is one of the few games where I carried on after playing the main campaign and continued some of the side missions which there are a total of 17 side missions, this is where it brings me to my complaint. I mainly focused on playing the main story rather than focusing on side missions, I did do some side missions here and there but mainly focused on the main story, however after the short 5-6 main story campaign you are allowed to go back into South Park and finish off the side missions, however, you feel like you are doing the side missions for nothing. The XP level is capped to level 15 which I reached in a matter of a handful of missions, then... nothing. You basically do the side missions for nothing and it made me kind of say, "Wow, after the main story, you literally do nothing, what a shame", which is rare for something like an RPG Adventure game like this one, it basically felt like an empty game after finishing the main story
But, South Park: The Stick of Truth is a must buy for any fan of the wonderful TV show, I'd might not recommend it to people who have never heard of or seen at least a few episodes of South Park, because you will have no idea what is going on. Also, this is not a game for the easily offended, this game and the TV series go into subjects that are deemed offensive to many people, but if you have an open mind, you would find it hilarious! South Park: The Stick of Truth stays true to the franchise and makes it even better!
Can't wait for the sequel!

I really wanted to enjoy this game.
The game makes you pick up coins, ammo, and health packs (which are just small for you to notice), and you can buy power ups during the stages to help you. But every time you die, you go to the beginning of the game, however, rescuing new characters gives access to the stage you rescued them, but since the characters are mostly the same, the stages keep getting harder and you will not have enough coins to buy power ups, the logical answer is to replay old stages for help which is really annoying.
The controls are decent and, the sound is okay and there isn't much to say about the graphics.
However, these things are badly implemented. The sound is just there, the gameplay becomes confusing when you have so many enemies on screen at the same time, sure they look different, but that only makes it more difficult to identify yourself on the screen.
The game also lacks feedback on many places, you hardly notice when taking damage, picking a weapon gives only a small prompt on under your life bar that becomes really annoying when everything blends together.
Speaking of weapons, they aren't really great, sometimes I would find myself avoiding them because my standard gun is more straightforward even though the shots don't go too far.
Also the achievement system requires you to have a certain objective for it to count as an achievement.
The worst offender though is time. Yep, everything has a weird timing, mine quickly beep twice before exploding, enemies take too long to disappear after dying and only drop items after disappearing, and, though these items stay on the screen a good amount of time, just like the mines, they blip too fast for you to pick up before disappearing. Enemy choppers come too fast and you need to destroy them using the environment.
To me, all of these design decisions make the game too frustrating for it to be fun.

FTL is a modern rougelike in which you embark on a journey across space, fleeing the ever - present danger of a pursuing rebel fleet. You jump through randomized sectors from beacon to beacon, encountering giant alien spiders, hostile space pirates, and everything in between. Strategy and luck come together in FTL's combat system. What do you do when your enemy disables your shield and then beams its crew onboard to wreak more havoc? Do you reroute power to your engines to increase your ship's evasion or power up the medbay to fend off the pesky intruders?   What impresses me most about FTL is that it caters to a million different play styles. There are nine playable ships (eight of which must be unlocked), each with two different layouts. The game will do everything in its power to crush you, asphyxiate you, set your entire ship on fire until that fateful moment when your hull (HP) reaches zero and your journey ends. You'll laugh and you'll cry (mostly cry), but you'll always come back for more. FTL does a great job with the visuals (combining retro and modern themes while avoiding clichés) and the soundtrack is simply amazing. Definitely worth whatever they're charging for it nowadays.

one of the best first person shooters of all time, maybe even THE best.  This game was a huge tech demonstration in  a a way when it came out, the physics and graphics were WAAAAAY ahead of  their time.  There are physics based puzzles, mirrors and magnifying glasses work, and the gravity gun is charming and fun beyond words (I want one for realz).  The plot is never really laid out in nitty gritty in either dialogue or in writing, but if you pay attention the story and world are artfully crafted, and engrossing.  The Combine (the bad guys) are a fascinating foe, as cruel as they are alien, and they get fleshed out a good bit in this game and even more in the expansions (totally worth getting BTW).  whether you are burning headcrabs in ravenholm (we don't go there anymore), banging it out with Combine soldiers, or running over ant lions in the car, this game is a total blast.  The levels are linear, as is the style of the older shooters of that era (Halo, call of duty MW 1 or 2's story), but they are large and complex enough you dont feel trapped in a corridor and the world seems real and alive enough for you to buy into it.  The pacing is also notable, sometimes you bust through a door, amped up expecting a fight, only to find a welcome dialogue sequence, and the vehicle sequences and puzzles that break things up from time to time are a treat too (exceptionally well done, the puzzles will only bother really, really stupid people).  Last, but not the least by any stretch of the imagination, the audio is EXCELLENT!  Gunshots echo realistically in canyons and alleys, the chatter from enemies is really cool (especially the flatline when they die), the screaming and howling of the headcrab zombies is terrifying and unsettling, and the audio for the weapons is top notch.
overall, 9.8/10, and if you want to get all picky and don't like decimals, 10/10
