Lego Marvel Superheroes is a advanced combot RPG game developed by Bethseda studios what combines advanced lore with fun mechanics of gameplay. The lore is rich and the open world elements make the game outstanding, also the next-gen graphics make it look straight out of the Unity engines cupboard. The story is about a teenager named Chad, who discovers on a week of mountain biking and parachuting that he has super mutant powers, the first power he gets is the ability to score sweet hatricks while playing football on the beach. The second power he gets is the ability to change into Elvis whenever he wants. I've saved the last for the best, his last power is the ability to turn into a biscuit when ever he so pleases. As it says in the game description it was highly inspired by Bad Rats, most of it is like Bad Rats, basically a upgraded version of Bad Rats.
The story revolves around Chad and his gang of extreme skateboarders. He lives in Canada and there is a very big skateboarding competition coming up and Chad is feeling insecure because his Girlfriend dumped him. Then, Chad requires his powers and fights all the evil crime in Canada, he doens't have to use his powers that much. Alot of childhood character make a appearence what can bring nostalgia into your brain, such characters as Johnny Neutron, and Ben 10. Like I said, the lore is awesome, when you come across a a landmark, you'll get a snippit of lore to find out about the certain object/landmark. My favourite was the bodybuildingorange because it supplied with lore that was not known to me, and it made my day. For the story I'd say it makes the game, but I've still got Gameplay to do, and other stuff, but the story is spectacular and I spent countless hours washing my body in it.
Lego Marvel Superheroes takes a change from the other lego games, adding in a XP system with a leveling up system, at first you begin at the NOVICE stage with very little perks, but as Chad progresses he levels up unlocking powerful abilities to defeat evil people, in his quest to become popular and win the Skateboard contest. The combat is amazing, including bloody finishers and great visual stunning takedowns (Non-Lethal and Lethal). One of the characters called Spider-Man can do a sick flip and snap someones neck, what personally I think is quite cool, plus it looks cool in awesome but blocky graphics. But, that's another section, for gameplay I'd say it's fantastic, good combat, good mechanics, and good takedowns?
The graphics are visuallly stunning as I mentioned, everything has a reflection, when I say everything I MEAN EVERYTHING it's like the floor of a bathroom toilet on every model, seriously it is. But anywho, the graphics are nice and saturated and colourful and really bring in the life to this game, this game in black and white wouldn't be as fun. It was obviously made on the Unity engine, making it stunning graphics and really demostrating what the Unity engine can do when you put lego blocks and make a game with them, cool.

. Indeed it has... this intriguing isometric RPG is a great combat system wrapped in a rollicking mystery that although has a few stumbling points, it is very much worth your time. Returns comes with a built-in campaign that will last you 10-12 hours if you take your time, and with plenty of mods in the community to keep it fresh.
Shadowrun Returns has a basic isometric movement system, just click where you want to go/interact with. It's when you get into the easy-to-learn combat system that the game really opens up. You can create your Runner to be a Sorcerer, a Drone-using mastermind, or just a guy with a shotgun that shoots people in the face. The RPG system is good, not overly complicated, and has good conversation trees that can be affected with different levels of Charisma. You can even role-play what type of things your character is knowledgable in. Overall, the gameplay of Shadowrun Returns is slick and stellar.
Shadowrun Returns has a story that doesn't quite work on the empathy stakes... there's no reason really to care for any of the characters you meet, and some of the Runners you can hire are simply generic. If they die, it's just a *shrug* and leave them behind. However, the actual mystery behind the game and what's going on I found to be motivating enough... although it starts off slow, you want to meet the 'Ripper' until you actually stop playing the game- though after you've met him, things really start to get interesting...
The graphics of Shadowrun are servicable; sure, they won't dazzle you, but they aren't bad either. It has a nice art-style to make the world come to life, and the character portraits help give you first impressions of the characters, as well as the information that comes through text-wise.
The atmosphere is great, with dank hotels and rain-drenched streets beckoning your Runner on. The characters are as fleshed out as you can get in a 'short' campaign as the Dead Man's Switch, but personally, I won't miss any of them.
The music quality in this game is impeccable. If you are a fan of electronic music, you won't regret listening to the tracks that are on offer here. 'Double Cross' is my personal favorite track. The additional sounds of guns and sorcery that permeate the air whilst fighting adds to the atmosphere.
Shadowrun Returns, A Dead Man's Switch, is a joy to play, and although the story has a few hiccups and the companion system leaves a lot to be desired, the game is overall a solid reccomendation. Worth your time indeed. Ready to deck into the system?

Coming from a huge fan of the SNES Shadowrun, this game is solid. Much more detailed than the SNES version, as one would expect from a newer game with old RPG influences. More detailed attributes to distribute your karma on. More spells and different ways to use them. Weapons have multiple firing modes which have positive and negative effects. And though the main storyline is reasonably linear, there's several conversations that either trigger or avoid side missions. The attacking is turn-based and is pretty well executed. Almost has a final fantasy tactics feel to it. Moving a certain number of squares costs a turn, which may get you closer to the target, which increases your percentage to hit the target with an attack. Though you do have unlimited ammo, you do have to reload firearms, which costs a turn. Nice touch I thought. You can select your characters class and abilities from the start, which gives flexability to your play style. But more importantly, replayability to play the game as a completely different character.
Now for my complaints. First and absolute foremost, IT'S TOO SHORT! First time through, taking my sweet time, and I clocked 10.4 hours start to finish. Super bummed. Second, computer decking is only done like twice in the whole game. It's well executed I thought, better than the SNES version for sure, but provided you have one decker in your squad, there's never a reason for you to spend any karma on improving those abilities OR spending any money on any of the gear. Lastly, difficulty. It was too easy. There are four difficulty settings and I played on the 3rd one AND did all the raids down a shadowrunner so I didn't have to pay them. No problem. Smoked through the game while using a minimal amount of medkits, let alone the trama kits to bring people back to life (used zero of those). Run and gun the whole way without issue. EDIT: I have since completed the game three times. 2nd time as strictly a shaman on the hardest difficulty. Much more difficult, but in a so-so fun way. All magic users are stupid weak for the first 80% of the game. The shaman can summon demons to act as another player on your team. But after about 3-4 turns, they end up turning against you and now you're more effed than you were to start. lol It was fun to do just to see if I could beat the game this way. Yes is the answer, though I died several times. Right about the same ~10hrs to complete. My 3rd run through the game I went insanely run and gun just to see how much I could dominate the hardest diffculty level. I was a huge troll and spent every single karma point on body and shotgun combat. 40 damage per shot was common. I smoked the living isht out of that game. Done in under 7hrs and the final battle was a joke, again on the hardest difficulty.
All in all, I thought there was a bit too much talking and not enough fighting (SNES suffered from that too). There's plenty of battle, but lots of discussion too. The storyline is ridiculously easy to follow, so spare me the multiple paragraph conversations. That's all I'm saying. I loved the game, obviously as I played it three times through. And best part? LOTS of replayability! Even though I've played it three times, there's draw to try out a 4th time as a different character type. Also, it seems as though there's 3rd party add-on stroylines that can be downloaded and played. I haven't downloaded any yet, but the reviews look positive. Antichamber is an original kind of 3D puzzle/platformer game. The style is often compared to portal; it's simplistic but also beautiful, clear, and the environment can create subtle yet effective hints about the puzzle-solutions. A lot of "rules" set for platformers and other games are broken, played with or showed for what they really are.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is heavily focused on puzzles. These puzzles range from easy to very difficult, and it is usually important to keep thinking about the things you're doing. Often, when you think you understand the "rules" of some of the puzzles, a surprising twist makes you look at the next puzzle completely different.
Besides puzzles there is a minimal amount of platforming. Most platforming is easy and can be done by anyone picking up gaming for the first time. However, by clever use of platforming and manipulating puzzle elements, new solutions can be found and whole parts of the game can even be skipped or accessed early.
This game throws a lot of surprises at you, especially at the start. During the late game you do expect most of the "twists" but the puzzles themselves still manage to find new ways to baffle you nonetheless.
Graphics:
There is nothing bad to say about the graphics. The style for the game has purposely been chosen as very simple, which keeps the environments calm and soothing. The game is white, with vibrant primary colours scattered around for several purposes. Everything you see serves a goal. Overall, it looks beautiful.
Sound:
I did not notice music, but there are sound effects and background "noises" such as water/birds/animals. Like the graphics, the sounds are very soothing and complement the style of the rest of the game. Sometimes sounds and environment do create mystery elements, which
Replay value:
Sadly, I find that this game has little replay-value. After completing the game, you know all puzzles and all paths. The most interesting thing about the game are the surprising solutions, which will now be clear from the start. A second playthrough can be fun for purposes such as a timed run (speedrun) or for a more thorough understanding of some of the meanings of puzzles. After this, you are done.
All in all this game was very enjoyable and surprising, and if you like puzzle games this is certainly something I can recommend you to play. However: keep in mind that this games takes about 4 to 5 hours to complete, after which most of the replay value is lost.

Oh look, it's Diablo 1 HD! With papercraft!
Seriously though, as someone whose first gaming true love was Diablo 2, I always felt bad for being unable to appreciate the original Diablo 1 for what it was, always seeing it as an inferior Diablo 2 prototype. This game, however, gives me that feeling I know I should've experienced when I played D1, but didn't. Its setting, characters and story are as close as you can get without getting sued by Blizzard, and gameplay is a weird kind of streamlined hack'and'slash, where the main character can only move forward and backward on a corridor "rail" of sorts. Which could be unfamiliar at first, but really doesn't take away much from the experience.
All the spells, gear and consumables in the game are called "cards". There are 3 classes (guess the archetypes), and the "cards" you can get are determined by those. What I liked about this system is that you can put on any card in any slot, so if you want, you either can get loads of spells and survive without any gear at all or, on the contrary, you can ditch the spells, gear up all the way to the teeth, and go left-click everyone to death. Both these possibilities require lots of mana to be viable, but in different ways - spells cost mana as you cast them and you have to refill it once in a while, and gear passively locks some of your mana up, so if you don't have enough free mana, you can't put on any more gear. It's an interesting simplification of the classic level/stat requiement on gear that falls into the whole "streamlined" feel this game goes for.
In short, I'm glad I found this little gem, and I hope one day to see Book of Demons 2: Archon of Ruination, if anything, just to see a papercraft Necromancer raising paper skeletons.

Well, I have to say I'm glad to be able to change my thumbs-down review of Shadowrun Returns to thumbs up. The fix for save files has been working fine for me with some flaws, but you will decide for yourself if this suits you fine or you might get DRM-free version that appearantly doesn't have these problems... I've used several different solutions and my own experiments to come up with the fix that works.
So, this is my story with Shadowrun.
I saw a few promotional posters here and there. Nothing more. Then one day, a good buddy of mine gifts me Shadowrun Returns and Shadowun Dragonfall. I didn't touch any of these in a long time because my reviewing and gaming queue was really choke full.
But one fateful night I decide to check out the playing order of Shadowrun games and I install this one. After creating my character, I've found myself in my smelly apartment wiith a dead friend asking for help. And I immediately fall in love. TOTALLY.
Shadowrun universe is one of the best I've encountered in a long time. This clash of tech and fantasy was something I even dreamt of writing about myself (until I've realized it's been done before and better). When I've figured out there are BOOKS out there about Shadowrun world... I nearly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants and figured out I'll die happy. You will be entering the strange cyberpunk retrofuturistic world filled with noir style crime mysteries, corporate thrillers and technology ruling the flesh.
The storyline and game itself is fairly linear, but it made me care more about roleplaying - there's never a dull moment and nobody asks you to milk the cow (read: nonsensical sidequests) when you're in the middle of exciting main mission. That way you truly feel like you're doing something important.
Battle system is similar to that one seen in XCom games (turn based combat), and RPG system is decent and effective, making you care how you distribute your Karma points.
The only true problem I had with Shadowrun Returns on Steam is the fact that at certain point I've started having major problems with save files - to cut the story short, game stops recognizing your saves. By doing this, you will be able to play the game, but Steam time tracking will not work. If you're into tracking your time (as much as I am), you can always run a Steam edition of the game beside second one.
I am playing on Windows 7 64bit. I am not responsible for any accidents or nuclear meltdowns caused by copying and pasting. BACK EVERYTHING UP.
If you all of a sudden get greyed out CONTINUE button and you are not able to load your game, try this.
1. Go to C:\Users\YOURUSERNAME\AppData\Local\Harebrained Schemes\Shadowrun Returns\Saves and copy all the files. These are your save files. COPY THEM.
2. Go to your Steam folder. There, find the following folders \userdata\YOURPERSONALNR\234650 . Inside 234650 folder you will see two folders, one named Local, the other named remote. Back those up, just in case. You're bound to find some save files in these folders, but sometimes it's not the case. Now, paste AppData/Local... save files to both of these folders. If system asks you to overwrite, overwrite.
3. Now, most people say you need to restart Steam and start it in admin mode. This may help you once, just as it helped me, but then you'll encounter greyed out buttons again. The way I made my saves work is that I ran my game directly by clicking Shadowrun.exe from \Steam\steamapps\common\Shadowrun Returns.
Pros: your save games work.
Cons: no Steam overlay, no time tracking.
I would usually not lose this much time to figure things out, but Shadowrun is SO GOOD and when I heard Dragonfall and Hong Kong are even better... oh, happy times!!!

Spectacularly inept and ill-considered attempt to make a gritty third person shooter. The game's director said he was sick of goody two-shoes video game protagonists and wanted to do something different, but it feels like some pretty fundamental lessons of characterization and dialog were lost in translation.
Even if you overlook the fatal flaws in the narrative, however, the gameplay is clunky, repetitive, and entirely linear, with swimmy controls and fitful feedback. Maybe it could be chalked up to age if not for the fact that I've played better third person shooters that came out years before this one - and they still hold up even a decade+ on.
Skip it and try a Max Payne game instead.

I just finished playing Antichamber, and I decided this world have not enough review of this game yet, not on Linux at least.
Plot
The game has no plot, it's something that I would define an introspective journey. When the game starts, you see no introduction, you just spawn in a black and white room with four walls. One of the walls is the settings menu, then here is a a black wall, another wall with a strange symbol, that will become a map in future and another transparent wall behind what there is an "exit" door. Your adventure starts when you click on the first available room of the map. From now on, your goal is to solve multiple puzzles to gain access to deeper areas of the maze-like game world, until you get access to the last stage. At the end of every puzzle on the wall there will be a panel with an image. If clicked, an aphorism related to the puzzle you just solved will show up. Some of those signs are extremely nice, and they are probably the soul of the game somehow: they seem like telling the story of a life, from the beginning to the end. I really appreciated them. Some of them are also useful, and give some hints for the puzzles to come. The structure is non linear, and the puzzles can be solved in almost-arbitrary order. Only some puzzles depend on items you find from previous puzzles. Some of the puzzles lead to other puzzles, and some lead to dead ends. Some times those dead ends are "dev-rooms", where there are pieces of artwork showing you the development of the game.
Gameplay
The game looks like a classic 3D first person shooter, but there are no enemies to kill, no hurry and no stress situation: it's just you and a non-euclidean world to explore. Yes folks: non-euclidean. It means that if you go a way, then you turn and go back, you may end up in a place which is not the place you came from. Sounds strange? And that's not all! It also means that the place where you are may depend on the direction you are looking at: if you are not looking at a wall, such wall may well cease to exist. Sounds confusing? Well, it is, but it's funny confusion: since the games is not random in any way, the only point is getting used to the structure of the world. It is a continuous side-thinking exercise, and what I liked most is that there is absolutely no hurry in any moment of the game. I really hate having to complete levels within some time limit, or having to redo the same thing over and over because the difficult part is not understanding the puzzle but doing the incredibly complicated sequence of very stupid actions in the right order at the right time. This is very rarely the case for Antichamber: look at the world around you, think how to go through the situation with the tools you got, and do it. Some puzzles are obviously simpler than others, and many of them look totally impossible at a first sight. After you have been able to solve the first puzzles, you will be given a strange ring-like gun. This gun is able to absorb and fire little cubes of the world, and will be key for being able to solve many of the puzzles. Further in the game, you will get upgraded versions of such a gun, with ability to quickly suck and spit cubes, move cubes around and create entire walls. The gun will be your only companion in this adventure: as I said, it is introspective.
Controls
Classic mouse and keyboard combo is the way I suggest for playing Antichamber. I don't think there is controller support, and if there is I don't recommend it: there are many other games where a controller will work very well, but in FPS-like games mouse and keyboard are what you want - unless Valve does the miracle.
Controls are easy and there are no problems with the defaults. The time you will spend struggling to understand how to do what you want to do is near zero.
Graphics and sound
Graphics is minimally beautiful. Nothing too complicated, and basically no textures. Colours, colours, colours everywhere! I'm generally not much a fan of games that willingly look old-fashioned or minimal, but Antichamber is definitely nice, and this choice totally fits the spirit of the game and enhances the feeling of being in a strange, mind-driven world where geometry is broken. The graphic makes you feel like you are living in one of those dreams where you look behind a door two times and see two different places.
The game runs on Unreal Engine 3, that seems to run pretty well on our beloved Linux operating systems. I played on Sabayon Linux using hybrid graphics and Bumblebee / Primus GPU for offloading the graphic tasks to my GeForce GT 630M. The frame rate have always been pretty stable. The game crashed a couple of times, though.
The sound is nice but nothing that will make you scream of joy. The soundtrack is embracing and relaxing, and helps you dive in the world, although is not the aspect of the game that you will remember most favourably.
Longevity
I am a slow player, and I finished the game in about 12 hours. Once the game is finished, there is little reason to play it again, or to re-do over and over the same puzzles. It is a one-shot experience.
Conclusion
Antichamber is a very good game. In these times of clones and clones and clones, creating something really new is a good achievement per se. Creating something that is new and good is much more difficult, but Antichamber reached the goal. If you are searching for a testosteronic shoot-to-eveything-that-moves, move along: this is no place for you. If you feel like experiencing something new, dive into a world shaped like a dream and stress your brain with side, thinking, Antichamber is what you are searching for.
Final rate: 8/10.
How much is worth™: ~ 5 Euros.

There are two things it does right: combat improvements and the narrative presentation. There are just so many things at your disposal when it comes to free-flow combat, and yes, odd stuff happens still, but the tight rhythmic gameplay is just better with enemy variety as well as gadgets you can use during the combat (plus, some levels have you fight along side your sidekicks and these sections are really sweet). It balances out the flow of the combat, intensity as well as strategy. As for the narrative presentation, Arkham series has always been a knock-out when it comes to fusing gameplay with cutscenes, and Arkham Knight does it best here.
The problem is, the story itself is lackluster. The wholly unsatisfying ending aside, the main story fails to incorporate various characters and the world, and instead sidelines potentially very interesting villains away from the main story. Arkham Knight himself is an interesting character, yet, really, I don't think anyone who has read the comics (or like me who hasn't but knows some stuff from them) found it a revelation. Scarecrow's character seems to be a bit different, more like Hugo Strange with an obsession for fear gas. Not to mention that Riddler challenges are tied to the true ending to the game, they wasted Deathstroke on a stupid Batmobile section?
And yes. Batmobile. Batmobile is made well. The control on that thing is marvelous. But there are way too many Batmobile sections. If they were varied or require methodical approach like some of on-foot sections, I wouldn't complain: except they aren't. Most of Batmobile sections are incredibly one dimensional. You attack all the drones almost exactly the same way, meaning you approach almost all Batmobile combat sections exactly the same way. Some of Batmobile puzzles are good, but seeing how most of them are associated with Riddler, you get tired of them.
And that's what the game feels like: tiring. This is basically Arkham City with Batmobile. A lot of the level design is still the same (and they are still good), and that's not a bad thing seeing how Origin basically is like that and it's fun to play. But it has stupid needless stuff sprinkled throughout, plus the Batmobile. Playing all the filler stuff, I can't help but feel like I'm playing an Ubisoft open world game with better core gameplay mechanics. They even have bloody towers all over the place you have to tackle. Except I somehow found Syndicate worth getting 100%; this I just couldn't.
Oh and if you don't have a PC with more RAM than 12GB, don't even bother playing it on PC. I have i7-6700HQ, GTX 1070 and 8GB RAM, and the game still stutters like crazy when moving fast through Gotham in Batmobile or flying.

I want to like this game, I really do. I paid 30 dollars for it and I was hoping to get at least 20-25 hours of gaming out of it. Unfotunately, while the game isn't bad per se, it has some flaws that for me impair the game's playability and longevity. Firstly, the game, while graphically impressive, is very badly optimized. Some gamers can run the game flawlessly but my system has a 780m. The 780m falls between a 660 Ti and a 770 GT. The game itself recommends(not requires...recommends!) a vanilla 560 so consequenly, I should be able to run this game at 1440p, high settings and still get 60 fps.
But I simply can't. The best I can manage is 1080p, medium settings and 60 fps. In a twitch shooter, those settings neither look good nor play well. In short the game is a fat bloated pig on mobility architectures and lots of people play on mobility architectures. This is an oversight that strictly shouldn't have happened. I suppose if you're running a 970, this game isn't a problem but if you're one of the many mobility gamers out there, be wary of this game because the architectures are different and even if you do have the horsepower to run it beautifully the game may not be designed to take advantage of it.
Secondly the game is very repititious. The classes lack significant variation. Each round plays almost exactly as the last as you buy the same gear and get the same weapons. The fighting is frenetic, which on the surface seems great, until you realize that it's simply spamming everything with firepower until it drops. The maps are uninspired and level advancement is slowed. Thematically, the concept of people spontaneously turning into zombies with drills for arms doesn't do it for me either, personally.
Mass Effect 3 has a similar multiplayer component but has literally 60 different classes and over 50 different weapons. Did I mention that at least 25 of the class archtypes play *completely* differently? Some have a staggering array of powers and others are weapon specialists. The range and variety is truly wonderful. Characters feel well, handle well and shooting play is flawless. Graphics are attractive and the game runs on modest systems. The game has over 15 different maps that all feel/play differently and you can play against four different races which all attack/behave differently.
When combined with four different difficulty modes, lots of ammo types, equipment/character bonuses and a complex branching power/skill system, the game has every advantage over this one. So why am I bringing it up? Because the games are almost identifcal in their design and yet Mass Effect 3's multiplayer component was a throwaway mode that few players extolled or gave credit to. And yet the game comes bundled with a long, rich campaign and costs 10 dollars on Origin.
You could buy this, get the inferior product, for 30 dollars. Go play ME 3 multiplayer. It's ultimately the same product but better and you'll be a lot happier. If you've played Left 4 Dead 2, or Mass Effect 3 multi, this game is simply no great shakes.
By all means post why you think this commentary/review is wrong. I'd love to debate why it is.

People will spend a lot of time citing how bizarre Zeno Clash is, rightly so but it also overshadows the fact that this game is also a great brawler, with interesting characters and story to match the strange setting. Visually it's indeed a splendour, wierd and wonderful with all kinds of cool details to the world and it's inhabitants. Despite it being such an odd place you get really immersed in it thanks to the physiciality of the combat and your interactions. Even the games guns are clunky constructions made of bone and wood. In all, everything has weight. There are also a host of welcome improvements over the first installment. We get to spend less time with the Corwids of the original but in exchange we visit so much more of the land, get more challenges and tools at our disposal. Keeping this fighting game interesting, mechanically for it's dozen hours is quite the feat. Side quests often reward you with valuable items and weapons. Totems too encourage you to explore, to level up and make the game a bit easier given how tough the combat can be.
It's a little clunky though and overall the game lacks the polish of AAA titles. Voice acting ranges from good or solid to the outright bland but it never got distracting. It also strains at the seams to hold the games scale in place. But for the breadth and depth of it's ideas, as well as the colourful execution, it's absolutely a must play for those seeking something different.

There's a lot of confliction when I first looked at the Zeno Clash series. I didn't know whether to buy one or two. If this is your case and you don't own both games and you do end up buying one copy... buy the first if you can. If you liked the first, you'll definitely like and buy the second. The story line gets exponentially better and relates to the previous story.
The second Zeno Clash takes place with a continued story line from the last. Ghat is now able to roam freely unlike the first which guided the player and jumped place to place. If you've played the first, those places that you went to, you are able to visit freely again. New enemies are created that suit their terrain wherever you go along the world. I like how the first literally did not need any free-roaming, it was nice to have something different in the second one (as you were able to continuously run).
The game-play has changed I would say about 50% from normal. You can now call up allies when you fight, which sort of takes away being smothered by opponents. The first one really felt like you hit your opponent, that same effect is still there but not to that satisfaction of that from the first (that pttchhhhh sound when hitting someone good and that dynamic camera movement). What I did like though (probably the best upgrade), is when you were being attacked from behind, you were warned and were able to press both mouse buttons to counter the opponent hitting your back. This is huge as Zeno Clash you'll find yourself sometimes surrounded by many enemies. I would definitely like to see more of this type of feature (hopefully with one button control or kick control) if a new Zeno Clash comes out.
The fighting scheme is somewhat the same and both hands now are able to power punch. Weapons are as far out as they were before and 3 new weapons are added to your "special" arsenal. One is a chain which comes very handy and is fun to use, the other two are two special Golem weapons which I won't spoil. The fighting is a bit more decorated in the second, and I feel more freedom was given. The grab function has also slightly switched.
I would recommend this game if you are a real Zeno Clash fan or just really liked the first. Unless your the guy who likes newer games instead of older version of games then grab number 2.
RATING : 7.8/8
Would give it an 8 if the game was slightly more different than the first. I would also like to ask kindly that the creators the Zeno world make sure a Zeno Clash 3 comes out :)!
For future Zeno Clash games I would recommend multiplayer, and maybe even dare to try to incorporate local co-op. To add to the fighting, perhaps add kicks or even allow for players to hold down the mouse button, then use the mouse to swing to determine the type of swing. Don't make it to the point where people start snapping their mouse cord, but something decently close enough.

There's a lot to be said on both sides with Killing Floor 2.
Take my points with a grain of salt, as you may feel differently about some of these features but some things that personally disappointed me in KF2 are:
-The heavy, powerful feel of the guns in KF1 is somewhat gone, or at least comparatively lacking
-Despite characters being more unique and diverse, their personalities still seem flat compared to KF1
-The voice menu from KF1 has been severely downgraded to an awkward, minimalistic Overwatch-style communication wheel, which is lacking extremely basic options that were included in KF1 such as "Thank you", "Run" or "Look out"
-The gritty, horror-esque atmosphere of KF1 is replaced with a somewhat unfitting shiny, clean, futuristic sci-fi style
That being said, Killing Floor 2 still has many redeeming qualities that, in my personal opinion, outweigh the aforementioned letdowns.
+In my personal experience, when playing on Suicidal or higher, the game actually feels more challenging and fast-paced than the first game.
+Gore physics
+Great soundtrack
+Vastly improved graphics (obviously)
+-Significantly less grindy perk progression, though it almost feels a bit too fast at times
Overall, Killing Floor 2 is lacking a lot of the personality that made Killing Floor so great, but other than that, it delivers more of (and in a few cases, improves on) the violent, fast-paced, co-op horde-shooter gameplay that Killing Floor 1 did so well.

If you have some money to sink into the game, you will enjoy playing this game since (at it's core) it is still a better game than Hearthstone (even though that is not really saying much).
However, if you dont feel like spending money and you are not lucky enough when you open the free boosters, prepare your heart and patience to grind through some very horrible and frustrating times until you can actually get a good enough deck to even feel like you are competing against other players (took me several days to get enough money to buy enough boosters to be lucky enough to make a quasi-mediocre completely luck-based Royal Banner Swordcraft deck where I may or may not actually draw those freaking cards so I can actually do something with my awful officer cards after turn 4).
Also, it feels pretty tricky to get vials and money to get those decks since you (again) have to grind through cheating bots, you gotta be really lucky to get good cards when you play in the arena and you have to be lucky with the missions you get (only "consistent?" way to get money since you only get exp in matches) because you will get a lot of missions that consist of getting a win with a particular deck......good luck with those if you dont even have 1 mediocre deck xD.
The game also suffers from a few not well-balanced cards like Prince of Darkness, Mordecai the Duelist (this one is particulary disgusting to go against with a bad deck without banish cards) or Cerberus and some incredibly stupid mechanics (like the second player getting 3 evolution points, leaving the first player at a huge disadvantage most of the matches that get to late-game). Also, sometimes you will feel like you are playing Candy Crush because the RNG will simply NOT give you useful cards a lot of times. But of course, that comes with the territory, this is a card game, after all.
Also, I find people netdecking almost constantly. For every player with a meme deck or trying to make a good deck of his own, I find 20 guys with tier 1/tournament winning decks. This is bad because, again, I was one of the unlucky ones who didnt get a decent enough deck to play against those mega-decks.
All in all, its not a bad game. But it isnt a particularly good one either.
It is a pay2progress game at it's heart and that will always offer a frustrating experience for a lot of players if they are not lucky enough to get an actual competitive deck with the initial free boosters.
If you are not a patient player and dont feel you want to spend money on this game, I really do not recommend it.
If you are very patient and insanely lucky in your free boosters, sure, it is kinda playable as a F2P (you need to be incredibly lucky though....like...ridiculously impossibly lucky).
If you want to spend money anyway then yeah, you can actually be competitive without being stupid lucky, but why not play MtG instead? hehehe

I am fairly certain this is the worst game I have
played. Often even bad games may be worth a low price, but this game is not worth a single penny or moment of your time. It fails on every level, from technical issues to braindead gameplay. Avoid at all costs.
Let's start at the beginning, the launcher. The highest the resolution can go is 720p. This can be forgiven if the game is good enough or it's heavily dependent on 2D art (such as visual novels), but no such excuses exist for this game. And as far as I can tell no option for a windowed mode either, so I hope you like stretching. And even with all the options maxed out here the screenshots do not begin to describe how terrible this game looks in motion.
Moving on to the game itself, the UI is hideous and clunky. Once you've managed to get past that, you are stuck with the longest loading screen I can recall in anything short of a Source game in many years (and the art you're stuck looking at doesn't help pass the time). Then you are in the "game." Unlike virtually every other single racing game from a behind-the-car perspective, you control both movement and acceleration with the left stick of your controller. I suspect this was done to lazily match the keyboard control scheme, rather than taking consideration for what plays well (a concern you will see equally ignored throughout the rest of the game). The driving itself is incredibly lifeless, from the physics to the track design. Other tractors will come towards you and slow you down if you hit them. You get points for doing so, but it doesn't seem worth it considering how much they get in your way. If only you could plow through them and watch tractor and driver alike careen through the air, perhaps that would have been one sole redeeming factor for this game. There are also anti-power-ups (why would you do this?) in abundance in this game. That floating thing in the middle of the road that looks like it'll be fun? It apparently makes you so drunk your controls lock up for around 15 seconds, leaving you with nothing to do as you stare at a wall. Between the time it took to figure out the travesty of the controls and discovering which of the power-ups actually help you (only one), I failed the mission. Blissfully though, the game gives you the option to quit to desktop right then and there. That is the best design choice the developers made in this whole trainwreck of a game.
In short, do not buy this game. Do not even redeem the key if you buy it from a bundle, like I did, hoping for a quick joyride. Do not let this game anywhere near your computer. It is, frankly, less playable than Bad Rats. If you do end up with a key, give it to someone you don't like or something. Maybe prank a friend with it. Do not play it.

Risk of Rain is a game you will either love it or hate it.
In my opinion, this game is amazing.
The gameplay is simple and easy to understand, but at the same time it is really difficult.
You crash land on an alien planet and must get of the planet by activing the teleporter in each biome and collect gear to help you fend off the monsters that inhabit the area. There are 12 playable characters that each has thier own play style and a ton of variety in the items, enemies and bosses. Each item, enemie and boss has it's own description which I found very interesting to read as it gave a little back story to the world with the occasional joke. The one thing about the game I found annoying is the game doesn't have a save feature and you have to keep playing until you die. This means if you exit to the menu or quit the game you lose all your progress. I guess it could be called a game feature, but I wasn't to keen on it.
The graphics are great for the retro pixel feel the game is going for and felt familar, but special in it's own way.
In my opinion the developers didn't cut any corner here either.
Another unique feature was the music. The music fits in so well with all the planet that you explore and most of the time it fits in so well you don't even notice it. It just feels like it should be there. The devs reused a few tracts for a couple biomes but I was fine with that as it they had all ready put a ton of work into it already.
There is also a multiplayer feature, but you have to use a program like hamchi or portforward and god is it hard to portforward.
In conclusion, Risk of Rain is a fantasic game that is great for killing time and has a lot of variety so it is hard to get bored of. The indie devs have done a spatacular job on this game, which is relatively cheap and is a worth getting.

When it comes to surviving the hostile alien planet, time is against you. The name of the game in Risk of Rain is to speed your way through power and escape the dangers before they overwhelm you. Kill to adapt and grow stronger against the alien hordes before they outgrow and kill you, and hurry your way back to your drop-ship.
The lore behind the game is pretty impressive and depressing at the same time. Your concern and hope for mercy is cast aside, knowing you were guilty of stealing everything from an uncharted planet. The one who caught wind of this decided to put your in your place. It's merely a moral summary of greed, consequences and evolution.
There are various classes to unlock with each and every play-through, and every area is chosen in a random matter to hinder your progress. Eventually, though, when you find all the secrets within each and every area, you can gain an even bigger advantage or challenge yourself even further within every starting play-through. So the replay value can grow over time as long as long as you're curious and adventurous enough to explore every nook and cranny.
Graphics are deliberately primitive, but performance is good enough even for a 2009-based computer. The old, rusty look of the wastelands and the survivors that dwell in it, with various creatures that glow, surprise and potentially shock the players with mini-bosses and special item drops. It would suck to walk these dull and hazardous worlds. But the struggle lies in the hands of the player. Your knowledge of each and every area in the game can also be advantageous depending on your monitor size and display resolution.
Unfortunately, because of permanent deaths within every play-through, your time to think before you act may end up getting you killed before you make it to the end in one go. Once you've died enough times before learning everything and then finally beating the game, it can be satisfying. But only if you're patient and persistent enough to adapt.

Positive:
+I really like how you can adjust how long your run will be, and that it calculates this based on your personal time completing runs.

+Nice card upgrades/mechanics, make sure you properly seat each card tightly into it's slot!
+Enough random goodies to be interesting, but not overdone like Diablo or Torchlight.
Neutral:
I have to say I am a bit worried about Corpse Runs!  I had a real bad flashback to the late 90's playing Everquest. In Everyquest you die 18 levels down in some dungeon and have to painfully run back down and get your ... naked.  This is somewhat similar.  However you don't have to start over from the entrance, and it is not really too painful to get your stuff back.  I died in a room with the mage full of nasty armored dudes, took me a few tries to get my stuff back.  All in all it was NOT very painful.  This could have been a huge turnoff for me, but I think it's done well.
Negative:
-I use a steam controller for almost everything I play.  I was happy to see they included a Steam Controller profile, I love it when a dev puts some time into making a really nice profile.  However my first run or two in the demo was really not fun.  The buttons are ALL labeled wrong!  So it kept telling me to smash armor with the Y button , when it actually was the B button!  Not a huge negative, but really annoying.  I'm old, it took me a while to remember which buttons to hit when due to the on screen prompts always being wrong!  An hour or so of messing around and it was not really a problem any more.  And I could always make my own steam controller profile for it.  Not a huge issue. Maybe there is a way to set this in options, I did really dig for it.
-Targeting.  Once again this may just be a steam controller issue.  I had a little difficulty using the right track pad to target.  WIth some practice this was not a terrible issue, I just felt like there could still be some improvement to it.  Not a game breaker for me.
-Atmosphere.  It's early access, and I'm only four hours into the game.  I'm hoping there is a lot more variety to the setting.  It all seems similar.   Maybe I'm not far enough into the game, not sure, just beat the first boss at 4 hours.
-Also probably because it's early access.  Not a lot of character types to choose from.  Only two at the moment, a warrior and a mage.   A 3rd one says coming soon!  What would make this game absolutely perfect for me is about a dozen unique character types (maybe even DLC packs).
I am really having a lot of fun with this game.  I rarely buy things full price, took a shot at this after playing the demo.  The game mechanics are unique.  I would have a hard time comparing this to another game, although Diablo comes the closest, if it used cards instead of gear.  I think the difficulty is just right.  My negative points are all very minor.  The corpse run I was worried about seemed to be a non issue (was more my fault dying 4 times in a row, have to learn to play the mage better).

Antichamber is an original kind of 3D puzzle/platformer game. The style is often compared to portal; it's simplistic but also beautiful, clear, and the environment can create subtle yet effective hints about the puzzle-solutions. A lot of "rules" set for platformers and other games are broken, played with or showed for what they really are.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is heavily focused on puzzles. These puzzles range from easy to very difficult, and it is usually important to keep thinking about the things you're doing. Often, when you think you understand the "rules" of some of the puzzles, a surprising twist makes you look at the next puzzle completely different.
Besides puzzles there is a minimal amount of platforming. Most platforming is easy and can be done by anyone picking up gaming for the first time. However, by clever use of platforming and manipulating puzzle elements, new solutions can be found and whole parts of the game can even be skipped or accessed early.
This game throws a lot of surprises at you, especially at the start. During the late game you do expect most of the "twists" but the puzzles themselves still manage to find new ways to baffle you nonetheless.
Graphics:
There is nothing bad to say about the graphics. The style for the game has purposely been chosen as very simple, which keeps the environments calm and soothing. The game is white, with vibrant primary colours scattered around for several purposes. Everything you see serves a goal. Overall, it looks beautiful.
Sound:
I did not notice music, but there are sound effects and background "noises" such as water/birds/animals. Like the graphics, the sounds are very soothing and complement the style of the rest of the game. Sometimes sounds and environment do create mystery elements, which
Replay value:
Sadly, I find that this game has little replay-value. After completing the game, you know all puzzles and all paths. The most interesting thing about the game are the surprising solutions, which will now be clear from the start. A second playthrough can be fun for purposes such as a timed run (speedrun) or for a more thorough understanding of some of the meanings of puzzles. After this, you are done.
All in all this game was very enjoyable and surprising, and if you like puzzle games this is certainly something I can recommend you to play. However: keep in mind that this games takes about 4 to 5 hours to complete, after which most of the replay value is lost.

There are two things it does right: combat improvements and the narrative presentation. There are just so many things at your disposal when it comes to free-flow combat, and yes, odd stuff happens still, but the tight rhythmic gameplay is just better with enemy variety as well as gadgets you can use during the combat (plus, some levels have you fight along side your sidekicks and these sections are really sweet). It balances out the flow of the combat, intensity as well as strategy. As for the narrative presentation, Arkham series has always been a knock-out when it comes to fusing gameplay with cutscenes, and Arkham Knight does it best here.
The problem is, the story itself is lackluster. The wholly unsatisfying ending aside, the main story fails to incorporate various characters and the world, and instead sidelines potentially very interesting villains away from the main story. Arkham Knight himself is an interesting character, yet, really, I don't think anyone who has read the comics (or like me who hasn't but knows some stuff from them) found it a revelation. Scarecrow's character seems to be a bit different, more like Hugo Strange with an obsession for fear gas. Not to mention that Riddler challenges are tied to the true ending to the game, they wasted Deathstroke on a stupid Batmobile section?
And yes. Batmobile. Batmobile is made well. The control on that thing is marvelous. But there are way too many Batmobile sections. If they were varied or require methodical approach like some of on-foot sections, I wouldn't complain: except they aren't. Most of Batmobile sections are incredibly one dimensional. You attack all the drones almost exactly the same way, meaning you approach almost all Batmobile combat sections exactly the same way. Some of Batmobile puzzles are good, but seeing how most of them are associated with Riddler, you get tired of them.
And that's what the game feels like: tiring. This is basically Arkham City with Batmobile. A lot of the level design is still the same (and they are still good), and that's not a bad thing seeing how Origin basically is like that and it's fun to play. But it has stupid needless stuff sprinkled throughout, plus the Batmobile. Playing all the filler stuff, I can't help but feel like I'm playing an Ubisoft open world game with better core gameplay mechanics. They even have bloody towers all over the place you have to tackle. Except I somehow found Syndicate worth getting 100%; this I just couldn't.
Oh and if you don't have a PC with more RAM than 12GB, don't even bother playing it on PC. I have i7-6700HQ, GTX 1070 and 8GB RAM, and the game still stutters like crazy when moving fast through Gotham in Batmobile or flying.

Many people do not find the story interesting, but I commend EA for trying something different with a new IP and the story is more than servicable.

Although still in Beta, Book of Demons is a well-polished, beautiful, and nearly complete game. It’s story and intro adds a fantastic ambiance that stays true through the game. The card collecting and upgrading system adds goals, gives satisfaction, and forces you not only to use hand eye coordination, but also strategy to complete this epic game. The difficulty curve isn’t something you would expect a game still in Beta to do right, but, to my astonishment, I found it already perfected. Although basically complete, book of Demons will wait to be released until February 2018 but, to the joy of the community, the long expected Ranger Update will be added sometime before the new year. But this update will only add more play time so you might as well pick up the game now and enjoy saving the world from a duck wielding demon!
Like a typical hack and slash RPG, you’ll be fighting multiple enemies at once while using different abilities (cards) depending on your current circumstance in game. Simple right? Well of course things are complicated whenever enemies start summoning hordes of skeletons, exploding into poisonous clouds, freezing you’re buns off, and burning your mana with hell fire! With each different level lays a different challenge and, thus, demands a different strategy. All of this forces you to have good planning skills along with proper knee jerk reactions. Although this sounds like it would make the neigh impossible, it only adds a level of challenge without making the game seem impossible. Because of this, It’s difficulty, and how beautifully balanced it is, greatly enhances the gameplay enjoyability.
Perhaps one of the most praised things about Book of Demons is its soundtrack. I’ve read many raving reviews about how it’s better than the philharmonic orchestra, professional bagpipers, grandpa’s snoring, etc. Perhaps this set my expectation to high. I found it subpar, neither here nor there. It certainly fit all the themes but it was nothing that wowed me. As for the sound effects, I was pleasantly surprised. Often this is a corner cut by developers but I would give it a seven out of ten, a good deal above average. On top of that, on the developer’s timeline he clearly states that he will further improve them. Moving on, the art for Book of Demons is not only original, but simplistic and elegant. The combination of 2 dimensional characters in a 3D environment adds personality, depth, and contrast that most art styles lack. The unnaturalness of this design compliments the dark, brooding atmosphere that really sets apart this game from the masses.
I know everyone’s wondering about how finished the game is and what’s missing at the moment. Well, there are only three major changes that will be made to the game. 1, the developer is making a “star mechanic” that will probably give you a rating/score upon completing each dungeon depending on how well you did. There are already achievements for this and it should add to your drive to complete each dungeon as perfectly as possible. 2, more achievements!!! This ones pretty straight forward, it’s going to add more goals for you to complete, more play time, and more ways to prove your superiority over your friends. 3 (the big one!), this update will add The Ranger as a playable class. Now this might not seem like a big deal but I promise you it is! Whenever you slaughter the innocent demon of death and doom, you’re encouraged to play through again as the mage. So, adding another play through will increase how much game time you get by 50%! Not only that, but it will also make it possible to get tens of currently walled off achievements. When will these updates come out? Sometime between now and February of 2018. So, as you may for surmised, the game is complete but how long you can play it will be lengthened in the future.
Hours of entertaining game play, beautiful graphics, challenging combat, character and card upgrades, and so much more! What not to love? Truly, his game is a hack-n-slash RPG junkie’s dream. However, like most people, I worry about purchasing games still in development. This is because some companies like to take the money they made and leave the game unfinished. Not so with this game! The game, in my opinion, is ready for release right now and the updates are still pouring in! Honestly, this game is just a treasure. So go ahead, snatch it for its very reasonable price, help support the kindly creator, and have a heck of a time playing Book of Demons!

I just finished playing Antichamber, and I decided this world have not enough review of this game yet, not on Linux at least.
Plot
The game has no plot, it's something that I would define an introspective journey. When the game starts, you see no introduction, you just spawn in a black and white room with four walls. One of the walls is the settings menu, then here is a a black wall, another wall with a strange symbol, that will become a map in future and another transparent wall behind what there is an "exit" door. Your adventure starts when you click on the first available room of the map. From now on, your goal is to solve multiple puzzles to gain access to deeper areas of the maze-like game world, until you get access to the last stage. At the end of every puzzle on the wall there will be a panel with an image. If clicked, an aphorism related to the puzzle you just solved will show up. Some of those signs are extremely nice, and they are probably the soul of the game somehow: they seem like telling the story of a life, from the beginning to the end. I really appreciated them. Some of them are also useful, and give some hints for the puzzles to come. The structure is non linear, and the puzzles can be solved in almost-arbitrary order. Only some puzzles depend on items you find from previous puzzles. Some of the puzzles lead to other puzzles, and some lead to dead ends. Some times those dead ends are "dev-rooms", where there are pieces of artwork showing you the development of the game.
Gameplay
The game looks like a classic 3D first person shooter, but there are no enemies to kill, no hurry and no stress situation: it's just you and a non-euclidean world to explore. Yes folks: non-euclidean. It means that if you go a way, then you turn and go back, you may end up in a place which is not the place you came from. Sounds strange? And that's not all! It also means that the place where you are may depend on the direction you are looking at: if you are not looking at a wall, such wall may well cease to exist. Sounds confusing? Well, it is, but it's funny confusion: since the games is not random in any way, the only point is getting used to the structure of the world. It is a continuous side-thinking exercise, and what I liked most is that there is absolutely no hurry in any moment of the game. I really hate having to complete levels within some time limit, or having to redo the same thing over and over because the difficult part is not understanding the puzzle but doing the incredibly complicated sequence of very stupid actions in the right order at the right time. This is very rarely the case for Antichamber: look at the world around you, think how to go through the situation with the tools you got, and do it. Some puzzles are obviously simpler than others, and many of them look totally impossible at a first sight. After you have been able to solve the first puzzles, you will be given a strange ring-like gun. This gun is able to absorb and fire little cubes of the world, and will be key for being able to solve many of the puzzles. Further in the game, you will get upgraded versions of such a gun, with ability to quickly suck and spit cubes, move cubes around and create entire walls. The gun will be your only companion in this adventure: as I said, it is introspective.
Controls
Classic mouse and keyboard combo is the way I suggest for playing Antichamber. I don't think there is controller support, and if there is I don't recommend it: there are many other games where a controller will work very well, but in FPS-like games mouse and keyboard are what you want - unless Valve does the miracle.
Controls are easy and there are no problems with the defaults. The time you will spend struggling to understand how to do what you want to do is near zero.
Graphics and sound
Graphics is minimally beautiful. Nothing too complicated, and basically no textures. Colours, colours, colours everywhere! I'm generally not much a fan of games that willingly look old-fashioned or minimal, but Antichamber is definitely nice, and this choice totally fits the spirit of the game and enhances the feeling of being in a strange, mind-driven world where geometry is broken. The graphic makes you feel like you are living in one of those dreams where you look behind a door two times and see two different places.
The game runs on Unreal Engine 3, that seems to run pretty well on our beloved Linux operating systems. I played on Sabayon Linux using hybrid graphics and Bumblebee / Primus GPU for offloading the graphic tasks to my GeForce GT 630M. The frame rate have always been pretty stable. The game crashed a couple of times, though.
The sound is nice but nothing that will make you scream of joy. The soundtrack is embracing and relaxing, and helps you dive in the world, although is not the aspect of the game that you will remember most favourably.
Longevity
I am a slow player, and I finished the game in about 12 hours. Once the game is finished, there is little reason to play it again, or to re-do over and over the same puzzles. It is a one-shot experience.
Conclusion
Antichamber is a very good game. In these times of clones and clones and clones, creating something really new is a good achievement per se. Creating something that is new and good is much more difficult, but Antichamber reached the goal. If you are searching for a testosteronic shoot-to-eveything-that-moves, move along: this is no place for you. If you feel like experiencing something new, dive into a world shaped like a dream and stress your brain with side, thinking, Antichamber is what you are searching for.
Final rate: 8/10.
How much is worth™: ~ 5 Euros.

If you're looking for the literal grandfather of the stealth genre you've found it. Not to be fooled by that modern reboot crap made by Eidos Montreal.
A game where you the player are thrown into huge multiple levels and left to your own devices after a short training mission, there's no handholding here no big pointy arrows or minimaps or ability to take on multipe guards at once you are a thief not a fighter and this is really emphasised through your character's physical weakness. So if you're a fan of hardcore stealth where any moment's detection could mean your last this is for you. See Thief as a trilogy allows the player to live this power fantasy usually gotten from video games in this case by allowing the player to be somewhere they're not supposed to be and doing something they shouldn't which by not getting caught in the process allows them to feel so much more powerful over their enemies.
Thief 2: The Metal Age basically improves upon many of the flaws found within Thief: The Dark Project. If you like me were first put off by The Dark Project's focus upon the supernatural and magic, then Thief 2 is for you. This game retracts back from The Dark Project's more labyrinthine level design but mind you that does not mean the scale of the levels within this product have been reduced in fact some of the missions I've come across in this game really make me wonder what the hell has gone wrong with the industry nowadays. For a game released back in the good old year 2000 I would never have expected to be breaking into three-floor banks with a whole network of tunnels to be found underneath, to buildings which are roughly 6-7 floors in scale as well as to have a whole sequence beforehand set on the rooftops of a steampunk dsytopian city in which I the player can eavesdrop and break into these buildings, hear guards argue across the streets to one another as well as witness another group of thieves taking goods from another house which yes being the master thief that I am I pilfer their goods without them noticing. Which may I add is all completely optional, the sheer volume of methods in which you can tackle your objectives as well as explore the world is quite astonishing and in retrospect a player can really see how Looking Glass studios as a company was well ahead of its time.
Cutscenes are the most beautiful and original concept I've seen and I've yet still to this day to find a game that hits the same level of atmosphere through design as found within the works produced by the team at Looking Glass in which through the style of rotoscoping some of their cutscenes where others are just narration over still images allows the artstyle of this game to really blend with the physical game itself through both shape and tone intertwining the overall Gothic/steampunk direction the sequel took.
Soundtrack which is done by Eric Brosius is really something else which words cannot describe, the game is worth buying for it's soundtrack and sound design alone which still to this day not one single stealth game has for some reason nailed one of the most simplisitic sound design choices that Thief introduced to gaming; the ability to listen and hear your enemy approaching the same way in which Thief conveys.
It's a game you've got to at least try for a few missions to get into its very unforgiving and this can put some people off but stick through it and I guarantee you this will be one of the top games you've played.

Why does this keep happening to me? And by this I'm referring to the fact I can't seem to play a game where I can say, in clear-cut manner "this is good or this is bad", but always have to keep a balancing scale in my head and actively weighing positives and negatives against each other. Well, in one more attempt to remain consistent such is the case with Shadowrun Returns so let's get down to it, chummer.
First thing first – it's GREAT to see Shadowrun make a proper return to the world of video games following its less than stellar last entry. That does come with a caveat or two because Returns was funded thanks to a Kickstarter project and this fact seeps through almost every aspect of the game, but we'll get around to that in due time. If there is one major Achilles heel worth noting it's the fact the entire game feels like a very light venture into the world of Shadowrun, but also one that makes only a token effort in explaining inner workings and setting itself to the uninitiated. If you don't know much about Shadowrun you'll get a brief 101; only for parts pertinent to what you're dealing with and delivered to you at a snail's pace primarily through loading screen text. This goes beyond matters of fluff and extends to systems themselves  - it's a borderline RPG-lite experience compared to what many have come to expect these days, eschewing things like looting fallen bodies and any great interaction with the world that surrounds you aside from few mechanics-related interactable points. This goes hand-in-hand with very light-weight tutorials which you'll have to actively seek instead of them being naturally introduced to ease you into the game. This may or may not be a relevant sticking point depending on your level of familiarity no only with Shadowrun but also with RPGs in general, though.
To keep everything in perspective it is important to note this game was not made on a multi-million dollar budget and that should exempt it from some of the problems, even if things such as sometimes unresponsive functions and somewhat uninspired takes on certain elements like implementation of the Matrix remain annoying throughout the game. Speaking of which, as much as I love to see everything ranging from Adepts to Deckers presented not all Archetypes were created equal as far as unique selling points go and neither were Etiquettes aka your social "specializations" which unlock specific options in dialog. Game really could have used more of these options in general, but I guess it functions acceptably well with this overall linear structure of the game taking you from location to location as story demands and not letting you re-visit older ones, local quasi-hub notwithstanding.
That was enough nagging about the game, where's the good stuff? Returns is not a bad game and you may have noticed I gave it a thumb up recommending it despite my incessant complaining in paragraphs above. Why? Because it's a still a competent RPG with great flavor and decent character building options. It smartly offsets the fact you only customize the main character by letting you choose who to take with you on missions from a roster of contracts, quality ranging depending on how deep your pockets are. Even though it kinda takes a while to kick in, game's story certainly delivers on everything from standard Shadowrunner fare to more... out there revelations and twists you will probably not see coming, but which still have absolute basis in existing lore.  Relatively short by RPG standards, but succinctly to the point and with no filler to waste your time. Characters? They definitely take a backseat to events unfolding although I have no doubt you'll find favorites among them.
Last advice, chummer – never EVER cut a deal with a dragon if you value your sorry existence.

So, Thief 2 is weird. Apart from some minor tweeks, The Metal Age is not that different from it's predecessor: it's basically the same thing, only with robots instead of zombies (which are equally as terrifying, don't get me wrong).
Now, Karras' machines are quite dumb, easy to kill and easier to sneak past but if they spot you, you are good as dead, babe. This means that the game focuses much more on ghosting this time around, going as far as giving your a couple of missions in which sneaking past every enemy without interacting with them is one of the objectives required to beat the level.
In Thief 2 there are many more enemies, more convoluted puzzles, more branching paths and it is overal more criptic and harder than the first game but you also have more gadgets to help you along the way: Invisibility potions, slow-fall potions, Noisemaker arrows that actually work, exploding frog eggs that I've never used once and my absolute favourite: water arrows. I know they're not new to the series by any means but if you start a level and you buy anything but water arrows you're an idiot OR a masochist. Also I feel like they should have used Garrett's fancy mechanic eye a bit more. It smells like wasted opportunity right there, even because it was Karras himself, the main antagonist, to design it. It could have been a strong plot point and a great way to renovate the old game mechanics but instead it's just kind of there.
The graphics are improved a bit, still not that great but, I mean, for the time they were decent. Again the maps are incredibly large, labyrinthic and detaled so that's understandable but what I find inexcusable though is how repetitive the level design is. In the first game every level was memorable and unforgetable but here they are all kind of mhe, a part from a couple of exceptions ("Life of the party" is just fantastic).
I feel that the problem here is that they went for a more geometric and specular design. Every corridor looks the same, every room has the same props in the same places so yes, you get lost easily, which is good in a thief game, but it's just not fun in this one in particular. Maybe this is the reason why they decided to include a marker on the in-game map that tells you where you are, I don't know but I'm really glad they did. It totally makes the "notes" feature useless but at least the game is playable like that.
The plot is, well, good? It's quite an intricate story and I think it needed a bit more breathing space: it starts too late into the game, so it gets rushed near the end. The plot itself is not bad at all, it's probably even better than the original's, I just feel it could have been told better.
In conclusion, Thief II: The Metal Age is not as good as the original but it's still worth playing! The subtlety, the creepy atmosphere, the ingenious puzzling, the great voice acting, the amazing sound design, it's all still there, it's just a bit lazier this time. I know that you shouldn't fix what's not broken in the first place but still, this game could have been so much more!
If you like the original Thief you'll like this one too, that's for sure and if you're into modding as well, then you may want to explore the modding community that this game has: it's huge.

If you can't afford hallucinogenic drugs, this is a good cheap alternative. I think I may well be having nightmares about FatherMother for a long time to come.
As far as the gameplay goes, I found the controls tricky (getting the right sequence of mouse clicks to pass the tutorial took me far more time than I'd like). Though it turned out that didn't matter anyway, as pressing both mouse buttons down at once to perform a double punch, followed by kicking my enemy once they were on the floor, did the trick most of the time.
The gun design is very intriguing, reminiscent of the weaponry in the film Videodrome. But firing the guns was mildly disappointing, to say the least: they have the same kind of effect as a child's popgun, both in terms of haptic feedback, sound and damage done to enemies. And they break after firing them about 4 times. I decided to stick to fists and feet.
I didn't play for long, but during the time I did, I didn't have a clue what was going on. Working out where to go next seemed next to impossible, and I got around mainly by chance. I wasn't really sure who anyone was, who I was, where I was, or where I was supposed to be going. The dialogue didn't help: it is extraordinarily difficult to follow, obtuse, bizarre, and poorly translated, with the quality of subtitles from a Chinese martial arts film translated by someone who speaks English as a second language. But charming nonetheless. I didn't play the first Zeno Clash, but I get the feeling that if I had, I would still not have a clue what was going on.
Despite all these flaws, I found it entertaining for an hour or so. The experience of playing it is kind of like being inside one of those avant garde Czech animations you sometimes see on TV at 3am, but with fighting.

Well, this is going to be long and unstructured. It's here to relay relevant info about the game, not give an arbitrary number and talk about immersion like some of the idiots on here.
I haven't 100% completed Dying Light yet, there are still some challenges, skills and a couple of quarantine zones left but that's still given me a good 46 hours of fun. (All main/side quests completed though)
Dying Light (apart from the obvious Dead Island base) takes from both Mirror's Edge and Far Cry 3, though thankfully the gameplay is deeper than Far Cry 3. There are a few guns but most of your time will be spent with melee weapons and jumping along favelas like a monkey jumps through trees.
Keybinds are generally pretty comfortable (yes you can rebind). The visuals are a mixed bag, yes, it's a REALLY nice looking game but maxing every setting will never hold 60fps. I have a GTX 980, 16GB RAM, SSD and an i7-4790 running at 4.00GHz, this should NOT be happening. Most of the chug is caused by the draw distance setting but even with it at minimum the fps still sometimes drops under 60. If you've got an older PC beware. Also they tried to trick PC users with a fake "optimisation" patch, go look that up if you're interested in that.
The movement/climbing feels good (no Assassin's Creed auto climbing garbage) and the quests/side quests are reasonably varied and fun. You have a visible lower body (the correct way to make a first person game). You'll probably spend way less time with the game if you just mainline the story quests. Combat feels alright though it's been streamlined since Dead Island, it's faster and less nuanced in exchange for the extensive climbing stuff being added. All weapons have finite usage and there are a ton of craftable one-time-use items, weapon upgrades and weapon effects. The scavenging aspect is diminished later on in the game so it's not a huge problem.
The Day/Night cycle is interesting and at night there are areas in complete darkness and WAY tougher enemies show up. You can stealth it up, try to outrun them or cop out and go to bed until morning. Though with some effort they can be killed, fighting them is never a viable option at any point in the game. When you aren't avoiding night monsters, there are many ways to have fun messing with enemies and the environment; spikes that zombies can be thrown/kicked into, dropkicks to send them flying, various environmental traps (electrified puddles, exploding cars, UV light traps etc). There are a lot of skills to unlock, some are really fun to use, others are just stat boosting. Human enemies can't be properly snuck up on which is a shame. There are isolated levels called quarantine zones that are kind of difficult and a nice addition.
There are 2 main areas and a couple of smaller areas to explore. Even with the city environment, a surprising amount of buildings are open to run through and made the world feel dense. I really liked that almost every landmark visible in one area is directly accessible in another. I wanted to see more boss fights. I didn't play much of the co-op and only played one "Night Hunter" match but that was pretty fun at the time.
I loved the music. Synthy, 80s B movie style tracks and it even has sort of a theme song. The main menu theme is remixed in various ways and that's super rare nowadays. (I'll buy the soundtrack if it goes on sale) It's a big budget title but has a lot of nice little quirks. Similarly to the music, the story also feels like an 80s B movie story with some fun events in it. The dialogue and voice acting don't really lend too much fun to it though, the main character is completely unremarkable apart from their situation and is kind of a schmuck. Most other characters apart from Jade and Rais are bland and boring.
The city being based, at least partly on Rio de Janiero is interesting, not only because favelas are cool to run along but also because of the not-olympic games set to be hosted there, letting people of disparate nationalities show up. (Rio was set to host the actual olympic games recently)
Recommended to Open-World, Parkour/Freerunning and First Person Melee enthusiasts.
