2 years after coming out with the great first game "Thief: The Dark Project" Looking Glass had decided to take another try on this brilliant stealth series. But not before they do a different type of game which was "System Shock 2" a sci-fi, horror, sort of rpg type game. It was good in it's own right, but during that process it seems they may have forgotten some of what made the first Thief game good. Also to clarify this is more or less the same time period as the first game.
First of all the simple stuff, in the 2nd game we still have the great drawn art style for most of the cutscenes and we still have the store and briefing intros, we also still got Garrets great voice and personality. However the level design, atmosphere, and enemies (for the most part have changed). In the first game you had a mysterious, sometimes horror, sometimes just cold and lonely, sometimes funny atmosphere all at the sametime. The pagan factions and their creatures really brought a unique feel to the game. However in this one, it will feel much more generic where you only have normal guards and robots. The fantasy element and mysterious part of the world is almost completely gone. Now it feels much more like System Shock 2 rather than Thief. In fact many of the new enemies are just re-used and re-skinned assets from System Shock, which is just lazy. Another change to the gameplay is that the levels are GIGANTIC, some levels easily overstay their, welcome, either having their best parts at first or at the end, but some will easily feel like a slog, even if you are liking it, you will find yourself saying is it over yet? This gets worse in a game series that already was balanced perfectly now has random robots all over the place and cameras! So now you have to worry about that while there is so many more guards than there should be walking around. Because it's not just the size, it's the amount of stuff in it. So many more enemies that it begins to force you to play a certain way rather than thinking things out. Not too mention instead of using a great mixture of how the sound works with different floors, so many areas and levels have nothing but marble floors which are so loud that you end up having to either waste money on so many moss arrows or you have to cheat and do the thing where you barely tap the keys to move in half animation to make no sound. Big levels are great but not so big they feel bloated. They even admitted to wanting to make it bigger and tougher but this isnt how they should've. They honestly should have made their AI better, but this is something all companies do even now, make the game artificially harder rather than fixing their braindead and limited AI. However i will say the levels still have the great art style and look from the first game and thankfully they did find a way to push the engine to be able to allow them to correctly furnish the rooms, house and banks look like real ones from the time period, no longer do you just have a random table with a chair or two in the rooms like the first. So that's one good thing, otherwise the gameplay is mostly the same, just boring cuz of the mostly poor level design, enemy types, and enemy placements. Also considering how the engine works, they are certain parts that will make you really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ without spoiling, it's a part later on that requires "some masks". Another positive, the music and sound quality is still great. At certain points you do get great brilliance with how this is used but is often ruined by everything else i mentioned. The dialogue for voice acting is also still great and funny.
Now i already mentioned the robotic minions of the great enemy...or not so great enemy. The new big bad guy, has no real precense in the game and once again will remind you of system shock. Think  Atlas from Bioshock but even worse. This guy has a terrible voice that just makes him annoying to listen to, he isn't intimidating at all unlike the spooky pagan god from the the first game. And there is just not real rising action, or climatic event like the first game. The last mission is easily the worst in the game and series. I'll just tell you, that you spend the last mission to "defeat" the bad guy by crafting..... CRAFTING. No portals, no real race to the clock, not spooky atmosphere. Just mundane running around crafting.
It's so sad but it's obvious it was either made by different people or they did forget the brilliance of the first game. It's sad too cuz still has traces of first, has pretty and somewhat interesting levels, has mostly the same ideas and feel but gets ruined by their changes and lack of imagination. It's the sophmore slump, the lets return to what game was great and praised and try to do everything bigger and better rather than fix things. In the end i wish steam (once again) had the maybe option but im gonna give this one a NOT recommended. If you loved the first and wanted the 2nd, get it cheap and realize it's gonna be different and will only have a few moments of great feeling like the first while the rest of the time you slog through, just keep that in mind. There are great fan missions for it, 100s of them, so that might be the only real good reason to get this one. People often say deadly shadows went the wrong way, but this game was the start of that. So keep all this in mind. Thank you for reading my review and here's hoping for more fan missions.

username: Thief 2 is the best stealth game
text:
This is going to be a long one so sit down and relax! As my name entitles, this is probably THE best stealth game ever made! I will go in depth why it is and why YOU should be playing it:
Let's start off with a list. What makes a stealth game one of the greats? In my own personal opinion it is: Have engaging and functional stealth mechanics. Provide the player with alternate routes and methods of completing an objective. have interesting, unique levels. Have said levels progressively provide challenges to overcome. NO FORCED combat! And most of all, have an engaging story and setting that makes the player WANT to progress. Every stealth game I have ever played usually doesn't have all of these things checked marked on the list. MGS has forced combat and has a questionable story that tries to be over the top yet subtle at the same time. The first two Splinter Cell games were far too linear and also forced combat at times. Not to mention the sub par stories. Conviction tries way too hard to uncheck every thing on this list. Dishonored's story is cliche and is WAY to easy any way you play it (Yes, even the non lethal no powers run is too easy). Death to Spies has barely any atmosphere or story. The list goes on. That's why everyone's favorite stealth games usually are Splinter Cell Chaos Theory, the Hitman series, and other games that manage to check the checklist. What about Thief 2?
This game checks every single thing on the list and for some parts, even goes BEYOND the criteria. Every level is HIGHLY unique, replayable, massive, and intrigueing all at the same time. From a shipping warehouse to a bank to a police station and more, no two missions are ever the same(except two that uses the same map). Not only are the locations unique, the objectives are as well. You are sneaking into the warehouse to lget enough money foryour RENT. You are sneaking into a bank to get evidence on the sheriff. You are going into a police station to frame a guy by placing evidence in the VAULT. Almost every level is VASTLY open and there are not two, or three, but usually FIVE ways to get into the building and there are always two ways into every room. Is there a guard in your way to the staircase to get upstairs? Go take the other two stairs and your good. Although not all missions are quite heavy hitters.( Tracing the Courier in paticular) Not to mention, Only TWO out of FIFTEEN missions in this game require you to knockout people. That means you have THIRTEEN ghostable missions. This makes this game one of the stealthiest stealth game I have ever played ( Say that 5 times fast). This game is so stealthly, the community has made terms like "supreme ghost", where you have to put back items you USED. Compare this to MGS, where they force you into combat every so often.
Now, I wouldn't give this game the huge praise it deserves if the world and story were crap. NOPE! it is one of THE BEST settings to play in. An industrial, steam punk, fantasy world. An interesting story about how the industry is taking over the town. And interesting characters. The protaganist, Garret, is a smart mouth, no ♥♥♥♥♥ given guy that you WANT to play as. He has a personality that makes you want to check every nook and cranny just to see what he has to say. The factions in this game are also unique and interesting and you can probably remember their names instantly. They have their own weapons, armor, and even the way they talk. The Mechanists worship metal and technology and so they use enhanced armor and talk like a Shakespear character.(" Who art thou?") The main villian has a good purpose and is highly threatening in his own way.  The City guards are bumbling idiots who talk slow and usually get agitated easily. It just goes on and on.
Speaking of the Mechanists, their inclusion in the game provide a great big help to the checklist. Their technology creates challenges to overcome. First you'll start off by seeing their version of "security cameras". Later, you'll see little robots of sorts that set off the alarm when spotted. There is some more, but if you have played the game you know what I mean. The levels get more massive and require more from you each time. Each gadget has it's purpose and yet is almost completely optional to help you in most levels. Using the light and shadow stealth is robust. But more importantly, the SOUND is what shines here. Different floor types have different noise levels. You can sprint on carpet, but once you get on a metal grate, expect trouble. It truly is a inspiring sound system not only to stealth games, but to game design in general.
The ONLY problem I have with this is not even with the game itself. It's getting this thing to work on modern PC's. If you do decide to get this game, be prepared. Get the Taffer Patch and Tf2Tool patch or else this game will probably not work for you. There are also some HD packs to help make the game more beautiful. Do I even need to say it? GET THIS GAME!!!

Xcom is an amazing game, the graphics are neat, gameplay is off the charts, overall its a pretty prominent game.

Gameplay is a nice test of true tactics, one small step into an unknown area and it could be your captains last. Personally, thats why I dont play much, to punishing, but not enough to siphon any entertainment out. There are enough enemy varities to employ different strategies for them, and each of the soldiers classes are special, as they should be. Each class is balanced enough that 3 of any is very redundant in any mission, the max being 6 so there will be overlap. Custimization is ok, enough to make a somewhat look alike of that friend that will 'accdently' blow himself up when surrounded by a small squad of xenos.
My biggest gripes with the game is this, when your soldeirs panic they have a chance ( for me it was every other panic) to shoot one of their fellow comrades and since i tend to have my squad close to each other, the accuracy is in the high 70's usually. To me, when someone is panicing they aren't going to shoot the a friend, they blindly fire at the enemy. The last problem is willpower, i dont want to spoil it but its a big factor later on, and when a soldier is critically wounded, they lose willpower, and theres no way of recovering it afterwards, so if you have an unlucky captain, chances are he will panic as much as a rookie. I guess thats it.

A tale of two halves.
The first half is a basic-yet-intriguing cyberpunk XCOM-lite game. The second is a tedious, monotonous, dragged-out affair that completely spoils everything and made me very glad it was only $2.50 when I picked it up.
PROS
-Crisp art style that lends itself fairly well to the setting
-Some interesting characters (kind of)
-The music is decent the first time around
-Neat outfits
-It's less than ten hours....
CONS
-Environments/levels are 99% static and lifeless
-The dialogue/script is wildly inconsistent in terms of style, going from grandiose to vernacular at will. It's like two or three different guys were writing without consulting the design document. Then at the end they were just like "♥♥♥♥ it, too hard to redo all this work"
-After a couple hours, the music grates
-Combat is far too simple to be enjoyable for long
-Lack of cool loot/drops
-Exceedingly linear
-Most characters are neat at first but then it becomes obvious there's no depth
-The narrative takes a wild shift in the second half, and it's not for the betterment of the game
-The second half is only more difficult because gobs of enemies are thrown at you, rather than anything clever or original
-Puzzles can all be solved by holding down Alt to see what few things are interactive
-Terrible ending that made me uninstall immediately after closing the game
-Along with the tonal shifts, most of the scant humor isn't funny, and the cyberpunk/Shadowrun terms were used in a tryharding manner rather than making sense or adding atmosphere
-Lots of typos and generally-lazy writing
-Decking is uselessly dull
Overall it's a game that starts out strong and finishes way after boredom sets in. The combat is stale with little-to-no tactical depth, and level design is so narrow-sighted and basic that I can't help but think these guys are out of their league. And this is from someone who views cyberpunk as the best genre in all of media.

Shadowrun Returns (SRR) is a story-driven linear RPG with turn-based tactical combat. You play a Shadowrunner (something like a private detective or a hired special agent) who's thrown into the investigation of an ex-colleague's murder only to find himself wrapped in a much greater plot...
For those not familiar:
--Wikipedia. I would add the "Noir" keyword in that passage, as well.
SRR is best played with a mouse and is entirely built into a third person isometric engine, just like the original Fallout games. The visuals (scenery, character portraits etc) are very well made and capture the atmosphere of the world, resonating in its depth and mystery. The music and SFX are just OK, and note that the game has no voice-over at all. The mechanics of the game are solid but they could use some more balancing and polishing. What annoyed me most is that the game tends to "lock" you in turn-based combat mode, even when all enemies are downed, until you reach a specific map location. Also, the stat-system (the so-called "Karma" points) is kinda inflated, not all skill-trees are well structured, and many of the items or skills you acquire become obsolete quite fast as you get better ones. The game is not very difficult: It took me 15 hours to complete on Normal difficulty and I only failed and had to reload a couple of times. You can quick-save/load anytime with F5/F9.
The plot itself is interesting and keeps you motivated to see what's next. Each time you think you're close to the ending, something more pops up, throwing you into a bigger plot! Role-playing is quite varied and there's usually multiple ways to progress in the story which, however, is fully linear. However, I played the game only once, so I am not sure if the consequences are really that different if you pick other dialogue options... Most of the characters are memorable and well developed but I think that the lack of voice-over kinda limits their profoundness. Finally, I like how the game borrows elements from classic books/games, e.g. Gibson's Neuromancer or the Fallout universe, and how it renders stereotype characters, e.g. the "corrupt cop", the "badass waitress", the "taciturn bouncer" etc. Well written!
In overall, SRR is a decent game, mostly recommend if you're into that theme (cyberpunk) and/or that game genre (story-rich RPG with tactical combat). There's not something really special about it, but it was surely worth my time! If I were to rate it, I'd put it around 70-80%. They say that the second game, Dragonfall, is much better than SRR, so I got high hopes for that one!

The LEGO series games are what I'm using to introduce my five-year-old to video games.  They all have roughly similar gameplay dynamics - each figure has special attributes that you use to negotiate the level (use Human Torch to melt ice, use Thor's lightning to jumpstart an electric turbine), then you come back through again with your choice of characters and you can do more things to unlock more characters and rewards.
A solid, entertaining romp, largely targeted at the 6-10 set.  The game offers a reasonably large cast of Marvel heroes, including pretty much every one of the company's heroes to ever make it to film, from Blade to the X-Men to Spider-Man to the Guardians of the Galaxy.  It's all set around a LEGO-scale openworld recreation of Manhattan, which is pretty entertaining in and of itself.  You can unlock various vehicles and race through the streets, or do the various game missions, all of which have at least two playthroughs to ensure you find all the goodies.
The plot in this one is wafer-thin.  Baddies Loki and Doctor Doom are up to no good, assembling a doomsday device, the goodies have to team up to stop them, blah blah blah.  The point of the game is to get your favorite heroes and bash them together in a lovely digital toybox, and the game succeeds at that.  Some of the puzzles might be a little too complicated for younger players, and the controls can be a bit prickly, especially on the "racing" missions.
Still, a nice gateway drug if you're looking to take your young one into the dangerous world of 100% completing games...

An RPG that takes place in the Shadowrun setting, which is a mixture of Fantasy and Cyberpunk. Humans, dwarves, elves and other metahuman races walk the planet, while corporations rule the world. The setting is definitely solid, and has a lot of background knowledge, that makes for a rich world.
Gameplay consists of navigating your characters across an isometric map, interacting with people and objects, and fighting. Combat is turn-based and relies very much on cover, although there are playstyles that do not.
Character is freeform, but starts with a certain archetype, which you can then customize as you gain Karma, the resource used to develop your character.
The story is good, but the greatest charm of the game has got to be writing, and the various side quests and dialogues, that make up the universe. However, none of it voice-acted, so if you do not like reading, don't buy the game.
All in all, its definitely worth the price as intro to the series, but I will not be held responsible if you get addicted.

Batman: Arkham Knight is (ostensibly) the final chapter in Rocksteady’s Batman: Arkham X series. In it, Batman faces off against Scarecrow, who is seeking revenge for Batman throwing him to Killer Croc in the first game, and the titular Arkham Knight, whose identity you can guess without even playing the game if you are familiar with the comics, and whose identity becomes obvious somewhere in the middle of the game even if you’re not.
This game continues on in the tradition of Arkham City and Arkham Origins in that you play Batman in an open-world city. The map is even bigger this time around, and you are given the Batmobile to drive around in.
The Batmobile is the big new feature of this game, and is very similar to the one seen in the Dark Knight trilogy of movies. It can turn into a tank and move around in any direction while in tank mode. This is essential for fighting the army of tank drones, autonomous vehicles which attack you and the city throughout the game.
Alas, while these sections are okay, they suffer from one major problem: it doesn’t feel very Batman-y. Given that these games are about feeling like Batman, this is something of an issue.
Alas, the rest of the game has little meaningful innovation. The fights in this game are bigger than ever, with a fight in the Batmobile against 60 drones, and fights against large numbers of goons appearing at various points in the game, as well as even more complex predator encounters, where you sneak around and pick off armed guards, including medics who can revive their allies, people who you can’t see through walls with detective vision, and huge goons with miniguns. The biggest innovation in the predator sequences is the so-called fear takedown, where you can take down a whole group of goons in sequence from hiding without them being able to shoot you while doing so.
Alas, this isn’t very innovative, and the predator sequences and the fighting with goons sequences don’t feel very fresh or new. And while that’s okay to some extent, the lack of really interesting new enemies is kind of discouraging.
Added onto this are the boss fights, or rather, the lack thereof. This game is very obsessed with the Batmobile, and unfortunately, a lot of the new boss fights are Batmobile centric. And indeed, the main boss of the game is the Arkham Knight, who you fight over and over again in various guises. This isn’t so bad – the fights are actually all unique – but they’re big on flash and not so big on substance. Cool fights – like the Mister Freeze fight from the second game – aren’t really on the menu here, and while some of the fights are okay, and sneaking around blowing up tanks in the Batmobile is kind of neat in its own way, in the end, it feels a bit repetitive at times after a while.
The other villains are by and large much less interesting, sadly. Two-Face and Penguin make an appearance, but they’re just reskinned mooks, and are taken out in the same way. Deathstroke shows up again but is in a tank which is mostly a rehash of a previous fight in the game, Man-Bat is not really a boss at all, and while Firefly is a different take on the fight, it doesn’t feel terribly boss-like and is more of a racing sequence. Indeed, apart from the titular Arkham Knight, the only real boss-feeling enemy in the game is the Riddler, who pilots a gigantic mecha to take you out after you solve all of his riddles… again. This is actually a somewhat interesting fight, in part because it makes use of the switching mechanic which shows up in a few fights where you fight as two characters in the same fight, switching from one to another as you do team attacks, or just when you feel like it.
Unfortunately, the Scarecrow himself doesn’t show up in any meaningful capacity as an enemy – gone are the cool sequences from Arkham Asylum, replaced by and large with cut scenes. There are a couple of neat sequences, particularly towards the end of the game, but ultimately the game doesn’t do a whole lot with Scarecrow.
And indeed, this leaks over into the story as well – Scarecrow and the Arkham Knight are both pretty generic and uninteresting, and the game as a whole is a mostly bland revenge plot with one real twist which is kind of neat and involves the (deceased) Joker. Indeed, the Joker is again the highlight of this game, which is kind of sad because he’s, well, dead the whole game. On the whole, the plot isn’t terribly interesting or exciting, and it feels very much like you’re just bludgeoning your way through, rather than taking control of the situation in the way that it felt like you were doing in Arkham Asylum.
The game as a whole isn’t very tight. I 100%ed the game and took about 70 hours doing it according to my Steam play time, though I suspect it was less than that and I just left the game running for a while a few times while alt-tabbed out. And unfortunately, this game felt long, and not in a good way – the game doesn’t have a whole lot of interesting tricks to it. Instead, there’s just a lot of content, but it is all the same content – drone fights, brawls, and predator encounters, and frankly, only a few of them are really memorable. There are over a dozen bombs you need to defuse while fighting waves of drones, but these fights are all very samey. There’s a neat sequence where you need to sneak around and take out “cobra tanks”, which are only vulnerable from behind… and then you end up doing it five times or so. The fights with goons quickly wear thin and don’t offer much new, and the predator encounters basically all feel very similar, with little meaningful variation. Sure, ostensibly the later ones are more difficult, but I never felt very threatened and they basically felt pretty rote, with only the invisible to x-ray detective vision enemies really mixing things up at all.
There are tons of side quests, but they ultimately almost all feel samey, and only the DLC ones really felt like they did anything interesting. The DLC ones felt much more interesting, offering more divergent experiences, such as dealing with the Mad Hatter putting you in a pop-up book (which was, while basically a bunch of mook fights, at least visually interesting), going through a downed zeppelin prison ship, and racing through frozen waters to save Mr. Freeze. These are all much more memorable than the main-game sidequests, which were pretty repetitive and more or less followed the formula of “go to location and fight a bunch of mooks 3-15 times.” There wasn’t much in the way of interesting story to them, and they felt pretty superficial.
Likewise, the Riddler has left something like 240 trophies around the game, plus dozens of destructible objects. Most of these just feel like they’re there – just a trophy lying around somewhere for Batman to pick up. Very few felt like actual riddles, and while there were some vaguely interesting puzzles, and the Riddler was actually kind of fun in his pretentious way, there were just an enormous number of them and collecting them felt like a bit of a drag. It might have been better if there had JUST been the Riddles, or if there had been something clever about the whole thing in a problem solving kind of way… but alas.
And really, this is the case with pretty much everything in the game. There’s a huge amount to do here, but a lot of it is just the same thing, over and over. It is an open world game with a huge area, but the dungeon type areas – the places where you go inside and fight through a place – are actually pretty small and are few and far between. Why spend so much time on a huge open world when you could instead create interesting environments for Batman to navigate? Is it really fun flying around over the city, or driving through the city in the Batmobile, when there’s nothing terribly interesting to do in most of it?

When I first started the Thief series, I started with the newest one called Thief.  While I enjoyed it a lot as a stealthy game with an interesting setting, I was bothered by how so many people said that it wasn’t a true Thief game.  Unconvinced, I was told to play the originals and see for myself how different they are.  So when I saw that the series was on sale, I bought it and have been playing Thief 2 for quite some time now.  And my initial thoughts after finishing the game, is wow.  Wow, this IS an amazing game and it puts the new game to shame.   With that said, lets get into the review.
You play as a thief named Garret.  Your goal is to perform various tasks that typically involve stealing valuables or performing sabotage.   While not all jobs require you to steal, it is a profitable activity to do.   As the story progresses, you are told about a man named Karras who is using machine-men (Robots) to do all sorts of things.  He is a worshiper of some unusual faith and thinks that making these robots will help him win favor and help the world.   Simple plot, but it's enough to make each job related and important.
No music, only sound effects and ambience.  For a stealth game, this is perfect because you need to focus on sounds, not music.  The sound effects used are pretty simple and hardly have any variation but it IS an old game so it was good for its time.  The voicing is pretty cliché and not that good but once again, its dated.  I believe that this was the first Thief game that had female guards whom had unique voice lines.   Footstep sounds are distinct enough to know if you are loud or not, and it varies based off what you are walking on.
Let's be honest, its dated, period.  For back then, it wasn’t that bad, and even when using a mod that enhances the various textures, it still isnt the best.   However, the mod does make a lot of the textures look better.  On a
er note, the lighting is very important in knowing if you are visible or not.  Some spots had issues where you appear to be in the light but are hidden while other times you are in the shadows but the game thinks you are visible.
This is going to be fairly lengthy since this is the MOST important feature of Thief 2, which is why I saved this for last.   What Thief 2 gets right, are all of the mechanics for a stealth game.  The only issue right off the bat, is the enemy AI which can be exploited if you choose to.  Outside of that, the game forces you to focus on a variety of factors when playing.  Sound levels are important in knowing how loud you are.  If you walk or run on tiles, you will be heard.  If you walk or run on carpet, then you won't be heard.  If you run on a wooden floor that is above guards who are in the floor below, then they will hear you and eventually run upstairs to see who is causing all those noises.  This also has an effect on the robots in the game.  There are big robots that can hear and see you, but there are small robots that won't see you unless you make noise.   This leads you into making sure to walk carefully around the tiny bots as they wont see you and thus you can evade them, no sweat.  The game even gives you tools that assist you with these noise issues, and its in the form of an Arrow that spreads moss all over the floor, making it possible to walk, run, jump without being heard.
Another aspect to the game, are lights.  Like with any stealth game, lights are important to have and to be cautious of.  There are plenty of light sources in the game.  Some can be turned off, some can be put out by a Water Arrow, and some cannot be put out.   When many of these lights are out, they are out period, but one type can be relight so you have to be careful of guards who want to light it up.
As mentioned earlier, the enemy AI can be wonky or unfair for human AI, but the enemies themselves are interesting.  The Human enemies typically function the same.  They respond to loud noises, dead bodies, etc.  But it’s the robot enemies that are worth mentioning.  In the game, there are about 5 or 6 robot enemies.  First type is a camera that moves back and forth and will lock onto a target if they are not hidden.  Stay visible for too long and the silent/non-silent alarms will go off and you're basically screwed.   The second type are large robots that react to sound and sightings.  They are deadly if cornered but are predictable.  The third type are the 'mini me' versions of large robots.  These type are blind but react to sound a lot faster.  Once they hear something, they will open up their eyes and look for the source.  If spotted, they immediately run to the nearest large robot or guard to alert them.  The other bots are far and few in terms of use but they have their own unique abilities like one is a child robot who cannot be stopped or destroyed, and another is a spider shaped robot.
The last basic mechanic is the archery.  I won't sugar coat it, the aiming with the bow, is pretty bad.  Some arrows have trajectory while others shoot straight.  There is no crosshair to use and often times its trial-and-error inorder to figure out how to aim.  Also, some of the hit-boxes for torches can be off too if hit at the wrong angle.  In the game, there are various types of arrows and useable items.  The arrows range from basic arrows that damage, to fire that explode, to vine arrows that allow you to create a hanging vine to use to climb places.  As for the items, they mostly consist of mines you can place to set a trap, and throwables that can help you see around corners or flash bang an enemy.
And finally, I wanted to talk about the last design aspect for the game, and that is level designing.   The maps themselves are usually fairly large in size and feature a lot of ways to approach a situation.  Just like with most games, there are your path meant for non-stealth, true stealth, and opportunists stealthers.   Its amazing how well designed the levels are because it feels like there are so many routes to take and after playing each mission for so long, you start to realize how often these paths converge into each other and that’s when it all makes sense.  Speaking of this,  secret pathways are used throughout the whole game as well as secret rooms.  Some can be obvious due to massive switches and handles, while others require some more, out of the box thinking to find.   The tricky ones are the places where the switch used is very tiny and blends in well with the background or is tiny and well hidden behind flags and posters.  For a game that was this old, it's simply amazing to see how detailed and well thought out the map creators were when designing the places.
After playing this, I still enjoyed the modern Thief game but now I can agree with others who say that Thief (2014) is a good game but NOT a good Thief game.  I won't go into details about that game, but what I can say about this one, is that it definitely set the foundation for what a true stealth game should be about.  Few games can come into comparison to it and while yes it has dated graphics and an exploitable AI thing, it’s a really damn good classic game that all stealth fans should play.  If anything it will give them a better appreciation for stealth games in general.  However, my final bit of advice is to make sure to install the Mod that patches the game and enhances the textures.  The patch itself will help prevent certain levels from being incompletable while making sure to fix issues that can cause players to escape the map or get stuck

Thief II, in my opinion, is one of the greatest stealth based games ever made.  Every level is lovingly crafted and filled with character.  Thief II keeps the wonderful stealth and exploratory elements of Thief 1, but improves on them by making levels large, sprawling, and fun to explore.  Stealth is more than crouching around, its keeping to shadows, avoiding noise, distracting people.  BUT, more importantly, it is very very fun.
This game has multiple difficulty levels, so if your looking for a challenge, or just want to experience an age old classic, it is all fun.
If your looking for story, this game will fill your needs.  Thief II builds upon Thief I's lore, but you don't need to have beaten that game, though I also suggest it, in order to enjoy Thief II's story.  Plenty of wonderful fantasy as well as intrigue, all delivered by the wonderful voice of Garret, master Thief.
Thief II is an old game, and rigid polygons, show it.  But while the graphics might have aged like milk, the rest has remained a goldplated master piece.
If you are looking at Thief II you have probably already heard about it, as it is a cult classic stealth game that modern stealth games often get compared to.  If you've ever wondered why every one says this game is benchmark for Great Stealth Based Gaming, I highly suggest picking it up and finding out.

"Teleglitch" is a weird game - it really enjoys being unfair, but after a while (as is usually the case in such destructive relationships between gamer and game) you will start enjoying its unfairness too. Make no mistake: "Teleglitch" will make you work hard to even survive its first level and will spring some nasty, cheap and lethal traps on you as soon as you start feeling comfortable. It will always keep you trembling and terrified of opening doors to unknown rooms. "Teleglitch" will crush your spirit by making all those "you'll learn how to play this game and feel deep satisfatcion"-phrases sound super-dumb. "Teleglitch" will do all these things because IT HATES YOU. The only thing for you to do is to hate it back passionately and beat it. You won't find peace untill you do.

I've anticipated this game for a long time but elected not to purchase it on release due to a lot of triple A games not being so good lately. (*cough* AC: Unity, Evolve and Lords of the Fallen *cough*) Of course, the moment I decide to do that the game I wait for turns out to be good. There will be no spoilers in this review but I may accidentally mention something that would give away late game content so if you are wanting your experience completely unspoiled, take my word for it that the game is good and leave this review now. Otherwise, hello.
Okay so let me start off by saying; this game is effing excellent. I must admit, from the gameplay I'd seen and the reviews I'd read, I was expecting a semi-decent FPS survival that would take maybe 10 hours to complete with some repetitive hack and slash combat that had been over-hyped and blown out of proportion like most other triple-A games these days. I admit it, I was dead wrong.
Let me get the only two negative things I can say about this game out of the way. The multiplayer is pretty unbalanced, (although having someone join your game is a blast,) and the performance is sometimes lacking (fixed with Dying Light Manager 0.10a, google it for more info. It may have been updated to a newer version by now.)
The graphics in this game are so, so beautiful. During the day the shadows are gorgeous and at night the game has such intense and terrifying shadows that even though it is really difficult playing at night time, I still end up doing it just to enjoy the game's wonderful aesthetics.
I'm not huge on "horror" games, but this is the perfect mix of terror and action for me to enjoy without freaking out and quitting. (I'm looking at you Dead Space.) I hate slow paced horror games but since this game is always moving forwards, I could actually enjoy the scary areas a bit more than I can in other games.
The movement system in this game is fantastic, every time you jump onto a ledge or platform you immediately have 3 other options to jump to, which in turn have 3 more and so on. Freedom is the word when it comes to parkour in Dying Light and there is nothing more satisfying than jumping 150 meters down into a pile of garbage only to take no damage.
Dying Light was built on Chrome Engine 6. I have to say, I love this engine. Zombies have amazing ragdoll physics and being able to cut a zombies head, leg and arm off on one swing, then kick each individual part around just adds to the immersion. To this moment, if I see a zombie at a ledge of a building I will run up to it and kick it off just to watch it fall to the ground; no exceptions. It is glorious.
10 hours into the game and I still hadn't even found a gun yet I was enjoying the game immensely, guns are just a bonus late game. The progression in this game is absolutely perfect, you start off using sticks and wrenches to attack things and you mainly avoid zombies, but by the end of the game you are an absolute zombie murdering monster complete with a grapple, guns, super powerful melee weapons that slice zombies into two pieces with a single swing and the ability to go all the way across the city without stopping or touching the ground. (Still scary going out at night time although the monsters are a bit more manageable.)
The skill trees in this game are really well thought out with almost every skillpoint you get changing the way you play the game. No more of that, "5% damage increase while wielding 2h weapons" etc. You always get something meaningful, like a new ability, increased jump distance or a new finisher. I also like that there are 3 skill trees rather than just 1 and they are all leveled separately. So you have to go and do parkour to level up your agility tree and you have to engage in combat to level up your power tree. The trees are pretty damn big too. At 22 hours into the game and I was only 14-18/25 and it gets slower as you level, but like I said, almost every single level up adds something useful to your arsenal. Not to mention that the final perks on each tree are extremely useful so that adds incentive to level all your skill trees.
The story itself in the game was pretty good, but the real depth I got out of the game was the side missions. That being said, the actual campaign goes for around 17 hours so there's that. There are so many side missions all with interesting rewards and interesting storylines. You can also find survivors around the world and just sit and listen to them talk, they give insight into how the outbreak happened and a lot of them have clever things to say that will get you thinking. Clearly someone put a lot of effort into the dialogue for this game.
Overall I'd give this game an 9/10 and if the performance was a bit more optimised I'd be giving it easily a 9.5/10. I highly recommend you get this game if you are at all interested in survival FPS games. It's worth it.
TL;DR: This game is fun and has zombie babies in it.

As is the case with many games, I bought Teleglitch on a whim and for a few measley bucks. On the surface, it promised me the usual cache of indie-game features: a unique art style, a tried-and-true, marketable gameplay type (roguelikes are all the rage these days) and so on and so on. Imagine, then, my surprise when Teleglitch: Die More Edition turned out to not only be decent, but this year's answer to 2012's fantastic Hotline Miami. Technically, Telegitch was a 2012 release, but this shiny new version adds a host of features that personally, I don't think the game could really live without.
We play as some space marine doing what space marines do best: answering distress calls and blowing things of varying size into as many pixel-y bits as possible. We learn, slowly, that some wacky experiments were going on with teleportation and mutation and blah blah blah, you've heard it before. The story is bland, but well-told through audio logs that mark the first time I've actually stopped to read the darn things. A dark sense of humor certainly helps.
Gameplay is really why we're here though. Teleglitch, as I hinted in a rather blatant manner at, reminds me of last year's incredible Hotline Miami. Mutants don't approach; they charge head-on. Hostiles with guns shoot without stopping to check if perhaps you're friendly after all. Dodge their bullets, and they begin leading their aim. There is very good reason the subtitle of this game implies we're going to die. More.
None of this is a bad thing. This is a challenging game, one I may never see the final level of, but it is so without being unfair. The controls are responsive, your aim is reasonably accurate, and if you're conservative with bullets the first few stages, ammo's never a problem. Nope, every death here is you screwing up, as every death should be. The levels are just randomized enough to keep things interesting, but not so much you run the risk of being unable to defend yourself. You have the tools you need, it's all down to how you apply them.
Visually, Teleglitch is kind of surprising. Screenshots would have you believe this could have come out alongside Doom as a cheap pack-in. In motion, however, this game looks fantastic. It packs a retro feel, sure, but it's overlayed with effects as you explode and shoot and otherwise murder things that warp the pixels around you. This is probably the first time I can actually say post-processing effects really add something to a game, but here they really do. Each bomb and bullet looks as though it's tearing the world apart.
Indeed, Teleglitch: DME puts me in the difficult position of having to admit I can't really think of many faults with something. It falls under the umbrella of that rare caste of games with perfect difficulty, meaningful visual design, and just plain visceral fun. Teleglitch may have run me just over $2 at the time I purchased it, but I think, of all the titles I've given a go this year, it just might be the one I'll keep installed.

Teleglitch is a stylized little top-down shooter with roguelike elements that has a pretty neat engine. That's about it. What you see is what you get, basically some cool particle effects and pixelly stuff with a limited selection of weapons, rather weak procedurally generated levels, and enemy AI that while interesting at first, isn't too challenging or intense.
There's not much content here, it's not like Binding of Isaac where there's an absolutely ludicrous amount of unlocks, items, and other stuff to keep you busy, it's a very slim product. It's like the developers created the engine, fine-tuned it, made a pretty great, responsive, and crunchy feeling run and gun, then just left it at that without actually developing content.
You'll enjoy a runthrough or two, but it's really just not that compelling. The atmosphere is nice, but the writing is dull and basically everything about this game is dull.
Lack is the word, just lack, lack of a soul, like me, that's why I'm marrying Teleglitch.

The full game has only a campaign mode that plays kind of like the game "Simpsons Hit and Run" if you took out EVERYTHING that made that game charming. All it is, is a "do various flavors of a driving mission, dont collect X, collect Y" and attempt to keep the brain damage at bay.
After beating a mission you are rewarded with a handfull of currency, in which you can buy all of 2 or 3 things TOTAL. You can upgrade your (stat-less) tractor with "quicker engine" and "better brakes" OR you can drop ungodly large amounts of moeny and get a new (still stat-less) tractor.
The power-ups are mostly "power downs" as you can get spun out (oil can), reverse your steering controls (whiskey/moonshine bottle) OR can speed you up with what is probably supposed to feel like turbo (a barrel).
Also, the "hillbilly rock" soundtrack gets very old, VERY quick
Once you grow sick of the campaign (which will happen VERY quickly) you are left with nothing else to do except exit the game and try to come to terms with wasting 2 bucks on such a game that would only be suitable as a FLASH game.
TL:DR
Do you like racing games? If so, dont buy this game as you can go to a flash game site and get much more enjoyment out of a free game.
If not, really really do not buy this game

A stunning sequel to a fantastic game.
Zeno Clash 2 takes the land that you started learning about in Zeno Clash and stitches it all together to make it an open world. You can feel so much more connected to Zenozoik with the ability to freely travel around and explore. The battle system has been overhauled to make it much more interesting. The story is expanded massively, showing that Zeno Clash was just the tip of an iceberg. The new weapons are very unconventional, which makes them extremely interesting. I am so sick of assault rifles, but I digress. The characters feel unique and interesting. Characters from ZC1 come back in higher definition, with tons of new friends. Even the non-speaking denizens of Halstedom are still in place, keeping the feel of the first game. The music is incredible. It does an outstanding job of conveying the surrealism of the world you're exploring as an uncivilized, misplaced protagonist who is learning more about the world than any of his equals could begin to fathom. Massively recommended.
Shame that Rimat's lines were recorded in a bathroom though. Also I miss Deadra's old voice, and it was a little jarring to be without her for so much of the story, considering she was a central plot-mover in ZC1. It kinda felt like taking Alyx away from me if I was playing HL2.

Ce tactical-RPG du studio Harebrained Schemes a été kickstarté en 2012 et est sorti en 2013.
Parmi les designers et fondateurs du studio on trouve Jordan Weisman qui n'est ni plus ni moins que le créateur du très célèbre jeu de rôle sur table..."Shadowrun" !
Ce "retour" de Shadowrun est donc bel et bien organisé par son papa, en garantissant ainsi l'authenticité.
Shadowrun est un mélange de cyberpunk et de fantasy se déroulant dans un futur dystopique (imaginez par exemple un hacker elfe se promenant armé d'un flingue dans des décors à la Blade Runner pendant qu'un shaman orc l'observe depuis une ruelle sombre...). Par-dessus ça on trouve de l'horreur et de l'espionnage industriel (mais survitaminé, à base d'attaque de bâtiments pour y voler des données par exemple) avec une touche de film noir, de film de détective, ou policier (imaginez donc que notre elfe est suivi par un humain en long manteau, mâchouillant une cigarette sous la pluie, enquêtant sur des meurtres commis par ce qui semble être un démon...).
Bref, dans le futur proche de Shadowrun, la magie, les races typiques de la fantasy, etc. sont devenus réalité. Et les mega-corporations ont un statut et un pouvoir équivalent à celui de grands pays.
C'est donc un univers sombre, très riche, et qui est très bien exploité dans le jeu. C'est d'ailleurs une des grandes qualités de ce dernier : son univers mais aussi son atmosphère, son scénario, ses dialogues, ses personnages.
Le jeu est bien écrit et profite d'une ambiance très réussie.
Malheureusement tout cela est très linéaire pour un RPG et ne donne souvent pas au joueur l'impression que ses choix de dialogues et ses diverses décisions ont réellement de l'influence sur les événement... Dommage.
Le jeu est par ailleurs plutôt court, comptez une quinzaine d'heures de jeu en mode "very hard" (sinon c'est vraiment trop facile...) pour en venir à bout.
On aurait aimé pouvoir profiter de l'histoire un peu plus longtemps, on se sent un peu stoppé net dans notre élan quand la fin arrive.
Malgré la linéarité du jeu, la création du personnage laisse place à la liberté. On peut créer un cyber-bagarreur, un tireur d'élite, un hacker charismatique, un magicien, un shaman (invocations à la clef), ou un mélange de tout ça (un techno-mage !). Pas de classes, c'est au joueur de construire son profil et c'est plutôt cool. On améliore ses compétences avec les points de "karma" obtenus au fur et à mesure des missions. Ils arrivent vite et en grand nombre.
Le joueur a aussi la possibilité de s'acheter des implants cybernétique : oeil artificiel, jambes ou bras mécaniques, peau pare-balles, etc. Cela possède un coût financier mais aussi un coût en "essence", au détriment de l'efficacité de la magie...
Pour la plupart des missions, on pourra se constituer moyennant finances une équipe de shadowrunners à piocher parmi des profils nombreux et complémentaires, il y en aura pour tous les goûts. On devra aussi s'équiper et là aussi l'arsenal est varié, que ce soit les armes, les sorts, les différents items (soins, grenades, drogues).
Les combats sont nombreux dans Shadowrun Returns et constituent au final l'essentiel du gameplay. Et j'ai aimé !
Par contre c'est du classique : On est sur du tour-par-tour avec un système de grille et de point d'actions. Les personnages peuvent se déplacer, tirer, attaquer, lancer des sorts (offensifs, ou de soutien) ou des grenades, etc.
Les situations sont relativement variées et leur résolution intéressante, le tout demandant un minimum de planification et de réflexion.
Graphiquement c'est correct : En vue isométrique, éloignée, les décors et les persos sont plutôt jolis (quand ils sont vus de près sur certains écrans, les modèles 3D des personnages sont bien moches par contre...). Les portraits des personnages sont très réussis !
Niveau sonore c'est assez quelconque, avec des sons corrects pour les armes mais globalement rien de transcendant. Mais la bande-originale est de très bonne qualité ! Avec ses synthés et son côté futuriste des années 80, elle contribue parfaitement à l'ambiance du titre.
Deux défauts à mentionner quand même pour finir : une déception concernant la Matrice, l'internet sous forme de monde virtuel auquel on accède par certains terminaux, qui est une idée potentiellement intéressante mais dont l'implémentation est plutôt un échec ici (que ce soit le gameplay, le level-design ou les graphismes). Et un système d'inventaire assez mal fichu qui oblige par exemple à distribuer les items entre les membres de l'équipe en début de mission, sans possibilité d'échange une fois celle-ci commencée. Ça serait excusable si les items qu'on ramasse en cours de mission, dont on ne connaît pas la nature avant de les avoir récupérés, pouvaient eux au moins être répartis, mais même pas... Du coup on envoie untel ramassé un item en espérant que ça soit par exemple le kit de soin dont on voudrait qu'il s'équipe... Pas dramatique, mais un peu bizarre.
Au final Shadowrun Returns peut donner à juste titre l'impression d'un produit pas complètement abouti.
Mais, bénéficiant d'un gameplay tout à fait correct et d'un excellent univers, il est en fait très agréable à jouer et je le recommande aux amateurs du genre.
Il dispose en plus d'un éditeur, que je n'ai personnellement pas utilisé, mais qui semble avoir permis la création de contenus très intéressants par la communauté (des campagnes supplémentaires notamment). Je vais essayer tout ça très bientôt.
Les épisodes suivants de la série, "Dragonfall" et "Hong-Kong", ont reçu de très bonnes critiques et améliorent différents aspects du jeu. Hâte d'y jeter un oeil également !

This review is for all three of the original thief games (Gold, Metal Age, Deadly Shadows).
If you liked Dishonored, Bioshock, Prey (but mostly Dishonored), the original thief games are what started all of that. These games were what really kickstarted the stealth/combat rpg genre and they've aged relatively well. Yes, the graphics look like crap compared to today's options. Yes the gameplay can be kind of clunky at times-let's face it, they were breaking new ground at the time. But the bones of the game-the story, characters, voice acting, and basic gameplay-are all fantastic and really enjoyable. The games are so cheap rn I'd recommend buying them all and playing them in order, but that's not a requirement. Individually:
Gold: best level design. Really cool areas that shine despite the terrible graphics. Also the glitchiest
Metal Age: my personal favorite. Best characters, best story. Also the best in terms of female charcters, if you're looking for that

While most people may look over this as being "Yet another zombie game", let it be said that it isn't. While some may skip over it, thinking back to how unpolished Dead Island was, one would be pleased to know that they have not made the same mistake.
This game sets an example that needs to be followed, the amount of bugs are fairly low, and yes, there may be performance issues, but no game shall ever be perfect. The polish in this game is unlike i've ever seen, to the way the particle effects react, such as smoke slowly spreading to a room in an abandoned apartment after opening a door, the way the lighting is done, where a flashlight isn't just shining light on the nearest wall, but actually providing a cone of light, even in the void of night. The way the enemy strength isn't shown to you with a number, but by changing their appearence subtly, to the point where i only noticed the pattern over halfway into the game.
Sure, some of the enemies might be a bit easy, and some may be annoying in a very unfair way, such as one enemy being able to fire upon you, yet being nowhere to be found, they have however kept the fear in the night, to the point where once you are at the highest power you can be, you think to yourself you can take everything on without trouble, but the Volatiles, they are always kept as terrifying as in the beginning, because while you may kill one or two, more will come, and you will not be able to stop them.
The movement system, being from someone who absolutely loved Mirror's Edge, was brilliant,  and while one may want something such as horizontal wall running, it may have felt a bit too unrealistic if done wrong, and while you get a grappling hook, you cannot use it to completely bypass any obstacle, which i feel is fair, for why would you want to get away from such a massive part of the game?
The story manages to be original, considering the medium is very heavily used, you actually grow to like the characters, which many games fail to do. And finally, while Troy Baker might be becoming the new Nolan North, this might be one of his greatest performances, especially near the end, the emotion in his voice is something many voice actors cannot replicate.
As for the problems, there are performance issues, some of the challenges in the game can be anger inducing due to focusing on a specific mechanic, such as cutting zombies in half, and there are some inconsistancies in the story (one of which, is  only due to keeping a gameplay mechanic in, for removing it for the second half of the game would have been a horrible idea), but overall, 45 hours, none of which was with repetitive gameplay such as grinding or multiplayer (be the zombie), which is much more than many games can provide in this age of gaming.
Let's just hope that this game sets a new bar, and that we get to see more games with this level of care put into it.

An old game, but the community is still making new content in the form of new and/or improved missions, and they do this because this game is one of the best of all time, and is, in my opinion, the best stealth game ever. If this was a book, it would be considered as much a classic as "The Lord of the Rings", "Narnia", "Dracula", and "Frankenstein".
Before "Assassin's Creed" had its parkour, we had Thief II, where you can climb boxes, barrels, and ladders to get to the aptly named "thieves' highway" and traverse the level safe from the City Watch and Mechanist presence below. (Some of this does require some creative effort and a lot of trial and error, but it can help to get a bird's-eye-view of the map.
Gameplay is pretty-damn spotless, but you may experience some difficulties with graphics and controls, in which case I recommend you search the web for "Tafferpatcher", a fan-made patch for the game that also provides you with some tweakable files if you'd like more control over the settings.
It is a hard game, but it is rewarding, as all good games should be. The stealth aspect of the game is paramount to your success, if you are playing on the harder difficulties especially, as if you get caught, you do not stand a chance in combat, although a well-timed flashbomb, blackjack, and sprint to the shadows can help. It pays to plan ahead and have 2 or 3 escape routes memorised, otherwise you'll be as dead as a burrick in Constantine's Mansion!

Shadowverse is (insert another unoriginal Hearthstone comparison here).
But, in all seriousness, Shadowverse is one of the greatest card games I've played in a while.
This'll be a pretty lengthy review. If you want something shorter, skip the TL:DR and the edits.
Most of the others just feel slow, or just way too hard to get into (*cough* Hearthstone *cough*). Shadowverse is what every other card game should be. The game starts with a short tutorial, giving you an explanation on everything. It's very easy to understand, and the card descriptions will explain the rest. After the tutorial, you get an insane amount of packs compared to other games (*cough* Hearthstone *cough*), making it easy to start getting into multiplayer and climbing the ladder.
The solo modes, of fighting AI and short story modes. I, myself, didn't pay much attention to the story mode, but the rewards are not bad, things like rupies to buy packs, vials to craft cards, and extra things like card sleeves and Take Two Tickets (more on that later).
Fighting the AI also has nice rewards. Through their achievement system, you can get 200 rupies per elite AI killed (edit: and the new Elite 2 difficulties), which is nice because you can buy two of any pack with that amount.
Multiplayer is great, unranked is your usual "fight whoever you wish," with no regards to rank or level (from my knowledge).

Ranked is also pretty good, about what you'd expect from ranked, fight players and gain rank for winning. My only issue with it is that I seem to get paired with people wildly higher or lower than me (currently rank 5000, just fought a rank 11000), which may just be due to either the popularity of ranked, or that the game considers that who I should be playing against.

They also have private games, which are actually really easy to use. You simply give anyone you want to play with the match code, they enter it, and you're ready to play (you can also play Take Two against a friend this way without using a ticket).

Their arena system, Take Two is the greatest arena system I've seen in a card game (*cough* Hearthstone *cough*) you start by choosing you deck type ( the "crafts" or "classes"), then choose 15 sets of 2 sets of 2 cards (makes sense?) to create a whole deck. Tickets for Take Two are easy enough to obtain, as you earn one at the end of every storyline, and get one after logging in for 15 days (not in a row, as long as you come back, you get another daily award).

Now, again, the card packs. Compared to other card games (*cough* Hearthstone *cough*) they are extremely fair. Each pack gives you 8 cards, with an 8% chance of be animated, or golden, if your familiar with other card games (*cough* this is getting old *cough*). The packs are easy enough to get, only 100 rupies (and you get 20-40 whenever you log on daily). They have 2 (edit: now 3) card expansions that have come out so far, and the game is constantly getting updated. Fixes come when the community says a single card is overpowered, underpowered, or bugged. They also give out free packs whenever they have to shut the servers down for patches, just adding to how easy it is to get into the game.
The game also brings a new feature called evolving. You can spend an evolve point to "evolve" a minion. This either just adds to their stats, or adds a special effect that can change the game in major ways.

The card art is also pretty good (if you're into anime). You can tell that they put a lot of thought and work into it. And, despite this game not having a big series behind it (*cough* Fireplace Pebble *cough*), I can almost imagine these characters in their own world, sustaining their own lives, and forming their own beliefs (like Daria's satanic rituals). The animated cards are also pretty sweet. Despite having ~100 hours over all my devices, I still have yet to get a useful animated legendary. Although, this makes sense. Animated cards are beautiful, and, thus, only makes sense to be rare.
Shadowverse is a great card game that is very easy to get into, especially if you've played other card games (*cough* Hearthstone *cough*), but still has unique features of its own. Card packs are easy to get, and buying packs is anything but mandatory, unlike other card games (*cough* Hearthstone *cough*).
All in all, it's free, even more so than other free card games (*cough* you've heard this before *cough*), it's worth a shot.
(btw, don't pay attention to the play time, I have it on 3 seperate devices, two of which are mobile.)
Edit: Tempest of the Gods came out.
Like most of the other packs, it's pretty good.
You have you're stray OP card, like Heavenly Aegis, but even those have their downsides (like high play point costs). Most are decently balanced though.
The game is still great, and they're still super generous with their card packs (*cough* over used joke *cough*).
Edit: Tempest of the Gods hasn't been out long.
Heavenly Aegis seems to be what most players are complaining about. I don't see why they're complaining so much though. I play a mid-range swordcraft deck and all I do is play Roland the Incorruptible, and they need to take double the turns to take me down, and by that point my horde of ambush minions have been buffed to one-shot them.
The meta is still way better than Hearthstone's, no having to deal with unbeatable decks (*cough* Pirate Warrior *cough*), just some difficult to deal with decks. And even that isn't too bad, because of the large number of packs you'll be getting, making new decks to counter said decks is super easy.
Also, for your reading pleasure, I split apart different sections. No need to thank me.

First off, the only way to describe what was running through my head when I first started playing Teleglitch was “WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥?!!?” Saying that, this indie roguelike from developer Test3 Projects rabidly eats your half alive corpse and then spits it out leaving you wanting more. Strangely addicting, you find yourself drawn to Planet Medusa 1C left in awe by the pixellated madness that is Teleglitch. So strap up and make every shot count, and I’ll tell you why this is one of my top 5 picks of the year.
Teleglitch is one of those games where watching “Lets Play” with some youtube♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bag in his mothers basement isn’t going to suffice. Best played with a keyboard and mouse,  this top down shooter is reminiscent of GTA but put together with the savage intellect of a guerrilla militia planning its next terrorist move. To be honest, I was standoffish when it came to this game at first, it didn’t catch my eye, and I wasn’t really sure what it was all about. During a sale on Steam I was able to purchase Teleglitch for a good price and give it a chance, and I’m glad I did. After getting the hang of this game I felt like Rick Grimes or Daryl Dixon on a rampage blowing off zombie’s heads and throwing pipe bombs at anything in that got in my path.
In a cold, dark future dominated by mega-corporations, a place 30 light years away from Earth, Planet Medusa 1C is on the edge of habitable space and the site of a shadowy research facility specializing in necrotic tissue reactivation. You are a scientist who has suddenly awoken to the realization that you are the lone survivor. The rest of the facilities personnel have all been killed, micro-chipped and reactivated as combatants by the facilities central processing AI. An in-depth storyline keeps you constantly informed of your surroundings and almost adds a sense of excitement through your adventure. The story of Teleglitch continues throughout each level and grows deeper and more involved as you progress on your quest.
This game is hard and involves a lot of tactical thinking on the fly. An advanced crafting system helps you build explosives among other various weaponry based on the materials you collect throughout each level. You are also able to craft other tactical items like the Detector which helps you locate enemies on the map in close quarters where you would otherwise be ambushed.  Combining health kits or different materials can result in health upgrades or even steroids. These crafted items are a key element of Teleglitch making later gameplay almost impossible without them. The map is another vital piece of gameplay and by using it as a constant reference I found that it not only allowed me to keep my bearings but also helped keep track of any missed rooms I may have passed on the way. You will also encounter databases that hold crucial information regarding your mission, or maybe some tactical advice regarding secret locations which also make up a large part of the game.
The “Die More Edition” of this game alters gameplay slightly making each of the enemy creatures slightly more powerful to increase difficulty, as well as offering more weapons and items to craft with. Weaponry is a large part of the game, but in a small way. On Medusa 1C there is a lack of ammunition so every bullet counts and depending on what you are wielding you may not put down what is attacking you in one shot.  Without the “Guns & Tunes” DLC you start off with the standard 9mm pistol, then with continued play you are able to find more ammo and other weapons or explosives. Something that sets Teleglitch aside from other roguelikes of its kind is the unique crafting system I had mentioned earlier, and with this you are also able to build upgrades to your guns, which gives them more power or a special ability.
Some might think the pixel graphics in Teleglitch belong in 1981 but I look at them and see a visual masterpiece. Nostalgic, with flawless gameplay that keeps you on the edge of your seat Teleglitch is an amazing example of a simple pixel game that took it to the next level. Seemingly so basic, Teleglitch is a breath of fresh air to the retro movement and another essential in the library of any indie game. Like many roguelikes the map and environment change with every new game. Thousands of zombies and mutants deliver hours of gameplay making this game another instant classic and comes highly suggested to any gamer.

This game is pretty bad. I'd say 3/10 single player. 5/10 co-op.
Pros:
>Fun villain protagonist and even worse "buddy"
>Break all the rules and be a general♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥while running and gunning
>Starts in the middle of the action
>Good set ups to levels, such as running a heist and fighting through a civil war
>Really, the heist level is pretty fun.
Cons:
>Campaign is less than 4 hours long (Most of my play time is from accidentally leaving the game running over night)
>Clunky controls and gun mechanics
>Grenades have a kill radius of about 2 ft, but good luck throwing them with any accuracy
>All the guns have absurdly short ranges, even the rifles (except the scoped sniper rifle)
>Even on the higher difficulty, most of the threats come from enemies positioned right around corners or in cages over your head, or snipers. These guys will kill you before you can react, even on the lowest difficulty. Thanks for the help
>The AI is rough, and your companions will manage to kill about 1 person a level.
>Because the AI is crap, its obvious that most of the moooks, snipers, tanks, helicopters, etc. are gunning for you only 99% of the time, which really takes you out of the game and negates any strategy you may attempt in using the squad commands to draw fire or get a crossfire set up.
>All those awesome level set ups and concepts devolve into so-so gunfights with little strategy or positioning possible.
>To limit the use of gun emplacements you find through the game, the rate of fire slows down until the gun finally stops firing after about 10-15 seconds like the thing was battery powered. The bullets come farther and farther apart, and the last few pretty much dribble out of your gun like the last few drops of water from a bottle. Just wait 5 seconds more for it to charge up a bit! But the enemies can use these emplacements without any slowdown to mow down your companions over and over. Really awkward. I'm not the fan of typical overheat mechanics in games, but that would have been much better.
>Not enough back story to understand your reputation, or why your character chooses to trust certain people over others.
There are a lot of good ideas that weren't executed on well:
>Using RPGs to knock out armored vehicles and helicopters. This seems AWESOME, in practice its tedious. The explosions from rockets and grenades are lackluster, and the vehicles don't appear different or damaged even if they are knocked out. Sometimes you pump extra shots into them for a bit before you realize the helicopter is slowly crashing or the armored vehicle has stopped firing.
>At one point, your allies radio that they found a tank after you left them at the base of a building so you could clear the way. AWESOME! Time to rock a tank! WRONG. By the time you get down from the building, they have driven the tank to the other side of the buiding for no reason and have abandoned it. They literally drove it about 30ft after you had cleared out most of the threats. But you get to look at it! That's just as fun!
>High stress jeep ride through the jungle while you man the gun on the back. AWESOME. How could this be boring? Well, it feels like the jeep is going about 20mph, the gun (like 90% of the guns of the game) can shoot accurately at about 10 ft, and its super scripted, so if you die, you can expect everything to happen the exact same way again.
>The ending happens the way it happens no matter what, it fits the story, but is set up in a way that makes it seem like if were faster or chose a different route, things would happen differently. But scripted events and even an invincible enemy ensures the story happens just as planned.
In all, it was a fun break from more serious games, but you'll probably play it only once, or maybe twice if you want to run back through with a friend.
Buy it on a steep discount sale, or move on.

If I could, I would give this game a "sideways thumb".
Kane and Lynch is an odd game. For every good idea it has, there is an equally bad idea to balance it out. As the title suggests, the game is about Kane and Lynch, two mercenaries trying to get revenge on a mercenary group they used to work for. This plays out in typical third-person shooter fashion, with genre standards like cover system, squad mates, etc.
The gameplay is a mixed bag. The guns themselves feel and sound punchy when they hit what you're aiming at, but all of them are almost comically short ranged, making for an odd combat dynamic. It's not particularly bad, mind you, but it did feel like I was running out into the open more often than what was sensible. Speaking of running out into the open, this game's cover system is completely broken. You're sort of supposed to push yourself up against whatever you want to duck behind, but I can count the number of times that actually worked right on two fingers. It's easier to just stand or crouch behind whatever you're trying to hide behind than to mess with this game's broken attempt at cover. The game also has some weird design choices, for example, the tutorial is actually in the second level, after you've spent an entire level shooting your way through enemies. The problem is, that first level doesn't give you any kind of instruction on what button to press when it wants you to do things like go into cover or climb onto something, so for that level, you're constantly checking the options menu to find out what button you're supposed to press, only to have the game try and teach you after you spent all that time trying to figure things out on your own. The one thing this game does to genuinely well is the squad system. It's fairly standard, you tell teammates where to guard, what to shoot, whether to hang back, but it's useful and works well. I also have to commend the game's inclusion of split-screen co-op. I haven't played this mode myself, but it's fairly rare to see split-screen on a PC shooter, so I respect its inclusion. Overall, the gameplay is odd, and broken in places, but it's playable and even has bursts of "hey, this is cool"
The graphics are another example of how this game is all over the place. It came out in 2007, so looking a bit dated is excusable, but this looks like it got trapped in a sort of awkward tranitionary period between PS2 era graphics and Xbox 360-era graphics, something more akin to a game from 2004. Other games from 2007, such as Call of Duty 4 and The Orange Box were much more consistent and generally looked a lot better than this game does. The characters themselves look decent, except when beards (which look terrible in this game) are involved, featuring reasonably modern graphics techniques such as normal maps and whatnot (basically, the old wrinkly people you play as look old and wrinkly), but props and environments (including weapons), look like something from a PS2-era game, blocky and angular, with basic, low-resolution textures. Outdoor environments actually look fairly decent, being reasonably large and detailed, with good use of color and decent lighting, but indoor areas have a barren, almost abandoned feeling. This would be fine if you were supposed to be going through abandoned areas, but this game sends you through heavily populated areas such as banks and nightclubs, making these segments of the game feel odd and empty, and failing to convince me that I'm moving through and actual world. The buildings feel like they were just constructed and no one moved in yet, devoid of many of the props you would see in other games. One cool graphical thing this game does have going for it is that it features absolutely massive crowds. There are tons of people in places like the aforementioned nightclub, and they move out of your way and react in a surprisingly convincing way.
Finally, let's talk about the storyline. I just could not care about this story or any of the people in it. It's cool that you get to play as an unambiguously bad set of characters, but the storytelling is poorly executed. Basically the group of assassins Kane and Lynch worked is trying to get back the money they think Kane took. When Kane fails to get the cash, they do a bad thing (I won't spoil what on the off chance someone actually cares), so Kane and Lynch try to get their revenge. It's an interesting setup, but none of the characters are ever fleshed out enough to make me want to care. The past relationship between Kane and the group isn't explained much, so their rivalry fails to be interesting, and neither Kane nor Lynch are interesting enough for me tor really latch on to either. You can have an interesting story about a complete amoral character (The recent film, "Nightcrawler" is an excellent example), but that's not the case here. Every character is kind of an idiot, and the worsening of their problems is always their own fault, making them more annoying than cool. You eventually pick up three side characters who serve as your "squad", and while their gameplay function is interesting, they serve almost no purpose to the story, and are basically nothing more than names. Their relation to Kane and Lynch is never explained and other than one or two offhand lines, they get no characterization other than "unpleasant". The game wants to be a Michael Mann crime revenge story, but has neither the style nor charm to do so.
Overall, it's not a terrible game, but it's not particularly great either. It's certainly not worth the $7 price being asked, but if you can get it for $1.25 (which it drops to frequently), it's not the worst thing you could play. The game lasts about 6 hours, so it's okay as a "weekend game" that you can beat and forget about.
