I decided to wait until Killing Floor 2 left early access to voice my opinion of the game. And it is safe to say that Killing Floor 2 (KF2) lives up to its predecessor’s name.
The game excellently builds upon the predecessor, and competently tackles the themes of the previous game. Gore, guns, and gameplay are all enhanced over KF1, being able to literally “paint the town red” is one of the most fun things to do. The addition of a new boss character is great to see, and all maps are well designed. Gunplay is excellent, and zed time is more appealing. The breakdown of perks and the expansion to the levelling system is a great contribution to this game.
Killing floor 2 does lack in some areas to the original (for me). These include, but are not limited to, inferior music. The iconic “abandon all” unfortunately does not make a return for the sequel, along with many other classic tunes. While fleshing out an expanding the perks was overall a fantastic idea, the survivalist perk is perhaps the weakest perk in terms of execution. I feel that this game has less heart than killing floor, however this could be the nostalgia of the original game.
Things I hope to see soon:
•	Xmas, summer and Halloween events. (tripwire has promised a return of these)
•	The return of some classic maps (Wyre, west London, water works and other such classics).
•	The option (or mod) to add classic KF1 music.
•	A more expanded arsenal (this too has been promised)
•	More characters
•	More game modes (objective mode was fun, and I’d like to see a return!)
In all, KF2 is a very competent sequel. I think it is perhaps unfair to compare KF and KF2 as they currently stand, rather it is more fair to compare the 2009 Killing Floor release and the Killing Floor 2 release. And in this respect, it is a wonderful game that truly expands the franchise. I hope that the longevity of this game lasts as long as killing floor!

It was a bumpy road during the Early Access - two steps forward, three steps back. Although,
has fixed some of the balance issues by the time of release, I have grown so tired of all the monotonous gameplay and numerous tiny annoyances that I'm not even excited about the full release. I still return to this game from time to time only to get bored of the same stupid community behaviour and superficial attempts by the devs to get their numbers right (because, in their opinion, if too many players are winning, it's bad, and changing damage stats, economy numbers and zed spawn rate is enough to make the game balanced).
"Early Access done right" - they said. Wrong!
did an ill service to themselves, antagonizing their own previously loyal fanbase in the development process, by breaking their promisses and adding things no one asked for. Never again am I buying an Early Access game.
Nevertheless, I'll put a "thumb up" for this game. It's fun in the beginning, until you grow tired of the same routine.
had many of the same problems, but, in overall, it was a slightly more enjoyable Co-Op experience than
.
========================================
PROS:
- Cool, detailed, shiny maps.
- Cool, detailed, shiny weapons, which feel good.
- Cool, detailed, shiny and various zeds.
- Fast paced zed slaugther
- Reasonably faster leveling up (than in KF1)
- Perk-specific skills
- Modding is allowed, encouraged and relatively easy to learn
========================================
CONS:
- ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ community (see more below)
- Balance issues (see more below)
- No easy way to launch private games
- Game is too easy on Normal and Hard
- It requires a good team to win on Suicidal and Hell on Earth, but it's not easy to get a good team in random games
========================================
NEUTRAL:
- PvP
- Skins
========================================
BALANCE ISSUES:
- Game Conductor: it punishes you for being high level, fast and accurate. Well, I'm absolutely sure that there are plenty of masochists out there who enjoy being grounded into a pulp. But I'm not one of them. If I'm getting a headshot after a headshot, I'd rather see myself rewarded with a victory instead of being surrounded by zeds, 'cause reloading is slower than zeds are running (I'm talking about HoE and Suicidal here).
- Game intentionally spawns zeds in a way that makes players surrounded or overwhelmed, limiting kiting options. Maybe, it's not anything bad as a principle, but the way it is implemented in this game, strongly limits options to prepare for and counter such situations
- Perks are designed in a way that you are forced to play CoOp, because not all perks are good for solo and require support from other perks. I think all perks should have more or less equal chances of surviving on their own, especially, in solo.
- Balance in overall. Cluster spawns of husks or sirens dosn't seem like evenly distributed system to me.
- Knockback is way too strong and shouldn't apply to small zeds.
========================================
COMMUNITY:
- Lack of communication
- Lack of cooperation
- Players not playing according to their perk function
- Players who are playing on Suicidal or HoE, although they do not have the skill and/or level for it
- There is an influx of bad players after the final release
A few examples of common and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ behaviour:
a) low level (0-5) players on Suicidal;
b) medics who focus on kill count, instead of healing;
c) firebugs who enrange the zeds, create chaos and stand in the way of commandos, whose function is to take out trash zeds from distance;
d) low level players who join the game towards the end, ask for dosh and die within the first two minutes of the wave;
e) players who don't group and don't hold their positions, but are trying to do everything on their own;
f) players who run away from the boss or fleshpounds instead of joining forces with others and taking out the enemy fast;
g) excessive force on trash zeds (e.g., an RPG launcher against a crawler, a grenade on 2 clots) or wasting a magazine on a bloat without a head.
Those are just a few examples of annoying players you will encounter on the servers. They are a burden on the team, by spawning extra zeds and increasing the difficulty, but not doing anything substantial to counter that. (Although, I must admit that CS community is much, much worse).
I hope the devs will implement the private match function some day. Meanwhile the only solution are the dedicated servers, which is not a very convenient option.

For those times when you just wanna get killed by marauding Space Pirates...FTL is a wonderful little Indie game. You play the crew of a small vessel seeking to escape the clutches of the powerful Rebellion that has taken over the galaxy. Your goal is to reach the safety of The Federation Fleet on the opposite side of the galaxy. The whole while the clock is ticking and your fuel dwindles as the Rebel Fleet marches across the map in an attempt to capture you, the last remaining hope for defeating The Rebellion. You must navigate your way through 8 sectors of point and click encounters stopping along the way at star systems inhabited by various races with varying attitudes on you and your crew. Not every system has an encounter and not every encounter turns deadly, often the choice is left to you. Do you flee and move on to the unknown quantity that is the next star system or stand and fight in an attempt to garner valuable scrap and weaponry with which to better arm yourself for what lies ahead? It all culminates in Sector 8: The Last Stand, where you finally link up with The Federation Fleet and are pitted against the mighty Rebel Fleet Flagship. Can you triumph and restore order to the galaxy or simply fade into history as a simple sidenote to the conquering Rebel Empire? Spool up the Hyperdrive and power all weapon batteries because it's a dangerous galaxy out there!

Almost identical to  the original, this game rarely fails to sate my current tactical and strategy needs. Careful planning rather than lightning reflexes is the theme of the day. This is an impressive clone of a classic 90's game series, which was the first isometric viewpoint genré of game. For dinosaurs like myself, this really is such a trip down nostalgia road, and for this reason it should instantly appeal to anyone who liked the originals.
However, XCom Enemy Unknown wields a double-edged sword. It is this same loyalty to the original game that also means this is little more than a re-skinned re-build. As great as the 3D cut-scene and in-game sequences are, they are little comfort  from the fact that the user has forked out at least £30 for what my old nan used to call, “money for old rope”.
That being said, there are few releases these days that aren’t old themes rehashed instead of original concepts and ideas. This doesn’t mean that those same said releases are not worth buying. Quite the opposite. We may have reached critical mass for game concepts in the gaming world yet much like in the art world - we can still see dramatic results through technically minor changes.
In summary, XCom Enemy Unknown is a worthy, (nay, essential I daresay!) addition to any wannabe special forces tactician.

Ce tactical-RPG du studio Harebrained Schemes a été kickstarté en 2012 et est sorti en 2013.
Parmi les designers et fondateurs du studio on trouve Jordan Weisman qui n'est ni plus ni moins que le créateur du très célèbre jeu de rôle sur table..."Shadowrun" !
Ce "retour" de Shadowrun est donc bel et bien organisé par son papa, en garantissant ainsi l'authenticité.
Shadowrun est un mélange de cyberpunk et de fantasy se déroulant dans un futur dystopique (imaginez par exemple un hacker elfe se promenant armé d'un flingue dans des décors à la Blade Runner pendant qu'un shaman orc l'observe depuis une ruelle sombre...). Par-dessus ça on trouve de l'horreur et de l'espionnage industriel (mais survitaminé, à base d'attaque de bâtiments pour y voler des données par exemple) avec une touche de film noir, de film de détective, ou policier (imaginez donc que notre elfe est suivi par un humain en long manteau, mâchouillant une cigarette sous la pluie, enquêtant sur des meurtres commis par ce qui semble être un démon...).
Bref, dans le futur proche de Shadowrun, la magie, les races typiques de la fantasy, etc. sont devenus réalité. Et les mega-corporations ont un statut et un pouvoir équivalent à celui de grands pays.
C'est donc un univers sombre, très riche, et qui est très bien exploité dans le jeu. C'est d'ailleurs une des grandes qualités de ce dernier : son univers mais aussi son atmosphère, son scénario, ses dialogues, ses personnages.
Le jeu est bien écrit et profite d'une ambiance très réussie.
Malheureusement tout cela est très linéaire pour un RPG et ne donne souvent pas au joueur l'impression que ses choix de dialogues et ses diverses décisions ont réellement de l'influence sur les événement... Dommage.
Le jeu est par ailleurs plutôt court, comptez une quinzaine d'heures de jeu en mode "very hard" (sinon c'est vraiment trop facile...) pour en venir à bout.
On aurait aimé pouvoir profiter de l'histoire un peu plus longtemps, on se sent un peu stoppé net dans notre élan quand la fin arrive.
Malgré la linéarité du jeu, la création du personnage laisse place à la liberté. On peut créer un cyber-bagarreur, un tireur d'élite, un hacker charismatique, un magicien, un shaman (invocations à la clef), ou un mélange de tout ça (un techno-mage !). Pas de classes, c'est au joueur de construire son profil et c'est plutôt cool. On améliore ses compétences avec les points de "karma" obtenus au fur et à mesure des missions. Ils arrivent vite et en grand nombre.
Le joueur a aussi la possibilité de s'acheter des implants cybernétique : oeil artificiel, jambes ou bras mécaniques, peau pare-balles, etc. Cela possède un coût financier mais aussi un coût en "essence", au détriment de l'efficacité de la magie...
Pour la plupart des missions, on pourra se constituer moyennant finances une équipe de shadowrunners à piocher parmi des profils nombreux et complémentaires, il y en aura pour tous les goûts. On devra aussi s'équiper et là aussi l'arsenal est varié, que ce soit les armes, les sorts, les différents items (soins, grenades, drogues).
Les combats sont nombreux dans Shadowrun Returns et constituent au final l'essentiel du gameplay. Et j'ai aimé !
Par contre c'est du classique : On est sur du tour-par-tour avec un système de grille et de point d'actions. Les personnages peuvent se déplacer, tirer, attaquer, lancer des sorts (offensifs, ou de soutien) ou des grenades, etc.
Les situations sont relativement variées et leur résolution intéressante, le tout demandant un minimum de planification et de réflexion.
Graphiquement c'est correct : En vue isométrique, éloignée, les décors et les persos sont plutôt jolis (quand ils sont vus de près sur certains écrans, les modèles 3D des personnages sont bien moches par contre...). Les portraits des personnages sont très réussis !
Niveau sonore c'est assez quelconque, avec des sons corrects pour les armes mais globalement rien de transcendant. Mais la bande-originale est de très bonne qualité ! Avec ses synthés et son côté futuriste des années 80, elle contribue parfaitement à l'ambiance du titre.
Deux défauts à mentionner quand même pour finir : une déception concernant la Matrice, l'internet sous forme de monde virtuel auquel on accède par certains terminaux, qui est une idée potentiellement intéressante mais dont l'implémentation est plutôt un échec ici (que ce soit le gameplay, le level-design ou les graphismes). Et un système d'inventaire assez mal fichu qui oblige par exemple à distribuer les items entre les membres de l'équipe en début de mission, sans possibilité d'échange une fois celle-ci commencée. Ça serait excusable si les items qu'on ramasse en cours de mission, dont on ne connaît pas la nature avant de les avoir récupérés, pouvaient eux au moins être répartis, mais même pas... Du coup on envoie untel ramassé un item en espérant que ça soit par exemple le kit de soin dont on voudrait qu'il s'équipe... Pas dramatique, mais un peu bizarre.
Au final Shadowrun Returns peut donner à juste titre l'impression d'un produit pas complètement abouti.
Mais, bénéficiant d'un gameplay tout à fait correct et d'un excellent univers, il est en fait très agréable à jouer et je le recommande aux amateurs du genre.
Il dispose en plus d'un éditeur, que je n'ai personnellement pas utilisé, mais qui semble avoir permis la création de contenus très intéressants par la communauté (des campagnes supplémentaires notamment). Je vais essayer tout ça très bientôt.
Les épisodes suivants de la série, "Dragonfall" et "Hong-Kong", ont reçu de très bonnes critiques et améliorent différents aspects du jeu. Hâte d'y jeter un oeil également !

Coming from someone who's really a Marvel fan through the Cinematic Universe, it's awesome to have all the heroes available without such pesky things as licensing rights. The second level for example, features Mr. Fantastic, Captain America, and Spider-Man.
LEGO Marvel Super Heroes is a great LEGO game, creating an original plotline requiring the help of all the major Marvel heroes (plus you can unlock some minor ones in side-quests like Ghost Rider and Moon Knight), going against villains like Doctor Octopus, Loki, Doctor Doom, and MODOK. Even when you're not going and re-going through all the levels for minikits (which create a comic book page when completed), you have a huge Manhattan hub world, where you can do side-quests, do vehicle races (note: the Hawkeye's Skycycle and Spider-buggy races don't give out Gold Bricks), and unlock new characters and vehicles (though the number of flying characters, including Iron Man whom you start with, make the air vehicles redundant). I do love the Cloud Rider, it's like a pink and blue light cycle.
Also, like the MCU, Stan Lee just has to cameo, so you have to rescue him in every level, plus some 24 more times around Manhattan, and naturally, he's voiced by Stan Lee himself.
Great game, whether you're a comic book enthusiast or a casual fan of superheroes. One of the best LEGO games I've played too.

Picked it up on a whim during one of the sales.  Have always been facinated with Cyberpunk/Steampunk and high fantasy, and this is a wonderful mix of the two.  Obviously the lore and history of this series go back further then my couple of hours into the game, none of which I knew, but I was instantly engaged and curious where the story was going.  It's full of cliches and used tropes, that doesn't make it any less wonderful. A little wordy, with 0 voice acting or any other story telling device we take for granted now a days which gives it a old school tabletop feel.  You could almost close your eyes and hear your DM describe the torn up world or your companions demenor, but then you couldn't read the story...sooooo..you know.
If you're a fan of RPG (table top or videogame) and Cyberpunk, you honestly can't go wrong here.
Running at 25 km/h with electronic music blasting in the background, leaping on top of buildings in the tokyo skyline (almost) without a care in the world. Mirror's Edge is that game.

This is a fantastic game marred by some significant flaws.  Thankfully, they don't really interfere with the gameplay except in a few small spots.  It's an extremely immersive experience and is surprisingly adept at preventing the player from feeling disoriented.  Overall, here's my breakdown:
Overal:  6.5/10 (5 being average)
Sound: 8/10.
The sound design in this game is nicely done.  The voice actors don't sound super rigid, the sound effects give subtle clues that can help you when you're in danger, and the music that plays is perfectly atmosperic.  My only complaint in this department is the fact that with the exception of the main theme (Still Alive) there really aren't any songs that would be good to listen to in any other context.
Visuals 9/10:
Art Direction is beautiful and extremely cohesive.  The use of strong colors contrasting against stark white makes for a very pleasing aesthetic.  Additionally, it's the only game I've ever played where I had to turn the brightness down instead of up for me to be able to see things clearly.  Textures are appropriately high for things that you will be looking at closely, and with the texture setting on "Very High" never saw a texture that took me out of the experience.  Biggest complaint is that everybody's faces are very rigid and feel a little out of place with the world.  I feel as though a bit more stylization on this front would have been extremely beneficial overall.  2D Cutscenes that occur between chapters aren't what I'd call incredible, but it's a nice way to handle incidents that are focused on interaction or that don't work well with the standard first-person perspective.
Gameplay: 6.5/10 (Averaging 9/10 and 4/10)
Free Running gameplay and Art Direction are the two biggest places where this game really shines.  The free-running/Parkour is a unique gameplay concept executed well, and contrasts extremely sharply against most modern games that give you the option of looking around, strafing and ineffectually jumping.  You really develop the sense to see where you need to get to and exactly how to get there.  Executing the perfect set of moves to get where you need to go is extremely satisfying.
Unfortunately, Combat mechanics severely detract from the overall experience.  Faith has the ability to defend herself by either countering melee attacks by armed enemies, picking up dropped weapons, or simply punching/kicking them into submission.  Unfortunately, the combat mechanics in this game feel extremely tacked-on.  While playing through the game, I constantly dreaded the sections where you are forced to fight "Blues," the in-game slang for Police or Security.  Early on, it's not that difficult to counter somebody swinging a pistol, but in later levels the fights are painfully unfair and just not fun at all.  The game seems to think that players will play Mirror's Edge as either a stealth-based combat approach or a run-and-gun approach.  Sadly, the stealthy approach simply doesn't work.  There's no measurable capacity for sneaking as enemies will autmatically become aware of your presence should you wander closer than 6 feet regardless of any other circumstances.  Going for a no-kill run in this game isn't a fun and unique way to beat the game, it's pure masochism.  Using dropped weapons becomes the only viable option for a lot of the game if you don't want to have to restart the segment 10 times or more.
Level Design:  7/10
Again, later areas of the game begin to suffer relative to earlier portions.  In the beginning, runner vision helps guide you around levels without heavy-handedly walking you through an entire level.  In later segments, Runner vision will highlight maybe three objects the entire chapter, and typically only in absurdly obvious configurations.  Instead of being helpful, it becomes a cruel taunt.  There are also several obstacles that have to be overcome using a specific move (Wall jump-reversal-wall jump) in a context that was never revealed to you, you're expected to just figure it out.  In the final couple of chapters there are challenges that completely disregard the natural flow that has been established up to that point and instead force you to take random long jumps and blind swings.  It feels unnatural and out-of-place.  And that's only when you're not stuck in a generic room ignoring Parkour moves and fighting off an obscene amount of the police force opening fire on you with infinite ammo.
Story: 3/10
Falls flat on its face.  Several major plot threads are introduced over the course of the game, but only one of them has any sort of resolution to speak of, and an unsatisfying resolution at that.  I'll avoid spoilers for those that haven't played yet, but the way the story plays out really feels like the development team had gotten to the climax of the story and then was forced to ship it.  On one hand, it leaves a lot of threads open for a sequel, on the other hand it leaves those who care about the story and are playing now with what feels like a cop-out.  The best way to play this game is to completely disregard the story in its entirety, at least until a sequel comes along that addresses the four major unresolved plot threads.
Overall, Mirror's edge is a great game that feels undeniably rushed in the end.  The average person could play up to chapter 7 and be done with it and then check out youtube videos of the ending scenes if they really want to know what happened; they wouldn't be missing anything significant.  I still recommend it due to the unique assets the game contains, despite its drastic shortcomings.

After you play this game, you won't be able to find another 'Stealth' game that would satisfy you, just saying.
I played it, and now I can't find anything else to do with my life. It's like this game doesn't age (and probably won't many years into the future).
-The graphics may seem bad at first, but it only takes about one or two mission(s) for you to realize how good this game is. The amount of paths you can take in each area or level is just uncountable. You can try different approaches everywhere and the arsenal of items given to you makes it extremely fun to experiment. (Just save the game often because trust me, by doing some reckless things or trying them for the first time you might die or fail the mission, and you there are NO checkpoints, so you need to load the saved game to be able to play from the right moment.).
-The Sound is. Absolutely. Perfect. This is the only game I know that concentrates on you paying attention to your surrounding at all time. You listen, trying to figure out where the guards are in the area or if there are any sorts of machines working, like cameras. Also each surface is either loud or quiet, forcing you to think through your actions before you walk in some direction. Guards can hear you if you're not patient enough and it's probably going to end ugly for you. (Also remember to stay in the shadows, Trust me, game rewards you for being slow and quiet.)
-The movement in this game is much better than in the first one. Now you don't have to turn(camera) to be able to make turns, instead Garrett is able to walk right or left, which really makes the game more fun to play.  At least for me it was a bit of an issue, so I was relieved to know this was fixed in Metal Age.
-The Main character is extremely memorable. You can't get enough of him and some of his lines. The jokes he makes at some moment of the game are just hilarious. He's extremely likeable and his voice actor is well picked. The Great Master Thief Garrett leaves a great impression throughout the entire game.
-The Story is well written and contains a lot of plot twists and locations you're going to visit. Not all missions are simply about stealing something without being noticed or dying, there is a huge variation to each and it's circumstances. You're going to be visiting old building, some which are filled with extra high security, giant open areas, as if they came from some sort of a fairy tale or fantasy story, or even the big city at night where the entire action takes place.
Overall this game is addicting as hell and I still can't cope with the thought of the idea that there are no more games with such brilliance and so much effort put into creating a perfect stealth environment. Maybe I'm way too blinded by its 'greatness' but Even though I can't give it anything less than 10/10.
Also, this is the first game that made me make such a long review. lol. It deserves a 10/10, Get it as soon as possible. YOU. WON'T. REGRET. IT. --- Unless you're a taffer. ( Just Kidding, I'm one too and I don't regret it even a bit.)

Well, LEGO Marvel Superheroes is a brilliant game! Today I will be doing a long in depth review that will hopefully get you to spend your precious money, and trust me it's worth every penny!
Plot:
The plot is all you would expect from a Marvel game. The world ( or at least Manhattan) is in danger from supervillians, and Nick Fury, Agent Coulson and S.H.I.E.L.D must gather the very best heroes to defeat the evil. The story moves quickly, and you're straight into the action in Level 1 as you face Sandman as Iron Man and Hulk. Each level brings in new characters with different actions and abilities and soon The Avengers, Spider-man, the X-Men, the Fantastic Four and loads of other side heroes are involved. In the game you will face many villians such as the manipulative Loki, the evil Magneto, the destructive Venom and even Doctor Doom himself while shooting jets of ice as Iceman, flying through the sky and shooting lasers as Iron Man, slinging webs to climb even the Empire State Building as Spiderman, and turning yourself into a teapot as Mr. Fantastic.
Gameplay:
Each superhero has unique abilties like wrecking, lasering, hammering, regenerating, clobberin', shrinking, web slinging and even....throwing squirrels! Outside of the action packed levels lies a huge open world - all of Manhattan! There's hours of activities to do in the city from skydiving to boat riding and sightseeing to car stealing - it's just like GTA except there's no sex, drugs, swearing or death...seriously, you can fall from the S.H.I.E.L.D Helicarrier into Central Park with no parachute and you will still survive. I find myself spending hours inside Manhattan visting Times Square, the X-Mansion, even a circus! If you have no idea what im trying to say, just think of it as New York Simulator + superpowers.
Pros:
- Open world.
- Levels with lots of puzzles and boss fights
- Good replay value as there are quests and items to collect in Free play and the open world.
- Fun for Marvel fans of all ages.
- Fairly original story.
- Unique LEGO models at the start of each level show where the mission takes place.
- Agent Coulson and Maria Hill tell you all you need to know to carry out the mission.
- Over 200 Gold Bricks to collect.
- Character designer can make Iron Man have Hulk size and ability ( no need to buy the Hulkbuster, it is available though)
- Ant Man shrinks - enough said.
- Drivable cars, buses, boats, trains, helicopters and jets.
- Voice acting is everywhere in New York, from gossip to road rage.
- Stan Lee makes about 50 cameos.
Cons:
- World does kind of cut off and the idea of the bridge being down is a bit lame, I'd rather have Loki put a barrier round the city.
- Flying and driving can be a bit haywire sometimes e.g my helicopter tipped over once and I crashed down into a crowd of people :(
Conclusion:
Overall, great game, seriously, what are you still doing reading this click that green button!
9/10 - Would Marvel again.

I've anticipated this game for a long time but elected not to purchase it on release due to a lot of triple A games not being so good lately. (*cough* AC: Unity, Evolve and Lords of the Fallen *cough*) Of course, the moment I decide to do that the game I wait for turns out to be good. There will be no spoilers in this review but I may accidentally mention something that would give away late game content so if you are wanting your experience completely unspoiled, take my word for it that the game is good and leave this review now. Otherwise, hello.
Okay so let me start off by saying; this game is effing excellent. I must admit, from the gameplay I'd seen and the reviews I'd read, I was expecting a semi-decent FPS survival that would take maybe 10 hours to complete with some repetitive hack and slash combat that had been over-hyped and blown out of proportion like most other triple-A games these days. I admit it, I was dead wrong.
Let me get the only two negative things I can say about this game out of the way. The multiplayer is pretty unbalanced, (although having someone join your game is a blast,) and the performance is sometimes lacking (fixed with Dying Light Manager 0.10a, google it for more info. It may have been updated to a newer version by now.)
The graphics in this game are so, so beautiful. During the day the shadows are gorgeous and at night the game has such intense and terrifying shadows that even though it is really difficult playing at night time, I still end up doing it just to enjoy the game's wonderful aesthetics.
I'm not huge on "horror" games, but this is the perfect mix of terror and action for me to enjoy without freaking out and quitting. (I'm looking at you Dead Space.) I hate slow paced horror games but since this game is always moving forwards, I could actually enjoy the scary areas a bit more than I can in other games.
The movement system in this game is fantastic, every time you jump onto a ledge or platform you immediately have 3 other options to jump to, which in turn have 3 more and so on. Freedom is the word when it comes to parkour in Dying Light and there is nothing more satisfying than jumping 150 meters down into a pile of garbage only to take no damage.
Dying Light was built on Chrome Engine 6. I have to say, I love this engine. Zombies have amazing ragdoll physics and being able to cut a zombies head, leg and arm off on one swing, then kick each individual part around just adds to the immersion. To this moment, if I see a zombie at a ledge of a building I will run up to it and kick it off just to watch it fall to the ground; no exceptions. It is glorious.
10 hours into the game and I still hadn't even found a gun yet I was enjoying the game immensely, guns are just a bonus late game. The progression in this game is absolutely perfect, you start off using sticks and wrenches to attack things and you mainly avoid zombies, but by the end of the game you are an absolute zombie murdering monster complete with a grapple, guns, super powerful melee weapons that slice zombies into two pieces with a single swing and the ability to go all the way across the city without stopping or touching the ground. (Still scary going out at night time although the monsters are a bit more manageable.)
The skill trees in this game are really well thought out with almost every skillpoint you get changing the way you play the game. No more of that, "5% damage increase while wielding 2h weapons" etc. You always get something meaningful, like a new ability, increased jump distance or a new finisher. I also like that there are 3 skill trees rather than just 1 and they are all leveled separately. So you have to go and do parkour to level up your agility tree and you have to engage in combat to level up your power tree. The trees are pretty damn big too. At 22 hours into the game and I was only 14-18/25 and it gets slower as you level, but like I said, almost every single level up adds something useful to your arsenal. Not to mention that the final perks on each tree are extremely useful so that adds incentive to level all your skill trees.
The story itself in the game was pretty good, but the real depth I got out of the game was the side missions. That being said, the actual campaign goes for around 17 hours so there's that. There are so many side missions all with interesting rewards and interesting storylines. You can also find survivors around the world and just sit and listen to them talk, they give insight into how the outbreak happened and a lot of them have clever things to say that will get you thinking. Clearly someone put a lot of effort into the dialogue for this game.
Overall I'd give this game an 9/10 and if the performance was a bit more optimised I'd be giving it easily a 9.5/10. I highly recommend you get this game if you are at all interested in survival FPS games. It's worth it.

I purchased Killing Floor 2 during a weekend sale which meant the purchase price was around £14.00. Having really enjoyed the first Killing Floor and looking at the reviews for the second one, I anticipated that I would like it but thought I didn't really have enough time to play yet another game on steam. Had I known the game was this good, I would have replaced one of my 'usual' games in place of this immediately.
The zed time has a Sin City feel to it which makes everything black and white with red as the only colour (awesome!). As a healer by nature, I was pleasantly surprised to see a better arsenal available to the medic class including a trusty shotgun and assault rifle. This certainly increases survivability during the higher waves and difficulties.
My quarrels with the game could be recognised as minor but I was quite sad to hear the voice packs were now in French accents? Being developed in France, I see why it would have been but it would have been great to have an option between British or French accents because I really loved the Londoner version.  Also, I saw there is now an XP system with achievements similarly to other games. In the first Killing Floor, the way you leveled up was to do a set task with your chosen perk - for healing you needed to heal a certain amount, for support you had to both weld and do a certain amount of damage. That said, I do like the max perk level of 25. I found after 200 hours of Killing Floor One, that I had all perks set to level 6 so I'm looking forward to leveling all my perks to 25.
I am a massive fan of zombie games, as are my friends - we play Left 4 Dead 2 also as we like the objective mode available. I think if Killing Floor 2 had dedicated Objective mode which didn't bug out (like was the case in Killing Floor One), I think I would more likely to stick to KF2 as opposed to switching between Left 4 Dead 2 and Killing Floor for the different modes.

Antichamber is the very definition of trippy. It is a living surrealist painting that sucks you in, forces you to play its games and won't let you go, and that's okay, because by the time you get to your third 'chamber' you won't want to leave. You'll need to uncover all its hyperspatial geometries, discover all the rooms and all the impossible ways that they are connected, and figure out all the entrances and exits.

Have you ever played an Elder Scrolls game and wished you could play a dwarf? Swinging an axe around, drinking your weight in ale and plundering caverns for the treasures of your ancestors and maybe sacking the hidden banks of some dirty elves? Well stop. You won't ever be able to play a dwarf in Elder Scrolls.
Instead, hop into Regions of Ruin and become the most badass pixel dwarf ever. Unite your people against displacement caused by ravaging orcs, goblins and other freaky and goulish fiends. Build a community and slowly retake back both the underground and the sun backed soil your people were driven from.
If you ever played games like Kingdom: Classic or New Lands, or side scrolling adventure RPGs or maybe you want to try something differrent, pick this game. It is incredible and worth every penny.
Pros:
* You're a dwarf with a badass beard.
* Skill Tree (providing many ways to build your dwarf and play the game)
* Extensive Loot system
* Easy to use inventory
* Forge (you can dismanle items for resources or create your own)
* Great resource management + options of obtainment (send out workers while you adventure)
* Village building (build and upgrade your community with resources + expand populace by rescueing and recruiting dwarves)
* Open world map exploration (uses a map based on resources)
* RPG with main story and lore (with references to Dwarf Fortress!)
* Impressive soundtrack/SE and pixel art (with a night and day system)
* Frequent updates and content patches!
* Devs love this project (and so it won't be neglected)
Cons:
* Platforming can be a bit tricky to ascend elevations of any kind, especially if enemies are mounted above you.
* Throwing is a bit janky but not impossible/hard.
* No "sprinting". You can use a Dash but that's more of a quick jump forward.
* Resources become hard to gather the further you go as they become very scarce.
* You can't customize your dwarf body. I want a red beard damn it. xD
* You get an itching for more when you need sleep.
I cannot imagine what this game will become out of early access and all of the content and features it might add since I'm already really impressed with it.  However, I am excited for the future! Great work devs, you made a wonderfull game!
5/5

Almost identical to  the original, this game rarely fails to sate my current tactical and strategy needs. Careful planning rather than lightning reflexes is the theme of the day. For dinosaurs like myself, this really is such a trip down nostalgia road, and for this reason it should instantly appeal to anyone who liked the originals.
However, XCom Enemy Unknown wields a double-edged sword. It is this same loyalty to the original game that also means this is little more than a re-skinned re-build. As great as the 3D cut-scene and in-game sequences are, they are little comfort  from the fact that the user has forked out at least £30 for what my old nan used to call, “money for old rope”.
That being said, there are few releases these days that aren’t old themes rehashed instead of original concepts and ideas. This doesn’t mean that those same said releases are not worth buying. Quite the opposite. We may have reached critical mass for game concepts in the gaming world yet much like in the art world - we can still see dramatic results through technically minor changes.
In summary, XCom Enemy Unknown is a worthy, (nay, essential I daresay!) addition to any wannabe special forces tactician.

Book of Demons is a twist on the old dungeon crawling hack and slash RPG's. What will be familiar are the dungeon types, monsters, debuffs, levelling system and so on. But that's really where it ends. In Book of Demons, you are stuck to the 'pathway' or 'roads' in the dungeon level. You move around this path fighting monsters and bosses and gathering gold. This is different to usual games like Grim Dawn or Diablo, as in those you're free to go anywhere in the dungeon, rather than stuck to a path. This means using tactics in order to defeat monsters as you're unable to dodge as well as you could in other games.
The next difference is that instead of collecting loot, like swords or armour, you collect cards. These cards provide passive buffs or active buffs. They have rarity levels. Each active card costs a certain amount of money to use; while passives will 'lock' a certain amount of mana constantly. This means you have to be careful with how much mana is reserved and how much is available for active skills. The use of these cards is further limited by how many card slots you have unlocked, you start with 3 and each one costs increasingly more gold to unlock. Cards can be upgraded by the NPC's using money and Rune Cards (crafting mats). Furthermore one NPC can identify certain rare cards; for a price.
Book of Demon's is presented in a rather unique style; with a cardboard cutout, popup style graphics. It's pleasant to look at and is enjoyable. The game is humorous and full of character.
Overall the game is very enjoyable and the only reason I'm writing this review is because the game asked me to! I would be carrying on playing if it wasn't for that!

I imagine when the folks sat down to think about a new RPG to create (this back in the late 80s-early 90s), they figures hey...Cyberpunk is big!  But D&D was still the king of RPGs.  Why not mix them together?  So you had a Gibsen-esque world  of hackers, megacorps, and gunplay...mixed with D&D tropes.  It makes for a nice mashup.
This particular game is a combat RPG that has the same sort of polished turn/action based combat of the new Xcom games, but with a content creation toolkit and a very nice character creation system.  Combat is fun, paced and sized so you can focus on controlling a few units with some interesting synergies.
Plus:
-If you like Shadowrun, or Cyberpunk in general, or Cyberpunk with fantasy races and real magic, the world is fun.
-Interesting classes, and you can create your own classes based on how you develop stats.  Some good synergies.
-Toolkit means that like the original Neverwinter Nights game, plenty of user created content.
-Combat is just detailed enough that you can think out your moves without getting bogged down, but still be rewarded by thinking them through rather than click attack on the nearest enemy.
-I like that this game (at least as paced in the first campaign...have yet to play the later two), is paced that I can play, save, and log off and come back to it without a huge mental investment.  The advantage to being on rails and having few and focussed goals is you don't have that problem with full quest logs for 100 quests all miles away from where you're standing.
Minus:
-Initial adventure somewhat lackluster.  Ran but 17 hours on my first playthrough and I am a talk to everyone, open every box type of player.  Some good segments but some of the NPC motivations made little to no sense until it was all over.  It was the definition of "on rails" as well.
-Inventory management stinks.  You need to distribute items before the quest starts, you can't trade in-game and whoever finds loot in-game gets to hold it...which also means hired mercenaries may walk away with very valuable loot that should be yours.
-If you're someone who needs super duper graphics, or can't stand turn based games, this isn't for you.
Overall, if you are the target market, you will like it.  If you aren't, you won't.  I'm not sure how they're packaging the game lately but I hear the Dragonfall DLC (haven't started it yet) is a much better and much longer RPG campaign, and they have a new one coming out soon (Hong Kong).  I can't wait to try them out.

There are several things Dying LIght does well, but on the whole it's a frustrating experience.
THE GOOD:
- The parkour model is implemented well, which lends itself to one of the best parts of the game: running around at night and either sneaking by zombies or running for your life.
- Everything looks great. The visuals are appealing and distinctive.
- The 'upgrade trees' work well and allow for a good learning curve.
- Voice acting is well done.
THE BAD:
- The story is pretty bad. It tries to pass itself off as not taking itself seroiusly, which is fine, but it doesn't follow through; it's almost as if part of the writing team wanted to do the Saint's Row of zombie games while the other part wanted serious and thought-provoking. It ends up succeeding at neither. The villains are cartoon-level, moustache-twirling Evil and completely unbelievable (even within the context of ZOMBIES) and there is no foundation for any of the characters (including yours) or the factions to which they belong; there's the guys you help, who are angelic, and the guys you kill on sight, who deserve the dismembering they get. One NPC gets better treatment and ends up being the most meaningful, but the game squanders the capital it earned with her on a nonsensical interlude about the value of life and death -- an appropriate subject for the zombie apocalypse but one too weighty for Dying Light to handle gracefully.
- The combat model is finicky during the middle portion of the game. Once you've made it to the end, you have enough tools at your disposal to manage most any scenario; and early on, you're so starved for resources or moves that fighting anything at all is an undertaking (as it should be!). During the middle bits, it's particularly frustrating to be grabbed, not because zombies shouldn't grab you, but because of how it's implemented; you purchase an upgrade that allows you to escape unharmed, and until you do, you're at the mercy of the AI that will interrupt whatever movement you're making to submit to the grab animation. It's a little tough to describe, but at any rate it feels very gamey.
- While Dying Light deserves credit for being difficult, it goes overboard in a few areas not in legitimate difficulty but in capitalizing on gamey exploits: for instance, there are 'challenge missions' where you can only throw zombies to their death, or only sneak up behind them, or where you must cut off their arms. It's a good idea but the engine doesn't support doing it right: while the running and climbing challenges are fun, the combat challenges are either very easy ('kill everything in sight with this awesome machete') or, mostly, frustrating: often these very specific instructions also have very short timers, and the cumulative effect of a handful of these challenges is to make you avoid the rest of the challenges.
- The folks behind Dying Light are clearly proud of their 'tons of craftable weapons' system, but it feels arbitrary to be constantly replacing your broken weapons. It's a problem with the concept; it's implemented well, but what is intended to be 'look at our variety' ends up leaving you with no particular attachment to anything you find.
- The ending. Not the story portion, which is bad but was already covered; rather, the grand finale is the game's one-and-only quicktime event. It doesn't reflect well on a fighting game when the engine can't manage the fight that they want and so an entirely different system must be found to handle it.

Regions of Ruin is a platformer-rpg-townbuilder mix with an engaging (and growing) amount of backstory in the form of a vibrant atmosphere and plenty of lore. New content usually arrives at a weekly pace, including new locations to explore, additional enemies to slay and interesting items to slay with / help with the slaying. The devs are very active, supportive of their fans and open to suggestions, something which is sadly lacking in many modern games and developers.
I have high hopes for this game's future, and wish the devs the best of luck for their future endeavors.

There's a long and short to my review of this, the short answer is that this game hits every single spot that i look for with beautiful music and art, tight, highly enjoyable gameplay and exceptional replayabilty.  It's a shining example of a game that has endless potential to replay, but is incredibly fun from the first minute and will always provide a fair, but exceptional challenge.  Yes it has a couple problems with RNG and a grind for content at some points, but I love it all the same.
That's longer than I'd expected.
The long version is a lot more analytical.
So to kick it off, the game is a rogue like/light platformer, which are words that turn a lot of people off quickly, but if it helps. the platforming is fairly easy and there are plenty of items in the game to make that part of it drastically easier, from jetpacks to double jumps, near endgame, you can pretty much get around anywhere with ease, but the added mobility adds an element of fun back in that was lost with the challenge of actually having to try to carefully make some jumps.  And of course there are plenty of optional items and drops that will still require some skill with platforming to reach.
As for the Rogue like/light elements, it works like this:
You start off with access to 1 of 12 classes, and a few starting items (we'll get into items later)  You collect these by completing certain tasks (earning achievements basically) like "die 50 times" "collect 15 monster logs" and "beat the game 20 times"  these unlocks help vary the game and allow you to have a stronger end game character by stacking different active abilities and passive (again more later).  Now this is one of the problems, some if not most of these items can have fairly difficult achievements so you sometimes go a while without any progress or without seeing anything new, some of the drops are RNG dependant (the monster logs for example) and some are just downright difficult (beating the game 20 for example).  however many of them are fairly reasonable and so it can space out relatively well.
Now the items, and gameplay, are extremely satisfying, the character abilities are fun to use and have real weight to them, and the items offer varied and interesting buffs to allow for interesting builds (such as "crits heal you, enemies explode on death, fire a missle when you take damage)  these make most if not all characters fun to play.  and allows for 12 classes to be possibly split into dozens if not hundreds of differnt play styles and sub classes.  Yes the fact that the items are random can be an issue, and many items have fairly similiar effects, which feels a tad lazy at times, but there is a modifier that you can earn to eliminate some of the RNG.
And i have to mention the graphics, i personally enjoy them, however, they can get busy near end game and i'd understand if some people can be turned off by the style, and yes pixel does get old quickly.
The music, however, is another story.  Many of the soundtracks i can best describe as haunting, or otherworldly.  Each piece perfectly accents the level it's paired with as well as the energy of the situation the player is in.  They all build in intensity to a perfect peak without ever overwhelming the actual gameplay.  The soundtrack is a must buy.
Wow that got longer than i thought, TLDR the game has a couple of problems, but in all honesty they're towered over by the simple fun and challenge every single other aspect brings to the table.  The developers deserve every bit of support they've gotten and more.  This game is in my top 10.

The demo got me hooked within the first few minutes! Book of demons has a unique art style and great voice acting, the intro is short but beautiful, building a nice atmosphere, dragging you into the game. Gameplay is as unique as the art is. Book of demons tries to do things different than your usual dungeon crawler or hack and slash game. It is generally slow paced realtime gameplay but with lots of bells and whistles to keep you busy. The core challenge of the gameplay builds around various mechanics that monsters and boss monsters can spawn with and the strategy how to take them down.
Everyone who sees a slight overlap in gaming interests should at least check out the demo. The download is small and absolutely worth it. The game has huge potential and with some serious work it could evolve into a classic.
But yeah for that some work is required, yes it is still OA, but we're here for feedback right?
Disclaimer: I haven't approached the game in completionist mindset yet, so there may be some lack of knowledge on my side. Also some spoilers incoming.
What you get right now with the demo is actually better than what you get with the full game. The demo covers the first third of the story mode. The first levels are challenging and you actually feel scared because you have so little life. At the time you get around 40 life it is pretty hard to die. In fact I played through story mode with both chars and didn't even die once (I think I triggered Death Rage twice). Not even in the slightly overtuned archdemon boss fight. Simply put: Later in the game the fights get longer but not harder. Longer to a point where it is draining to facetank a mob for 10 seconds. Don't get me wrong, I am not into games that are super challenging all the time, but if a mob poses no threat to me it is just boring to shoot them down. I feel the player has - at least in the second third of story mode - slightly too much HP.
Golden/fire/cold hearts and shield mobs are the main mechanics that slow you down. While this is intentional and not a bad idea, the ways to cope with can be impairing. I found myself often picking the right elemental skill manually from the card pane, sometimes switching back and forth mob by mob. With mage I later opted to solely rely on basic attacks with level 2 lightning/fire/cold passive cards. While this solved the constant manual switching I felt cheated. I could also have used the fire/cold attack skills and just switch projectiles but in some messy fights it can be quite hard to hit the right mob. Which leads to golden heart mobs. First of all I wish I could completely disable auto attacks in the options menu. Reliably hitting them in a messy fight can be impossible due to overlapping mobs and I haven't seen a card yet to help with them apart from hard hitters. I see that this is probably hard to fix, maybe this mobs can be just super scarce?
Overall I found the fights starting normal difficulty and also some story mode parts can happen to to be a bit too lengthy just spamming a single mob or a small pack, quite a bit of boredom came up.
It is a mess. Surely intentional. The grand strategy is to camp fountains, have a crowd control skill and shoot mobs or the archdemon if possible. Each time i tried to clean the area after the archdemon was down I got into trouble and left. Is that even possible? Idk, but anyone who claims to know what is going on in that fight is either a liar or a prodigy. While it is doable I feel it is overtuned and out of control. I cannot suggest any fixes here because I don't understand the mechanics of the fight, maybe thats part of the problem but it feels odd to me.
Endgame is where the game begins. I expected more difficulties and got em. More grind, more levels more loot. But the core difficulty mechanic was quite an disappointment. Locking cards? Completely disabling playstyles seems to be trendy right now and it is a mechanic I have a huge personal grief with. Let the player develop his style of playing and then take it away from him is just not cool. Ok there are cards that can protect neighboring cards. Fine. But then again you easily end up reconfiguring your controls because you are forced to put cards on certain slots, which could even contradict between mage and warrior. Not cool. I like for example the nudist achievement, something I seriously would do for the luls. Maybe it isn't that bad in long term because you get plenty of cards that protect your playstyle core cards. I don't know if this is set in stone and I would hope for something different. But one thing to consider: Make the keyboard icons below the cards draggable just like cards.
So this are my thoughts for now. Hope it helps. Keep going the good work!

A very good cRPG based on the classic Shadowrun tabletop game; it almost makes me want to play the original, minus the crappy combat system which is thankfully simplified in this version.
For those unfamiliar with Shadowrun, it is a cyberpunk RPG very strongly based on 80's views of the future, not surprising considering when it was made. Mega corporations are basically nations in their own right, law enforcement is handled by private corporations, and the population is strictly divided between poor and rich.
Also, thanks to an event in the mysterious year of 2012, magic has appeared on Earth and some of humanity has mutated into "meta-humans": Elves, dwarves, orks, and trolls.
Shadowrun Returns's base game puts you in the cyberpunk future of Seattle, on the trail of a brutal murderer. Naturally there's more to it than that, and you end up involved in some deep drek before the story's end.
Despite a jarring jump in difficulty at the end of the game, the experience is a wonderful example of how cRPGs can and should be done, and I would easily recommend it to any RPG fan.

As stated in the opener, this is a glorified game of collectibles. Most levels will have random loot scattered across levels and it's your job, if you're OCD inclined, to collect everything, all while avoiding the guardians of said loot.
+ Trying to find loot in and of itself is a lot of fun. It's a great feeling to find a huge stash behind a hidden door that you almost overlooked, or discovered while backtracking. The game's name holds up.
+ Stealth mechanics, for how they're designed, work great. Stay in the shadows to avoid the guards; if you enter the light and they see you, they'll attack. Simple.
+ A nice supply of items to help you "thief your way around" each and every level. The Rope/Vine Arrow was my favorite.
+ For a game that is extremely repetitive in it's nature, I was pleasantly surprised as to how happy I was to dive into the next level after finishing a previous one. This game does repetition correctly, and I can't even fully understand why. I just had a lot of fun.

This is big deal for a stealth game. -2

I'm a huge fan of classic DOOM and Quake, the latter particularly because of its unique atmosphere of eldritch horror. Not many games capture it quite as well, but Teleglitch gives it a terrifying run for its money. Between the gritty brown surfaces, the spilled gore, and the silent uncertainty of what lurks around every corner, this title takes that otherworldly horror and mixes it with hectic action and classic roguelike tension. Creepy, intense, and challenging, this is a worthy entry in both the roguelike and survival horror genres.
Posed like a top-down version of those classic shooters already mentioned, Teleglitch sends you through branching, randomized levels in search of escape. The science colony you're stationed on has gone completely to hell thanks to some questionable teleporter experiments (sound familiar?), leaving you as the only level-headed person alive among killer cyborgs, ravenous zombies, and worse. Along the way you'll find and assemble an arsenal of space-age weaponry as you learn more about the fate of the colony and the bizarre anomaly consuming it.
No matter how seasoned a space marine you might be, Teleglitch will have you forever dreading what's around the next corner. The top-down perspective is based on lines of sight, so anything not directly in view of you is blotted out by thick, sharp shadows. You start with naught but a pistol and knife, but over the course of the game you collect weapons, ammo, and other junk that can be combined into a huge assortment of gear to help you survive. The crafting system is robust, easy to navigate, and has a number of meaningful choices and secrets to work out. It's a refreshing addition to the game, as opposed to a lot of modern crafting systems unceremoniously bolted onto their games.
You'll need every tool at your disposal too, because nothing in Teleglitch holds back. You'll be facing waves of mutants, zombies, cyborgs, robots, and far more exotic things at every turn. While the first few levels pit you mostly against melee enemies, you'll soon start running afoul of gun-wielding foes that can drop you almost as fast as you can drop them. The limited sight lines become a real terror as you creep down the derelict corridors, tensed for the next shootout. It's one of those games that really, really makes you work to beat it, and it's intensely satisfying when you finally pull it off.
This is one of those rare pixel art games that's ugly as sin, but once you start counting bullets in your clip and learning how to construct quad-barreled nailguns, you won't even notice. The minimal graphic design does do it some favors, leaving effective elements of horror to your imagination. The sound design is incredibly on point, with ominous cues and snaps of static in just the right places. And if you like the combat, they even added a series of arenas to blast your way through. There's a lot of secrets to discover, a lot of monsters to fear, and a lot of ways to mow them down. All told, these features combine to form one of my all-time favorites on Steam, spanning the roguelike and horror genres.

The card art is beautiful, the different classes feel and play completely differently to one another, and the Japanese voice acting is superb. There are some minor gripes I have with this game, such as the main menu interface being terrible, and that there's no in-game option to switch to Japanese voices so you have to mess with the game files, but all in all, Shadowverse is definitely the strongest CCG available right now.

Kane and Lynch is one of the most memorable games to me, yet not exactly one of my favorites. I enjoyed it back when it was released, beating it several times on Xbox 360. I was impressed by how they managed to create such violent and depressing atmosphere in a story about characters who are downright insane in a disturbingly twisted way. The game feels like it was planned to be actually big, but after going through rough feature cuts it turned out to be what it is, a story-driven cover-based TPS with plot holes and the most basic of TPS mechanics you can find.
But the story and atmosphere is what deserves some attention in K&L. Heard of the night club level? Or sieging a business skyscraper dressed as window washers? Give this game a shot. Seriously, it deserves to at least be tried.
The reason I give it a thumbs down though lies in this exact Steam version. This is not actually a Steam version, to be exact - it probably won't even work when you buy and install it before you get Microsoft's Game Marketplace installed. I still own a disc version and can confirm that it's the same edition with absolutely no differences (except the MS Game Market is installed along with the game not making you confused about why it doesn't launch). For best experience get it on used disc or play it on your console of choise. Putting aside all technical details, the atmosphere deserves your attention. Just give it a shot.

Kane and Lynch is a pretty bare-bones action game. It doesn't bring anything really great to the table.
The story is really lacking - its just a typical 'my daughter's kidnapped by the bad guys I used to work for; they want us to do X job or she dies'. Throw in a sidekick that's a sloppy ripoff of the character Waingro from Heat, and that's Kane and Lynch for you.
The gunplay is wildly erratic at times; shooting long distance is frustrating as most bullets are off quite a bit. The engine is more or less the same as older Hitman games (same company) so the physics, especially when shooting bad guys, can be downright comical.
Overall its a forgettable game, without achievements or trading cards, and it taking about 4 hours to beat (even on its toughest setting). it's a tough pill to swallow.
However if you like mindless action, you really can't go wrong - just don't pay more than a buck or two. It's better than some movies and games I've experienced. It's not Bad Rats...

Killing Floor 2 drops the players in Europe after an amalgamation of events which occurred due to the tampering of genetic material by the Biotech Company called Horzine Corporation. Through genetic manipulation the company was able to create dangerous mutant clones known as “Zeds”, classified as failed experiments, who eventually were able to breakout from the labs where they were kept in captivity, later on these Zeds overran violently London, spreading through the rest of Europe with murderous acts. These occurrences crippled Europe leaving civilization in chaos, all communication cut-off, governments dismantled and military forces utterly decimated. When all hope seemed lost, the last remaining civilian survivors, a group of soldiers and mercenaries decide to come together as a team, and create a movement who swore to eradicate these creatures from the face of the Earth.
Killing Floor 2 is a wave based combat game, where you can play in survival mode up to six players in a team or twelve players in versus survival mode (six versus six). In the versus survival mode players will be separated into two groups, the Zeds and the Humans, the mechanic has a close affinity with Left4Dead versus mode.
In Survival mode, you and your five friends have to fight and survive ten waves of mutant clones (Zeds) and with each Zed you kill you earn money so that later on, at the end of each wave, you are able to purchase beefier weapons and combat armour. The Zeds that give you the most earnings are the muscled ones, but watch out with these guys, they are tough as nails to take down. At the end of 10 waves you will encounter an eleventh wave where you will have to battle against one of two bosses.
In this game players have to grasp the magnitude of teamwork. If you are not a team player than this game is not for you or maybe you will eventually be kicked out of a server for not contributing for the survival of the team. The effectiveness of teamwork and constant communication will prove dire in the team’s survival abilities. Recklessness in is not approved. In other words, your team work will dictate if you struggle, die or survive in this game.
The new system implemented in Killing Floor 2 is called the Zedconomy System, where players can receive daily random drops of weapon skins and wearable cosmetics. This is actually a huge advantage to any player due to the fact that these items can be traded or sold in the steam market for some extra money.
In Killing Floor 2 there are 10 perks which vary from each other, so coming up with a diverse team will always benefit in the outcome of the teams survivability. Each perk has a cap level of 25, with two abilities to choose from in every five in five levels. There is a unique array of perks you can choose from in Killing Floor 2 which are: Berserker, Commando, Demolitionist, Field Medic, Firebug, Gunslinger, Sharpshooter, Support, Survivalist and S.W.A.T. Keep in mind that some perks are built to confront specific Zeds which will make your functionality in the team utterly crucial and overall will contribute for the teams survival. The monstrosities in this game put modern horror movies to shame. The enemies you will face in this game are the following: Cyst, Alpha Clot, Slasher, Crawler, Stalker, Gorefast, Bloat, Gorefiend, Husk, Siren, Scracke, Fleshpound, Dr. Hans Volter and last but not least The Patriarch. These enemies will use every means necessary to eliminate you, by using their bile to vomit acid on you, gash you with their claws while invisible, use supersonic screams to cause you pain, sever your locomotion by grabbing you and even muscled like monstrosities will run after you, armed with chainsaws or massive steal mallets to pound you to the ground. When you select higher difficulties you will notice that all Zeds start to work together to corner you, they will evince new abilities, possess more health and deal more damage. In the eleventh wave, you will face one of two abominable bosses. The Patriarch is armed with a mini-gun and a rocket launcher, as for Dr. Hans Volter, he shoots canisters of poisonous gas or explosives. If a team does not work together, both bosses can easily dispatch players in a matter of minutes.
Killing Floor 2 sounds and graphics have been embellished comparing to its predecessor, there are over 40 different weapons you can choose from, all of them are well designed and arrantly fulfilling to use, they are true blueprints to the real things. The sounds feel realistic and the amazing animations run smoothly on any Pc.
Killing Floor 2 is duplicating the experience of its predecessor but this time with more jazz, providing the player with memorable moments that seem to come out of an Oscar winning horror movie. The game is an incredible sight to behold, utterly challenging, fun and a fast co-op shooter with vivid maps. Once you enter this game it will feel like you are experiencing your own horror movie. Do you dare?

I'm currently sporting a really well equipped level 11 Daredevil warrior, and just beat the Cook, which was easier than one of the rooms leading up to him, where I had to fight about 50 arachnids, 8 medium sized Golems, 6 Archers, 12 Lumbering zombies, 2 Giant Skeletons, 3 Frozen Warriors and 2 skeletal mages in a cramped room. Certain things, like the RNG, should be fixed up a bit to make the game a more pleasant experience. Examples:
I did not enjoy getting a Legendary card that turned out to be a skill card named "Throw", when I've never even used that ability, or shown any interest in it. (:'c) I was really hoping for a legendary shadow blade (:c)
Sometimes the game is way too easy, and sometimes you can't help but think to yourself: "How are humans supposed to beat this?"
Edit 1:
I'm now currently a level 16 Daredevil Warrior, and let me tell ya, the closest I've ever gotten to dying was when I was prevented from moving by tons of small spiders whilst having 2 bosses, one of which spawns whatever spider that arachnods spawn along with arachnids. My favourite Card Layout is:
Heavy Strike, Helmet, Mana Amulet, Health Amulet, Cuirass, Shadow Blade, Buckler, Fire Axe, Frost Flail, Boots.
Overall it's a great experience for HC players, since it will, as time progresses, have challenges better suited for you.

You dont play the game for the story mode, but for the freedom and all the fun you get from the Lego games. I used around 40 hours to collect everything and the game was really fun. There are so many characters to play, vehicles to drive, aircrafts to fly etc. The free play mode gives you a big city to play with. From there you can acess story mode missions, races, get challenges/task from bystanders and do common super hero stuff.
If you like to collect/achieve and are a fan of Lego/Marvel Super Heroes, I strongly recommend this game. I hope you enjoy the game!

I think the biggest thing I was impressed by with Dying Light coming in after having played Techlands previous games was the improvement to the combat. Due to the combat being more melee focused than ranged it requires the combat to have the mix of mechanical, responsive, visual and audible feedback. Something that plagued the dead island series was that the combat did not have good feedback, hitting enemies in those games looked and felt weak, it seemed as if there was no real impact to hits. Dying lights combat is tight, hitting an walker around the head with a baseball bat looks and feels impact-full. Everything from the movement, hit detection and fluidity of the overall system is massively improved. Nothing feels more satisfying than completely decapitating a zombie with a electrified sword in one hit.
Dying light core mechanics work from day and night cycles. During the day while walkers are still a threat, mutated zombies known as volatiles are not in play but they can be found in dark areas. The day is when you want to get most of your travelling and quests done as its much safer to travel by light. At night however its a different story, Volatiles are out in force all over the city, they are quick and dangerous. Fighting anything other than walkers at night is a big no, volatiles will kill you at night in a couple of hits as they are damn strong. You are very much the prey at night and it pays to stick to the rooftops and not linger. While going out at night is much more deadly, there will be quests that involve going out at night, so if your thinking you can avoid it completely you can't. While the deaths you have at night and the subsequent loss of survivor points can be frustrating it is in my opinion a fantastic experience. The thrill of being chased, the tense survival moments of hiding are done superbly. You certainly get that tense panicked feel that I haven't felt since playing Left4Dead for the first time.
The story of Dying light is pretty unoriginal and clique. While there are some funny, interesting characters in there and most of the voice acting is not terrible, overall the writing is not that inspired. There are often cheesy, unessential moments of conversation and then suddenly complete jumps in the characters relationships to the point of a guy you barely know dying and then being refereed to as a close friend, I'm sorry but at what point did he become a close friend? We talked like four times. The way the story is told and indeed the quest system overall gives the game a very much far cry 4 with zombies feel, which I did not particularly enjoy. I found the plotline interesting enough to go through it but in my opinion it was the combination of good combat, survival and parkour that kept me playing, not the story. I certainly believe that had the mechanics of the game not been fun, I would not have stuck around for the story alone. I mean the bloody story had me climbing a radio tower at one point for goodness sake. I was having bad flashbacks for Kyrat, I was nearly waiting for Pagen Min to start yammering on at me over the radio, it almost had me thinking it was a Ubisoft game for a moment. Game developers need to learn that things like parkour are fun, the slow tedious process of climbing high towers is not.
The game features two multiplayer modes, one is co-op so you can play with a friend though the game doesn't knowledge that another person is playing in anyway which is quite annoying but it works fine and is fun killing zombies with a friend. The other is be a zombie where by you enter a friends game as a zombie and try and hunt them down to kill them. Its basic multiplayer and while fun for a time won't hold you for particularly long periods of time.
Overall I will say this about dying light, it held me. It has its problems like many games do, but it was fun enough that I kept coming back. The game is fun in fact I would go as far as to say that it's the best zombie game I have played in years. It's immersive, running from rooftop to rooftop is fun, combat is tight and while the narrative and indeed the mechanics are unoriginal, they are executed for the most part very well. It's what the original dead island should have been but wasn't and I certainly would recommend it, particularly if your a fan of the zombie apocalypse genre as it's probably is and will remain the best one out there for sometime. I am now however done with all these bloody zombie games, can we have something original please?

A very enjoyable and addictive game. It can be beaten fairly quickly, but all dungeons are randomly generated (I haven't even gotten close to running into all the monsters and cards you can find yet), and after you've finished it, you can continue playing with more customization in level generation.
Yes, it will become obvious very quickly that this is in part a spoof to a big dungeon game (whose name starts with D and is currently on the second sequel), but only as extra flair (anyone else find the voice of the Sage by the fountain somewhat familiar? Hehe).
The concept and the game play are quite new from what I have played before. The concept is that the game is based on those popout books where you open a page and a whole scene opens up in 3D before you with characters, objects and scenery popping out in glorious cardboard cutouts. Well, everthing in this game is made to look like that, some with a hint of origami paper folding.
You don't have weapons or potions - you have cards instead that you can emply like a weapon or potion or spell, and there are a few features that you could only do with the concept of cards - some monsters can knock you over and by doing so throw some of your cards out of alignment, so you can't use them until you notice and put them back in their places by clicking on them.
The random dungeon generator (that supposedly learns from how you play) is quite fun. You get to define how much time you have to play, and while I haven't timed it, it seems reasonably accurate. I have not encountered any issues with the generator at all. Unlike most games, you can only go along a predefined path within the scenery. Sometimes the path will split and give you options where to go first. Sometimes this pathing system can get a bit irritating when a monster straight ahead fires at you, and you can't evade, but that's part of the challenge.
There are three character classes - fighter (available from the start), mage (available after you've reached level 5 with the fighter), and archer (which doesn't seem to be activated yet as of the time of me writing this). Interestingly, the fighter can reach as far with a sword as the mage with spells - I guess they had to find a way to avoid the fighter getting swamped.
Otherwise you have a lot of the typical features - loot gets dropped, e.g. money (wich you pick up just by moving your moves over it), potions, charges for various skills, upgrades, XP boosts.
Beware the last level - it's REALLY challenging!
I'm glad I found this game and will keep playing it, and I'm sure that after I take a break, I'll enjoy coming back to it again.

The battle system is turn-based, grid-like strategy fight. You control up to 4 players, and fight againts enemies either by using guns, melee weapons, or spells. The battle itself isn't hard to understand, but it is very challenging if you are playing harder difficulties with an unprepared party.
The main character is very customizable, it takes my first playthru a lot of times struggling on how to develop my character. However, after one playthru, I find the customization choice is pretty unnecessary, since you can always hire a full team of balanced shadowrunners to do all the work.
The story or dialogue choices make very little difference to the plot, most of the time they just affect the next NPC sentence and that's all.
The plot is interesting and fit in the game setting pretty well.
