Very fun game, especially for Marvel fans, be they long-time comic followers, or new fans who just follow the movies. The story is mostly comic-friendly, and the roster includes over a hundred characters (more than any other Marvel game, I believe), including favorite icons like Spidey and Deadpool, and some lesser known classics like Moon Knight and Silver Samurai. And of course, the King of Cameos and Generalissimo of comic books, Stan Lee. :)
Gameplay is similar to just about every other Lego games. You go into various levels, collect studs, and defeat foes. And afterwards, return in Free Play to use other characters to earn minikits, red bricks, and new characters. Rather than having a central hub, like earlier Lego games, it follows the newer trend of having an open world, in which you can enter races, finish puzzles, and assist NPCs with tasks to earn Golden Bricks, which unlock bonus levels featuring new characters. And of course, it has the ever-popular custom character creators, which allow you to make your own character by mixing parts of other characters. It's very fun to see what combinations of superpowers you can create.
While Lego games tend to lose replayability upon hitting 100%, I'd definitely say this one, with a massive, diverse roster and many different extra tasks both during and after the story, is one of the most replayable. I would recommend this game to any Marvel fan, and to people who enjoyed other Lego games.

++The sound design in this game is phenomenal. The propogation engine, the voice acting, how it effects gameplay, everything is just at the highest standard possible which is to say totally unmatched.
++The cutscenes in this game are, again, and I'll be repeating this a few times, totally unmatched within video games as a whole

++Levels can take an hour or more to complete and are totally rewarding the whole way through
++The sneaking is just plain fun
+Graphics are a noticable improvement over the Dark Project more so in consistency and art style then technical acheivement.
+Using Tafferpatcher, I couldn't ask for smoother performance on modern systems
+Levels are huge, but not for the sake of being huge
+The addition of officially marked secrets is awesome
+A lot of the new equipment is really cool
+I've always liked the animations in these games, but some people seem to think they've aged really badly
+-The soundtrack by Eric Brosius was made to be more musical than ambiant and it doesn't work nearly as well. It's in no way bad though.
-+The Life of the Party is just disappointing, but I guess it's not its fault it got hyped so much. Plus, it's not bad by any stretch of the imagination.
+-What the hell are the point in vine arrows? I used them like once for metal surfaces the whole game.
-One level is turned into two which is utterly lazy and unenjoyable considering how the level wasn't even that good the first time
-Movement seems to glitch on surfaces more than the first game which is quite frustrating
-Physics tied to framerate (60FPS)

I've played Thief II multiple times and never get tired of it.  I have the game on CD but bought the Steam version because my CDs no longer play the end mission videos.  Those videos push the story along and the plot is much better with them.  The game is similar to a first person shooter but the best way to play is on the hardest difficulty level in which you aren't allowed to kill any humans--you have to play by stealth.  I have to say, knocking out a guard with a blackjack is much more satisfying even than killing a boss in many other FPS games.  At the same time, it's still a lot of fun to kill a guard from a distance with an arrow at lower difficulty levels.  I never did succeed at killing guards with a sword--I just take too much damage.
Every mission is different--reconnaissance, rob a mansion, escape an ambush, blackmail someone, follow someone undetected and more.  Weapons are varied and most are useful for things other than killing enemies--a rope arrow to climb, water arrow to put out torches, moss arrow to dampen sound on hard flooring etc.   Don't worry, you still get to kill nonhuman critters (and humans in lower difficulty levels).  While all of these elements make for excellent game play, Thief II's plot is wonderful.  One of my only critiques is that the plot should be advanced farther within the missions than through the end of mission vidos.
The look and feel is not outdated even though the game is almost 20 years old; in fact, I hope there's a 20th anniversary edition--I'd buy that in a heartbeat!

Batman Arkham Knight is the 4th and final title in the Batman Arkham franchise action-adventure series that follows Batman through Gotham. I had a lot of skepticism playing this game because all I read were bad reviews from every PC user bashing the game because of the horrible launch that had a plethora of glitches and technical issues with unoptimized performance problems. Locking FPS at 30, crashes, lack of rain shader/ambient occlusion/AA/antisotropic filtering etc etc. I've never myself experienced any of these issues albeit I did play this game a year and a half after it came to PC via port (Release date 6-23-15 vs my gameplay 3-13-17). I sport a pair of Nvidia 970 GTX Sli'd and I don't have a single issue playing the game.
Graphics:
The plus side of the high-spec card is that the graphics are amazing. It has a certain cinematic authenticity to it, a movie level gloss and immersion that takes you directly into the game and makes you feel like you're truly in Gotham. From the smallest dust particle to the sweeping bridges and skyscrapers, Gotham City truly feels alive. Every crack in the sidewalk, every fierce tattoo, each choppy wave, an craggy wrinkle tells a story that makes you want to know more. The people may not be as attractive as in previous installments, but they are more realistic, and they truly have character.
The devs have introduced a photo mode, where you can pause the game and do a nearly 360-degree rotation to get just the perfect shot. Just use the Steam shortcut you set up (F12 default) to take screens, and it removes the ugly interface when you take the shot.
Gameplay:
They added the Batmobile! What a great addition to the series! Not only can you zoom around Gotham City like a boss, you can destroy half the city as you go! I had great fun running down criminals, blowing up cars, knocking down trees, fences, support pillars, you get the idea. It's basically a fast tank, and it acts like one. In addition to a new form of transportation, we have a great many quests, riddles, and fights to win using the Batmobile, which is not only a car, but a BATTLEmoblie! At the touch of a button we can transform it to a highly-maneuverable tank in order to destroy. We can even do Batmobile-assisted takedowns with Wayne's patented non-lethal rounds. "It's like being punched in the chest by an angry gorilla!"
As far as manuverability the game itself feels so much more fluid, totally engaging and immersing you into the gameplay from being able to fly and grapple across the world. It feels so big yet so small at the same time, it's a huge map but everything is accessable easily and quickly.
Combat:
As usual for the series, combat starts off deceptively easy, then amps up in difficulty as you progress. We have the new Fear Multi-takedown ability, which enables you to take out up to six enemies within seconds, provided that you can come upon the group by surprise. There are also points in the story where you can play two characters at once, and during this time you can do multi-character takedowns, one of the more fun parts of the combat system.
Story:
When the game started, I felt that the side missions were much more engrossing than the main storyline. I went through the game knowing not only exactly who our mystery assailant was, but why we were being attacked. Absolutely positive right up to the moment of the unmasking, and then, everything changed. That which had been mildly interesting was suddenly fascinating. My mental shift was profound, as far as such things go, and it pulled me into the story in ways I had never considered. Although one aspect of the story I had totally nailed, there were several real surprises throughout, something which I really cherish. A good story is something that I truly appreciate, but you have a good story with great gameplay. They also do a great job of including the rest of the villianous roster to the game that they previously left out.
Pros:
+ Amazing level of detail, environmentally and graphically on characters
+ Each character is unique with the exception of the occasional thug
+ Fluid gameplay
+ Hours of exploration and more riddler quests to keep you engaged to 100%, doesn't feel too tedious though you may want to use a guide or youtube
+ Introduced Batmobile and all the glory that comes with it
+ Interesting and engaging plot
Cons:
- A little repetitive to get the 100% ending
- A little frustrating to get certain challenges done, but then again, it is a CHALLENGE
TL;DR
9/10
Great graphics, good plot, good combat. I had 0 issues with graphics. Tedious to get 100% ending but definitely doable. I'd say it was the best of the 4 in the Arkham series imo.

In my older days, this game was the absolutely best game I have ever played! It was not so long time ago I actually replayed this game and it did not quite live up my expectations of what I remembered.
The game is about a criminal, who is in jail writing a letter to her daughter Jenny. Some dudes, help him escape and he found himself in a chair bounded and is asked to deliver back the money he stole from his old teammates. They have kidnapped her daughter until Kane delivers it back to them. To guard him, they hire a watchdog (Lynch) to look out for him and the journey begins.
The gameplay is not as snappy you would probably like. It feels all a bit clunky and not responsive at all. The cover system is a bit average and so is the gunplay. It takes your through some interesting levels (locations) in the game and design of the levels is quite good. You have a squad you can use by calling commands, but it never never really used properly, and you are in most cases better of alone.
It is worth pointing out that this game still uses Windows Live. It is quite frustrating and a battle to get this game to work on newer machines. I do not know if is a bug. It has been so long since I used Windows Live that can probably not remember my password. I had to do a work around to play it. A shame, since you buy in Steam.
The game has not really aged very well. I feel like this game had a decent graphics for its time. The texture quality is low and it looks like you are playing on low quality.
The writing of the game is not really interesting either. They use a lot of swear words, not there's anything wrong with that, but they constantly use it. The guns sound awful and they much louder than the game itself. I throught the soundtrack was pretty good. It gets you hyped and fits the levels well.
Yes, Kane and Lynch falls flat on pretty much every level, but it's not a bad game per se. It is just so average and does not bring up whole new set of stuff. I am going to recommend this game anyway, just because it holds a nostalgia value for me and I would probably also have picked it up sometime anyway.

Out of the digital card games out right now, I believe this is the best one.  I have played Hearthstone, Duelyst, Eternal, Elder Scrolls Legends, Gwent, and Shadowverse.
I feel like Shadowverse takes a lot of inspiration from Hearthstone, without making too many of the same mistakes.  Hopefully anime girls don't bother you because you'll be seeing plenty of them.
The main mechanic that makes Shadowverse stand out from Hearthstone is 'Evolve.'  This gives a follower +2/+2 and allows them to attack an opposing follower immediately.  Some cards even have effects that activate when they are evolved.  In addition to drawing an extra card, the second turn player will also get one more opportunity to evolve.  First player gets to evolve twice, second player can evolve three times.
Right now the meta game is fairly balanced.  It seems like all the classes have viable decks.  If you care about being super competitive the best class for aggro is bloodcraft.  That would be the best/cheapest deck to try and rank up if that's all you care about.

The most garbage Xcom wannabe game ever made.
Cover in the game is irrelevant, the game has no real cover, only %chance reduction to alien hitting you. Play in harder modes and the aliens hit you 99% the time even if you are in high cover areas.
Aliens do not teamwork at all, the only aim they have is to kill one of your soldiers, no actual planning behind the moves.
The his %chances that the player team has, are all lies, even with 100% chance to hit you still miss, even when standing right next to an alien with a shotgun resulting in dead operatives in a full game.
Xcom operative moral is a joke, like when one of your operatives walk into poison cloud, your full team goes into panic mode (possible). Or one of your operatives takes a hit from an alien and your full team goes to panic mode.
Weapons, there is only one sniper, one shotgun, one pistol, one rifle, and one heavy machinegun in game, there is no option to use different amount of ammo magazines. There is no variation in weapons at all, only research new type of above weapon as laser/plasma etc etc and gain +dmg +hit etc. and that +hit actually does not matter at all, as the hit chance% is a lie in this game, actually now when i think about it, any %chance that you see in the game is a lie, the % chance is not what it shows and the hidden modifiers in this game are hardcoded and not showing to the player. PLUS all rolls are from a preterminated random seed form, meaning you can load your savegame 10 000 times and you miss everytime. (this has an option in the options screen where you can turn new random seed generation on after a load save game ;guess the developers got cought being lazy).
Thats pretty much some of the pointers, that makes this game an utter garbage xcom wannabe.
If you want to play an Xcom game, i suggest playing the older titles, they are much more rewarding even with crappier graphics but the actual GAME is good. This cannot be said about Xcom: Enemy Unknown, as its in a nutshell only made to get money from fans of the XCom series who crave for the old xcom games in better graphics only.
Also i think that the developers should be ashamed of making this game, this is the worst game i have ever played from this genre.

A lot of words will be wasted voicing outrage over the game's subject matter. I suspect an equal number of words will be wasted pointing out the ostensible hypocrisy of people who think nothing of shooting digital humans, but feel the need to howl over the killing of a digital bull. I won't bother injecting my point of view because many of you, like me, just want to know if it's worth 4.99.
The simple answer is no.
Bull fights are essentially made up of two mini games. The first has you taunt the bull in order to get it to charge your cape. The basic idea is to perform strings of combos in order to increase your score as well as crowd favor. The second is a series of timed button presses. Both are repeated over a four round match.
Overall it's a fairly shallow game. The controls are extremely stiff and somewhat non-responsive . Matches lack any depth while managing to feel too long. What's more the actual killing of the bull isn't shown. The Tercio de Muerte is nothing more than a couple of button presses ending with the bull charging off camera followed by a score card. I imagine some people will view this as a good thing.
Why am I giving this a thumbs up? The game isn't totally devoid of entertainment value, but mostly because I welcome the chance to experience something different regardless of what side of the line my moral compass points towards. I can appreciate someone trying something different, but if I were you I would wait till it's on sale.

Pros/Cons
+ Cool world and lore
+ Decent visuals and soundtrack
+ Noir-style storyline
+ Large number of player customization and play style options
+ Simple, easy to learn tactical combat system
- Linear and short, very little player choice in how the game progresses
- Characters are likable but shallow and onenote
- Story takes a turn for the ridiculous in the last act
- Overly simple tactical combat, too easy
- Broken cover and accuracy systems
- Dragonfall, the far superior standalone DLC, can be bought for the same price
This is my first experience with the world of Shadowrun, but it’s easy to understand why it’s so popular. It’s a unique mix of gritty cyberpunk and whimsical fantasy, mechanically enhanced soldiers and mages, futuristic hackers and magical elves. It’s a weird combination, but it works. There’s a cool world here worth exploring, enhanced with atmospheric, if unmemorable, visuals and music. Unfortunately, the gameplay and story don’t quite do it justice.
This is an old-style isometric turn-based RPG, and it’s about as simple as they come. Battles are simple, your team versus a host of enemy goons, and consistently satisfying to complete. But battles are also small and take place mostly in linear corridors. With a cover system that appears useless and an accuracy system that rarely makes sense (my characters have missed shots that the system rated as having a 95% chance and above far too often), the tactics rarely amount to anything more than who can hit/stab/shoot/burn the hardest.
The game has a large number of classes, races, etiquettes, weapons, armors, and cyberware to choose from, but in combat, they all play very similarly, and the differences are mostly aesthetic. The variety is great, but it’s too bad that variety never translates into a difference in gameplay. The linear progression, lack of choice or sidequests, and similarity between classes means there is little to no replay value.
The story starts off well. It’s a basic noir-style murder mystery, held up more by the strength of its setting more than its writing, but it’s nonetheless compelling enough to carry the gameplay. It progresses standard enough, with the player following leads, interviewing suspects, battling bloodthirsty gangs, up until a certain point towards the end when the game takes a dramatic turn for the silly, and then an even more dramatic turn for the ludicrous. It remains compelling, but suspension of disbelief is broken and never repaired. You’ll meet a wide cast of characters who are for the most part likable and interesting, but lack depth, which is representative of the game’s overall problem.
It lacks depth. It has a cool setting, but that’s never satisfyingly explored. It’s a got large variety of classes and equipment, but which mostly play the same. It has decent gameplay, but it’s overly simple and linear.
But the game is also cheap, and worth a purchase if you can find it one sale. If you’re a fan of the Shadowrun universe or simple tactical RPG games, you’ll likely enjoy this. If you’re looking for something with more depth, that’s more open, with a better storyline, you should look elsewhere and be willing to spend more.
The most damning criticism of all is that you can buy the standalone DLC, Shadowrun: Dragonfall, which is an enormous improvement over this game in every facet, for the same price. There is no reason to recommend Returns over the far superior Dragonfall, which is more open, has a better storyline and characters, and better tactical combat. The developers improved so many things in Dragonfall they made Returns obsolete.

There's a lot to like about this game. The fantasy meets cyberpunk setting and lore are fantastic. The tactical style combat similar to Fallout 1+2 and Wasteland 2 is also quite enjoyable. The ability to recruit a team from a wide variety of runners is a nice feature. But despite all these the game still feels disappointing. The game is incredibly linear and is quite short especially when you compare it to similar games and towards the end boredom set in and i struggled to stay interested.
Good Points:
- Great setting with some beautifully animated background. The lore is interesting as well.
- Tactical combat is a pretty decent
- Being able to contract party members gives you a lot of options to tweak your team to meet the tactical requirement for each level.
Bad points:
- The game is extremely linear which is a bit jarring considering these types of games tend to be more open.
-Pretty short game.
- The last couple of hours things start to feel a bit repetitive especially when the game introduces a really annoying new type of enemy.
Overall this is ok. Although the linearity lets it down massively theres still enough here to save it from being a bad game which is why i've leaned more towards recommending it. I wanted to love this game so badly. The SNES classic is still, in my opinion, one of the greatest video games of all time. I think the biggest failing of this version is that it didn't look to the SNES (or even the Genesis) game for gameplay.
This game has a decent story and interesting characters, but if this is all I want, I'll read a book. Where this game really falls down is the game play. I have no idea why turn based combat was opted in place of the real time SNES style combat, maybe because XCOM made it 'flavour of the month'?
However, I can deal with the combat, it's okay. The thing that really lets this game down is that each environment just sits in a linear series of bubbles. The SNES and Genesis progenitors were much more open world, and as such, much more interesting, immersive and engaging. I'm very disappointed that there's no real 'world' to this game, just a series of XCOM-esque highly contained areas, that serve no real purpose outside of combat.
If you like XCOM you might enjoy this (though I think XCOM is the better game). But if you're looking to re-live the classic 16 bit Shadowrun games - just go play those instead. They might not have the fancy graphics but they have a world of atmosphere thats sorely missing here.

This game is so addicting.
Imagine the gameplay style similar to the game known as Kingdoms without the hastle.
You are a dwarf trying to build up his city to get stronger and stronger.
Like most RPGs there are XP progression and gear progression.
When you level up your can add a stat point and use a skill point which can only be done at a firepit.
As for exploring the mechanic involves getting food from towns/areas then using that food to unlock parts of the map (Based on distance away from the city you are building). The further the town the more it costs (kind of obvious). Once you unlock that part of the map it is free to travel to the nodes at any time. (HIgher campfires mean your search area gets bigger so it becomes more efficient to use food).
As for the fighting. So far i've only played a melee character where i am using a shield and a melee weapon. Cutting down enemies left and center. Though the games difficulty increases dramatically as the more damage you take the less you can sustain. If you take no major injury (text on screen) it means you can regenerate your health to perfect health.
Meaning Magic attacks even though brutal damage it doesn't cause permanent damage.
Bosses are just named enemies with a higher health pool, hits harder and has a few unique tactics.
As for building up your town. After you explore for abit you'll see dwarves trapped in cages (Only release them after you've dispatched all the enemies) these can be used to automatically gather resources from completed zones. Each dwarf is 1 resource per 5 seconds. Until that resource pool has been used up.
Not going to say more about the game as I'd like you to experience the game yourself. I'd recommend this game for it's game mechanics even though the combat is kind clunky to get your head around at the start.

Where to begin?
Let’s start with that this is a Massively Multiplayer Online (Action) Role Playing Game that grabs you instantly with over the top, limb scattering, screen shaking abilities that decimate hordes of monstrous humanoids, ogres, demons, undead, fluffy rabbits, crocodiles and… of course, spiders!
Then if that’s not a full game in itself, it features an incredible diversity of skills that players can pick and choose from, not a simple ‘Fireball or Lightning’ choice that most games; in both of these genres pride themselves on, but a choice of ANY skill (About 16 Primary for each class – along with a minimum of 3 separate variations on each skill, with the additional secondary class choices as well! I think it’ll take a bit longer than I’ve been playing to get my head around that.)
Now, who needs more? We do apparently! They go and throw along an almost infinite number of possibilities for loot: completely randomized, no two weapons are the same in this game, which means that we aren’t all running around with the ‘War glaives of Azinoth’ or of course more recently the ‘Ashbringer’, we get to make our characters unique!
Plus, Housing – Crafting – Enhancement – Enchantment – The Compendium (Not enough hours in the day for this one! And I love it.) – PVP – Group Survival mode – Dungeons – Public Events – One of the most responsive community teams ever - Enough story and side quests to entertain you for at least 25 hours (At the time of this review* and I personally don’t think I’m even half way through the main quest line!)
But as always – Nothing’s perfect right? – I agree, and that is why I cannot review this game as anything other than amazing! I have never played a game that hasn’t had some rough edges, or some bugs, let alone a MMORPG – I remember Lord of the Rings Online at release, I managed to play maybe 2 out of 7 days each week because of game breaking issues for the first few months.
My point is, though it has its flaws, it is a perfectly enjoyable game, that I was immersed in as soon as I watched the trailer, let alone when I switched it on for the first time.
If you want an optimised and rigid, game/MMO where your opinion is drowned out amongst everything that is the p2w business model – join one of the many that’s focussed solely on profit and not a work of love NOT Guardians of Ember!
BUT if you want to enjoy a fast paced, community focussed MMO, that’s just that little bit original – chuck £11 over to Runewaker Entertainment /Insel games and lose a few weeks of your life!!
Not a perfectly constructed review, just passionate! Enjoy the game everyone, and a huge thanks to everyone at Runewaker for my new favourite pastime.

A fantastic sequel to thief gold which improved upon its predecessor with better level design and made it less about combat and more about stealth.
The most interesting part I found in this game, like in thief 1, the increase in difficulty gives you more objectives to do and restriction on killing or being detected in a few missions which will test your skills.
And although the graphic didn’t age well, this can be remedied somehow with the fan made patch for better textures and compatibility with modern systems (check the PCGAMINGWIKI site for more info).
In addition, you can add the Shadows of the metal age mod which will add great fan made levels.
The only problems I had with the game is the final level design which in my taste was too long, too labyrinthian and had too many highly religious steam powered killer robots.
Also, the controls for jumping and climbing stuff are not OK but dodgy – when you think you should be able to grab a ledge while jumping or try to go down ropes or ladder, it will not always register as such and you would likely fall to your death or loss some life.
But other than those things, it's an excellent game, an excellent thief game (where you can jump) and I really suggest to those who like proper stealth games with good story to try to get past the graphics and play thief gold and its sequel thief 2 the metal age.

After playing the game to the end, I thought I would put in my 2 pence and give my personal opinions of Batman: Arkham Knight.
Story: As for the storyline, Scarecrow basically causes Gotham to be evacuated due to threatening to disperse a toxic fear gas that will cause everyone to become overwhelmed with fear and start killing each other. This, if you’ve played any other Batman game, means Gotham is only home to the sort of people Batman likes hitting in the face. As the game progresses, you run into old characters and enemies, such as Two-Face, Penguin, Mr Freeze, Riddler etc. All of which you will eventually hunt down as side missions while slowly working your way to Scarecrow. I won’t go too much into the story if you don’t know already, but I thought it to be very enjoyable and the impact of Scarecrow’s fear toxin on Batman makes for a very interesting story.
Gameplay: The gameplay is very similar to all the other Batman games made by the same company. Multiple gadgets, massive street brawls, and the Batmobile. The gadgets, unfortunately, don’t really differ much from previous games, apart from the disrupter gun which can disable guns/turrets etc. and the voice emulator to open voice activated doors. The fighting revolves around knowing what button to click when someone comes at you swinging while mashing the punch button. And now for the Batmobile. Now many reviews regard the Batmobile as an annoyance and would rather it not be there. Now I fully agree that sometimes the game forces you into scenarios that make you use the Batmobile, but I saw it as a welcome change with puzzles requiring you use it and tank battles which are, at least in my opinion, very enjoyable.
AI: The AI is very similar to other Batman games. Not revolutionary, but good enough for them to be a welcome addition to the game, instead of a hindrance. For example, when you are in predator mode, the AI will listen out for you. If they see you grapple up to a ledge, they will shoot up at you. If they see you in a vent under the floor, they’ll chuck a grenade under the floor and blow you up (or just the vent depending if you got out the way in time). Like I said, not really any different to previous games. In this game there are more variant enemies though. Normal soldiers/thugs, ninja samurai, soldiers invisible to your detective vision, big guys with miniguns. All sorts. They make for very enjoyable brawls.
Graphics/Issues: Now the graphics, for me at least, they were perfect. I will list my PC spec at the end of this review but I was getting over 60FPS with everything maxed out. Now from reading reviews, I think I was lucky as others have stuttering and crashes that made the game unplayable for them. In my nearly 20 hour play through, I only had 1 crash to desktop and everything else ran smoothly. I’m not saying the issues don’t exist however, so please be ready to refund if things don’t go your way.
Overall: Just to make everyone aware, I purchased this game from a 3rd party website and only paid £4.99 for the game with all DLC, and for that I was extremely pleased. The story is good, the gameplay, if you like it like me, is fantastic, and the Batmobile isn’t as bad as everybody says. I think it was unfortunate this game launched in the state it did. If they would’ve delayed the release for another month to sort things out, it would be a brilliant finish to the series, but they were too concerned with pleasing shareholders and not consumers. I think it’s lucky this is the last game, as I don’t think another would’ve sold well after the mess that was Arkham Knight’s release. To conclude, the game is very enjoyable now it’s been patched (for the most part) and if you want to play the end to the series, you should definitely get it.

After finishing the campaign and all of the storyline DLC, my overall view of Resident Evil Revelations 2 is that it is good but far from great. Realistically, it's a game that didn't need to made and exists purely so Capcom can profit off of the RE name between major releases.
The story is actually pretty good (if you get the best ending, otherwise it's anti-climatic) and really the only thing that kept me going.  Each episode plays similarly which got boring fast. The only real difference between episodes are the environments which were sometimes interesting, other times dull. The more interesting ones had a very scary feel to them and had you worrying about what could be around the next corner. The gun play felt good but enemy diversity is low and enemy design is strange. Most enemies didn't look like something from the RE universe.
The skill upgrade system is a cool idea but most of the skills are useless. There's a lot of unlockables which adds replayability but the game isn't really enjoyable enough for me to want to replay. The game is very linear and everything in between the story's progression sequences feels like a pointless timesink to get to the next storylind progression. That's not the way I want to feel playing a Resident Evil game.
If you can get the game on sale and are dying to play an RE game since you've already played everything else, I'd say check it out but I'd be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if I paid full price for this. Especially the "Little Miss" DLC which was a total joke.

The main mechanic that makes Shadowverse stand out from Hearthstone is 'Evolve.'  This gives a follower +2/+2 and allows them to attack an opposing follower immediately.  Some cards even have effects that activate when they are evolved.  In addition to drawing an extra card, the second turn player will also get one more opportunity to evolve.  First player gets to evolve twice, second player can evolve three times.
Right now the meta game is fairly balanced.  It seems like all the classes have viable decks.  If you care about being super competitive the best class for aggro is bloodcraft.  That would be the best/cheapest deck to try and rank up if that's all you care about.

The last part of the Arkham Saga.
Probably the darkest of them all.
The whole athmosphere got a lot more sinister, than it's predecessors.
First, I was sceptical, because I felt rather unfamiliar, and Arkham City, Origins or Asylum had a diffrent athmosphere,
but when the story in it continues, it matches perfectly.
From the gameplay side I have nothing to complain.
The freeflow combat system is in here again, and makes a solid job, even though I had the feeling, that it worked a little bit unfinished, than in City, or Origins.
I had more situations, when my combos broke, than in Arkham City, but maybe I was just out of practice.
From the graphic view, you get all the visual aspect, you expect from a Batman Game.
The textures are sharp, the explosions and details are amazing, and the character models are breathtakingly realistic.
I loved the small detail's like the raindrops landing on your cape, or the facial animations.
The Batmobile felt a little out of place.
Of course it was essential to the storyline, but still; a Batmobile, which transforms into a tank, destorying Drones, with rockets and machine guns, felt a little awkward at the first, but I wasn't so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of from it, like other fans of the game.
Also I can't believe, that thugs survive a car crash with that thing, so it killed the immersion a little bit.
But you can cope that fact, when you play through the storyline.
The voice acting in it is on top; especially John Noble as Scarecrow.
His soothing voice, brought goosebumps on my skin.
But also Kevin Conroy, as well as Troy Baker as the Arkham Knight and of course Mark Hamill as the Joker;
they just made a fantastic job, and I really enjoyed that voice acting.
From the open world aspect, you get 3 Islands, all are accessible from the start,
but when you want to drive with your Batmobile through them, you have to play through the storyline first.
The side missions are fun to play, but the riddler challenges get's the lion's share in it.
There are a tedious lot of them, so they eat the most of your playing time.
All in all it is a deserving end for the Dark Knight, but the ending leaves questions open, so maybe we get another Arkham title soon.
I would hope so.

Super Hexagon is a game by Terry Cavanagh were you play as a small triangle rotating around a hexagon. That's all there is to it and by now you have guessed that this is very minimalistic game. The goal of the game is to survive for as long as possible as walls and shapes approach from all around. This sounds simple and easy enough you start up the first level and are met by pulsating chiptune music and a few seconds later a resounding "Game Over". Super Hexagon is a difficult twitch based game and you will fail to survive the goal of 60 seconds many many times. Avail ye not however as the game is the modicum of fairness. With practice and memorization you'll learn all the patterns it throws at you and your times will increase. By surviving longer and longer you start to enter into a kind of zone were everything fades away except the game and you eventually get highscores in the high 200s! Since on avarage one round doesn't last more than a minute, this game is a great timekiller, and with enough practice can become a way to reach a cathartic state of focus and relaxation. S'probably one of my favorite games.

Teleglitch is an intense game. It packs the story and thrills/chills of Doom 3 and the top down insanity of Smash TV into a visually retro title that is as relentless as it is fun. The fact that they have titled this update the Die More Edition is telling. You will die.... a lot.
Another great aspect of the game is it's nod to roguelikes. While there is a linear progression to the story, each time you play the various levels will be altered. Unlike some of the fps horror games like Doom3, this means that surprises will actually surprise you after your first couple plays.
Don't let the blocky graphics fool you however, the game comes complete with incredible kinetic effects (mainly through the firing of your various weapons) and an intensely tight control system. It also has a beautifully simple crafting system that gives just a little bit more to that feeling of hopelessness while you die, and die again.

A really good time!  I've obviously put quite a few hours into this game, although the lack of a save+quit feature means that I spent only 50 hours
playing the game, and the other 40 hours were spent in the pause menu, so I didn't lose progress when I had to stop mid-game.
Lots of interesting enemies, abilities, and items.  The difficulty curve is quite steep at first, but once you've died a dozen times or so, you'll have unlocked a few more characters, and some useful items.  The 'story', as told via the Monster Logs you collect from enemies, is straightforward and simplistic, but the world-building/detail about the monsters and their lives is nice.  The item log is also pretty fun, since all the items are cargo, scattered when your ship crashes, and come with little descriptions detailing their sender, recipient, and generally a 'letter' accompanying them.
Very much worth the $10, and it seems to go on sale fairly regularly if that's still too much.  Good for filling a spare 20-60 minutes, very replayable.
One issue with the multiplayer is (allegedly, I haven't tried it much/only played local) fairly poorly implemented when it comes to game creation.  No server lists, so you either need to have friends who own it, or organise a game in the steam forum.  The actual multiplayer gameplay is very fun, since you can get some good synergy between characters that you just can't have playing solo.

The first thing that came to my mind when I saw Zeno Clash 2 on Steam was;
"I definitely have to get this game."
Now, I have played the first Zeno Clash, and the second. I have completed both and there's quite a bit of things to say about both of them.
The vivid, quirky design of landscape, buildings, characters and items/weapons is present in both games, and it's truly something refreshing that you don't actually see in every game out there.
The storyline, too -- is connected. The two are connected, so I suggest you play Zeno Clash before picking up on Zeno Clash 2, as you most likely won't understand the story behind Ghat's 'family' and what happened to it in the events of the original.
Now, onto the mechanics themselves. The game is a first-person brawler, and it's a bit easier than the original. (At least as I remember it, I've played it ages ago. Literally!) The mechanics of the brawling is actually great. Rarely ever will you run into a bug, and the new tools of the trade (Grenades, Chain, as I like to call it the Sun/Moon-strike gauntlet and the Golem Link are all amazing tools that are (later on) at your disposal. The game is very responsive and plays out well, the punches connect when they need to connect, and the special moves that you learn how to use in the tutorial or later on come to play when you fight a bit more advanced enemies.
Onto the world;
The world of Zenozoik is truly amazing. It's a 'civilization' between barbarism and chiefdom as described by one of the game characters you will (later on) absolutely love and root for. The locations! They're absolutely amazing, quirky and detailed just how they were in the first Zeno Clash. Now, for a fan -- this is not a bad thing! This is absolutely amazing as it has freshened up my memory on the world itself, especially the 'city' of Halstedom.
Now, if you're familiar with the game you'll notice a lot of old characters appearing, such as Rimat, Father-Mother, Pott and others. And they're spanking new amazing in the second edition. Also, guess who you'll encounter as well? Chneero! That's right! You'll meet Chneero, the one-legged Corwid! And you will love it.
The game sparkles with detail, and it's absolutely stunning. It has taken my breath a few times when I was watching the horizon over Zenozoik. Why? Well, you'll notice the level design -- which is actually original, and the character/monster designs that you haven't seen anywhere else, really.
Zeno Clash 2 blooms with originality and is truly an under-rated and under-appreciated title on Steam.
Worth the money? Definitely worth even more.

Extremely BAD game. Avoid at all costs. The only thing that kinda works in this game is running and even that feels horribly slow paced.
Things that are completely broken (by design):
Jumping and climbing: The game is full of these and I have never ever seen worse climbing. Far, far superior versions can be
seen for example in games like Saboteur, Assassin's Creed, Tomb Raider.
Combat: Even though combat is rare as most of the time you are meant to run past the opponents you still have to fight them some times. It's all just so unbelievably bad that I have no words to express it. IF you play this game, play it on easy. Difficulty only applies to combat and the combat system has nothing to offer to this game (except for grief).
Level design: Supposedly you are a good runner which means your character should probably know the city pretty well but frankly the character is completely clueless. Sure, there is a 'hint' button that shows in what direction you should go but in many cases its' just the general direction ignoring all obstacles. Also a lot of times you have to *guess* if you can make a jump or not. More often than not you can't which brings you to last autosave which probably was pretty far back.
Field of view: Horrid. 70 degrees maybe? In any event whatever you are doing you can't see anything. If you are hanging from a pipe or something all you can see is the damn object you are holding on to.
Enemies: They know where you are at all times and many times they keep firing at you even though they have no line of sight. They won't hit you but they know in what direction to shoot. Also, when arriving to new locations the enemies will be shooting at you long before even you know where you are. The police will turn from 'it's a nice day' to 'shoot to kill' mode in about 0.07 seconds.
Any good things? Fresh concept I suppose and the graphics are nice. Well, except that the game uses FAR too much white.
Overalll assessment: There should be no reason whatsoever for anyone to ever buy this game. Even for 50 cents the game would have nothing good to offer. Seriously.

My very first review of a Steam game, so please forgive me if i forgot to mention something. Also this is a pretty long review so ignore it if you dont like reading too much. Here are my Pros and Cons:
Pros:
-Insanely fun and addictive gameplay.
-Zed Time (short slow motion period), makes the game so much better when you see all that gore in its splendour.
-Different perks with different guns allowing you to have an overall team that can fill the weaknesses of each individual perk with the strengths of another.
-Zeds getting gradually stronger every wave, allowing you to get powerful items to fight them, climaxing in a boss battle worth your time and money.
-2 Bosses, each with individual strenghts and weaknesses that require a lot of teamplay and tactical preparation to defeat.
-25 levels on each perk, with 2 options to improve your current perk being unlocked every 5 levels.
-Being able to switch from one perk to another and configure your perks skills between waves, so that you dont start crying when someone from your team has to leave and ruins your team comp.
-Good music that will put you in the mood for some brutal action.
-Carefully designed official and community maps offering unique opportunities.
-Different difficulties for new players to get the hang of the game and for hardcore veterans to satisfy their thirst for blood and dismemberment.
-Different types of Zeds, each with different skills, strengths and weaknesses.
-Many characters to choose from, each with his/her own jokes, remarks and battlecries. They can also be customised from top to bottom.
-Active developer team and community, offering a variety of new content to keep you interested.
-Fun boss and player character chatter, making this game less horror and more fun.
-On higher difficulties some zeds have special attacks and powers, making the game much more challanging and volatile.
-Great AI, very flexible, the zeds often try to outnumber you or sneak up behind and make your job harder, and they also try to find weaknesses in your position or comp and take advantage of them, sometimes succeeding and exterminating your team.
-You can browse community servers or just let the game search for a server automatically based on your preferences. Also works while in a lobby.
Cons:
-After a while it becomes repetitive.
-Not as many guns in the game for now (i think 5-6 for each perk), adding to the repetitiveness until it becomes sort of a norm or monotony.
-Leveling up your perks takes a while, and it may be rewarding at the end when you get to enjoy them but until then you're stuck killing on community made perk training maps or normal ones.
-Some perks are unbalanced.
As you can see this game has a lot of good and a little bad, which can be improved and most likely will. Overall a great game. If you took the time reading this you should definitely buy it right now,

I bought this game fairly early in development, when the current update was adding the Volter Manor map. Early on this game was in a pretty rough state with updates being months apart for small amounts of content being added. However, as of the last few updates, Tripwire Interactive has been on point with listening to the community and for the most part, fixing all of the issues that tainted this otherwise amazing game.
This game is a great example of a sequel taking the formula of the original game and improving on it to better the experience. Compared to the first game, the overal pacing of the game is much faster. Also instead of 7 perks that have scaling bonuses across 6 levels, we now have 10 perks with 2 choosable skills every 5 levels spread across 25 levels total. There are now two alternating bosses (50/50 chance) with a possible third one on the way.
Some Pros-
The new classes are fun to play as well as the returning ones(other than Firebug lol)
The official maps are very well optimised
Just like KF1, there is an active custom map community
The weapons and ZED time animations are gorgeous
Some Cons-
Cosmetics no longer come in packs and must be either found via random drop, opened from a case/crate(USB flash drive in game), or bought from the Steam Market
Official maps are generally much smaller than KF1 maps, though TWI has said they may be adding larger ones
The Trader Pod doesn't shut up between waves
Overall I think if you liked the first game and don't mind it being faster paced, this game is a sure buy.

X-Com: Enemy Unknown is an excellent tactical/strategy game by 2K Games. The basic story surrounds the idea that aliens are invading earth and you are the last, best defense. A spiritual re-imagining of a classic, X-Com takes squad-based combat and mixes it with resource management. While in the base view, you play the role of the Base Commander that must manage research, base construction, and troops. When aliens attack, the game switches to an excellent turn-based combat mode.
Both the base management and the combat are excellent and offer enough challenge for even the hardest core strategist. The expansion X-Com: Enemy Within deepens the original game by adding genetic modification, Mec’s, and another opposing faction. The highlight of these new additions is easily the Mec’s, which made me smile for an hour the first time I deployed one of these monsters.
X-Com: Enemy Unknown is a wonderful game that is well worth a purchase and I recommend it completely.

Preview (Early Release) This newest game in this sug-category of sidescrolling rpg/strategy games is shaping up to be something out of the ordinary - even this early in development it's becoming clear that this is a passion project and I have seldom (if ever) enjoyed an early release this much. The game is a well balanced mix of exploration, rpg, strategy, citybuilding and crafting. This game however doesn't fall into the trap of oversimplifying combat - which while seeming deceptively simple actually has a fair amount strategy and complexities below the simplistic surface and  well demand more of you than you would imagine from a game of this type - but don't be fooled on higher difficulties it has enough challenge to make you rage. It is a ton of fun to build/improve your colony through adventures, rescues and crafting and while many of the features are still being implemented/completed  its easy to see where the game is going and I suspect i'll end up doing  a lot of complete playthroughs - this is the kind of game you can enjoy over and over. This has easily been my favorite early release in 2017 - Hell I'd go as far as saying this game is my personal favorite of 2017. The game grabs you and before you know it hours has passed and sure they have a ways to go before this game is done but these devs are as welcoming and appreciative of feedback as any I have ever seen. I wholeheartedly recommend you join their discord if you have ANY questions and/or feedback. If you have enjoyed games like Kingdoms, Era, Starbound etc - then you will easily fall in love this game. This is definitely a game and developer worth supporting and were I to rate it I'd have to give them a 9.5 / 10.

Improves on the first one mechnically in every way, lots of refinement on a solid foundation. Character models and textures still not great, but world building and design still top notch. Negative is lack of closure and sudden ending which leaves a lot to be desired, see this as the second act in a trilogy but the third act is way different mechnically and stylistically to the first two.

This game i a great homage to diablo (yes, the first one).
But don't get it wrong - it's not a remake in style of a popup book, it differs some more.
The greatest issue at starting i had was that you only can follow the „path” through the dungeon, while the monsters can roam free. I got used to it fast and had lots of fun with the game.
Unlike in other games you dont have equipment in traditional sense here. You only have lifepoints, mana and cards.
The cards can be spells or can be equipment. If you cast spells, your mana is consumed and you have to refill it with potions, wells, regenerating amulets (nothing new here). If you choose to wear some of the equipmentcards, a portion of your mana gets „locked”. This mana is required to wear the equipment and can't be used for casting spells any more.
This leaves you with  some place for tinkering with your equipment and spells (if you upgrade your equip, it will consume more mana).
Another nice part of the game shows up after the first tutorial. Unlike most games of this type, you can choose how long you want to play for progress in one session. You have to get down into the dungeon to a specific depth to reach a boss. You can choose how big your journey will be from small to really big - 10 minutes to an hour. Depending on your choice the dungeonfloors will get bigger or smaller and your progress will be more or less.
The enemies differ quite a bit and require slightly different tactics to defeat them - especially the bosses.
In deeper floors it can get a little bit annoying / crowded. (Number of enemies can escalate quickly).
<<<<<<<<<<<<<< Storytime >>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
It was a day like any other, as i wandered deep into the dungeons, entering a room suppressing a yawn.
With a broad grin i greated my old friend Mr Gargoyle. „Hi there, what's up? Wanna chill a few minutes?“
I casually walked in, ready to pat Mr Gargoyle gently on his shoulders with my mace of frosting and shaking his hand with my axe of flames.
A few steps in, i noticed another visitor. Startled i looked at him, sighing „drat, this guy again”. Louder greating him „Oh, hello, Mr Priestboss”. With a dark and somehow chilly voice he answered nonchalantly „ah, great you could make it, Mr Warrior. We just wanted to invite you to our party. Please, .... take a seat.”
„Thanks alot. I will. Just have to greet Mr Gargoyle properly.”
I dashed as fast as i could - meaning walking speed - over to Mr Gargoyle and started smashing my club at his read. He shrug if off with a damp thud and a slight crack in his grey and stony skin.
„How impolite,“ roared Mr Priestboss, „you even did not let me finish my introduction,“ he continued slightly agitated.
„Do you know my friend over there?” He was pointing to another corner of the room and waved his friend over. “May i introduce? Mr Other-Priestboss.”
At that time, i was whacking the second time at Mr Gargoyles Skull. THUDDDD.
„Oh, and we brought some other friends....“ i heard him thundering across the room.
Turning my head i saw him and Mr Other-Priestboss chanting. Both of them conjuring some Bodyguards (as we all know the law of the adventurers prohibits attacking bosses while they conjure reinforcements).
Drat.
I was whacking furiously at Mr Gargoyle now. Big chunks of stone flying left and right.
Some hits later i managed to look back at Mr Priestboss and Mr Other-Priestboss, again. Their Bodyguards hat just arrived. They greeted with a slight nod of their head and echoed in a chorus „We.... got.... friends..... too...”
Still  pummeling Mr Gargoyle - or like he is called now Mr Gravel-on-the-Floor i slightly panicked.
Think Mr Warrior, think.
A few seconds later  forming a plan in my mind: First, kill the bodyguards of the bodyguards, then kill the bodyguards, then kill Mr Priestboss, and another go for Mr Other-Priestboss.
Starting with full running speed - walking the same pace as ever- i charged the first bodyguard, which exploded. Having a run, i smashed a second one with my mace, a third with my flaming axe, leaving a blazing trail in the air, melting the snowflakes of the mace.
At that time, i noticed the error i made. I charged into the room, uncovering more of the floor to come. Some of the monsters in front of me, some closing in from behind. I was trapped, for i could not leave the trail in the middle of the room don't get too close to the walls they teach us in explorerschool. Damn that mental imprinting,
No time to turn back!
Swinging my mace and axe in unity, i made a few steps.... and the world exploded.
Some of the bodyguards conjured more of their pals, mages at the other end of the room spitting magic missiles at me.
Bonearchers shooting flaming arrows of doom at me, some spiders - where the hell did they come from? Are they pals of pals, too? - started to freeze the ground i was walking on. With a meteorite from the sky a bunch of imps came crushing down, immidiately starting to set the floor ablaze - a floor can freeze and burn at the same time? .... i never knew from the books at adventurerschool. More spawns of hell were throwing vials of poison at me....
THUDDDDDD. Darkness surrounded me.
A few moments later i came to my senses again. I was lying in one corne of the room inside a flaming fiasko in front of me stalagmites out of ice, behind me the massive boulder a gargoyle propelled at my head.
Poisonous gas everywhere.
The room filled to the brim with Mr Priestboss, Mr Other-Priestboss, their friends, friends of their friends, friends of their friends friends....  and me lying in one corner, sobbing tremendously, whining with soft voice between the sobs.
„All i wanted to do, is chill for a few minutes.”

Look, I dont usually go for this pixel crap, but like the golden rule always proves:
Gameplay>Graphics.
And there is no better example of that than in Regions of Ruin. A pixely little game in which you must go around the lands running amok, grabbing resources wherever you can, saving your peon gatherers and eventually, rebuilding your lost above-ground(???) dwarven kingdom.
Along your travels you will encounter many quest givers, collectibles, puzzles to unlock and chained events.
As you build up your town you can take advantages of the perks from each building (taverns give companions for hire, apothecary lets you craft medkits; blacksmith lets you tear down and recreate better weapons, refinery allows you to smelt ores for better ingots, better craftings, and a library allows for saving your recovered pages to books.
You may be thinking that's a lot. And for a pixel game, it is. Which is why I felt the needed to review this ambitious little gem.

Thanks to the free weekend, my wife and I have given this game a try. Though we have not played that long, we end up buying the deluxe version. This game is far from perfect. I would only recommend this game if you can look beyond its cons.
Pros:
- It is kind of a mix between WoW, D3, and GW2. Mobs get respawned and some are elites like WoW. Gearing and skill design sort of like D3. And the public events and art direction reminds me of GW2.
- Graphically pleasing. Pretty decent customization on characters (very much like GW2).
- Accessible for casual gamers. So far it is pretty easy to read through the stats detail.
- Deluxe version comes with the freedom of reseting skill and stats - which I think that should have been in the base game.
- Deluxe version also comes with a perm mount - which I also think that should have been in the base game.
- More importantly, deluxe version comes with a pet that helps you collecting loots. I think it is very essentia. Extra stash is also a big plusl. I would strongly recommend deluxe version to the least if you want to play this game.
- I get to team up with my wife so the experience is pretty nice. Dungeons come with 3 difficulty levels. We pick the middle ground. Actually, it is pretty challenging!
- Challenging in a sense that we have to observe the boss mechanic. And there is some strategy in the mob aggro.
- Build variety seems interesting. I am spec'ing to a bit of tanking and self-heal. My wife is spec'ing to a lot of dps and a bit of team heal.
- Player's housing is a plus.
- Figuring things out is fun. This game seems to have a bit of depth.
- Oh, jumping is an option (without sound effect though).
Cons:
- My wife and I both have yet to experience a smooth game play. The game play freezes a lot as the frame rate drops regardless of graphic setting. We have played many MMO / ARPG. This is the only game that has that kind of issue. We have contacted support. It is likely due to AMD graphic cards.
- To further elaborate, I have observed consistently huge FPS drop during casting. In town, my FPS could be 70+. But when I pop a shield for my dark knight, FPS drops to below 30 and then goes back up. The end result is the my screen appears to freeze for that moment ... all the time. Even as I set my graphic preference to very low, the frame rate would drop from 120 to 80. That still freezes the screen.
- Movement is kind of slow, even with mount.
- Story is pretty forgetable.
- No voice over.
- I don't usually play with sound on. Some have pointed out that there is no footstep sound. It is kind of odd to have RPG games these days without that.
- Also, there is this constant message on the screen saying that the ability is not ready. That is when you try to fire off an ability before the cooldown finishes. I didn't realize it at first. But when my YouTube viewers pointed that out, the message (large font) can be rather annoying.
- I don't think there is ability queuing like some other ARPG / MMORPG (i.e. firing an ability just before a cool down completion should be fine).
- Primary power and secondary power both share a 1 second cooldown. In short, you can't hold the LMB like other ARPG. Very strange design.

Antichamber is an incredibly mind-bending puzzle game that uses Euclidean geometry (too hard to explain, Google it if you haven't heard of it) to present a huge challenge to the player. There are many secrets to be found, and what you see might not be what is real, such as a dead-end hallway that actually lets you pass through the wall into another room. This game is very confusing. I would highly recommend Antichamber to all fans of the Portal series and anyone who likes indie puzzle games. Be warned: it's confusing, tedious and difficult, but it's fun nonetheless.

The first Thief game was an innovation, a pioneer in the field of stealth games. Its sequel surpassed it masterfully. (Some spoilers ahead.)
In 2000, at the turn of the century, Looking Glass Studios were not looking hot. Despite their massive successes with Thief: The Dark Project and, one year later, System Shock 2, the studio was nearing bankruptcy. They were only kept afloat by Eidos as part of their contract, but their sacrifices, and eventual closure almost immediately following Thief 2's launch, were worth it, as this game can be called their swan song.
The idea behind the game is simple. Instead of killing the enemies you encounter, you're mostly supposed to sneak by them instead, pilfer whatever they're guarding, and make your getaway. The gameplay is almost exactly the same as Thief 1, with some changes I will write about in a few paragraphs.
At the end of the first game, Garrett is warned about the dawn of the Metal Age by the Keepers. As the second game starts, The City is seen in a full industrial revolution, spearheaded by a breakaway faction of the Hammerites, known as the Mechanists. Their leader, Karras, is a gifted inventor, and directs his Friends, as they call each other, to work on new technology to benefit all. At the same time, greenery in The City begins to fade as part of this wave of changes. Garrett will re-enter this world as usual, doing contracts for his 'pals' or just for himself, but becomes pursued by an emergent police force, possessors of Mechanist technology and a zero tolerance policy on crime.
One thing I should mention about Garrett is that he definitely comes across as more fleshed-out. His personality is mostly the same gruff, darkly-humoured realist-cynic, but he takes plenty of opportunities to display it, in the game itself and in cinematics. Speaking of cinematics, they, and really the entire game, are a lot more polished than its predecessor's. Together with a change in theme from darkness and abandoned places to more homely, cozy areas made colder by the sound of metal grinding on metal comes a facelift in texture work and art style, marking Thief 2 as a clear sequel.
This change of technology has brought about a few new toys to play with and plenty of obstacles that stand in Garrett's path to riches. Flares exist as items that can be activated, carried and thrown to help with pitch black areas. Additionally, Garrett's eye can now interface with another new item called a Scouting Orb, which can be thrown like any other item, allowing the player to see through it. Scouting Orbs can even be picked up and re-used!
However, with new toys come new enemies they must be used against, all of them mechanical in nature, ranging from rudimentary cameras called Watchers to patrolling automatons armed with cannons, impervious to simple swords and arrows, and requiring Garrett to think of some other way to eliminate them or sneak by them.
On the graphical front, the game uses the same Dark engine used for Thief 1 and System Shock 2 before it, albeit made to look pretty for the times. Otherwise, it's exactly the same as Thief 1 on all fronts. What Thief 2 has instead of innovation is a gripping story, with some unexpected twists and turns, more human locales to be visited, conversations to be overheard, and mysteries to be discovered. Even the enemy AI has improved visibly from the first game.
To sum up, if you liked Thief 1, you'll love Thief 2. The developers' experience shows, as the game has been improved on all fronts. And if you finish the game and want more, check out Thief 2X, a fan-made expansion released in 2005, or any number of other fan-made maps.

Make sure your computer meets the specs, and that EVERYTHING on your computer is up to date. If you do, you'll have no issues playing this game now. I'm aware of the issues it had, but my computer is just a Google search result for "best PC build for under 700" and it runs flawlessly on my computer. You won't need some $2000 dollar machine to get past it's issues. It's just a drivers problem.
All that aside, this game is fantastic. A little too much emphasis on the new Batmobile mechanic, but they at least made the Batmobile a delight to drive around in and battle in.
Something that you might not be aware of is that this game is very much a horror game. Scarecrow has returned, and it FEELS like a story where Scarecrow is the main villain. Contains genuinely disturbing imagery, and is by far the most adult game in the Arkham franchise.
All of the features you know from the previous game, and the game treats you like you've played an Arkham game before. Everything you know and love about the game has also been enhanced. New counters, new uses for gadgets, new takedowns, new weapon neutralization techniques. Altogether much more strategic choices for e very single situation you're in. Never do you feel like you're limited to doing the same thing over and over (other than the Batmobile battles, which do get somewhat tedious after so many have passed).
Somewhat smaller rogue's gallery than previous games (I think), but does feature a few surprise entries, and enough easter eggs to keep you searching through this game for months.

So let's start this review by criticizing the story-module they offer with the game, since its the only story provided with the game and while yes you can acquire others from the Workshop, you'd expect something more solid, At this time I have about 10 hours I believe put into this game and with that I was able to start a first game, went maybe a quarter to a third of the way thru, than decide to restart with a different character and finish it... all in 10 hours, its very short overall, and the logevity of the game depended solely on the players themselves building new stories, which is not a good idea, since players didn't program the game or get paid for it, their work will most likely not be up to par... typically, but in this case, I am not really sure of the quality of the module provided with the game.
Look at the Deadman's Switch story, effectively it has alot in common with Robert E. Charette Secrets of Power Shadowrun Novel series, you have a Sam Watts, instead of Sam Verner, heck you see one of Verner's buddies in there too, also with one of your runners named Coyote, somehow a connection to Sam Verner, however indirectly this time. Ultimately like that Novel series you are a man (or woman) on a hunt, in the Secrets of Power it was Sam Verner on the hunt for his sister, in here it was your Shadowrunner on the hunt for Sam Watts murderer, and in the end just like with the novel you end up dealing with some creepy spirits and it became the main issue to deal with at the end of the story. Frankly I am shocked nobody else saw how they merely copied various elements from the Secrets of Power novel series and recreated a cheaper story based on such elements but of far more mediocre result and with a far too cliché ending for the genre. So story wise the single module provided is a enormous let down.
Now for the Gameplay, well its not too bad, but felt fairly limited, you have effectively a single Shadowrunner you can buid and equip, those you can hire are pre-made entirely and you can't even modify their gear, shouldn't you be able to buy weapons and stuff and loan it to them or something? It would make sense... rather you are stuck with whatever they want. Also they don't level up along with you, but as the game advance the entire list of potential runners is updated at a few spots in the storyline, also you only have two runners that have any connection to the storyline mostly, those two are involved in it and one of them is only available for a couple of missions, the other is only available after the first is not available anymore, which mean you never truly feel involved with your crew all too much and they are very much expandable assets. Also a problem is the bits of the story in the Matrix, unless you make your char a Decker, or at least update one to be a Decker on the side of anything else you want it, well you are going to have issues, the few spots where you have to deal with the Matrix would have to rely on pre-made chars that you don't have any choices over the build for, which can be a serious issue. They shouldn't have made the Matrix runs a necessity if you only have one custom char and that char might not be a Decker.
Another issue is the game sometimes bugs and those bugs can be dire, at one point I wasn't able to do anything anymore during a fight, I couldn't attack or anything, so I had to close the game and load my auto-save, only happened once, yet its still annoying.

Alright, so. I played this game for the free weekend, and I can say I had a bit of fun with it at first, but as time went on, it just kind of felt like a slog. Instead of boring you with a wall of text, I'll point out The good, the bad, and the ugly of this game. Take what I say with a grain of salt, it could be that the game gets way better later, but I couldn't bring myself to go past the play time I have.

-I enjoy the class variety, multiple classes for each role.

(It consumes the armor) You can hide pieces of your base armor without costume bits if you want to, so much as to run around in your underwear at all times. BUT...
-Breaking down a normal armor item costs 100 Frozen ember, the real money currency of this game.
-EDIT: Forgot to add this point before, but you can't remove your clothes when you're creating your character. If you're gonna let me modify my body, at least let me see what I'm modifying, so I don't get in game and see I've made them into a monstrosity.
-Questing feels pretty generic. Go here, Kill this, Talk to this guy, Go to the dungeon, new town, do it all again, etc.
-Gameplay feels pretty slow paced. (Compared to other aRPGs)
-
-

-
-First hour of the game feels like a slog to get through, and I honestly couldn't.
-Cutscenes are very... weird and there's no voice acting anywhere.
-Need treasure keys to open an additional chest at the end of the dungeon, but you only get them through dailies and... fishing, apparently?
-
-WHY IS EVERYTHING IN THE MARKET SO EXPENSIVE? (Mind you, its mostly all cosmetic, but still?)  If I've already paid for the game, why is things still being locked from me at THIS price?
-For refernce, some costume sets and mounts can get upwards of 30-40 dollars.
-Not only is it expensive, but awkwardly priced. Instead of something being 1400 Frozen ember, so you can get it just by spending 15 dollars, its 1499, forcing you to buy another 10 dollars worth of ember just to get it. (20 dollars total)

Thief 2: The Metal Age is definitely a diamond from its time. The game is heavy with atmosphere and immerses you within minutes. The story is told through cinematic cutscenes but mostly and solely through the gameplay. You take on the role as Garrett, an experienced thief who steals for a living, throughout the story Garrett becomes entangled within the conflict and mysteries of people and factions. The stealth is very well done, every type of terrain emits a different level of loudness whenever you step on it and allows you to think more strategically for every level. You different types of equipment each with their own uses. For example, you have moss arrows that when shot on the ground it creates a soft surface for you to walk on (very useful for marble floors), water arrows to put out torches and provide more darkness, flash bombs to disorient your enemies and knock them out, and so forth. If you are spotted by guards you'll die in three to four hits, so your best chance of survival is staying behind the shadows. Once you get the hang of everything, you will feel like a master thief.

Moving on from gameplay is the characters, some are actually very good with characters like Jade who helps you out at the beginning... however, some of the characters you'll probably just glance over until something happens to them that gets the feels going.

Speaking of weapons... WHY DON'T YOU START THE GAME WITH A BASIC PISTOL?! Seriously, some of the enemies in the game actually have guns which can kill you pretty quickly, and I know its a game about keeping quite and not attracting Zombies but I mean come on, just give us the bloody option.
Another thing that bugs me is that if you want the dodge ability... you'll need to upgrade first which I didn't know as I thought you'd have the ability straight away but nope, you'll need to upgrade for it... which was a pain in the as trying to escape from a massive horde of NightClawers.

Every door I open leads to another possible death trap. Metal grating against metal, scratches echoing across the open cultivated on-base gardens. All it takes is one zombie with a really good ear to come investigate and with it comes a dozen more. All filled with inhuman rage, all hungry. Fitting that my armor plating is constructed of Militech’s ration cannisters hammered together.
This game does not ♥♥♥♥ around. Through each of its 15 stages (10 stages with 5 alternates) it'll force you to scavange as much weaponry and seemingly useless junk as you can without letting your guard down. All it takes is one wrong move and you're dead, back to square one. Strap some tubes to your guns and make them shoot more boolits, drizzle meat and bloody juices over a plastic explosive to create a savory trap. Enjoy a flexible crafting system while also learning why it was a bad idea to convert your weapon without any proper ammo.
This is what it would be like if Quake 1 running on software render mode got together with Hotline Miami and they both wanted to ruin your day over and over again after watching Alien a couple of times. Play smart and be ready for all manner of things that want you dead - from reanimated corpses to giant robot squids with laser weaponry and more. They'll come at you fast and by the dozens.
This is easily the most terrifying game to come out this year. And even if you are sick of roguelikes, you haven't played one that was like this.

Extremely BAD game. Avoid at all costs. The only thing that kinda works in this game is running and even that feels horribly slow paced.
Things that are completely broken (by design):
Jumping and climbing: The game is full of these and I have never ever seen worse climbing. Far, far superior versions can be
seen for example in games like Saboteur, Assassin's Creed, Tomb Raider.
Combat: Even though combat is rare as most of the time you are meant to run past the opponents you still have to fight them some times. It's all just so unbelievably bad that I have no words to express it. IF you play this game, play it on easy. Difficulty only applies to combat and the combat system has nothing to offer to this game (except for grief).
Level design: Supposedly you are a good runner which means your character should probably know the city pretty well but frankly the character is completely clueless. Sure, there is a 'hint' button that shows in what direction you should go but in many cases its' just the general direction ignoring all obstacles. Also a lot of times you have to *guess* if you can make a jump or not. More often than not you can't which brings you to last autosave which probably was pretty far back.
Field of view: Horrid. 70 degrees maybe? In any event whatever you are doing you can't see anything. If you are hanging from a pipe or something all you can see is the damn object you are holding on to.
Enemies: They know where you are at all times and many times they keep firing at you even though they have no line of sight. They won't hit you but they know in what direction to shoot. Also, when arriving to new locations the enemies will be shooting at you long before even you know where you are. The police will turn from 'it's a nice day' to 'shoot to kill' mode in about 0.07 seconds.
Any good things? Fresh concept I suppose and the graphics are nice. Well, except that the game uses FAR too much white.
Overalll assessment: There should be no reason whatsoever for anyone to ever buy this game. Even for 50 cents the game would have nothing good to offer. Seriously.

Brilliant, cruel and very tense. Essentially what you'd get if you put the real-time shooting back into Doom: The Roguelike. Ten randomly generated floors of sci-fi research complex, and a hojillion monsters, zombies, mutants and robots between you and escape. It's very hard, and it's very good, and kinda terrifying until you get a feel for it.
It's a game of resource management, really. You're always low on ammo, enemies are dangerous, healing is scarce and as you get deeper into the complex, enemies become more resistant to low-caliber firearms, meaning you either have to scavenge carefully or use a basic crafting system to bodge together custom weapons.
The art style can be pretty divisive - it's a concious decision to make things as minimalist as possible while still being visually parseable. Whether it achieves that goal is a point of much debate, but I've never had much trouble with it. The excellent audio (everything has its own audio cue) helps cut through the noise, too.
The Die More edition is a general tweaking, tuning and polishing update. There's a few new weapon types, and five of the levels have alternate exits that lead to 'B-side' version of the next level, giving it a little more replay value.
Totally worth it, especially as it's on sale right now.
