E-sports is a sensitive topic, and it was a tricky task for Valve to characterize the people who shape the community belonging to it: the professional gamers, their families, the fans. What I particulary loved about this film was that Valve put souls behind the names on the scoreboard, and it was touching and effective. This film also touches on something crucial to the gaming community: the credibility of E-sports. It's a big deal, it's a risk, and Free to Play show it. The tug-of-war between "real life" and what's on the other side of the screen is a source of tension for professional gamers, and as is said in the film, will only be alleviated with time and with the acceptance of E-sports as another type of team-based play.
As a whole, the film had soul. It was great. It's another start for movies about games, like Indie Game. I don't play DOTA but found the language and visuals to be accessible, and I didn't feel like the film was trying to sell me on DOTA as a game I should play. It was more like DOTA was just this one specific example of a competitive game that serves as a form of escapism to the discomforts of real life and growing up. This could be ANY game. These could be any people. I recommend watching it, if only to gain more insight on the long journey E-sports has to go in order to be accepted into the wider internaitonal community.

Zeno Clash 2 has two things going for it. The story, which starts to reveal truths and secrets about the world at large and had the interesting characters of the golems, and the addition of permanent weaponry which gives you powers that open up tactics and a Metroidvania-esc progression/exploration. Unfortunately, that’s pretty much it.
Nearly everything in this game is done worse. The combat, while having more layers to it, is plodding and uninvolving. The AI is near braindead and instead of the aggressive and quick opponents from the first game we get plodding enemies that tiptoe around you and throw attacks that often have no chance of hitting. The ally AI is somehow worse and good only for distracting mobs. The combat is also less diverse than the original. In the original there were some enemies that were simply too dangerous or untouchable and had to be defeated with weapons and at one point a magic torch you had to relight, adding needed combat variety. In 2, every single enemy is defeated by punching them. Every single one. Even the giant enemy crabs.
The visuals… most of the environments look great, especially that one open field area near the beginning, and the texture work overall is improved. But the character models look awful. I firmly blame the switch to the unreal engine. I really don’t know whose bright idea was it to use an engine that's notoriously bad at rendering flesh and hair for a game that’s primarily hitting fleshy hairy things in the face.
The voice acting is atrocious. The female lead sounds almost exactly like the one the female lead in the first game had that everyone hated; I’m not sure how even non-english speakers could’ve missed that. The world APPEARS to be open world but is actually restrictive and closed in maps, and the continued absence of a jump button highlights this. The music is simplistic and lifeless compared to the first, with quite a few bad remixes of tracks from the first game. And to top everything off the game is designed around Co-op when the first game was single player, and done is a way that makes it feel like they were just jumping on the Co-op fad (which is already started to die off). I shudder to think of how much of the development probably went into this.
I really enjoyed the first game. It didn’t matter if it was short or limited or somewhat ugly, it was an exciting new type of game with a setting that’s more exotic then what you generally find in video games. I can tell they were trying to expand things with the sequel, but I also felt like they were trying to do something that they simply didn’t have the budget, manpower, and experience to do. In the end I was disappointed by a clunky and ugly game with a big empty lifeless world and questionable design across the board. It’s not BAD persay, but it’s a mediocre experience that definitely wasn’t what I expected or wanted from Zeno Clash 2 .
Worth it on a steam sale? I guess. Personally I’m hoping one day that it’ll get a Witcher-esc revamp and rerelease. Though with the death of the publisher who even knows if that’s possible.

no doubt, not even me and my facepunching fetish can deny, that the magnitude of the zeno clash series lies in the strangeness of its world. perfectly realized oddities inasmuch that they’re not even strange, different, yes, but it’s only surprising for a moment. the first zeno clash strived to keep that feeling aback by quickly introducing things and leaving them esoteric. playing zeno clash 2 without the first’s context may feel the same, however, less is introduced through narrative in this game, making it feel more friendly and inviting. in this we gain some things and lose some things. the original zeno clash felt like an exceptional turgid mystery, the clouded world fueled pinings and unsureness; though a player you felt a voyeur. zeno clash 2 doesn’t wish to obscure things. it doesn’t brilliantly hold information back or overload in complexities. it wants the player to take in and understand the strangeness. enjoyment of zenozoik’s surrealism relies on the player’s projections. the sequel is a hell of a game in a traditional sense, but much less of a new age experience.
the stylistic difference doesn’t matter if you want to punch things in the face. animation and contact is more solid in zeno clash 2, which I consider the greatest part of the combat. the fists are even more furious; heavy punches and uppercuts are absolutely brutal. options are still sectioned around light and heavy attacks. heavy punches no longer require an absurd wind up. they're versatile as pokes, as guard breakers, and as finishers. light punches are jabs. left click is left punch, right click is right punch, allowing for a few different combos but losing a touch of natural simplicity. it's an easy concept to pick up on and uppercut kick finishers make alternating punches so worth it. the greatest addition to zeno clash 2 is the special move meter. it fills a bit as you fight and a lot if you get hit. these allow you to perform various wind up attacks and finishers. they add utility to your combat and make you more suited to take on masses of enemies. if the bar is full, you can go beserk. this makes the special and endurance bars infinite - allowing much more attacks than a full bar - but tactically timing special moves goes out the window, for when it times out the lack of special may leave you defenseless.
models, visual effects, and environments are generally stunning, on that note. though I highly doubt eclipsing the potential of the unreal engine, they show off a great sensibility. there is a slight sheen to the models that is reminiscent of bioshock, but in a way that’s less overboard, so it comes off as a great effect. zeno clash 2 is an extremely colorful game that doesn’t rely on cell-shading or a cartoon aesthetic and that is what’s striking at the end. though, it comes at a slight dissatisfaction that the barren areas look the best. canyons, darkened scablands, caves, and a flowered desert have the most cohesion. the city and the coast are accomplished, but the forested areas mar my disappointment. the flora and fauna, though unique, are plain low-res. and on my computer, for no discernable reason, my framerate seriously stuttered through the forests. no other time or area was affected, so I firmly place the blame on the game. enemies and npcs have a bizarre, entitled sensibility that you will only be able to find in zenozoik, and that is still the best visual aspect of zeno clash. at a risk of spoiler, the golem designs in the game continue to impress me as I look back. they’re intense, otherworldly, striking, I plain love them. father-mother is as weird as he is pitiable, your various ‘brothers and sisters’ are so alien, yet recognizable. somehow, this time, even ghat seems more capable of expressing emotion, which is hard to believe.
with that, there’s a price to pay. the dialogue in zeno clash II is generally rubbish. I don’t know how that happened. the dialogue in the first game was fantastic and thoughtfully placed. words weren’t wasted, even the made up ones. things occurred logically, at the same time, a dash of the unpredictable, but the dialogue always sat in accordance to the situation and usually inflecting a caveman’s poetic sensibility. there is none of this in zeno clash II. only the golem is permitted to be well-written, everyone else, in taking background roles, sound like background characters. ghat is strung pathetically by rimat for no good reason at all. he contributes nothing more than wanting to beat people up when problems face his way. although that’s how he acted before, he was considerably more pensive about it. rimat has no clear ambition, besides wanting to help father-mother, except most of the things she does do not seem to accomplish anything. I guess, in the sense of their aimlessness, rimat and ghat string eachother along, but that doesn’t mean anything good. it’s all fueled by the nonsense desire to have sidequests. these give you more things to do and places to go, but they’re not well written or thought out, so level progression seems random, and how the characters justify it doesn’t sit very well. I’m quite certain rimat never had a good line throughout the entire game. at least ghat wanting to punch people is entertaining.
however, though the dialogue is incredibly simple, even lacking, the story is still competent, and near the end, great. does that make sense? somehow, I lean towards: not really. zeno clash II has a habit of presenting things that don’t make sense. it deals with personal satisfaction, it deals with unshakable ideals, it deals with duty over honor, it deals with intellectual rebellion, it deals with living in a rut. most of  this stuff is in the shadows, told over half-meant quips of long lost history. the distance and at the same time casual immediacy of the story surprises. though it cannot be forgiven how bland the dialogue is or how sudden the plot developments come, it still manages to be convincing by the end of the game.
yet, clear as day, plot and dialogue take a backseat in zeno clash II. the game is entirely about exploration. although accepting your first sidequest within city walls gives the game an air of a strange, barren western rpg, it isn’t the case at all. zeno clash II’s open world ends up more like zelda than anything else. there isn’t really anything open about it, the sidequests themselves being entirely linear and missable. it’s only an interconnected overworld. there are, oddly out of place, treasures to find. personal stat upgrades are hidden as totems and offer lukewarm progression. the amount they improve ghat is negligible and it starts to take far too many to see any improvement, yet the effort to giving things to collect is fine. that sentiment rears its ugly head with two other kinds of collectables, butterflies and cubes, that feel forced and relatively pointless. while the elegance of the world is a far shoot from, say, metroid prime, if you enjoy taking in the strangeness of the world, zeno clash II is incredible. you and impossibilities get to journey together. that’s the most important part about playing zeno clash II. experiencing another world that’s an otherworld, while punching people in the face.
if you have no greater goal in life than punching faces, this is a sublime work. there quite frankly is nothing in the beat ‘em up genre that provides such a well-rounded experience. however, entirely, it is just a well-rounded experience. unless you have a particular love for the very strange or, once again, for punching in the face, you might even feel a little bit let-down with zeno clash II. the gameplay is fantastic despite its simplicity. I very much loved the game, so I want to defend it, but I lack the words to do so. it’s a collection of somewhat good things, which might make a great thing, but only to a very weird person.

Antichamber is one of the finest puzzle games I've ever played. It's easily equal in stature with Portal in my mind. The way you learn mechanics is incredibly organic, and there are no artificial barriers to your progress - if you can figure out the final puzzle without completing the rest of the rooms, you progress to the finale. While the ending was rather silly, the rest of the game is joy to play, and the a-ha moments make the experience incredibly gratifying. In addition, the games lasts just about as long as it needs to; there's a really solid base of content here without any filler.

My very first review of a Steam game, so please forgive me if i forgot to mention something. Also this is a pretty long review so ignore it if you dont like reading too much. Here are my Pros and Cons:
Pros:
-Insanely fun and addictive gameplay.
-Zed Time (short slow motion period), makes the game so much better when you see all that gore in its splendour.
-Different perks with different guns allowing you to have an overall team that can fill the weaknesses of each individual perk with the strengths of another.
-Zeds getting gradually stronger every wave, allowing you to get powerful items to fight them, climaxing in a boss battle worth your time and money.
-2 Bosses, each with individual strenghts and weaknesses that require a lot of teamplay and tactical preparation to defeat.
-25 levels on each perk, with 2 options to improve your current perk being unlocked every 5 levels.
-Being able to switch from one perk to another and configure your perks skills between waves, so that you dont start crying when someone from your team has to leave and ruins your team comp.
-Good music that will put you in the mood for some brutal action.
-Carefully designed official and community maps offering unique opportunities.
-Different difficulties for new players to get the hang of the game and for hardcore veterans to satisfy their thirst for blood and dismemberment.
-Different types of Zeds, each with different skills, strengths and weaknesses.
-Many characters to choose from, each with his/her own jokes, remarks and battlecries. They can also be customised from top to bottom.
-Active developer team and community, offering a variety of new content to keep you interested.
-Fun boss and player character chatter, making this game less horror and more fun.
-On higher difficulties some zeds have special attacks and powers, making the game much more challanging and volatile.
-Great AI, very flexible, the zeds often try to outnumber you or sneak up behind and make your job harder, and they also try to find weaknesses in your position or comp and take advantage of them, sometimes succeeding and exterminating your team.
-You can browse community servers or just let the game search for a server automatically based on your preferences. Also works while in a lobby.
Cons:
-After a while it becomes repetitive.
-Not as many guns in the game for now (i think 5-6 for each perk), adding to the repetitiveness until it becomes sort of a norm or monotony.
-Leveling up your perks takes a while, and it may be rewarding at the end when you get to enjoy them but until then you're stuck killing on community made perk training maps or normal ones.
-Some perks are unbalanced.
As you can see this game has a lot of good and a little bad, which can be improved and most likely will. Overall a great game. If you took the time reading this you should definitely buy it right now,

I bought this game fairly early in development, when the current update was adding the Volter Manor map. Early on this game was in a pretty rough state with updates being months apart for small amounts of content being added. However, as of the last few updates, Tripwire Interactive has been on point with listening to the community and for the most part, fixing all of the issues that tainted this otherwise amazing game.
This game is a great example of a sequel taking the formula of the original game and improving on it to better the experience. Compared to the first game, the overal pacing of the game is much faster. Also instead of 7 perks that have scaling bonuses across 6 levels, we now have 10 perks with 2 choosable skills every 5 levels spread across 25 levels total. There are now two alternating bosses (50/50 chance) with a possible third one on the way.
Some Pros-
The new classes are fun to play as well as the returning ones(other than Firebug lol)
The official maps are very well optimised
Just like KF1, there is an active custom map community
The weapons and ZED time animations are gorgeous
Some Cons-
Cosmetics no longer come in packs and must be either found via random drop, opened from a case/crate(USB flash drive in game), or bought from the Steam Market
Official maps are generally much smaller than KF1 maps, though TWI has said they may be adding larger ones
The Trader Pod doesn't shut up between waves
Overall I think if you liked the first game and don't mind it being faster paced, this game is a sure buy.

I would love to see more games like this.

Currently have ~250 hours in game.
Pros
* Dual Class System that is simple to understand and allows some choices
* Group or Solo Dungeons (Story and Randomly Generated)
* Isometric MMO - this is a plus for me maybe not for most but I enjoy this
style of game.
* Crafting System with meaningful gear and items
* Talkative GM's and Dev's - They tend to respond on steam and are often in
game.
* None P2W item shop and an in game currency can buy some items off the
shop
* Public Quest System
* In game events - GM's have been doing events seems like every other
weekend for players in game. I have ran into the GM's at some of the events
in game and been able to talk with them after the event.
* Enjoyable game play (until I get the short end of the stick on RNG).
Cons
* Small Dev team - means long time between updates, patches, and bug fixes
often take awhile.
* Numerous Bugs - Some bugs have been in game for awhile now and haven't
been addressed or have been fixed and then show back up in a later patch.
* Server Lag  - Server lag is something that most online games deal with from
time to time and can be fixed by changing to different servers or a different
server architecture (they are currently exploring different options for this).
* Game Engine Optimization - The game engine seems to be poorly optimized
for a large number of actions to be going on at once. I have ran into several
issues with FPS when pulling large amounts of enemies together.
*  Item Shop in Buy 2 Play game - While I do not see this one as a big con since
the items in the shop are purely convenience and the game is often times on
sale it is still a minor complaint of mine.
There are also a few other things about the game that tend to irritate me like the whole stun mechanic in game (every enemy attack regular or special has a chance to stun your character with no diminishing returns which often results in your character becoming stun locked until your HP reaches 0). I have been very vocal about this mechanic and see it as an annoyance and a way to give the game the impression of being difficult. Another thing that I have an issue with is the way the item upgrading works. Many times I have gotten my item up to a +6 enchant and then get -1 on the next 5 or 6 attempts to end up back at +0 or +1. I really wish there was some kind of safety net or some way to more reliably upgrade gear. Some have also expressed concerns with the enchant reroll system and how RNG based it is and from personal experience the RNG in game is terrible (swords rolling +crossbow mastery for example).
I still log into the game almost every day and find my time in game enjoyable. All of the cons that I have listed and the issues that I have with the game can be fixed or addressed later down the road nothing on my list is not correctable. Plus it is very likely that some of the issues will correct themselves over time once we get the next act added and the level cap raised with the next tier of crafting/enchanting mats.
As far as does it make sense to purchase. I'll leave that decision up to you. I will say that I do not regret my purchase and still find the game enjoyable and think that the game still has a ton of potential.﻿

XCOM is an interesting game to play.
It's definitely one of those old school turn based strategy games where you need to go in with a strategy at the beginning or things will be terrible before the end. It's easy to lose countries in the project if you neglect to build satellites in favour of troops and research/tech.
The combat gameplay can be annoying as hell especially when shots where you have an extremely likely chance to hit your squad will fail to, yet others involving flanking shots and hitting through walls with a low chance will work fine, and the aliens will also experience this same weirdness.
The graphics are decent, the mechanics could do with a little more telling if it's to appeal to a more casual audience. The storyline is basic at best and sadly the environments for missions all tend to feature the same places over and over again. It's a good time sink if it can hook you in.

Antichamber is an incredibly mind-bending puzzle game that uses Euclidean geometry (too hard to explain, Google it if you haven't heard of it) to present a huge challenge to the player. There are many secrets to be found, and what you see might not be what is real, such as a dead-end hallway that actually lets you pass through the wall into another room. This game is very confusing. I had trouble understanding some of the puzzles, but thinking through and trying again (and again and again...) is what got me through the game. I would highly recommend Antichamber to all fans of the Portal series and anyone who likes indie puzzle games. Be warned: it's confusing, tedious and difficult, but it's fun nonetheless.

I've never left a review on a game before. But I have been long desperate to find a replacement for my previous addiction, Diablo(s) 2 and 3. Between Blizzard's many poor business practices regarding D3, and their especially poor PC support for the game, I've been wanting an excuse to uninstall it once and for all. And I have found it. This game perfectly recaptures that feeling of the procedural dungeon crawler with plenty of loot and leveling to be had, but with those systems amazingly polished and simplified to the point where it feels greatly satisfying, but doesn't feel like you're managing an Excel spreadsheet to min/max your character. Now, it is still early access, and there are still some missing features and rough edges to sand down, but it feels amazing already. This is a real diamond in the rough and one of the few times where Steam Early Access actually does what it's intended to do. I would easily buy this game at full price but if you can get it on sale, it's an absolute steal.

If you want a turn based combat game that works a lot like the old Fallout 1 & 2 series, but set in the future where there's cyberpunk meets magic, you'll want Shadowrun. The game lets you choose to build your character by sinking points into different categories and skill branches to get better at something (ie, don't play the pre-made stuff, make your own, it's better in every way). You can mix and match, be a generalist, or a hyperspecialist. You can be a support character, the front line, or something in between. The game plays like a RPG, but it's not as deep as some RPG's. Kind of like how Mass Effect would be, if it were an isometric game. You can make choices and follow different dialog trees, but ultimately you will do the same thing at the end.
Warning, the game can be difficult towards the end. It can be frustrating if you're not prepared for lots and lots of combat. This is not a game you talk your way through. No matter what.

Its free weekend, so I decide to give a try. Overall, the game itself is cheap, only $14 in full price. Is it worth the price? maybe. You can get a few hours of fun from it. Is it a MMO I would recommed? no.

The skill system is interesting, and there are a lot of things to explore. It has everything other common MMO games have, like crafting system, instance, etc.
However, here comes the one biggest issue I have with this game: the game is no where near polished. If it is year 2010, I would call it a good game, but we are at 2017 and the game just don't feel like a finished product. The character animation is stuttering, and there are all kind of small issues with mobs on the field. I have encountered weird clicking bugs here and there, and saw goblin half buried in the ground, within only a couple hours of play.

The concept is really original. The only lack that I can think of is the similarities between classes. Yes the spells differs, but I would like to see a bigger difference in gameplay between a mage and a warrior other than having different cards. Maybe introducing some unique passives? Anyway, the game is great!

A fantastic stealth game which fans of the genre will still love to this day. If you do not enjoy stealth games, this won't change your mind. Thief 2 is all about staying in the shadows and navigation. Combat is present, but ill advised as you are so pathetically weak that a single guard is likely to end you. What you must do is use a plethora of tools with multiple uses to your advantage in getting through a situation.
Due to its pure focus on stealth, the enemy AI holds up. They'll patrol, they'll linger, they'll get into banter with each other, they may even be hostile with one another depending on your level. Speaking of the levels, they are simply enormous, packed full of secrets, loot, and supplies you may put to use. Monsters from the first game which you had to fight have been all but removed, which takes away plenty of the tedium they presented, along with their cave based, fairly confusing level structure. Every level is distinctly designed and presents their own challenge through getting in, navigating, and getting out.
If you're a fan of stealth based gameplay, Thief 2 is all you've ever wanted.

They switched from Valve's source engine to the Unreal engine, and I have no idea why. It doesn't look any better than the first game, and causes a terrible shadow bug on all AMD cards. Now beyond that annoying bug, I love the visual style and the tribal soundtrack. Very similar to the first game. I can't say I cared for the open-world aspect. Score this one for less than $7 and you'll be happy with the experience.

Quick Summary: Play an anti-hero like a poor man’s Max Payne in a third person shooter with a gritty semi-realistic storyline.  The game appears to have co-op functionality, but I don’t think you can go through the single player campaign with a friend. Also, the game uses Games for Windows Live.
You play the campaign as Kane, a former mercenary indebted to a powerful crime group with international dealings. By indebted, I mean they own you and will kill your family if you don’t pay them back what you owe. The group has tasked Lynch, a low level thug as your new partner, and he’ll be tagging along with you to make sure you behave. Unfortunately Lynch has some serious problems, which add considerably to your own situation.
The game is played as a third person shooter where you can pick up the weapons your fallen enemies drop, and/or request ammo from one of your allies (usually Lynch). There are maybe a dozen guns to choose from but some are noticeably better than others (stronger, more precise).  There’s even a rocket launcher on a few levels to take care of tanks/helicopters. An important distinction is that unlike the Max Payne games, you have a “regenerating health” system instead of a standard health bar. This means if you take damage, you just have to hide for a few seconds and you’ll fully recover. This of course means the game is faster paced and you’re going to be more likely to try daring Rambo style attacks or charge enemy positions.
Pros:
+I mentioned the gritty storyline, and I actually enjoyed it. The “hero” Kane makes all sorts of stupid but believable decisions, and his new partner Lynch is even dumber. There are no “good guys” in this game, as is probably the case among real world criminal thugs.
+This is straightforward action, no puzzle solving or map exploring. You won’t get “lost” while playing this game, which I appreciate when I want to just blast my way through a mediocre game in one afternoon.
Cons:
-The game’s graphics are lackluster for something less than 10 years old, and the gameplay can be kind of clunky. I am told that if you have Windows 10, you will not be able to adequately run this game.
-I mentioned blasting my way through the game in one afternoon, and by that I mean the game is like 5 hours long. Hope you got it for a cheap price because there really isn’t that much replay value.
Overall, I don’t regret playing the game, but I’m glad I got it from a Humble Bundle because there’s nothing about it that’s “awesome.” Not horrible either though.

I've been playing card games for most of my life. Mainly Magic and Hearthstone, but I've dabbled in Eternal and Duelyst and ESL and others. And Shadowverse ticks a lot of the boxes for doing a game right. It's fun, has great variety in classes and strategies, is easy to learn but complex to master, has a great community... but one of the things that REALLY sets it apart is the time and effort the developers have put in to making it a top-shelf experience. The original Zeno Clash actually surprised me on how good it was.
It was overall a clunky mess. The guns--while powerful, were clunky and unwieldy, just like the hand to hand combat initially. But just like the combat, the plot, art, and enviroment deepen immensely with time. Half way through the game, no spoilers, I found out exactly how deep it was.
The story isn't extremely well written...However it is worth weeding through, thorns and all. It's almost deeper than itself, the protogonist, Ghat is justified in his anger but doesn't handle correctly and gives us a cliff to jump right into the plot.
This time however, the attemps to streamline the gameplay serve to it's detriment. The combat got quite the downgrade and turned me off to the core gameplay. The story didn't grab me either, being a "Path to redemption" as I saw it. The Gameplay and the story together make for a rather unappealing engagement, and it lost me just after the first chapter. I cannot say I can reccomend this game.
Now let's talk about the invidual points. Combat's up first. In the original game, you could easily see your reach, your blows felt like they had weight to them and each punch was satisfying. Countering was worth the practice, managing groups of enemies isn't even worth it a quarter of the time. You can just kyte them out, swing one punch to stall one of them. That's not the worst part. Your character has no reach. You literally have to stand chest-to-chest to engage your foes, the effect of your punches feels light, combat isn't worth it.
Plot wise, it's a false call of retribution. For what little I was able to stick through, it was just another half-way written attempt to undo what the first game did in some way. I lost interest the moment I got the synopsis of what I was going to be doing in these first thirty minutes.
The combat along with the plot are what got me to charge on in the first one, but this game's was far worse than the original.

Mirror's Edge is an extremely enjoyable game that provides great freedom to the player in regards to speed.
This game is a first person game where you are able to run as fast as you can to get to point A to point B. And it does not disappoint in doing so. You can climb over many obstacles, gaining momentum as you zip through your mission. Speed matters in this game, and Mirror's Edge does a good job at bringing parkouring to life. You can jump to buildings, climb on pipes, wall run across billboards, and sprint your way to the goal. There is so much you can do in regards to running and the adrenaline you get from it is amazing. There are not a lot of games out there that solely focus on freerunning (InMomentum and the Assassin's Creed series only come to mind to me) but this game harbors a great experience. The story is neat, and you can enjoy some time trials to beat your old times or top others. There are some puzzles in the game that you have to go through, but it's what makes the runner experience just as fun.
There are some issues that I would like to point out. The story is short. I was disappointed when the game had ended to early, and would like it if they added more to the mix. The combat system could have been improved as well. In some instances in the game you would resort to killing your enemies via gun or hand-to-hand combat. The gun mechanics are okay but lack the ability to aim down the sight (but that shouldn't matter since this isn't an first person shooter). The close quarters combat is really clunky with only one animation to combo some punches and a kick to knock your enemy down. Fighting in this game wasn't really satisfying, but it didn't ruin the experience for me. I had more fun sprinting freely through obstacles than punching guys who sometimes are not worth fighting.
I hightly recommend this to those who love freerunning and a fast paced adventure game. Mirror's Edge brings up a nice take to a type of game that has not been touched upon in a while.

Killing Floor 2 is a really good sequel to the first game and it captivates me a lot more than the first game did. It does what the first game did but it improves on some aspects. At least they are improvements to me, and that is why I actually prefer this game over the first one.
"Money, money, money"
The game is a bit faster and more frantic now. Unlike the first game, you now have a sprint button and some of the zeds are also capable of sprinting. This makes the game a bit faster and it also encourages movement. And that was a gripe I had with the first game. Because people had figured out every single mechanic of that game, you would most often that not just stand in one place for the entire map, and that bored the hell out of me.
The shooting feels really, really good. Definitely something they have improved as well but they've also been getting better with it overall as I also enjoyed the shooting in Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm. Combined with the gore system and the heavy soundtrack, it really amounts to hours and hours of fun. And of course there is also the fact that you can cover large portions of the maps with blood and it stays. Simple but effective.
Pathing is better than the first game. In KF1, a lot of rounds would end with there being 1 zed left and you had to go all over the map and find the plod. However, in this game I can count it on one hand when that happened. KF1's pathing bug was never really fixed, and now they've implemented a sort of "teleport mechanic" so when that little bugger is hard to find, instead of you treading all over he'll be teleported to you.
"Dosh! Grab it while you can, lads!"
Like the first game there's also a bunch of community maps. Of course, some is better than others but it keeps it fresh. And thank you to all the map makers putting in the work, and also serving some nostalgia with making old KF1 maps in KF2. We also get 2 bosses now instead of just 1 which is great for shaking it up a bit.
Microtransactions are present as well. Of course this is not a plus. At the time of this review it is only cosmetics, thankfully. Unlike in KF1 where some weapons were paid DLC. Way, way back I think I remember Tripwire saying the learned from that in the first game and it will only be cosmetics for KF2. Emphasis on "think".
It is disappointing that the Martial Arts perk did not make it into the game and was replaced with the Survivalist perk. It seems like there's been a lot of turmoil with the Early Access period for this game. I only played it briefly back then and waited for the full release, so I have not investigated it that much. A lot of people say Tripwire banned a ton of people, and Tripwire said that they had only banned a couple, and Steam moderators had banned the others. But again, it seems like it is claim against claim. Feel free to dig into it yourself, I'd rather just play.
"You're pathetic! Like a bunch of Millwall fans!"
Finding a game through the "quick play"-ish option is a bit buggy but I haven't had any problems with the server browser. The Firebug's Microwave gun also needs a fix as the pushback bugs the hell out of Scrakes.
I would definitely recommend this game. I find it hard to get bored of a shotgun combined with zed-time and heavy metal. There are a few things that needs to be ironed out but it is not things that get in the way of my enjoyment of this game, far from it. Give it some time...
Yep, this game is not bad.  But it need time to get good and all the bad review aren't going to help his progress.
I'll try to be clearer.  The game is a MMO before its a ARPG and most negative critics seem to be based on the fact the game is not Path of Exile or Diablo 3.  The truth is that it was not designed to be like that.  I mean, as all MMO when they start, the content is rather limited, voice acting is mainly absent, minor bugs are present... but if my memories are good... World of Warcraft had his lot of problems when it started too...
But the game shows a lot of promises.  Its beautiful, lightful and great change of pace from the usually very grim ambiance ARPG usually offers.  I feel a bit like in an japanese anime when I play.
But if you wanna give it a try, don't forget the game is a MMO first.  Monsters respawn very fast, map is not random, quests are rather very basic, the story line is in background around all those mini-quests you do to get xp and items.  Crafting, fishing and the likes are present but not very developped for now.
Major bugs that are pointed out by other reviewers seems to be a thing form the past... still have some minor glitches, but nothing that would hamper seriously your game.
Overall, I can only tell you that of you expect to find Diablo 3, Grim Dawn or Path of Exile here you will be very disappointed.  You must like MMO character designs and economy to appreciate this game.  The ARPG feel is almost only present from the isometric view.  Combat pace is much slower than ARPG styles too.  The objective are not to clean the maps ; its impossible as monsters respawn pretty fast.
Tha game has its niche.  Its not for everyone but if the bad critics do not kill it, the game shows an incredible potential.  If I was the designers tho... I would switch right for Free to Play mode because they are not BLIZZARD and do not have their millions of zealots.  MMO and forced fees do not mix well in this era ... Better to focus on pricy cosmetics and stash extensions (that 80% people will forfeit) in exchange of a populous game that will attract real players and fans that will gladly pay for it.

First of all, I want to say I am writing this review not out of nostalgia. I have never played a Thief game before, this was my first encounter with it. I skipped part I because most people said part II was the high point of the series, and improved a lot on the first.
What can I say, even though this game is 17 years old, it still delivered me with an experience I have rarely found in todays games. Its atmosphere is absolutely incredible. This is mostly thanks to exceptional level design. Not a single level felt like it was borrowing from the previous one. For a game with over 35-50 hours of gameplay, that's pretty exceptional. Especially regarding that the levels are filled to the brim with secrets, loot, characters, passageways, etcetera... Remarkable. Garrett is an excellent protagonist, and the game really gives everyone a solid backstory, be it through excellent dialogue or in books/scrolls you find lying around.
The game is not without its negative points though: some parts of the story feel a bit overly weird or convoluted, and the graphics are, even with the HD mod pack, a bit of a hurdle to get over.
But don't let that stop you from playing, what is as I now know, rightfully called a "classic gaming experience". This is a stealth game to which all others owe so much, I can see that now.

This is a fantastic game.  I haven't played the pen and paper (P'n'P) version, but I'm dimly familiar with the lore of it.  I also didn't play the old Super Nintendo game, which I heard was quite good.  All that said, I can definitely say that this game is a lot of fun.
The main campaign included with the game is interesting and does a good job of introducing you to the game's world, without being too obvious for players already familiar with the setting.  The story is decently engaging, and -- thankfully -- doesn't turn completely into a "THE FATE OF THE UNIVERSE IS IN YOUR HANDS, CHOSEN ONE" narrative.  There's a teensy bit of that, but it doesn't get too over-the-top.
My only real complaint was that the Matrix aspects of the main campaign are fairly underdeveloped.  For those not in the know, the Matrix is essentially the in-game version of the internet, where the Decker class really shines.  Deckers are meant to interface with technology and perform various hacking activities, all of which takes place in the Matrix, and which plays like a sub-game where you as the Decker operate almost like a magic user within that world (even though you can only use normal weapons in the real world, a.k.a. "meatspace").  It's a cool concept and decently implemented in the game where you get to use it...but if you're playing as a Decker class character, there's not as much use for your actual decking skills in the main campaign.  This amounts to, in traditional D&D terms, having a thief class with not too many combat skills, and a campaign that only has a few locks to pick or traps to disarm.  It's a minor complaint if you play a combat or casting class, but it's one of the things that really makes Shadowrun more than just "Cyberpunk D&D."
The art design is well done, given the overall thrust.  You can get a pretty good feel of it from the store images and elsewhere online.  Sound is fine, with some nice, atmospheric musical tracks, too.  The guns can sound a little plinky, but I expect that can be modded.
Speaking of modding, I'd say that's the game's main selling point -- or at least it was when last I played (which was probably about a year ago).  The game was designed to support user generated content (UGC), and there are several modules available through the Steam Workshop, as well as -- I believe -- a ton of other assets.
The one caveat I'd offer is that continuing UGC development may have shifted to the Dragonfall Director's Cut standalone game (depending on the development team), but there should still be plenty of stuff available for this game, even if development has moved to the newer game.  And, of course, with the upcoming Hong Kong expansion, development may shift again from Dragonfall to the Hong Kong game.  We'll see where all that goes.
All of that aside, at $15, this game is a steal with solid gameplay and plenty of UGC to explore.

I kind of enjoyed this game, but overall I have to say that it is NOT worth it.
First of all, just to get the game running you need to download Games for Windows Live, which is pretty annoying in itself, but I've heard that some people (namely those on Windows 10) can't run the game at all.  That by itself is enough to make me not really want this game, but I decided to play it anyway.
As for the actual game, it's nothing great.  The gameplay is alright.  It's a mediocre cover based shooter at best.  I only really had trouble with one area of the game.  My biggest complaint about the gameplay is that most of the guns feel the same.  You have pistol, shotgun, automatic weapons, and single shot weapons.  They made several different automatic weapons, but they all handle roughly the same.  The game is also really short.  It only took me about 5 hours to beat, and the replay value is almost nonexistent, which sucks.  It's also annoying how the HUD only shows how much ammo you have for your weapon, not how many bullets are in the magazine.  A lot of minor inconveniences come together to really bring the game down.
Despite how bad the gameplay is, the story is probably what disappointed me the most.  Kane gets busted out of prison and is forced to work with the men who betrayed a while back (you never find out what he did).  One issue that I had with the story was that there was little to no foreshadowing.  Now foreshadowing isn't necessary for a story, but you have no idea what's going to happen until it happens, and then you feel confused because you don't really know why it happened, or if there was any hint to it before.  The story wasn't anything great, but it was the main reason that I played to the end...  and boy did it let me down.  The game lets you choose between 2 endings, both of which leave a bad taste in your mouth.  I won't spoil it if any of you want to see it, but just take it from me it isn't worth it.
Overall, this game just isn't worth your time.  If you want a cover based shooter, there are thousands of better ones, and if you really want to know the story, just look it up.

An incredibly unique experience, Zeno Clash 2 is now one of my favourite games of all time.
The game's design and world is one of the most original you'll ever play in.
Around every corner, you'll catch yourself going "what is that?" or feeling awe-inspired by the environments.
The music is fantastic, accompanying the game's atmosphere perfectly when needed.

During boss fights and such, the game doesn't take you by the hand and tell you how to defeat them, which is great. You need to figure everything out for yourself, and you really are put into the main character's shoes. The game has co-op, although not particularly benefiting from it, it's a welcome feature to a game that is equally fun to explore on your own or with a friend.

Although the tutorial will fill you in on the story, I would advise playing through the first one beforehand to really feel immersed in the world.
I can't recommend this game more, it oozes polish and brilliance. Give it a try!

I was put off at first by this game simply not being Zeno Clash 1, which used a different game engine, more linear environments, and what felt like an entirely separate combat system. I don't personally like the Unreal engine, and feel that there are arguably few games that it works well for. The entire time I played it I could feel the anguish of the designers when something couldn't be realized exactly as they had imagined it, but what they truly gained from the switch was too great to ignore and I imagine was quite a point of conflict for the ACE team because really, for the game they were trying to make, they
Unreal.
It took me a long time before I could appreciate the sheer brilliance of the game as a whole. Gating through upgrade acquisition, skill-ups through exploration, and an insane amount of little details throughout to help the world feel alive. Not necessarily anything new on its face, but the deeper you get into night the clearer things become. The more I played, the more I appreciated the lessons the team took to heart from their first game. Literally every part of the game bleeds thoughtfulness when scrutinized.
This game felt like it was made for
and I am notoriously difficult to please. I'm not dumbly impressed by beautiful vistas or flashy combat, but by the subtleties of fine details and overall execution. I'm not running from one exit to another, I'm standing in a field and observing how each individual part makes up the whole. I'm watching that bird, tethered to the exit, and thinking about how in this world that's how the inhabitants mark their boundaries.
From the other side of the game, I can see that Zeno Clash 1 is a cave painting compared to the masterstroke of its sequel. One is not necessarily better than the other, so much as they each merely exist in entirely different contexts. Zeno Clash 2's story both surprises and delights, which was admittedly an unexpected and welcomed extra when all I really set out to do was live in that uniquely backward-but-forward world for awhile. 8/10.

Zeno Clash 2 retains the same absurd atmosphere and wildly creative art design of the original, but unfortunately that isn't enough to keep the game from being a disappointment. The core hand-to-hand combat that was one of the main draws of the first game returns here with some improved depth, but the overwhelming enemy counts make battles more of a chore than anything and renders the lock-on system mostly useless in larger fights. The AI (both friendly and enemy) seems to be surprisingly incompetent and a noticeable step down from the original.
The game's environments are impressive and fun to admire, but they're also shallow and lack substance. Whereas the first game was purely linear (which in turn led to a more focused, interesting story), the sequel decides to go the open-world route with side-quests scattered about that makes everything feel like a mess. The game places skill totems throughout as some sort of incentive to explore, but it comes across as a poor attempt to mask the overall emptiness of the world.
Zeno Clash 2 is a game that tries to be more ambitious than its predecessor and ultimately fails as a result. Gorgeous to look and a combat system that is quite strong, but compared to the original, there are far too many changes for the worse.
You can run, jump, kick, punch, and run some more. The graphics are great, gameplay is smooth, and you will always come back for more.

I think ive played the game long enough at this point to finally write a proper review. Like most people, I started playing Shadowverse after Hearthstone became a game I wanted to play less and less. I disliked how the game was paced, I was displeased with the lack of viable options for decks (IE: Meta decks) and overall the game just became who could SMOrc faster (going face until they either win or lose).
Thats probably my second favorite thing about Shadowverse, bulding decks that just rely on going face are both viable AND very cheap to craft, making them perfect for free to play players that want to get into the meta quickly BUT they are not the end all be all of decks. Every hero has at least 3 meta decks each and they all play differently.
Playing differently leads into my favorite thing about Shadowverse, there are more than one win conditions. Instead of bulding decks that solely focus on killing the player you can instead build decks around cards that end the game or altering the game in a way where you can win using precise usage of cards. Examples of decks like these (at the time of writing) are Seraph haven (where you babysit an amulet you drop at turn 8, keep it on the board long enough and you win the game), D-Shift Runecraft (Revolves around playing cards to reduce the cost of really high cost cards and then gaining a second turn, killing the opponent in a single turn) and roach forestcraft (this revolves around playing cards to make your roachs gain more and more attack and decimating your opponent). Ultimately, I like that there are many different ways to approach defeating an opponent.
The biggest thing you will notice between Shadowverse and other card games is that they are extremely generous to free to play players. You have many different ways of attaining currency in order to buy packs, just starting the game (as of today) will net you around 30 packs for free just to get you started. Even just recently they had an issue with the latest expansion where a few cards were not working correctly and they had to disable and fix them. To thank the playerbase they gave everyone free packs. When is the last time any other CCG you have played has given free cards for a mistake? On top of that they gave out tons of currency for the new years and frequently offer sales to buy packs cheaper. Overall this game is VERY nice to its players and you dont even need to spend money to get into the meta.
Overall, if you are looking for a fun card game that isnt Magic or Hearthstone then I highly suggest you give this game a try. Putting your feelings for the art aside (I know some dislike the "anime" look) its a very balanced game and can be very fun to play with friends. Couple this with how generous the developers are to players and the community itself its definitely my favorite card game of 2016 and forward.

I grabbed this game on sale thinking that it was a good deal but in fact, any discount won't ever make it any better. I still played it to the end so I will give you a quick review -no spoiler- of why you should not get this game, whatever the price.
The game is a shooter, with some extremely limited squad management involved. You play as an inmate on the run from death row. Now with that in mind, I will start with the qualities of the game:
-It is fairly short and believe me, that's quite the relief.
...and done.Now, that's out of the way, I will list some of its many shortcomings:
-Its a port from the console and it shows. It's not very ugly but it is still pretty bad for a 2007 game. The optimization is non existent and the fps will drop even on a modern mid-range rig.
-The control are truly inadequate and moving around is really frustrating. Commanding the squad is not too hard but there ain't much you can order them anyway.
-Aiming is a royal pain, you always find yourself in a particular angle that prevents you from firing at the enemy. It is so cumbersome that you will find the cover system more effective at protecting the ones you are shooting at.
-The AI is stupid both for your enemies and allies. This makes the game really easy very often, especially in corridors. To compensate for this, you are regularly thrown in arenas where inordinate amounts of bad guys will spawn from all sides. Your teammates will be of very little help. It makes it more irritating than interesting.
-Finally, the scenario is very unoriginal and full of clichés. The English dubbing is only semi-convincing.
In short, better you replay one of your old favorite rather than trying this poor, generic game.

Killing Floor 2 is a really good sequel to the first game and it captivates me a lot more than the first game did. It does what the first game did but it improves on some aspects. At least they are improvements to me, and that is why I actually prefer this game over the first one.
"Money, money, money"
The game is a bit faster and more frantic now. Unlike the first game, you now have a sprint button and some of the zeds are also capable of sprinting. This makes the game a bit faster and it also encourages movement. And that was a gripe I had with the first game. Because people had figured out every single mechanic of that game, you would most often that not just stand in one place for the entire map, and that bored the hell out of me.
The shooting feels really, really good. Definitely something they have improved as well but they've also been getting better with it overall as I also enjoyed the shooting in Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm. Combined with the gore system and the heavy soundtrack, it really amounts to hours and hours of fun. And of course there is also the fact that you can cover large portions of the maps with blood and it stays. Simple but effective.
Pathing is better than the first game. In KF1, a lot of rounds would end with there being 1 zed left and you had to go all over the map and find the plod. However, in this game I can count it on one hand when that happened. KF1's pathing bug was never really fixed, and now they've implemented a sort of "teleport mechanic" so when that little bugger is hard to find, instead of you treading all over he'll be teleported to you.
"Dosh! Grab it while you can, lads!"
Like the first game there's also a bunch of community maps. Of course, some is better than others but it keeps it fresh. And thank you to all the map makers putting in the work, and also serving some nostalgia with making old KF1 maps in KF2. We also get 2 bosses now instead of just 1 which is great for shaking it up a bit.
Microtransactions are present as well. Of course this is not a plus. At the time of this review it is only cosmetics, thankfully. Unlike in KF1 where some weapons were paid DLC. Way, way back I think I remember Tripwire saying the learned from that in the first game and it will only be cosmetics for KF2. Emphasis on "think".
It is disappointing that the Martial Arts perk did not make it into the game and was replaced with the Survivalist perk. It seems like there's been a lot of turmoil with the Early Access period for this game. I only played it briefly back then and waited for the full release, so I have not investigated it that much. A lot of people say Tripwire banned a ton of people, and Tripwire said that they had only banned a couple, and Steam moderators had banned the others. But again, it seems like it is claim against claim. Feel free to dig into it yourself, I'd rather just play.

Wonderful, just wonderful.  Traveler's Tales released yet another LEGO game, what a bore.  Hmm? What's this?  It's based on Marvel Comics?  Hmmm...then this game might have a chance.
Unfortunately, it doesn't. If you have played (most of) the previous LEGO games made by Traveler's Tales, you'll see what I mean.  Every single LEGO game that comes out is the same thing: Break stuff, build stuff, get studs, buy stuff with studs, use specific characters to unlock secret stuff, etc. and the series just gets crappier and crappier. Nothing really changes in the LEGO games, but hey, at least they talk in this one.  The gameplay in LEGO games never change, sure this game is one of the first open-world hub LEGO games, but that doesn't change its gameplay. The puzzles and things you do are still the same silly, unoriginal, ridiculous things  that actually make it feel like LEGO, but not the thing that's in LEGO form, not for one moment in these games can those puzzles and stuff you do be serious and original.
A lot of people say the controls are crappy in this game, but I kind of grew up with PC gaming so I am used to any PC controls no matter how bad.  Yes, the flying and vehicle controls are kind of weird and eventually get annoying, but I don't really care and it doesn't bother me anymore.  By the way, who gives a flying rats crappy behind about mouse control?!  Seriously, it's a LEGO game, they never have mouse control, deal with it you freakin' idiots!
The story is original, I'll give it that, but terrible. The humor is weak and there's too much of it. And some of the story doesn't even make any sense, for instance, Doctor Octopus and Agent Coulson cleaning up the Daily Bugle, seriously?  I know this game's audience was heavily targeted at children, but they could've been a bit more serious with this game. Come on, it's Marvel, treat it with respect you loony-toony game developers. And what the heck is Howard the Duck doing in this game?  Better yet, what the heck is Howard the Duck doing in Marvel in the first place?!
Now I want to go on record and say that I LOVE the Marvel films, but this game just makes a mockery of all of it. They even left out some key Marvel characters: Quick Silver, Ultron, Scarlet Witch, Vision, and other important characters.
Oh wait, you want to get %100? Oh hoh hoh hoh hoh hoooooh! These games are RELENTLESS when it comes to secret content. It will take you MONTHS to unlock every single little damn thing in this game. I only own ONE LEGO game where I got %100, ONE. Trust me, don't waste your time unlocking all that crap, it's just not worth it. I would rather watch Disney's Frozen a thousand times so I can play the whole damn movie in my head while having Let it Go stuck in my head in the process than get %100 in LEGO Marvel Super Heroes.
This game is crap. Don't you DARE buy this game, because if you do, you'll be giving Traveler's Tales money and giving them another reason to create another one of these LEGO-shaped garbage cans.
If you're a kid, this game will probably be the best thing that's ever happened to you. If you're an adult, not so much.

To start with 40 hours in i have 1 level 25 char and one level 10.
Guardians is a competent ARPG. As an MMO ,it would need a larger player base.
As many have said it has a Titans Quest pacing and feel.That is not a bad thing at all.
It is little more than competent  however and lacks the depth of skill tree ,items and crafting of other similar games.
The skill tree is very small and I have found the same skills I leveled at 15 I still use now.
This is balanced with the fact you can respec your skills anytime for free. So you can certainly fine tune and change as much as you want from the limited choices offered.
Loot is a big draw in ARPG style games. There is lots of varied loot in the game but almost nothing is an improvement over 5 or 6 level old stuff you have added some bonuses to. In 25 levels NO quest has given me a single item better than what I have either.
Crafting is very average as well. As you get a bit of a late start at it,again it has little appeal.With no player market to sell or trade items all your loot and  all your craft items you end up breaking down to upgrade components.
Upgrading is interesting BUT...then they throw in a RNG mechanic rather than make it skill based and you have to feel like gambling instead of feeling like you are a better craftsman.
Final thoughts.  Guardians is a game well worth having a look at.It is a good amount of play time for the price even to get as far as I have. With some new areas that were less like the old (I am looking at you dungeons) and some added skill varients this can only get even better.

I'm not going to mince words here, this game is amazing.
Pros:
+Challenging, but not in a punishing way.
+Great art.
+Great diversity in enemies.
+Some very unique combat mechanics that I've not seen anywhere else.
+Easy to grasp controls and mechanics.
+It's actually quite atmospheric for a game populated with paper people.
+The card system is awesome, and actually feels a lot more rewarding than, say, finding a leather belt that gives you +2% to gold find or some such nonsense.
Cons:
-No sprint feature. Character movement is... Rather slow, but this is only really a problem when you're having to backtrack to 100% a dungeon because you missed 32 gold behind a pillar.
-The sound effects are a bit dull. Not a huge deal either. The music is fine and fitting, but hearing the same casting sound for fireball over and over again gets rather tedious.
-DOORWAYS. This is honestly my biggest gripe with the game. Doorways are deathtraps in dungeons (I've not died because of one yet, but there's been some close calls.) From time to time you'll come across these structural sadists and on the other side there'll be just a metric booty load of enemies.
So to anyone who's bothered to read this far into my review, if you've been putting this game off because of the art style or the concept - stop. It's worth the dosh, the developers seem to be quite competent (there's even a feedback feature you can use at any time during your gameplay) and they have definitely poured a lot of love into this title.

I'd say it is one of my favorite games ever in the past few years of gaming. I'm sick of overhyped games that try to get by on amazing graphics but nothing else. When all the game devs are prioritizing visuals over no substance, Harebrained Schemes decides to stick to what made a great game in the past. Good writing, imagination and a perfectly imperfect world. And they prove that it still works, inspite of what games are believed to "require" in order to be considered "great games".
There is no other way to say it. Shadowrun Returns packs everything we "pen-and-paper" geeks have craved for years and more. Breathtaking artwork, music and overall ambient sound effects that combine to hit that intended mood perfectly when exploring a dark and mysterious future. This also serves well during its tactical, turn-based combat. Character growth is a fairly easy to understand while maintaining the depth of what you'd expect from the actual roleplaying game. For the video game side, if you liked the classic SNES or Sega Genesis games, this also might be up your alley.
What I like most about the game is that it is easy to learn how to play, but it remains a reasonable challenge. The flagship story that comes with it 'The Dead Man's Switch' has a bit of criticism with some players but I found it enjoyable, especially the first half or so of it. The only criticism I had with Shadowrun Returns is the last 20% or so of said story. Which the remaining parts felt slightly "tacked-on" after the main focus of the tale. Despite that nitpick, the game has tons of replay value (due to the different characters you can create and play) and the game editor helps contribute to this, User Generated Content and the ability to make your own stories for others to play helps give this title more to do beyond just the story it comes with.
For fans of role-playing games (especially dark futuristic, dystopian or cyberpunk settings)... is this game worth picking up for its price? Most definitely!

Bought this game based on some screenshots and what little information there is out there on it. That being said I thoroughly enjoy it. The class system and stats allow for extreme customization.
You wanna be a Ranger that uses dodge as mitigation to tank with a specialization in traps and turrets?
You can do that.
You want to tank using holy magic as your source of damage?
You can do that.
The quests are all very simple and the dungeons are as well for most of the game. It's a bit grindy but very fun especially with a friend or guild mate.
The dungeons are where everything you've made your class into are really tested. There are two types of dungeons. Blue dungeons contain one simple boss while the red dungeons contain many bosses with complicated mechanics which become especially fun and challenging on nightmare. *I'm looking at you Vexx from embergarde sanctuary*
Each dungeon can be tried on 3 difficulties ranging from Easy (1 star) to Nightmare (3 star).
Most classes and builds can solo the 1 star's and even the 2 star dungeons while 3 star dungeons require a party for the most part. The tanking classes can spec into pure tanking or sacrifice some tank power for self healing, damage, or party buffs. This is true of all roles.
The game is very early in it's launch and as such contains some bugs and a few QoL improvements it could use (Occasional CTD's, No dual spec or gear swapper) but, overall, this game is incredibly fun for a group of 2-5 friends.
My only immediate note to the devs would be MOAR QUESTS.

To start things off: Civ V is a good game. This review is very nit-picky and is probably going to upset SOMEONE in SOME WAY. Just don't crucify me, alright?
Starting with the good things about Civ, I can easily claim that it is an immediate gateway game to not only 4X titles, but also Grand Strategy and various other games based around resource management and the like. Easily approachable from any angle at any difficulty, the game has one of the most indepth in-game tutorial-esque messages that the user has the ability to leave on for the sake of direction or turn off if they become annoying. The game even has its own encyclopedia of information about everything in the game (cleverly named the Civilopedia). Also available in Civ V is the astounding range of difficulty options, be it complete baby-mode or nigh impossible. (I will have to tie this subject in later, as the functioning itself of the difficulty scale is not too perfect.)
Civ V players have the ability to pick from a wide range of various nations that can all accomplish different goals in different ways. For example, if I play Boudicca of the Celts, my most viable options are usually domination through religion and culture or combat, though I could easily change my focus to maybe a science victory (however unviable that would be). Some nations even limit themselves to only becoming amazing at certain periods of time, such as Darius of Persia and his amazing functionality during Golden Ages (which are acheived via an excess amount of Happiness in your nation that usually take a while to get to). Basically, there is a Civ for everyone. As is usually the case with strategy games, more options means more chances to show your prowess.
Now that I've discussed a few positives of Civ V, I feel as if it's time that I tell you about the not-so-great. For example, while the difficulty scale covers a wide range of playing levels, higher difficulties usually involve some cheesing strategies and various trial-and-error starts. This is because that if you choose one of these more challenging modes, the game REWARDS the AI so that they can actively compete against you. A popular argument that has become ESPECIALLY relative when it comes to modern games pertains to the idea of "artificial difficulty," or making unfair advantages that only serve to hinder the player by adding a sort-of fake challenge. To say the least, artificial difficulty is not fun. At all. To award the AI and give it a bias over the player at the start of the game WITHOUT improving its functionality or basic awareness of ingame events is unbelievably lazy.
While on the topic of AI, I'm not going to lie to you; it's ♥♥♥♥ing garbage. Never has a game gone by where I win without having to deal with some stupid war over a Wonder I built 700 years ago or borders that have been cemented since the start of the game. Never has a game gone by where I win without being denounced for not helping someone with something they wanted or for not agreeing to their cries for charity (by the way, the AI will ask you for money like a ♥♥♥♥ing street bum. It's fairly annoying). Countless times have I seen an AI raise an army and simply deal with their -87 income, and countless times have I seen the AI settle a city in the middle of tundra for reasons unbeknownst (until Uranium rolls around and surprise! That barren wasteland of a city has found two sources!). That's another matter that concerns me personally and it only occurred recently to me during a multiplayer session with a pal. I'm pretty sure that the AI can simply see into the future as well as ignore fog of war. This idea became especially prevalent when one of my naval vessels found itself spontaneously surrounded by six ancient caravels, that of which killed themselves in order to take out my one boat.
The AI also has an issue with not blobbing at all or blobbing MINDLESSLY, especially Pocatello of the Shoshone. I understand that Pocatello's AI is programmed to expand at a VERY fast pace, but come on. There is no reason he should have twelve cities (yes, twelve) in his Renaissance. It's excessive--unbelievably excessive. Some nations you would expect to expand, such as America, Rome, or Arabia, usually stay within about three cities (atleast, that's the most I've seen come from Washington). Do not even get me STARTED on the Zulu.
Also, many Civilizations that I talk about in this review are DLC, which would be acceptable if the DLC in question only added Civs. Some of the DLC, however, add extra mechanics that should have been included in the base game, such as religion or ideology or even Wonders. If you have only the base game, you're not going to have that great of a time when put in comparison to the fun with DLC.
Now that the rant is finished, I probably should explain why I recommend the game if so many things are so terribly WRONG. While Civ V is a good game, as stated previously, it also serves as a gate to BETTER games, like Crusader Kings 2, the Hearts of Iron Series, and its predecessor, Civ IV. That being said, I recommend it for the sake of getting interested in the Strategy Game genre, not for its gameplay alone.

Zeno Clash is a very odd, very surreal, but overall very interesting experience with plenty of pleasant gameplay moments to balance its flaws.
Good:
It's odd, the combat works well, it's amusing, a bit silly, and you get to beat up wild animals with your fists; for those of you who want to skip the rest.
The core concept of being a somewhat mentally unhinged brawler in an exotic alien world is fun on its own, and deserves a special mention for the game. What makes it funnier is that people actually expect this sort of punk behavior of the protagonist Ghat. Nobody ever calls you out for getting into random fights, shooting people in the streets, or chain-whipping wild animals into submission.
Fun/cruelty factor aside, the combat is pretty interesting on its own; if somewhat easy. You have a good number of different punches, combos, and special attacks you can use, while still not overwhelming the player in any area. There is a very bare-bones rpg stat system which, while not really necessary for the game in the first place, doesn't get in the way of anything.
The levels are very unique and entrancing, ranging from busy alien cities, flower-covered deserts, high-tech ruins, and something I could only describe as a river of soap. Every other character in this strange world has a different way of speaking and some little quirk or design that defines them and makes them stand out. The levels and characters combined make for an even stranger story that only gets weirder and weirder as it goes along; and take that for what you will.
In summary, it's fun; especially if you are the easily amused sort or just really stressed and want to play as a guy who likes to punch things in the face. The setting and story are very unusual and alien, and while it might not leave you glued to your keyboard eager to see what happens next, it is certainly worth going through it just to see all the exotic locales and see how the whole thing plays out. It's jus an overall amusing and odd experience.
Bad:
Poor balance, bugginess, and lackluster voice acting if you aren't reading any more of this.
Depending on how you play, this game can be stupidly easy. Sometimes it feels like Ghat practically cheats. Between the absurd melee skills, being able to chain-whip six guys at once, special attacks that can send about anyone into a ragdoll, and being able to call down laser beams from the sky, it felt like the slow and bumbling enemies I faced never stood any chance. Weapons get an extra mention: While the various hammers, scepters, and guns are very pretty and fun to use, they practically allow you to cheese your way through even the most difficult fights. To counter this, the game makes weapons finite. Once you break your hammer or use your gun's ammo, that weapon is gone for the rest of the game forever. Once you use all the weapons in the campaign you don't get any more, and that felt a bit cheap since they were still a lot of fun and I wished there were ways to acquire weapons to use just for fun.
But on the note of balance, allies actually can be useful outside of cannon fodder distractions, and it can actually be worth it to put points in the leadership skill for that reason.
The game is just a little bit too buggy and slow at times. There was a time where I found a way to kill a boss without him being able to hurt me on pure accident. Some of the sidequests, which I looked up online and know for sure I did not have the items to complete, let me complete them anyways. Enemies in some areas got stuck on terrain. Weapons I had not picked up (to save them for later) would vanish when I left an area (adding to my dismay that fun weapons are cheaply limited). I also got a few visual glitches related to the lighting. One in particular caused me to have background images burned onto my screen like a picture. So there are some very frustrating and jarring bugs that one could encounter on a regular basis.
Finally, the voice acting. I'm not an expert, but I sometimes felt like it wasn't possible for Ghat or Rimat to show any emotion outside neutral or slight frustration. Every other character in the game is fine and has some unique verbal tic or speech mannerism that makes them interesting to listen too, except the two protagonists. Maybe the Golem isn't any better, but at least he sounds like what he is supposed to be. Sounds in general just feel a little muted sometimes, but this is the only thing really bad enough to stand out to me as far as the overall goes.
So the voice acting is a little bland at times, bugs and balance decisions can be frustrating, and the game can be a little too easy at times. I won't nag too much on the difficulty because I wasn't on hard, but the main thing for me is that it felt easy for the wrong reasons. There are just a lot of little bad designs and difficulty flaws that mar the surface of an otherwise fun game.
Overall:
On the freeroam rpg scale, it's certainly not Skyrim, and if you come into this with any sort of high expectation it will disappoint. The game requires you to overlook some flaws
But while it has some moments when it will make you sigh in disappointment, but you can always shake that off by punching some giant crabs. The weirdness and silliness is the main charm here, and the focus on the brutal fist fights combined with the unusual setting full of furry, scaly, and just plain freaky alien creatures just makes the whole thing fun; despite how simple and unbalanced it is.
As a person who is easily entertained by first person fighters such as this, there is nothing not to like. At the very least, it's cheap and a good way to kill some time punching random things in the face. I recommend it.
