TL;DR:
Before I begin, please take a second to read this quote I found from another review. In literally 3 sentences, this reviewer has completely summed up Mirror's Edge.
"It's easily understandable why many reviewers give Mirror's Edge relatively low scores. They buy the game "about parkour", in other words 3D platformer, and expect some challenges inspired by Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time or Psychonauts with lush environments and a quaint story a la Assassin's Creed. They get ZILCH of it."
I DO NOT RECOMMEND THIS GAME. If you're looking to pick it up anyway, then honestly pick it up on Steam when it costs like $5.
------
Let me do a brief overview. You play as this asian cutie named Faith, and she is a "runner", which is basically a messenger that uses parkour in order to get information to your clients, it is assumed the information is probably illegal because the game takes place in a dystopian futuristic city where information is HEAVILY monitored. Basically, the game is about your sister, who is a cop, gets framed for a murder and now you are public enemy #1 and you are being hunted down all whilst trying to clear your sister's name.
Story: 6/10
The initial idea of the game, fine. I can handle cheesy cliche storylines, that's no big deal, but what they tried to do was force feed you while all you really want to do is parkour the hell out of a gorgeous city. Whatever, I've played worst storylines, at least it gave a reason why you had to run your♥♥♥♥♥off all the time.
Sound: 7/10
The music, not bad. Sound effects, not bad. Constantly hearing your character grunt and moan, REALLY DISTRACTING. Realistic, don't get me wrong, but my god I feel bad for people who are attracted to the type of girl Faith is, I couldn't imagine being able to focus long enough just to beat it (the game, badum-tish).
Graphics: 9/10
Aesthetically speaking, this game is gorgeous. Everything is clean and white, which is cool, and then you get sudden bright flashes of vibrant color (usually showing areas you need to go to). It would have been great to have a fully colored REAL city, but this game would have been impossible without the colors sticking out to show you where you need to go. It actually does a really good job 80% of the time making things really obvious/intuitive of where you need to go. Major thing that annoyed me, no windowed mode. I alt-tab often, having to restart the game as often as I did because it crashed is really annoying.
I'm going to write a second paragraph for graphics. On a gameplay side, yeah the game is beautiful, but on a cut scene side they flip it and turn into an amazing art-style that really looks good. This is the main reason why I give this game such a high graphics score.
Gameplay: 3/10
I don't really know how to score this fairly. I remember the commercials, I remember trying this game before. The game looks and was sold to me as a "parkour" game. It barely is. It is like a first-person Assassin's Creed where you can't just climb whatever, you have to find the EXACT thing to climb. The game is SO linear that instead of Assassin's Creed you think "okay maybe it is more like Prince of Persia" except there is no TIME REWIND POWERS. I promise you that you will die the most stupid deaths either from mistimed jumped or the gunfights they force you to participate in. I'm not someone who usually hates police, but in this game, seriously I killed every one I could find. In the training or early level the game preaches about not fighting and trying to just get away, screw that. It is so easy to die in this game it really gets tedious repeating the same thing over and over again.
Honestly my biggest problem is how linear it is. It would have been great to free-roam the city, and I understand how overly ambitious that is for this game, but that would have been AMAZING. The game is more of a deeper, symbolic artstyle than a parkour game, and I get that too, but that was not what I wanted when I played this. The game is relatively short, what took me 8 hours to do was how many times I kept freaking dying.
Overall: 4/10
This game had potential, and in an artistic sense, it is really good. I play on minimal settings and the game STILL looks really pretty. I don't want to go on a huge long rant because I kind of already did slightly. You want a fun game, go play something else because I don't understand how some people can rate this game so high and claim it is good.

First, I need to be clear that this is a review on day 2 of early access.  The game is not finished.  There are many places you cannot go and get a message that the area isn't in yet.  Items and abilities have numbers attached to them, but none of those numbers have actually been balanced yet.
That being said, core mechanics are in place and feel well thought out.  Given only the broad outlines of a goal to gather dwarves together to stand against the goblin king, it feels fun to explore locations to see what I'll find.  As you explore locations, you rescue dwarves that will help you gather resources to grow your town.  The little mini quests in areas I explore are varied enough that exploration is its own reward; I don't feel like I'm just clearing identical areas in some sort of resource grind.
What makes the casual exploration gameplay really work is the art syle.  How you feel about this game is going to depend largely on how you feel about pixel art.  Personally, I am amazed how expressive the low pixel count characters are.  It takes a particular talent to create features by altering the color of individual pixels.  My favorite is the dwarf who is clearly dressed as a plague doctor.

If you’re a fan of Michael Manns films, then rest assured, you’re going to enjoy Kane & Lynch: Dead Men. From the L.A Bank heist shootout to the Nightclub showdown, you’ll have a vague idea what rests ahead.
Visually, the Hitman: Blood Money game engine has dated well. And holds up to many games this current generation with well-rounded reflections, shadows and environmental destruction which add a sense of realism and immersion into the game world. Cut scenes suffer from audio cutting out resulting in the end of the conversations missing, while the addition of sub-titles makes this issue smaller, the end result is a still mildly frustrating. As for the voice acting, Lynch leaves something to be desired but the voice acting for Kane adds much more to the character of this flawed man.
Mechanically, while it works, the cover system is “clunky” at best; resulting in poor cover mechanic and a sub-par targeting system with precision targeting is almost non-existent in the game.
Gameplay-wise, Kane & Lynch is a kinetic and non-stop experience, shooting and seeking cover is exiting whenever you can control it. Although it can get repetitive at times, there’s no stop sign to show at you by the constant number of henchmen coming at you. The command system that plays out in a strategic way where you can command your team mates/NPC’s to target selected enemies or take cover; however it was an under-exploited system because you will find yourself doing all the shooting due to the poor AI.
Kane & Lynch is a thrilling but very violent and masochistic action game. You have the opportunity to end the lives of innocent bystanders to even hearing the voice of a cop beg for their life because they have children; all while the wife and daughter of Kane are held captive. The story follows at a psychological drama emotional vibe, and certain strong elements that would put the player in enough stress if it isn't by the story's way of destroying up the characters’ lives, and although it doesn't grab enough interest on its character development it does at least satisfy you with those individual personalities of each that makes a credible duo that are not precisely role models nor does it glamourize the lifestyle of the protagonist which many games or movies lean towards to justify their actions.
Exciting, ultra-violent, masochistic guilt, pulse pounding vengeance, searing vulgarity and Japanese gangsters in leather motorcycle outfits, this game has every top-notch action film element one could ask for.

So far, this game has surpassed my expectations by quite a bit. I got it for $10 and just assumed it was going to be pretty bare-bones but, so far, it has proven to have a lot of variety and depth. The class and stats system along with gear variety seems to allow for a lot of build variation, with varying effectiveness I'm sure, though.
I've been looking for an ARPG MMO for a long time and so far, this has been exactly what I've been looking for. The leveling isn't trivialized, it's actually feeling rewarding as I hit each new level as opposed to D3 where it's just a race to max level.
The game does have a lot of room for improvement, however. It is not highly polished but it's still very fun to play. There are some bugs and it seems like a lot of skills are probably not useful. I would also like to see some gear restrictions to use certain skills. I can currently equip a melee weapon as an engineer and still use skills that fire a gun. This breaks the immersion and makes my weapon choice feel pointless.
Overall, the game is well worth the asking price. I like where it's at right now and can see it having a bright future. A large part of me wants to upgrade my edition to help support the games' development because I see so much more potential with it.
If you have the $15 to spend and have wanted that ARPG MMO like I have, this is well worth the investment. I am excited for the future of the game and can say the devs have been updating the game frequently and been in good communication with the community.
Also, a lot of people mention the game has a low population. I'd definitely say this is true but it has also been refreshing. I think it will help build a better community with slow and steady growth and not a massive influx of people that cause people to compete for everything that brings out their nasty sides. The game also has significant updates in the works that should get publicity to continue to bring more people in.
All in all, if you're on the edge, give it a shot! With its price point, you can't go wrong.

Let me start this by saying I've never played the Shadowrun RPG.  I found the swords and sorcery meets cyberpunk theme interesting and the writing felt a lot like William Gibson, if a bit overdone.  Tho overall plot was  quite good and kept me wanting to play to find out what was coming next.
This game has a very similar feel  to the  original Fallout and Fallout 2.  This is probably because it is in the same 3rd person isometric perspective with turn-based combat.  One of major differences was that objects in the environment can provide partial  cover.  The world is  also done in squares instead of hexes, which does feel a bit more natural, even if it limits the combat options a bit. There is no special  targetting though - you shoot at the person and either miss, hit or crit - so headshots and going for the vitals  is out.
There are lots of options  for  how to develop your character.  You can pick a race, but that seems to have minimal effect on the game.  The far bigger choice is your class, but really what that does is pre-select a few skills. You can easily go a different way or create a "class" of your own.  Definitely be careful to be focused on what skills and abilities you choose to improve the game is short (more on that below), so you don't have time to diversify your skills.  Be excellent at something rather than a jack of all trades.
There are lots of "crunchy bits": armour, weapons, spells, cyberware, consumable items, etc. to buy and help improve your character.  The economy seems quite balanced as well so you don't get to the end of the game with too much money and nowhere to spend it.  On the flip side, I did have enough to buy exactly what I wanted.  Those going the cyberware root may have a different opinion as that equipment is  quite expensive.
There are a few flaws with this game.  Annoyingly, the behavious when clicking on interactive items in the game world is inconsistent.  If the little icon for it is not displayed, you can't interact and often the icons disappear, even when you cursor is right on top of them.  Other times, you click on them, your character goes  over to interact, and nothing happens until you move the cursor away, move it back, wait for the icon to reappear and click again.  Annoying.
The other main flaw is that the story is both very linear and short.  There are a few side quests, but with the exception of one that I noticed, it was almost difficult *not* to do them as they required very little exploration and were almost  always  on the path you were already following.  That leads to the flaw that the game is very linear.  The levels are very small and there is really very little reason to explore as you generally don't find stuff tucked in dark corners - most of it is right on the main path.
The biggest flaw is the game is very short.  I played throught the whole game, doing all the (very limited) side quests that I could and was done in less than 15 hours. In the RPG world, that is very short.  Still, it left me wanting more which is better than slogging though a padded game that goes on too long.
Overall, I recommend the game, especially if you are an RPG fan and have a passing interest in the subject matter.

I like this game. The parkour and the combat system make it feel like a more polished Dead Island. Content-wise it's very meaty and you get a good chunk of story to go along with several challenges and side quests.
The game gets a bit too easy once you reach survivor rank 25 though. Weapons (when upgraded to the greatest extent) can kill Volatiles, Goons, and Demolishers in 1 or 2 hits. It makes the night phase a joke.
As of writing this review, there are currently a handful of achievements that are bugged and one is definitely broken. Various players report very different experiences when it comes to how some of their achievements are tracked. I had a friend who I played co-op with for the entirety of the game and he ended up 1 quest short on his progress bar (we were stuck at 44/45 while he was stuck at 43/45) even though we played every single quest together.
There's also a few glitches that were mildly annoying. I fell under the map once while travelling near a fishing village. A friend also has demonstrated the grapple hook glitch that pretty much sends you flying out of bounds.
Now you may be thinking that with half of the interview mostly being about achievement bugs and glitches, I may not even recommend this game. Nevertheless, I'm still going to recommend it. I've enjoyed my fair share of zombie games and while the Dead Island games were kind of 'meh', I still enjoyed the open-world setting. Dying Light is a better version of Dead Island. I'm recommending the game because Techland's games are progressively improving. They just need to bring their A-game when it comes to the aforementioned bugs/glitches.

Even though this game caught my attention back in 2008, I didn't get the chance to play it until recently. I am glad I took the time to go back and try this, because it was definitely a great purchase.
The story was certainly good, albeit a bit too short for my tastes, but what truly made this a good purchase was the unique "puzzle" aspect of the game. There were plenty of brain stumpers sprinkled throughout and gave it a good challenge so it wasn't too easy and rewarded the player with a sense of self-satisfaction when getting through a level. The fighting/gun mechanics could've been a lot better, but for what the game was made to center around; it definitely hit the nail on the head.
The environment and music certainly immerses you in the experience and sets the tone for an exciting/fast-paced game that will keep you playing until the very end. I say if it's on sale, then it's worth picking up and trying for yourself.

In short, this game is Flappy Bird from the 10th circle of Hell.
You're controlling a small pointer that rotates around a central hexagon (though shapes can change!) and you're trying to avoid oncoming radial barriers. This can be stressful enough, but go ahead and add a voilently spinning playing field, changing colors, and one of the best electronic soundtracks to complete the Super Hexagon experience. You will fail, a lot, and very quickly, but luckily the game has a Hotline Miami-esque R (spacebar) to restart style, so you'll be back in the action faster than you know it, usually just to fail again in the first 5 seconds. This game is made to throw you off, and it will. You'll slowly get the hang of it and go back to earlier stages and think "I struggled on this, really?".
There are some issues such as the lack of null movement cancelling (might be intentional?) with some control styles (namely mouse and some controller controls) and the fact (this might just be me) I have to have my controller plugged in for my keyboard and mouse to work. The Shift-Tab Steam menu is also kind of buggy and can not work or freeze the game.
I totally recommend it to anyone looking for a challenge, but be prepared for dizziness, frustration, failure, and that one glorious moment when you FINALLY beat a stage.
Don't play if you're prone to motion sickness.

Pros:
+ mostly well-balanced. Every clan sees moderate to significant use, but no clan is deemed as useless
+ Visuals are well-made
+ Account link to the phone app, letting you play wherever you want and maintain progress on the same account
+ Generous rewards, dozens of free card packs to kickstart your deck, relatively simple missions for money
+ Ability to play in Japanese (With a workaround for Japanese voices with English text)
Cons:
- Most card illustrations are obviously inspired by Anime, making visuals polarizing: you either love it or you hate it
- Interface is very phone app-like
A new virtual card game in relative infancy, but already proven itself to be quite balanced. The publisher, Cygames, write blog posts regarding balance in the current meta-game with each expansion. The balance changes so far made sense, and the effects were as intended, without collateral damage or being excessive.
The rewards and starter package is plenty (17 Standard packs and 26 Darkness Evolved packs when I started), and new players can get close to 4000 rupies (Standard currency, 100 rupies = 1 pack) with simple one-time missions, and daily missions (which have individual timers) almost always amount to at least 100 rupies a day, though there is no "3 wins = some money" system like that of Hearthstone.
Overall, the card game is fantastic, and it certainly felt much better to start off on this game than on Hearthstone.

There are still some frustrating missions in the game that are nowhere near as good as the others which greatly ruins the games pacing but other than that, this is still a good classic stealth game.

Risk of Rain is a fantastic game. However it has a serious flaw in the way it saves your progress. The game is fast first person platformer. A fresh new adaptation of true and tried platforming. Rather than moving slowly and timing the jump from the edge. Speed is what counts here. You need to be moving at a constant speed to kick open doors, catch a drop wire etc. etc. Every thing is setup for constant nonstop movement. The level designs are so perfect; once you get hang of controls there is no need to stop. The game takes you through roof tops, A/C vents, malls, office walk ways and lots of other varied setups. At every stage there are multiple paths to move forward. There is a lot of freedom and it is tied well with risks.
A critical thing to understand here is that the start-up period of the game is ROUGH. You are expected to be able to wall-jump, balance on thin rails, jump over chasms, and do other challenging things. The controls are going to be hard to get used to. Don't give up. It could be frustrating. Stick at it, and give yourself time to get used to those controls. Keep working through the initial levels. The reward is well worth it.
Once you become used to the controls, the game really becomes captivating. You're expected to race top speed through a variety of obstacle courses. You have to think on the fly, react instantly, and pay attention to clues. It draws your mind in to focus on the moment.
You can replay levels to try different paths, to try to get a better speed, and simply to have fun. So even if you "solve" a level in one way, there are reasons to go back and replay them multiple times.
This game has been agony and ecstasy for me, and when I beat it I felt exhilarated. If you are a high-energy gamer who has the patience to try and try again, you will find yourself rewarded. If not, you should know ahead of time that there's no cathartic blasting your way out of trouble in this game.

After one playthrough, its obvious this game is flawed, and it fails to be as tactically complex (And for me, enjoyable) as its previous installments.
The X-Com series has always been known for its solid and difficult strategic layers.  Often dubbed the "greatest PC game of all time", it aimed to combining simulation and management with tactical sqaud-based shooting. You were given a set of eight soldiers, which could be upgraded to a squadron of up to thirty, with a host of intricate weaponry, equipment, armours, and tanks to accompany them.  You fight battles against a persistent alien threat in an isometric viewscape with a sort of action-currency monopolizing your movements and shots, making this strategic battle hair-pullingly difficult, as well as rewarding and fun.  All the while, you are to keep countries happy with your performance, and manage peace and tranquility across the world, or you risk losing the support of funding nations, and then, inevitibly, facing bankruptcy.
In Enemy Unknown, you get six soldiers who fight random packs of enemies who show up in pre-determined locations who will not move an inch on their own accord unless activated by your soldier's movements.  The isometric grid-movement has also been radically simplified, as you get two movements, the first one can move and get into cover, and the second can shoot, or move out of cover somewhere else, then the soldier's time has been expended, and you end your turn.
With a host of bugs and glitches that have not been fixed, even in to the expansion pack.
I continue to have frustrating glitches such as soldiers stustore.steampowered.com20getting double-turns, buttons refusing to respond, mouse sensitivity issues, and a host of graphical and animation artifacts.  Not only does it have technical problems, but in execution, it hosts a horrid system of enemy spawning which is based on activating random packs, and an outstandingly shallow soldier load-out that lacks in comparison to the first.
The alien AI works on a shoot-on-site basis, and there is a painfully obvious bias towards the power and accuracy of the aliens, as when you lose a soldier, you do not feel like you messed up and made a bad decision, you feel like you were cheated by the aliens.  Your ticket to success is not skill, it's farming a few powerful soldiers and using them the whole game.  However, this all would be okay if the game was not close to ten gigabytes, but the original was four megabytes, and was the home to an exponentially larger amount of content.  The games graphical fidelity can't even be the reason for its size, as the textures are simply bad, and its obvious they were designed and compressed with console in mind.
This is most definitely designet to be baby's first strategy game, but that's not even valid, because its mechanics are broken from the start, and its price point is outstandingly high.  This is not something you should expect out of the strategy genre's most potent developer, but honestly, I expected this after hearing it was slated for a console release. The AI works on a shoot-on-site basis, and there is a painfully obvious bias towards the power and accuracy of the aliens, as when you lose a soldier, you do not feel like you messed up and made a bad decision, you feel like you were cheated by the aliens.  Your ticket to success is not skill, it's farming a few powerful soldiers and using them the whole game.
This does not capture the spirit or greatness of its infinitely superior elder, X-COM: UFO Defense, which is available for purchase on Steam.  Buyer beware though -- It is ran through DOSBox, and the emulation is very shoddy, and due to this fact, I recommend you look up ways to enhance it, as there are many popular guides to making it the perfect X-COM experience.  It's elder is also close to twenty years younger than it, which is another reason Enemy Unknown disappointed me so greatly.

X-Com Enemy Unknown is a rare type of game that only come's around once in awhile. It is gripping, crafty, and terrifying. An engrossing, deep turnbased combat game, married neatly with a real time strategic base mechanic makes this one of the standout titles of 2012.
X-Com is a successor of the classic X-com titles from the mid to late 90's. While this new title has been developed by a differrent company, Firaxis, they have managed to preserve what was so enthralling about X-Com and the alien threat. With a new engine,powered by Unreal Engine 3, Firaxis brought X-Com to a new generation with slick graphics and fresh gameplay.
X-Com has two main layers. The first is the "meat" of the game, which is the tactical combat. Players are tasked with squads between 4 to 6 elite soldiers, each with varying skills and abilities that are unlocked as they get kills and survive more missions. A range of custumizable options are in the game, such as changing their appearance or names, and choosing different skills as they become available. On the battlefield players are faced with the ever imposing alien threat, which is intelligent and ruthless. The aliens have many different species, which act as the classes. From the lowly sectoid to the fearsome muton, players will be constantly challenged with ever increasing numbers and powers. All the aliens feel very distinct, and the ai does avery good job of keeping players on their toes. They will use any advantage they can get,be it suppression and flanking, or simply ganging up on one man, and will remorselessly destroy the unprepared squad. Thankfully X-Com has a few tricks of their own. As players progress, new armour and weapons become available, such as the S.H.I.V, a mobile weapons platform that replaces a soldier in the field and can act as agressive mobile cover, or the skelton suit, which allows soldiers to use a grapple hook to reach elevated positions. Perfect for getting that sniper in for the kill. Late game will players will see even more advanced alien technologies be adapted for your soldiers use, and even delve in to phsycic abilities.
The second layer of X-Com is the base management. This is where players are tasked with monitering global panic, issuing promotions to vetrans, researching alien technologies, and contructing a fortified base from which to launch operations. It is here that all new weapons and tactics become available, so it is crucial to manage X-Com's limited resources wisely, as one mistake could leave you without the proper weapons or technology to survive the increaing alien menace. As permadeath is in the game, players must strive to keep their soldiers equipped with the latest and greatest if they hope to achieve victory. Missions will occur at random and vary from seek and destroy, a timed bomb diffusal in which the player must find and diffuse bombs scattered around the map before an alotted amount of turns, to Vip escorts. Each mission takes place on a randomly chosen map, so no two playthroughs are the same.
X-Com Enemy Unknown is a a fantastic title that will challenge and entertain, and I highly recommend to all types of gamers.

The interactions between Batman and the villains, Batman’s inner monologue and the dissection of Batman as a character are just fantastic. It really tries to delve into who Batman is and why he is who he is. It does get it’s head up it’s♥♥♥♥♥in the end but the rest of it’s just fantastic and the story genuinely left me afraid and tense at points.
The ending, however, is kind of disappointing because it’s an anti climax. Scarecrow is shown as weak, which as a villain makes sense, but story-wise doesn’t. It shows Batman overcoming his obstacles but we already knew Batman was strong. It’s the weakness stuff that is interesting.
It’s basically what the previous Arkham games had but with more danger. Thugs are packing guns, drones, and artillery so you have to sneak around more. There aren’t many more systems added here but it’s more a refinement of the system into something really great. The opportunities for takedowns, silent takedowns, and gadgets is something I want speedrunners to use because it’s going to look amazing. The combat is just about the same but you have more enemy combinations (electric, shields, brutes, medics).
They do introduce driving in this game and unfortunately, it's boring. The control itself isn’t too pleasant and the missions are tedious really. The ones where you have to act as a tank and take out other tanks is challenging but it never changes. All of the missions related to driving are just boring and they repeat without change. At least the stealth missions use different locations and layouts.
Now the biggest pile of horse♥♥♥♥♥♥ You have to complete the entire game to get the real ending. That includes the ♥♥♥♥ing riddler “puzzles” which can go ♥♥♥♥ themselves. There is an ending which requires you to complete half of the possible mission trees which also sheds some light on the ending. This isn’t much of a problem with the various villains you interact with as each one has voiced cutscenes and makes sense in a story progression sort of way. The annoying part is that you have to complete at least some of the UNMARKED tedious car side quests and that means riding around the city trying to find the mission until you give up and just YouTube the endings.
The game looks good but not great. Faces look oily for some reason but the mechs, villains, and the suits look great. The city is ok but usually there is either plant stuff or rain covering it up which is annoying and plus, it drops the frame rate which jumps around between 60-90. It did crash a bit for me but whatever.
I enjoyed my time with it and am glad I did. I am also glad they decided to end the series here because it shows that they are coming to the end of their good ideas well.

First off lets talk about optimisation. The game had a terrible release 2 years ago, which has been widely documented.
If  thats all that is keeping you from picking this title up then have no fear! , it took them long enough but its fixed.
I hold a solid 60fps with a 970 asus strix, all settings maxed except the extra nivida fluff. If you have a monster rig go ahead and turn those on but I don't see much difference between on/off and it hogs VRAM. That being said..
Almost immediately ingame you are introduced to the batmobile, get used to it apparently the dev team fell in love with their creation as it is USED ALOT. I really liked it myself but near the end it really is a bit much, I would have preferred some more hand to hand fights with the super villains of Gotham.
The combat is pretty much unchanged from City which is no surprise as they have influenced other games with this system. Some new gadgets are introduced though which is neat when it comes to puzzle solving or taking down groups of henchmen.
The storyline is fantastic and shouldn't be spoiled, you need to go in unaware and get ready to be shocked! Strong voice acting supports this especially a stand out performance by John Noble as Scarecrow.
One big thing that everyone should know is the whole mess with the ending(s).
If you are not going for 100% completion then do NOT and I repeat do NOT finish the main storyline with all side quests complete.
Doing so leaves you only the riddler trophies  and the game locks you into the 100% game completion to see the ending/credits. Which means you need to hunt down 243 riddles across all maps/buildings....
Solution - Leave 1 side quest incomplete while you finish the main storyline and then you can avoid the riddler and his riddles.
If you do go for it then don't worry, some of the puzzles are fun, it took me 20 hours extra but it wasn't really that boring at all.
So in summary -
+ Great Graphics
+ Marvelous soundtrack and voice acting
+ Arkham combat system
- Riddler trophies for complete ending

It's a decently fun game, but I actually had to stop playing after I cleared 1 of the dungeons because the hitbox issues and tiny little items on the floor that's hard to pick up. There are also graphic issues that other aRPGs share with environmental clipping mobs making them invincible as well as a pillar in the foreground that blocks the view of a gorup of mobs and stuff like that. I'd suggest have a faster dissolve of the walls and doorways and such.
The Dual class system is good, but then I wouldn't really want to restart a new char to try a new combination because that first 15 levels of questing was extremely tedious and not all that intuitive. You are sent all over the map trying to do quests while mobs are packed everywhere with a pretty quick respawn timer. I'd hack n' slash for like 10 levels, and then just end up running pass the mobs afterwards. In the traditional non-MMO style aRPG, the mobs don't respawn unless you reset the instance, and in a MMO, the mobs are spread out a more sparsely to allow people to travel, but this game took those two elements and try to smoosh them together.....It just became a game that doesn't give you any downtime (to even clear your inventory or upgrade skills),  and wasting all the killing on trashmobs that really drop nothing useful.
Also the quest rewards are really lacklustered. If the gear drop from the dungeon is higher than the quest reward, then either tune the quest reward higher or the dungeon drop quality lower.

This game was awesome and definitely exceeded all of my expectations. Honestly, I was a bit apprehensive when it came to buying and playing this game. This game initially came to be known as one of the greatest examples of why PC gaming ports can be either be hit or miss. It was buggy, had frame rate issues, and was at times downright unplayable. As a result, I waited a long time before I decided to buy and eventually play this game. Honestly, I had no problems with the game and it was smooth sailing the whole time.
As for the game itself, it was awesome. This may have been the best game out of all of the Batman Arkham series. The game wasn't perfect, but there were a lot of moments in this game where I was truly enjoying myself.
One thing I disliked about this game was how the boss fights were completely different from the other games. The boss fights in the first three Arkham games were a big part of what made them great and in this game it felt downplayed. There were instances where I realized I was fighting a boss character, but it just didn't feel like a boss fight.
Another thing I disliked was being forced to play through the sidequests to beat the game. Even then, if you don't 100% this game, you won't get the true ending. I realize a lot of games do something similar, but I just hate being forced to play sidequests. The sidequests in this game weren't repetitive, but it was a hassle trying to look for tiny things in such a huge map. At times, I had to look up sidequests locations online to simply get on with the game.
One huge complaint I heard prior to playing this game had to do with the batmobile. For me, it wasn't that bad, but it also wasn't perfect. The batmobile is a beast in this game, but with the way that Gotham's streets were designed, it wasn't ideal. Trying to drive the batmobile at ridiculous speeds while you tried to stay on the road was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The streets were too narrow and I frequently found myself crashing into buildings and all sorts of stuff. Not very ideal gameplay when you're required to tail a car and crashing gives the AI an opportunity to get away.
Overall, this game was awesome and it's a must play. I played it with an msi rx 480 8gb card along with an i5-4590, not too bad game performance.
I give this game a 4/5 and if you're any type of Batman fan, I recommend that you play this and the three other games in this series.

One thing that must be said beforehand is that I'm a suspect concerning indie games. I absolutely love them. And also hardcore games. And games that allows you to create your own stories and tales, games that even defeat is a playthrough worthy of rememberance. And FTL is all of the above.
Although music can be a little bit repetitive at times (it's not bad - it's just repetitive - I do love the main theme on the menu tho) and the sound effects are weirdly annoying, it's a fantastic games in all other aspects. The pixel art (which I also love) is adorable although it has a few flaws on animation and pixels with different sizes, which looks a little "out" of the "old-school" aesthetic, but all the designs and visuals are worthy of the title.
But the aspect of the game that launches it faster than light into success (no pun intended ;) ) is the gameplay mechanics and the style. Faster Than Light can bring to you the same feelings and rapid thinking that only the captain of an Enterprise or the Firefly could ever have. All the tough choices, the difficulties and facing the consequences of these - it's all there. Spare fuel for someone in need and risk being stranded yourself later? Avoid battles by accepting deals that make you question your own ideals? Hand over one of your friends to a slaver or face certain death in battle while your crew desperately try to prepare your ship for a jump?
Despite a few flaws, FTL is an amazing game and certainly a must buy if you enjoy the thrill of space-faring stories and has the courage needed to make decisions without ever looking back.

Prior to getting this, I'd played all three of the previous Arkham games on PS3. So I'm quite familiar with the series.
To begin with, let's talk about the three most common complaints about this game.
First, PC performance. When this came out, it had horrible performance on PC. I can't speak for anyone else, but by the time I played it (early 2017), the performance issues seem to be addressed. That or having a ton of RAM (which I bought in anticipation of eventually buying this) and maybe having a Nvidia graphics card (there's a Nvidia splash screen at launch) is what makes it work. My specs, FWIW: Intel Core i5 4570, 16GB of RAM, 2GB GeForce GTX 960, a 250 GB SSD, and Windows 10.1.
Second, the Arkham Knight reveal. Rocksteady made a big stink about how the identity of the titular villain of the game was a big secret. Batman fans were pretty sure we knew who he was but Rocksteady insisted the Arkham Knight was a new character. Turns out, they were lying. If you’re a Batman fan and already have a suspicion that you know who Arkham Knight is, you’re right. There really isn’t a big mystery. It’s just a new name and costume for an existing Batman character.
Finally, the Batmobile. Yes, it’s absolutely absurd that the Batmobile has a tank mode. Yes, it’s both contrived and ridiculous that the Arkham Knight sends a bunch of unmanned tank drones after Batman for him to blow up in the Batmobile. Yes, the Batmobile is massively shoehorned into all kinds of things in the game (both Riddler puzzles and the story itself). That said, did it ruin the game for me? No, but some of the game’s weakest/most frustrating moments were centered around the Batmobile. In fact, some of the biggest boss fights in the game were tank boss fights instead of legit actual boss fights like we got in the previous Arkham games.
Other complaints: Some of the race tracks are obnoxiously hard. (Yes, there are racetracks. For some reason.) And there are too many Riddler trophies (which you have to get to unlock the best ending.) The city looks great but is devoid of civilians again. (If inFamous could do civilians in a city on PS3 back in 2009, why hasn't Rocksteady found a way to implement them yet?) Most of the side quests are repetitive and not terribly interesting. The thugs' banter is good but repeats so many times and so often that it gets maddeningly annoying at the end of the game. Particularly if you're getting all the Riddler trophies. (Fortunately, you *can* mute dialogue to avoid hearing it.)
Despite that, it was quite enjoyable. It isn’t terribly well-written but it isn’t ruinously badly-written, either. It’s in line with the kind of writing you find in a typical Batman comic (i.e., not the standout good ones) but made more tolerable by the fact that it’s interactive. And their presentation is top-notch—Batman looks suitably awesome, the musical cues and cinematic camera angles are dramatic, and so forth. (The only hangup there is that the facial animations got a little weird sometimes. Particularly Batman's mouth. As my wife put it, he sometimes looks like he had a botched botox job.)
In line with the previous Arkham games, Batman is such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ed loner that I don’t know how we’re supposed to believe he ever trained three Robins and Batgirl. Which is a shame because when Batman *does* team up with one of his allies, it’s quite fun. Speaking of Batman's allies, it got really old how everyone who wasn’t Batman got captured and had to be rescued—find a new plot device to move things forward, guys.
The voice acting is generally very good. The Arkham Knight can get annoying but I can’t fault Troy Baker for that—he’s done great work in many other games.
While the fundamental mechanics of combat and predator challenges are the same as they’ve been in the previous Arkham games, Arkham Knight adds enough new features to make it interesting. It doesn’t have the same “been there, done that” feeling that Arkham Origins had. I had a good time with it. Hell, I'd say I enjoyed the Predator challenges more in this than I did in Arkham City.
Arkham Knight also has one of the best-looking Batsuits out there, which is something I appreciate. So although the Premium Edition came with a ton of alternate ones (there's 20 Batsuits in total), I found myself mostly sticking with the canon one for game. (Although the '89 movie Batsuit is totally awesome and my favorite alternate in any of the Arkham games.)
While I can see why a number of people had serious complaints about this game (particularly when I read how it was at launch, both in terms of the bugs and features they hadn’t added yet), I enjoyed it. If you really liked the previous Arkham games, or are a huge Batman fan, it’s worth getting. If you didn’t like the previous ones or hate open world games of the Ubisoft variety, this probably isn’t the game for you.

This shadow-based stealth game builds on everything its predecessor began.
To start, I'd like to say that this game is the masterpiece of its series and is a must-buy if you are even somewhat interested in the stealth genre.
Almost everything about this game is perfect.
You play as thief, god-killer, absolute legend Garrett and try to get to the bottom of the schemes of Karras, a shady figure who really likes steampunk and selling robots and cameras to ♥♥♥♥ing everyone.  As a sneaky boy who likes to hit fleshy people with blackjacks, these robots and cameras will present a large problem to you.  Funnily enough, if you beat the absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a robot with your blackjack for long enough, it will break, but it is easier to incapacitate them first with one of your water arrows (which are in limited supply) to their engines.
Level design is fantastic, better than the first game's.  Each level is nonlinear and massive in size.  The enemy AI is good, and does not fall apart when they start to look for Garrett (unlike this game's predecessor in which they simply moved toward Garrett while they looked for him).  Just like the last game, you have an arsenal of gadgets at your disposal that allow for unparalleled creativity in how you can approach an objective, including the iconic rope arrow (which allows for tons of creativity just on its own).  Enemies are diverse and challenging, and the levels often require you to find hidden areas or encourage you to find secrets.
Sword combat returns almost unchanged, which is good for the most part, but the abusability of overhead swings on human targets is the only flaw I can find with this game.
One of the greatest stealth games of all time: 9.5/10

Gaming "journalists" (read: glorified blogger) are busy latching on to games like Bioshock Infinite, The Last of Us, Gone Home, and the like because of their insecure need to validate their existence. "Look games can be art, 10/10," and "like art but with guns, 9.5/9.5," media coverage for gaming has some of the worst critical thinking skills in almost any media outlet. While those games are receiving all the limelight, games worthy of praise/discussion are swept under the rug if they are too difficult to understand or write articles on. Zeno Clash is one of those games and it is a game that should be discussed.
It's not easy to understand, the combat system may come across as divisive to some, and the world is a bizarre caricature of itself. The story, which I normally don't enjoy in videogames, is thought-provoking and handles it's themes well (if you can ignore the questionable voice acting). Bioshock Infinite glanced over it's themes, never actually questioning either side of the argument. It gave the player a peanut gallery of "hey guys, racism is not good" in-between slaughtering a brainless police force and moved on to the next thing without getting more than ankle deep. Whereas, Zeno Clash has a few themes and they drive the narrative. The violence in the game is explained in the world itself, which is a lawless, wacky, maybe post-apocalyptic setting where people use their fists to solve their problems. You rarely kill anyone, but still manage to fulfill your videogame violence quota in-between plot points.
So instead of the narrative driving the gameplay around like a cripple being pushed by an obtuse nurse, they work in unison. The controls in Zeno Clash can be janky at times and I would highly recommend a controller, but the combat is inventive, satisfying, and overall fun (buzzword, buzzword). Punching some weird bird-man in the face after he throws rocks at you is my new favorite game mechanic. I stated this before, but it's worth mentioning again: YOU RARELY, IF EVER, KILL ANYONE. You just beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of them.
Zeno Clash v. flavor of the month games is a lot like progressive v. pop music. One is easy to tap your foot to straight away and usually burns out quickly, the other is difficult by design and takes time to appreciate.
TL;DR Get Zeno Clash, play Zeno Clash.

I was worried from the first impressions that people on youtube had about this game. Having really enjoyed the first one, I was really excited with a sequel's potential, and yet, the general opinion was that this was a far less enjoyable game than the first Zeno Clash. Regardless, since I had the game, I decided to try to right after finishing the first.
So, let's say it has a pretty confusing and "not as exciting as I hoped for" beginning. Even having played the first one, this game throws you into the wolves right from the start in regards to its story, and that sort of continued through the rest of the game... That's my biggest complain.
There's a string of events between the first Zeno Clash and this one that they simply don't tell you. In the first one, Golem helps you through the journey and everything seems fine in the end. When this game starts, Ghat's feelings towards the Golem have changed entirely, which puts you in a weird position of not knowing why exactly that has happened.
But I'll go into that later.
The main focus of the last game, was the world they've built, which was weird as hell, but also beautiful in its own way, despite not having the opportunity to explore its full potential. I'm satisfied to say that the said issue has *mostly* been resolved with Zeno Clash II. You'll meet many more characters that give you more pieces towards understanding the world, and have many more different areas to roam around.
This time, however (and much to my sadness), the Corwids weren't given as much atention has in the last game, although there's some contact with them as well (read my impressions of the first Zeno Clash if you don't know what they are).
The scale of their world and story is far more grandiose in this game. Instead of worrying about your little world, doorways are opened into a larger world than zenozoik. You'll be able to understand the origins of this "tribe", and that was a great drive for me, the whole way through.
From the first game, you learned the world. This time, you learned how that world came to be, and that's pretty awesome.
My advice for playing the game: look for every Cube, and then go into the Secret Tunnels in the desert (do it towards the end). Also, find it by yourself, it's not too hard, and it's a great part about the world discovery! In that tomb you'll find more information that complement what you learn through the story nicely.
So, the world is still great, if not greater. What else? Characters!
This time, you'll meet other beings similar to Golem, you'll know their purpose, their origins, and to a point, their deep characters.
My main problem, as I said, was the main character, Ghat. At least for me, a Player vs. Player-Character conflict arose for me. (read more about it here
My own beliefs through playing the game were in a constant conflict with the actions that the game had me do. Those beliefs came to be from what I played in the first game... I came to play a certain Ghat that is incoherent with the actual Ghat, and that was a bit awkward, and something the designers should be more careful with next time around.
This may very well be a personal problem, but it contributed to my initial confusion, and detriment of the experience in the first hour or so.
Apart from that, the characters were as great, this time with a focus on Golems instead of Corwids, both unique and great to the world of ZenoClash.
So, the world and the characters have once again carried the game for me, and I loved it the whole way through. If you've enjoyed the first game, you definitely have to try this out, since the same aspects that made the first a great game, make this an even better game, since it has improved its flaws with a richer and more open world.
The combat system was fairly the same, with more combos, and a bit of Cooperative play, but not too much to make a big difference. It does not hinder the game, and it's a nice change of pace from most FPSs out there.
You still have primitive weapons which look great, although they're not really a necessity to go through the game.
Final thoughts:
The art direction was still awesome, creating a really rich world (both visually and conceptually), with its own backstory and look to it. The music didn't really standout for me, but it's not a major issue in any way.
If you haven't played the first Zeno Clash, go play it, and then play this. They're both very much worth your time if you enjoy having a completely different world to explore and great characters to talk to.

Remember when FMV arcade games were popular? I do, but that's because I'm older than dirt. Seriously though, I think that there's a certain charm to QTE-based FMV games. A lot of them feature dozens of ways to die, and it's amusing to see just what can go wrong, simply because you pressed up instead of down. It also helps that some games - like Dragon's Lair 2 - have really interesting visuals.
There's nothing amusing or visually interesting about Stay Dead Evolution. The developers of this game probably would have been better off trying to license some old Shaw Brothers films, and just slap a big red X on the screen whenever the wrong button is pressed. At the very least players would be treated to awesome fight sequences. Actually, I take that back. If there were fights worth watching, who would want to be forced to press buttons at the right moment, just to keep the action going? Admittedly, I'm going off on a tangent, but think about it for a second. You're given the choice between playing a videogame, or watching a Martial Arts movie. If you wanted a little of both, you'd play a fighter, or maybe a beatemup.
If you play this game, you're making a commitment. You're sacrificing your free-time in order to play a game that offers no entertainment. Even if we take away the amateurish production values and the boring fight-scenes, we're left with a game that's just really frustrating to play. Basically you hit the arrows when they appear onscreen and a little moving indicator is in the right spot. If you double-tap the keys when the right colors appear, you can perform combos or counter the opponent's attack. It's a pretty simple system to figure out, once you browse the tutorial.
So let's say you beat the first opponent. No wait, you humiliate him. He can't even land a hit, and you deliver a stunning combo that drains almost all of his health. So he forfeits the match and you're feeling pretty confident. However, when you face the next opponent, the QTEs speed up at an alarming rate. Your brain needs time to see A) what arrow-key to press B) the color of the box (which determines if you can combo/counter) and C) the little moving indicator that flies across the box. Even when your brain has gathered all of this information, you still have to press the key. This is where a lot of players are going to be tripped up. There's a little randomization and the window to press that key seems to vary in size. If your timing isn't super-precise, then you're going to take damage.
Apparently this is one of those games that you're supposed to play frequently. After a long enough period of time, you can adapt to the poorly-designed difficulty, and the absurd timing requirements. Your reward for mastering this game? Oh right, the snore-inducing fights.
In short: This is just one of many games in my library that has earned the rating of "YIKES!"

Review is for Enemy Within DLC:
This full expansion pack adds  new layers of strategy to the game, making the campaign much bigger.  It adds new enemies, mission types, maps, upgrades, soldier classes, and bonuses.  Everything is well balanced and integrates seamlessly into the original game, just like the great Civilization V expansion packs that have come out recently. The MELD resource is a new addition to most of the missions, there are usually 2 of them to capture on every mission and they have expiration timers, so you will constantly have to decide whether to turtle up, reload, overwatch and play it safe, or send some poor expendable to dash to grab it despite the danger.
I was surprised that this expansion pack was so big, and would recommend it to anyone who already owns the game, or is purchasing it for the first time.  If you have never played before, I'd recommend just ignoring the enemy unknown campaign and jump right into the Expansion Pack, you won't miss out on anything.

Really decent game. I've never played a game like this, and recommend it to anyone also unfamiliar with the genre. With the resurgence of the genre with games like Pillars of Eternity, Wasteland 2 & Divinity: Original Sin, I recommend Shadowrun Returns because it's pretty simple, and gives you a great idea of the style of gameplay.
It is fairly linear. Like, it's pretty much impossible to NOT do sidequests, as everything is laid out before the player. And as far as combat goes, there are a lot of different options, but they all kinda end up towards the same execution. Again, as someone unfamiliar with the genre, I didn't mind at all. Just a heads up if you are expecting something really deep though, the game might seem underwhelming for you. The story and setting are great though. Definitely really well written (though at times the dialogue was pretty cheesy) and the environments are really well detailed. Music was pretty good too.
A big downer for me was the techincal issues. Lots of restarting as the main menu wouldn't load properly. And even though my MacBook surpasses the requirements by a mile, sometimes there would be random drops from a steady 60 fps to 30 fps for no particular reason. (That was with I had no AA on.) I eventually turned up AA all the way, and it sat at a steady 30-40 fps and never went below. But still, would have been nice to have more optimization. And while the backgrounds and environments look nice, models are really ugly.
Either way, while the game isn't perfect, I definitely recommend it to beginners of the genre. There is more than enough in the game to make me interested in purchasing Dragonfall, which i hear to improve upon every aspect of Returns. I'd give Shadowrun Returns a final score of 6.9/10.

“Deux Ex” meets “Arcanum” — and there are few ways to see that.
Most obvious is the setting. Cyperpunk with magic, elves, orcs, dwarves, etc. Though I am not a huge fan of fantasy, it goes perfectly in such a blend. And the world lives. People react to latest events, there is a sense in visiting your acquaintances over and over.
Then, “Shadowrun” has a great story with lots of thoroughly written dialogues, impressive characters and plot bends, turns and twists. The tale that is told is mature, but not over the top gore fest (just the right amount of gore fest!). And the soundtrack is appropriately nice.
Then, there are many ways to complete each task. They depend on what class you choose — there are some of more classical ones and some more setting-specific, or you can create your own character build, selecting your own mix of skills. Beside that game gives you many choices to solve tasks — governed by how much you are willing to explore, dive into story and the world, in wide sense — globally, and narrow — in a current mission and location.
Overall a great experience for someone who like aforementioned classics and doesn’t mind reading lots of text. Like a book, y’know. Where you shoot and burn people.

This is a great game. An RPG Dungeon Crawler. You run along the paths, left clicking enemies to attack, and using cards against them. In the game, spells, skills, consumable items, and equipment come in the form of cards. You can find cards in chests and the occasional bookshelves.
One thing I like is that you go down the dungeon in 'quests', where each quest is a certain amount of floors, but before the game generates the next quest, you can use what's called the Flexiscope to adjust how big it'll be. When you choose the size(there's a button and a slider), it'll change how many floors there are, how big those floors are, the minimum amount gold and exp you'll earn on that quest, and roughly how long it'll take. It's done this way so people can choose their preferred size, and feel accomplished when they finish it. Only have about 10-15 minutes to spare? Choose the 'Small' quest size and finish it within that amount of time. Got plenty of time or prefer longer quests? Choose the Large size and it'll give you an hours' worth of Dungeons. Also, before you click to descend into a Dungeon Floor, it'll show you what type of monsters to expect, which is useful.
All Cards(spells, items, etc) can be upgraded with Rune Cards you find in the dungeon, increases their power(and mana cost) and in the case of items like potions, increases the amount you can carry at once.
Due to the procedural generation of the game, there's plenty of replayability. Theirs also 2 character classes at the time of this review: the Mage and the Warrior, both of which play quite differently from each other. Also, in the future, the Rogue Class will be added, which I know uses a bow, but I don't know too much else. Each Class has 3 character slots, so other people can create their own character.
This game has a distinct Diablo I/II feel to it. To the characters, the Dungeon(which is obviously the Catacombs from Diablo I), and even the cards.
I highly recommend this game to any fan of RPG's, lite hack n' slash games, or Diablo.

This is a great re-vamp for the series. I played this game day one and it was riddled with minor combat bugs which were ironed out in the coming months.  Each new addition to the Steam collection is priced and sold like a novel.

The people who made the game do a good enough job advertising the pros, so I'll just list the cons for the people who are looking for why they might not enjoy the game.
Cons;
-The biggest issue I've had is that some story missions will tweak with your current inventory for story purposes.  While this isn't an issue in itself, (and your gear is put aside for you) the problem is that not all your items will be restored.  It seems to be exclusive to equipped items and weapons, but I've lost rare items as a result.  Until it's addressed, don't take your rare equipment with you on story missions.
-Occassional glitches that might lead to you getting stuck in the enviroment.  Happens rarely though, and there's usually a way out.
-Exploding zombies that kill you instantly.  Not too many, but enough that they almost always catch you off-guard.
-Personal tastes on this one, but I dislike that the variety of melee weapons is bottle-necked based on survivor level.  The issue here is that, unless a lower level player drops them for me, I no longer have access to lower level melee weapon varieties.  I enjoy my katana, but I can longer purchase bats, cleavers, machetes, crowbars, etc, nor do I find them from loot.
Those things aside, this is one of the best games I've played in a while.  I'd give it an 8 out of 10.

"Why should I bother reading your review?" (Skip this if you want)
I've had video gaming as a hobby for 20 years, crossing all genres with a big appetite for survival, horror and RPGs. Hence why I decided to review dying light. I try to stay objective and neutral. Give credit where its due and use the stick where the game deserves to be criticized. Note that I'm a Non-Native English speaker.
The Good
The game has great graphics and the gameplay is fun. Despite the gameplay being repetative, the fun is not severely diminished  - because at its core - it is a very enjoyable "grinder" / sandbox all the way through. The crafting system is very basic, but better to have a basic crafting system than none. The upgrade trees was something I found alarming because though I do love RPG elements, I was afraid the game would become too easy with all these upgrades. However, the game managed to keep the challenge at a rate that always kept me at my toes even with a ton of upgrades. As for sidequests, they are actually kind of interesting in this game. Even a fetch quest can become fun through dialogue or challenge.
The Bad (VERY MINOR story spoilers)
The variety of opponents in this game is too low imo. But that becomes nitpicking. Because the biggest flaw this game has - is actually the personality of the main character. Though the story isn't that great or imaginative, I would consider it kinda good for what you'd expect from a Zombie game. The main character however, is a nightmare.
Your character is a whiny, unprofessional moron who gets emotionally attached to the doomed people of this ruined city. He cries when a story character dies, as if he cares. I had to roleplay that I was faking it. The main character is introduced as an agent whom sole purpose is to retrive a file. Then he starts crying and caring for the people in the city instead of doing his job. The white knight in shining armor of your main character becomes tiresome and obnoxious as he spews out ultra-moralistic crap as if he was the human embodiment of self-rightiousness. The main villain is also uninteresting and cliche and suffers the opposite, by being completely void of humanity and just "evil for the sake of evil".
TO SUM UP:
Though I personally never cared about graphics (i still consider Fallout 2, Morrowind and ff7 the best games out there) the graphics in this game is really good. But you need a decent rig.
The gameplay itself is great. It is fun despite being repetative.
Crafting system and upgrade system is good.
The challenge is not so hard that it becomes overly frustrating, but neither as easy that you risk to become bored.
Enemies are varied enough, but just barely, there should have been 1-3 more types of enemies.
The story itself is average, but better than I expected for a zombie survival. Side quests are surprisingly satisfying!
What really pulls the score down imo is the lack of some things in the story, like joining factions or faction vs faction assault/defense in the storyline, NPCs you genuinely care about etc.
BIGGEST OFFENDER is the main character and the main villain, they are both horribly written and it is impossible to symphatize with either. Your character is too "good" on the morality scale, at the point of it almost becoming repulsive. The main villain is unimaginatively written and is the standard one dimensional "evil for the sake of evil" boring archetype. Near the end of the game I hated the main character more than the villain.
All in all, 7.8/10 - I recommend this game.
If you like sandbox games, zombie apocalypse scenarios, survival games, horror and RPG elements and have a good PC, you will probably find this game worth the money. Do not however - expect the story, the main character or the main villain to provide any intellectual or emotional satisfaction on any level unless you are younger than 16 years old.

In Kane and Lynch you play as Kane, a convicted and hardened criminal on his way to death row for killing a man. On the transport truck to the prison Kane is broken out by Lynch, under instruction from a group known as “The 7”. The 7 are a powerful group of people and have it out for Kane, accusing him of taking money from them, and in turn have taken his wife and daughter hostage. Kane, under the supervision of Lynch, is given the order of getting The 7’s money in three weeks however he can, or they’ll kill his family. Kane can’t do it alone, so he enlists old friends in the trade to help him. The rest is up to you to find out, but I will say the title characters have great chemistry in their own screwed up ways, which is very enjoyable to see play out in their interactions together.

Kane & Lynch was such a polarizing game at the time of its release, you either absolutely hated it, or you liked it. The story itself is depressing with the twists and turns it provides making you feel upset, hopeless, and sad, much like the main character would feel like in those moments I’d like to think. There was no real hero to root for, the characters played true to their parts are very unlikeable, generally being the worst of criminal scum for their own reasons. The controls were at best wonkey and hard to control on console, with the PC release having technical issues of their own to overcome to ‘enjoy the game’. Even with this in mind I still highly recommend this game, it’s not for everyone, but for those that will enjoy it as I did and can see past some flaws, you’ll find a very gritty and interesting game that isn’t afraid to see its bleak narrative course to the end.

Normally, I might be saying wait for a better sale on this one -- or for a couple of updates.  It's a little slow right now, and I just did the dev survey saying as much.  It'd be nice if they added some more town options or sped up ways to level or access better cards sooner.  A tiny bit grindy, but then I'm an old dude who doesn't have tons of patience for hack and slash.
But here's why I don't regret paying the $14 summer sale price.
1. There was a free demo that let me see what I was getting into.  Yes, I know I can get a refund if I really don't like something, but a refund is a hassle compared to the no-hassle demo.
2. It's a unique indie.  The pop-up book graphics, the card system, the story-- these are what made me want to continue after the demo.  (The unique graphics kind of make the combat a little clunky, but again, the demo will let you know if you can handle the combat or if it's too awkward.)
3. Unlike countless other 'early access' games that haven't changed in years, this one seems to be under active development.  I mentioned the survey; the devs are aware of the potential areas for improvement, and they want to be responsive to the opinions of the players.
4. Why does the archdemon have a duck?
5. After the initial game start, the levels allow you to choose your own game-play times.  Have 8 minutes?  13?  Longer?  Good feature.
6. Did I already clear that area?  Did I miss anything?  This game answers those questions as you go. No more wondering if there is something more to see.
7.  I'll probably think of another item or two the next time I get into the game.  I'm also just scratching the surface of the game, and I haven't seen everything it has to offer.  I'm sure there will be plenty more to add here.

A charming Diablo inspired dungeon crawler with a unique art style. The game is polished enough to be released, except for the additional class (Warrior and Mage are currently available, Ranger is on the way) which is a welcome suprise amongst Early Access games.
Gameplay - Point and click, accessible enough to be turned into a mobile game. However, the card system is what stands out, loot and skills are placed into a pool of cards that can be equiped to your character. Think of this pool as your "hand". Your hand can be increased to equip more items and skills (healing potion, necklace of mana regeneration, etc.) making it so you can easily change a characters build, while maintaining anything you have upgraded back in town. Both of these elements bring a more casual feel to the game, which is complimented by the fact that dungeon crawls can be set to a certain time limit. If you want to go on a 5 min crawl, you can. Want an hour? Go for it. In the end, it comes down to managing your characters movement and skills, while adapting to the various types of enemies. And, if you feel like adding an extra edge, the option for perma death is available at character creation.

I first know about Shadowverse from my Facebook timeline, lot of friends play it. My first impression of Shadowverse is that it is "Hearthstone for weebs". But, one day, I was bored and try to find a new free-to-play game and decided to install this Hearthstone for weebs.
It was the best decision ever!
At the beginning, Shadowverse give you a tutorial; you know, like how to play the game. After finished the tutorial, they'll give you a LOT of freebies like Rupies (gold), Crystals, and even pack (booster) tickets; if I remember correctly, it was 20 pack tickets for two expansion (Standard & Darkness Evolved). You can spend Rupies to buy an extra pack (1oo Rupies for a pack) or buy new Leaders (in-game character; cosmetic only).
Shadowverse is a fast-paced card game, kinda like Yu-GI-Oh! in XYZ/Synchro/Pendulum era. You can choose one from seven playstyle (each playstyle have different Leader) that have its own power and weakness. With combination and strategy of cards (Follower, Spell, Amulet) in deck, you must deplete enemy Leader's shield (20 point). There's also a evolution mechanism that evolve your Follower to have more Atk/Def point or even new effect.
There are Solo and Multi mode. In Solo mode, you can experience some in-game story/lore for each Leader or do Pratice versus any Leader of you choice. In Multi mode, you can choose unranked match, ranked match, or private match with your friend. There is also an Arena mode in which you play Take Two by building a 30-cards deck by choosing one of two pairs choice; there are total five match in Take Two and you'll get better rewards for every win.
In the latest update, you can now buy a pre-built deck which is good for starter. Each pre-built deck can be bought for 500 crystals for the first time and 750 crystals for the second and third time (you can only buy each pre-built deck three times).
Oh, don't forget that you can sync the game data with the mobile version (Android/iOS) so you can play on the go.
It's gorgeous! The artwork of every card is beautiful and cool. There's even some animated card which make it more gorgeous than a standard card. If you like some "fan-service"artwork, you'll find it here too.
Most of the card have its own voice; the English voice is pretty good in my opinion (my favorite is the voice of "Aurelia, Regal Saber" and "Oathless Knight"). If you prefer, you can switch to Japanese voice by choosing Japanese language in Steam' Properties settings.
Like other free-to-play games, there is an in-app purchase options for you. You can spend real money to buy Crystals that can be used to buy pack, pre-built deck, and Leader. Cygames usually offer a good deal (like one-time offer and new year's sale) to buy crystals.
In summary, Shadowverse is a must-try card game for you all!

This is an extremely early review into their Early Access stage. In the future I will probably change my review.
I have extremely high hopes for this game! It's fun and quick, but not without fault. I'll split this into positives and negatives.
Pros:
+ Extremely easy to pick up
+ Pretty neat aesthetic
+ Most if not all of the promised features in the game already work (I feel like this is important to note with Early Access titles in 2017)
+ Devs are definitely devoted
+ Love the health system. There's something great there! It's not a simple health bar, but instead an immersive and in-depth overview of how screwed you are. Not enough RPGs take that into consideration!
+ Every dwarf has personality!
Cons:
- Changing controls doesn't seem to work. I've tried three times to change my controls and have been unable to.
- The attacking/counterattacking system doesn't feel very satisfying, as combat usually is 1v3-1v6, not allowing for any sort of attack other than spam left clicks and kite. Throwing is extremely useful in this regard, though.
- The sound is all over the place from quiet to explosively loud
- Compared to Kingdom too much, the game is way different than Kingdom. I totally see where the comparison is from the aesthetic, but gameplay-wise it's very unique.
- Pacing is very poor as of right now, you can play 30 minutes and already have a great deal of buildings built. As a result, it doesn't feel very rewarding to build the next one.
- The resolution of the game itself feels too low, and could be a little zoomed out.
- Any problem your character has from battle is instantly cured by a little apothecary dwarf for a few coins. It kinda removes the intensity of the health system they have in place
The cons will probably will be worked out with a little polish. I don't often say that, but I get a good vibe from these guys. All in all, this game is shaping up quickly. At the rate they're going, it looks like by it's release it'll be an extremely solid game, and a steal at the asking price!

X-Com Enemy Unknown is a rare type of game that only come's around once in awhile. It is gripping, crafty, and terrifying. An engrossing, deep turnbased combat game, married neatly with a real time strategic base mechanic makes this one of the standout titles of 2012.
X-Com is a successor of the classic X-com titles from the mid to late 90's. While this new title has been developed by a differrent company, Firaxis, they have managed to preserve what was so enthralling about X-Com and the alien threat. With a new engine,powered by Unreal Engine 3, Firaxis brought X-Com to a new generation with slick graphics and fresh gameplay.
X-Com has two main layers. The first is the "meat" of the game, which is the tactical combat. Players are tasked with squads between 4 to 6 elite soldiers, each with varying skills and abilities that are unlocked as they get kills and survive more missions. A range of custumizable options are in the game, such as changing their appearance or names, and choosing different skills as they become available. On the battlefield players are faced with the ever imposing alien threat, which is intelligent and ruthless. The aliens have many different species, which act as the classes. From the lowly sectoid to the fearsome muton, players will be constantly challenged with ever increasing numbers and powers. All the aliens feel very distinct, and the ai does avery good job of keeping players on their toes. They will use any advantage they can get,be it suppression and flanking, or simply ganging up on one man, and will remorselessly destroy the unprepared squad. Thankfully X-Com has a few tricks of their own. As players progress, new armour and weapons become available, such as the S.H.I.V, a mobile weapons platform that replaces a soldier in the field and can act as agressive mobile cover, or the skelton suit, which allows soldiers to use a grapple hook to reach elevated positions. Perfect for getting that sniper in for the kill. Late game will players will see even more advanced alien technologies be adapted for your soldiers use, and even delve in to phsycic abilities.
The second layer of X-Com is the base management. This is where players are tasked with monitering global panic, issuing promotions to vetrans, researching alien technologies, and contructing a fortified base from which to launch operations. It is here that all new weapons and tactics become available, so it is crucial to manage X-Com's limited resources wisely, as one mistake could leave you without the proper weapons or technology to survive the increaing alien menace. As permadeath is in the game, players must strive to keep their soldiers equipped with the latest and greatest if they hope to achieve victory. Missions will occur at random and vary from seek and destroy, a timed bomb diffusal in which the player must find and diffuse bombs scattered around the map before an alotted amount of turns, to Vip escorts. Each mission takes place on a randomly chosen map, so no two playthroughs are the same.
X-Com Enemy Unknown is a a fantastic title that will challenge and entertain, and I highly recommend to all types of gamers.
