tldr: a fun unique game that brings back memories of Kingdom combined with a skill based open world RPG. Enough available content alrady in the Early Access version, lots of unique areas to visit, enemies to fight, quests to do, loot and resources to collect in order to gear up fight bosses, level up and unlock more skills to complete quests and build your dwarven kingdom.
If Kingdom and Elder Scrolls had a baby, that would be called Regions of Ruin. RoR is hevily inspired by Kingdom but it's a completely different game at the same time, it's a side-scrolling RPG where you explore, fight, level up, and build your town. The world has a ton of unique areas, quests, loot and resources waiting for you. You will die a lot or you can change the difficulty if you are not into fighting signigicantly better than you enemies, you can visit and complete each area in the order you chose and you can recruit mercenaries to assist you in combat and workers to farm resources for you.
The combat is trickier the higher the difficulty you chose, you can dash to avoid enemies, or sneak to sneak attack them, you have a power hit and the ability to throw axes in your enemies face. When you level up, you unlock abilities that will make your job easier. The skill tree has 4 categories: melee attacks, ranged attacks, shield and power hits and you can chose the path that fits to your playstyle. There is a good variety in the enemies already in the Early Access version and bosses that you can find the more you explore the map in the further away areas.
You "build" your town by spending resources for buildings that automaticaly get build there for you. Some of them offer you different things for example a tavern to hire recruits to assist you in combat, or a forge to make your own equipment and an apothecary to make bandages. There are 8 buildings currently available that can also be upgrated to provide more perks.
There is an open world, you visit new in the order you want and all of them are handcrafted not procedurally generated. That means that everything is placed there for a reason. There isn't an infinite world but it has almost 60 areas already in the Early Access version for you to explore. The areas can be forests, deserts, caves, farms, ruins, strongholds but each one of them is different from the previous ones. You always have new stuff to do and find.

There is a good variety of npcs (50+?), most of them with unique dialoque. Some of them offer you quests to help them in one way or an other, some of them come and stay in your settlement to be used (medic, blacksmith, vendors etc) and some others you can used as workers to farm resources for you.
The lore is a mystery you have to figure out by talking to people and collecting some book pages. Currently not finished in the EA version but there are some good amount of text already written. You can also notice a subtle sense of humor in some area's signs or in the gameplay itself, for example your injuries names or that you can apply your skill points by pressing P (peeing) in the campfire etc.
The art style you either love or hate, it's a decent pixelart with some nice scenery and lots and lots of different hand drawn areas, buildings, enemies, npcs, items and biomes.
The music is fantastic, gotta love it when a game has a good soundtrack that fits the games universe and hypes you.
Controls offer you a variety of options, i use keyboard but as far as i know the controllers will be fully supported too. I tested it in windows but also as far as i know the game runs smoothly on Linux and Mac too. Performace is great in my 5+ year old laptop with an i5@1.80ghz and a gtx970m, it will probably run smoothly in any pc.
The game still needs a lot of work to extend the content, new areas to visit, new quests and maybe more weapons, armor types and buildings for your settlement and of course the lore, the ending and everything story-related but i'm sure everything will be there in the full version.
The developer is a solo-dev, very passionate about this game since the day i met him he is fixing bugs left and right and adds new content in regular basis. The current version of the game offers you at least 12-15 hours of play time that can be easily reach the 20 depending on your playstyle and difficulty (edit: apparently some people after the EA launch are finishing it in 5-10 hours so it's totaly up to you how much it will take to you for now). They plan to make the content triple during the early access, the map is huge and only 1/3-1/4 of it is available currently so i expect it will need 40-60 hours to complete it after EA. The game is fun, unique and if it seems interesting/promising for you i would highly recommend it to you to check it out and give it a chanse.

This game is an odd one. Every single criticism that you've heard about this game just might be valid, but that still doesn't hinder my recommendation of this game.

Yes, the recoil on the guns is absurd. This isn't a problem, because bullets are much more damaging when they actually hit what you want them to.
Yes, the graphics are dated, but it's early 360/PS3 graphics, so that makes more sense than it would otherwise.
Yes, the characters are all but unlikable. However, this seems to be intentional, as IO interactive stated in an interview before release that you shouldn't be trying to do so. Think about movies like The Departed. There's nobody to root for, not even the titular protagonists. Fortunately, the further you progress, the more that Kane and Lynch ♥♥♥♥ up. The characters, not the game.

Yes, the story is confusing, but it's only confusing if you don't bother to put the puzzle pieces together and try to figure out the facts from what little information. It's like the story in Dark Souls in that way. The only difference is that this is fresh territory that nobody has bothered to theorycraft yet, so go nuts blazing a trail that nobody's blazed before.

LEGO Marvel SuperHeroes is a extremely fun LEGO game with a funny and wonderful original story containing alot of the big names of the Marvel Comics universe and a tiny bit of their movies. - Large open world of Manhattan with recognisable comic locations
- Large roster of characters such as The Avengers, The X-Men, The Fantastic Four, or even the bad guys such as the Sinister Six or the Brotherhood of Evil. Even little extras such as Stan Lee himself, Deadpool, Venom, Doctor Strange, Ghost Rider, etc.
- 15 Fun Story levels
- Good soundtrack

- Deadpool Missions after completing the story
- A bundle of fun sidequests

I must say it's been quite the pleasant surprise.
I was a bit scared at first with the slightly lame intro sequence, but the game play is solid.
It's a diablo style game, mixed in with a cards=powers style gameplay at a glance, but there's a lot to like beyond that.
The levels are very much a completionist paradise, where it tracks how many monsters, loot piles and whatever are still remaining (you get bonuses for leaving nothing behind) and there's no Inv really.  You level up with a very basic system but there's some elegance there with the trade off of mana maximums for artifact items (which are like passive buffs).
Also strangely at first, your mouse is where your character kinda is, as opposed to where your icon on screen. You move the mouse over loot, power ups, or monsters to attack them, and dont have to endlessly walk up to stuff to hit it. Once you get the hang of it, diablo's old school 'using my legs like a sucker!' seems pretty lame by comparison.  There's still dodging and so forth, but having to quickly click on a shield icon for enemies to bypass defenses, or click on your own health orb to try and rapidly remove poison becomes a game in itself as the madness of♥♥♥♥♥♥on the screen everywhere takes over.
Gives you a few levels to get into the swing of it, and early game pacing is good.

A classic that any fan of the stealth genre should play. Thief II offers an experience that feels fresh even today thanks to its in depth stealth system. The stealth mechanics rely on both sound and sight so there is always a moment where you're in the dark but a guard is coming towards you. Do you remain in the dark and hope that he does not get close enough to see you? Or do you move and hope that he does not hear you? Way too many games simply forget about the sound detection. Combine this with an interesting story and good level design and you realize why Thief II makes for a timeless classic.

Interesting game with a very tiny target audience.
Super Hexagon is a very basic "Don't Collide!" game, similar to early racing games where all you do mechanically is to steer left and right.
You do that with under the most minimal of error margins.
Prepare to die not only very often but in repeated succession that makes 'Dark Souls' feel like 'Barbie's Adventure in Teletubbieland'.
On the flipside, you'll be thrown right back into the fray in about a second.
Visuals are boldly simplistic but fitting and form a chic symbiosis with the soundtrack.
Menus, controls etc are well done as is the level design.
CPU load is surprisingly heavy.
If you have lots of spare time on your hand, enjoy the classic vg inspired beats, have a masochistic streak and enjoy a healthy hand-eye coordination, check out the store video if you're into Ilynxesque reflex games.
As Steam ratings are binary, I have to assume that the dear reader of this review is probably not among this l33t hardcore crowd .
Shame the game would not feature an easy mode or an editor.

Everything below is just my honest opinion. Everyone has one.
TL;DR:
The game is worth the money. Go get it. Go find 5 friends to play with. Go spend a couple of dozens of hours, or more if you feel so. 8.5/10 (see, you dont even have to scroll down :>).
Now, a bit more expanded:
CONTENT
Some people like to compare KF1 to KF2. Here's my comparsion.
By the date of release, KF2 has:
- 12 maps (KF1 had 5)
- 10 perks (KF1 had 6, they added Demolitionist later on)
- All the KF1 enemies + 1 more boss (and 1 more coming in the future) + 2 more variations of the weakest enemy (and 1 more variation of another enemy coming soon)
- 4 guns for each of the 9 "unique" perks + a few offperk weapons (I'm not sure how many did KF1 had on release)
- a unique grenade for each of those perks (KF1 had like 3 types if I recall correctly: regular grenade, Commando's HE grenade and Support's grenade; later on they added healing grenade for the Medic)
- 2 game modes + 1 probably coming in the future (KF1 had 1 + 1 more was added later on)
Sure, at the moment, KF1 has way more content than KF2 (atleast map- and gunswise), but let's not forget that all this content was added into the game over the course of many years. I, ofcourse, cannot guarantee that KF2 will have that much content in the future too, but TWI (developers) already promised us more content in the future. It's up to you to trust them or not. But my opinion: they did it for KF1, there's a high chance they will for KF2 as well.
GAMEPLAY
For people who are new to KF:
It's great. Fast paced destruction of waves of enemies that seem to never run out of livestock using various methods of creating holes and scorchmarks on things and making different parts of the same fleshy object suddenly move in completely different directions.
It can get repetitive in time, but it depends on how much you love that kind of stuff. When it does, you can switch to Versus mode for a different perspective one the game. Though still, Co-op is the main thing to play KF2 for.
For the people who played and are familiar with KF1:
The basic formula is the same: hold out hordes of Zeds by correctly distributing the responsibilities over the team and eradicating everything that comes close. And then defeat the boss. Personaly for me it's enough to call it a KF game. Then it adds some other touches like: Stumble/Knockdown mechanics, enhanced melee system (Block/Parry in particular), Perk skills system, sprinting, and other stuff that I'm too lazy at this point to recall. All of this is what's required to call it "KF2" and not "KF1 with pretty graphics". Otherwise the game would have no sense. If you don't like these changes, then it's probably better to save the money and stay in the good old KF1.
SOME CONTROVERSIAL MOMENTS
Microtransaction and Versus mode in a Co-op game.
I dont have anything against MT's: they're purely cosmetical. Don't like it? Don't need it? Don't use it. Simple. That's what I do.
I don't have anything against VS mode either. It's just the same. Don't like it? Don't play it. Any balance changes made for VS don't affect Co-op. You can set the filter to Survival and forget about VS forever if you feel so. Though I personaly enjoyed VS quite a bit. It's a good change of pace after dozens and hundreds of hours killing Zeds.
GRAPHICS and SOUND
The game looks gorgeous. 'Nuff said. That's something that everyone will agree on I think. Persistent blood, 19 (?) points of dismemberment on each enemy, cool guns sounds and reloading animations with high tickrate to look even coller in Zed time... and Zed time! KF's slow-mo that makes it look like you're in Sin City movie.
Music is any metalhead's dream (can always turn it off if you feel so).
VERDICT
Sure, it has many differences from KF1, but if it didn't, it would be just an expensive graphical patch for KF1 and, therefore, wouldn't have much point of existing.
Sure, the devs didn't bring everything they promised (Crawlers still can't traverse the walls and ceilings; Martial Artist will not happen, though developers never officialy announced it as far as I remember, it was rumored by the people who were surfing the game files, I may be mistaken here), but I'm looking at the game in it's release state and what it turns out to be at the moment and not what it might have been if things would go different.
Overall, I don't regret the money and hundreds of hours I spent on it.

Any first person puzzle game situated in colorful, abstract environments that promises to bend your mind is instantly appealing to me. Antichamber won't be a game I'll have to sell to anyone - it knows its audience. I'm more interested in explaining why it's less successful than I had hoped, and why, nearly a year after my feverish desire to start it, I have only just picked it back up and finished it.
Antichamber is a game best enjoyed on a calm night with a cold beer. Progress may or may not happen in any given session, and there is a distinct possibility that you'll just wander around in circles for an hour and give up. This isn't because you're obtuse, but because Antichamber partakes in very little handholding, and the speed of your success is largely going to depend on your grasping some of the game's fundamental mechanics, which you'll need to discover mostly on your own.
The highest praise I can offer about the experience is how satisfying it is towards the last couple of hours. Antichamber relishes in teaching you concepts and mechanics throughout its entire length, and while I'm not a big fan of how it's set up (more below), in the end you'll feel like you've conquered one big puzzle chamber, rather than just a series of its constituent parts. The payoff is a really cool ending sequence that is mostly worth the effort to experience.
Antichamber's environment is one large interconnected labyrinth. (Large in the $20 indie game sense, which means fairly small, equating roughly to the size of the original Portal.) Its passages and puzzle rooms loop into each other in an abstract way. Any area can lead instantly to any other, and while this sounds good in theory, as you advance and discover new rooms, it's progressively harder to remember and understand how exactly to get back to a previous area you want to go to. Oftentimes, it's literally impossible. The game alleviates some of that frustration by allowing you to access the game's hub room with the Esc key, which features a map of the entire labyrinth and all its rooms, each of which you can instantly link to. The map itself is close to useless for typical navigation, since in this game, rooms can connect in ways that can't be depicted in two or even three dimensions.
The problem with this approach is that it breaks the flow and immersion of the game, since you come to realize that backtracking (and forwardstracking, I guess) through the puzzle rooms is largely inefficient compared to immediate access of any given puzzle. It winds up being largely inconsequential how all the rooms connect, since there's no real way to understand Antichamber as a whole structure. The only way to grasp it is by viewing each room as an island - it doesn't matter how it connects to the others, since each room's puzzle is an isolated affair and can be accessed with a simple click of the mouse on the map.
Early on in the game, you start to run into unsolvable puzzles that you may or may not understand are initially unsolvable until you tinker unsuccessfully with them for a while. This is because your only tool is a gun that absorbs and shoots little cubes that you need to interact with in various ways, and while you (again) may not realize this at first, the gun itself has hidden upgrades that make said cubes act differently. It becomes a Metroidvania style of exploration - running very frequently into inaccessible areas you'll have to take note of to try again later when you've failed to figure them out.
Oftentimes you will solve a puzzle in Antichamber, only to have the exit lead to a place you've already been. In other instances, working on a solution will lead you to a secret room that has no exit or reason for existing, or again to an elusive "pink cube" that (spoiler) serves absolutely no purpose in the game. The game's exit itself can be accessed before a good portion of the game is even solved, rendering the whole thing a bit inconsequential in my mind. There's no justification to much of the game's environments, and this is where a bit of linear design would have helped. I can hear the counterargument, the idea that a good labyrinth will have a plethora of dead ends and red herrings, but ultimately a sense of concrete progress can be hard to feel, robbing you of much of that satisfaction inherent to solving puzzles.
There are various panels scattered throughout the labyrinth that can be activated to display an image and some text. Finding every one of these panels (a feat kept track of in the hub room) is this game's version of completion, and once you figure out how to interpret the map (it's not obvious), you can busy yourself in the endgame by revisiting all the incomplete puzzle rooms to search for those last missing panels. It's just enough to get you to explore the entire labyrinth front-to-back, yet the rewards for finding the game's secrets just aren't that interesting - rooms filled with concept art, 3D model museums, and other frivolous filler. Some sort of overall reward for finding all the secrets, like maybe a bonus ending or extra challenging puzzle sequence, would have been better.
What's unique in Antichamber, yet falls a bit flat in my opinion, is that your Cube Shooter is the main puzzle of the game. The behavior of the cubes you absorb from and shoot back into the environment follow a set of specific rules that are not always explained. These rules form the bulk of Antichamber's challenge, and to be quite honest, the rules aren't very logical. You have to interact and tinker enough to figure the rule sets out, but it's entirely possible to solve a puzzle accidentally without comprehension of the rule in play, or even solve one in a way the developer did not intend. With a limited set of tools, you can break the game several times and access areas too early if you're clever enough.
So with regards to the gun/cube manipulation, I never found myself in that wonderful "AHA!" moment when comprehension suddenly dawned on me - I was always a bit behind what the developer was hoping I would understand, and I was getting through the game in such a way that I wasn't even sure if it was actually CORRECT. Having completed the entire game and having found all of its chambers and panels (resorting to a guide in only one instance), I am still unsure of precisely how a few of the cube mechanics work, and that's not saying anything good about the principal gameplay factor.
And honestly, all of this comes by choice of design, I think. The developer was probably aiming for a nonlinear puzzle game that offered numerous possibilities of solutions and ways through. In this sense, the developer succeeded. It was just a less satisfying approach than I would have hoped.
I'm still recommending the game though since it did a lot of things right. The visual style is interesting, with its mostly sparse environments accented with flourishes of color. I think this game is about life and death, so while the environments are very rigid in architecture, the sound design is intentionally organic, often evoking outdoor environments and weather phenomena. The music is perfectly ambiant, and some of the puzzles are genuinely exceptional.
It's an easy recommendation for fans of the genre, and while my overall impression is definitely positive, there were times it just left me a bit cold.

TL:DR - this game is a Diablo clone. Not of the game mechanics & look, weirdly, but the setting and general story. Pointless. Anything original about the game is killed by the Diablo setting and story which is so heavily used it's overwhelming.
Long Version:
I really love the look of this game, the mechanics are novel, work very well and are pretty exciting. The voice acting is great, and overall I would give this 100% for presentation and gameplay. I want to love this SO MUCH.
So why am I not recommending this game? The story setting is basically just Diablo. I mean, almost exactly. The only thing they haven't done is use the same names. The village is recognisable, there's a kindly old sage advising you, and a friendly barmaid, a healer, a witch (sorry... fortune teller), and the Cathedral. The few townsfolk left suspect their Bishop has been kidnapped and is under the cathedral, then in the level preview you see you'll be fighting "The Cook", a demon who looks exactly like The Butcher, and there's the corrupted evil Bishop! And under it all, is a devilish boss who looks pretty diabolic. Even with his rubber ducky. The dungeon look and contents feel painfully familiar and unfortunatly take away from the few original and novel monsters. Even the music is just a re-arrangement of Diablo's. It's really killing the joy of the new mechanics for me.
Look, I love a homage as much as the next person. But I've played Diablo for the last 20 years. A few clever references, a loving homage here and there to some beloved character like Cain for example... that would have charmed and delighted me. But basically just copying everything? It feels lazy and tired. I'm not able to really enjoy all the original things done with the mechanics or the novel bosses (like the big Gargoyle and his minions). I feel like a HUGE ball got dropped here and I don't understand why this game is getting such ravingly positive reviews honestly. The unoriginality of the story and setting take away a huge chunk from what otherwise would have been an exciting new game which brings new mechanics to a very "done" genre (done as in, there's a LOT of hack & slash games out there, not as in no one wants to play them).
There are enough Diablo clones out there, and even then most of them only clone the gameplay, I don't get why Thing Trunk thought it would be a good idea to just use the Diablo story instead of come up with something original. I also wouldn't be surprised to see them getting contacted by Blizzard with a C&D, you can't just change the names and pretend it's an original story when it's so painfully recognizable. It's not like they have done a really clever parody of it, it's just the same with different names.
I only hope that each additional "book" they add isn't a slavish recreation of something else like this one is.

Dying Light is a zombie game which isn't shy of upholding cliches but does so in a fun and innovative way. Comparing the game to Dead Island (: Riptide) the game has fixed a lot of the core flaws and completely rebooted the story in a new setting with new parkour mechanics. The game does this very well, you start up with a character which is fumbling around in the dark, has no idea what to do and your parkouring still has to evolve. The pacing is really good for the first few hours. However this turns into disaster real quick. If you start co-op and do a few side-quests, your leveling will lead you to overpowered skills much too fast, obliberating minibosses with a few hits while that shouldn't feel possible as it makes the kills majorly disappointing. It goes from bad to normal to holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I'm a biotic spiderman with guns parkour, which is fun for new players to the freerunning scene but doesn't feel as fun for the purist parkour-only Mirror's Edge players.
The story, as-is, is a bit lackluster. It doesn't include backstory (just a bit in the side-quests) and you don't really feel as if you're involved in a greater world with a lot of things going on. The architecture and levels reflect this, have a lot of conflicting design choices. Of course, this is Techland and they did not think this through, no biggie, the gameplay makes up for it. Smashing zombies in and running around the place with the day-night mechanics makes for a very fun game where you just want to run around and explore every inch.
Even though the scaling isn't brilliant and the story isn't up to par, the gameplay, gunplay, graphics are all awesome and fun. If you can see through the 00's zombie action movie cliches, love blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up with your fists and traps and you really like freedom of movement in a game, Dying Light is just for you.

I had high hopes, and still, the documentary is as good as I thought it would be.
Valve already accustomed us with high quality games, sometimes even teasing and toying with fans about their releases. But they follow one rule, they officially release their products when they are done.
This documentary has been in the works since 2011, teased and thought to be released in 2012, but they still fine-tuned it and finally released on March 19th 2014.
The film brings us to 3 different worlds, we follow the emotional journey of 3 e-sports players, from their home countries to the first million dollar prized gaming tournament, set in Cologne in 2011. We watch these professional gamers personal histories, we get to know the reason for their ambition to become the champion, and why they set that goal. It's 3 different stories of 3 pro gamers, with totally different backgrounds but with one goal in common.
The film directs us to one question, are e-sports that different from the normally conceptualized sports? In the end, aren't the struggles the same when we compare a professional gamer to a "normal" athlete? When going down a professional competitive road we all have to make the tough choices. You cannot be a good gamer if you want to stay on E-sports, to survive you have to be the best, and the film shows how our subjects clearly have that in mind and how they constantly on internal conflict, sometimes requiring a leap of faith to get your dreams.
I wholeheartedly recommend this film, Valve managed to make me feel, get excited, and make me sad, in a space of little more than an hour. It's really well done and beautifully captured. Be sure to notice the players reactions and expressions throughout the film, sometimes you get more answers just by looking at their eyes, witnessing their feelings of despair, loss, and happiness.

This game, like its predecessor Thief 1, grasped the essentials of stealth gameplay almost 15 years ago. No game since has done anything like this, which is why Thief 2: The Metal Age remains at the top of any list of games with stealth focus even today.
Aside from the fantastic stealth gameplay, it is the atmosphere created by the interplay of level, sound and lighting design that serves to fully immerse the player into Thief's steampunk setting after the initial shock of the dated graphics has worn off. The textures might look blurry, the particle effects on streetlights like something out of an 80's arcade game, and the polygon count in single digits, but none of it matters once you have sneaked past the first guard, relieving him of his purse in the process.
The horror elements of the first Thief are a bit more subdued in the sequel, and more emphasis is placed on the pure stealth and thievery aspects, which is something I personally prefer. However, the story is just as gripping as in Thief 1, with old aquaintances making an appearance and old feuds buried for the sake of new make-shift alliances. I would definitely recommend you play Thief 1 first, and then return to play Thief 2, if only to be able to fully appreciate the story of Thief 2.

What to say about XCOM-Enemy Unknown? I loved it. I've sunk, nearly 40 hours or so into it so far, and Just Finished off the main story for the first time.  The Basics - Aliens attack Earth, You are the Unnamed Commander of the XCOM Project, a secret shadowy Paramilitary Unit that is created to defend the earth from the unusual, the strange and the alien. your goal - Protect Humanity,
The Good - The strategic overlay is very in depth, the GUI is pretty tight and you have a fairly deep customization options at your disposal, you can change what your guys and girls look like, what they take into battle and there skill sets over time as they go for Rookies to battle Hardened Vets. its this deep system that really makes you attached to the characters and their story even though the game doesn't tell  you one, you very easily make it up as you go within the overall story arch of the game, you will develop favorites, and you will feel bad if you get one of them killed. the difficulty curve is significant, the games job is to kick your♥♥♥♥♥and that it does very well.  The Combat system itself is tactical turn based and you have to think sometimes several turns ahead to make the best use of your squads skills, doing so can turn a furball of a firefight into a much easier time than just rushing in headlong guns blazing. The Graphics are also pretty Good, and if you run an ENB you can get some quite lovely visuals out of it.
The Bad? There are Bugs. Oh Yes. Some of them Frustrating as hell. One in particular that I ran into frequently was the game glitching up during a squaddies turn and unable to do anything, or switch to another soldier, usually because of elevation issues, requiring a reload, Also sometimes it can randomly CTD during Tactical Gameplay, though speaking for myself I did not run into these until I installed the slingshot and elite soldier packs, so take that for what it is, perhaps I was just lucky up to that point either way many hardships can be avoided by saving often.  The main story itself is also rather confusing and you will be as confused at the end as you were in the beginning for why the aliens invaded in the first place. So if that's a deal breaker for you then, you have been fairly warned, Alas it is also not very Mod Friendly.
All of that said However, The Fun and enjoyment I am getting out of this game are by and large vastly out way the negatives I highly recommend it. :)

This was a pleasant surprise.
It's a FPS Puzzle/Platformer with minimalistic graphics, but that doesn't mean it's not a "pretty game".  The lack of details help it accomplish some of the dimension-bending puzzles that make Antichamber such a trippy experience.
The best comparison I can think of is Portal, but only in game mechanics.  Otherwise the games are complete opposites, and yet both still work beautifully.
Portal = Fleshed out story; Antichamber = No story provided at all (you make your own guesses on what's going on)
Portal = Humorous characters and script; Antichamber = No talking or other characters (you are completely alone)
Portal = The game provides direction on where to go or what to do; Antichamber = You get no help.  Explore and figure it out yourself.
Both games = You get a nifty "gun" to help you
Like Portal, Antichamber ends up being a fairly short game (the gameplay is mainly from exploration and trying to figure out what to do), but if you enjoyed Portal and can get Antichamber for a good deal, then I definitely recommend picking it up.

Everything below is just my honest opinion. Everyone has one.
TL;DR:
The game is worth the money. Go get it. Go find 5 friends to play with. Go spend a couple of dozens of hours, or more if you feel so. 8.5/10 (see, you dont even have to scroll down :>).
Now, a bit more expanded:
CONTENT
Some people like to compare KF1 to KF2. Here's my comparsion.
By the date of release, KF2 has:
- 12 maps (KF1 had 5)
- 10 perks (KF1 had 6, they added Demolitionist later on)
- All the KF1 enemies + 1 more boss (and 1 more coming in the future) + 2 more variations of the weakest enemy (and 1 more variation of another enemy coming soon)
- 4 guns for each of the 9 "unique" perks + a few offperk weapons (I'm not sure how many did KF1 had on release)
- a unique grenade for each of those perks (KF1 had like 3 types if I recall correctly: regular grenade, Commando's HE grenade and Support's grenade; later on they added healing grenade for the Medic)
- 2 game modes + 1 probably coming in the future (KF1 had 1 + 1 more was added later on)
Sure, at the moment, KF1 has way more content than KF2 (atleast map- and gunswise), but let's not forget that all this content was added into the game over the course of many years. I, ofcourse, cannot guarantee that KF2 will have that much content in the future too, but TWI (developers) already promised us more content in the future. It's up to you to trust them or not. But my opinion: they did it for KF1, there's a high chance they will for KF2 as well.
GAMEPLAY
For people who are new to KF:
It's great. Fast paced destruction of waves of enemies that seem to never run out of livestock using various methods of creating holes and scorchmarks on things and making different parts of the same fleshy object suddenly move in completely different directions.
It can get repetitive in time, but it depends on how much you love that kind of stuff. When it does, you can switch to Versus mode for a different perspective one the game. Though still, Co-op is the main thing to play KF2 for.
For the people who played and are familiar with KF1:
The basic formula is the same: hold out hordes of Zeds by correctly distributing the responsibilities over the team and eradicating everything that comes close. And then defeat the boss. Personaly for me it's enough to call it a KF game. Then it adds some other touches like: Stumble/Knockdown mechanics, enhanced melee system (Block/Parry in particular), Perk skills system, sprinting, and other stuff that I'm too lazy at this point to recall. All of this is what's required to call it "KF2" and not "KF1 with pretty graphics". Otherwise the game would have no sense. If you don't like these changes, then it's probably better to save the money and stay in the good old KF1.
SOME CONTROVERSIAL MOMENTS
Microtransaction and Versus mode in a Co-op game.
I dont have anything against MT's: they're purely cosmetical. Don't like it? Don't need it? Don't use it. Simple. That's what I do.
I don't have anything against VS mode either. It's just the same. Don't like it? Don't play it. Any balance changes made for VS don't affect Co-op. You can set the filter to Survival and forget about VS forever if you feel so. Though I personaly enjoyed VS quite a bit. It's a good change of pace after dozens and hundreds of hours killing Zeds.
GRAPHICS and SOUND
The game looks gorgeous. 'Nuff said. That's something that everyone will agree on I think. Persistent blood, 19 (?) points of dismemberment on each enemy, cool guns sounds and reloading animations with high tickrate to look even coller in Zed time... and Zed time! KF's slow-mo that makes it look like you're in Sin City movie.
Music is any metalhead's dream (can always turn it off if you feel so).
VERDICT
Sure, it has many differences from KF1, but if it didn't, it would be just an expensive graphical patch for KF1 and, therefore, wouldn't have much point of existing.
Sure, the devs didn't bring everything they promised (Crawlers still can't traverse the walls and ceilings; Martial Artist will not happen, though developers never officialy announced it as far as I remember, it was rumored by the people who were surfing the game files, I may be mistaken here), but I'm looking at the game in it's release state and what it turns out to be at the moment and not what it might have been if things would go different.
Overall, I don't regret the money and hundreds of hours I spent on it.

Well that sucked. I noticed before even playing this game, that Steam was warning me, by the game not even starting up. "We're warning you! It sucks! Just back out while you have the chance." This is actually a big problem for a lot of people who buy this game (And the solution is so simple. You just have to install the Xlive folder in the actual game.) But, where does one begin with Kane and Lynch?

... Probably with Kane and Lynch. They suck. They are the least-likeable a-holes I've met in a game. And I'm supposed to connect with them, according to the game. Look! Whenever Kane get's shot down he thinks about people yelling at him. I'd rather call him a wuss than an empathetic character. I started to like Lynch for his dark comedic moments, but as the game went on, he just turned into this hate-spewing jerk that would ruin a lot of missions and cause them to go on far longer than they'd have to (In the actual script). He also ruins a lot of tries I've had at levels, because the AI is so off in this game. Enemies are not only really dumb, but the "tactical" system of the gameplay turns into babysitting, since most of my squadmates wanted to go out and shake hands with the enemy. And if an ally is shot down, they're on a timer for you personally to heal them. I never found out an alternative to have my other allies heal them, but no. I'd have to run in the middle of enemy fire in the next 15 seconds or I fail the mission.
Also the cover-shooting sucks horribly in this game. The game is incredibly picky about where you take cover, and even when you successfully take cover, most of the time enemies will shoot through your cover. I had a helecopter shoot through solid concrete and kill me. Solid concrete. If you can't take cover behind something that'd make sense to take cover behind (like bales of hay or low walls that just can't be used for cover, because it hurts their feelings) you could always duck behind them... after Kane hesitates a few moments to get his head shot. The whole time, I kept thinking about much better games I could be playing like Grand Theft Auto, Uncharted, or Mass Effect with much better characters and mechanics.
Oh! And what's the biggest problem in the game? The story. It's a floppy, predictable mess. The places you go to have very loose connections and you can end up in the middle of Cuba dressed as a guerilla in the middle of a firefight with no explanation of how you got there, other than, "We need to get so-and-so." And all the characters besides Kane and Lynch involved in the story are just as unlikeable or just flat-out forgettable. The game tries to make me feel all emotional when bad things happen to Kane's family, but I had no reason to care for them OR him. In fact, I personally think that the more horrible things happened to Kane and Lynch, the better. They really deserve it. I like Niko Bellic, Tommy Vercetti, and Trevor- because they have redeeming qualities.... Well, maybe not Trevor, but still. Kane and Lynch have no redeeming qualities. They're just heartless jerks that kill tons of people.
K&L also wanted to go with the choice-influenced ending, where you choose to stick with your mates and tough it out or go with the coward's ending. After playing this muddy game for so long, I didn't really care about the moral implications of my choice or the "good" or "bad" ending coming about. I chose the one that ended the game faster. Yeah, I'm a coward. Deal with it.
This is a horrible game. The characters, story, and gameplay are all over the place and poorly put-together. Do yourself a favor and buy a Grand Theft Auto game. It's got better elements in all three of the categories, and you can feel like the a-hole for killing tons of people in it- not hate the characters for being a-holes.

Hello! I'm pretty "experienced" semi-hardcore but very min-maxing liking ARPG player writing my first review :)
I've purchased game cuz it's released and was pretty cheap and so far i've totally Had my fun for the money i spend.
Eveything what's written is based on my opinion and the experience i had with the game so far.

The game is surely wasn't made for casual players, but also it's not as "hard" to understand as it seems at the first glance, i believe this is caused by the random stat(except weapon Damage) itemisation system the game uses, which is pretty similiar to the Diablo 3 in it's release era (prior to patch 1.0.4) but not as bad as it was back then due to one great future which devs(thx god) provided called "Enchanting" which allows you to re-roll stats if you're unfamiliar with it from other games.
In the beggining game feels very slow compared to the like's of D3 or PoE in the endgame builds :) This also is caused by the itemisation system which i mentioned earlier, add to that lack of good clearing skills on earlier levels on the most of classes, needless to say if you can survive in such enviroment for the first few hours the game will reaaally open up @around ~17-23sh lvl's and will start becoming more like traditional arpg's where you make few hits, destroy the pack of mobs, and move on to the next ones. Properly using "Enchantment" feature to re-roll trash stats into good ones on early gear you'l find, speed's up that process alot.
Some text about skill system : it has pretty good design, but suffers alot from most of the skills (i would say around 60%) being straight up garbage, ~20% are very good and another 20% could be efficient in group play, currently this is the weakest aspect of the game by far, which really needs attention imo.
Truth to be told it's made even worse due to passive stat boosts, which is provided in the skill "lanes" due to "Demon" being in them which i believe... must be exorcised :)  As it's stated in the Holy Book "knowing the Demons true name gives you control over it" and the demons name in this case is the "Critical hit chance +0.5%". That is just disgunstingly OP and unbalanced to the point it is better than any other stat u can find there by atleast twice amount O_O That Demon's power renders every skill lane where it is present to be maxed out w/o even looking at skills that lane provides and honestly that is just sad.
I didn't find game to be 'clunky' like some people say, but it feels like there is some kind of undrlying server issue where server sometimes does not register your hits (either it's caused by ping or "server/client sync tick rate"), most of the online games(i think) adress those problems by chunk of netcode called "lag compensation" to prevent this but in this game it feels like there's none and that thing i would say is more negative than positive one.
Another aspect which requires some attention of devs is the Professions, which is for now atleast - completely useles. They does not provide you with anything and grinding for gear is much better/faster/etc option than trying to craft it.
That being said, i still liked the game much more than i expected to, it's totally not perfect and has the room for improvement but it's a good game with potential to become great one in future, i would rate it 8-/10 right now and will hope it becomes better in the aspects i've mentioned while still enjoying playing it.

Summary: Short, uninspired, buggy.
Kane & Lynch as an idea has all the elements that make Hitman, developed also by IO, work. A contracted killer, here a mercenary that worked as part of a group rather than a lone hitman, bound for death row, gets out of prison by his old group to make amends. His family is kidnapped and he has to comply to save them. Although a bit cliche, the story could work, but it simply doesn't. The characters are underdeveloped, the plot never gets deeper, while large gaps are left to fill in with your imagination.
Gameplay-wise, the gunplay isn't anything to write home about, reminding of linear FPS that were considered outdated even by 2007 standards, with bullet-sponge enemies. The guns are often inaccurate, even in short distances and while firing with discipline (aiming, short bursts etc.). The cover system doesn't always work and sometimes while you are in cover you still get shot without the situation justifying it (e.g. when covering behind solid rock or cement that shouldn't be pierced by bullets. The AI is laughable, with some covering the wrong way opening themselves to shots, or when in groups just running straight at you, which diminishes any sense that you are fighting actual opponents.
The game requires Games for Windows Live, and in newer systems you have to find out on your own and download the client yourself in order for the game to launch. Multiplayer is long-dead, co-op is off-line only, the campaign is short (I finished it in ~6 hours while really taking my time). There's also a few crashes and glitches, although this is an afterthought in the game which is already dissapointing.
I got this as part of a bundle and it was as good as a movie you let play in the background. You can skip it safely and not miss anything, if you really want to play the second one (haven't played that yet, so no idea if it any good), just read the plot online, you're not missing anything.

An excellent adventure.
Shadowrun is an incredible world of Blade Runner meets Dungeons & Dragons and this game does it great justice. The world feels huge and full of quirky characters with their own agendas and this particular story does a great job of touching each of the varied aspects of this game.
It's a fair criticism that a lot of the dialogue options feel like different routes to get to the pre-defined outcomes - the story is not nearly as branching as a true pen'n'paper RPG could be - but those failings are made up for by a well written thriller that keeps you wanting to move forward to see the resolution. What starts with a simple murder escalates into a fight of world-changing proportions.
Could have been an excellent platform for UGC, but has been rather surpassed by subsequent Shadowrun titles.

The game is good but not perfect. If you can handle the fact that it is not the most polished game in the world and there are a lot of skills that just flat out sucks and need a rebalance (i would say 15% of all skills are imba, 15% of all skills are niche and have an use in parties only, 15% of the skills are useable but still kinda weak and 55% of all skills are trash tier) Then you got a good game
Graphics. They are fine and looks quiet good. They have a really western look even if the game was created in Taiwan and i got zero problems with the graphics and the artstyle
Sound/Music. Sounds sounds fine but i do agree with other reviews that crits need to sound better. Music is quiet good (i like one of the dungeon themes and the menu theme) but there are too little of it and after some time i just ended turning it off
Now for the gameplay. Early game (level 1-14) can be quiet boring because you dont have a lot of skills and the skills you do have feel quiet boring to use, but the game do pick up later on. Guardians of Ember is a MMOARPG where you follow the story quest like other MMORPGs but there are optimal quests and optimal dungeons that you can do. While the areas are not super open ended they do feel more open than Devilian or MU Legend where there are no real secrets to the maps and just you walk from A to B. Here there are some secret missions and dungeons that gives cards (get all cards of a type in an area and you get a permanent stat boost that scales with level, higher level means higher stat boosts) While the game do feel like a generic MMOARPG like Devilian when you start playing it there are some standout features in GoE
One such feature is the dual class system. After you get to level 15 (2-4 hours play) you can pick a sub class. What that do is that you have all active skills of the sub class as well as all the skills of your main class. That works really well and while it is not the first game that have done it it still works really well here. You can however only use the passive skills of your main class so take a look in the guides if you are unsure what passives you want (all classes are viable in endgame so dont worry about endgame class balance, the endgame class balance itself is balanced well with no class feeling super weak or super strong)
One more standout feature GoE have is player housing. It is not super fleshed out as you might expect but it still works fine here
One more standout feature is the lack of pay2win. Unlike other buy2play games (BDO is the most wellknown game that does this) You dont need to spend any money after you buy the game to be competitive and there are zero pay2win in GoE as well. You cant buy power in the cash shop at all unlike 99,9% of MMORPGs (and even more of newer MMORPGs that are with very few expections pay2win) You cant even buy gold for real money like in WoW or buy any instant level boosts like WoW so GoE is less pay2win than pay2play sub games like WoW
The final standout feature is that while i did say that skill balance itself is bad the game do give you more freedom with builds compared to Devilian or MU Legend (based on cbt 1) You put stat points like in good old Diablo 2 or Grim Dawn and that gives you something to go with. Do you wanna deal a lot of damage or do you wanna be really tanky for parties? Thats your own choose. And it is still true that there are a lot of skills for each class so with the dual class system you can feel quiet unique compared to other players rather than generic warrior 67
If you can handle the lack of polish (it is not super unpolished or anything but it is not as polished as something like MU Legend/Lost Ark because Gamewaker/Insel dont have as much money as Webzen/Smilegate (those 2 companies have tons of money and Insel/Gamewaker did not spend much money to make the game and that is easy to see) And want a game that mixes MMORPGs and ARPGs well then GoE is a great buy with a lot of content to do and even more content like act 6 and tower in the future

Shadowrun Returns is a cross between an RPG and XCOM-style combat.
It's not bad at all, even though there are obvious flaws and limits: you can tell the budget was not sky-high, but Harebrained Schemes managed all the same to create a game with a lot of character.
The combat is a bit simplistic compared to XCOM, but it's decent. There's quite a bit of variety involved, since you can build your character to be a melee fighter, a gunner, a decker, a mage or a mix of everything.
Dialogues are the game's strong point, for the most part (even though there are a couple of bad lines), and the story is relatively compelling: I liked the ending too, because it's more nuanced than expected.
Shadowrun Dragonfall is probably the best point of entry for the series, as I hear it's improved under every aspect, but still, this is a good game.

I love the Shadowrun universe, so I was pretty excited about the kickstart campaing and the eventual release of this game.
As an old school gamer, my gaming history is based on games like Fallout(1&2), Shadowrun(original), XCOM(originals) and many other genre-defining legends, my expectations were pretty high I must confess.
Once I finished the game (about 10h or so) I couldnt believe that it was over, it felt like something was missing.
It was the realization that the experience I hoped for was never going to be delivered.
The game is not a total waste but it's tremendously shallow, as linear as it can possibly be.
Character creation doesnt feel deep enough: generic 3D models, character photos that do not represent your model, lack of customization, lack of classes information...
During the course of the game you do not interact with the game-world but with overlays on it, you will never go up or down a stair, you interact with the overlay near the stair and then you go up or down.
Leveling up feels boring, most of the time you don't feel like getting stronger. Also the possibility to wait for a stat check barrier (the game tells what values are needed) to spend your karma points feels really sad.
All around It's an excessively minimalist game: graphical engine, art, interface, world, combat, skills, progression... everything.
If it was a mobile game it would've been a fair accomplishment, but at this point in gaming history, a "return" to Shadowrun universe as a PC game shouldn't have looked like this.
This game lacks depth for a Shadowrun universe PC game.
Two good aspects of the game though:
- story: Does a good job immersing you on the plot.
- content creating community: The level editor and the content created by the community can keep you entertained if you happen to like the game. The community made a lot of other adventures for you to run if you wish.
For me, that is not enough and, most importantly, not what I was looking for on this "return".
For people with high expectations as mine I cannot recommend this game.

To be completely honest. I love the art style. That was the biggest reason I had given this game a shot. However, the single player campaign is extremely difficult. As there is some sort of learning curve as well as the fact the difficulty of the computer is absurd immidiately after the tutorial. You are given access to a card shop and when I played (I was playing to collect cards). I was given around 130 free cards right off the bat. Thus diminishing my drive to play the game to get more. Regardless, the cards were useless until you gain experience and know a ton more about how to us them.
It will most likely take around 8-10 hours before you get a hold of the mechanics and have significant knowledge on how to win. After that, I predict the game will become immensely reptitive.

To defend the points I made.
1. I had played the single player campaign, beaten the tutorials and thought, yeah, I got the hang of this. Then after the tutorial I met a vampire opponent. He always beat me in 3-4 turns. I played him around 7 times before I figured out how to organize my deck. Thus the learning curve.
2. Given the currency and rare currency, I bought about 80 high level cards, 20 Mid level cards, and 30 low-level cards. Rating: 8.5/10
Overview: Open World Action Adventure
The Good:
+ One of the best looking open world games I have ever played.
+ This game handles one of my bigger criticisms I had with the previous games, the open world feels a lot more alive; cop cars chase criminals, military and thugs patrol the streets, etc.
+ I love the story and how many of the characters make a return and the roles they play. A fantastic way to finish the series.
+ The batmobile looks and plays incredibly well. The ability to call the car at a moment’s notice, seeing it drive through the streets as it turns right before you and then jump in and drive off without missing a second feels awesome.
+Solid sense of progression and upgrades. Gaining experience unlocks more powerful combat moves and gadgets.
+ AR challenge maps further the replay value giving you extra challenges. You can play as many different characters
+ Riddler trophies makes a return. Many of these collectables have a little puzzle associated with them making them fun to collect if you are into that sort of thing.
+ Great voice acting and sound
+ New Game Plus- Upgrades carry over.
The Average:
+/- Given the calibre of this game I was a bit disappointed with the graphical and gameplay options.
+/- Side quests that deal with villains are fun, however other side quests suffer with open world syndrome, i.e they start to feel repetitive over time. You can only disable so many road mines, military checkpoints, save so many fireman before you start getting tired of it.
+/- The game is heavily designed around using the batmobile. Many objectives have you using the batmobile whether for driving or combat. If you don’t like the controls or using the car in general you may be disappointed with a lot of the missions.
+/- Combat remains mostly the same. You can strike, counter, dodge, use gadgets and do a variety of special moves all while trying to maintain the combo meter.  The new addition is that you can now fight with a partner and do a special takedown moves. There are also a few new enemies to keep things fresh. The developers decided to make changes to the camera, timing and some changes to certain move sets which lead to a more frustrating experience.
+/- This game features a ton of DLC, yet most of them never felt substantial. Most of the arkham episodes can easily be beaten in under 30 minutes and most of them play out exactly the same.
The Bad:
- This is not a well optimised PC game.  This game is one of the worst pc ports in recent memory and even after many problems were fixed the game still struggles to play sometimes. You need a system above minimum requirements to play this game at a somewhat decent performance.
Conclusion:
I love Rocksteady Batman games, they are some of my favorite games and if this is Rocksteady’s final Batman game then they should be very proud of their efforts. Though I love the game, the formula is starting to wear thin for me. If you played Arkham City and even Origins this game offers little surprise, you’ve done it all before except this time you have the batmobile.

Surprisingly, this game is really great and the best of the RE series that I played so far. Why? Because this is a true horror survival - not a action oriented shooter horror like RE 5 - but more true to the originals and as one of few horror games out there that works perfectly in co-op mode (Once you are ingame after the intro, press start on your two gamepads and you are set) ! The split-screen co-op with gamepads is fantastically implemented, the roles for the two players are very different making it more interesting. The pace of the game is perfect. Most importantly though, this game has NONE of those ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous quick-time events that I hated so much in RE 5 and 6. Good riddance to those.
This is just a really good survival horror game with a good story that goes on with a good pace. It has none of the weaknesses RE 5 and RE 6 had, such as silly dialogs, action sequences and story. Instead it just comes off as well polished.
The only thing I miss a bit from RE 5 is the ability sell items and upgrade your weapons and this feeling of general ammo scarcity. This is perfectly made up by the fact that this game is overall much better than RE 5 and probably more true to the first RE parts. The upgrading in RE:Revelations 2 happens via items you find, and the upgrades can be attached / detached when you find a bench. There are also skills you can unlock globally for certain/all characters, using XP you collect by completing missions.
Imo, this game should have been named RE 6, and RE 6 should be named as some action spin-off of the series. This game is the real dea l and catches the real spirit of the series, forget RE 6.

Stay Dead Evolution is a fighting game developed by the italian company Brucefilm.
There isn't really a story to the game: you play as generic action hero number 21 who kicks and punches bad guys. The end.
When I started playing, I was literally laughing at how easy it was. You press three arrow keys to attack or defend, defending on which prompt appears. While simple at first, the harder the game gets, smaller and faster the prompts are. When you miss a prompt, the enemy parries or counters your attack. The round is won when your enemy has no energy left. You can achieve a humiliating victory by hitting the enemy seven times without getting hit: that will unlock a triple combo against that character. The game has an addictive quality to it.
As you probably noticed by watching the video, the game is made entirely of FMVs, just like in the good old days. I must admit that the fight choreography feels like that of an actual fighting game, with the characters always jumping around in their fighting stance.
The only problem with this game is the lack of content: there are only four opponents to fight and four difficulty levels, as well as three aesthetics: Modern Days, 90s Look and 80s Look. The latter two, while fun at first, make the game even harder to play.
The music is pretty generic, with the exception of the one that plays during the fight with Dagon.
Overall, this is the most original fighting game after Divekick, featuring increasingly challenging combat, good coreography and okay music but a lack of content. I recommend it to fighting games fans and to someone who's looking for something different.

I’m going to slap on a recommendation, despite not enjoying the game as much as I expected. I guess listening to other people talk of the largest cathedral in some distant country as an awe-inspiring piece of human ingenuity for half of your life usually results in you finally entering the halls and thinking to yourself: “What an old building.” Still feels kinda cool nonetheless, but can’t help but thinking you would enjoy it a lot better if you found about it yourself. Half-Life 2 is largely a study case. A Citizen Kane of video games, if you will, absolutely revolutionary in its time, properly crafted and well presented, but suffering – for very much the same reasons. In a post-Half-Life 2 landscape, ideas that made the game so good are thanks to it just so commonplace, this game can hardly blow you away anymore. But when you think about all the clever and non-intrusive storytelling, pacing, level design, even the range of stuff you do in the game, you realize its genius. But unless it’s one of your first games evarr, this realization will always be an afterthought. No self-respecting gamer goes through life without playing Half-Life 2 and that’s why I recommend it, but at the same time, I now know better than to shove it down people’s throat.

In 2016, it’s hard to say something about Thief II that hasn’t already been said. While Looking Glass Studios may have invented the modern stealth genre with Thief: The Dark Project, they perfected it with The Metal Age. This game’s innovative use of sound, sprawling level design, and impressive amount of player agency, create an experience that still immerses me to this day.

Metal Age’s missions consist of sprawling sandboxes that allow the player to pursue objectives in whatever way they see fit. Along with the wide variety of tools spread throughout these missions (arrows, mines, bombs, etc.), there are practically infinite ways to traverse any given level. The levels themselves are set in a wide range of pseudo-medieval locations. As master thief Garrett, you’ll be robbing banks, breaking into manors, trailing people through city streets, and so much more. What's really incredible about The Metal Age is that in all of its vastness and player choice, it always manages to feel organic. During my time with Thief II, I never felt like a guy in his computer chair, I really felt like a master thief. This feeling of total immersion is greatly aided by Looking Glass‘ creative and dynamic use of sound. Your footsteps make different noises at different volumes depending on what surface you walk on. You can lean against doors to hear a muffled conversation between two guards. Every coin, key, chest, door, and ladder, makes appropriate jingles, creaks, and thumps. Eric Brosius’ composition work deserves special mention here. While not traditionally musical, Thief II‘s soundtrack expertly creates a nocturnal and ominous ambiance that never really comes to the forefront, but is always present.
While it should be clear by this point that I consider Thief II to be a classic, I don’t believe it’s a perfect game. The Metal Age‘s most glaring flaw is in its visual fidelity. As a 3D game that's over a decade-and-a-half old, the graphics have aged somewhat unfavorably. Models are low-poly, with rigid animations and less than great texture work. While the dated graphics didn’t break my own personal immersion while playing, if you’re the kind of player who finds low-poly graphics to be distractingly jarring, this game may not pull you in as much as it has others. While not as much of a sticking point as the visuals, Thief II has one more notable flaw. The two missions prior to the final mission are practically identical, down to reusing the same map and having dangerously similar objectives. Neither mission is particularly bad, but the needless redundancy so close to the game’s conclusion may be frustrating for some players.
That being said, these two flaws are relatively minor tarnishes on what I consider to be a nearly perfect game in terms of player choice, level design, and use of audio. Some classic games are recognized for their influence on the medium of games as a whole, whether it be a innovative mechanic, or even inventing an entire genre. However, we often return to these games and find them to be dated or unentertaining. Thief II: The Metal Age serves as a welcome exception to this trend, and has stood the test of time to become one of the greatest stealth games ever made.
Overall Score: 9/10
+ Huge Levels
+ Multiple Paths / Choices Through Missions
+ Great Setting Variety
+ Good use of Sound
+ Highly Immersive
- Dated Graphics
- One Redundant Mission

This is the best squad-based strategy game I've played in... EVER! And any sci-fi fan will dig the entire theme - Stargate fans reminisce as the story unfolds over humanity's first encounter with extra-terrestrial species. Battlestar Galactica fans relish nostalgia as you research and adapt alien technologies to aid your war-efforts.
Assuming control of the XCOM project, you will manage the program's resources, facilities, and war assets in seeking to shape the program into a weapon capable of overthrowing the alien invasion of Earth, all while juggling international politics and responding to emerging situations across the globe.
The graphics are fantastic, and the over-the-shoulder action sequences are impressive. The characters and voice-acting are believable, if slightly comical. With over 100 unique and well-designed hand-built maps in the game, you're hard-pressed to feel locked-in to repetitive missions in a couple (several tens-of-hour) run-throughs of the game. Combining the detailed maps with the large range of gear and tactics available to your squads in addition to destructable environments (with consequences), there are a large variety of different means by which you can accomplish each mission. I find myself frequently re-loading in-mission saves in order to achieve a better outcome, but you can also play the game in Ironman mode - a single save that only moves forward; all deaths and decisions are final.
The game has a solid and logical plot-line, and the serious air is lightened with an occassional injection of humor (in one of my favorite moments, as I was outfitting soldiers in the barracks Central Officer Bradford chimed in criticizing a Mission Control officer, "Are you REALLY using your situation monitor to play Civilization? Well, I hope you're aiming for a military victory, at least.").
My chief complaint is the simple lack of a level-editor for the game. Mod and Steam Workshop support would add a ridiculous amount of content and replayability - I would love to play through alternate storylines.
If you like turn-based tacticals or are a fan of science fiction, you must play XCOM: Enemy Unknown - there is simply no way around it. I look forward to playing through again with the expansion, XCOM: Enemy Within.

Similar to "The Stanley Parable" this is a puzzle exploration game where all you basically do is try to find new paths to take that are different or unique to what you have previously completed.
The game itself is not all the "fun" or "exciting", but Antichamber does a good job of psychologically "breaking the mould" that other games have put onto the player.
For example, when a game tells you to pick a path typically as a player you will choose one or the other. This game however likes to play mind games and will show you there is always another path. (back the way you came)
Then the game gets more complicated as you progress and turns into a "Portal Like" game where you have a gun that can shoot blocks that you can use to hold doors open or block lasers to solve various puzzles.
As an experience this game is great, especially if you enjoy watching your friends fail seemingly obvious puzzles.
As a game...it's lacking on many levels.
- no story
- no objectives / goals
- no death / failure state
- not much to do besides walk around, and sold various block puzzles to get to more puzzles
- no replayability once you solve everything
- puzzles get extremely complicated causing the user to just stop playing after a while
In short....
This is a game you experience once, and only once. It's a great experience, and you will love it at first, and want to show your friends, however... you won't want to ever play it again, and you'll likely just forget it even exists.

+ A character-driven story starring Kane and Lynch, which make this game series memorable.
+ Environment is never repetitive: each level is set in a different location.
+ Shootouts are spectacular, and some are quite large-scale (like the Tokyo and Havana levels).
+ Splitscreen co-op.
- Single-player story is short.
- No online co-op.
- Clunky gameplay and gunplay.
- AI has some issues that sometimes break the immersion.
- You have to manually install GFWL through the game's folder in order to play the game.

By the date of release, KF2 has:

- 10 perks (KF1 had 6, they added Demolitionist later on)
- All the KF1 enemies + 1 more boss (and 1 more coming in the future) + 2 more variations of the weakest enemy (and 1 more variation of another enemy coming soon)
- 4 guns for each of the 9 "unique" perks + a few offperk weapons (I'm not sure how many did KF1 had on release)
- a unique grenade for each of those perks (KF1 had like 3 types if I recall correctly: regular grenade, Commando's HE grenade and Support's grenade; later on they added healing grenade for the Medic)
- 2 game modes + 1 probably coming in the future (KF1 had 1 + 1 more was added later on)
Sure, at the moment, KF1 has way more content than KF2 (atleast map- and gunswise), but let's not forget that all this content was added into the game over the course of many years. I, ofcourse, cannot guarantee that KF2 will have that much content in the future too, but TWI (developers) already promised us more content in the future. It's up to you to trust them or not. But my opinion: they did it for KF1, there's a high chance they will for KF2 as well.
GAMEPLAY
For people who are new to KF:
It's great. Fast paced destruction of waves of enemies that seem to never run out of livestock using various methods of creating holes and scorchmarks on things and making different parts of the same fleshy object suddenly move in completely different directions.
It can get repetitive in time, but it depends on how much you love that kind of stuff. When it does, you can switch to Versus mode for a different perspective one the game. Though still, Co-op is the main thing to play KF2 for.
For the people who played and are familiar with KF1:
The basic formula is the same: hold out hordes of Zeds by correctly distributing the responsibilities over the team and eradicating everything that comes close. And then defeat the boss. Personaly for me it's enough to call it a KF game. Then it adds some other touches like: Stumble/Knockdown mechanics, enhanced melee system (Block/Parry in particular), Perk skills system, sprinting, and other stuff that I'm too lazy at this point to recall. All of this is what's required to call it "KF2" and not "KF1 with pretty graphics". Otherwise the game would have no sense. If you don't like these changes, then it's probably better to save the money and stay in the good old KF1.
SOME CONTROVERSIAL MOMENTS
Microtransaction and Versus mode in a Co-op game.
I dont have anything against MT's: they're purely cosmetical. Don't like it? Don't need it? Don't use it. Simple. That's what I do.
I don't have anything against VS mode either. It's just the same. Don't like it? Don't play it. Any balance changes made for VS don't affect Co-op. You can set the filter to Survival and forget about VS forever if you feel so. Though I personaly enjoyed VS quite a bit. It's a good change of pace after dozens and hundreds of hours killing Zeds.
GRAPHICS and SOUND
The game looks gorgeous. 'Nuff said. That's something that everyone will agree on I think. Persistent blood, 19 (?) points of dismemberment on each enemy, cool guns sounds and reloading animations with high tickrate to look even coller in Zed time... and Zed time! KF's slow-mo that makes it look like you're in Sin City movie.
Music is any metalhead's dream (can always turn it off if you feel so).
VERDICT
Sure, it has many differences from KF1, but if it didn't, it would be just an expensive graphical patch for KF1 and, therefore, wouldn't have much point of existing.
Sure, the devs didn't bring everything they promised (Crawlers still can't traverse the walls and ceilings; Martial Artist will not happen, though developers never officialy announced it as far as I remember, it was rumored by the people who were surfing the game files, I may be mistaken here), but I'm looking at the game in it's release state and what it turns out to be at the moment and not what it might have been if things would go different.
Overall, I don't regret the money and hundreds of hours I spent on it.

Preface: I liked mirrors edge and I have played a lot of shooters/melee games. I did not  like dead island but did like it's option to throw melee weapons and modify them.
Now that that I have declared the things which may lead me to have some bias we can get on with it. The game has a reasonably good storyline albeit somewhat predictable at times. The reason for you being in the situation makes sense, the interavtion with other characters makes sense. If I were to criticise any character ni the ggame it would be the main character for not developing much of a personality until about 60-70% of the way into the story. You may have heard that it relis upon a damsel in destress storyline, this is NOT the case with the "damsel" saving your life at least twice during the course of the game.
The combat is good and relatively fluid. you can equip 4 melee weapons at a time and 4 utilities ranging from a UV torch to electricuted riot shields. The stamina systems keep the game challenging and the different "special infected" range from irritating to down right deadly and maintain that position until relatively late into the game.
The weapon crafting is reasonable extensible with the ability to add effects such as fire or impact to weapons as well as modifications which add to damage, handling or durability to varying degrees.
The exp rewards are reasonable and the skills you can unlock are helpful with only one of them, the grappling hook, really detracting to the difficulty of the game bar the ultimate upgrade from each tree, which essentially give you infinite stamina for their associated ability e.g. agility gemoves running and climbing stamina costs.
The different skill trees do add a lot of different playstyles to your arsenal and I will say it again none of the upgrades feel boken.
There is a reasonable amount of humour in the game including one of my favourite insults I have heard in years from "the twins" who are a pair of intelligent yet condescending brothers with an inability to relate to other people.
The co-op is a good laugh and saves any progress you make to your campaign evein if you are not the host.
Overall I would recommend this game a lot. It may not be original but it has taken the best parts of a lot of games with only a few issues that I have noticed.
