To start off, I should point out I never played an xcom game before, so I can't really compare it to the other versions.  That being said, I enjoyed this game a lot.  I put about 25 hours into it, and I'm working through what appears to be the final mission for my first playthrough.  This game actually has a surprising amount of variety to the enemies, that scale in difficulty as your gear improves and your soldiers become better trained.  From what I know of the previous games, it seems they have added a couple more classes, making there be four in total (five, if you count the robots known as SHIVs), all of which are unique and have completely separate abilities.  One of the things I really enjoyed about the game was the customization.  I know in previous games you could only change the name, but in Enemy Unknown, they take it a step further and allow you to change the look and voice of your character.  Additionally, they also get a nickname once they reach a high enough level.  It may not seem that important considering you have an isometric view the entire time, and therefore can't see that many details, however it does help you feel more of a "connection" to your long-standing soldiers, especially when they get one-shotted by a floater because you wasted your cash on weapons rather than armor.  Speaking of which, this game is BRUTAL.  One mistake can cause you to lose an entire squad of low to mid quality soldiers.  I highly reccomend iron man mode, as you have to live with the mistakes you make, therefore making you more likely to learn from them.  As much as I love this game, however.  I have to admit it's not perfect.  This game, at least for me, suffers from freezing and crashing.  A lot.  The game runs perfectly fine at 60 FPS, until suddenly it decides that it doesn't approve of your commanding skills, and crashes the game.  Unfortunatly this can be used to exploit iron man mode, because when you come back to the game you are usually a few turns back, giving you another chance at a potentially fatal move.  Unfortunatly I have no experience in multiplayer so I cannot comment on that, however rest assured I'll be sure to update this review if I ever give it a shot.  From what I've played though, this game is definetly one of my favorite purchases on steam, and I would highly reccomend it to pretty much everyone.

There are some funny situations also, like when you break into a shop, alarm goes of, and you find yourself surrounded with cop-zombies. Finally, you will be amazed how many people keep grinder blades and nails in their dirty laundry ;)
It is hard. I already mention that I died 131 times - game keeps the statistics for me ;) What is more,
For a plot, I would tell that guys from Techland could teach some of Hollywood directors how action movies should be done. It's not that it's unpredictable, but follows Hitchcock saying that story should start with earthquake and tension should rise from now on.

The other thing that bothered me, was that no building was destructible, no plant flammable, and so on; but for this plot it could became disastrous, if it was.
Never tested it in coop mode, though. But someday i will.

It would be odd to call this game linear when it all but eliminates any conceptions of what a straight line is. Antichamber is very exploration-based; if you find you've gotten to a dead end, you can almost immediately go to a different unfinished puzzle. This is all helped by an expanding map that, once you figure out what the symbols mean, can show you where you've missed stuff and where you don't need to explore any further.
In terms of puzzles, the description of the game is a good explanation: nothing can be taken for granted. Rooms change when you look at them, fake walls and floors are everywhere, and many other elements get thrown at you at just the right time to impress you. The solutions to the puzzles are sometimes unique, but I encourage you to mess with what you're given and find solutions that feel like they're unintended.
Overall, a solid game; it accomplishes what it set out to do.

My first impressions of the game were similar to most...great visuals (especially for its age) with interresting and unique gameplay. However to me the game became boring pretty quick. For me it was because the game resorts to the same "puzzles" repeatedly and each chapter feels very similar to the last as far as in the way you are required to progress. (same jumps utilizing a select few repeating environmental features, elevators).
The story doesn't do this game any favors but I can see why so many people are hungry for a sequel (I won't spoil anything here). I think that they really had a missed opportunity to have an engaging story involving such a promising setting.  The story just never really explains things, or maybe a better way of putting this is that the scope of the story is very narrow.
One last thing that I thought hurt the game was allowing you to engage enemies in direct combat. The shooting mechanics were so weak that they should have been removed all together. I think that engaging enemies should have been reduced to using the characters abilities to circumvent combat with more impressive disabling moves and removing sections in which you were trapped in a room with enemies waiting for an elevator door to open or having the chance to turn a wheel.
Overall I would say the game is a bit overrated but worth picking up at a cheap price, and with a campaign length of 5-7 hours you really won't be wasting your time. Good concept and I still have hopes for the sequel. I wouldn't recommend this game due to all of the other great titles available...but I wouldn't discourage someone from picking it up.

Wow! two breakouts released  in a day.  Breakout/arkanoid games  have always been one of my favorite  arcade genres ever since the first one was released  way back in the late 1970's.  I've played hundreds of them over the years and have some particular favorites (e.g. Acky's XP Breakout, Ricochet infinity, Arcmania 2,  Reaxxion, Hyperballoid 2, Arkanoid: The Virtual Isles, Incrediball:The Seven Sapphires, Magic Ball 3 aka Smash Ball 3,  plus several others).  All of those mentioned had something different or special about them such as a  never before seen power up,  a level editor, hidden levels, great level design or mini games, most of which   gave them  a lot of replayability.  That said Caromble has an innovative addition called leap motion, which requires you to purchase  the leap motion hardware that'll set you back  just under 90 Euro's.  I like the idea, it would go well with my Track IR, but for this game, I doubt i'll be spending a further 90 euro's.
The  level designs are  nice and I like the color scheme, which reminds me of  the  colors used in Borderland and Borderland 2.  There's nothing spectacular about the game play, in fact I found it a little tedious, though there are some nice features;  for example,
i) ... A request window pops up  for  suggestions and feedback  when you close the game down  (this will probably disappear once the game comes out of  early access),
ii) ... Level navigation is simple
iii) ... You can avoid the last few  awkard to get bricks by hitting the portal at the top of the arena, that appears when there are only a few bricks left.
iv) ... The way you can curve the ball by slicing the ball as it hits the bat.
v) ...  The end of stage bosses.
vi) ...
Unfortunately I don't think the overall ball  physics are good, and   the bat  seems a little sluggish.  I've been playing breakouts frequently for over  30 years  and  consider myself an experienced player,  yet I  missed   quite a few balls  in the first 10 or so minutes due to the bat sluggishness. It's nothing major and changing the sensitivity of your mouse can  sort the problem somewhat.
:
It would be nice if there was a count down indicator showing how long there was left of   any power-ups  captured and I'd love to see a level editor. I'd also like to be able to select or deselect power ups.  I've only ever seen this  functionality in a few breakouts  and it added a lot of replayability.  Also  some idea's for new power-ups include   ball shape changes and bat shape changes to add to the randomness of  ball flight.
I will return to this review to update it once I've  added a few hours of game play and when its out of early access.  Hopefully we will see lots of updates and additions.   Overall I give this a thumbs up.

Kane & Lynch: Dead Men is a third person shooter game with a few interesting twists, but ultimately the poor execution of some elements drag it down quite a bit.
First off I've played this game a bit when it came out on Xbox, did a little bit of coop back then, but never finished it. It has been sitting in my Steam library for a while now until I recently decided to finish it. The game itself was released in a time where things were still good in the gaming business and companies churned out games at a fast pace. It was also a high time for Xbox and most relevantly coop was the thing every game needed to have.
STORY
The game takes an interesting perspective from the bad guy who gets broken out of prison and is confronted with his past. Needless to say life as a mercenary is shady and he did some things his former employers couldn't agree with. His wife and daughter are leveraged and he is blackmailed into retrieving something. Beyond that the story gets rather predictive with failure and revenge as central pivoting points.
GAMEPLAY
As said the game is a third person shooter and the controls handle a bit slow and rough, but when playing with the controller everything runs pretty good.
Cover mechanics however are poorly done and for some reason you can only get in cover on the edge of a wall, even the lower ones. This is very frustrating since enemies are abundant and aim pretty good, even on the lowest difficulty.
On the other hand most of your weapons have such low accuracy you really have to get very close to hit something. Result is that moving from cover to cover gets you killed most of the time, luckily your team-mates revive you almost every time.
And that is pretty much the only thing they get right, other than that they're pretty useless. You have a few basic commands, but anything other than 'Stay here' or 'Come over' is pointless. You can order them to attack a specific target, but this just results in them rushing towards it and shooting them in the face with a shotgun. The animation however is pretty nice though. That's mostly the gameplay throughout the game, aside from a few vehicle missions.
VISUALS
The game is a bit older, but it still looks acceptable, but nothing special. There is some destructibility, which was also very popular back then. Most animations in the game appear somewhat crude, but then again acceptable for it's age. It should run pretty good on today's laptops as a counter argument.
AUDIO
The audio is nothing to be noted specifically, no orchestral scores. Just your standard background music with a few tension increasing tempos. The voice acting, including lip sync, is actually pretty good for the standard of those days. But the dialogs happen mostly during game, which can be very incomprehensible at times. However most of them are restricted to a lot of swearing and banter, so you won't miss much.
MULTIPLAYER
As said the game can be played coop and it will be waaaay more fun when playing with some buddies, like with much of these coop games. Also the online versus mode is very original, especially with a name like Fragile Alliance, things can get interesting. You can view the tutorial and get an impression of what it would be like, but that's about it. Servers are dead, both coop and versus. So sadly I cannot divulge into this any further, but I can expect it would change my opinion of the game.
VERDICT
Buy it cheap if you want to experience the beginning of the franchise, but other than that just skip it and go straight to the next one. If you have enough friends who are willing to play it with you I would probably recommend this one for sure. Most coop games from previous generation are well worth it just for that.

Besides that the incredible physics-based destructions, you fight your way through either with keyboard, mouse or controller to beat the evil at the final boss rounds. The game surely has a offering when we talk about challenges, since every area is designed differently.
If you enjoy a fresh brick break game, with a fast Ping Pong mechanic, then this game is for you.

Let me start by saying that I didn't intend to write this review as I feel the games quality speaks for itself. However having purchased it the day the EA started, I was on ground zero when the somewhat irrational hatred and minor trolling of this game started and recently noticed a negative review that boiled down to ' This game is fantastic but EA OMG WTF BBQ! '. To try and balance out this odd reaction I am going to go into length and address some of the hate with some common sense and some facts. It's up to you to chose to read it but the TL;DR is that this game has been consistently fantastic and has grown into a decent successor to the original.
- The game was in EA for 19 months. Compared to other titles that is a standard amount of time allowing for staff changes at some intervals.
( EA Done Right ) - It is often complained that when Tripwire announced that Killing Floor 2 was going to be Launched in Early Access and that it would be ' Done right ' that that would imply anything from having the game out faster to there being no bugs and that tripwire failed the community by not releasing the game fast enough. However, when the EA launched it did so will multiple levels, multiple perks and a fully working core game. Contrast this with many other EA titles on Steam. The difference is night and day. You were able to play KF2 straight out of the gate allowing the dev to steadily improve and add perks, levels and so on. When you purchase an EA game on steam you have to expect to run into issues you normally wouldn't have to deal with in a fully released product. As far as I am concerned I have thoroughly enjoyed the EA time and feel that they more than fulfilled this promise.
- During the EA Micro Transactions were added into game. Initially with very limited cosmetics however over time this has been expanded to include crate drops etc. Now, as far as I can tell, there seem to be three different hate groups on this subject. Those that believe that Micro Transactions are fine in a full release but not EA. Those that believe Micro Transactions are fine in a full release but not a highly priced full release and those that believe Micro transactions are never ok.
Micro Transactions are everywhere. They have become a fairly common thing in gaming and like it ( CS:GO ) or hate it ( Mostly any other game ) they seem to be here to stay. The EA addition of MT's happened about 7 months into development and to this date provides only cosmetic changes that also have a chance of dropping for free during gameplay. As far as MT's go this is a pretty decent and standard approach. They had a solid playerbase and provided MT's to those players. At no point in the game does having a particular skin improve your gameplay or have any affect what so ever. This issue comes down to choice and to me the choice seems simple. If you don't approve of MT's then do not purchase any skins. Let them drop by chance. I believe black listing a game for adding in Micro Transactions that do not affect gameplay is a little daft. But, as I said, it depends on your stance.
- This one baffles me. A fair few people in the community hate that a new game mode was added to the game. The main concept and mechanics of the game were nailed down early on in development and by the time Vs was added the traditional Killing Floor gameplay was solid, save tweaks and bugs ( EA ). The Vs mode ( Player controlled Zeds vs Player controlled Humans ) had balancing issues ( EA ) but, again, was not forced upon players but rather is an option. It was an often requested mode for the original Killing Floor and is an enjoyable addition to KF2.
- During EA the devs were often accused that they were not listening to the community. This is a problem in most game communities. The devs have acknowledged that while they do answer questions not everyone receives the answer. To combat this, as well as reiterating their views and answers on frequent live streams they also have a development schedule that shows where they are putting their work into. In my view they have gone beyond trying to accommodate the community and are very open with what is in the pipeline.
This game is rad. Its a savage and bloody mess of lovely graphics and fluid gameplay. Equally easy to jump into a quick game before work or chain up a long stretch of gut ripping madness! I was a huge fan of Killing Floor and am a huge fan of KF2. The community can be a bit brittle and daft at times but the vast majority just want to enjoy the game!
The company itself has a pretty decent track record and supported the previous Killing Floor for years with additional content, both free and DLC. You can tell that this was a passionate project for them and to my mind they have been very connected and open with the community. Sitting in Live Streams and watching them effortlessly answer the bizarre demands of some of the community shows their commitment.
Full disclosure. I have played KF2 since the first day of EA and as soon as I could I purchased the Metro Police Officer Skin from the MT store for like £4. Do I regret it ? Hell no! I look like a policeman now!
Nothing beats hitting reload just before Zed Time hits and you slow motion throw your empty magazine into the face of a charging Fleshpound!
The sound design and music are spot on. The community complained about the sound the starting pistol made when fired and Tripwire reworked it. ( And rightly so, it sounded like an empty plastic bottle hitting a slab of Gammon! )
The use of Perks in this game are far better than the original. Progression feels solid and the rewards are actually useful.
Gameplay swings wonderfully from gliding around one shotting Zeds with ease to soiling yourself as you run past the corpses of your team mates while being chased down by Fleshpounds.
Seriously just play it. I mean if you don't like it just get a refund but if you enjoy FPS action and plenty of limb ripping madness then hop on in!
: you may disagree on my views ( I am counting on it, really ) and that's cool! Because you are handsome and life is good! Take care champ ; )

I rolled the dice on this ARPG, and have been pleasantly surprised.  It scratched that itch that so far only Torchlight and Diablo II have been able to scratch for me. Pros
- Pleasant to look at
- Huge number of skills to choose from
- Dual Classing (which you can swap on the fly)
- Interactive devs very open to suggestions
- Online (party mechanics etc)
- No inventory tetris (1 item is 1 slot)
- Player Housing
- Casual friendly
- Surpisingly deep enchanting and crafting systems
- Tons of content/things to do already
Cons
- Not many players yet
- Later content is much more enjoyable than early content (more interesting montsers/bosses/story etc)
- Overworld map is static
- Cash shop (although the free currency used to buy shop stuff is super easy to farm)
- Minor bugs (rare crashes, typos, getting temporarily stuck on terrain)
I've read alot of reviews of this game, and most of the negatives ones are really more on the fence. That or people who play for less than an hour and give up without seeing what this game really offers.  If you don't mind the issues common with early access titles, you'll find a very rewarding game underneath.

I'm glad I waited to play this for the first time, and on PC for that matter, so i'll run it down. WB Games has always been a pain in the butt with the PC communitiy, and this port started out like a train wreck. I saw it all over the place.  Luckly for me, i'm paitent, and this was one reason I was glad to be. The PC Port has been fixed up nicely, and it runs great, and i'm running a 970GTX. I get a good 60fps with no issues. I had no stutters, and the gameplay was smooth as butter.   Now, let's talk about the actual game!
So, I got the Season Pass edition for like $17 on the Summer Sale last year, and now i'm around to playing this. I bring this up because I want to talk a little about the DLC.  Well, I can say, it's not terrible, and blends nicely into the game, with all the voice acting and setups well added.   The main story from where I am is a lot of fun, and I just love the fact they got Commissioner Gordon's voice actor to be the guy who played Mike from Breaking Bad.   Driving actually runs pretty good, and controls are not too jerky, which I liked. I enjoy the Battle Mode on the Batmobile, because it's not only fun, but I like driving in it for those small roads.   The Joker being back again was so a nice choice to add to the supposed final entry in the series, and he still plays the role like the master he is.     Riddle Challenges are always my jam in each game. I always determine myself to get them all, and this is way more expanded comepared to Arkham City, so props to that, and the opportunity to grind and make EXP from all over.
Sound is on point, and well done. The radio chater is fun to listen to for clues.  Music is excellent, and well orchestrated.
Overall. now at this point of the Port, and how time has fixed the game up for PC users, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND this game. WB Games may have to mend wounds with players, and I can understand it, but if you get it cheap enough like I did, you'll be glad to play it on PC now.

I have toyed with playing Resident Evil games on a number of occasions before but this is the first one I have bought. The first episode was on sale for 79p whilst all the other episodes were not discounted at all. The publisher must be extremely confident that you will get hooked after the first episode to do that. However this did not work on me, after the first episode I was left with the overwhelming impression that it was okay but had no desire to buy the rest of the game.
The campaign's plot so far is intriguing, the way the story is told by splitting it into two parts is excellent. The combat is mostly uninspiring shooting dribbly monsters in the face. The character switching felt a bit forced in the first half where one character had guns and the other had a torch with no good reason why they both couldn't have guns and a torch. However the switching worked much better in the second half where you had a tough guy with all the weapons and a creepy child who can see monsters through walls. So overall it is reasonably enjoyable.
There was also a boring raid mode where you need to just repeatedly kill a bunch of monsters to level up your character and unlock things to kill more monsters. This didn't hold my attention for long.
So overall I feel I got my 79 pence's worth out of this first episode but I am in no hurry to spend twenty odd quid to get the rest of the game.

Despite not really enjoying any of the Dota series or most MMO's for that matter (including the recent +The Elder Scrolls Online, Strife, etc), this documentary film speaks far beyond it's content, revealing in just a bite size length a rather heart-filled insight of our much loved and forever evolving 'games world' {}♥__♥}
Free to play shows like any obsession how damaging to yourself and your loved ones it can be, through three gamers all competing for a million dollar prize.
What is obviously shown, but not mentioned, for any gamer you are not judged by anything, but your gaming skills. It's not what or who you are, but what you can do. Unfortunately I can not say this about real life, with experiences of being chased by gangs with fire touches, planned knife threats, rejected by primary schools and sadly many more.
Like great films and novels, they help us escape temporarily, but with games, you can actually be someone or something else. ‎Residual self-image. Your avatar. A predefined or self created gaming character. The 'other/inner' you. For a quick example, this is me in Saints Row IV:
or as our Bengal cat Kitt in The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim:
When you see, join or simply just talk (typing or voice) to a random human player within an on-line game, in your gaming character form, you completely ignore those fictitious "differences" that so many of our beautiful world (in real life) judge upon first, even though we all know these so called "differences" don't actually exist.
Racism, sexism, disability discrimination, homophobia, prejudiced, or class (based on wealth) ...for my short thirty years of gaming (twelve of which gaming on-line now), I've not experienced any of these disgusting man-made discriminations and have never felt scared, conflicted, a shammed or unwelcome. If I could literally live on-line, full body, Lawnmower man-like I would ...with a running start, eyes wide open and jump in head first \[]O__O]/
I'm probably typically alone with these thoughts and emotions from watching just one documentary film about gaming, but I'm also very curious to what non-gamers who watch this think and feel? Is this how you see us all or had no idea? Scary? Alienating? Intriguing? The early shots of LAN parties brought back some seriously fun memories from my youth and how games can physically (in real life or on-line) bring so many of us together for endless entertaining, collaborative and mind blowing fun experiences, one that no film or book can match.
Unfortunately for me, the majority of my family and friends (in physical real life) don't play games, so without choice, that makes me (and for a very long time) a 'Lone Gamer'. Some of them play those awful mini-games on +FaecesButt or prefer mobile device based games and even just games consoles, because it's easier (so they think), but this to me is like looking a photocopy re-production of a great painting or listening to a stunning piece of music on the radio. It's nothing like the real thing, which in this case is a home desktop computer that's used to it's full scale potential, regardless of it's OS. Sure, +Steam on Windows offers 'currently' without a doubt, the best home entertainment possible on our amazing planet, for audio, visual, compatibility, customization, upgradability and importantly, cost effectiveness. The almighty Linux and of course the hybrid alternatives like Steam OS and Android even will soon change this giving us all more and most likely, better options ()^__^)
What do you think ...three more years of Windows OS and DirectX only games? DirectX 12 is already a year late and it's still not even officially available publicly yet {}¬__¬}
The slight anti-climax of Free to play is the paltry prize that's divided between the five team players, which would barely buy you a bedsit in London ...however ...this momentous and continuously growing event is truly the beginning of far greater international gaming events to come. I remember coming 5th in a Soul Calibre tournament in my youth and walking away with a 'goody bag' that contained a T-shirt, a mug, a couple of CD's and some random stationary (something called a pen?). The first prize was Namco's back catalogue (about forty games at the time) including 'some' of the games consoles to run them on ...so yeah ...it's certainly come a long way since then thankfully. However, unlike those who entered the Dota 2 International Tournament, I did not train daily, travel far and no team or teamwork was required, hence (the only thing that survived is) the very used "collectors" mug that sits proudly in our kitchen {}o__o}
It also would have been nice to see the great Gabe Newell say a few words during the film, rather than appear briefly towards the end walking off stage without a word, but understandable ...I guess {}o__o}
You may never see me play Dota 2, which does not mean it's not a gg (good game), which I'm sure it is, just not for me, but Free to play is a remarkable 'free' documentary and is truly worth it's weight in '+Steam Achievements' ()^__^)

for giving this 'openly' and 'freely' to the world \[]^__^]/

This game is marvelous. I have loved turn based games like this since I can remember. If you enjoy tactical games with lots of customization and real difficulty then XCOM is for you. Buy Enemy Within as well. Most games have an easy, medium and then hard difficulty and I find it does not properly convey what those words mean. People are have become too reliant on "ITS RIGHT HERE" markers and things that take the fun/use out of playing a video game. Xcom gives you your easy, normal, and then Classic which is the way its supposed to be played. Then there is impossible which means...I ♥♥♥♥ing dare you. Ironman mode (one save so if you botch up or impatient, there are consequences) is even better. I never thought I would have close to the hours I have spent on Skyrim for another game but Xcom makes me come back for more every time.
The story however, could use some major work and polishing. There also could have been more storyline battles and I find that even with enemy within's map usage that I would like more of them. Modding could heavily help this as I know developers can only do so much when it comes down to making a game and putting it out for people in time. Modding increased and currently increases skyrim's playability a hundred fold. StarCraft 2 also allows for the public to make maps and those maps even see professional play when selected by voters/professional gamers. It could also use even more customization for troopers. Armor decoration/paint schemes and types of looks were a big coolness factor when customizing your guys/gals.
My only other complaints that I can think of are that aliens did not scale well after you began powering up and gaining gear. Even in impossible once you get over the first month or two hump it starts to become very easy to gain ground and keep it and I only found battles becoming hard if I just made insanely dumb decisions or was engaged by two or so big mechs. Even then if you have a couple suppressors, it still becomes trivial. The other is that a few boss battles for the extra epic feel of accomplishing things as well as a way of seperating the missions up into phases or just aquiring a badass weapon at very high risk would be great. The end "boss" as well needed severe revamping and was far too easy and I was very dissapointed when I found that they did not fix this battle in Enemy within.
TLDR: 9/10

Unlike most games where pickups and guards are very evenly distributed, stuff in Thief is actually where it would be in real life. This is not a good game, while the concept is sort of fun it's just way too messy and intentionally frustrating and time-wasting.  The tiny peripheral field of vision, jumpiness, quasi-random generation, absolutely no checkpoints within level, random rotation switches and splitting/joining points when the field switches to pentagon or such makes this frustrating without equivalent reward for me.  Hard for all the wrong reasons.  And while it certainly is addictive, it is not fun. There is way too much, "grinding" if you will, if what you need to practice (since that's what the game requires in a bad way) usually shows up in the latter part of a level but you have no problem with what's before, you'll still need to spend the full time doing everything before for most attempts.
In other words, this forces you to practice to win or progress (not a bad thing in of itself), but with no practice mode or way of isolating problem events, it forces you into the worst kind of practice habit possible.  Certain events tend to show up later (or earlier but if all the difficult events showed up in the beginning it woulnd't matter) in level, therefore making isolatating the problem event and for most attempts wasting your time grinding the same beginning sections which  over and over, which numbs the mind and causes you to perform worse on everything fairly quickly.
I would be interested to see in the code how fast exactly what your maximum and mimimum required reaction times would be in a number of the situations it generates based on your best-or-worst-case prior positioning (based significantly because of the random generation engine).
On top of this, some of the music (first level) isn't that good.
If you don't mind being frustrated and spending an inordinate amount of time practicing something that isn't fun and likely has no relevance elsewhere, get this game.

I'm not going to pretend that this game is perfect.  Read enough of the other reviews and you will clearly see that people are mixed on this game.  I'm also not going to touch on the review scandal.  That was an ugly bit of business, but it doesn't impact the game on its own merits.  It showcases how scummy the company is that made the game.
I like the characters overall.  The gang of mercs that you build up has their own personalities and each one adds to the story a little bit, but the center is on Kane and Lynch.  The banter between these 2 during the course of a mission can be a lot of fun to listen to and it helps drive the story a little bit further.  Games like this usually don't have much of a story to them, but this one has little pockets waiting to be seen, if you give it a chance.
It's not without issues, though.  The cover system, while functional at times, does not always work and sometimes you will snap into cover at odd angles or stupid moments and it won't work when you always need it to.  Gunfire definitely drives your aim skyward, but that is a relaistic idea (even if it seems too aggressive in this game).  Enemies do take a fair number of hits to put them down, but if you're in that much of a bad situation, you can always switch to your pistol and go for headshots.
The music and sound effects are great and, again, the banter between the characters will keep things moving.  Sure, profanity abounds in this, but given the source material, what did you expect?
Overall, a mix of locations (and the club shows how many people you can put on a screen at one time... nice chaotic atmosphere that makes it harder to get by without killing any innocents) keeps things interesting and varied.  There aren't too many guns, but there are enough to get the job done and give you a little freedom to determine what works best for you.
Is it perfect?  Hell no.  Will you get frustrated with the things that don't work well?  Quite possibly.  But is it worth giving it a try to enjoy what does work?  Yes, I think it is.

When I think of Thief:TMA, I think of being aggravated that I can't move around. This was something that happened in Thief:TDP, but in that game, it wasn't a problem. Not only were there breathers were I could sprint across open grass, or swim in relative safety, but also I was immersed and excited by the locations and the many many hidden secrets and background I was constantly happening across.
"I wandered around lost and unsure a lot, but there was nothing that was unenjoyable about doing that. The game encourages you to do so, and there is a lot to discover (and steal) while you unlock the greater picture of the mission. I played slowly and patiently, but I missed a lot of content and could easily play it again for a new experience."
I don't feel the same way about TMA. There are a lot of reasons for that.
I don't like metal floors constantly placing me in danger of being heard. I don't like more guards and cameras everywhere. I don't like metal and concrete factories as settings to explore. I don't like the notes and conversations by normal goons about normal grounded things. I don't like having no "free range" areas. I don't remember enjoying the stories or notes and background. I don't remember finding many hidden objects or spots I didn't expect to be able to access. It all feels a lot more empty and a lot more tedious.

Thief II: The Metal Age is a 2000 stealth game, developed by the now-defunct Looking Glass Studios, the successor of the widely acclaimed yet underrated Thief The Dark Project (1998), considered by many as the pioneer of modern stealth game, released along other amazing stealth titles such as Tenchu and Metal Gear Solid.  Being the least known of those 3 (at least from my point of view), Thief, for me,  is the most advanced on how a sneaking game should be, and that’s coming from someone who don’t have nostalgia glasses attached at all.
You take the role of Garrett, the cynical, sarcastic, and somewhat selfish master thief, with his only goal is to steal enough goods to pay his rent. A pretty interesting hero (or antihero) in the get go isn’t he? That very attitude, skill, and notoriety is the source of the problem on both games. You start off by having a couple of disconnected missions, before the real problem takes off. Thief Gold (I’ll just call the first one Thief Gold from now on)  has a pacing issues in the first couple of missions, because they’re kind of a long ”introductory” missions. Setting up the Thief universe, Garrett as a character, and it’s gameplay mechanics, and then it becomes a bizarre and intense supernatural horror story.
With all the universe building stuffs is done by the first one, and all the supernatural mumbo-jumbo gone (not completely, but it put in bare minimum). Thief II doesn’t have to suffer with all of these, it has a better pacing, more focused, more intricate dystopian-thriller story, set in an even more well realized steampunk setting. From a “modest” manor to a high security, 6 story towers, from stealing lowly goods to ancient mask, Thief has a unique storytelling, we all are as clueless as Garrett is,  all the story elements dropped in the perfect time and place. Take example for Karass, the antagonist, the common people only know him as “The guy who leads The Mechanists Order”, and so does Garrett, and us, the player view him, and he becomes a more threatening figure, and that’s through texts and overall environmental storytelling only.
While Thief Gold is a thieving game turned-supernatural stealth-semi-platformer halfway, The Metal Age is a “thieving simulator” all the way to  the end. Thief II is simply a much more refined version of Thief I, minus the annoying zombies, and maze-like location, my biggest gripe with Thief I. Improved graphic, making a more beautiful contrast between light and dark, and improved sound design. All thanks to  the amazing “Dark Engine”, an engine designed for Thief, and Thief alone, and yes, I know System Shock 2 use this engine too, but Dark Engine truly shows it’s technical prowess here. It has a unique aesthetic and probably the best “built-in” directional sound design ever. Even until now, I can’t think of any game that has a directional sound so spot on even without the help of a software and hardware
Thief is a stealth game at  it’s purest, most immersive form. Your ear, eyes, patience, and common sense is your greatest strength. Thief is a slow, I mean, really slow stealth game, especially on expert where you can’t kill any humans. Stay in the shadow, lean on every corner, creep your way around, and be patient and spatially aware, because once you’re caught, well, you're one dead thief, especially if you play on expert
The interface is minimalistic, there’s your health, your light gem, and inventory. No mini map and quest markers.  That help a lot with the immersion, you are lead to appreciate and respect the surrounding area, the unique art style and layout in each level, heightened your spatial awareness.
There's one flaw in this game and that's the AI, they are... inconsistent. Ranging from nearly blind/deaf (or both), to superhuman sense. You might think the AI gets smarter every time you advance to the next level, well.. to an extent yes, but for the most part, it's "unpredictable".
Two defining characteristic of Thief, that Thief II managed to improved, as I said earlier are the sound design and level design. I won’t delve deeper into sound design, because there’s not much to write about. It’s simply amazing, spot on, and overall has a defining "exaggerated" sound design. Let’s focus on level design for now. It’s FANTASTIC, it’s huge, titanic huge, believable, follows architectural logic, and has an "oppressive" atmosphere throughout that fit with the theme very well. Unlike the second half of Thief Gold, when the level goes total mind♥♥♥♥, in a good way, mostly. In term of level scenery, Thief Gold has more variation, from tomb, prison, cathedral, ruins, and mansions. Thief II levels are all worldly architecture. Only one level that goes to Thief Gold territory and that happens to be my least favorite level. As I said, it’s huge, more complex, but logical complex, that what makes Thief II a more fun experience than Gold. It’s harder to get lost, even if I do it’s easy to get back on track, making the exploration much more enjoyable.
The level verticality is simply astounding, so many paths, some is more obvious than others, some require keen eyes and careful exploration, some requires you to hear conversations and reading notes. It’s so rewarding every time you enter a room, and realize there are 3 or more ways to get in / across. There is a vent that connects that room to the basement, the celling that connects to the attic, there’s always the so obvious ground hallway, or you can move through the interconnected rooms and picking up loots and notes, and oh! There’s a secret passage if you put out that fire, saves my time from creeping out this place!  Every route is fun to take on, making every level looks larger than it is. Besides there’s no better feeling when stumble across some loots on the way.
One major flaw in the gaming industry trend nowadays is the fact that a lot of today’s games forget the phrase “Less is more”, the removal of an element hold the same importance, or even greater importance nowadays, as adding one. They take a shotgun approach, throwing everything that looks cool hoping it will sticks. It’s not necessarily bad, but with that design philosophy in mind, a game will become a “Jack of all trades, master of none” and directionless. That’s a plague that need to put in moderation.
Thief in the other hand, is already set out to be a hardcore stealth game from the very start. It’s simple and humble in presentation, and that’s what makes it works in perfect harmony.  With a “realistic stealth/thieving game” in mind, Looking Glass can focus on what’s important on  a stealth game. The combat is terrible, the gadgets are mostly stealth oriented, you are “forced” to do the stealthy way, but it’s fine, it’s a stealth game after all. It’s not about playstyles in Thief, it’s about the route you take and they deliver.
If I have to pick what’s the most underrated game developer for me, it’ll be a tie between Looking Glass and Black Isle. Though I might choose Looking Glass, because Thief, System Shock, and Ultima Underworld are less known than Black Isle’s Fallout series alone. Without them, there’ll be no Ion Storm (Deus Ex), Irrational (BioShock), and Arkane (Dishonored), it’s no coincidence that all of them are such  a hit. So short lived yet so influential, A timeless stealth game Thief II Is. A more than worthy successor of an already near-flawless game, and a perfect game to end an era.

I've had my eye on this title since some time last year, as a huge fan of Diablo and the C/ARPG genre as a whole. I eventually caved and purchased Book of Demons last week and have just started playing it tonight.
I'm not far through, I've just slain The Cook and got my first Legendary card (an enhanced copy of Mighty Blow for my Warrior) and am so far totally loving my time with the game! I am enjoying all the old Tristram vibes with the Sage and the Demon infested Cathedral, the obvious but well spiced up Butcher reference and many other little touches that solidify the tone and feel of the game as being something akin to the original Diablo or Darkest Dungeon, but with a very firm tongue in the cheek.
I find the card based system quite interesting and entertaining. As a Warrior at the moment I am spending almost all of my card slots and mana on artefacts (weapons and armour) and an essential slot dedicated to Healing potions, but I honestly haven't felt the need to use many spells or abilities. Not that I would have enough mana to do so with the amount of enchanted gear I'm wearing. I don't think this is a problem for me, per se, but I imagine some people may find the trade off between passive bonuses from artefacts (green cards) and active abilities from spells (blue cards) to be... unnecessary?
The game is well paced, allowing for relaxing and cathartic monster slaying in just the right sized chunks, and with the dungeon lengths easily customised to be tailored to however long you wish to spend playing.
I haven't tried the Mage yet and as of writing this review the Rogue class is unavailable, but I am very much looking forward to trying both of them out and seeing how the game feels different. Presumably with the Mage class I will find the balance shifting more heavily towards the use of Blue Spell cards for active abilities. I may be a bit disappointed if this was not the case and I still felt that passive bonuses were worth more than spells and abilities on a Mage character.
I adore the art, which is heavily stylised in a Papercraft fashion and even down to the way the newly generated dungeon literally unfolds before you like a folded up game board being unfurled across a table. The music is very reminiscent of Diablo and the voice acting is actually very impressive compared to my expectations, with the Barmaid sounding very sweet and compassionate and the Sage being a dead ringer for a certain other series' iconic well-leaning identifier of unknown bric-a-brac.
Overall I give this a healthy 8.5-9/10 so far and anticipate that I will be playing this for a good while to come. Rating slightly lowered for the so far perceived imbalance in the usefulness of green cards vs blue cards and small number of playable classes, though of course I know the Rogue is still in development and will complete the dungeon delving trio that matches off against the original Diablo. More classes beyond those three would be amazing.

They were clearly meant to feel exciting, but to be honest they didn't really, too easy to perform in some places and always too linear. There was one path, one direction, one speed, one action permitted at all times which I was playing. The correct path was even usually highlighted a nice bright red just to make it incredibly obvious which way you had to go and what action had to be performed to avoid forcing your poor little brain to have to do any amount of thinking at all.
The story bored me almost immediately, it just felt so generic, "omg, those stiff shirts and their law and order are horrible, lets dress like punks and run across rooftops to change teh world!". It was like the story was written by a fashion design company, all about look and style and lacking any sense of substance almost immediately.
As for the main character, I couldn't even remember her name later on, and while I wouldn't say she got to the point of being annoying, I would say I have no reason to count meeting her as a positive experience.
Overall, very pretty, sounds kinda nice, and there's the usual production values from a DICE/EA game, but at the end of the day it felt like this game was designed to look fantastic in game trailers without any consideration for how it actually played. Fantastic take on 2D rogue-like action. Each of the 12 unlockable characters feel unique and the "Artifacts" found distributed throughout the randomly generated levels allow you to change the game's parameters (often drastically) and makes for a versatile and customizable experience. One of the game's defining features is the time-based difficulty. As time elapses, the game becomes more difficult until reaching a threshold.
The game play is responsive and satisfying, whether gunning down enemies from afar or bombarding them with robot fists or hunkering down behind a shield with a shotgun. Controls are fully customizable.
Item variety is fantastic and lends a unique feel to each playthrough, granting your characters different strengths to compliment their abilities or plug up their weaknesses.
Simple yet inspired graphics and art direction set a gloomy, sci-fi mood reminiscent of classic metroid.
The music is stellar. I mean really a wonderful achievement. Play with headphones.
My only minor gripe at this point is that there should be a hotkey for cycling through the different zoom levels.
Also, taking screenshots via steam does not seem to work in this game.
Buy it and buy copies for your friends.

The video game for board game fanatics.

You know Civilization; begin at the dawn of civilization and rush to new technologies, racing through history in a turn-based environment. Leading your people to victory through science, technology or war.

The appeal of Civilization 5 isn't necessarily the technologies, combat units or different civilizations on offer. The story you create is the appeal of this game. Thrown into a randomly generated world, pitted against barbarians, allying with other civilizations,experiencing peace, war and treachery. This game is very diverse for such a simple concept.

A single play through could take days to complete. As a result most people will find themselves playing against AI. The game feels like it was designed for multiplayer, with the ability to trade and create agreements. The AI does not take advantage of these options, unless taking from you to have the scales tipped in their favour.

Unless you have a group of friends who want to play, you will find yourself facing off against the one dimensional, aggressively selfish AI.

With the content available in-game, the AI will be an afterthought for you, until there is a hundred hours logged and you begin to look past the surface of Civilization 5.

This game gives you a lot of content and replay value. There is something here for any turn-based strategy enthusiast or board game fanatic.

Stick of Truth is an immersive South Park episode. If you like South Park you'll love this game. If you loath South Park avoid it like the plague.
As you'd expect from Stone and Parker the story is well written and the challenges fit into it seamlessly.
You play "The New Kid" in town. The South Park gang is embroiled in a roleplaying game that you are invited to play.The elves and humans are waging war (playing steal the flag) over a stick (of truth) and you are the New Hope  that will turn the tide of battle. You traverse the vastness of horror that is the realm of South Park. You battle Elves, Humans, bums, rats and sixth graders. You get to give a princes a flower, and you find Jesus.
Oh yeah, and you make a lot of friends on facebook.
You have stalwart allies who stand by you in your in your epic quest. From Paladin Butters to The Grand Wizard fatass they will aide you in your trials. Even Cartman.
You run into many of your favorite South Park characters and some of them have fun things for you to do.
The special abilities, equipment and spells are hilarious parodies of those in 'serious' role-playing games. They kept me laughing through the whole game.

The turn-based method of fighting slowed combat so that it did not outpace the flow of the story. It also allowed the NPC'S an opportunity to make  snarky comments if you take too long to attack. It was kind of cool. I wouldn't want to see another game use this method, but it's Awkward silliness seemed to fit.
Although the game is exactly as long as it needs to be to tell the story, it is too short for the price they were asking. If you're on the fence about the game, wait until it comes down. Way down. I pre-ordered it, and even though I loved the game, I still felt I had  been ripped-off. Then again, what was it that Cartman said about pre-ordering games? It had something to do with a d|ck in your mouth. . .
One more thing. If you buy this game for your children: Bad Parent! BAD Parent!! Didn't you learn a thing in parent obedience class?

First of all, let me tell you, that HARDWARE REQUIREMENTS are ONE, BIG LIE. I have completed the whole game on much weaker computer than it was specified in requirements. Not only that; it was stable 30-35 fps with 1920x1080 with all set to medium on my FX-6300 and Radeon HD 7770 1GB GHz edition.
As there are some problems with other, even more powerful Radeon cards reported, I would say that the issue is that game cannot take all the best from Intel-Radeon setup, on AMD-Radeon setup seems running smoothly.
Then, about game, it is fun. I personally never enjoyed zombie themed games, yet I enjoyed it.
It is addicting, since I've played 4 days straight for 60 hours, and it has not happened for a while for any other game (I'm 25 yr old, with girlfriend and job), not to mention that to complete it, I only died 131 times and still enjoyed the game.
It is funny. You will enjoy every different freak you will encounter(it's paradox, but it seems that to survive in a place like Harran, you have to be somewhat insane, or you have to become insane). For some dialogues, you will laugh hard enough to fell from chair(Gazi and his mother, Lykenthrope, ommander jefferson, and so on). There are some funny situations also, like when you break into a shop, alarm goes of, and you find yourself surrounded with cop-zombies. Finally, you will be amazed how many people keep grinder blades and nails in their dirty laundry ;)
It is hard. I already mention that I died 131 times - game keeps the statistics for me ;) What is more,
For a plot, I would tell that guys from Techland could teach some of Hollywood directors how action movies should be done. It's not that it's unpredictable, but follows Hitchcock saying that story should start with earthquake and tension should rise from now on.
About running system, one word - AWESOME.
It's bad game for you, if you want just to kill zombies though. There are literally everywhere. They are tough. They are getting tougher and more ferocious as the main plot advances. You cannot kill them all. You cannot shoot them, because noise will bring vast amounts of Virals, even more agressive ones.You cannot kill them all, because your weapon eventually breaks, what is expected(especially from simple gas pipe, after breaking spines of 4 not-anymore-people). And during the nights, it's getting even tougher.
Of course there are some glitches, but what game does not have them. For example, while I was completing the game, there was one closet from which every time i walked by, zombie broke through door from that closet. Funny that in zombie-infected area someone had enough time to repair them, and close zombie inside 3 TIMES A DAY ;)
The other thing that bothered me, was that no building was destructible, no plant flammable, and so on; but for this plot it could became disastrous, if it was.
Never tested it in coop mode, though. But someday i will.
To sum up, this is great piece of game. I would give it 9/10, and if you read it, you should try it.

(This review only covers the four main episodes of the game, and not the two bonus episodes that slot in between those chronologically.)
I was too young to get involved with the Resident Evil franchise at its inception on the original PlayStation, and have only ever engaged in the franchise via Resident Evil 5.  My girlfriend is a huge fan of the movies and games however, and picked this up for us to play on the Steam Link in the living room together, so I figured I'd give it a whirl.  The original game was released episodically, so a base purchase will get you just Episode 1, and you can purchase each additional episode (a total of 4, plus 2 "extras" that are more side stories than the rest) or pick everything up in a bundle like she did.  Its interesting as a gamer to see the episodic model slowly coming back into style after the model kind of petered out in the 00's with Half-Life and SiN.  Early Access games can take the model to the extreme end of things, while developers like Tell Tale, and in this case, Capcom, can push out an entire campaign over the course of a year.  Now that the full game is available though, you won't have to worry about only getting the first taste and being left hanging for X amount of months.
Resident Evil 5, while enjoyable, didn't overly inspire me to go out and play every other title in the series I could get my hands on, although I will admit Resident Evil 4 continues to rot in the depths of my Steam backlog, so SOMEDAY I'll get to see what all the fuss is about there.  Revelations 2 was a lot more pallatable in terms of pacing though, and did not burn me out or get frustrating after long sessions of gameplay like some games do (especially when played on the TV, never been able to handle console marathons for anywhere near as long as on a monitor on a desk somewhere).  The gameplay balances itself between desperate "don't let the boogie man get me" gunplay and some puzzles that can range from basic to quite clever without being overtly infuriating, with dramatic pre-rendered cut scenes peppered in as bookends between it all.  I actually quite enjoyed the episodic nature as it put the game in nice bite-sized chunks I could sink my teeth into and feel satisfied with putting down the controller after a couple hours of gameplay until the next night.
The game puts you in control of two protagonists at a time that you can switch between at-will like other RE titles, but there are two duos in the story, each exploring the same maps separated by several months of time.  Each of the four characters has their own unique abilities and ways of working together with their respective partners to explore the maps, unlock doors, find ammo, etc.  Typically, one pair plays through an area for about an hour or two of gameplay, and then the story will jump to the second pair revisiting the same area, but possibly from a different angle, which made focusing on combat and puzzles for the second pair a lot more enjoyable as I knew where I was going, though sometimes the areas visited are dramatically different to prevent you from getting that feeling of retracing your steps every two  hours.  Ammo and inventory management is still a thing, you'll have to be choosy with how you engage enemies (especially when half of the playable teams do not pack heat), though boss battles tend to get a little more generous with keeping you adequatly stocked in case if you run out.
Between Resident Evil 5 and reading about the older games in the series in gaming magazines growing up, I was able to piece together enough of the story to make it enjoyable.  However, a lot of the finer details are relegated to journal-like collectables, and if you try to over-analyze the plot in the universe proper it might make for a headache for a casual fan.  Thankfully, the writing and overall themes of the game focus a lot more on this being a story about the four characters involved as people, rather than a piece of the giant Umbrella tapestry that Capcom has woven over the years, and for that the story comes out much more tolerable than other sketchy dubs of Japanese titles.
I did experience some technical difficulties with massive frame drops and skipping in early gameplay, and have seen people having issues with it.  The final fix turned out to be V-sync related, and though I had it disabled in game, I still had G-sync enabled on my monitor and it was causing issues when played on PC or streamed to the Steam Link.  Disabling G-sync before playing eliminated all of my technical woes and the rest of the game ran fine, so I won't hold it against the developers.
Though the game didn't completely convert me into a huge Resident Evil fan, Revelations 2 might have actually made me more willing to try other titles in the series like the stream of HD re-releases Capcom have been publishing.  Who knows, I might even finally get around to playing Resident Evil 4 HD.

In a beautiful and colorful world, you play the part of the girl that gets to see the world on the underside.  While things might look calm and nice in this city, it's really not.  Information is being suppressed, communication is always monitored, and if you want to be able to have an open mind and not be killed for it, you have to get your message out in secret.  That's why you, the main character, exist: to run secretive information around the city.  You'll get caught up in a plot about catching the last of your kind, the Runners, that involves potentially the death of someone close to you.  You have to run and dodge, shoot and kill when necessary, incapacitate when not, in order to save the city from the man who wants to silence truth, incidentally the leader of the city.
The gameplay is really neat, being able to traverse the city's rooftops as the main character; the controls are usually intuitive, making it easy to pull off all the complex stunts that will get you from building to building, or up a wall, or across a pipe, etc.  The story is immersive and unexpected.  And, what's more, the game makes a serious connection to the real world that we live in, what with all the stories of NSA spying going on.
I give two thumbs up.  I had a lot of fun with this game.

Why I repurchased this product:
1. Its been around a year and half since I last touched this game for a prolonged period of time and it seems my burnout has worn out and the game has changed since post-launch (and I'm a cheap wiener.)
2. While MTs are still in the game, that problem has sort of been redeemed as they've added a crafting system in which you can complete objects. This includes dailies, weeklies and seasonal events and once you fill up the meter, you earn a vault crate that gives you random cosmetics, which you can keep or scrap to save up for higher quality aesthetics. This is a grind, but it does gives give players a sense of accomplishment for long-term play. You also still do have a pretty good chance to gain rare items in the crates, but they're not tradable as that would understandably ruin the game's economy.
3. I still think they should have went with the community's idea of adding another melee class instead of survivalist as this would have given each class a specific role, but I can see its purpose. The class is flexible and gives new players a taste of whats to come from the other classes as its a mixture of all them.
Conclusion: I probably jumped the gun, but I don't think they should have introduced MTs mid early Access and, instead should have put out more cosmetic bundles as they have now along side the MTs.

They really need to have a 'in the middle' rating option instead of yes or no. With that said, I did select no, but that isn't my real impression of the game. Also remember that this is in EA, so anything I say here may be addressed at a later date by the devs.
Setup:
- Download/patching was pretty straightforward. Not sure of the of the issues people had mentioned about it, but I didn't have any issues downloading, updating and then getting right into the game.
- Character creation was underwhelming. You basically select one of the 6 classes (which are kind of flat feeling; more on that later), one of 4 races who from what I read have absolutely no difference between them other than physical appearance, select male/female, pick your hair, eye, lip color, name and thats that. Unless I totally missed a big section allowing you to personalize your appearance, you basically look the same as anyone else with your race/class/hair color.
- Available classes were also a bit meh. The selections are pretty basic things you see across MMO and hack/slash games. Other than the dark knight which is a little bit of a DPS/tank melee hybrid, we've seen everything else a thousand times. With that, I'm also surprised that there wasn't a rogue/stealth type or more specialized magic types like a necro, all sorts of elementals or just something new and creative.
- I am still under the impression that unless the different races have inate skills/bonuses/benefits that aern't mentioned during the character creation page, there is zero difference between them other than you look like a human or something else. Kind of disappointing if this is simply for cosmetics.
Gameplay:
- There is little to no actual story setup. I know some people want to get into the lore and everything and some can't push the enter button fast enough to bypass it. So that that for what you will. When the game loads, you're basically at a fort and goblins have overrun the area, blah blah blah you've heard this a billion times already. The overall gist of the game is to get the sacred ember McGuffin and save the universe as usual. But this is a hack & slash game, so I know the story matters as much as the acting does in a p0rn movie.
- The graphics/artwork are good. The game was nice to look at and on my system (i7, GTX 780) everything ran at full graphics without a problem.
- Good on the devs for making it possible to allow key rebinds on everything. Not sure why this is sometimes not available (other than pure laziness).
- One of my biggest gripes was that even when max zoomed out, it felt like you could only see 10 feet in any direction. I'd really love to see more ARPG games where if you have discovered/cleared the FoW on an area you can zoom out much further than just whatever is currently right by you. It really felt like everything was ontop of me.
- The aggro ranges of mobs are rediculously short. Probably due to what I mentioned above, but you basically have to walk up and smack an enemy before they react to you. Then again, with having a close in max zoom, if the aggro was further you'd basically spend the entire game having things run at you from off screen.
- The skills system is pretty straight forward and you quickly realize that you need to formulate a strategy on how you want/need to set up for your specific playstyle. I'd suggest having all of these skills be shown on more of a bottom to type chart where you unlock X to unlock Y istead of the weird left to right bars that are there now. There should also be multiple skills to pick at the unlocks you get at 10, 15,20, etc instead of just 'this is the skill you get at this level'.
- The loot and armor/weapons system is surprisingly one of the most simple straightforward approaches to it, yet its rarely used. Have you ever asked yourself in a RPG/MMO, 'why cant I put this dumb shirt on' and the answer was because you weren't a cleric or whatever class it was for? Well, anything you loot (as far as Ive seen) you can equip it; the caviet is that the bonuses are more geared towards the class its meant for so while you may enjoy a huge AC jump on those pants for wearing a warrios pants as an archer, you aernt getting meaningful bonuses/stat increases from them because they are geared towards the stats a warrior uses. But you can still wear them!
- Actual combat is straightforward. Bind attacks, do work. My issue outside of the too much zoom problem was that this game was basically, start at X and there are 2/3 people with quests. Go do those quests and move to the next spot, rinse/repeat. Ontop of this, the map you are fighting on isn't large; you have quest givers wanting you to check things out/kill problem mobs that are 20 steps away or go and check if my house is ok when the house is the equivalent of being a block away from the person. it made me want to call the NPC questgivers lazy azzes and made me wonder how they manage to get dressed in the morning.
Overall, I want to like the game. I really do. That's why I'm doing this review in hopes that eventually things get being developed and/or that I am wrong about this later in the game and the zoom zooms out 5x as much, the game feels more challenging and I'm not running errands for people too lazy to go check the mailbox. The way it sits right now, it has potential, but there are game play issues like those I mentioned above that just makes me think twice about spending any real time playing or investing in grinding out gear because I've seen this all already.

On the surface this seemed like it would be an incredible game but it just did -not- deliver.  The art style is brilliant, the soundtrack is incredible and the gameplay intuitive; but shoddy cutscenes, bad checkpoint locations, and hotspots with -tiny- windows that don't seem to trigger consistantly on PC make this game incredibly frustrating.  Maybe this feels like a bad port, or maybe the development was rushed; either way the result was my rage quitting ~2/3 of the way through the game and haven't picked it up since.
A game which contains enough bugs to actually make me -angry- is not a good thing.  I'm sure I'll pick it up again another time to complete the story in preparation for Mirrors Edge 2 (which looks like more effort will be going into it), but outside of that - I don't recommend this game.
TL:DR - Great atmosphere and style; sloppily made.  Only buy if you have a high tolerance level for frustration.

Its more a of Titan Quest/ Grim Dawn Meets Guild Wars 2.
I have not spent a lot of time in the game, but 3ish hours sitting at level 11 i feel as though i got an ok Taste to leave a review.( yes i know there is muuch more i have to explore)  I would like to start this off with the negatives becuase the Devs are very active so I want to make sure they see the dislikes.
NEGATIVES
1)  Loot - What the hell is going on here? there is WAY to much, i never thought i would say that about an ARPG but i did, Your Bag will be full in a matter of minutes, which makes for constant trips town, and no with stash (atleast not one that i could find) , and no crafting until later levels , it becomes a chore.
2) Gear- again what the hell is going on here? Like some other reviews its just very hard to understand and very confusing for new players, Im sure this could be simplified in a number of ways,
- lower level gear should be just your average attack/defense with slight buffs
- mabye add a gearing tutorial that shows players why they should use light or heavy ( just when you pick up your
first )
- add another gearing tutorial about the buffs they offer ( again just when you pick up your first one)

4) Skill Tree- PLEASE GET RID OF THE FULLSCREEN! for a game that can not be paused this is very very annoying.
5) Map- ( not the mini ) This map is 100% usless! It does not show current location or objectives it is just a pretty screen
6) Mounts- While i love the mounts, We need a mount hot key( nevermind this has been added) slotting it into the side bar just does not do it for me.

THE GOOD
1) Its is a beautiful game! and runs smoothly for me.
2)  Being able to zoom in and out freely

Fantastic take on 2D rogue-like action. Each of the 12 unlockable characters feel unique and the "Artifacts" found distributed throughout the randomly generated levels allow you to change the game's parameters (often drastically) and makes for a versatile and customizable experience. Plus it's co-operative locally and online.
One of the game's defining features is the time-based difficulty. As time elapses, the game becomes more difficult until reaching a threshold.
The game play is responsive and satisfying, whether gunning down enemies from afar or bombarding them with robot fists or hunkering down behind a shield with a shotgun. Controls are fully customizable.
Item variety is fantastic and lends a unique feel to each playthrough, granting your characters different strengths to compliment their abilities or plug up their weaknesses.
Simple yet inspired graphics and art direction set a gloomy, sci-fi mood reminiscent of classic metroid.
The music is stellar. I mean really a wonderful achievement. Play with headphones.
My only minor gripe at this point is that there should be a hotkey for cycling through the different zoom levels.
Also, taking screenshots via steam does not seem to work in this game.
Buy it and buy copies for your friends.

Edit (October 9, 2017):
A recent update to the game allows players to vote out the leaders of their guild.
The ability to vote out guild leaders is a terrible addition to the game. There is no incentive to invest time and in-game resources to build up a guild if a group of players can band together to vote you out at any time. This discourages guild leaders from allowing open recruitment since they don't know who they can trust. All round, a terrible update to the game. If meeting new people and building a community is what you want, then stay away from this game.
Original review (August 21, 2017):
This is a solid Diablo-like game, but there are a lot of bugs and glitches and the client will crash at some unfortunate times. The content at the moment is a bit minimal. There are a lot of activities such as crafting, fishing, mining, growing plants, potion making and cooking, but none seem too important yet. The end game content currently consists of running a dungeon for loot, leveling up those activities I mentioned earlier in preparation for future updates and completing a compendium of enemy-dropped cards that gives bonus stats.
I'm not sure that I recommend this game at the $20 price point. If you can find it cheaper, then it is worth trying.

I feel more than a little weird writing this because I am clearly in the minority compared to the other reviewers, but I expected (and wanted) a thought-provoking puzzler and what I get is a psychedelic zoo.
While extremely clever in some of the "puzzles", my own experience was that the majority of the rooms are just smoke-and-mirrors tricks.  Plowing ahead like a bull in a china shop seems to be the #1 way to "progress".  I wound up in an enormous mobius strip, chasing my tail and being patted on the head by the signs for doing the right thing for like 10 minutes. Stick of Truth is an immersive South Park episode. If you like South Park you'll love this game. If you loath South Park avoid it like the plague.
As you'd expect from Stone and Parker the story is well written and the challenges fit into it seamlessly.
You play "The New Kid" in town. The South Park gang is embroiled in a roleplaying game that you are invited to play.The elves and humans are waging war (playing steal the flag) over a stick (of truth) and you are the New Hope  that will turn the tide of battle. You traverse the vastness of horror that is the realm of South Park. You battle Elves, Humans, bums, rats and sixth graders. You get to give a princes a flower, and you find Jesus.
Oh yeah, and you make a lot of friends on facebook.
You have stalwart allies who stand by you in your in your epic quest. From Paladin Butters to The Grand Wizard fatass they will aide you in your trials. Even Cartman.
You run into many of your favorite South Park characters and some of them have fun things for you to do.
The special abilities, equipment and spells are hilarious parodies of those in 'serious' role-playing games. They kept me laughing through the whole game.

The turn-based method of fighting slowed combat so that it did not outpace the flow of the story. It also allowed the NPC'S an opportunity to make  snarky comments if you take too long to attack. It was kind of cool. I wouldn't want to see another game use this method, but it's Awkward silliness seemed to fit.
Although the game is exactly as long as it needs to be to tell the story, it is too short for the price they were asking. If you're on the fence about the game, wait until it comes down. Way down. I pre-ordered it, and even though I loved the game, I still felt I had  been ripped-off. Then again, what was it that Cartman said about pre-ordering games? It had something to do with a d|ck in your mouth. . .
One more thing. If you buy this game for your children: Bad Parent! BAD Parent!! Didn't you learn a thing in parent obedience class?

I have played this game since 1992, not since today's Steam release.  It's a DOSBox version of the original game, in all its glory.
RIGHT-CLICK THE GAME IN YOUR LIBRARY.  This is extremely important, because that's how you can configure the keys, which is also the best way of knowing what they are.  It's also how you access Super Melee - 'Play Game' takes you to the campaign.  And since you're unlikely to 'view manual' before you start, it's worth knowing that the campaign starts with your ship arriving in the Sol system, after being isolated far from Earth for decades.  Earth is the third rock from the sun; you don't have to go there first, but it's not a bad idea.
If you don't love early 90s techno, then I guess you turn the music off, but each race has its own theme music, and there's some nice tunes in there.
But what is the game actually like?  It's a arcade/story game, with RPG and customization elements.  You get to discover a galaxy that is full of surprises and wonderful backstory and wonderful fun.  And if you complete it on the first playthrough without using a walkthrough, then you're a genuis.  (But don't worry, there's a race that sells clues!)
Pros:
A faithful restoration of THE standout game of 1992
Amazing storyline
Soundtrack and graphics were revolutionary at the time, and are still not bad
Arcade gameplay that is just plain awesome
Two-player shared keyboard experience is great
You're paying maybe 1 cent per hour of campaign gameplay
Cons:
No in-game tutorial or other modern comforts
My wife hates the soundtrack, even though I still love it
The campaign is LONG and hard to win
Working out how to play the game is a critical part of the experience, and many people don't go for that sort of thing.
