Zeno Clash 2 successfully improves on all of the shortcomings of the first one. And let me tell you; I had a blast playing the first one and I had even more fun playing the second one, even if it had a slightly higher learning curve in the beginning. Let me sum it up:
First; the graphics have been improved. It now runs on UE3 and it shows. It's sharp, runs at 60fps and looks gorgeous. The environments and characters are simply amazing. What a great world ! ACE Team sure knows how to build an intriguing, weird world.
Second; the world is now bigger (unfortunately still a bit too linear) and has sidequests.
Third; Ghat (main character) has more moves, including the awesome looking and easily executed piledriver.
Fourth; you can now bring allies into some of  the bigger battles. It also introduces co-op, so you can run around and fight bad guys with a buddy.
Tell me that that doesn't sound cool, right ? Hell yes !
At the same time it also has some flaws, thanks to these new additions. Let me sum those up:
The world is bigger, yes, but it's still divided into hubs. So instead of using one big world, it's split up which throws you a bit out of the experience every time you have to travel. These portals also look a bit out of place.
Since battles contain multiple enemies it's hard to use some of your newer moves. And while your allies are somewhat helpful, they can also get in the way when you're fighting (inconvenient when friendly fire is on). The game also locks onto enemies automatically, so you'll have to switch around a lot. My advice is to disable this in the options menu so you can move around freely and lock when you feel you like it.
And like always, whenever a game is awesome, we don't want the experience to end too soon. Zeno Clash 2 isn't short, it's about 8-9 hours long (including all sidequests), but still on the short side for an 'open world' game.
I had a great time playing it, and I truly hope ACE Team will earn enough money to give us a third game of this wonderfully realized world. We'll know in a few more years.
In the meantime; buy this and show them your support.

I didn't play this game until I was 26 years old, so I like to think that my opinion on it is unbiased by nostalgia. That said, this game is absolutely fantastic. Easily one of my favorite stealth games of all time. The levels are large and incredibly organic, with several hidden passages and ways to traverse them. The difficulty is challenging but not tedious. The graphics are dated, but more than makes up for it in incredible sound design and ambient music, wonderfully composed by Eric Brosius. Not only that, but the game is filled with character. The atmosphere is dark and the fantasy world presented here is creative and interesting, but the game also has a very dry sense of humor that keeps things from getting too grimdark. Thief 2, The Metal Age was a game that I very much enjoyed playing, and although it’s quite old, I still think it holds up very well.
In Thief 2, you play as Garrett, a master thief who must overcome recent trouble involving a corrupt Sheriff who has cracked down on crime, and who seems to have a personal grudge against Garrett. Throughout the game, you must sneak around in various missions and locations, all while uncovering a potentially much larger problem that goes beyond Garrett himself.
In terms of gameplay, it plays similar to the first Thief game. You sneak around, completing various objectives, all while trying to remain unnoticed. While combat is an option, Garrett is rather unequipped when it comes to fighting enemies, and stands little chance against more than one foe at a time. Stealth is by far the best option, and Thief 2 still holds up as one of the best stealth games i’ve played. Guards have long, unpredictable patrols they take, meaning they don’t simply walk from one end of the room to the other making them easy targets, which keeps the game tense and forces the player to always be on their toes in case a guard shows up unexpectedly. Guards are always alert, and will investigate a noise they hear. If they catch a glimpse of you, they may decide to look around, forcing the player to keep moving so that they aren’t found. Garrett’s main means of hiding is darkness. By hiding in the shadows, guards won’t be able to spot the player, allowing them to sneak around unnoticed. The mechanic of hiding in darkness and being exposed in the light works excellently in the game, and it was quite revolutionary for its time. Another interesting mechanic is how not all floors produce the same amount of noise when stepped on. Things like carpet and grass will produce little noise, while marble floors will produce more noise, potentially bringing guards over as well. As you progress through the game and begin stealing from richer people, more marble flooring will be found and more electric lights will be used, meaning it will get harder to keep quiet and stay in the dark.
The level design is some of the best i’ve seen, even an improvement on the excellent design of the first game. Levels are non-linear, large, and open, and can have many different sections, each with their own ways to sneak around undetected. The levels are also very varied. Some you may find yourself in a huge mansion, some in the streets of the city, and in many other locations as well. Garrett will have a large array of tools at his disposal to help him through the levels, including many different types of arrows such as water and vine arrows that will help in certain scenarios.
Thief 2 also wisely gets rid of the more paranormal settings and enemies that were common in the first game and replaces them with more stealth focused ones. In the first Thief, many of the levels revolved around ruins and caves filled with enemies such as zombies. These levels didn’t offer much in terms of stealth, and for the most part involved simply running right by the enemies while avoiding their attacks. Enemies such as zombies are rarely seen in Thief 2, and luckily don’t break the flow of the stealth gameplay. Thief 2 does use new enemies in the form of robots, but luckily they can be snuck around, making them similar to guards. They also offer a good challenge, because they cannot be knocked out, and throughout playing the game I never once destroyed one. I don’t even know if it was possible to destroy one in the game at all.
The game and the people in it also have a lot of charm. Garrett isn’t some lifeless protagonist; he’s a man who can take a moment seriously, but isn’t afraid to make a few cynical remarks about the people he’s stealing from. He isn’t some special hero who people shower with praise, he’s just a guy trying to make enough money from stealing to pay his rent. The guards in the game also have excellent, sometimes quite funny dialogue, and the drunken tone of their voice is a great way to get across their character.
The story itself is also very good, and is often told in a non-direct fashion, meaning the player will learn more about the story and world by reading notes left on people's desks, listening to guards talking to each other, as well as other ways. This also gives players more of a reason to look around and explore the environments. While the story itself may seem simple at first, it slowly builds up and becomes something more. It’s rarely a flashy story, but it’s subtle, as well as intriguing and interesting at the same time.
I can only really think of two complaints about the game, and they're both pretty minor. First, climbing in the game can be a bit difficult, and if you miss the ledge your trying to grab, the character may jump by accident and alert guards to your location. Second, it seems a bit unfair that taking one step on a marble floor brings every guard in the nearby area to your location, especially when guards are already walking over marble floors without anyone caring. Still, these are only small complaints and they didn't get in the way of my enjoyment of the game.
Overall, Thief 2 offers a great improvement over an already great game. It’s one of the best stealth games around, and it has gameplay that still holds up today. The graphics will seem quite dated by today's standards, but if you’re able to get around that, it shouldn’t hinder your enjoyment. One of my favorite games.

Thief 2 is a pretty old game. You'll have to re-bind controls right away (F is crouch, for example), movement is less smooth than today's games, and combat kind of sucks. Luckily, the movement is easy to get used to, and you're never supposed to engage in combat anyway.
There is a bit at the end where the same map is used for 2 levels, and I'm not a fan of the final level, but the rest of the game is so excellent that it outweighs all the negatives in my eyes.
Seriously, this has to be the greatest stealth game in existence. Stealth is based on line-of-sight, whether you're in a shadow or not, how much noise you're making, and even if you have something reflective in your hands.
There are also a metric buttload of different entryways and routes that you can take. You could play this game over and over for years and never know about a certain ledge that you can jump on if you jump just right that gives you an entirely new perspective on a level. There are also a ton of secrets in the vein of Doom and Doom 2. The great thing about these secrets is that they're never hidden in a way that makes no sense. If there's a wall that slides away, then there's a button, or a movable torch-holder, or a bookshelf with a pullable book, or something else similar that's somewhere closeby.

With most things, you expect, as time goes on, that they will improve. Newer cars are better than old, that sort of thing. The stealth genre is the only thing where this doesn\'t seem to be the case. Not to say that there aren\'t good modern day stealth games, of course there are. However, as of right now, none of them have seemed to surpass Thief 2, just offer and equally good experience, despite Thief\'s age.
I won\'t go crazy on this review, but here is an example. Hitman is a stealth game of sorts, and as most games do, it discourages you from killing bad guys. The less bodies the better. How does it do this? With points, a negative effect on your over all proformance review, just some numbers on the screen. And thats all fine and dandy. But what about Thief.
Thief is entirely organic, as it encourages you to be as stealthy as possible in a totally realistic way, that is much more planned out, while avoiding the whole issue of pulling you out of the experience, reminding you that \"this is just a game\".   If you encounter a guard, you could try to sneak around him. One small mistake could get you killed though, so why not knock him out? You could, but then you have to worry about the body, which if not well hiden enough, could ruin everything. Meanwhile, killing him would be even worse, since that would not only make a body, but also a blood stain, which would require a water arrow to clean. This natural progressing of actions and consequences encourages you to play with as little encounters as possible, instead guiding you to learn to sneak past guards without ever interacting with them in the first place, being the ultimate ninja. But this doesn\'t feel gamey, and doesn\'t feel arbitrary or tedious.
This is just one of the many reasons why Thief 2 still stands up as a great stealth game. Buy it, then download tafferpatcher, a program which helps the game run on modern computers. Don\'t worry, it is stupid easy, just download the file, and launch the executable, it takes all of 30 seconds. Plus, there are thousands of fan made levels which the community has made, providing hours of gameplay beyond the base game, so have fun!

A flawed but strangely enjoyable game. Follow a ruthless ex mercenary who's family has been held hostage by a mysterious group known as "The 7" and a medicated psychopath who is prone to blacking out and going on murderous rampages. A crazy series of missions from bank heists, hitting up clubs in Shanghai, to fighting in a South American civil war - the story is over the top, such as rapelling down an office building to blow up the window and fight your way to the bottom, and the characters pull the story together just enough that you'll be happy to follow along. The weakest point in the game is the combat, and lacklustre gameplay mechanics. Shooting is mediocre and hard when your shots don't hit their mark (usually making you rely on a lucky shot or two that hits its mark), the cover system is practically useless and very tough to use, and the ability to command your fellow criminals doesn't have enough of an impact to be worth doing since they can often take care of themselves.
Regardless, this game oddly captured my interest and held onto me for the span of its short, couple hour campaign.

Why I repurchased this product:
1. Its been around a year and half since I last touched this game for a prolonged period of time and it seems my burnout has worn out and the game has changed since post-launch (and I'm a cheap wiener.)
2. While MTs are still in the game, that problem has sort of been redeemed as they've added a crafting system in which you can complete objects. This includes dailies, weeklies and seasonal events and once you fill up the meter, you earn a vault crate that gives you random cosmetics, which you can keep or scrap to save up for higher quality aesthetics. This is a grind, but it does gives give players a sense of accomplishment for long-term play. You also still do have a pretty good chance to gain rare items in the crates, but they're not tradable as that would understandably ruin the game's economy.
3. I still think they should have went with the community's idea of adding another melee class instead of survivalist as this would have given each class a specific role, but I can see its purpose. The class is flexible and gives new players a taste of whats to come from the other classes as its a mixture of all them.
Conclusion: I probably jumped the gun, but I don't think they should have introduced MTs mid early Access and, instead should have put out more cosmetic bundles as they have now along side the MTs.
Edit: Oh ♥♥♥♥♥♥ apparently you can also craft crates that require cash too and sometimes get better
crafting material.

I played a lot of tactics based games and this is one I would have gladly skipped had I known how linear and miniscule any choices presented were. The game is really narrow in terms of forward progression.
You can move anywhere when it isn't in battle mode. This requires clicking everywhere. It's like a point and click adventure.  You are lead along the way towards spots that present "treasure" and mini events that require skill points to unlock. Moving is really slow. And you have to move everywhere. There is no speed adjustment. Just click, click, click.
Leveling system is almost a joke. You are presented with multiple stats to improve and to put it into the playstyle you want. The most special class that this game gives is the decker class which lets you jack into the cyberspace. I didn't want to play anymore after a few hours.
I didn't play too long until I realized how pointless most of the "choices" i made were. There isn't a cause and effect scenario. It's more of a just kill everything you see. The story line is supposedly good. It wasn't strong enough to make me want to play the boring aspects of the game.
Combat is nearly okay. They got something here almost done right. If you're going to play your first run i would recommend just being able to kill everything. A game like this was meant to be played multiple times so you can choose to be somewhat weaker and try to unlock everything the first time or play strong the first time and go again and be at the optimum level of power and be able to unlock a lot of stuff.
Story is the driving factor of this game. the story dictates every move your character makes. There is no FREEDOM and the character you make is driven by the storyline. You can't go somewhere and level and make money and do whatever you want. The game forces you to keep moving on with the story. You make do with the resources you have and keep moving the story forward. It's an okay storyline. I did not care one bit about any of the characters after the first two hours. It must be me who is having a hard time connecting with the story.
The graphics look good but executed a little poorly. I have to zoom in to get a good look (2560x1440) and don't bother playing this game on multiple screens (i had it on triple screens and this game was not built for it). The mood and atmosphere is almost on point. I'm not big on cyberpunk stuff so it didn't quite pull me in.
I lost almost all interest piece by piece. The only reason I would finish the game is because I like to finish games. I will not be playing this game anymore. Maybe another campaign to see if anythign had improved though.

A bunch of Magic: the Gathering pros sat around a table and worked out where existing CCGs like Hearthstone dropped the ball and have provided an incredibly polished card game with lots of variety without all the bullcrap RNG we've come to expect from the genre.
With strong class mechanics and powerful card synergies as well as the flexible and powerful evolve mechanic there is a lot of fun to be had with what initially appears to be just another CCG.
In terms of free-to-play options there's the story mode (6+ hours of gameplay with story, let's you try each character), completely free arena-style drafting with your friends and plenty of freebies to get you started (packs and arena tickets). If you're not interested in spending money out the gates there's plenty to get started with and the developers do just hand out packs from time to time.
If you're a bit more hardcore with your cards building a collection is relatively easy, with more cards per pack than Hearthstone and the ability to put more than one of each legendary card in your deck there is a lot of flexibility with deck construction. Duplicates can be converted to vials which can be used to craft cards you don't have. Currently there are two sets: the core set and Darkness Evolved. Another set is being released on the 29th Dec. That leaves you with a massive card pool to experiment with - giving varying levels of power and synergy in both draft (Take-Two) and constructed formats.
Overall this game is a must try for card game fans and I see it sticking around for a long time. Well-polished gems of the genre like this could one day give Magic and Hearthstone a run for their money.

Play if you enjoy: First person brawlers, good story, interesting characters, developed worlds, and a twist on each you don't normally see.
Not recommended if the following bother you: it's not everyone's cup of tea.  The characters and world are a bit different, a bit out there.  You've got to do some thinking, and some digging, for the whole plot to make sense.  The game's a bit rough, the voice acting is good enough but not great.
It's a first-person brawler done fairly well, but that's not the primary thing that attracted me to the series: it's the level of imagination.  The game is as much art as it is video game, creating an alien world filled with bizarre animals, plants, people, and architecture whose imagination is astounding; it won't be like any place or game you've seen before.  ACE team have always impressed with their originality: world, art, plot, and to a lesser extent gameplay.  Zeno Clash 1 was a story in itself, not requiring a sequel to be complete, but it asked questions and laid the groundwork for a much bigger story, which is what Zeno Clash 2 delivers.  ACE team are from Chile, a country we don't normally see games from, and this different culture shows through in a way I find interesting and refreshing.  They also have their own creative style reminiscent of more fantastic works of art, literature, or hallucinogens.  I spent almost as much time enjoying the geography, flaura, fauna, and characters as I did playing the game.  It's also one of my favorite plot structures, where we're introduced to a fantastic world then delve in to real and equally fantastic story behind it.  World and plot are the very high points of this game.
Gameplay lines up with the form and objectives for the game: a first person brawler with an emphasis on fists, combos, and multi-opponent fights.  You are provided with some weapons, which are either limited ammunition or permanent but with interesting limitations.  The game does break down a bit here, however; the fighting has some hiccups, is not always intuitive, and the weapons start to steal the show, overall being more effective and easier to use, as the game goes on.  There is a basic character upgrade/skill point system, putting points in to four different abilities focused around fighting, but it doesn't feel like it adds much to gameplay.
Voice acting is good, but not great; it serves to move the story along and where it performs less well it's not bad enough to pull you out of the story.  Characters have extremely defined appearances, and with this extremely defined voices.  Music is very well done: different areas have different themes, these themes fit those areas very well, and there are a few scenes that are absolutely defined by the themes that go with them.
In closing: both this and its predecessor remind of 80s/90s low/mid budget fantasy and sci-fi flicks: the sets and costumes are odd (intentionally), it's kind of off the wall, they could afford to try something different, and they could make the game they envisioned.  If you like interesting and new world and characters, an intriguing plot, and aren't bothered by sometimes clunky gameplay than give it a shot.

Mirror's Edge is just like it's heroine. It attempts to hurdle some pretty significant obstacles, however, unlike Faith, Mirror's Edge doesn't always succeed.
The story is somewhat straightforward, but it's interesting enough to keep you engaged. However, a cliff-hanger ending and an only just announced sequel make for a slightly unfinished feel. However, more intriguingly, what did catch my interest was the way the story played out between missions; through stylishly animated cut-scenes, as well as scenes within the game engine itself, which also look attractive. While, as I am an animator myself, these cut-scenes are a pleasant addition, they feature a completely different art style. Both types look good, but the disparity is a little odd.
Mirror's Edge is a first person perspective "free-runner" platformer whereby you take the role of Faith, making countless sequences of jumps, grabs and slides to reach the end of a partially open world stage. As a "Runner", it's all about speed and momentum, with keeping your moves streamlined, flawless and silky smooth a top priority if you are to finish a stage in a set time, or outrun a team of enemies. This is an infinitely satisfying and thrilling game play formula that rarely misses a mark, inflicting gleeful vertigo in the process. To back this up, the controls are as tight as you could want, with sharp turns and tight slides feeling so, so right. On the PC, the game's graphics are phenomenal, the clean and crisp visual style perfectly enhancing the atmosphere of the futuristic, post-reform utopian city, and cleverly immunising the game's visuals to ageing textures. PC only PhysX capabilities only add to this, with rippling flags and shattering windows adding an increased sense of surrealism. Most of the time, you'll want to avoid tangling with cops and SWAT teams, instead using your agility to out manoeuvre them, but now and again you'll need to fight your way out. Hand to hand combat is generally the best method, with jump kicks and slides being the most efficient and elegant, however punches and kicks feel weighty and satisfying, but with no combo system or progression this feels somewhat paper thin.
The second halve to combat is found when hijacking a cop's gun, however, despite what you might expect, these weapons are in fact less effective than using your fists, especially seeing as how you cannot reload them. These guns are difficult to control, possess no sights or method of active aiming and are generic as hell. I don't usually feel this way, but the game could have been far better off if they were left out entirely and replaced with a better hand to hand combat system. Mirror's Edge has a way of bringing the pace to a halt. Unfortunately, for a game that relies on so much forward momentum, Mirror's Edge has a way of bringing the pace to a halt. It has a tendency to trip over its own feet, keeping you slipping and sliding blissfully along, only to have a intricate but tedious jumping puzzle or hazy objective put the brakes on. These aren't bad, but they're not particularly engaging, either; you're likelier to feel relieved rather than fulfilled when you complete one. In *all*, not some of these cases, you're torn from the experience and reminded that this is, after all, just a game.
Mirror's Edge is many things, and it stumbles often for a game that holds velocity in such high regard. But even with all of its frustrations, it makes some impressive leaps; a unique and adventurous game that makes some brave moves that pay of immensely. Having set a solid foundation, we can expect an impressive improvement in it's upcoming sequel. The first game however, as GameSpot might say... "it just doesn't nail the landing".
+ Amazing concept and seamless, exhilarating game play design
+ Clean and crisp, visually pleasing visual style
- Flawed combat system
- Lackluster and flow interrupting platforming sections

Ok, there are few games that I really enjoy and this is one of them.    Anyone that is familiar with COIN ops should know that it's not all about killing the bad guys.   It's about fighting a war yes but the battle field is political as much as it is conventional.   The designers here seem to have struck the correct balance between the two.   It focuses primarily on the field operations side of things but behind the scenes your strategic decisions are based on how much political support there is available.
This leads to some very crucial decisions.  What types of troops and operations should I employ?   How do I accomplish my mission and support my troops when political support is weakening?   These decision are dealt with very effectively in Vietnam 65.
If your interested in this type of game or even if you are not sure pick it up during a steam sale and try it out, you might be pleasantly surprised.   I would give this game a 9.0 score

This game is awesome in so many ways. For starters, this isn't your average point and shoot game. This isn't just run and gun and hoorah you saved the planet. No, Kane and Lynch: Dead Men is gritty, dark, with a twisted story and completely mad characters. Kane is kinda calm and smooth talking, but when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, man he gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Now Lynch... wow, Lynch is just too bananas for the game. At first he'll struck to you as a hippie but oh he so isn't... And when you combine those two shot-out mercenaries against the world: just trust me, you won't regret the story that comes out of it.
About the game itself: even though it's a third person shooter, the controls are very fluid, as is the gameplay. When it comes to weapons it's a bit meh: you always start with an assault rifle and the same bloody pistol, but you can trade with Lynch for his shotgun and badass revolver. And hell, you could always pick up a machine gun from a dead guard and just blast everything and everyone because who cares, you're a mercenary! "But what about ammo?", you may ask. Well, that's covered too: your allies are always carrying ammo for you. Always. Oh, and if you're downed in battle, they'll come up and revive you. And there you go again, shooting everything and everyone.
Final veredict: 9/10. It's just that good.
EDIT: after installation, you will most likely be unable to open the game: you'll hit play, and nothing. Just go to your SteamApps folder -> Common -> Kane & Lynch: Dead Men -> XLiveRedist and run the setup. There you go, up and running!

I'm about to finish it and I have to say, it turned out much better than I anticipated (especially because of one particular character who wasn't even mentioned on the store page but I'll get to that later). One big difference setting this game apart from the other open-world Arkham games is the Batmobile. When I first started this game, I played it for an hour and stopped after seeing the Batmobile. It just seemed unnecessary. Why would I use a car when I can fly?
A few weeks passed and I decided to give it another go. Imagine a 55gb hole on your SSD, I either had to delete it or get it over with. And I'm glad I did the latter. Storywise it's not as strong as previous games since the main villain isn't Joker here. Scarecrow is trying to release a fear gas to Gotham, he has a dumbass ally called Arkham Knight (he really is the weakest point of this game, acting like a 13yr old emo kid who can't find his eye liner) and you're trying to stop them. There are other villians trying to take advantage of the situation and that's about it. That's the story in a nutshell.
Combat is similar to previous games (which is a good thing at least for me because I don't need Dark Souls levels of combat here). There are new gadgets and the way I see it Batmobile is one of them. It's not just a car, it's a multi-purpose tank. Literally. You get into combats with it, take down enemy convoys with it, solve puzzles with it, you race with it. After spending couple hours with the game it started to make sense. I really liked the way they implemented it.
Audio is meh. Visuals are alright. That is, if you're running a Nvidia GPU because this is a Nvidia "optimized" title (meaning it has some extra graphical features, mostly to make the game look better). Speaking of optimized games, this isn't one of them. It runs fine and looks fine for the most part but some bits of the game are clearly not optimized.
Oh and there is no SLI support.
Okay 'member the character I mentioned earlier?
So anyway.. Because this game was released in a poor state and at the same time, steam refund policy was introduced, it's quite cheap now. They stopped supporting it but as I said, it runs fine for the most part.
DLC wise, I would recommend "Season of Infamy". You basically take down several villains scattered throughout the city. They are nice distractions. I haven't played the other one yet.
All and all it was quite fun mainly because of the surprise I mentioned above. I can't wait to see the end. If you're into open-world games, grab a gamepad and give it a go.

The first in a series of games for Shadowrun, this game for me was not only nostalgic but also a great link to the original tabletop RPG game. Being an absolute RPG nut, I am really particular about my games of that genre (such as engaging storyline, character development, some form of progression, a mix of linear/open world missions..) and I have to admit that this game fullfilled that quota really well.
Firstly, there is the aforementioned character development. Whilst you create your character form the start and choose their stats, etc. You interactions with the world can change your characters persona somewhat and also the storyline of the game adds to the development of all the NPCs around you, actually making you "care" about some of the others and wanting them to make it to the end.
You also get to do missions with a crew, which you hire. Making money is not easy, so you do need to be a little carefull with purchases, but most missions start off with a down payment (which was handy when I decided to do missions with about 30 creds). This allows for you to get different classes to work for you and you control each member of the crew. As it is Turn-Based, much like the tabletop game, it works beautifully.
The world itself is vibrant with different characters and the things you will see. Some of the responses that you have as an option can open up some hilarious dialog and whilst you usually have a goal in these discussions, some responses just can not be ignored... although like in life, once you have said it, you can't take it back!
Overall, the game is really enjoyable and you will be hooked to the storyline, as it is very well written. If you like sci-fi RPGs then this is both a classic and a new wave of excellence in this department, this game being a great starting point before going onto the other games in the series. The price is pretty reasonable to be honest, but with 2 other games currently avaialble, bundle deals are the order of the day - you will not be disapointed!

I bought this game specifically because I had heard that Shadowrun Dragonfall was such a good game and this was first in the series. After reading reviews about the rough edges of Returns I wasn't expecting much but to my surprise I found myself really enjoying this title. Everything negative you've heard about SR is true but despite the negatives the game is still tremendous fun. The game combines the CyberPunk fiction of a William Gibson or Neil Stephenson (including a little fantasy thrown in for kicks) with the turn-based RPG combat of the early Fallout or Jagged Alliance games. Shadowrun Returns certainly has its flaws but this little game is absolutely worth the ride! 7/10
Pros
+ Writing - Some of the writing is a bit rough but overall they really captured the cyberpunk vibe well
+ Turn-based Combat is superb and reminds me a lot of the original Fallout games
+ RPG Elements are really strong and it is fun building up your character
+ Character Design is well done and there are a great many models to chose from
+ Atmosphere/Artwork - Definitely won't win any graphic awards but this game really does transport you to this dystopian future
+ Music is perfect for the game
Cons
- Plotline - It seems like the overall story was written by different teams and then pieced together at the end. There is no consistent flow from start to finish and while each individual piece is interesting, ultimately the sum of its part is actually less than each individually.
- Replayability - This was one of the more frustrating aspects of the game. The mechanics are phenomenal but the slow start to the story means that you have to wade through a lot of garbage to replay. This is a shame because the core gameplay just begs for multiple playthroughs
- Ran into a few bugs with the game but only one ever forced me to restart a game
- Difficulty is a little sporadic. Most of the game was a breeze with the team I put together but there was one scene in particular  (the cemetary) that I ended up replaying for almost 2 hours because my team kept getting slaughtered! I actually found this scene to be far harder then the end boss.

The Metal Age is stealth game perfection. Even though a lot of the stealth mechanics don't make much sense, such as a guard not being able to see you should you be standing inches away from them if you're in a dark spot of a brightly lit room, everything about this game is FUN. You'll spend about 40-60 minutes in each level, and that's if you're ignoring picking up all of the loot that's scattered around.
The story, in comparison to the original Thief, is very well written and intriguing. The plot in the original had you fighting zombies and tomb raiding, while in this game, the focus is on the transition from a dark ages fantasy game to "The Metal Age". You don't feel so much like a spelunking knight with a sword and bow and arrow, but an actual thief, taking on bank heists and even sneaking through a medieval police station and stealing from the evidence vault.
The screenshots displayed on the Store Page really don't do the game justice. For a game from 2000 the graphics have aged tremendously, and the lighting and texture work look fantastic to this day. My favorite level is the bank, just because of how spectacular the green tiled floors, wooden walkways, and red carpeted offices look.
Not only do the levels look incredible, but they have some pretty great layouts and the level design is ingenious, inventive and sprawling. After replaying the bank mission so many times I've found six different ways to enter the building, and there are so many different routes you can take to get to the vault without being spotted it's insane. From crawling through a vent and dropping down into the offices adjacent to the vault room, shutting down the mechanical faces (which act as cameras hanging from the ceiling and spinning around trying to spot you) by flipping a switch on the third floor and going through the teller gates, or going through the lions den and using a rope arrow attached to the ceiling to cross the Guard's Room and into the backdoor of the vault room.
I also love that each section of the immensely huge levels has a little nugget of dialogue to be heard that are entertaining to listen to and informative. The voice acting isn't great, but I always ended up quicksaving each time I heard a guard speaking with another guard so I could hear the full thing and then quickload so I didn't lose any time. What is really well done however is Garret talking to himself, usually stating the obvious but it helps players stay on track when he explains something to himself the player might not already realize. His little quips and things he says never get old, even after you've played the same level three or four times.
In conclusion, this is an outstanding gem of a game that you would be doing yourself a disservice not to play.

If you are looking for a good story, or at least one that isn't inexcusably cliché at every single opportunity, as well as solid/likeable characters- look elsewhere.

The graphics were a little muddy, but that was easily forgettable after an hour or two of gameplay. Additionally, the damage you deal to zombies was exquisite- giving you proper visual feedback of the damage that you are dealing versus obviously predetermined death animations.
All things considered- this game has many high and many low points. If you liked Dead Island's gameplay, you will love this game as it is a logical upgrade to the development team's previous work.
I would recommend Dying Light if you have a group of friends to play with, but I would hesitate to recommend it if you are just playing on playing the game solo.

Thief 2: The Metal Age is a direct sequel to the Thief: The Dark Project, this one released in 2000 and made by Looking Glass. At the core it uses same mechanics and even same techonology of engine as the original, so some might think of it as expansion pack. Yet it's upper level of design is different, being designed like a proper stealth game and having more steampunk setting.
Also, yea, you probably heard that this version doesn't have credits music. It's not a false statement, but it's not suppose to have one to begin with. It's just that localizator of German version decided to add some song from some German band. Doesn't sound Thief-like at all.
Technically, it's released as-is and thus has some problems. Like, it doesn't support widescreen resolution or anything more than 800x600.
I think that just like with Thief 1 on Steam, to see cutscenes you have to run .exe file with admin rights. But I think it already does it?
I also noticed that the gamma slider doesn't work either. And in this one I felt that the game is way too dark by default. Or maybe Thief 1 is the one which is too bright. Not sure.
Also, yea, enable fogging in options, it's art-improving graphic option, not "hide things if far away".
Then again, you probably should use one of a community patches. Not sure how much do they change, I was there for Vanilla experience, but people love those, so.
Plot once again follows our cynical thief by the name of Garrett in the mysterious City. In the first game he had to destroy the Trickster, god of Pagans house of nature, who wished to destroy everything man-build. This heroic deed shifted the balance of powers toward the path of progress, to a dawn of the twisted Metal Age. Pure fantasy elements and monsters are almost not seen, The City is being cleaned by the City Watch and a new Mechanists sect emerges out of Hammerite house to lead the age.
And yea, the story continues, as everything here shifts to steampunk and Victorian setting. And Thief is focusing more on just being a thief, rather than adventurer. No more adventure, you now have big houses and mansion to rob and even your maps are always accurate and provide good description to let you. It even feels less linear due to this, albeit actual levels are less dragged due to less maze-like qualities and less of fetching and puzzles. But hey, this is what people expect Thief to be.
And it futher embraces the fact that it's more focused on stealth. You got new tools of trade, like Invinsibility potions, slow-fall one. There is a scouting orb that you can throw anytime and see from it's point of view, which I always forget to use even though AI never notices this so there is no good reason not to. Remember kids - don't be like me, that's not smart choice.
You can now lean into door to eaversdrop. Guards pretty much always mumble something to themselves, futher giving you audio hints. Some rare guards even wear special helmets that you can't blackjack them. Althrough they are so rare that I don't remember any such encounter. There are even occasional patrol that have more than one person.
And it's a Metal Age that we are talking about, with Mechanists bringing new toys to watch out. There are surveliance camera, security systems and robots, which can be divided into huge dangerous robot that can't hear and small robot that can only warn others, but only after first hearing you, activating their vision and seeing you. All mixed with humans, giving more stealth-focused variety instead of monsters. All while you are cracking the bank level with it's ceramic tiles and three floors of complexity.
Albeit, it does mean that it lost some of the charm. There isn't much of wonderful immersive mystery that made me fall in love for Thief. That, and I am not fan of this theme, it's just feels too Victorian. It mostly has to do that it actually lost some gameplay variety. There is only so much mansion that you can crack at before it gets a bit old. Which isn't to say that there is no rare mission which goes out of this style. And it also varies the stealth objective that you have, even having this single awesome police station mission where you actually supposed to ghost due to knockouts limit. And it has this awesome mission where you travel on rooftops of a city.
But I still can't help but to feel monotomy setting after the half of a game. After all, it still ends up too much with you blackjacking everybody you come across. Or maybe it's because of the plot. It starts nicely, with some conspiracy going on, but soon it's all same grey Mechanics, Mechanics, Mechanics, who lack some charm. Even though their leader is kinda awesome and robot carry it along, but the environment gets you after a while.
That, and I am still dissapoint that the plot didn't explore relationship between Hammerites and Mechanics. At least I never seen any actual conflict. Kinda hoped to see the clash of ideals ever since I overheard one of the very rare Hammerites complained in the second level. But oh well.
That, and in the last one third of a game it simply farts out. I don't know, it feels like the quality and excitement suddenly drops. Then again, Looking Glass studios was in deep financial trouble and was rushing out, I bet this is the impact to it. The Kidnap level is both boring looking and boring to play, in a cave with more mechanists, where you run all over the place to find the needed NPC. Not to mentioning that I had sudden framedrop because of some trouble with AI pathfinding, until I found the guard who was hogging game up.
Then you have two levels in a row that take place in same mansion, in both cased you enter it and exit in. The thing is that the first level of it feels like an earlier development version of the level, while the second time around it doesn't differenate enough to hold interest. Like plot-wise you sneak in to find a secret stairway toward the third floor so you knew where it is to snack masks on next day. After that you are supposed to leave yet you can venture futher into the third floor where you find many glitchy things, with flying decorations, misaligned models and you can even steal the already-present masks, but no one will care. As if you aren't supposed to be there.
Final level isn't bad though, at least on second try when I learned how to exploit big robots into blowing up themselves. And when I knew to take it slowly. Kinda like a little nightmare of steel, albeit I can see how some may decide that it goes too long, as well as being a challenge course. It's actually is quite awesome. But then the ending feels dissapointnig. It leaves you with no satisfication of victory and doesn't hype you up for next title. Just ends immeditly, with no music. Unlike the perfect Thief 1 ending.
But hey, I don't think that the main point of the games lies in ending. I would say that the Thief 2 is more than worth beating, even if it leaves you a bit sour. It's a Thief game, the one with complex levels, no hand-holding and more focus on stealth. And even though stealth core gameplay is still a bit on simple side, knocking everybody out, despite having excellent audio design that futhers gameplay, it's still a greatly enjoyable game.

Hi,
I've spent some time in it and I overall currently enjoy it, but there is a variety of issues with this game that desperately needs to be addressed, otherwise these things will likely cause me and other players a lot of grief later on in the game. These issues are:
1. Hit Detection Problems = It appears this game suffers from the same problem Dark Souls 2 did; to the player it will appear you avoided the hit but the game still considers you within range and hits you. Thus, in this game, running past an enemy often results in it hitting you in melee, despite you no longer being in melee anymore. This is often a problem where the render thread (renders everything onto the monitor) and the update thread (performs all the calculations) of the game engine are processing frames at different rates. This is a game crippling problem for an ARPG, as you need very precise hit detection in order to pull it off; this is a priority for fixing.
2. Input Delay = It appears that there is a delay in all forms of inputs from the player. For example, I'm using Whirlwind, and when I take my finger off of the button, I keep whirlwinding and consuming energy for another 0.33 to 0.66 seconds. This causes a whole variety of issues, and again, like Hit Detection, this makes it hard to properly transistion from Whirlwind to close-quarters combat and then hit targets with a precise Hammer Strike (or w/e its called), and I often miss my intended target as a result.
3. Loot Delay = Again, there is a delay between when an item drops on the ground and the time when you can pick it up. Often I have to wait anywhere from 0.25 to 1.00 seconds to pick up an item or auto-pickup a chunk of gold.
4. Imprecise Hitboxes on Terrain = There has been numerous times I've gotten hung up on terrain, and thus ground right to a halt. Objects that look like you can pass under them, you can't, and I've seen enemies use ranged attacks through a solid object and hit me before, while I on the other hand can't hit them. Or, there is these overhanging tents, that you can enter, but you can't attack targets that are inside it and their attacks cannot escape out of it either.
5. Energy Potion Cooldown = You have a metric called Energy and it is used for all your attacks. It regenerates over time, or you can use the Energy Potion. The issue is that I'm frequently running out of Energy, and the most basic potion only restores 20 energy, but has a full minute of a cooldown. I could understand a full minute, if it restored all of my energy, but 20 energy for 1 minute, when that 20 energy barely powers my Whirlwind for a single 360 rotation? Thats harsh, which often results in me running in circles while my potion is on cooldown, as running back to your body takes FOREVER.
6. Stat Allocation Problems = As a Knight, that uses shields, I've found that I'm able to play much more easily by dual wielding, rather than by using a shield... which is odd for me as I'd expect that if the class is built around shields, I'd do better with a shield, but I'm not. This of course leads to the problem of how to allocate my stat points. Up to LV 15 I can respec them freely, but, the reality with this game is that it only starts getting "good" after LV 15, so I could potentially screw up my Stat Allocation because I'm currently focusing on augmenting my dual wielding as I'm being just much more successful with it. Unless there is some way to respec my points for a cost later on, I think this mechanic of only allowing stat relocation until 15 is too harsh.
7. Imprecise Hitsboxes on Items on Ground = I find it often very difficult to pickup an item off the ground. In other ARPGs, like Diablo 2, Diablo 3, Baldur's Gate Dark Alliance, or even Grim Dawn, items have a sillouhete that highlights the item to make it easier to grab that item. Not so here, and thus I will frequently grab the wrong item, and as I'm in the second area and haven't found a vendor anywhere, I'm frequently tossing items out to make room for 1 more item. See the problem?
8. Breakables = Some crates or barrels in the environment are breakable and produce loot. Some can't be broken, but you can pass through them freely as if they lacked a hitbox. Still others can't be broken or passed through, but I've seen enemies pass through them which is very annoying. Some consistency would be nice.
9. Hidden Chamber Items = These are a misnomer; there are no hidden chambers that I could find in any of the dungeons, but they are a potential drop from the final "boss" of the dungeon. Renaming that to maybe "Potential Rare Loot" would be better, unless, well, the Dev Team intends to actually add hidden chambers to the dungeons, and have that loot in those chambers.
There is a lot of depth and interesting mechanics to this game, so I'll keep pushing myself to play it as I do mostly enjoy it. But, the above things will likely cause a lot of problems later on in the game, where enemies hit harder and overall various gameplay systems are more punishing, like durability repairs. There is potential here, but it all depends on the Dev Team. The first 4 issues, will often make OR break an ARPG, and if not addressed WILL turn away a lot of players as these problems will lead to people feeling the game is unfair and mechanically broken.

This is my first review ever on steam and i feel i needed to help promote this game, sorry for my spelling in advance.
quick summery,
pros:  fun and absorbing gameplay,  nice graphics, "old school" kinda feel,  an open "meta" for those wanting to make their own build and see where that leeds,  NOT P2W.
Cons: there is alot of polish still needed, lack of information can be disheartening for new players, the first 27 levels feels like a pure grind fest, small playerbase.
so with the summery out of the way id like to go in to details of mentioned pros and cons above.
pros.
1. gameplay & absobtion, as a lover of ARPGS and lootbased games having played games like devilian, RO, poe, diablo1-3, tree of savior and so on, i feel it's super easy to get absorbed in to the world of GoE the splendid artstyle and fun and "deep combat"
the rason i call the combat deep even tho at first glance it looks super easy and straightforward, is that aproaching mid/late game (lvl 28 onward) you can make combat as deeps as you feel like, mixing abilities from the main/subclass distributing stat points, passive skills and so on there is ALOT you can do with what feels like "not much" at first.
2. graphics, this point i feel i dont need to go to deep into detail, the artstyle is just right for what this game is trying to get across and works well with the animations of your spells.
3."old school"  with the lack of a better word i feel this is the closest term i can use to describe it, the game feels like a blend mix between Dungon siege/ Ragnarok / diablo,  what this means ( to me ) is that there is a easy to follow quest chain through the game with alot of opportunities to go and grind a dungeon for some loot or exp, min/maxing your clear speed and finding and learning about all the differant stats that gear can roll. this is a system i just love, even tho i know this might not be a positive note for everyone.
4. "open meta"  what i first noticed when i started playing this game what the lack of " top 10 builds" which gave me mixed feelings when i started due to not knowing what to do withy my levels afraid of "destroying" my character before even reaching mid game, tho i quickly found out that with a litle bit of common knowledge it's easy to basicly make any build work, notice i say "work" and not omg everything destoys everything,  when u reach further in to the game with a mediocre build you will get a feel for what your skills do and how stats work with said skills, and making a upgrade to your current build would be easy to do on the spot. This all is something i like alot, when the game says "hey you wanna be a hunter with pets that heals?" you can just go ahead an do that and it would work.
cons.
1. Polishe.  The game is not "done" in anyway and there is alot that still needs to be looked over most of this is the way how you character and the world seems to work against eachother in alot of places, getting stuck on wierd invisble hitboxes, ( like vanilla wow and mage blink. ) Even tho this can get on your nervs alot of the time, you acctualy start to learn what to lookout for in the terrain to avoide this as much as possible, even tho thats not something you should need to do.
2. lack of information,  this is probebly the biggest Con of the game currently, as you might have noticed is that i use the term "learn" alot and even tho that is fun in it's own way, it's not what everyone wants and can be a real bonerkiller for some players, there is no skill calculator for the game so finding information about the classes can be hard to obtaine.
to be honest this bit almost made me skip this game going in to a game with the mindset of a semi hardcore player wanting to perform well and doing everything i can to be "good" at the game and and i cant for the life of me find the information i wanted to get a build idea from the getgo.
But i stuck with the game and followed the only build i could find with information from (ghazzyTV) and as i reached lvl 28 i feelt i hade enough knowledge about about 2 of the classes i wanted to play to make a new char and make my own build.
3.early levels,  i have 2 characters above 30 and i have had the same feelings with both of them that the questing/grinding before lvl 28 feels really "empty" theres not much going on and it feels super slow, tho as soon as you reach 28 the pace picks up and the game becomes more enjoyable, try to get to 30 before you decide if you want to keep playing or not i promise it is so much more fun after that.
4. playerbase, Currently the playerbase is not large by any means, but its a solid base non the less alot of helpfull people willing to share information or point you in the right directions or just simply having a conversaation while grinding.
Endbit,
I decided to write this review after playing this game for 70~ish hours in hope of explaining the current state of the game and maybe be the make or break point for some players.  There is alot of hope for this game partly because of the games devs are really amazing with taking ideas and oppinions from the community while also keeping the development of the game really clear for all the players to see and to comment on.
im going to dedicate the summer to this game and will update me review at the start of fall or if i find something worth mentioning before that.
Again sorry for my spelling and thanks for reading, Good luck in the game !

Vietnam '65 is a great hex based strategy game which marries simplicity well with an engaging theme and diverse gameplay opportunities. As the name indicates, the game is set during the Vietnam War and constructed around the premises of maintaining popularity among the local population of the South, represented by a Hearts and Minds (H&M) score. This score is the centre of the game and you are required to keep it at 50 or above to win. Alongside this, an additional resource called political capital is used to purchase and maintain units in the field. Both are effected positively and negatively by actions in the game such as clearing mines, killing enemy units, suffering damage to your own units, and allowing Viet Cong (VC) units to infiltrate villages. While H&M can be effected my many factors, political capital is only effected positively by the destruction of enemy units and negatively by the destruction of friendly units as well as the constant drain of unit upkeep. This represents an inability to really effect the political capital available to you and while this is not a major issue, the lack of control over this resource was clearly recognised, as the mechanic has seen revision in the follow up game; Afghanistan '11.
The units available and strategies you can employ with these units are both numerous and diverse. Though the expenditure of political capital, you are able to purchase units such as US G.I.s, UH-1 Huey Slicks, M48A3s, M113s, Green Berets and more. Each of the units available have their own abilities and unique role to play. For example, Green Berets act as reconnaissance and can train Army of the Republic of South Vietnam (ARVN) troops, UH-1s and CH-47s can lift vital supplies to keep units in the field, and the engineering variant of the M113 can clear jungle, build roads, and construct bases among other things. The units available are all well represented and each serve their purpose with none feeling like fodder.
In Vietnam '65 logistics and mobility are vital to success and go hand in hand. Each unit, if outside a base, must stay supplied otherwise it will simply be destroyed when it reaches zero supply. Though this is somewhat of a crude system, it fits the simplicity of the game well and emphasises the importance of logistics, as well as adding another layer to the gameplay. Vehicles such as UH-1s, CH-47s and M113s are all capable of delivering supplies which can be acquired at the main base or a firebase. While each game starts with the player controlling a main base, the construction of a firebase, and forward operating bases (which operate as training camps for ARVN troops) are done by engineering units. These bases are vital as they allow resupply of all units, as well as firebases allowing the stationing of artillery pieces, thereby extending the range at which you can transport and supply units, allowing you to increase your influence over the villages furthest from your main base.
Vietnam '65 is somewhat limited in that it only has a skirmish type game mode, with the single objective of maintaining your H&Ms score. However I do not think this is unreasonable considering the cost. Additionally, randomly generated maps, a levelling system offering in-game rewards, several difficulty settings, and the ability to create custom difficulties, editing elements of the map and gameplay, all add to Vietnam '65's replay value.
In summary, Vietnam '65 is a great hex based strategy game at the lower end of the price market with polished, satisfying, quick, and simple gameplay to jump into and a reasonable degree of replay value.

Vietnam '65 is a turn-based strategy war game set in the la (sic) Drang Valley of the former Republic of Vietnam.  (South Vietnam, if you prefer.)  You start with a US Army base with some units inside, and expand from there.  Expansion involves setting up a fire base to extend your zone of control and (if you prefer) forward bases where you believe they'll do the most good.  From there, you fight against Viet Cong (VC) and North Vietnamese Army (NVA) units of various types, send US and South Vietnamese (ARVN) infantry into villages to get intelligence on the enemy and/or raise support from the locals (called "hearts & minds"), purchase more units (or perform some actions) with the game's version of currency (called "congressional support"), make sure units are supplied, and hope that you have at least a 50% score in hearts & minds when the mission ends. End of mission screens (win or lose) feature a US Army officer's uniform and medal case that shows the rank you've achieved and progression to the next rank, along with progression to earning future medals and decorations.
There's absolutely nothing special about the graphics of this game, which is the reason Vietnam '65 normally doesn't retail for over ten US dollars.  (I was lucky enough to get Vietnam '65 on sale.)  There's nothing I particularly like about Vietnam '65's graphics, but the worst feature has to be direct fire combat.
Combat animation would have been much better accomplished by featuring an independent animation featuring firefights between US/ARVN aginst VC/NVA units.  (The same is true with non-infantry.)  I'm sure I would watch every time, even if it was the same animation with the only difference being skin color and uniforms of personnel.  The sound in Vietnam '65 is nothing interesting.  The one thing I really like about the sound, is the roar of F-4 Phantom jets you can call in to bomb enemy units and structures.  Not that Vietnam '65 needs music to be enjoyed, the music is next to non-existent. The main complaint about the sound, is while it does have an authentic military vibe to it, the radio voices of people is out-done from what I experienced in a Vietnam War game I bought over twenty years ago for a DOS computer.
Writing positives for Vietnam '65 is the most difficult job I've ever had in writing a Steam review to date. If my childhood and teenage years of gaming are any indication, I think the overall military experience of Vietnam '65 is the game's best feature.  Hearing noises reminicent of a jungle in southeast Asia, rainfall, and brief radio chatter is nice, but I do enjoy looking at my uniform at the end of every mission.
Vietnam '65 has a great replayability factor to it.  While the game takes place in the likeness of a real life geographic location, the map is randomized in regards to village locations and terrain. Difficulty settings can be customized to make things more interesting. Medals (and other uniform decorations) mean new things to try and accomplish at the player's whim.
The ability to create ARVN companies from forward bases (through training from Green Berets) was a good move by the programmers.  (ARVN infantry units are also better at dealing with villagers than US infantry at the expense of being less adept at combat.)  No matter how old I get, looking at real life military equipment and uniforms never loses it's interest.
Landmines are plentiful in Vietnam '65, and rightly so.  I can only imagine paranoia was high for US and ARVN who had to deal with booby traps of all types.  (Both explosive and non-explosive.)  Fortunately, the game allows engineers to detect mined spaces, and foot solders can remove them.
Probably the biggest negative, is the potential that was wasted in this game.  While a ranomized depection of the la Drang Valley is fine, I personally thought there should have been more theaters of operation, which may mean removing the "'65" part of the name, but variety is good, right?  Certainly Navy and Marine Corps settings could work.
Rivers aren't the same dangerous terrarin they were in the real life Vietnam War, and while you can't call on the ubiquitous "swif boat" for support, river crossings also aren't hampered by fortified positions that the US and ARVN had to deal with in real life river engagements.  Although I do not know how many US helicopters were shot down by RPG's in the Vietnam War, air travel (at least in veteran mode) is quite dangerous, and perhaps moreso than what it was in the Vietnam War.
Although I have no problem with the game featuring the patch of the 1'st Cavalry Division on the player's uniform, I don't think it's right that units that weren't a part of the division are directly usable by the player.  Maybe it's better that the game isn't 1'st Cavalry-centric, but it's a shame that there's only two types of US foot solders:  Infantry and Green Berets.  Why not also allow for Rangers (which would function like Green Berets, but cannot train ARVN)?  That way, players can earn a Ranger stripe for their uniform.  (Many high ranking US Army officers have earned them.)
I personally don't like how helicopters cannot spot enemy units under any conditions.  I'm sure that VC and NVA were easily visible on foot in open areas and crossing rivers to US helicopters!  While I am fine with the enemy being difficult to spot in jungles, I'm dismayed by the fact that jungle spaces can only be cleared with engineers.  The player can call on the Air Force to air drop supplies to units and bases or bomb enemy units and bases, but no ability to defoliate jungles with napalm and Agent Orange.
Unsuccessful attacks from artillery and airstrikes cause a drop in hearts & minds from villages, which makes no sense.  Maybe if a strike went awry and hit a friendly unit or a village, then yes, I can see why hearts & minds would be affected.  Units receiving wounds (or damage) also cause a loss in hearts and minds.  That would make sense if a unit is lost through combat, but otherwise still being able to function?
There's two issues with medals:  You can only earn them once, and you can't tell which medal is which by hovering the cursor over them.  I say the game should allow for devices (like stars) to be placed on top of their respective ribbon band on the uniform to signify multiple awardings of medals.
Wounded units can only be treated back at base.  Field hospitals cannot be created, medics do not exist, yet vehicles can be repaired anywhere by engineers.
The tutorial was simply wrong.  The names for "basic training" and "advanced training" were backwards.  The former is more "advanced" than the latter.  Basic training isn't controlled enough to teach the player well.
The thing that stands out as being most incorrect about Vietnam '65, is the difficulty settings.  When I first played, I selected "custom," and I made everything as difficult as possible.  (Even moreso than the "veteran" difficulty setting.)  At least my experiences were similar to the Vietnam War in that regard:  It didn't matter how many enemies I killed, my apprval rating fell like an anvil in Loony Tunes, and combat became unsustainable.)
Fire bases get supplied like headquarters at the end of every turn, but do not directly receive howitzer munitions.  Restocking howitzer munitions is accomplished by helicopters flying to and from HQ and bases containing howitzers.
If you see this game on sale, buy it!  Vietnam '65 is the example of a niche game.  There's things you know are wrong about it, yet if it's in your niche, you will still love it.  Just be careful of when you're supposed to sleep.  The first day I played, I was playing until 8 AM the next morning, and finally got sleepy at the end of a mission.  Now I can't wait to finish typing to play this game again.  (I'm tempted to skip on proof-reading just to get my fix!)

I have completed this game on the PS4, but have also played this game substantially offline.
Now, Arkham Knight, to me, is one of the best games to come out next to The Witcher 3. Not only is it a fitting conclusion to Rocksteady's Batman-trilogy, it's also an all-around awesome game. Everything that City did right when it came to the basic essence of being the Batman, Knight amplifies and brings to another level. The story, to me, was the best out of Arkham games, just perfect in its exploration of how far Batman has had to go, and will have to go, in order to save Gotham and himself. Scarecrow is a terrific villain, somebody who truly has lost all regard to anything outside his ultimate goal. John Noble was amazing as his voice-actor; soemthing that Rocksteady is industry-leader in. Though, yes, Arkham Knight did not end up as great of a villain as he had been billed up as, his backstory and the reveal surrounding him was still magnificently achieved. The story hits new highs, and struck an emotional chord in me, making me want sad thinking that I would never have that "first time" feeling again.
The side missions, concerning various villains both small and well-known, were excellent. Varied and interesting, they used everything the game had taught you at their highest level. From having to chase Firefly throughout the city on the Batmobile (which happened to be my least favorite mission series), to stopping Two-Face's crew from robbing various banks and utilising every stealth mechanism known, and finally investigating a series of rather ghastly murders; one does not easily become bored in Arkham Knight. One minor gripe comes with the Riddler trophies & riddles. Having to find ALL of them, of which there are many hundreds, to achieve the final true ending was a tad too much for me. Thank you, YouTube.
The combat of Arkham Knight is the same amazing thing it has been since Asylum, but made with just that extra-dosage of perfection. It feels even smoother this time around, and the addition of dual-teaming with various allies is an awesome experience. And a sight to behold as well. The overall gameplay itself, as Batman (et. al) is the games highlighting feature, and a standard for the industry.
Now, to the most controversial aspect of the game: the Batmobile. I personally love it, and believe it's usage was just right. But, I also can see the criticism, and can understand it. The feel of the Batmobile itself is incredbly smooth, and the rush of just driving around Gotham, drifting around corners and shocking random rioters, is amazing. The tank battles, though not cumbersome at all, do get a little trite. This especially comes to light when the final battle against a major villain, after the end of the main story, is just another tank battle. I would have much preferred if he had been fought on the rooftop, for example, man el mano.
The music of the game, composed by the amazing duo of Nick Arundel and David Buckley, is an amazing accompanying aspect to the game. Though not as bombastic as the score for Arkham City, Arkham Knight's score aids the somber and almost-futile feel throughout the game. Gliding through the city, the music gave off a true sense of "this is the end", whether or not Batman and Gotham would pull through victorious.
Overall, Rocksteady has done what many thought impossible not just once, but thrice. Three awesome games making you The Batman; with a story to match the best Hollywood has to offer; and with an ending as shocking and fulfilling as possible, Arkham Knight sends The Dark Knight off most beautifully.

+ Thoroughly enjoyable main story.
+ Inventive characters.
+ Beautiful (dystopian) gameworld.
+ Good game mechanics.
+ Karma system is neat.
+ Even with all its flaws, I still want to play this again.
- Main story is too short. The campaign can be blazed through in a single session on Easy. This game could have used at least five campaigns of similar length added as DLC. (And not suddenly swapped from DLC to standalone.)
- Linear storyline. I don't think my actions influenced more than whether a side character turned vigilante or not, which had no relevance whatsoever to the continuation of the main storyline.
- Not nearly enough use of the Deckers' Matrix to advance storylines. At some point you end up in a 10x10 (if that large) space in the Matrix to meet up with someone... and that's the only time you really meet a story character in the Matrix. How about a Deckers' program market in the Matrix? Swap programs around with online merchants? An information market where you can buy or sell information obtained via Matrix hacks? It could have been so much more.
- Constantly have to re-hire runners between missions, have to re-equip them, and they run away with their equipment at mission end.
- No real bonding with side-characters as you don't team up with them but have to consciously decide to hire them for a job again... if you can get them to join you in the first place. I found only a few missions where they need to stay alive, which only annoyed rather than invoked empathy for them. I had more empathy for my team in Baldur's Gate or my soldiers in XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
- Dragonfall DLC was replaced with Dragonfall standalone game, breaking workshop content. I would like to see a fix rolled out by the devs to remedy this. I'd personally much rather play Dragonfall with the Shadowrun Returns GUI.

is pretty much an rpg dungeon crawler, but with some twists:
- you need cards to unlock special abilities, spells, pots, armors, etc.
- each time you level up, you can choose between two upgrades: health and mana. Health makes you stronger, mana gives you the possibility to equip more cards and cast more spells. You need to balance them in order to get to the deeper rooms of the dungeon.
- you can only move on a certain path and your attacks are dealt by clicking on the enemy you desire to attack.
- enemies have different strengths and you need to adjust your strategy to prove yourself victorious.
Right now there are two classes available to play (warrior and mage) and one under development (rogue), each one with peculiar abilities and cards.
I'm really enjoing this game and I can't wait to see what this growing indie team can bring to the table.
