Well after about 50 or so hours of playing this game and grabbing everything I pretty much can, I feel like I need to write a review on it! (With lots of Dead Island hate)
Short review: It's basically what Dead Island should have been but mixed in with some Far Cry, Mirrors Edge, and a little bit of Assassins Creed elements.  If you want a superior Dead Island get this.
LONG REVIEW TIME:
PROS:
Better story (as far as a zombie game goes): As far a a zombie game story goes this is a lot better than Dead Island.  Basically- oh yeah SPOILER ALERT -you're a man named Kyle Crane who is dropped into the infected city of Harran to find some guy that has stolen a very important file from the GRE.  And guess what happens the minute you get dropped in? You get bit, of course, lazy pr^$k couldn't move fast enough.  There aren't many twists and turns in the story, but there are some very interesting parts here and there but not much else.
Characters: Compared to Dead Islands bland Characters, these actually have some soul to them (Take that for what you will) each one is pretty interesting, some are kind of bland, but not as bland as the ones in Dead Island anyway.  Each one seems to have some weight to it or at least some emotion.
Fighting the Biters: Fighting the zombies actually feels like it has some weight to it, with each hit you make, each gunshot, everything.  It doesn't feel as lifeless as it does in Dead Island with swings or with guns.  The hit sounds are solid, the impact and weight with each swing you make, the bone breaking for biters, everything, it feels pretty solid.
Scavenging for items: To craft good weaponry or even some distracting tools, you need items found throughout the world.  Aerosal, sawblades, chemicals, ductape, everything you find is useful in someway or another.  This is how you make throwing stars, strong elemental weapons, explosives, and more.  Plus my OCD says "GRAB EVERY DAMN THING YOU SEE."  Not only that but almost every single building you go towards you can go into and scavange for some loot, very nice touch that you can enter most of the buildings to get stuff.
Traps: There are traps riddled throughout the world that you can use to your advantage, like a car trap.  It sets off the alarm and the zombies gather around it, after about 5 alarm horns it goes off with an electric shock, pretty much killing everything in the area around it.  Or like the electric fence, which makes a loud high pitched screech to draw enemies over, then zaps the fences below them with electricity, useful for dealing with enemies on your tail.
Different enemy types: There are different enemies instead of just zombies.  There are the Spitters from Left 4 dead except they are even MORE ANNOYING.  Demolishers, which as basically just really big buff zombies that can knock down a lot of your health and get quite annoying.  The Runner Zombies, they are basically runners that have been infected, they're as fast as you, and can climb up buildings to catch you. The prison zombies (I suppose this is what they're called) they are basically just a beefed up version of the regular biters except with a big piece of Concrete Rubar that will hurt you with the swing and knock you over if you're too close.  Hazmat zombies that can't get caught on fire, but have a air tank on their back, hit the tank, and BOOM.  The Volatiles, they come out at night to patrol and can sense you if you get too close, this basically goes as a cop system like GTA, the longer they chase you the more will follow, and the longer they'll try to search for you if you lose them.  And then my most HATED ENEMY EVER, the Suiciders, which can kill you instantly if you are within like 2 meters of them.
Weapon Variety: There are a lot of weapons you can get, each has it's own little property based off what it is, bone breaking, slicing off body parts, etc.  AND THE GUNS ACTUALLY WORK LIKE F%#KING GUNS.  Headshots apply to pretty much everything except for volatiles I believe, they do have some damn good sounds, and the impact of shooting a enemy is very rewarding.
Parkour!: How could I forget one of the most entertaining things of this game?  Years after Mirrors Edge came out i've been trying to scratch a very unbearable itch mainly because that game left me with wanting more of it, and since Dice is lazy with making the 2nd game, I kept hearing about this game and it has free running properties, thankfully it's done correct.  It doesn't feel like a mess, it feels very fluid, except for when you start off when you trip over every thing you see and grab onto, but it keeps you on your toes when you are being chased by the Volatiles.
Progression/level up: Progressing with your level in this game is pretty good, there are 3 types of levels.  Survivor, Agility, and Power, and each is leveled up based off of what you do.  Survivor is for helping people out with quests, getting air drops and giving them to the quarter master for some experience, or exploring and helping people in need.  Agility is for parkouring around the place, the longer/more deadly the jump, the more points you get from it, meaning the more dangerous things you do the more point you'll get from it.  Power is what you do to hurt biters, can be throwing stars, your own melee weapons, guns, traps, anything, even just smacking the zombie with your fist will get you points for it.
Day and night Cycle: people complain about the Day and Night cycle because it isn't introduced at first, which it isn't, but I think that's a good thing, I don't want to roam around at night not knowing what's gonna happen.  After a few missions it introduces you to the day and night cycle and it works correctly, plus all of your Power and Agility points are doubled at night since it's so risky to go out.
CONS:
THE F#%KING SUICIDERS: I hate these damn zombies the most, not only are they a pain to get away from, they aren't obvious from the rest of the crowd.  Need a example?  I was on the bridge trying to get to the top, while walking on the bridge and going through the zombies, there was one with his back turned, I figured "Ah why not" I hit him, BOOM, dead.  Turns out it was a stupid suicider zombie, but THEY ARENT OBVIOUS ENOUGH.  They blend in with the common infected so well it just starts to get annoying, like if you're in a battle with lots of zombies and they are blocking your path and you have to kill them, and then a suicider just waltzs in behind them and you hit him you just screwed yourself because of it.  I'm not saying they should get taken out, i'm saying I wish they were more obvious to see and identify.
The grappling hook: This isn't a con becuase I don't like it, it works great, but it's Kyle when he uses it.  If you grapplehook to certain things Kyle I guess goes artard for a moment and doesn't want to grab onto whatever I aimed it at.  Like one time I aimed up near a building roof and hooked at the edge, but instead of grabbing onto said edge and climbing up he just decided he wasn't even going to try and grab it, and then just fell and broke his legs.  Good going Kyle, a%#$ole.
Throwable items: Most of the throwable items are really useless, like later you can make burning and freezing throwing stars, yet burning is the best out of them all since not just zombies but the enemy Humans will start flailing around a little giving you time to attack.  And then the explosives, the only useful one is the Explosive firecrackers since they gather around it and blows them all up.
CONCLUSION: After playing Dead Island and then Dying Light, Dying Light is clearly superior, and since i'm running out of a word length, i'll just say this, it gets a 8/10 singleplayer, and a 9/10 for Co-op, it's fun, it's entertaining, and I haven't gotten bored of it since.  I'm not going to let AngryJoe or Benjamin "Yahtzee" Croshaw get in my way of saying it's another zombie game.  It's a lot of f%$king fun.

I remember playing Hearthstone back when it first came out. It managed to hook me for a grand total of maybe 3 weeks. I'm by no means a pro when it comes card games in general, but Hearthstone didnt seem as monumental as CG's like Magic, where I allways felt the barrier to "getting somewhere" was way too big to bother going beyond playing it casually. But I never felt I got anywhere in Hearthstone. The Meta seemed to slide past me constantly, every expansion seemed to invalidate whatever I had built before and eventually I just stopped doing my Daily Quests and stopped caring about the game completely.
Shadowverse was the complete opposite.
The game has a decent Singleplayer Campaign. Not overly long or a story that would rock you out of your chair. But just long enough and with a decent challenge curve to serve as a great introduction and Tutorial. The game handed me some basic cards for each faction and a whole lot of Boosters. leaving me with enough cards to build a half decent deck for each class, and some to spare for optimizing one or two I was planning to "Main".
The game has tons of rewards it hands you just for playing. You get Gold for Boosters and Vials for Card creation just by playing a couple Matches each day, supplemented by dayily Quests. Even now, after exhausting all the "Newbie Bonuses" I still feel like I'm expanding my collection at a satisfying rate. I also get the impression Shadowverse is being nicer when it comes to rare and Legendary drops, when compared to Hearthstone. On the other hand, i might just've been unlucky with the latter.
The Classes are varied, and I do think theres a viable deck to be built for almost any approach you'd like, be it aggressive, war trough attrition or just dropping high cost cards. The Cards are also beatifully animated and voiced (I went for the japanese Vocals after a while, just because of my preference. But the english voice acting is just fine), with some cool effects for some spells or Evolutions.
Long story short. It's easy to get into, has a very nice F2P model in my opinion, and just looks pretty. Worth giving it a try even if you're skeptical, you got nothing to loose. Well, maybe your reputation for not being a Weeabo. But let's be honest, none of us care what the rest thinks anyway. *sniffle*

This is my second review for the second game in this eponymous stealth series, enjoy B's.
Pro's: This game, just like its predecessor before it, really makes you feel like a Thief. When all the cylinders in your brain are firing off at perfect formation you will honestly feel like no one can stop you from "borrowing" their precious goods. The game is a direct follow up to The Dark Project (Thief Gold) and continues pretty much right after the first game, give or take a month or two. One thing they really improved upon in this game is the level design. I didn't think they could make it any better but it's even more logical now rather than Maze-like. Thief Gold also had logical level design but some of the levels were more like Mazes than a real tangible place that you could believe existed. In this game it feels more grounded than the first and more tangible, you rob a Bank, Frame a City Watch guard, Tail an informant, Crash a party and rob the denizens of the City, and help a friend rescue his unrequited love. All of those things add up to an experience that permeates into something so immutably real that I almost forgot I was playing a damn game.
Another thing that really helps you get immersed is Garrett himself, he now talks and comments on things way more frequently and has more character depth overall. Which in turn makes him even more likeable than he already was. Without spoiling anything there is one part where you break into some ladies home and Garrett just calmly says "Don't mind me ladies, just passing through" it really makes you feel like he is more than just a cypher for the player. Another real huge improvement is the inclusion of proper secrets in every mission. Most missions can have up to 8 or more secrets for you to find and they can be as simple as a short-cut or something really nice like some loot for you to plunder.
Con's: Once again there is not very many faults with this game but if there is one thing I didn't like as much as the first game it is the villain. He has a voice that sounds like a mixture of Cartman and Meatwad. Hard to feel intimidated by someone like that when I have that image in my head. He isn't a terribly written character and I really dig his motives and behaviour I just think a better voice could have gone a long way to make him seem badass. Maybe another complaint I can say is the final 3 missions are kind of "Meh" overall and the ending as a whole isn't as awesome as the first game.
Overall Feelings & Score: I feel like this game is not only just a worthy sequel to the first game but it is also a damn fine game in its own right. I give the game a $ out of *...make up your own mind and decide for yourself if you can enter...The Metal Age. Mind your P's and Q's because your balls, are, about to drop sirs and madams, peace the F out!

The graphics for this game may not be as spectacular compared to other stealth games like Metal Gear Solid but the gameplay more than makes up for that.
Taking place in a Victorian steam punk era with limited amounts of magic, you have to rely on quick wit and your arsenal to advance in the game.
Two guards block a doorway you need to enter through.  You could carefully sneak through the dark and bypass them, you could use an arrow to make a sound, drawing them away, or find a hidden passage in the wall to sneak behind them.  This is what makes the game so great, you have options you can use and not keep things so linear.
The difficulty also makes the game great.  There is no indicater of any kind to tell you there is a guard on the other side of the wall.  You have to use your ears to listen to footsteps, occasionally whistling, and eyes to see if that guard is carrying a key to unlock a door with.
One of the cons I can say about the game is the controls at times can be a little frustrating to deal with.  Sometimes you want to climb up a short wall, quietly, only to have Garrett not only miss grabbing the wall, he may make some noise too, alerting the guards.  I had a similar problem with ladders, with him not dismounting from the well.
The cut scenes are kept short and in between each mission.  Most of the story is told from reading parchments, books, and listening to game characters talk amongst themselves.
If you're looking for a stealth game that IS superior to most other stealth games, like Metal Gear, I would highly recommend this game ot

I'm finding a lot to enjoy here for a small price.  Like most stuff online you need to do a little poking around to separate fact from fiction when it comes to opinions and what people will say about a title.  There are some negative reviews that tell fiction as if it's fact and some people read them and just believe them, which is always a bad idea.
You need to look at what you are getting for the money and how you play, what you want to get out of the game, etc.  Personally I think it still would have worked out better as a F2P game but that said you can pay one price and that's all you really do need to pay ever.  You have access to all the inventory expansions and things just by doing daily quests, and you can win mounts, pets, etc by doing them as well (I've won a permanent mount already so yes it's definitely something you can do with dailies).  Some chest keys you are given some as daily login rewards, and realistically you find a lot of the best stuff without needing them anyway.  They can get you there a tiny bit quicker but aren't really needed either.  There really are not any pay to win options here.  What little is being sold is for a bit of extra convenience and as mentioned here you can win or straight out buy most stuff by spending your daily quest currency.
I can say one thing for sure - you definitely very much do not know this game at all within the first few hours.  It doesn't start to open up until later.  There are a multitude of skills to choose from that open as you level in just a single class, and it's a dual class game (you're free to change your 2nd pick whenever you want).  The skill variety is really nice and there are so many different ways they work too, not just graphical changes on the same type of skill use.  You have to play quite a while to see this but the choices keep growing as you continue on in the game, not just in skills but in overall things to do.
I'll admit that It didn't seem all that exciting during the first 6 hours probably, it was pretty standard.  Still worth a base buy price of $20, but still not that stand out during that time except for the quest dialogue had more meat to it than most games.  The game opens up more slowly than a lot of others as you level, but once you've played a while you have a lot of fun things to do.  It gets better over time because of all the new things that open as you play.
There is a lot of lore and story here which always is enjoyable for me.  I like to get into the world a little bit more.  For some people there will actually be too much, but it's easy enough to skip quickly through and still see what you need to do in quests and things and just ignore the world diaries and stuff you find around if you want.
The game is absolutely beautiful.  When people write in their reviews that it's ugly, I'm wondering what the deal is exactly.  It's better lookin than any other Diabloesque game that I've ever seen and I've experienced most of them.  The world is extremely detailed and pretty and some of the models have some pretty crazy detail as well.  I don't know if it was setting issues they were having or what exactly but it's an extremely pretty game.  I've also not seen that much as far as reusing of resources except where it makes sense to have some of the same types of enemies over a few areas.  You're constantly hitting new original stuff to see and fight.  There is *some* yes, but it's not really that much and not any more than most of these types of games.
I've really been having a lot of fun in this game without many of the issues people in other reviews have mentioned.  I don't know if that means the things like Crashing to Desktop have been fixed, or I won the compatibility lottery, but I've had no crash problems and no lag problems. I have completed this game on the PS4, but have also played this game substantially offline.
Now, Arkham Knight, to me, is one of the best games to come out next to The Witcher 3. Not only is it a fitting conclusion to Rocksteady's Batman-trilogy, it's also an all-around awesome game. Everything that City did right when it came to the basic essence of being the Batman, Knight amplifies and brings to another level. The story, to me, was the best out of Arkham games, just perfect in its exploration of how far Batman has had to go, and will have to go, in order to save Gotham and himself. Scarecrow is a terrific villain, somebody who truly has lost all regard to anything outside his ultimate goal. John Noble was amazing as his voice-actor; soemthing that Rocksteady is industry-leader in. Though, yes, Arkham Knight did not end up as great of a villain as he had been billed up as, his backstory and the reveal surrounding him was still magnificently achieved. The story hits new highs, and struck an emotional chord in me, making me want sad thinking that I would never have that "first time" feeling again.
The side missions, concerning various villains both small and well-known, were excellent. Varied and interesting, they used everything the game had taught you at their highest level. From having to chase Firefly throughout the city on the Batmobile (which happened to be my least favorite mission series), to stopping Two-Face's crew from robbing various banks and utilising every stealth mechanism known, and finally investigating a series of rather ghastly murders; one does not easily become bored in Arkham Knight. One minor gripe comes with the Riddler trophies & riddles. Having to find ALL of them, of which there are many hundreds, to achieve the final true ending was a tad too much for me. Thank you, YouTube.
The combat of Arkham Knight is the same amazing thing it has been since Asylum, but made with just that extra-dosage of perfection. It feels even smoother this time around, and the addition of dual-teaming with various allies is an awesome experience. And a sight to behold as well. The overall gameplay itself, as Batman (et. al) is the games highlighting feature, and a standard for the industry.
Now, to the most controversial aspect of the game: the Batmobile. I personally love it, and believe it's usage was just right. But, I also can see the criticism, and can understand it. The feel of the Batmobile itself is incredbly smooth, and the rush of just driving around Gotham, drifting around corners and shocking random rioters, is amazing. The tank battles, though not cumbersome at all, do get a little trite. This especially comes to light when the final battle against a major villain, after the end of the main story, is just another tank battle. I would have much preferred if he had been fought on the rooftop, for example, man el mano.
The music of the game, composed by the amazing duo of Nick Arundel and David Buckley, is an amazing accompanying aspect to the game. Though not as bombastic as the score for Arkham City, Arkham Knight's score aids the somber and almost-futile feel throughout the game. Gliding through the city, the music gave off a true sense of "this is the end", whether or not Batman and Gotham would pull through victorious.
Overall, Rocksteady has done what many thought impossible not just once, but thrice. Three awesome games making you The Batman; with a story to match the best Hollywood has to offer; and with an ending as shocking and fulfilling as possible, Arkham Knight sends The Dark Knight off most beautifully.

V65 is a fun, litttle strategy game set in the Vietnam War that's easy to learn and hard to master. Like in real war, no battle plan survives contact with the enemy and you have to constantly adapt in order to keep your units alive, but as long as you remember that good supply lines are vital to any military operation you'll be able to win almost every game.
Except on Veteran difficulty. That sheet's hard, man. D:
Just thinking about how I was doing really well for the duration of almost an entire game and then losing almost all of my units on the second to last turn gave me Vietnam flashbacks. Which in this case isn't necessarily bad thing because I like a good challenge.
I only have four minor issues with this game:
1 - Obvious tablet/mobile port is obvious. The UI is clearly meant to be used on touchscreens and it shows.
2- Not enough unit variety. All you get really are two standard types of non-descript "Infantry" unit (one American and one ARVN)  plus one type of Army Special Forces squad (Green Berets) that isn't really useful unless you can afford to build several FOBs.
3- While the early game is fun to play, mid-game it tends to get a little repetitive. Once you've established a secure foothold on any map, there really isn't much else to do besides wait until the 45th turn. While you do have to be wary of ambushes at all times, as long as you remember not to build any more units than you know you're able to supply regularly, almost any damage Charlie does can easily be mitigated.
4- There is no campaign mode, only skirmishes. 'Nam was one of the most painful episodes in US military history that only a few games have explored so far. It has so much potential for good, historical storytelling by means of a campaign mode, yet this game has none which is a real shame.
However, the complaints mentioned above are probably just me nitpicking. Overall I would say that Vietnam '65 is an enjoyable game that I would recommend if you're into this particular niche of military strategy games, and that I'm looking forward to playing this game's sequel (Afghanistan'11) once the price drops. =)

I've been playing Diablo 3 since launch and i do still play that game occasionally, doing a comparison with the 2 i'd say that Guardians of Ember is what diablo 3 should have been graphically talking (concerning the graphic, this game is way above the avarage of other games of this category), about the gameplay they're pretty much the same, i must admit though that diablo 3 still a bit more fast peaced concerning fights and action in general, but since this game gets improved steadly i do believe that devs will take care of this aswell. Again not a big gap between the 2, as it is right now i enjoy the gameplay and it's at a right spot, just it can be even better.
About customization, well it has way more options than Diablo 3, so the point goes clearly for this game. You can assign attribute points as you wish, you can assign skill points wherever you want, you can combine your main class with a secondary of any other avaiable thus opening way more options for character's builds and skill combinations, and unlikley diablo 3, a lot of them do work efficiently so the choice is pretty wide. You can also switch your secondary class with another one at a free cost, you'll keep the skill points and levels gained on your current secondary class, just in case you want to go back to your previous class without starting all over again. Of course you can't use/benefit of a non selected secondary class skills, that goes without saying. So, once you reach the level cap on a class, you can start levelling up another one, thus you can unlock every possible combo of class skills on a single character (the only difference will be made by your main class, your main class has passive skills aswell, which are not avaiable for any secondary class that you choose, so when you create a new character you have to keep in mind that: your passive skills are based on your main class, that's it).
About itemization, items roll with random affixes and random values (i.e. crit dmg xxx to xxx, hit rating  xxx to xxx, etc.), but the cool part is that there is a rune system where you can combine them into an item thus increasing the power and adding more stats/affixes on it.
Another cool thing is that any class can use/wear any kind of item available ingame without any type of restriction (right now i got a Knight/dark knight using a 2h heavycrossbow on a Whirlwind crit build, i just changed the appearance of the weapon to look like a 2h sword, so basically, the animation and the aesthetic is of a 2h sword. For those wondering why i'm using a crossbow and not a real sword or axe/hammer, well because right now it is the best weapon that i've found so far, but as i said doesn't matter at all as you can change the appearance of any item slot to look like whatever you want... even a knight wearing heavy plate armor to look like a caster with robes).
Items may be enchanted aswell. increasing the overall stats and armor/damage on them, aswell as you can reroll one bad affix similar to what you can do in Diablo 3.
There's a craft system aswell, it's not some over complicated system, just a regular one where you choose your main profession and farm mats (there are a lot of them), so you can craft armors, weapons, potions, etc. (i heard that the best weapons like the legendary ones are obtainable trough the craft system, not sure tho, i'm not that far yet into the weaponsmith profession).
There's also a private housing system, where you can place your own main house and start to collect furnitures to put in there. You can recruit NPCs that will work and help you with the craft professions, so they'll farm some mat aswell while you're out doing anything else.
The other functions are similar to other MMO/aRPG games: Random pubblic events spawning across the world areas to complete in solo or with other players where you kill/do stuff in order to gain rewards, a guild system where you play togheter with others and level it up to unlock some beneficial skill for everyone, characters are capable of riding mounts so you move faster outside the world, there's a compendium system where you can get cards dropped by every mob and to add them to your collection, the more you get the more stats bonues you'll receive. And finally the typical achievement system where you unlock them to gain titles and/or items.
Right now the PvP ranked system is not yet implemented, apart from training/custom matches. The PvP items vendors are present tho, so it's a matter of time on adding it i guess.
A fast recap:
Pros
- High level of customization for characters (both, gameplay and aesthetics);
- Cool dual class system;
- many things to collect and to do while they add the real end game (horde mode for PVE, which is coming soon and a PVP ranked system);
- A very good graphic engine and cool musics.
Cons

This game is similar to most other open world LEGO games: it doesn't deviate too much from the formula, a lot of "been there done that" moments, and trying to 100% can be a little tedious. But if you are a fan of Marvel comics you will really enjoy this game. There is a ton of content that the casual to the most hardcore Marvel comic book fan will appreciate. References range from the most recent Marvel movies to obscure and almost forgotten storylines or characters.
Visually it is one of the best looking LEGO games I've played. NYC is faithfully recreated in LEGO form, there are dozens of characters to unlock and they all have unique ways to play, the music is top notch, the jokes and physical gags are really funny, and there is a lot more missions to play beyond the story. Also, there's a lot of Stan Lee, and the more of him the better. It's a really fun game, don't let the LEGO bricks fool you.
If you are a little burned out by the LEGO series, then really there isn't a whole lot of new things here to entice you. But if you are a fan of Marvel, you should play this game as it's one of the best comic book games around. If you never played any LEGO games, I can't think of a better one to start with.

By far the best Batman game of the Arkham series, despite Arkham City!
I've not suffered any bug (well actually one, which i also encountered in the other games) so I guess the game's been fixed since its chaotic release.
When it comes to the game in itself, well it looks gorgeous (playing in ultra 1440p), I'd even dare say that, in my opinion, it looks better than most AAA games such as the Witcher 3. And it's fairly well optimized. As always the soundtracks and voice acting are on spot, however gameplay's not evolved that much since arkham city and yet it feels a lot more fluid. Also Batman doesnt jump around as much as he used to, like a god damn ballerina.
The main feature in this game's the batmobile and, as in most games with cars/horses/any "vehicule", it's not that great yet not terrible. Maniability and physics are both meh, however the battle stance is well made and quite user friendly.
To my mind, the best part in Arkham Knight is the story. Even if i cant disagree with people (prior to arkham knight) saying Arkham City was the best Batman game, I still prefered Arkham Asylum mainly because of the story. And in this one, I wont lie it's the bomb. Plenty of charismatic opponents such as Scarecrow, great plot, a few plot-twists (easily guessable tho) and there are very good ideas which i wont spoil there but which help the story and immersion a lot.
It's a lot darker, both the humour and the characters (especially Batman) and to me it's a big plus.
In the end, I cleared the game from bottom to the end (100% + most AR challenges) and i really hesitate whether or not i should buy the DLCs since the main game's so good.
A few flaws tho. First of all the Batmobile is too prominent. Secondly, and as in every single BA game, the riddler trophies. Artificially keeping the game alive for a few more hours of wandering around the city, looking for thugs to beat up and riddles to solve.... it's tedious and boring. 243 trophies. Come on. Lastly the boss fights. Wont spoil, again, but the final boss and most bosses anyway are both easy and boring.
Strongly recommended, best Batman game. I'm actually fairly sad that they failed their port, because it has really ruined it for most players and their work on BAK really deserved both recognition and more respect from the port team.

The minute you get in the first thing you'll probably do is change the controls. The default controls in this game are set up fairly differently than the average first-person game, but you'll have little-to-no trouble after setting them up. The graphics are pretty dated, even as far as 2000 is concerned.
The stealth mechanics of Thief are much more interesting than the average stealth system, based more around light and sound as opposed to the cone of vision that other stealth games tend to employ. Garrett decides to wear his clogs on every mission, so stepping on stone makes you much more obvious than stepping on something like a rug, while stepping on tile is a death sentence. The light gem at the bottom of the screen lights up to tell you if you're being lit up by the light around you, or is dark to show that you're completely in the shadows. Very rarely do games use lighting and sound as effectively as Thief does here.
The missions in the second Thief, as opposed to the original Thief, focus more around simple thievery instead of supernatural missions involving zombies and cultists. This is pretty subjective as to whether or not it's a pro or con, but I prefer the thievery. The original Thief is more of the same, but with more of the aforementioned zombies and cultists.
It's easily one of the best stealth games to date. The original is preferable if you want more of the zombies and similar stuff, and Deadly Shadows is a little more forgiving. Overall, I'd reccomend it to anyone looking for an extremely fun and unique stealth system that's rarely contested, even to this day.

I will say it right off the bat. Bebop and Tempo is not a perfect game, but by no means is it a terrible game. Generally speaking, the game is very much like a platformer or arcade game on NES or any other retro console. Don't hold your breath for an in depth story, leveling system, or an inventory system. If you are looking for lots of eye candy, then skip Bebop and Tempo because you wont get it here.
So then what does Bebop and Tempo have to offer? A game with charm, retro feels, and death...lots of it. Bebop and Tempo is a challenging game. I sort of breezed through the first area, a couple of hiccups here and there. Let me tell you, the game gets much harder the more you progress. If you want to get the best score possible, which in this games case the lower is better, you really have to master controlling your character. Thankfully the controls in Bebop and Tempo are solid. 
You have your basic directions, left, down, and right. Then you have three action buttons, jump, switch, and attack. Let me take the time to say thank you developer for thinking that not everyone plays games like you. You can rebind your keyboard controls in the options menu. Also, I was able to plug in an Xbox One control and it worked no problem, but you can not rebind the Xbox Control layout. Anyways, each character you can switch between do different actions such as dodging vs stomping. It is very rewarding to smash through a level and realize that you are only pushing three buttons. but pushing them at the right point, place, and time. Again, it is not easy to do this since enemies will be throwing objects, flying through walls, and even blocking your attacks. I will say that I do find Bebop and Tempo to be fair. My deaths/mistake were easily correctable on the next play through. Although you may find yourself saying "stupid ducking turtles!" or something that rhymes with that...
In a nut shell, you have to clear each level as fast as you can by killing all of the enemies which then opens the exit door.  Levels can be short, have no enemies, maze like puzzles, long like a castle(literally), a ton of enemies, and any combination of the aforementioned.  Some levels have a secondary objective by collecting extra fruit things which then gives you a star for that level. I don't want to ruin too much but if you collect all the stars in an area and can complete what comes next...Please do let me know because it has already taken 100 deaths from me.
The music is great but may not be for everyone. You can close your eyes and listen to the music and feel like you are sitting 4 feet away from your old CRT and your NES. I don’t know much about music but I either like it or hate it, and I like it. So great job on that part.
As far as graphics go, Bebop and Tempo is definitely taking notes from classic NES games like Kirby and Mario. Unfortunately, the game is not pixel perfect. There are a few instances where some characters look different as if more detail was put into them. Almost like two different pixel sizes. There are also a few graphical glitches here and there. I mean I am really nit picking but its there and can be noticeable if you look out for it. Otherwise, all of the levels and characters are very colorful and charming.
 Oh Versus Mode...I had my doubts about you. The main menu for Versus Mode looks very simple. You can choose your game length, balloon count (which act like health), level, and whether or not you want enemies on or off. Take my advice, turn enemies off, select any time amount, and play with one balloon each. Your friend can squeeze along your side and you can both play on one keyboard. However, you can not rebind the multiplayer keys. Also, the button layout is different and unless you want to figure out what each button does for what player, it looks like you have to actually read the instruction manual that comes with the game, which is on Bebop and Tempo's website and Steam apparently. My friend and I also were able to play both with Xbox one controls and a combination of one player on keyboard and the other on an Xbox control.
So how long is Bebop and Tempo? I have unlocked all of the areas, modes, and multiplayer levels. I have played adventure mode for about an hour and a half and I am at 33% completion. My guess is that I can get to 100% in about 4-5 hours.
In conclusion, Bebop and Tempo is a great game and I do have fun playing it. The music and graphics may turn away some, but I love a game that challenges me. For an arcade/platforming game, Bebop and Tempo is by no means a 10/10 or even a 9/10, but I do feel comfortable giving it an 8/10 and recommending a buy.

I didn't play the Thief games upon their initial release and so am not reviewing this through the rose-tinted glasses of nostalgia. But I can safely say that these games honestly do still hold up today.
Pros:
- Light/Dark system is a great mechanic and leads to the player paying more attention to their environment.
- Static map, some areas are missing and without an all encompassing minimap you are forced to be more cautious, unsure of what lies around each corner and this adds to the game's  tense atmosphere.
- Your footsteps become louder when walking on harder floors such as marble, adds depth and makes you more observant of your surroundings.
- No zombies or supernatural elements (preference).
- Excellent level design, navigating is not a problem despite not having a full map or quest markers. This is because the levels are designed logically (as though they were not designed just for a game but to serve the purpose of the building e.g a mansion)  and loot is distibuted accordingly, e.g you can safely assume that there will be little to no loot in the servants quarters, but there will more than certainly be something valuable in the nobles quarters.
- Tells the story through level design and gameplay instead of directly through a cutscene or text.
- You can't choose to go in all guns blazing, you die quickly (2 sword hits) and thus feel more vunerable and this creates tension. You aren't invincible, their is no second option to just fight your way in. Only through the patience and intelligence of the player can Garrett succeed, as you play you become a better thief- not through "levelling up"- you are never given any notification of your progress by the game (this is a good thing), Garrett stays his same vunerable self throughout the whole game, but you the player learn how to handle yourself: which areas are low/high risk, when to blackjack guards, where to hide etc ... This is extremely rewarding as by the end of the game you (the player) have gone from an amateur burglar to a masterthief, this progression of the player instead of the character is extremely rewarding and makes you feel like you are truly getting more skillful- this progression is expressed not through a number or a level and Garrett doesn't become more powerful as you play, your growth is shown in the way you play the game.
- Amazing soundtrack.
Cons:
- May be too dark and hard too see for some.
- Not the greatest voice acting.
- Graphics whilst not awful do not compare with those of newer titles.
You owe it to yourself to experience this masterpiece.
Definetely not recommended for teenagers!

The true beauty of this game comes from renaming your soldiers after your friends and watching them die because of your recklessness.

The second wave feature adds a bit of spice to the challenge if you feel like you are up for it; don't forget Ironman mode to keep you from save scumming!

At a(n) graphical/aesthetic standpoint, it presents XCOM in an appealing way that even newcomers to the franchise can enjoy. The music keeps the situation tense and engaging during fights and helps deliver the needed ambience outside of it.

Epanalepsis lets you glimpse the lives of three different people across various years: they all encounter the same man in red, said man is trying to warn them about the choices they're going to make and how they might affect the future.
The game that follows is more of a slightly interactive story than anything else, you'll walk around, look at objects, pick a few of them up and be faced with a choice for each character: the gameplay is thin and the story is sadly way too cryptic to make up for it.
-nice soundtrack
-some interesting dialogues
-what few glimpses you get of the overall story, and their implications, are pretty intriguing
-very basic graphics, little in the way of animations
-lack of actual gameplay
-walking speed is too slow
-the white text often gets lost whenever it appears on a light background
-way, way too vague in its narrative to be actually engaging, you're left wondering what happened, why and how your choices affected the endings you get
-very short, I was done in an hour
I like "artsy" and daring games, as you can see from my reviews, but Epanalepsis totally missed the mark for me: the gameplay is way too basic but that'd be excusable if the story had gotten to me.
Sadly said story was way too vague for me to find it interesting, some references and bits of info were intriguing but that's all there was: the disconnection between each character I controlled, despite the fact they all seem to be involved in what's happening, and dialogues that dealt with things and names that were barely explained, if at all, left me disappointed.
In the end I felt as if the game was being so vague, to the point of coming out as obtuse, just for the sake of it rather than doing it in an attempt to challenge my mind: I simply lacked enough info to be challenged. Despite getting it on sale for around 3,50$ I still felt it was a tad too overpriced for what it does: I can't recommend it but who knows, perhaps you'll have better luck with it.

Epanalepsis for me personally was a very frustrating game, from art style, to its linear nature, there were things here I just didn't click with. The game is unabashedly a whacked out story and never really explains anything at all. I would love to tell you what the story of Epanalepsis is all about but it doesn't actually give you any answers. The story flows at a rapid pace and leaves it to your interpretation to get your answers. Now I have played games that feature short stories, The Charnel House Trilogy is a prime example of simple straight forward gameplay with a cohesive story and game elements, oddly enough also published by Mastertronic. It seems like Epanalepsis goes against the grain in just about every way, when it came down to it.
To sum up Epanalepsis, gameplay is rather easy. This isn't really a point and click adventure game but more a visual novel. You are essentially on rails but you determine how fast they move. Go straight to your objective in the next room or stop and examine things in the area. This is basically it from beginning to the end of the game. Occasionally a decision is given to you that may or may not affect the ending. Lack of interactivity also felt frustrating to me, you feel like your just moving from text box to text box. The game doesn't actually give you much to play around with other then a few moments of "Go find this item." I felt that the game could've added a bit more for the player to do other than just slide around.
When I finished Epanalepsis, I didn't have a sense of wonder or thoughtful inquiry, I was more shocked that it was just over and that was it. There is nothing wrong with a short story but it felt like Epanalepsis wasn't interested in me as a player. The tone and narrative on the other hand are done well. You really get a feeling for the three main characters who are stretched out over a wide space of time. From 1990s to the year 2030, each section/chapter of the game creates a unique feel and tone to the game. I wanted to know more about these times and characters but felt rushed and moved along, for the sake of mystery and vagueness. What ties the three time periods together are these supernatural characters who more or less say "Your decisions matter, but not really, because you have made them a hundred times." This sentiment is driven into your head several times.
For a game that is exclusively based off its story and themes, your connection to the characters is only represented in the every day objects of their abodes. From the 90's mixtapes to the online gaming of 2000s. Sadly, you're not really encouraged to look at these items littered about the environments. This adds much needed time to the game but isn't required for you to complete the game. You have to approach this game with a sense of investigation that is solely driven by you. The game will never encourage you to stop and smell the roses. There is no bonus or secret hidden anywhere, you simply just get to know more about that character in that time period. Then your ripped away to another main character and restart the process. By the time you get to the end, your exhausted by the fragmented nature of the game.
Moving on and breaking down the other elements of Epanalepsis, the price of the game is subjective. The truth is that you can beat this game within an hour, if you're looking for a game that offers replayability and length, the game is going to come up lacking. You are playing this game because you are interested in its story and message, whatever that may be personally to you. There is also additional DLC for you to purchase and enjoy. The well done soundtrack is available for purchase, as well as The Epanalepsis Papers. A collection of scans of the developers notebooks and essays/annotations on development of the game. These may give you further insight into the games story.
The soundtrack is something that I found to be done quite well, each track is played effectively according to the story. The tracks do repeat but never annoyingly. The music does a good job of making you feel like everything is normal but that there is still something amiss. Then the music shifts to an outlandish track and everything is suddenly trippy. This I liked quite a bit and wouldn't of minded more of in other areas of the game. Sound effects from moving, to walking through doors were there but nothing else that really caught my attention.
The art style is where I was also thrown off quite a bit. Perhaps its a personal preference but it never really spoke to me. The characters themselves moved oddly and looked strange sometimes, depending upon the environments they found themselves within. While there is detail in the different abodes of the characters, you can't help but shake the feeling that the game feels like it was made on Windows Paint. There are times where the game looks ornate but other times where it feels very uninspiring to look at. Again that is up to personal preference.
There are some technical aspects to the game worth mentioning as well. There is a slight bug where the camera isn't oriented with the text box. You have to shift your character to see what is being described/spoken. The game doesn't have any resolution controls or options whatsoever. Other simple features like being able to move quickly through a room is painstakingly slow. Your characters walk very slowly. You can't double click on an exit but must physically walk your character to the door or to the object you wish to interact with. This is fine for things such as doors and small objects but even larger objects require that you approach them to get a description. This feels slightly silly at times and could've been made a bit more convenient for the player. Speeding up the protagonist a slight bit would've fixed most of these issues.
The game does have quite the following, many people have mentioned they felt a connection and deeply impacted by the tones and characters of the game. I personally didn't feel that way but you may find yourself enthralled with its storytelling. What it boils down to for me was that there was no satisfying answers. You just have to accept the game for what it is. If you can't do that you may find yourself as frustrated as I was.
One thing that can be said about Epanalepsis is that it is unique, I haven't seen many games quite like it or dared to tell such a strange story for better or worse. It doesn't really try to innovate the wheel or add any interesting gameplay dynamics. What it does try to do is make you think about yourself and where you are. So with that in mind, if you feel like you can connect with this game and perhaps don't mind games that are open to interpretation, you enjoy weird stories, and don't demand answers, you may enjoy this game. Sadly for me, it just didn't click.

I got this and the second game reeeeeaaaaaal cheap, like £1 for both games, so yeah bargain, i don't regret the 50p spent on this game but it is...mediocre at best. The gameplay is really janky and a lot of the time when you shoot someone when they are behind cover your bullet won't hit them and just goes through them instead, causing you to either wait for them to move or you being forced to move into different cover to take them out.
There's a nice assortment of different environments and levels to play through including a prison, bank, a nightclub, the streets of japan and even some jungle levels late on in the game. I have to say actually that the nightclub level in this is probably the best nightclub i have seen in a game so far, it had really immersive strobe lighting and was packed with 100's of NPC's who then run around screaming when you inevitably have a shootout in it. Compare this to the clubs in games like Deus ex or Sleeping Dogs and there's no comparison, and this game came out in 2007 so that's impressive to me. Only the new Hitman game and the new Assassins Creed Unity has really played around with interactive crowd density.
It's weird though because the actual story about Kane and Lynch has had no effort put into it BUT the actual characters all have more personality than you would expect in a game like this and i found the voice acting really well done as well, i actually wanted to finish the game to see where the story went. It's just why and how Kane and Lynch continue to work with each other had me saying WTF!!!! Lynch is a psychopath who kills innocent people for no reason and then has a blackout where he doesn't even remember doing it. Later on in the game Kane has him keep his ex japanese girlfriend hostage, and without spoiling it you can tell that isn't going to end well. If they were brothers i could understand it but they just met each other and another character who you break out of prison even says he doesn't wanna work with Lynch because he's a crazy b*stard and killed his own wife. They have a character in the game who gets it! so why doesn't Kane? it's stupid and they could have made that way more believable if they just spent more time on the writing
I would actually recommend this game purely for the nightclub level, the rest of the game is ok if you can get past some of the jank.

I love short stories, little bit sized chunks of content that cut out most of the filler full length movies have and gets right to the meat and potatoes.  It's easy to make a short movie, anyone with a camcorder and some video editing software can do it, it takes a real artist to actually make a short story that tells a GOOD story.  This is one of those times when an artist made a GOOD short story.
The movie starts with a man named Paul Hamilton, he's sitting in a bathtub full of soapy water, he proceeds to put a gun in his mouth and BANG!!!....  (you could say they started the movie with a bang, watching the scene immediately brought up my memories of watching Ken Park, although this movies death didn't take place in a skate park, nor was it carried out by a teenager, nor was it bloody or gory)  The scene immediately switches to Paul sitting in a bar, he's obviously intoxicated....  after a few misadventures Paul finally finds his way home, heading inside his door, he prepares himself for bed.  Upon waking up and getting ready for work, he stops to kiss his wife good bye....  WHAT?  His wife is shocked, and doesn't know who he is, she sprays him with mace and tosses him out the front door.
That's the movie in a nutshell, Paul Hamilton is lost, nobody seems to remember him, and he's left to wander around a concrete jungle trying to figure out who he is and why nobody remembers him.   The movie is far better than my one paragraph can do it justice, it's a exciting, that will leave you wanting more.  The true sign of a good short film is leaving the viewer wanting more.  I could have easily seen this being a full fledged movie, it was already really good for what it was.
The movie was made in 2013 and has a running time of 26 minutes.  The main character of Paul Hamilton is played excellently by Joshua Koopman.
Like I said above, you should buy this, it's a well put together indie short film, good acting, good pacing, and great music.   All for the price of a burger and fries at McDonalds.  I know lots of people are apprehensive at buying films on steam, but I personally see no reason to exclude movies on steam, they've been on the platform for quite a few years now, it's only the past 2 or 3 years that we've begun getting some decent to good indie movies.  So buy this movie, take 26 minutes away from killing aliens, reading visual novels with half dressed aliens, or playing whatever f2p you consider your flavor of the month.  Trust me you'll enjoy it..

The achievements are not hard to earn over the course of about 10-15 successful games.
Logistics of your units is a big part of this game.  You need to dedicate a good portion of your available transportation resources (primarily helicopters) to supplying your units in the field.  Beyond that, your objective is to win "hearts & minds" of local villages by sending your infantry units out to patrol them and engage the enemy units nearby.  Successful engagement of the enemy units increases both the support from the villages as well as "political support" in the form of $$$ from Washington to pay for additional units and operations that you need for your campaign.
I am looking forward to this game's sequel "Afghanistan '11" which should be on the market soon.

Before I bought this game I didn't know anything about any of the Shadowrun games, but it was on sale for $2.99 so I had to buy it.
It started out a little slow, setting up the plot and everything, but I was patient and gave it time.  It picked up pretty soon and I was definitely enjoying myself with it.  I was running aroung shooting people and casting fireballs and then I could go and jack myself into the matrix, a cyber world where I could search for information. but had to use my techno magic to protect myself.  It was great.
My biggest problem starting the game was that the steam trailers and everything didn't give me much info.  It only showed a quick overview of 3 classes, and there are 6.  So this is my quick description of everything.
Street Samurai: The most basic class in my opinion, but it is still very powerful.  The Samurai focuses on weapons and that is it.  You can use shotguns to deal MASSIVE damage up close, or you can snipe from afar.  Definitely a good choice for those who want to get the job done quickly.
Mage: The mage is your offensive spell caster.  You get fireballs and lightning along with blinding spells.  Prettty straightforward, shoot fireball, burn enemies, repeat.  Sounds basic, but I've had some experiences where I needed to really consider my options with different spells.
Decker: The decker is sometimes considered a weaker class.  They are your hacker.  In certain places they can "jack in" to the matrix and go exploring.  When out of the matrix, they are a weaker samurai, but in the matrix you are an extremely powerful mage.
Shaman: I find the shaman to be a heavier utility spellcaster, with some summoning powers.  As a shaman, you can slow enemies, give allies extra actions, and create fog to make enemies miss their attacks.  I find shaman a tougher class because they have to manage a lot of different things to keep your team working.
Rigger: The rigger is a very fun class that controls drones to go fight for him, but sacrifices his own actions to do so.  I find him extremely powerful if you have a shaman with you, because the shaman can boost actions, so you don't give up as much when you're sending out drones.
Physical Adept:  I don't know much about the physical adept, but they're basically and mix between mage and samurai, they have passive skills that can help with unarmed combat, but also use machetes and other melee weapons.
Those are all of the classes.  All of them are definitely powerful and unique.  What I find to be a very interesting factor is that you can put karma points (points gained from completing missions and objectives to level up skills) into any of the stats, allowing you to multiclass and be multiple classes.  My first character was a decker, and I found myself to be too weak outside of the matrix, so I upgraded my drone control stat and bought a drone, outside of the matrix I can send out my drones to deal heavy damage while staying behind cover, and give=ing allies medpacks when the are low on health.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants a mystery type of game with fun turn based combat.  I rate this game 9/10 and think it was worth the money!

This game is fantastic!  If you like Hearthstone or Magic the Gathering you will love this game.
For new folks:
1.  Open the crate.
2.  Did you open the crate yet?!
3.  Go to store to "buy" packs with your free tickets.
4.  Do the campaign and some of the easier achievements, you will get a ton more packs of cards.
PAY STRUCTURE -
This game does pay-to-win correctly, you can pay for packs of cards, but just logging in and playing the game you get more than enough to make great decks.  With the starter items in the crate, completing main quest, and dabbling a little in multiplayer for achievements, I was able to quickly get about 60-70 packs of cards.  Beyond that you get a small amount of gold each day just for logging in, and daily missions to complete.  You can get 1-2 packs per day just from logging in and playing.  Furthermore, once per day you can buy a pack at half price.  So the guy that spends $20 and opens them all at once is going is basically going to get 20 packs, while the guy that spends $20 and logs in every day is going to get 40 packs.  It seems to work well.  I have given them only $5, and rarely feel out-gunned by somebody with a crazy deck.
GAMEPLAY -
It plays similar to Hearthstone.  Each player begins the match with 20 hit points.  On turn one you get 1 play point orb, meaning you can play a lowly 1-cost card.  On turn two you get 2 play points, turn three you get 3 etc.  Some classes can get more orbs.  The character classes are similar to MtG, Havencraft is like the white deck, Forestcraft is similar to the green deck, Swordcraft is similar to red deck.  Each class has followers which can attack and defend, spells, and amulets which provide boosts to your avatar or followers.  The follower abilities will be familiar to any Hearthstone player, Storm = Rush, Last Words = Deathrattle, Ward = Taunt.
TWO REASONS WHY THIS IS BETTER THAN HEARTHSTONE -
This is where Shadowverse wins by a longshot.  I haven't played Hearth in a long time, but I remember when playing against a mage EVERYTIME on the 7th turn they dropped Flamestrike, when playing against Shaman EVERYTIME on 2nd turn they dropped the snake taunt totem, etc.  In Shadowverse you will see some of this, but the Evolution points totally shake things up.  Each player receives evolution points.  Player going first gets 2, player going second gets 3.  Evolving a follower adds +2/+2 to attack and defense AND allows them attack followers on the turn they were summoned.  Additionally a lot of cards have a special ability when they evolve.  One evolved card might summon another follower instantly, or two followers, or even more.  Or the evolved follower could have a special effect that at end of turn they deal 2 damage directly to the enemy player, the variety of options is enormous.
Second most classes have a unique special ability or trick.  When playing as Bloodcraft, for example, you go into Vengeance mode when HP is 10 or less.  This significantly buffs followers in most cases, but you need to seal the deal quick b/c you only have 10 HP left.  Forestcraft boosts their cards by playing two other cards prior to the special card.  Dragoncraft reaches Overflow when they hit 7 play-point orbs, significantly boosting cards.  Shadowcraft deals in dark magic by gaining shadows when it's followers have been killed or sacrificed, the shadows are then consumed by certain cards, with powerful effects.
OTHER STUFF -
The game has a solid server for multiplayer.  I have only had it fail to connect me to an opponent once.  The music is good, although I wish there were a few more tracks.  The graphics are great, especially when you drop a legend or evolve a special follower.  The game includes a "dust" crafting system similar to Hearth, but it is vials instead.  Legendaries are quite expensive, but bronze and silver cards are cheap and can still be very effective.  I am not a fan of the anime art and girls with rediculously huge boobs, it just looks weird.  I wish they made them look like badass warriors, like the male cards.  But that is a personal preference.
Overall I highly recommend this game.  It's free, so why not try it!

Epanalepsis is some more damn fine storytelling from the creator of Catachresis.
It's a short story, cardinally structured with three POV characters who inhabit the same space in different times through a kind of Nietzschean reincarnation device. I like it because playing the game feels like a ritual; you repeat the same montage of events in each of the game's acts: an introductory dream sequence, a mundane fetch quest, and finally a walk down a street (the same street in each story) to make a delivery, before being yanked out of your life by the overarching science-fiction framing narrative which remains elusive even after the game ends.
(I'm going to spoil the general storyline from here on out.)
In the first story, we get a glimpse into the life of a young, independent woman in the 1990s. Typical point-and-click adventure narrative techniques piece together this archetype: the personal importance of Judith Butler, dealing with roommates, one-sided pestering calls from mum, zines, and rowdy rock clubs are all part of this tapestry.
Then we jump ahead to the near-present day, in which we live the life of a gamer whose escape from life is not dreams and cultural theory but his overwhelming immersion in the commercialisation of video games. His apartment is adorned exclusively with game figurines and posters, with contemporary cultural references (which if you're the sort of person who reads Steam reviews, you'd be intimately familiar with) that are at their thinnest-veiling towards Indie Game: The Movie and Monkey Island. The only books he reads are the novelisations of his favourite MMO. Then when we take the now-familiar trek down the street, what was once the rowdy rock club has been gentrified to a fairtrade, organic cafe complete with a pitch-perfect, bearded barista straight outta any such place in Melbourne. This centre act is perhaps where the game is at its heavy-handest, but the developer should be commended on his commentary on modern, commercialised life and gamer culture for being neither contemptuous nor shallow; it's simply how folks find meaning today, and the game treats it with the same reverence as it treats our first protagonist's tastes and priorities. And using the form of an indie game itself (or, if you won't, an art-game) is the most apt place to paint such a portrait.
In the final story, which is the most interesting and unique, we are placed in the shoes (or wheels, as it were, in a refreshing change of literal pace) of a robot in a near-future dystopia. The narration style of the classic, point-and-click adventure is twisted to mediate a robot's point of view of the world. Each mouseclick qua 'examine' verb sets off an overzealous desire to REPORT ILLEGAL TERRORIST ACTIVITY and interactions with humans takes on a Sam & Max 'little buddy' tone, undercut with reminders that... you *do* realise there's a human behind the controls of this, right? Yes, yes, but look at the cute, little guy zip around! Way to go! Yeah! Set off that bomb!
There are a couple of choices to make in the game and an ending of sorts and although I haven't played the game more than once, I get the sense that any divergence from the narrative ultimately won't change much; that these characters are resigned to fate, as the mysterious, sci-fi visitors keep trying to tell us. And I like that. It gives you something to reflect on and leaves unsaid what needs to be unsaid, rather than trying to cram a complex, branching narrative of choice and consequence into your brain. It absolutely succeeds in conveying a sense of place, tone, theme, and atmosphere. Don't come looking for a satisfying, resolving story, because there's not even the intention of that being on offer. Instead, expect good and stylish storytelling and plenty of thought and attention to carry a one-hour experience.

Video games are not defined by their interactivity, as so, so many suggest, but rather their repetitiveness. If there is one thing video games are primed to grapple with, it is the banal - it's getting players to do the same thing over and over, with very little difference, but fistfuls of novelty and spectacle.
Epanalepsis is a short meditation on that repetitiveness, and as a result, is probably one of the most fascinating explorations of player choice and acausal game design I've seen in recent memory. It's not clear why you're doing what you're doing, it's not clear how the things you're doing matter to the game, and it's certainly not clear how those things precipitate future game events.
If you've read the preceding paragraphs and said aloud, "who gives a ♥♥♥♥?" then Epanalepsis isn't for you. In fact, even if you feel like Epanalepsis IS for you, I'm here to tell you it's not. I'm a person who thought Epanalepsis was for them, and it's decidedly not. It's not a thing I will completely and fully understand. It's not something that was made-for-me in the way that so many games are made-for-players.
Look, do you like short stories? You might be into this. Were you ever unemployed for any length of time and worried about that? Then you might even be moved to tears. Are you into prodding at weird stuff on the internet that seems pretty smart and baffling and alienating and melancholy? Okay, you should probably give this game a look.
I've also read through The Epanalepsis Papers, and found all of that particularly interesting. But I'm also a game designer and sympathized with Kunzelman's anxieties and loved a front row look at his development process.
Looking for a game where you'll feel satisfied by solving puzzles and mastering the mechanics and feeling a full sense of mastery of a game's world, its mechanics, its context? Don't bother. This game isn't for you in literally every sense of the phrase. And that's rad and wonderful.

Okay due to complaints from multiple people I have decided to give the game another try.  Sadly, my NOT RECOMMANDED review stands.
In my original review I called the game "a very generic hack & slash RPG with dated low rez graphics and clunky controls - plays like a game from the last decade, or at best a cheap modern F2P mobile title, complete with ingame gems store."
There were issues with the graphics settings not saving properly apparently, resulting to my previous comment of the graphics being low rezed and dated.  Well, according to the developer, that bug has been fixed - my response?  Yes, and no.  The client is still buggy as hell, and it took me a couple of force quits and restarts before I got the graphics working as advertised.  However despite finally playing the game with higher rezed graphics I still personally find the artstyle dated and uninspired.  It's not bad per say, but very generic and uninspired.
The messy distracting texts and fonts; the clunky abstrusive UI; the janky animations; the floaty unresponsively controls that I noticed before are still present.  And sadly, playing the game in higher rezed graphics actually made the game's flaws a lot more apparent in my eyes.
I said in my original review that "frankly nothing I saw in my time here interested me.  This game is as generic and bland as they come.  The whole time I was playing I was thinking "why am I wasting my time with this when there are much better alternatives out there - games with much better basic mechanics, with much better graphics, much better story, and much more personality?"  THIS, has NOT changed.  The game still plays like one of those dime-a-dozen-Asian-copycat-F2P games released in the last decade (and beyond).  I did NOT have fun.  I was NOT impressed.
Remember folks I am NOT putting the game or its developer down here, just stating MY PERSONAL OPINION of the game.  If you happen to like the game, good for you.  Go play it now and leave me in peace.

I bought this game as part of a Bundle Stars Bundle and it was the one I was most excited to play out of the bunch. I read many of the negative reviews before buying, but figured I would still probably enjoy it despite its flaws considering it was my type of game. Lets just say that my experience with this game has been less than stellar.
The first thing I did after installing the game was attempt to change the resolution and display settings. There is an impressive amount of settings that can be tweaked and I was intially pleasantly surprised. After changing some of them, I was told that the selection would be resource intensive and that I would have to restart my game. Fair enough. I applied the settings but there was no way to exit the game. After searching for a while I decided to kill the program through windows.
I then reloaded the game for a second attempt. The program did not remember my resolution choice of 1920x1080 and didn't load the game into full screen mode like it did on the first load. For some reason it defaulted to a low resotion and moved the window mostly off of the screen to the point where the 'play' button was no longer visible. Luckily, a simple press of the enter button got me into the game.
Sure enough, most of my setting were not retained but curiously some of them were. I re-applied them, only this time the screen went totally black after changing the resolution. I was unable to minimize to windows or ever get back a visible screen so I had to do a hard reboot of my machine.
On round 3, after rebooting, I reapplied the settings and I figured this time I would just go ahead and make my character and exit out of the program once I was in the game in hopes that it would retain my settings then. Character generation was simple but fine. Even though most of my retained settings were maxed, the graphics were extremely blurry and didn't look anything like the images above. When I zoomed into my character portrait the blurriness got even worse - I mean read bad. Anyway, I got into the game, killed a goblin (at least I think it was) and promptly exited the game so I could enjoy it properly with nice graphics.
On round 4, when I loaded up the game it now asked me for my account name and password. Now I will admit that if I had read the Steam page fully I would have seen this requirement, but at this point, creating an account was the last thing I wanted to do. I was also curious as to why I wasn't asked to create an account on one of my previous attempts.
Maybe I will give the game another chance in the future, but in its current state, it is simply too much of a hassle to get into and make it look like something that was made in the last two decades. I know that isn't isn't fair to the developers - especially considering that this is in early access, but first impressions mean a great deal and you only get one of them. Its a shame because the screenshots look promising.
Another issue I noticed was that steam says I have put 2.2 hrs into the game. I must have been abducted by aliens or something because I would estimate that I was actually in the game menus for a total of maybe 20 minutes and in the game itself for less than a minute. Perhaps it counts the time spent downloading the files in the downloader tool, but even so, it didn't take me 2 hrs to download. I even received 4 steam cards (but maybe that is the appropriate amount of card drops for 2.2 hrs). It just doesn't seem right.
My recommendation is to let this one cook in the oven a while longer, at least until the developer sorts out the graphical bugs.
