Well after about 50 or so hours of playing this game and grabbing everything I pretty much can, I feel like I need to write a review on it! (With lots of Dead Island hate)
Short review: It's basically what Dead Island should have been but mixed in with some Far Cry, Mirrors Edge, and a little bit of Assassins Creed elements.  If you want a superior Dead Island get this.
LONG REVIEW TIME:
PROS:
Better story (as far as a zombie game goes): As far a a zombie game story goes this is a lot better than Dead Island.  Basically- oh yeah SPOILER ALERT -you're a man named Kyle Crane who is dropped into the infected city of Harran to find some guy that has stolen a very important file from the GRE.  And guess what happens the minute you get dropped in? You get bit, of course, lazy pr^$k couldn't move fast enough.  There aren't many twists and turns in the story, but there are some very interesting parts here and there but not much else.
Characters: Compared to Dead Islands bland Characters, these actually have some soul to them (Take that for what you will) each one is pretty interesting, some are kind of bland, but not as bland as the ones in Dead Island anyway.  Each one seems to have some weight to it or at least some emotion.
Fighting the Biters: Fighting the zombies actually feels like it has some weight to it, with each hit you make, each gunshot, everything.  It doesn't feel as lifeless as it does in Dead Island with swings or with guns.  The hit sounds are solid, the impact and weight with each swing you make, the bone breaking for biters, everything, it feels pretty solid.
Scavenging for items: To craft good weaponry or even some distracting tools, you need items found throughout the world.  Aerosal, sawblades, chemicals, ductape, everything you find is useful in someway or another.  This is how you make throwing stars, strong elemental weapons, explosives, and more.  Plus my OCD says "GRAB EVERY DAMN THING YOU SEE."  Not only that but almost every single building you go towards you can go into and scavange for some loot, very nice touch that you can enter most of the buildings to get stuff.
Traps: There are traps riddled throughout the world that you can use to your advantage, like a car trap.  It sets off the alarm and the zombies gather around it, after about 5 alarm horns it goes off with an electric shock, pretty much killing everything in the area around it.  Or like the electric fence, which makes a loud high pitched screech to draw enemies over, then zaps the fences below them with electricity, useful for dealing with enemies on your tail.
Different enemy types: There are different enemies instead of just zombies.  There are the Spitters from Left 4 dead except they are even MORE ANNOYING.  Demolishers, which as basically just really big buff zombies that can knock down a lot of your health and get quite annoying.  The Runner Zombies, they are basically runners that have been infected, they're as fast as you, and can climb up buildings to catch you. The prison zombies (I suppose this is what they're called) they are basically just a beefed up version of the regular biters except with a big piece of Concrete Rubar that will hurt you with the swing and knock you over if you're too close.  Hazmat zombies that can't get caught on fire, but have a air tank on their back, hit the tank, and BOOM.  The Volatiles, they come out at night to patrol and can sense you if you get too close, this basically goes as a cop system like GTA, the longer they chase you the more will follow, and the longer they'll try to search for you if you lose them.  And then my most HATED ENEMY EVER, the Suiciders, which can kill you instantly if you are within like 2 meters of them.
Weapon Variety: There are a lot of weapons you can get, each has it's own little property based off what it is, bone breaking, slicing off body parts, etc.  AND THE GUNS ACTUALLY WORK LIKE F%#KING GUNS.  Headshots apply to pretty much everything except for volatiles I believe, they do have some damn good sounds, and the impact of shooting a enemy is very rewarding.
Parkour!: How could I forget one of the most entertaining things of this game?  Years after Mirrors Edge came out i've been trying to scratch a very unbearable itch mainly because that game left me with wanting more of it, and since Dice is lazy with making the 2nd game, I kept hearing about this game and it has free running properties, thankfully it's done correct.  It doesn't feel like a mess, it feels very fluid, except for when you start off when you trip over every thing you see and grab onto, but it keeps you on your toes when you are being chased by the Volatiles.
Progression/level up: Progressing with your level in this game is pretty good, there are 3 types of levels.  Survivor, Agility, and Power, and each is leveled up based off of what you do.  Survivor is for helping people out with quests, getting air drops and giving them to the quarter master for some experience, or exploring and helping people in need.  Agility is for parkouring around the place, the longer/more deadly the jump, the more points you get from it, meaning the more dangerous things you do the more point you'll get from it.  Power is what you do to hurt biters, can be throwing stars, your own melee weapons, guns, traps, anything, even just smacking the zombie with your fist will get you points for it.
Day and night Cycle: people complain about the Day and Night cycle because it isn't introduced at first, which it isn't, but I think that's a good thing, I don't want to roam around at night not knowing what's gonna happen.  After a few missions it introduces you to the day and night cycle and it works correctly, plus all of your Power and Agility points are doubled at night since it's so risky to go out.
CONS:
THE F#%KING SUICIDERS: I hate these damn zombies the most, not only are they a pain to get away from, they aren't obvious from the rest of the crowd.  Need a example?  I was on the bridge trying to get to the top, while walking on the bridge and going through the zombies, there was one with his back turned, I figured "Ah why not" I hit him, BOOM, dead.  Turns out it was a stupid suicider zombie, but THEY ARENT OBVIOUS ENOUGH.  They blend in with the common infected so well it just starts to get annoying, like if you're in a battle with lots of zombies and they are blocking your path and you have to kill them, and then a suicider just waltzs in behind them and you hit him you just screwed yourself because of it.  I'm not saying they should get taken out, i'm saying I wish they were more obvious to see and identify.
The grappling hook: This isn't a con becuase I don't like it, it works great, but it's Kyle when he uses it.  If you grapplehook to certain things Kyle I guess goes artard for a moment and doesn't want to grab onto whatever I aimed it at.  Like one time I aimed up near a building roof and hooked at the edge, but instead of grabbing onto said edge and climbing up he just decided he wasn't even going to try and grab it, and then just fell and broke his legs.  Good going Kyle, a%#$ole.

This game is amazing in its simple controlling and yet solid gameplay. For a game that I understand was ported from tablet, this one really surprises me. I can understand the somewhat easy control interface for that reason, but how the game depicts the conflict of Vietnam really captures it from what I know about that conflict.
In the game you control the air cavalry in what I suppose is some part of the Ia Drang valley campaign, the one depicted in the movie "We were soldiers". While the movie focuses on the actual battle of Ia Drang, the game has the air cavalry, the year 1965 and the location in common with the movie, but the game is more about how the conflict turned out overall for the US troops in Vietnam, so the VC or NVA units don't attack your units in the way that happend in the battle. Instead this is about winning over the villages on the countryside through operations in their vicinity, wich can be different things.
To your help you have a set of US units, mainly infantry, and of course choppers, and it while either be that you haul troops around in choppers, station them to patrol some area and use the choppers to re-supply them, or a combination of both. Your force can be bolstered if you have enough political support, and you can choose yourself what kind of reinforcements it's going to be.
About the gameplay, drawbacks are that whatever game you start, it will be the same basic objectives, and although the map changes between games and differ alot, the main gameplay will follow certain principles, wich can become somewhat repetitive. Having an ability to assign a chopper to auto re-supply a certain unit f.x. would help here.
Now, the positives on the other hand is how this game plays out, because despite some moments can feel repetitive from time to time, the way VC and NVA troops spawn, how they decide to move, and your (in-)ability to find them will make every game feel like you always need to stretch out, always need that extra unit, and that you never can be really sure where the next Charlie will appear. The VC had vast tunnel complexes running below ground in the regions where they were active, and that's how it works here. In some areas the units surface and heads for their objective, and spotting them and pin-pointing the origin area is more than tricky. I've had numerous games where at the end of the game I've seen that spawn points have been close to my base, while other games I've been running around all over trying to get a decent fix.
Once an area (probably) is located you can deal with it it different ways as well, either use Special Forces to scout and then air-/artillerystrike whatever shows up, or just post infantry to ambush them. Taking out units will give political points wich is needed to recruit new units or reinforce old ones, so if you're successful in tracking down and taking out Charlie you'll have a smoother ride. If you're not finding anyone, political points are used slightly for moving around, so then you'll sooner or later be on a tightrope, and just sitting still will allow the VC to fully influence the villages wich will make you lose.
So that balance, and the need to actually track down VC and NVA units and destroy them to be able to continue running your campaign, that is what makes this game replayable. Nothing about what's going to happend is set in stone, no matter what the map will look like, and how you did it last time around. If you're lucky, then early on you manage to build and FO on top of a spawn area, otherwise keep looking, and beware of mines while doing it.
For anyone interested in the Vietnam war, this is a good purchase I'd say.

Never has a game given me such conflicted feelings. In many ways MIRROR’S EDGE is a great game, but in a few, significant others, it sucks big time. Firstly, it’s yet another buggy, console port, which is becoming par for the course, sadly, for us PC gamers. Despite this, however, the visuals are good apart from the character models, which are below normal PC game standards. But the most important aspect of the game is the gameplay. When you’re free-running through the city it’s a true joy to play. The recreation of parkour techniques is remarkable and DICE have created a truly immersive experience. But then you’re forced to fight, and that’s where the game fails miserably. The combat in this game is the worst I’ve ever encountered. It’s so bad at times that there isn’t room in a short review to detail the failings, suffice it to say it’s maddening, especially when you’re forced to replay a particularly tricky section because you have insufficient control of Faith when in combat, or because she transforms from a nimble athlete into a trudging hippo as soon as she picks up a gun. And yet, even though I wanted to throw my PC out the window many times while playing ME, I’m so glad I stuck with it because, at it’s best MIRROR’S EDGE is an inspired example of what computer gaming can offer.

Kane and Lynch is indeed made by the same guys who made Hitman series (they even let you know of that in the intro). One day, someone thought "Guys, we be makin dem stealth games but what if... a shooter?" and so the Kane and Lynch happened.
Kane (the protagonist) is an ex-mercenary. We meet him in a prison van that is taking him to (hehe what a plot twist) the prison where he will get fried for being a baddie hired gun. His thoughts revolve around his wife and daughter, both of which he abandoned and now he regrets it (good timing, bro).
In the same van we meet Lynch, pretty much a psycho who killed his wife during one of his "blackouts" as he calls them.
Then suddenly BAM BOOM KAPOW RATATA SOME MASKED GUYS ATTACK THE CONVOY AND GRAB KANE AND LYNCH WITH THEM AND OH GOD EVERYONE SHOOTS EVERYONE, COPS DROP LIKE FLIES, WHAT A FUKKEN CHAOS, JESUS CHRIST ALMIGHTY. Turns out that they were hired by some super top secret criminal organisation which Kane stole loadsamoney from in the past and now they make him get the money back.
Lynch is freed because Kane needs a sidekick and who would make a better sidekick than a psychopath?
Long story short: they set on an adventure to retrieve the money for the crime syndicate, making friends and enemies on their way. However, Kane faces a personal tragedy by the hands of the criminal people and that makes him upset enough to actually shift his focus on killing them instead of killing cops, Japs, and Jap cops as he did by that point. He then goes to South America and whoops their criminal a$$es. Lynch is with him all the time and he fuks shít up because he's a psycho.
Kane and Lynch then shoot the criminal men. The end.
If you ever played any Hitman game I think you can agree that shooting wasn't really the strong point of the series. It didn't matter, Hitman is about stealth anyway. Here however their lack of experience shows (well in 2003 they made this shooter called Freedom Fighters, it was rather good, you can look it up). It's not bad, aight? Not very good but not bad either. I had a feeling like weapons don't generally deal much damage and are very inaccurate.
When you get downed one of your mates can inject one marijuana into your eyeball to revive you, but once he does that, you cannot get revived for again some time because otherwise you overdose and die. Sounds fun and all but when you get injected and then get shot down quickly afterwards, instead of immidiately dying, you have to wait for a guy to come to give you another marijuana shot which kills you. WHY CAN'T I IMMIDIATELY DIE INSTEAD?!?!?!?! This works both ways. Sometimes your mates get knocked out too and you have to give them the medical weed, otherwise they die and it's game over.
You can give your men simple commands like "stay here", "follow me", "go there", "attack that nígga", etc. I generally didn't use them but sometimes they came in handy.
Kane and Lynch: Dead Men™ is not the best game I have ever played. It is above average, I'd say. However, despite some very questionable design choices both gameplay and plot wise, I enjoyed this title. The game looks pretty ok to me even today. The story reminds me the action movies starring Bruce Willis or some shít like that. It was really neat.

What an ENORMOUS game! My whole family (5,8,30-something, and 30-something-else) has a blast tromping around Manhattan as several of our favorite comic book heroes (but let's be honest, it's mostly Lego Iron Man).
There are some rough edges as with a lot of the recent Lego titles, which all feel like they were inflated in size and then not properly quality-controlled. The most glaring problems with this one are the co-op experience (which feels like it was not properly play-tested as one player's actions frequently interrupt what the other player is trying to accomplish), and the racing missions.
Fortunately, the co-op issues can be helped A LOT by disabling the dynamic screen-splitting and opting for the more reliable static-split-screen. And a little bit of IRL communication goes a long way toward alleviating these frustrations as well, so I guess it makes for a good learning experience for the young ones as well as those of us who are old enough that we should know better.
Unfortunately, the only solution for the dodgy racing mechanics (and underlying HORRIBLE vehicle controls) is to find some deep well of patience inside yourself... or perhaps cultivating the ability to accept that you don't need all the gold bricks to be a happy, well-adjusted person.
Still, the game-breaking bugs are few (especially compared to Lego Batman 3, which we have abandoned as unplayable, at least on the PS3), and the fun-factor is definitely worth the bumps in the road.
Overall, recommended at $15 or less... at least until there's a proper Lego Iron Man game.

Hello, avid tcg player here who has played almost every card game to date intensively and at top level. Here is my verdict for Shadowverse after having played in A+ tier every day for over 1 month.
First of all, I am writing this review because I feel that Shadowverse is extremely overrated. You can tell by other reviews that the people reviewing it have either barely played it OR do not have full knowledge of all the existing card games out there, how much luck is involved in them vs requiring actual strategy, and how stale the gameplay is at top tier level (meaning the amount of viable decks that you can play with + cards which you can tech into them). I feel like a lot of people are giving this game too much credit due to the seemingly generous introduction which the game offers, giving you 40 packs right off the bat. The negatives are also not noticeable at low tier ranked games (B and below), so everything seems great right? To be fair, I would've written a positive review for this game aswell early on. But I stuck around for the long haul, and boy am I disappointed with it. The following bit will cover the key parts of the gameplay which makes me give this game a negative review.
So there are some stat nerds who just love to throw "but going first had 60% win rate before the changes, it's much better now!" in your face when you state this fact, but what they do not realize is that Darkness Evolved introduced a bunch of cards which made going second on par for every leader with going first already tempo/combo wise. Not only that; it also opened up new combos with the base cards which makes those super aggro decks not viable to play at all now @top tier. This set was either barely released or yet to be released when the 60% win rate for going first was determined, when Cygames made these changes which now heavily benefits the person going second. Here are the advantages for going second:
-You draw an extra card
-You get 1 more evolution orb (crucial for turning the game around)
-You get to evolve first (this is the gamebreaking part)
But that's not all. I mentioned that this game is very stale when it comes to strategic options. For anything other than super aggro *go straight for the leader* deck builds, there are barely any cards in most top tier constructed decks which let you make full use of your play points every turn, which is vital for going first. That crucial turnaround extra evolution which the player going second gets turns into a flat out advtantage already if there is nothing to turn around. As an example of a game phase, it's going to be very hard as the player going first already if you don't start with a 1 point cost card @turn 1.
And not only that, the advantages of going first also get negated by plenty of instant impact cards (which do something the turn that you play them) and turn the match into player going 2nd's favour early on already. Few examples are:
-Elf Child May (cost 1, does 1 damage to opponent follower, 1/1 field presence, forest)
-Sylvan Strike (cost 2, deal 2 damage to opponent follower, put 1/1 fairy in hand, forest)
-Whole-Souled Swing (cost 2, deal 2 damage to opponent follower, spawn 1/1 knight on field if you have less creatures on field than opponent when playing this card - this is always the case when going 2nd and playing vs aggro, sword)
-Magic Missile (cost 2, deal 1 damage and draw a card, rune)
-Kaleido (cost 2, return a 2 point cost or less card to the owners hand and draw a card, rune)
-Fire Lizard (cost 2, deal 1 damage to opponent follower, 2/1 field presence, dragon)
-Blazing Breath (cost 1, deal 2 damage to opponent follower, dragon)
-Angelic Barrage (cost 3, deal 1 damage to all opponent followers, all decks)
Cards like these will prevent player 1 from having any kind of advantage, since there is a severe lack of instant impact early game (turn 1-4) cards available right now. Quickblade (sword) is ok but can be dealt with too easily, Wolf works well due to the nature of the deck that it is used in + stats of other cards (hope and pray for no Angelic Barrage if all field presence = 1 defence), and Pinion/Aria's amulet status + a countdown reduction card like Dogma allows for a strong start if you're not playing vs Runecraft like:
Normally, if opponent decides to take out all of your creatures with theirs, you'll have 1-2 remaining on the field by the end of turn 3 and maybe did a few points of damage to them. But then they get to evolve and put up one of those 4 cost power cards; a strong creature like Floral or Bishop. This curve suits 2nd player too perfectly with the play points vs cost of those cards, and being in a situation where you can use them since evolved creatures have Rush (can attack opponent creature on the same turn). The only cards for player going first which can deal with this evolved creature on turn 5 = Dance of Death, Demonic Strike, Will of the Forest (forest leader only), 2 storm cards (gives opponent 2 for 1 value though), + a few more 3+ insta damage cards. Almost none of these cards are used x3 in any deck so the odds of you having them in your hand at that moment = low. So, you will likely be forced into evolving one of your own creatures to take it out because your opponent will likely be able to retain field control + do damage every turn and finish the game at turn 7-8 if you don't.
Atm, the complete opposite goes for player going first if they also have such cards in their hand. They either have to waste a turn if they don't have anything else in their hand which they can play (remember they have 1 card less, so less to pick from) OR play a card like Fire Lizard/Healing Angel without being able to make use of its effect (no creature on opponents field, no use for healing early on since your opponent hasn't started to damage you yet and is focusing on keeping their life as high as possible + trying to keep field control equal until they can activate advantage of their evo power card which the game is currently offering by letting them evolve first). All power evolve cards cost 4 or 3 points though, so you will likely waste 1 play point here (having a 1 cost card to fill it up with at this point woudn't even be desired) aka it won't be a perfect curve.
Storm/insta damage cards let you sort of bypass this because they'll atleast do some damage to your opponent before being removed, which lets you work towards barely getting your opponents life down to 0 which will likely cost you all of your cards to do so aswell, and then rip if opponent has sufficient heals or throws up a ward if you only have a storm card left in your hand. And that is why Bloodcraft is currently the only succesful deck which can still manage to go first without being gimped under these circumstances.
Past the mid point of the game, there is only one thing you can hope for if the early game hasn't been in your advantage: You drawing into those big late gameish gold/legendary cards while your opponent draws into weak (at that stage of the game) early game cards which don't provide enough resistance or damage to deal with said gold/legendary cards. If it doesn't happen then you just flat out lose. So basically that comes down to pure luck, which is too big a factor in the game atm. There is less luck involved with Poker than with this game right now; and you know that a tcg is bad when that is the case. Tcgs should always have more strategy involved than with Poker, which is known as the game where luck matters most. So the Shadowverse "About this game" description stating that this is the most tactically rich CCG on the market is just a big lie.

It's difficult to say whether Batman: Arkham Knight is better than Arkham City. Traversal via gliding and grappling has been made easier to use, whether diving smoothly off a rooftop or shooting up the side of an entire building. Combat has been basically perfected and the player has more options than ever, and additions like environmental takedowns and being able to strike enemies on the ground are essential improvements. The graphics are gorgeous and Gotham City is larger and nicer to look at than ever before. Strategies for Predator encounters have been expanded. The voice acting is mostly on point. However, while the game has a lot to offer and everything looks good on paper, certain aspects will be a mixed bag for some. The story is a more psychological and personal one, which I appreciated, but the central twist of the game could be seen from a mile away and interesting ideas were wrapped up quickly without expanding on their full potential. Some of the boss battles were disappointing to me, with one being an exact replica of an earlier confrontation. The Batmobile is used in some exciting ways, and driving is fun for the most part, but the standard version is a little too slow, in my opinion, and things can get tedious after the twenty or thirtieth tank battle. If you've liked the other Arkham games, you will definitely like this one, and for some, it might be the ultimate Batman experience. For others, the total package might just miss the mark, but just barely.

How does one rave about one of their all time favorite games without sounding like a raving lunatic?
Look, there are 4 (sorta) Thief games.  If each of them gets 10 points (so a total of 40) and you break it up here's the ranking:
Theif II: The Metal Age 50/10
Thief: The Dark Project (Gold) 10/10
Thief: Deadly Shadows 5/10
Thief -25/10
But that includes 3 stories for another time.
I do have to mention Dark Project/Gold briefly since Thief II would not exist without it.  It really is a fine game in its own right, the best Stealth Game up to that point.  However, it still relies too much on combat (and those damnable undead). The story, however, is worth it.  Which leads to Thief II -- apparently Looking Glass Studios realized that the combat was the least favorite aspect of the game and made it so you can avoid it entirely in Thief II (if you choose).  You may get seen and want to fight your way out (or have to I suppose) and you are not entirely without resources.  However, you CAN get through it without ever swinging your blade.  That, in conjunction with the story, propelled Theif II to the top of the stealth charts for me.
Do not look for visuals that have withstood the test of time.  They are dated, but they are sufficient if you aren't a snob, and the aesthetic works perfectly.  Do not look for this if you want to run and gun through levels putting arrows into the eye sockets of every guard you see while simultaneously slicing and dicing others who happen to get to close.
DO look for an amazing stealth game with a solid story that builds from at first trying to scratch out a living to getting embroiled in events beyond your control.  DO look for secret rooms, safes, stashed of loot.  DO be patient and learn the guard's patterns.  But mostly -- DO PICK UP Thief II: The Metal Age (especially during this stealth game sale!).
One last thing -- DO NOT pick up Thief (the reboot) as it has in common with the true Thief games only the title and the name of the protagonist.  They are as different as having a fire and being on fire.

***This is an old part of the review for Resident Evil Revelations 2, look at the other bit of the review down below under this review. The general game is currently from playing the Switch version of Revelations 2***
The game is poorly optimized on average PCs, leading it to run really bad, and crash the game. It sucks a lot, because I am really excited to play this game
Grab yourself some good hardware for your PC, and you're good, it does not work on average PCs. I'm too lazy to upgrade mine.
***the updated review***
Soooooo, apparently, it turns out that the game DOES actually work; again, because my PC is pretty potato, there are some issues that happen. However, the issues are more or less unpredictable. It was able to run at a consistently smooth framerate, to make combat bearable, and the gameplay is just pretty awesome, being a heavy emphasis on survival horror as it's now trying to go for, unlike the other RE games, and even Revelations 1. However, graphical errors, such as pieces of the texture, flying everywhere, and sometimes covering my aim, can be annoying.
Unlike Revelations 1, where you can carry a large amount, yet limited amount of ammo and healing items, this game now allows you to have a proper bag space for the items to carry, from two characters. While you carry less ammo, healing items, and such, you're not restricted to carrying a certain amount of ammo in whole(example, you can carry 90 pistol bullets in total in Revelations, but you can't grab more pistol ammo, not because your inventory is full, but the amount of bullets you carry, is full. While in Revelations 2, you can carry more pistol ammo than you'd like to, it'll fill up space, and can waste spots for potentially more improtant items, which helps to make proper inventory management). With the healing items, especially herbs, you need to hold down the button to use herbs, instead of pressing the button, and healing you automatically, which gives you a bit more risk when using herbs, instead of being able to immediately use it, at the last second you get attacked, to heal before you die.
Gameplay has been changed quite a lot, compared to Revelations, and even other RE games. It still retains its survival horror elements, with a mix of action. However, in this game, the survival horror is a bigger emphasis instead, compared to Revelations 1, although not as emphasized with the survival horror to something like the original, or RE4. A new gameplay element has been added in the game; the ability to crouch. The crouch ability gives the player the ability to sneak this time, which in other Resident Evil games, you're not really able to sneak or crouch. This does allow the player to try to sneak past by an enemy, or sneak attack them. A kind of an interesting addition in the series, which can allow you to try to safely sneak by an enemy, whether to kill them or not, should you want to save ammo, without wasting ammo on shooting the unsuspecting enemy that can easily be killed with a stealth attack... unless that enemy is only able to take heavy damage from the attack, instead of being killed instantly, so caution is still needed.
The gun stats customization returns in this game from Revelations 1, allowing you to improve the stats of the weapon of your choice, in campaign, and in Raid Mode.

Arkham Knight launched with some technical difficulties, but they seem to have been ironed out now - I got excellent performance on a moderate machine.  This explains the mixed reviews - as far as I can tell, everyone who bought it before the fix gave the game a big thumbs down, but everyone after got a game that works, and is very good.
If you played any of the previous Arkham series, you know what to expect - this game is more of the same, at the same high quality (not counting Origins here).  If not, go play through them - they're superb, and although Arkham Knight works on its own, you'll get more out of playing the series in order.  There are a few additions in this instalment which don't change a lot, plus the Batmobile which is not great due to clunky controls, although not as bad as people seem to be making out if you switch to KB+M for battle sections.  Aside from that, there are a few new enemy abilities in Predator and Combat, a big pile of maps and challenges, and some pretty cool set pieces, making the gameplay the best in the series yet, but it's in terms of polish rather than adding anything fundamentally new.
However, the narrative here is just superb.  I'm not one to go for story in games but this one is a really excellent conclusion.  Touching, psychological drama fertile for interpretation, describing Bruce/Batman's final character arc with themes of family, abandonment, identity, and redemption.  This game gives a purpose to telling the Batman story far beyond the cool gadgets and gravelly one-liners.  Add the same superb quality of direction and acting of the previous games and you have a truly great game.

I am overall satisfied with this game although a few things did bother me.
Bad things:
- I felt the different types of zombies aren't realistic and aren't even original. They reminded me a lot of the zombies in "Last of Us" almost like exact replications.
- The crafting system, although cool looking, was somewhat mediocre. I didn't find that I could get too creative aside from adding electricity/fire to the weapons.
- No fast travel. One of my biggest complaints in open world games are when missions take you back and forth between the different ends of the map; especially when you can't fast travel or use a vehicle. It would be nice to travel from safe house to safe house, or keep missions in the general area so you aren't constantly trekking across the map.
- The open world map size didn't impress me, I love maps that are huge and unique throughout. Instead they gave us a mediocre size and the same buildings, this is obviously to save time and work for designers but in reality, buildings don't all look the  same.
- I would have liked it to be a little less combat oriented and a little more survival based. When buying the game, I expected to have to scavenge every building, but actually you didn't. You easily bought weapons or just found good ones from killing enemies. They could have made food more important, sleep a factor, and it necessary to search every house or building like it would be in reality.
Good Things:
- A good story filled with lots of emotion. I know I got attached to some characters and couldn't help but feel emotional during parts of the story. I loved that they did this!
- Graphics!!! They did an excellent job with the way it looked! I loved seeing the lake and the buildings even when standing on towers and looking out, you could see everything!!
- Combat, even though I wish it were less, the combat was amazing. I got such a satisfaction over throwing molotovs at zombies and watching them burn or just running up and slice and dicing them.
- I loved the leveling up system and the three tiered XP points, however I wish some of the skills were more useful than they seemed.
- Hours of fun!!!!
Overall, I had some complaints but minor at best. The game was done to completion and I didn't run into many bugs. It provided me with hours of entertainment and still does. Although I wasn't thrilled with the multiplayer part of the game, it's easily turned off so other players don't interrupt your game. Overall, I would definitely recommend getting this game!!!!

Never has a game given me such conflicted feelings. In many ways MIRROR’S EDGE is a great game, but in a few, significant others, it sucks big time. Firstly, it’s yet another buggy, console port, which is becoming par for the course, sadly, for us PC gamers. Despite this, however, the visuals are good apart from the character models, which are below normal PC game standards. But the most important aspect of the game is the gameplay. When you’re free-running through the city it’s a true joy to play. The recreation of parkour techniques is remarkable and DICE have created a truly immersive experience. But then you’re forced to fight, and that’s where the game fails miserably. The combat in this game is the worst I’ve ever encountered. It’s so bad at times that there isn’t room in a short review to detail the failings, suffice it to say it’s maddening, especially when you’re forced to replay a particularly tricky section because you have insufficient control of Faith when in combat, or because she transforms from a nimble athlete into a trudging hippo as soon as she picks up a gun. And yet, even though I wanted to throw my PC out the window many times while playing ME, I’m so glad I stuck with it because, at it’s best MIRROR’S EDGE is an inspired example of what computer gaming can offer.

Vietnam '65 puts you in the strategic seat of a U.S. commander trying to sort out the political and military wasps nest that is the local Vietnam village front. It is touted as a casual game for the milhist strategy player, and this is both correct and wrong.
It's certainly casual in the sense that it does not crunch numbers beyond a simple fight success percentage that is equal for all units, and there aren't many different units you can play( a simple division of infantry-specforces-engineer-gunship-tank etc. is more or less what you have to work with).
The atmosphere is really above par, with decent graphics and  good( if sometimes corny) voice acting and sound effects ramping up the sense of paranoia and urgency that a good Vietnam game should have IMO. The AI and game design keep you on your toes, as both viet cong and NVA units harass you while rarely meeting you head on.
There are some glaring problems, such as the logistics system. Unless you have a mind for numbers and a good memory, you will lose both infantry and helicopter units to food/fuel attrition, and since new units are expensive and money hard to get, a simple misclick or forgetful moment can cost you the game.
Also, the way your units interact logistically isn't as intuitive as it could be. Your APC run out of fuel? Dropping fuel on it won't replenish it, so unless you somehow figure out that you must drive an engineer out to it with a refuel action, you're stone out of luck. Do your forward bases replenish your units, or can only the firebase help you out? Such things should be evident without poring through a manual, but, sadly, they are not.
That said, the concept of mid-level strategic leadership in the Vietnam conflict is novel, and having to push your units to the limit to get kills, which in turn grants you political influence, which in turns help you buy new units to eventually win the game on a time limit - is both exhilarating and challenging.
It's a good little game, and one I still revisit on ocassion, but not as great as it could be with a more user friendly interface and design. I dream of a Vietnam '65 with the kinks ironed out and more units, for one!

What an ENORMOUS game! My whole family (5,8,30-something, and 30-something-else) has a blast tromping around Manhattan as several of our favorite comic book heroes (but let's be honest, it's mostly Lego Iron Man).
There are some rough edges as with a lot of the recent Lego titles, which all feel like they were inflated in size and then not properly quality-controlled. The most glaring problems with this one are the co-op experience (which feels like it was not properly play-tested as one player's actions frequently interrupt what the other player is trying to accomplish), and the racing missions.
Fortunately, the co-op issues can be helped A LOT by disabling the dynamic screen-splitting and opting for the more reliable static-split-screen. And a little bit of IRL communication goes a long way toward alleviating these frustrations as well, so I guess it makes for a good learning experience for the young ones as well as those of us who are old enough that we should know better.
Unfortunately, the only solution for the dodgy racing mechanics (and underlying HORRIBLE vehicle controls) is to find some deep well of patience inside yourself... or perhaps cultivating the ability to accept that you don't need all the gold bricks to be a happy, well-adjusted person.
Still, the game-breaking bugs are few (especially compared to Lego Batman 3, which we have abandoned as unplayable, at least on the PS3), and the fun-factor is definitely worth the bumps in the road.
Overall, recommended at $15 or less... at least until there's a proper Lego Iron Man game.

Antichamber is a mind-bending puzzler. The closest I can get is "it's like Portal but while tripping on at least 3 different drugs." It defies description. Don't spoil it for yourself, don't watch Let's Plays, don't ask for help, just get it and go. Beat it in one sitting if you can; it's better that way, and assuming you don't go for 100% completion (if there even is such a thing) then it only takes about 4 hours.
While some parts of the game can be a pain and some parts will cause headaches, there are only a few puzzles that you *MUST* complete to progress through the game. That said, the more you skip, the harder the remaining puzzles will be.
The first time I played it was a spiritual experience. I enjoyed watching some friends struggle through the asinine challenges and watched their minds repeatedly blown. It's a brilliant exercise in thinking so far outside of the box that you escape the bounds of reality and end up back inside the box.
And here's a hint: Pay very careful attention. Move slowly and take your time - you'll spot the solutions much more quickly.

These are the voyages of the starship Kestrel, its five minute mission: To explore strange new worlds, to seek out new life and exterminate it, to boldly go anywhere but the place where you just died.
If you are the type of life form who enjoys watching space opera - from Star Trek to Stargate, Firefly to Farscape - and have always wanted to command your own crew of expendable redshirts, FTL is the game for you. With randomly generated encounters and probability-based outcomes, not to mention a wide variety of ships, crews and equipment each with unique playing styles, FTL will give you hours of fun. 317 hours and counting, in my case.
Although some say the game is too difficult - and it certainly is difficult the first dozen or so attempts, with so many random encounters to thwart you - if you play long enough you will grow accustomed the numerous encounters and the focus of gameplay shifts more towards the combat system. Thankfully this is equally entertaining.
The only real criticism of FTL is the lack of DLC - and this from a devout anti-DLC zealot. Adding in new encounters, new ships, new equipment and new races would be a very simple way of increasing the amount of enjoyment to be had from FTL, and something very much worth paying for, yet the developer appears to have focussed their business model on an (admittedly impressive) array of merchandise instead.
Easily worth the standard $10 price tag; I picked it up on sale for half that and still feel rather guilty.
EDIT: And then they released some excellent DLC containing everything I suggested and more. For free.

Arkham Knight launched with some technical difficulties, but they seem to have been ironed out now - I got excellent performance on a moderate machine.  This explains the mixed reviews - as far as I can tell, everyone who bought it before the fix gave the game a big thumbs down, but everyone after got a game that works, and is very good.
If you played any of the previous Arkham series, you know what to expect - this game is more of the same, at the same high quality (not counting Origins here).  If not, go play through them - they're superb, and although Arkham Knight works on its own, you'll get more out of playing the series in order.  There are a few additions in this instalment which don't change a lot, plus the Batmobile which is not great due to clunky controls, although not as bad as people seem to be making out if you switch to KB+M for battle sections.  Aside from that, there are a few new enemy abilities in Predator and Combat, a big pile of maps and challenges, and some pretty cool set pieces, making the gameplay the best in the series yet, but it's in terms of polish rather than adding anything fundamentally new.
However, the narrative here is just superb.  I'm not one to go for story in games but this one is a really excellent conclusion.  Touching, psychological drama fertile for interpretation, describing Bruce/Batman's final character arc with themes of family, abandonment, identity, and redemption.  This game gives a purpose to telling the Batman story far beyond the cool gadgets and gravelly one-liners.  Add the same superb quality of direction and acting of the previous games and you have a truly great game.

Yes, it's good. It's damn good. It's very damn good. It's so damn good, you might as well spend your money on this immediately. Half-Life 2 does everything right that Half-Life does... and then goes even further, doing an even more fantastic job with its story. The graphics and level-design are both very aesthetically pleasing, and the actors all do their job very well (Though the best voice actor would definitely have to be Dr. Freeman's. Very excellent job). And the story, like it's predecessor, tells it completely through animations and no cutscenes to be found, giving the game a nice steady flow. The game also has a great atmosphere. It can feel hopeless, empowering, and frightening at appropriate times. And the world that is created outside of Black Mesa labs is well shown and characterized, to be a very believable place.
Honestly, I only have two very small qualms with this game and that would be the loading screens and occaisional glitches. I never found an actual in-game glitch in graphics or animation, but rarely the sound would cut out of a random NPC's dialogue. And for a game that flows so well, the loading screen for the next section of a level can bring all that build-up to a halt. But these are only minor problems, that didn't take away all that much from how great the game is. Half-Life 2 is definitely one of the best video games I've ever played, and I can guarantee it'll be one of the best games you'll ever play as well. I cannot recommend this game enough.

I am overall satisfied with this game although a few things did bother me.
Bad things:
- I felt the different types of zombies aren't realistic and aren't even original. They reminded me a lot of the zombies in "Last of Us" almost like exact replications.
- The crafting system, although cool looking, was somewhat mediocre. I didn't find that I could get too creative aside from adding electricity/fire to the weapons.
- No fast travel. One of my biggest complaints in open world games are when missions take you back and forth between the different ends of the map; especially when you can't fast travel or use a vehicle. It would be nice to travel from safe house to safe house, or keep missions in the general area so you aren't constantly trekking across the map.
- The open world map size didn't impress me, I love maps that are huge and unique throughout. Instead they gave us a mediocre size and the same buildings, this is obviously to save time and work for designers but in reality, buildings don't all look the  same.
- I would have liked it to be a little less combat oriented and a little more survival based. When buying the game, I expected to have to scavenge every building, but actually you didn't. You easily bought weapons or just found good ones from killing enemies. They could have made food more important, sleep a factor, and it necessary to search every house or building like it would be in reality.
Good Things:
- A good story filled with lots of emotion. I know I got attached to some characters and couldn't help but feel emotional during parts of the story. I loved that they did this!
- Graphics!!! They did an excellent job with the way it looked! I loved seeing the lake and the buildings even when standing on towers and looking out, you could see everything!!
- Combat, even though I wish it were less, the combat was amazing. I got such a satisfaction over throwing molotovs at zombies and watching them burn or just running up and slice and dicing them.
- I loved the leveling up system and the three tiered XP points, however I wish some of the skills were more useful than they seemed.
- Hours of fun!!!!
Overall, I had some complaints but minor at best. The game was done to completion and I didn't run into many bugs. It provided me with hours of entertainment and still does. Although I wasn't thrilled with the multiplayer part of the game, it's easily turned off so other players don't interrupt your game. Overall, I would definitely recommend getting this game!!!!

I studied history for years, spent days worth of time studying countless books and documentaries looking to find something meaningful in the past.
And then I found Civ 5.
I started as France. I never thought the French would be my choice, but with my mods refusing to work I couldn't play as something from something else. So France it was.
I gave my warriors spears, my settlers began beautiful cities. We marched upon the sunset with hope in our hearts, ready to crush any that were foolish enough to stand in our way.
And then, I found progress.
You know them as trebuchets. A beautifully simple weapon of war. I built my first, sieging my first city-state to build another illustrious city in the name of France. In the name of progress. But one trebuchet wasn't enough. Soon I'd built five, and not even that was enough.
Ten. Ten trebuchets. Ten glorious monuments to progress. Cities fell, farms burned, rulers ran away to nearly abandoned towns because their capitals were in ruins. All in the name of progress.
Gandhi with his "peace" and his nuclear weapons tried to stop me. But progress stops for no single man, or no single nation. India fell, her missiles sitting dormant in empty silos. All in the name of progress. I built planes, tanks, submarines. And yet, every city fell to trebuchets. Scores of them moving in perfect formation. China fell, Russia burned, America left to rot in a few tiles because they tried to take New Calais. Korea was but a husk of it's former glory, scientific projects long abandoned to preserve their own lives.
All in the name of progress.
And here we are. Giant death robots stand guard over Paris. XCOM units patrol the wastelands, annihilating barbarian tribes and hunting down the last remnants of my foes as the great French flag flies over scorched earth. The gods themselves quake in fear of missiles fired into the heavens. I stand alone on this wretched ball of dirt and stone, alone except for the leftovers of once great civilizations. My men grow restless from lack of hostile forces. No greater threat looms over our horizons, for we are the greatest threat of all.
All in the name of progress.
9/10 not enough aliens.

Lemme give it to y'all straight, who are on the fence;
- Yes, the game is very much worth it at full price.
- One of the first games in a long while, that has kept me up until 5 A.M. in the morning, because of how lost I get myself into it.
- Doesn't do dumb jump scares, save for a VERY FEW TIMES, and each one counted.
- The game is maybe one of the best zombie based games out there, so long as you do enjoy it with action.
- Parkour in the game is AMAZING. Sometimes I like just playing the game, so I can run
around, across roof tops, and attacking zombies while talking to friends.
- Co-op in story mode. Freaking amazing. No dumb lobby. Just click 'Join game' and bam,
you'll be thrown a few feet away from a friend without them sometimes even noticing you joined!
- Single play and Co-op have a huge impact; co-op feels fun, slightly safer, and adds a lot in the form of friendly rivals! Single player feels way more tense and everything you do counts, making you second guess some choices, for fear or death. Night time in either mode is fun as heck, though four co-op makes it pretty easy.
- Night and Day feel almost like two different modes. In the day, zombies shuffle around, falling off rooftops, being dumb, easy to avoid and kill. Night time? Get those UV Flares ready, and be ready to flee if they catch sight of you.
- Even after beating the story, I keep coming back for more, as it's super fun.
- Took me around 30 hours to do the story, which also included only HALF of the side missions. Still got a little over 50% left to go, and looking forward to it!
TL;DR - Get the game, find friends to play with, enjoy the hell out of one of the few games worth it at full price.

I'm going to use the dreaded word "underrated" to describe this game, because it is. It's 1:25am, I've just finished the game, and it does NOT deserve the hatred it got.
Graphics: 8/10
For 2007, I really can't fault it, the graphical settings are nothing special and the hair looks a little silly, but it's competent.
Style: 7/10
I'd give this a higher score but the awesome style is not used enough. For instance, a certain character dies and the screen goes into a frenzy as the protagonist does, but this only happens ONCE. Too much good stuff underused.
Story: 10/10
Here is where it shines. Kane and Lynch are possibly the most abhorrent, frustrating, aggressive and irresponsible protagonists in a game, yet I wanted them to succeed, I pushed for them to be better people and that's what emotionally affects you. These people are irredeemable, and they are in denial, and so are you. The story is a little cliche at times, but it touched my small, bullet-riddled heart, and I loved it, I forgive the game for all of it's flaws just for this and the characters. Although, it shouldn't really be called 'Kane & Lynch'. 'Kane & Friends' is more accurate.
Gameplay: 5/10
Here we go... The AI is frustrating, the gun mechanics are clunky and sometimes unresponsive, there are clipping issues galore and some enemies are too infuriating, even on easy, that's not being bad at gaming, that's developers screwing you over.
HOWEVER, this game is worth playing through to the end for the story and, while it may be an unpopular opinion, this game is great. Now I'm off to play K&L2, ta-ta!

Do you like board-game aesthetics?  Do you enjoy on rail games (sort of?)?  How bout Collectible Card Games that don't involve trading?  How bout Diablo?  If you said yes to any of those questions, you might be an ARPG addict like myself.  Enter Book of Demons, the 12-step program to itch that scratch for ARPG gameplay without the managing of eight million different skillsets, crafting all sorts of fun nonsense, and distill it into the most Southern distilled alcohol without the alcohol!
Pros:
+ The paper-y graphics are a really nice touch and makes the game stand out from ANY other ARPG out there astounding to be what Diablo III couldn't be
+ the card part of the gameplay (collecting/customizing what's on your belt/skills) is pretty cool.  I enjoy being able to collect cards and upgrade them as time goes on per dungeon and going back to town
+ the voice acting is actually pretty superb.  Nothing sounds overdramatic; all the characters so far have their own stories to tell and listening to them is less of a chore than most ARPGs
+ the actual dungeon crawling is... repetitive, yes.  But ARPGs past will tell you that dungeon crawling is repetitive anyway
+ Let's say... unique controller setup.  The left thumbstick moves you around the dungeon and your right thumbstick allows you to pick up items, target enemies and the like.  Overall not a bad button scheme for the controller
Cons:
- the actual roleplaying part of the game is out of touch just a bit.  Yes, the cards you place on your person do influence your character but as far as that goes that's it
- limited character customization to literally just your name (it's not a deal breaker but it does put me out of touch with the character a little)
- Male/female genders per character aren't a thing.  Doesn't bug me that much but it might some
- the "on rails" system may bother some people but this IS a distilled version of Diablo/most ARPGs so it's not THAT big of a con
666/666: would definitely kill demons from hell in any format again... and again... and again... and again.  And again.
Definetely a game that's worth buying, lots of items, characters, easy to setup multiplayer and artifacts that make the game a tiny bit different and interesting with each new one you unlock. 10/10

I enjoyed Kane and Lynch 2: Dog Days a lot, and bought the first game a few years after that.
I must say, I enjoyed the first game too, but I think that it's too short, and quite annoying at some places. The AI companions can't take cover properly, and they can't revive each other if they are downed - you must revive them yourself.
There's no reload button, the character reloads automatically. Which means, that sometimes he starts reloading when you are just about to jump out of cover to shoot. Or, he won't start reloading and you jump on enemies from behind with almost empty mag.
Cover system is similar to Mass Effect 1 - when you approach an obstacle, the character will take cover automatically.
I've only had slight problems with this, and that the camera angles from cover are very badly synced with your aim. Most of the time when I peak out of cover, the shots are hitting the wall which I was taking cover at.
Atmosphere is good, the game has the exact feel - dark, criminal, unfortunate. I don't like Kane, he's both uninteresting and makes wrong decisions. Also constantly refuses Lynch's suggestions, then he pays for it.
Had no technical problems, apart from wrong installation - I had to manually go to game's folder and install GFWL support. It also constantly ran at 60+ FPS on max details. The graphics are avarage, enviroments sometimes feel empty. Characters look good though.
Fortunately, you don't need to login to GFWL to play the game, so the presence of GFWL has no effect. Don't be afraid of it.
Overall, it's a good game, but I don't recommend it because of auto-reloading and auto-cover systems that can cause trouble. Also it's very short (4 hours), companions are dumb at certain situations, and Kane is annoying character.
The Kane and Lynch 2 is a great though, it pretty much gets rid of EVERY negative points I mentioned in this review for Kane and Lynch 1. I recommend checking the second game.

After the smash hit of LEGO Indiana Jones: The Original Adventures and the then upcoming release of Kingdom of the Crystal Skull came Lego Indiana Jones 2: The Adventure Continues:
Lego Indiana Jones 2 follows the stories of Raiders of the Lost Ark, Temple of Doom, The Last Crusade, and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull (which is the main focus), as you solve puzzles, break baddies, and build your way to victory. Although the game does redo some key levels from the first game, it mostly brings in scenes that weren't in the first Lego Indy game. With the scenes that have been done before (Like the bar fight in Raiders), it gets a new spin and is a lot different from the previous level. Whilst playing this though, it is clear that the focus was on the Kingdom levels. The three original movies are split up into five separate levels, while Kingdom has three chapters, each containing 5 levels. You have to complete the first level of the Kingdom levels to unlock Raiders. (Once you beat one movie, another unlocks (Temple unlocks after level 5 of Raiders and so on)).
There are generally four types of levels you will encounter. 1: the 'normal' Indy 1 type levels. These ones take a little longer than the rest and usually have puzzles in them. The second type is the 'kill all enemies' levels. These are really simple and take the least amount of time. All you have to do is kill the enemies it wants you to kill and you call it a day. There are usually about 3 waves. It's simple, but fun. The third type is the vehicle levels. These require you to destroy the vehicles the level tells you to. It's pretty much like the kill all enemies levels, just in vehicles. The last one is the boss fight. At the end of each chapter (except for some of the Kingdom parts), you will encounter a boss. Each boss has a certain weakness to find, and can be a lot of fun. You'll find at least one of all of those 4 level types in a chapter.
In order to play the levels though, you've gotta have characters to control. The game, like all Lego games, includes a wide varity of characters to unlock. You'll see many familiar faces from the movies on your adventures. The main character, Indy, has a whip that allows you to whip objects down, swing across dangerous areas, and even drag people around. He, like all characters, can also pick up weapons, like grenades, pistols, machine guns, spears, and many more! Also, something cool to note: you can hold more than one weapon/object (torch/shovel/etc) at a time (in your inventory, that is), unlike the previous installment! It comes in handy. You can also aim where you want the whip to go and where you want the gun to hit. (Unlike in Indy 1) Other characters include wrench characters (like Mutt Williams), who can fix objects, book characters (like Henry Jones), who can translate puzzles, shovel characters (Sallah) who can dig stuff, and many more! Characters can be purchased in hub worlds.
Yes, I said hub worlds. Each level pack has a unique hub world and more or less open world. In these worlds, you can find collectable items, vehicles to buy, minifigures, and the levels. In order to get to the next level once completing one, you have to find it. This, among other features, makes this game unique in comparison to the previous Lego games. There's lots to mess around with in the hubs!
Besides all of this, there is also a hub where you can create your own levels and mess around with blocks! This is a lot of fun and provides countless hours of fun. This is also one of the few Lego games to do this. (We have Lego Worlds right now, but still). The game also had the fantastic John Williams soundtrack from the movies and local multiplayer.
Overall, this is a fantastic and unique Lego game! It's definitely one of the most underrated Lego games.

So, why to recommend? Well, if you don't pay too much and do not expect great game, it is still relatively decent game, with some good moments, ending - although scripted - is fair and rough as you may expect for somebody dancing with devil. Should developers at least made shoot-outs more intense, gave you chance to flank enemies or force/allow you to move from position to position to get advantage it would be better game despite the flaws.

Thief 2: TMA is everything a sequel should be, and more! Though  it doesn't have the same 'horror' element that the first game had, it's still very atmospheric with an incredible ambience that will suck you in to its dark, treacherous world and it won't let go until Karras closes the doors to Soulforge, forever sealing his fate! (yeah, more on Soulforge later).
All of the original Thief gameplay mechanics are still in place w/ added features: the stealth is in full effect with deeply complex missions and large maps that allow for multiple routes to completing objectives, all the sexy arrow types you loved from the first game are back (now with vine arrows), all of your original gadgets are back (now with scouting orbs, and in rare cases explosive devices), there are new enemy types (most notably female soldiers) and of course a new antagonist (alas, Constantine is no more, but Karras is easily just as much of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥as he was, so it's cool, and there's even a ghost pirate at one point if you can find him and his glorious pirate booty....um....let me rephrase that, I mean his treasure).  Oh, and I almost forgot one of the coolest upgrades, the cinematics between missions (some play out like storyboard drawings but others are actual cinematics and there's sorta one when you die too, but obviously that's not as cool as the others).
Now back to the final mission, Sabotage at Soulforge, Karras' stronhold, his HQ, the locus of his nefarious activities, yeah you get the point.  Being a final mission you'd expect some level of challenge and complexity and Soulforge certainly doesn't disappoint. But seriously, this mission for me was so vast and complex that I spent nearly a quarter of my total game time wandering its darkened corridors with like negative 5 hitpoints at some points, all while trying to figure out where I should go next and how not to get killed by Karras' mechanoid creations. After finally beating this mission, I almost felt like I couldn't recall an earlier point in the game but Soulforge.  It was as though the entire game took place in this one hub-like area.  Mentally, I was nearly defeated by this final quest but I persevered in the end and so Karras can suck it!
If you like Thief you'll love this one just as much, if not more so.  Get it on sale when you can but as far as classics go, it's a must own even if you have to pay the full price and there is so much depth and challenge that you'll be glad you made the purchase in the end.

Following the massive success of Blizzard’s Hearthstone and the games that followed, Shadowverse is Cygames’ attempt to enter the CCG market. The game just recently hit Steam, but had already received some attention previously when it was mobile only. So just how good is Shadowverse and does it compare to the other games in the market right now?
Gameplay
Shadowverse has seven unique classes, called “crafts”. Each craft has their own hero and special ability which exist in many of their class cards. This makes the playstyle of every craft unique, and ensures that no two craft share the same roles. Shadowverse borrows some mechanics from Hearthstone, such as “mana”, and basic spell casting and minion combat remains the same. However, the key element in which Shadowverse differs is the evolution mechanic. The ability to give a minion increased stats and the ability to attack another enemy minion solves problems that plagues Hearthstone such as mid/late game minions being too slow to affect the board. This key factor sets Shadowverse apart from any other modern CCG. Another fact which Shadowverse pride’s itself on is its significant lack of RNG cards. That’s not to say they don’t exist, but they are far and few and rarely ever decide the game. Card collecting is largely unoriginal: liquefy cards for vials, use vials to create new cards, and opening a pack gives you eight cards. Shadowverse also has an alternate game mode, “take two”, which allows you to spend gold to draft a deck of cards two at a time, and battling with other players five times with similarly built decks for prizes.
UI and Sound
The Shadowverse UI is directly ported from the mobile version with no changes, meaning it sometimes feels clunky with how large some buttons are, among other things. The game does support both languages, but the English voice acting sounds quite dull and cheap compared to the original Japanese voices.
Art
This game having a very anime based art style to attract Japanese audiences should come as no surprise. When it comes to the West though, the art work reception is either “love it” or “hate it”, as those who are unfamiliar with Japanese media may be turned away by some of the art in this game.
Monetization
Cygames, like most Japanese companies, are extremely generous when it comes to free gifts. The latest Darkness Evolved expansion came with ten free expansion packs, and players were also given packs to celebrate a download milestone just recently. In game cosmetics aren’t credit card only, and can be obtained via ranked play or just regular shop purchases. That said, purchasing the premium currency is quite expensive as the pricing was set more for heavy whales as opposed to casual spenders.
Overall, I’d say that Shadowverse has a decent chance of being listed in the top online CCG’s very soon. Its generosity to the new players is unrivaled in the western markets, and its strategic mechanics and lack of random elements will attract long time players of this genre. The only major bump in the road I can foresee for Shadowverse is that its artwork may be enough to turn off many prospective players. That being said, I have faith that Cygames is capable of turning Shadowverse into a game capable of challenging the tyrants who’ve ruled over this genre.

God it started out strong and with some smarter design it could get there again, but Shadowverse is in a bad way right now.
It plays a lot like Hearthstone but with an extra "Evolve" mechanic that tries to encourage board interaction and smart use of resources, and for a while, it resulted in a CCG with a broad, multifaceted metagame that included so many different archetypes.
But as sets keep coming out, it feels like either the design team forgot the lessons that made Shadowverse great early on, or they've made mistake after mistake in trying to fix issues from before. Games don't feel very interactive anymore. It comes entirely too much to matchup and luck of the draw. The numbers of players continues to climb but the hours they put into it are dropping. Dying Light was pretty much exactly what I hoped it would be. It’s an effective free running survival horror game. The story is absolute crap, but the music, sound design & creature animation is outstanding. It’s fairly well paced too, as it gave me new areas to explore just as the first map was starting to feel old. The first hour or so of the game isn’t too exciting, but the further you get into the game, the better it gets. It doesn't show everything it has going on right off the bat like some games do.
I found the second half of the game more scary than the first. With new types of monsters, and an excellent second area to explore, the tone they were going for was executed with great effect. If only the story was better! It commits the worst offense, which is to be boring. I could feel myself nodding off during cutscenes, wishing they’d just get it over with. The story mission designs weren’t too bad, and I loved the music. It just had the least interesting villain in history. He even looked generic, with a face so devoid of interesting features I was struggling to take in his looks even while staring directly at him. Same could be said of the rest of the cast. Even Ubisoft at their worst do better than this. But I guess it’s still a step up from the story in Dead Island. That had a story so bad I remember staring at cutscenes, mouth agape at the incomprehensible♥♥♥♥♥♥that someone had written, and then animated.
What was missing from the story is characterization. You have no idea who the main character is, who the employers are, who your friends are, or who the enemy is. You know their names and what they look like, but that’s about it. It’s as thin as it gets. The protagonist is forced by his employer to do morally questionable acts “for the greater good”. But because you have no idea where he’s coming from, it’s hard to care. What’s at stake for him? This story and setting needed much more work. It leans heavily on cliché, which has a sleep inducing effect on the audience, without any meat to the story. When exploring, the music, sound and visual design creates a deliberate tone. You can “feel” what the developers were aiming for with this game. But they seem to have underestimated just how much work you need to put in on the story and cutscenes to not make them horrible.
The reason this game isn’t a complete disaster is because of just how much stuff is in this game, and because of how strong the other elements are. The music is like Hotline Miami and Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon, evoking the feel of 80s movies. And the sound has all the subtleties you expect from AAA games, like how the world seems to have layers of sound based on how far you’re elevated from the ground, giving you different types of wind sounds.
During the first half of Dying Light I felt I could only recommend the game with several caveats. But as I got further into the game I felt myself becoming more enthusiastic about it! It’s quite an “emergent” game, ie it’s a bit chaotic in a way that’s rare in newer AAA games. At one point I wanted to get into a building, and luckily a hostile human had spawned nearby. He was attacking zombies, and as he made noise the hordes kept wandering away from the building towards him, clearing the path for me to run inside. An entirely unscripted event, and just one of a ton that I saw during the game. This element of chaos, coupled with the free running system kept it fresh all the way to the end. It never felt like a slog, or that it overstayed its welcome, which is relatively rare in big AAA titles. If you like the idea of free running in a zombie infested city, with escape sequences like those in the late parts of Mirror's Edge, then you'll probably have a good time here.

Shadowverse is an interesting new card game devloped by cygames that makes use of many of the mechanics and features used in previous card games, while still adding enough of it's own changes to keep it feeling unique. The game was originally developed for the phone and has only recently been ported to the pc which is where I believe most of the (admittedly few) problems with the game stem from. Although I'm sure the anime artstyle will deter many from giving this game a proper try, it would be a real a shame to pass it up as I believe this game offers one of the purest and most enjoyable card game experiences available online right now.
Pros:
+Easy to learn, satisfying gameplay
+Overall well-balanced game
+Good class diversity and differentiation
+Extremely generous rewards system (F2P friendly)
+Good art and sound
+Decent story mode with a good amount of content
+The evolve mechanic adds a new layer of depth and strategy to the game
+Arena format offers more meaningful decisions during the draft phase
+Short queue times (<30s in the lower ranks)
+Minimal RNG card effects
Cons:
-Load screens between many of the menus on the home screen (mostly fixed with an SSD)
-Imbalance between going 1st vs going 2nd in Arena
-Barebones friends list system with no chat functionality
-Casual and Ranked queues share mmr
Overall this is an excellent card game with a solid foundation in it's core gameplay and the changes made to the game thus far have only served to improve it. Although it could use some polish, the game's future looks promising and it's well worth checking out for anyone interested in the card game genre.

This was an odd little game. Made by gaming and money stealing juggernaut EA, Mirror's Edge presents itself as a first person platformer, something that any seasoned gamer should react to with a quick and swift retreat begging for a third person perspective. Surprisingly though, the game actually works in this view and controls rather intuitivley as well. The levels are designed to make use of Faith's abilities and when the action gets going and the player has a firm grasp of how the game controls, the game truly shines as a innovative and exciting thrill ride. Now for the negatives and oh boy are there many. The game is very short, only about 5 hours. Granted if you can pick this up on a sale and you are intruiged to give it a go, by all means, purchase it, but at the full asking price it may be a bit too steep for the average person's wallet. The leves are peppered or should I say splattered with horrible combat sequences with clunky controls that honestly yield no fun to the player. These segments cannot be skipped and usually will result in death if the player messes up for more than a couple seconds. These sections are just plain not fun and really detract from the overall experience. The guns in this game handle as if Faith has never once picked up a gun and strip the player of the ability to parkour.
Now the games visual aesthetic is pleasing to the eye. The vision of a blank distopian future where no ones privacy is safe comes to life. I just wish I could've seen more of it. The music when it kicks in to full gear, does a good job of getting your heart racing and the ending song is very very good. Overall, this experiment of a game can be appreciated as a bold step towards innovating the platforming genre and the game can be mocked for its poor combat and afternoon-short length. I repeat, if you do find this one on sale and are interested in playing it, even if only for the moments of platforming, by all means, go ahead and enjoy. If not, steer clear.

I feel this game is worth... $5-10.
Review is up to level 30. Felt ripped off for $30. It's an mmo trying to be like Diablo. I read a lot about it being a "re-released" game, and decided to risk it based on some reviews. I should have listened to the bad reviews.
Tid Bits:
- You can make your own teleportation waypoints to go back to any spot on the map. Cool feature, but still can't figure out how to make the item to use it.
- Loot system is perplexing to say the least. Bow can have Axe+ Dmg?! My axe can shoot.
- Some skills enjoyable at first... most skills and abilities just seem rather boring with no depth to them.
- Characters can Jump! Yes!... but pretty pointless. Only 1 quest I’ve seen use jump so far. (Make it a sprint dev's…)
- Some cool boss fights but not very challenging.
- Works nice in 4k
- Fishing, simple and quick. Didn't try crafting.
- Housing editor is fairly decent.
- You get horses/mounts.
Meh:
- Characters run way too slow
- Many Crashes
- Server lags a lot.
- Player base seems dead. You see the odd person here and there. Lower price could help a lot.
- 1st Main city... extra large and empty.
- Pathing issues while running and getting stuck on objects/stairs the odd time.
Story/Questing:
- Your standard mmo style quests. Nothing innovative here.
- Wasn't really reading the story, cut scenes looked vintage.
Look and feel:
- Pretty decent for this style of game.  Lots of detail.
- Good variety of assets.
Combat:
- Combat is way too slow and clunky starting out but picks up at higher levels.
- Skills don't seem to tie together well, you end up just mashing available skills.
- Not much combat strategy.
Enemy AI:
- Nothing creative at all, as soon as you get close they all swarm you, except for some range enemies. Every enemy and battle basically feels the same.
- Enemies respawn a few seconds after killed in the same spot.
Maps:
- Very linear. Following 1 main path with quests and dungeons along the way.
- Becomes more intricate at higher levels but still fairly linear.
Dungeons:
- So far.. Lower level dungeons are simple (like 1 room simple), they get much bigger around level 15.
Sounds/Music:
- Some sounds could be tweaked (warrior class sounds like a vacuum cleaner when twirling) but overall sounds are ok. Nothing epic here but not overly appealing.
- Music gets repetitive and stale fast.
Challenge:
- Solo Fairly easy.
- Grouping even easier.
OVERALL:
- Overpriced. Game needs an overhaul. Seems to pickup around level 15-20.
