The game is about preventing the VC to move into villages and preventing things to escalate to the point the NVA feels daring enough to send troops through the border.
The player will essentially juggle with airmobile troops and helicopters : moving troops, supplying them and medical evac.
Now and then, your troops will have an actual contact with the enemy. Often it's an ambush, traps and gathering intel.
Intel is critical. You get it by moving into populated hexes. However, if you don't actively secure the populated area, the pop become hostile to you and won't feed you any intel.
Intel is used to reveal VC/NVA units. It's particularly needed for VC units who disband and vanish after setting a successful ambush on your troops. So you have to find them first. NVA is a bit easier because they are conventional and you can chase them later (provided you can divert the firepower to that).
Once you have your intel, you will have to fall on the VC units. At times, the task is tricky as you may have to drop your infantry into a hot landing zone (where your helicopters are attacked when entering the hex) or you may have to drop your ground troops farther, but then they may lose track of the enemy.
The other tricky part is the logistics. Refueling armor, giving ammo to arty or supplying infantry, the helicopter is your workhorse. Overextend yourself and you may have unsupplied units. In that game, it means they are eliminated. It isn't sudden, you get warnings. But if you didn't plan, you may not be able to fix the problem in time.
Logistics is then the backbone of your action. It hints where you should build your firebase and where your firebase is built tells you where you can hope to project your troops.
When the situation goes out of hand, you may face troubles : are you going to evac the worn units and their injured, or leave them and haul ammo to the artillery of your firebase instead ?
The rotation of helos in the game is actually critical. It is a micro-management system but limited in size. You don't have that many units to handle. But if you hate the idea of being forced to pay attention to supply and ammo and set your resupply carrousel, you may want to look for another game.
Finally, you win or lose based on the "Hearts and Minds" of the local population. Kill the enemy and you improve your rep. Have the enemy move freely around or, worse, destroy a unit of yours, and the locals will stop supporting you.
You don't build troops, you request them. The difference lies in battlefield results. Your political support is your currency to ask for new troops. The more you win, the more support you get. On the opposite, if you lose...
Getting new units is more and more expensive. Mostly, you get to conduct your whole operation with not much more than the starting troops. You may replace units, get a few new ones but that's all.
Your Green Berets can recruit ARVN units. ARVN troops don't cost your political support. They are also better at getting intel from the locals. But they are weaker than the regular US troops. training ARVN troops also requires a forward base. Just setting one, where and when, can be a little challenge.
Ultimately, you win or lose the game by decimating the enemy. Logistics, intel, it's all about being able to know where to strike and being able to strike.
Sometimes you win after a bloodbath where the VC and the NVA bleed themselves against your bases. Sometimes you win with a combination of patrolling and securing plus a handful of aggressive moves.
Sometimes, it just snowballs out of control, from an array of VC attacks to NVA armor coming across the border.
The game is simple but efficient. It has a bit more depth than it looks. Difficulty also depends a lot on map layout (you can also somewhat decide the map style when starting a game).
Replayabiliity is debatable. Some players will enjoy the same mechanics on a different map each time. Others will look for scenarios and all and there the game is lacking.
It's remotely historical but gives you a good feeling of what can be airmobile operations in Vietnam.
The price tag is still a bit high.

First I love Strategy games and I love historical war games.  I'm going to give a quick review and get right to the points.   Now I'm getting a start to this review since I only made it through the first tutorial because I played it out to the end which is 45 turns.  I was thinking there would be some achievement but there wasn't one  I also noticed that there was no progression after the tutorial.  So it's not worth playing it tout to the end.
The game really puts you in command of an Area of operation.  The down fall is that the Controls will frustrate you.  Example Click a Huey  send it to a base to refuel well if it still able to move after reaching the base it will remain active. So when you go to click on another unit that Huey will move out of position and it runs out of fuel the next turn it will crash.  This applies to all units.
Now there is no economy to worry about, You buy troops with political favor, the more units you have the less favor you carry.  Now for every unit or base you kill you gain political favor and support with the locals.  every unit you lose, lowers your favor and can slow your progress.

This caused me to lose more troops during the tutorial then anything.
Planning your distance will greatly help your supply lines, rotate troops off the front lines.
But also your artillary can only be set up at bases and they provide your troops fire support support.

So far its not that bad of a game but there is a good learning curve, while some might get it quicker then others. by all means this shouldn't scare you away from a small little game.  It's not fancy in the graphics department, but it really tries to capture the Essence of what it was like for are troops fighting over in Vietnam.  You'll  have no clue who or where the enemy is an at the beginning of every turn you Intel of potential  enemy activity that shows up on the map.  Guess what they could be there or not, this bring another depth of realism because your intel could be good or bad, hell you could even be ambushed, hit a mine field in an area you already cleared.  Even how the enemy forces fight NVA will always stand and fight while the VC will hit and run, or you just might have a squad or rpg that shoot at your helocopters then disapear.  The enemy can pop up anywhere no matter what you control or cleared on the map.

Let's say that Vietnam '65 is a miniatures tabletop version of Go.
The graphics are quite adequate and the sound is at the okay level. The voice over is not annoying and one can actually pump some good 60's blues and rocks on the media player to give it some added mood.
The game is asymetrical. The sides in conflict work by different means to achieve the same objective. This is a plus on my book.
The mechanics are, in my opinion, well designed. The rules are clear - win the hearts of the population by keeping territory "control". Sounds quite complicated and it is because it is not simply a question of moving what where. It is about moving somewhere, half blind and with a supply chain support.
It provides fun in the long run and some degree of replayability. For the new players the game can be merciless but it has a decently fair learning curve, not steep, not shallow.

Book of Demons is an RPG with a unique art style, allows for personallizing the game session, game play that allows it to be an ARPG with stratgic and tactical elements, and a equipment collection system that appeals to my gotta-catch-them-all instincs.
The game play is mostly a click based ARPG, but certain elements slow down time (such as accessing inventory).  This allows the player the time to make an intelligent decsision that they as a player cannot make as fast as the warrior of fable they are playing.
Everytime you delve into the dungeon the game asks how long you'd wish to play.  Want to play for 10 minutes? Sure. How about 60 minutes? That's great, go for it.  It does take a few delves to unlock the longer play sessions, but that's ok.  You need these delves to learn your character and the game.
The art style is that of a pop-up book.  This allows the game to be whimsical and sincere at the same time.
The equipment is represented by cards.  This is not a card game.  It just is part of the unique art style.  It does allow the player to fullfil the need to collect things.
I really enjoy this game.  I'm looking forward to when the game is complete and for the followup games that appear to be part of the series.

This is cardboard diablo 1. If you've played diablo 1 or are at least familiar with the diablo series hack and slash type of games or generally just enjoy a good endless amount of monster slaying from an isometric perspective then this game should definitely be on your wishlist.
The game adds a couple of unique features such as the boardgame style graphics and playstyle and the cool 'collectable cards instead of skills' as well as the ability to set the length of your dungeon according to your available time.
I think it's worth noting that this game doesn't offer you the 'freeroam' abilities afforded to you in other hack and slashes as the movement is restricted according to set paths in dungeons (kind of like driving a mining cart around interconnected rails). This can make dodging stuff a near impossibile task sometimes and also makes it easier to get boxed in by fires, icycles, rocks, monsters and anything else that decides to block your path.
All in all I am really enjoying my time in Book of Demons and see no reason to not recommend this to anyone who likes a straight forward hack and slash with filled with quips and references to it's spiritual predecessor.

There's a plot to this madness, but expect it to kinda fall by the wayside after the first hour and a half. It's clear to me that IO interactive had some great ideas, but they forgot to put it all together for most of the game. There's a prison bus escape, then some shoot-outs, there's a robbery, and then some more shoot-outs. The rest of the game takes place in Havana and Venezuela, and it plays out like every other 3rd person War game. To add to this, the PC port of this game is a bit crap. It's prone to glitches, poor graphic effects, and objects disappearing whenever they feel like it. I honestly thought they added to the game. It made for a very surreal atmosphere.
It's possible that I don't find the game nearly as appealing as the characters. A lot of the time with these 3rd person shooters, you have Nathan "Indy" Drake, Lara "Rambo" Croft, the men (and women) of Gears of War, and so on. These heroes are made to be charismatic, given aspects that people can relate to, and are basically good people caught in bad situations. I mean okay, I can buy it sometimes, but the idea of playing as a couple horrible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who make bad situations even worse? That's so cool. Would they be better off dead? Most definitely. However, I get the feeling that Hell wouldn't be an acceptable end for them. Hell is more like....stage 3. Somehow they shoot their way out, but manage to end up somewhere else, and shoot that place up as well. Along the way there would be a failed string of negotiations, heists, kidnappings, liberations, bar mitzvahs, and house parties.
As a shooter, Dead Men is merely competent. Aside from the odd difficulty spike or two towards the end and some primo snipers, most gamers will sleepwalk through the chaos. Mostly this game gets by on some neats moments, its engaging protagonists, and some really decent sound-direction(good music). If you're curious and don't mind putting up with more issues than Sports Illustrated, give this game a go. During sales it tends to cost about as much as a candy bar, and lasts slightly longer.

AK, ah the end to a series that introduced me to Batman and just how awesome he is. Before I touched AA, I've always thought Batman to belong to the 'boring superheroes' group. After playing AA though, all that changed. I googled every characters that I encountered in the game, villians/heroes/sidekicks alike. Slowly immersing myself in Gotham, learning as much as I can in order to relieve the true experience in the game, and slowly liking it more and more.
What really impressed me was AA's freeflow battles when I first took part in one. It was a first for me to experience such battles and boy was it fun!! So simple, yet so effective, some things are fixed, yet gives you the illusion that you are in control; ingenious, for lack of a better word. And I was glad things felt the same in AO and AC as well.
As for AK - Hits and misses, it's still freeflow, but things seems to have loosen up abit, as seen with the new introduction of rooftop hybrid-predator battles, as well as the controls not feeling as tight. I've made a couple of mistakes I'd never make in the previous three. But still satisfiying when you get no damage.
Also, what is up with the distance batman and team can cover? I can punch a man here and leap 10km away (exaggerated, but srsly) to kick another, I didn't know batman crossed over and took lessons from Spider-man, damn, kinda makes the magic go away during the first 1 or 2 battles I partook. It wasn't this unrealistic in previous titles, afaik.
They seem to have loosen up the grappling as well, you can pretty much grapple anything you can see right now, yep even things you never really wanted to grappled, lel. WORKS WONDERS when you are playing some of the hybrid-predator scenarios on rooftops /s
Let me just say most side missions including the DLCs were well thought out and extremely detailed, the heart and thoughts that were put into these were pretty much amazing, majority of dialogues that were around were unique and there were tons of pressing A (Xbox controller) whenever I was in GCPD. Seeing the cells fill up everytime I go back was defintely satisfying too.
HOWEVER when it came down to anything militia related, Good god they are the most annoying bunch I've ever seen, including Scarecrow and AK himself.
It really gets tedious towards the end.
Empty, meaningless threats - 'Muwahahahaha u will neber defeat me Batman!!' *throws 62 more checkpoints, 80 guard towers, 20 land mines and 32 Cobra drones.'
Militia commenting that 'haha batman thinks he can win', when I've already twarted 3 semi-major events including
Look Scarecrow, AK, in case you don't know, I'm already 85% in the game and have already destroyed 6,000 checkpoints, approximately 3,200 guard towers, 5 land mines and 80 cobra drones and an almost complete genocide of your militia army, I'd need 200 GCPDs to accomodate all of them, AND YET YOU ARE STILL RAMBLING ON AND ON ON THAT STUPID SCREEN OF YOURS SAYING HOW YOU WILL DEFEAT ME WITH THE SAME OLD THINGS???
Those fear gas of yours should be relabeled as dumb gas.
Now you may think I may be exaggerating a little, but as a completionist, I've 100% all riddler's challenges in AA, AO and AC and I'm already 82% in AK and intend to 100% to get the ultimate ending. So I don't use the word 'tedious' lightly.
And just FYI, Riddler's mission aren't tedious. As a matter of fact, it is the star of all side missions in Arkham Series, it's so varied, and you always look forward to progressing, just to see riddler's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off face and hear him scream. Ladies and gentlemen, that is how you make a seemingly tedious progression not tedious - innovation, surprise, mix it up.
Imagine all riddler's trophy sitting around only with no puzzles whatsoever, that is how all mlitia related side quests are.
It's annoying everytime I have to go through it, and I have to say this is the first time I felt this annoyed in an Arkham series.
4 letters - OP AF.
Yes I get that Batman is supposed to be OP, especially since he is already established in AK. But srsly when you are in a game this long, with what I've mentioned above, all these isn't really helping. Back when I played AA, you can never help but feel that Batman IS there, just not quite since you need to level up to unlock abilities to progress, get that trophy, or simply kick people's♥♥♥♥♥in a more satisfying way. and you worked hard and progress for it.
Well in AK It's 'here all these is for you' bruce wayne's parents died here's the deed and ten gazillion dollars style, now go kick some♥♥♥♥♥ Yep very fun inititally when you can already glide so high and travel so far, pull off all the abilities mapped to your controller in such complex ways, sometimes I don't even know what button I'm supposed to pressed.

Oh look, drones - here a disruptor

Serious review time.
This game is pretty good. It's not phenomenal, but better than RE6.
First things first though, this game does have some drawbacks.
Firstly, there's no online co-op for the campaign. I don't know why they thought that would be a good idea, especially since you can play Raid mode with others online.
Secondly, it's not exactly a great console port. If you run on a non-mainstream resolution you will most likely end up with a black screen, which can only be fixed by dinking around with the config file.
The aiming feels very weird when moving the mouse fast, this is due to the fact that this game uses joystick emulation (for whatever reason).
Also, a huge part of the game's graphics are getting rendered using your CPU instead of the GPU. Again, you can blame the fact that this is a port for that.
As you can see this port isn't too great from a technical standpoint, now that we got that out of the way, let's move on to the actual game.
This game takes place between RE5 and 6, you play as Claire, Barry and two other (more or less) new support characters. The game's pretty straight forward, you get a cheesy 3 minute intro and then the horror begins. Interesting is that Barry's campaign takes place 6 months after Claire's campaign. The actions you take in Claire's campaign might affect Barry's later on, similar to the zapping system in RE2. I won't talk much further about the plot, since it would just spoil things. Just saying this, the plot isn't exactly overwhelmingly good.
The graphics are okay, they are not great, but get the job done. The enviroments feel quite natural and fairly believable. Animations look smooth, although I would like to mention that both male and female characters have the same basic animation set, which makes movement look weird from time to time.
Gameplay is really great, unlike RE6, this game isn't a massive explosion/action fest. We actually get to feel some survival horror again. Your health won't regenerate by itself (except for the last 10 HP or so) and ammunition is quite rare, making stealth kills and evasions much more relevant. Enemies won't drop any items whatsoever, so it's encouraged to avoid enemies or (if you are forced to) shoot the enemie's weak spot.
Each campaign has two playable characters, Claire + Moira & Barry + Natalia.
They all have their personal strenghts and weaknesses, so working together is encouraged aswell. However, at some points it feels like the support character is just there to loot the hidden items, at other times it actually feels useful.
Gunplay and movement feel very good. Your guns have actual recoil (unlike RE6's crosshair jumping thingy) and can be upgraded with parts that you can find (just like in the first Revelations) throughout the levels.
You can trigger an evasion animation at (almost) any time, use your knife in close quarters, and hit stunned enemies with a melee move. The melee system has been simplified. Unlike in RE5, you can only stun enemies with headshots, and each character only has two melee moves (head stun and ground finisher). I would have appreciated RE5's melee system here, as I think it has a good balance between action and gameplay balance.
The level design is engaging. Often you'll need keys or other key items (like gears) to move on. This combined with the scarcity and the interesting, soviet looking enviroment makes for fun gameplay.
Now for the thing that will (probably) be one of the main reasons for you to buy this game.
Raid Mode.
This mode can be addicting, while not flawless, it has a great variety of characters, weapons and skills, that will take hundreds of hours to unlock and master.
You'll start off with a level 1 character, as you play through stages, kill enemies, loot items and gain medals, your character will eventually level up and you will gain better parts, skills and weapons to upgrade.
You can upgrade weapons with parts similar to the ones in the campaign. This gamemode reminds me a bit of VR mode from the Metal Gear Solid games. It's gameplay focused, and has a somewhat arcade-ish feel to it.
However, it also comes with a few flaws.
Most stages are just modified stages from RE6. If you've played that game, you'll recognize alot of locations from RE6, a few from Revelations and the game's main campaign. Actually, I'm not sure if there's even a single original stage.
It also becomes unchallenging at some point. Throughout Raid Mode, you'll gain better guns, parts and skills, all these combined with a small bit of gamesense will make you unstoppable even on the highest difficulty. Maybe a dynamic spawn system and less powerful assets would have made for a more challenging experience.
Overall I really like this game. It's a step into the right direction, and I hope Capcom will make a full-fledged Resident Evil game that is similar to this one, but improves on the weakpoints.

Below this line is a reply to the developer (steam limits comments to 1000 characters).
I'll start this by saying the review was actually based on my experiences a while back and it seems a fairly major patch has arrived since then. This seems to have, among other things, added some options to tweak the game settings on a new game and therefore probably helped with variation.
My major complaint is a lack of replayability. The new patch will likely help with that but, for the price, it still leaves only a single scenario. If you wanted to improve that the best method would be a simple campaign or two and really that isn't a huge amount of work. Essentially you'd just need to have a pre-made map/pre-placed units and certain restrictions/changes for each faction or in the weather etc for each mission (you could, in fact, just set the map generation options and unit-type limits for each mission and still have it semi-randomised). Throw a little piece of text (no voice acting required) to lead into the mission and you're done. You could do everything from time-limited standard operations, defence missions and even pitched battles. While, on paper, it looks the same as just having the user generate their own scenario it really helps give the game some length.
The second real issue (and what makes it only mildly entertaining) is the seemingly arbitrary nature of some of the gameplay. From what I've read it appears that everything is actually happening for a solid reason but this reason is almost completely behind the scenes. A slight increase in feedback about why certain things are happening would help.
Otherwise there isn't anything hugely wrong with the game. The units are a little unbalanced (from what I remember APCs weren't great while tanks and particularly helicopter gunships were too effective). Infantry are actually the biggest annoyance due to their constant resupply needs and slow movement etc. These points are again based on an older version of the game and might have been due to a lucky map.
Adding scenarios with changing limits would help here too as it allows you to limit access to certain units or toy with their effectiveness.
Finally larger maps to allow for longer games would be nice though that might require some changes to the cost/upkeep of units and limits on their price increases. The current size of maps doesn't help the general impression of a tablet game ported directly to the PC.

In my opinion Mirrors Edge is a game that tries to take a path towards a new genre, "born" out of jump n run and fps games but, first of all, focusing on atmosphere and immersion. And the last two are probably it's main strength! I haven't yet seen a game that, even when just watching the trailer, gives you a sense of wideness and open space high up over a city. The atmosphere is obviously created by the, I'd say almost revolutionary texturing and the minimalistic as well as great soundtrack.
I can well remember how exited I was when I first saw the trailer a little before release. I could not wait to get my hands on it and when I finally did, well, it was really great! At least at the beginning, then more and more "salt" got mixed into the "soup" in the form of not very revolutionary gameplay. It got so far, that I didn't even finish the game, it just lost so much of what was great about it for me. And that was the atmosphere and the feeling of speed. And the last wasn't held up through the game, the running felt a little too slow and repetitive, the levels feature a lot of indoor-action, which adds different challanges but also destroyes what made the game so great for me in the first glimpse: the roof tops!
Then the cartoon like sequences in which the story is told somehow felt missplaced.
All in all for me this game seems to be composed in two "worlds", one features almost perfect atmosphere, level Design and Soundtrack, and then there is the other part, the one that makes me not want to play the game, and that is most of the gameplay and fight parts. Because it does not feel really like a shooter. But hey, I'm happy they tried, it's still a fun game, and it's important that new ways are tested. (I just don't want to play another CoD or BF... It's just boring!)
Concluding I'd say that I'd love to see more games like this one, perfecting what makes this game great. You should definitely play in, in case that you search for new gaming experiences!

Lemme give it to y'all straight, who are on the fence;
- Yes, the game is very much worth it at full price.
- One of the first games in a long while, that has kept me up until 5 A.M. in the morning, because of how lost I get myself into it.
- Doesn't do dumb jump scares, save for a VERY FEW TIMES, and each one counted.
- The game is maybe one of the best zombie based games out there, so long as you do enjoy it with action.
- Parkour in the game is AMAZING. Sometimes I like just playing the game, so I can run
around, across roof tops, and attacking zombies while talking to friends.
- Co-op in story mode. Freaking amazing. No dumb lobby. Just click 'Join game' and bam,
you'll be thrown a few feet away from a friend without them sometimes even noticing you joined!
- Single play and Co-op have a huge impact; co-op feels fun, slightly safer, and adds a lot in the form of friendly rivals! Single player feels way more tense and everything you do counts, making you second guess some choices, for fear or death. Night time in either mode is fun as heck, though four co-op makes it pretty easy.
- Night and Day feel almost like two different modes. In the day, zombies shuffle around, falling off rooftops, being dumb, easy to avoid and kill. Night time? Get those UV Flares ready, and be ready to flee if they catch sight of you.
- Even after beating the story, I keep coming back for more, as it's super fun.
- Took me around 30 hours to do the story, which also included only HALF of the side missions. Still got a little over 50% left to go, and looking forward to it!
TL;DR - Get the game, find friends to play with, enjoy the hell out of one of the few games worth it at full price.

Keeping your units in supply is crucial, as they disperse if kept out of supply for more than one turn, but the enemy isn't going to make it easy for you to supply them either, attacking your choppers with rocket launchers.

I enjoyed the time I had with Mirrors Edge. While it manages to pull of a beautifully fluent free running and combat system that tie greatly into the world, it does have its host of problems.
The first thing I saw in Mirror's Edge was the controls. At first, I was hard on the idea that these controls sucked, and that they needed alot of tweaking. However, I learned quickly the game had a curve to it, and got passed the controls. When I finally got good at basic movements, I became absorbed in the world. The towering skyscrapers, colorful rooftops as well as the very dark secrets that were hid in this utopian masquerade. Cool right? Yes. However, it is really hard for me to appreciate the mythos of the game beyond its scenery, and beautiful scoring. This was because the story was god awful. Riddled with messy , sloppy, cheezy, and otherwise worthless dialouge, there was no way I was going to give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about the sister to sister relationship in the story. And to put the icing on the cake, I was utterly displeased with the ending. You will know when you get there.
Completely disregarding the story, the freerunning in the game was spectacular. With many ways to run on rooftops and build up momentum, I was very much envigorated when I pulled off the perfect string of moves. The blur on the sides of the screen when momentum building is a very amazing feeling. Then came the combat. For reasons I can not understand, people hated the combat in the game. And I agree and disagree at the same time. While pulling off ninja moves on a guard was fitting for the missons, the gunplay was stale. This could have easily been avoided by making weapons more sleek and getting rid of the heavy guns. It really brought me out of all the agility in the game when I lugging around a huge♥♥♥♥♥M249. So for Mirrors Edge 2, please keep the gunplay; but make it exciting! Make me feel like a badass when I finally get the gun out of the guards hands and run away from the firefight.
There is also one other problem in the game, and that was the Runner's Vision. While artisticly this was cool, I felt as a game mechanic I did not like this. However, this really comes down to personal preference. I personally thought Runner's Vision held my hand throughout the game, highlighting where I should go next. Being chased from rooftop to rooftop by guards is not very fun when you know exactly where to go - I want to have to think fast to move to my objective! This mechanic can only be turned off on the hardest difficulty too, which is a shame. However, this is totally up to you on what you want out of Mirror's Edge.
To conclude, Mirrors Edge is a great game. Free running is a wonderful time, and stringing together the perfect combo is simply rewarding as hell. The combat, while it can be vastly improved, is a good concept. And Runner's Vision is totally up to personal prefrence. The world is spectacular too, really putting a "POW" into the scenery with all its spectacular and vibrant color, while appropiatley contrasting the darkness that lies within the utopian universe. I really wish I could care more for the politics in this game, but the story is just too boring and dull for me to care! Characters are generic and unexciting, not to mention the cutscenes look like an All State commercial. But overall, this game is a gem, and the parkour is hands down the best I have ever been able to experience.

So the sequel comes out next week, for that reason I wanted to re-review this game. If you've ever played a Lego game, you know that the quality of content is top-notch and the humor is great too.
There is alot of different types of gameplay in Lego Marvel Super Heroes and essentially 2 storylines. There is a main linear storyline and then there is another storyline which you experience after you complete the main one. Pretty crazy huh?
What really impresses me is the initial depth that Lego and Marvel put into the game. There is around 40 to 100 hours if quality content. That's not bad at all, the untrained eye will percieve this as a child's game which brings me to the next point.
This game has some pretty hard puzzles when you get over 20 hours in. It will cause you to think and dare I say, may even challenge you moreso that classic point and click games.
What I didn't like? Hmmm... sometimes camera angle was janky, physics for planes/jets were wonky and ai for heroes can be dumb but perhaps all those things may be expected when you're dealing with this much stuff. The map can get boring to look at after awhile, fact is that Manhatten/NYC is overused in super-hero games or games in general.
Controls for flying characters can be a bit annoying. Sometimes, the camera can go "off-the-rails" while your character will move in a direction that you're not meaning to.
I also didn't like how some of the characters felt unbalanced or like a copy-n-paste of one of the more important or well-known characters. Thankfully all these complaints are fixed with the sequel so that's great to know at least.
I'm 26.5 hours in and only 30% through the game. That should tell you something. The top-quality content can give you many hours of enjoyment and while the map may get old to look at after awhile, there's never a shortage of fun things to do.
For the best experience, always keep your system updated with the latest drivers and newest version of Direct X and you won't have any problems with this game.

This game is pure rubbish. There is no other way to describe it. The controls are terrible. For example. Reload, pick up weapon, action, climb something all mapped to one button, and there is no button to take cover, which is kinda important in a cover based shooter, especially when there is a heap of snipers (like there is in KAL:DM).
The shooting just feels off. The crosshair gives no indication where the bullets are going to go, so no long range headshots. I understand guns aren't laser beams but when you character can't hit the broad side of a barn with his assault rifle, you know somethings off. They also lack a feeling of impact or power. They sound like toys. The only weapons that feel somewhat good to use are the AK and the SIG 552.
The story is just silly. You'll jump from location to location without any expliantion, and characters are thrown in with no introduction. Kane continues to trust Lynch even though he is a pyshcopath with no real skills and
I mean I know it's a video game but it's just too silly to take seriously, which is the developer's intention.
And then there's the actual missions. Each one leads to a dumb shoot out. Sneaking between outposts in a war-torn country? Don't sweat it, just have a shoot out. Bank robbery? Just shoot everything, including the cops. Night club kidnapping? Guess what, you'll just shoot everything that moves! Everything is just a gunfight. A gun fight with bad controls and idiot team mates that you need to keep alive. There are missions that imply the developers were going to have stealth, or something interesting, but nope, just shoot the cops/gangsters/brown people and go to point A to B.
This game's only redeeming feature is the fact that the concept is somewhat interesting. I mean having two guys who will just use people to get what they want is admittedly somewhat interesting, but in no way will carry this game.

A pixelated, side-scrolling rogue-like. Sounds boring, right? Wrong.
On the surface, Risk of Rain may come across as just another game that boasts 'rogue-like' as it's primary feature, but what it offers alongside it is incrementally challenging gameplay, an awesome variety of playable characters (each with their own unique moveset), very well designed enemies that can and will swarm you if you're not careful, and a surprisingly awesome soundtrack that compliments the gameplay.
You play one of twelve survivors marooned on a strange planet infested with hostile life. You must use the money you earn from killing enemies to purchase upgrades strewn across the enviornment in order to survive as the enemies gradually become stronger. It's quite surprising how tense this game can get, especially if you manage to reach the highest difficulty.
Upgrades vary in terms of rareness and potency, coming in the form of chests. White chests are the most common while the red are the most rare and valuable. A majority of items are stackable and can drastically change how your character controls, which only serves to elevate the challenge as the clock keeps ticking. This game is a must for anyone who enjoys a solid challenge.

I'll be honest, I preferred the first one. While here the equipment selection has been improved, the areas expanded, and the missions more varied, I felt that The Metal Age was a bit off in terms of atmosphere and occasional design flaws, on top of bugs similar to those of The Dark Project, which I have just come to assume are inherent problems of the Dark Engine, which both games utilized.
The levels are large, and use a color and texture palette more believable than that of the first game. Personally, I liked the fantasy-looking themes of The Dark Project, compared to the industrial feeling of The Metal Age.
More space brings more to do, and while more challenges are welcome, the gameplay feels weak when the levels only allow one entrance to a particular location, and this will happen much more here than in its predecessor. As much as I hate hand-holding, I hate a lack of direction a tiny bit more. The Dark Project was good at giving the player direction through in-game literature and dialogue, and this sort of help is not as available here.
I wouldn't have such a problem with confusing level design if I was given more freedom to explore, but enemies are quite plentiful in this entry, along with many types that are only susceptible to explosive weaponry, limiting possible approaches and damaging that appeal of the game. While human opponents are usually easily dealt with, the mechanical enemies frequently chew up inventory items, often resulting in death when there are just too many to either destory or avoid.
The inventory holds a larger variety of equipment, but due to the sheer volume it can be a pain to navigate when having to do so quickly. The usefulness of some items has changed. The game seems intent on giving me plenty of water arrows, even though most of the light sources are electric lamps, and there is very little blood to ever have to clean. Fire arrows are much more helpful, but now quite rare. Maps are a big improvement over the previous game. Rather than being given my general location, I am now told which room I am in, which is helpful in areas where the rooms look the same.
Overall, I enjoyed it, but due to its difficult-to-manage size, I felt like it lacked some of the cohesion present in The Dark Project.

Arkham Knight is the 4th main Batman: Arkham game to be released. It is the latest in the timeline, continuing after the events of Arkham City. Gameplay is very similar to previous Arkham games, with the addition of vehicular combat, races and navigation, thanks to the Batmobile. The world is larger, with 3 differerent islands of Gotham to explore, each with their own theme, side missions and activities to explore and do. Brawling based combat is just like other Arkham games, with some extra counter attacks added to the mix, while predator based gameplay is the same as ever, just more dynamic with more ways to navigate levels and trick enemies. This is an open world action game with focus on one man army fighting segmants against dozens of goons (Much like Kill Bill), adding Predator based moments were you have to pick off each goon one by one with strategy and quick planning in real time, then finally feeling like a tank while mowing down high tech tanks with your Batmobile using the much used tank mode.
There are a lot of things I like. The best things is the ability to play as either Batman, Robin, Nightwing, Catwoman, Azrael, Red Hood, Batgirl or Harley Quinn in the optional AR challenges. A lot of work went into making each character feel involved in the world, making them feel welcome in Gotham. Personally, I love the challenges from all the Arkham games, and this is just a treat!
The story is very cinematic. A lot of cinematography was used very well during cutscenes and even while performing environment based takedowns. By the way, these takedowns are the best, even if they are rare to come by. Not to mention, the main story mode allows you to fly anywhere you want on the 3 islands of Gotham. Each island is large and just looks fantastic. Each building looks like it means something to Gotham, like there's a past between every alley and sidewalk. Thankfully, this thoughtful immersion is enhanced by the side missions, which there are plenty of; focussing on some of the most iconic villains from the Batman comics, adding some new ones I've enver heard of before who have motives for being in the abandoned city in the first place, casually morphing the feeling of disgust with the GCPD as they hide away more than help with the struggle.
Jim Gordon is normally a favourite Batman character of mine, and his selfish vendetta is explored within the story, summing up the state of the GCPD. Yes, the GCPD is a small army, with only one building to work with. I love entering it frequently within the story, as criminals you've helped capture fill up the very limited cells the more oyu play the game and complete main missions alongside side missions. The cells are placed near the entrance (for some reason) and the noise builds the further you are into the story as more criminals clang on the bars and taunt you for not predicing Scarecrow's next plan. This is also a bitter sweet taunt to Batman as a character, who does not kill. He will live in limbo if all he does is throw criminals towards the GCPD. Batman spirals into madness later into the story, questioning whetehr he should let the Joker out within him and just clean the city up in an instant while he has the chance. I love this context explored in a more complicating manor that is easy to simply run by if you don't pay attention.
Metaphors aside, the on foot combat is still great, although a bit more fast paced, which I don't mind. As already mentioned, I love the new environment takedowns. One is to pick up and slam a goon head first into a barrel, as his legs stick out. It's always a magical sight witnessing that. Goons feel a bit more dangerous this time. Even the simplest goons can grab Batman and hold him still, or even rugby tackle him. There are easy counters for this,  but it actually reminded me of how humanBatman is. He must always be alert, just like the player, so I have a connection to how human he actually is now, unlike in other Arkham games. Not to mention, there are a lot of variety in different enemy types, all with different skins based on the faction they work for! That is amazing, yet making them easily identifiable at the same time.
Additionally, as you play through the main story, or even explore random locations, the vision of the Joker appears to question your morals and give background to specific locations of Gotham. I love listening to Mark Hamil explain how the storm blows in a poetic manner, or even how easy it is to just kill a guy.
Also, this port is actually really good right now. I don't own the best graphics card at all, but this game was very smooth and had plenty of options I could tweak. The graphics are gorgeous, even on medium settings. The only frame rate drops I had were while speeding in the Batmobile, which were very annoying, sice the game had to pause to load the map. That loading symbol was the bane of my experience with this game.
Also, what even are the DLC missions? They are about 15 minutes long each and offer very little to the main plot. While the Batgirl mission is the best and longest, it still offers very little context
Oh dear. Why is the Batmobile annoying, slow and boring? It's only somewhat fun to drive during a Firefly side mission, but even then the game had frame rate drops and made the illusion of fast paced driving feel sluggish. Heck, even while in tank mode I got tired after an hour of doing it. It's very repetitive shooting other tanks over and over agaiin in the many waves the game throws at you. However, the worst types of tanks are the larger ones with only 1 weak point at the back, during vehicular predator gameplay. Yes, you heard me. This is terrible.
Oh dear again...
One final thing. Why does Robin control weirdly in some AR challenges? Is it me, or does he just have no range for his punches or does the game not register his inpute correctly. I acn't control him most of the time and it's completely unfair to get less points because of this.

The most primitive game idea (I'd call it a clicker/runner game where you have nowhere to click or run), but implemented with utter ingenious mastery, making it a test for one's neuronal physioligy strength, a piece of psychedelic media art & an enlightment simulator. The coolest parts are those randomly changing visualization patterns & gauge dynamic fluctuations - they seriously challenge player's consciousness & self-control - to keep score flowing you'd want to get the gauge in risky positions where death is just a split-second away & everything depends on reaction times. You may try a more relaxed approach, but how long do you think you'd endure pushing gently & constantly on your Spacebar? 10 minutes? 20? You may be surprised to feel your wrist totally numb very soon!
That's when the stuff becomes spectacular - a man with exhausted hands swearing & laughing at a screen shaking with colors, switching scale, centering & design in constant attempts to overcome human willpower, judgement ability & the obsession for highscore. Man and machine provoking each other in a mad dance of jumping rhythms & twirling illusions! The action gets desperate!
You can only push Spacebar, but periodically you get opportunities to add a secondary gauge pushing Ctrl for massive score multiplication, the rhythms for the two change independently, you feel these changes through reaction times of the corresponding gauges - occasionately the space for their vibration gets limited & the sensivity rises or falls, the game performs pseudo-physics simulation - gauges tend to change their mass, while buttons variate in pushing power. The further you go the harder it all comes on you. Afterall, it's a mockery software, sarcastically funny both to play & to watch!

Hi Casual Gamers,
I recall playing this game when I was 14 years old. Stealing everything, hiding bodies in dark corners of the house, and a cynical gaming motive just made the immersion into this game that much better at the time. When this game was on sale, I just couldn't help myself by trying it again in this current age. This game had great stealth mechanics and I believe it was revolutionary for its time. Now with updated graphical stealth games this old and dusty game has its pros and cons.
The Pros
- Stealth game-play, with the higher difficulties not allowing to kill anyone. You play as a Thief not a Hitman
- Open ended map. There are many ways to get your objective(s)
- Secrets. The game has bonus secrets, either to benefit the mission or back-story on the game
- For a completion-ist, hours of game-play
The Cons
- The game's graphics is similar to Tomb Raider 1.
- Player needs to be patient
- The AI isn't the sharpest
Overall the game is fun, 1st person, single player game. The game is old and dusty but can keep a player, like myself, lurking in the shadows pickpocketing a guard. Just remember that those water arrows are more helpful than ordinary arrows. If you get tired you can save the game and come back later, or try a different route.

Certainly the greatest stealth game of all time......
Sequels usually are worse or hit the same beats as the original, only maybe changing the criticisms directed at the original. Thief II is pretty much a revamped Thief 1, feeling more like a mappack than a sequel.
It is, however, a much better thought-out game and feels much, much more secure in its concept and execution than The Dark Project. For starters, the levels are 100% dedictated to stealth and they feel a lot more fun to explore for it. Gone are the clunky combat sections and in place of that is fantastic level design that seems a lot more interested in attempting to replicate the experience of stealing from a rich guy's mansion or from a bank than the mystical weirdness from the many levels from the original. Levels also feel a lot bigger, with many sections and many, many different ways to explore them.
In terms of artstyle, this is Thief 1 with the occasional higher quality textures and the occasional better looking models, but neither Thief is really easy on the eyes, so a lot of that extra goes unnoticed.
Thief II's plot manages to be even better than the original, the focus still on Nature vs Science, but this time with Science being the main opponent and having an interesting (with an extremely annoying voice) antagonist that keeps you on your toes at every single opportunity he gets.
For it's more focused effort, the game feels a lot more repetitive than the original as the many city scenarios don't feel as alien as the organic-based levels, the contrast not as strong.
It is, in my opinion, for the best and Thief 2 is one of those sequels, that doesn't add or change much, but it doesn't need to, because for what it does, it does better than any other game out there.

This pains me to write this review, because I really REALLY want to like this game. But since there are things (mostly two BIG things) that are objectively wrong with it, I can't, in good conscience, recommend this game as much as I like the idea of it.
I'll cut right to the chase. There are a couple of game-breaking bugs that will prevent you from finishing levels. The ones I've run across have been "fixable" by restarting the game and doing the level all over again. The first couple of times it was forgivable. After I noticed a pattern, I couldn't look past it any longer.
To get specific, there are times where the camera will stop panning with the character LITERALLY blinding you to what you're doing. When you're doing a level with cliffs to fall from or enemies to stumble into, you are unable to properly complete the puzzle. This clearly isn't an intended feature because you can "cheat" the camera back into position temporarily by using the Milli mechanic (not worth explaining in detail, but it basically gives you a free look at the whole level) to figure out where your character is and then blindly move yourself upon resuming gameplay in hopes that you're doing the right thing.
Another game breaking bug I encountered involved doors that require keys. Sometimes the game would randomly decide that I've collected the key before I actually have. Then when I get to the spot where the key is supposed to be. It's gone. The game took it away because it assumed I had it. Go to the door that's locked and I can't open it because I haven't gotten the key. I'm donating chunks of my life away only to get punked by a game that wasn't properly QA'ed.
Now for the reason I still want to like the game: it's really fun. The mechanic is unique and provides some interesting and complex puzzles. The do get a touch repetitive, and the "boss fights" are definitely misnomers, but overall, I had a good time when the game was functioning properly. The art style is cool and the music is pretty amazing especially the main menu theme.
However, the story is pretty crap and the characters are all around unlikeable though which is only flicking salt grains into the wounds left by the non-functional aspects of the game. I stopped reading dialogue about two thirds of the way in because I had enough of the characters and was never really invested in the story to begin with.
So, with a heavy heart, I have to thumb this one down. Were it not for the bugs, I would absolutely be able to give this game a thumbs up and recommend it at sale price. I was lucky enough to grab it off of Humble for only a few bucks, thankfully.

I wanted to like this game, but I feel it really needs some polish to be good.  Conceptually, the game presents a neat world with a lot of potential for a good and intriguing story, however it's execution leaves something to be desired. As a puzzle-platformer, the movement mechanics are not as solid as they should be, which can lead to frustrating missed jumps and having to restart levels or segments again.  The puzzles while the core mechanic are often repetative and sometimes more trial and error than actually intuitive. Because of the trial and error and poor control, the first "boss" was less an exciting experience and more a dull trudge of figuring out what to do and restarting over and over at checkpoints. Other complains are more quality of life issues, such as the loading times, but also by design your character warps back in time to an established checkpoint but if you die by falling into a pit (which will happen) if you are unable to warp back in time the whole level has to be replayed, which can be monotonous since you have to do all the required actions of setting up clones, but then also waiting for those clones to complete their required actions.
TLDR it's a game I wanted to like, but I just can't get behind.

I found the story, mainly the ending, disappointing but did like solving the puzzles: recommended.

Guardians of Ember is a decent MMOARPG, though it's currently missing a class and fifty of it's planned one hundred levels. This obviously effects things like class balance and endgame, as there is none yet in this early form of the game.
It has a ton of potential, though, which is why I'm happy to recommend it at this point in development. The dual class system is awesome, there are many dungeons to explore, and the visuals, races and combat are all positives.
GoE does feel a little rough around the edges, though, as mob density feels a bit too thick around roads, and if you die you'll have to run across a zone to get back to where you were as the only ressurection point is at the zone entrance.
There's a cash shop, but the only things in the cash shop are reset scrolls and items to expand your inventory. These can EASILY be bought without paying extra money, as you earn cash shop currency for doing achievements, and some of these achievements can be re-done daily!
It's a fun game, with a ton of potential to become one of the best in the genre. You may want to wait and see what the last fifty levels and endgame bring, but it looks to be worth your money.

I thought the Dead Space Trilogy was bad when it came to a protagonist that always said: "Sure! I'll do it! No, don't help me, I'll do it ALL BY MYSELF!" Some villages may be uncooperative, or the helicopter ferrying your troops to a village may be attacked forcing a hasty retreat lest that helicopter be ambushed again, and you have to keep those troops supplied which means you'll need a fleet of helicopters, your base may be too far to efficiently ferry supplies and men so you need to build bases closer which need to be defended from VC or NVA assault.
My only major gripe is that currently the game is somewhat unclear about combat, only giving a % based chance that you'll successfully engage and destroy that enemy with no info on what factors increases or decreases your chances, although I do believe that this is being fixed in an update in the near future.
Despite this I like it and I'd recommend it to History nuts and strategy fans.

Racecar.io is an MMO version of Snake. You're at the mercy of anyone with crappy internet, if you start encountering these people, just stay far away on the other side of the map and let them do their thing.
Overall, a quick, fairly fun 100% that can be accomplished in under 10 minutes

Well, this is the 2nd LEGO Indy game from Travellers Tales. It is basically the sequel to the first game in the series. It was released in 2009, so it is kind of old to this date. This LEGO Indy game has some new features that the previous did not have: level creator mode, hub worlds, new fighting mechanics, and a new story that is introduced in this game (Kingdom of the Crystal Skull). Ever since I was a kid and after beating the first LEGO Indy game, I have enjoyed playing this game, and I still have memories from my childhood when I used to play this game together with my old friends. It was until I started to read critic reviews all over the internet, that I started to understand how disappointing this game actually is, and I understand why. The biggest problems I found with this game, is that the developers chose to put each movie into one single hub world (where you have to spend half the time playing through "the worst movie" in the Indiana Jones franchise), and that the levels that is based on the first three movies does not follow the original storyline that the previous game had. This to me felt very annoying and distracting, because it does feel more like a quick recap instead of including the most iconic parts of each movie. Though there are parts that I like about this game: the fighting mechanics are improved from the first game and works very good, the bonus hub where you can create your own level ect, and that the environments in the game look much more realistic. I would not recommend this game, because there are so many flaws that should not be in the game, and because the developers changed too much on the LEGO formula. I would rather recommend the previous (original) game, because that is more detailed when it comes to story line, and there they had the most iconic and important parts from the first three movies. I still like the game and would not say it is that kind of bad, but it is a very disappointing game compared with the first game in the series.

November, 1965 South Vietnam.
In the past two years the Vietcong
, with support of the North Vietnamese Peoples Army (NVA), established a foothold in southwest Vietnam, along the Cambodian border.
Running supplies and reinforcements from north to south Vietnam. Since December 1964 the South Vietnamese army repeatedly suffered major defeats against North Vietnam, to the point of breaking.
To prevent that a first deployment of just 3500 Marines in a defensive role in March '65, quickly escalated to 200.000 GI's by December '65. Marking the beginning of a full grown offensive ground war, of the US and his allies, against North Vietnam. In a plan to destroy the enemy and his infrastructure in 12 to 18 month.
10 years and 1 month later at April 30th 1975, the last US Soldiers left Vietnam by the largest helicopter evacuation in history.
This game recapture the events starting in November '65. When the US for the fist time implement Air-mobility doctrine & Air-Assault tactics. Trying to hunt down enemy forces and interrupt supply lines (Ho-Chi-Minh Path, HCMP), in even the most remote parts of Vietnam. By deploying, supporting and extracting an entire Battalion size force just by helicopters. Making the Bell UH-1D Iroquois (Huey) the maybe most iconic helicopter in the world.
You got 45 turns to secure the valley running from the Cambodian border, and win the hearth & minds of the civilian population. Stopping VC reinforcements coming down the Ho-Chi-Minh path, and the NVA from crossing the Cambodian border. Setting up bases and trying to wipe you off the map.
You see, it's all easy peasy. ;)
Vietnam '65 is certainly one of those addictive easy to learn, but hard to master games, with the excitement of a rogue like game. The game seems easy and simple at first, but soon you will find out real thinking and deductive skill are asked for. When trying to figure out the pattern of VC sightings, to pinpoint possible locations of Ho-Chi-Minh trail spawn points across the valley. Then building forward bases in strategic locations, from which your units will operate to lay ambush to any VC coming down the HCMP. Inviting a Claymore mine full of surprises.
For just $10 bucks this game is not only a bargain, but for me personally already amoung the best strategy games of 2015 with a high re-playability value. Almost like FTL back then.

with Mel Gibson, Sam Elliot Madeleine Stowe and Clark Gregg.
This movie depicts the first conducted Air-Assault in history, from November 15th to 18th in the La Drang valley
, near the Cambodian border. Leaving 308 GI's dead in just 4 days. One-third of the entire force.

Review based on version as of March 3/2017.
I recommend to anyone looking here - try the demo. You will get to see how the game works (quite a lot of it actually) so you can make your own mind up.
As for my opinion:
Graphics are nice - not too demanding, yet still very functional, entertaining and enjoyable to look at.  Only real complaint at this point is that the game is just screaming for more content. There are 7 major groups of monsters, with up to 15 variants of each (total looks to be around 65 to 70, I haven't seen the last group - the first 6 have 58 combined). These variants do use different graphics so they aren't just different colours).
Gameplay uses a mechanic of cards to represent equipment and spells, as well as "crafting" components - these are for upgrading your cards (each has 3 levels). The card system works pretty well - it forces you to make strategic choices, and you can tune these choices based ont he kind of opponents you are encountering in a dungeon.

As mentioned elsewhere, your character has to follow the paths, but you do get to choose which way you want to go on these paths. Its not as limiting as you might think (this is where the demo really helps the game shine). Level size is configurable which allows you some control over how long you want to play in a session (time estimates are provided, seem not too far off). And you can return to town at almost any time, your progress will be saved (you do have to either use an item, or walk back to the level entrance to get to town).
Combat works pretty good and is explained in the tutorial (make sure you follwo along or you will get destroyed!), with only a couple of concerns in the present version. The big one is that sometimes it is hard to get your charater to run away when you want to/need to - he may go a couple steps then stop, move nothing at all, or move where you want.  Also sometimes it is hard to target the monster you want to (or to hit their shield) when there is a crowd.
The character progression system seems to encourage play, and exploration. You need gold to buy some improvements (more card capacity, upgrades, identify cards, etc), while every level you get a point of health or mana. Mana is used for both spells and to power equipment. Makes you think strategically :-)
This is part of a series of 7 games (check the publisher's website) - so we will see how the rest goes. This one is a good start, and at this point is quite playable and looks to have a good future.
And most importantly, its fun!

Bought Risk of Rain when it was on sale... One of the best decisions i've ever made. If you're like me and like a challenging game that kind of tilts the tables of progress and difficulty, then this might just be the game for you. I never really got into platformers, always felt they were a bit too slow for me on gameplay but this game brings a fresh new look on platformers. First off, choose your survivor with unique abilities. Load one of the first maps which are random, find items, level up, and make sure to find the teleporter. Activate the teleporter and be ready for a HEAVY enemy wave filled with loads of mininons and as well a massive boss. Once clearing out all enemies, escape through the portal. Now, I know that sounds a bit linear but, what this game has going for it is that the longer you look around looting for items, the harder the game gets. It's up to you to figure out how will you be managing your time. Loot too long, enemies become ever more O.P., rush through the level and be ready to be unprepared for what the game will throw your way next. Did I mention that it's 4-player co-op? Online and local 4 player co-op are what makes this game really shine. Grab some mates, suit up as different characters, get out of the escape pod and take your first steps on this alien planet, gather items, and prepare yourselves to fight back to back against the unforgiving hordes of aliens that want nothing more to see you fall. Oh almost forgot, once you die, it's GAME OVER... G.L.
